concepts/anticlericalism-separation.title: Anticlericalism and the Separation (Laïcité)
concepts/anticlericalism-separation.content:
Anticlericalism and the Separation (Laïcité)
Anticlericalism was the doctrine and the policy of the Third Republic that sought to reduce the influence of the Catholic Church in public life and to establish the separation of the spiritual and the temporal powers. From Gambetta’s cry — “clericalism, that is the enemy” — through the Ferry school laws and the expulsion of the congregations to the Separation of Church and State of 1905, the laic programme defined the religious character of the Republic. Sabatier’s L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle (1911) reads the whole movement from inside its culmination, while Péguy adds a corrective: the laic and the religious were not simple opposites.
The religious question in the early Republic
The religious question was central to the Republic from its birth. The ordre moral ministries had bound the Republic’s Catholic and monarchical opponents together; the republicans answered by making anticlericalism a test of loyalty. Gambetta’s speech of 1872 at Grenoble, naming clericalism “the enemy,” supplied the formula; in the 1877 campaign and after, the charge of ultramontanism was levelled at the republicans’ opponents, and the Vatican and the Seize Mai were linked in republican suspicion. Hanotaux records the growing conflict between the Republic and the Church: the religious manifestations, the episcopal mandements, and the republicans’ resolve to break the Church’s hold on education and on public life.
The Ferry school laws and article 7
The decisive assault came under the republican ministries of the late 1870s and early 1880s. Article 7 of the higher-education bill, proposed in the Waddington ministry and pressed by Jules Simon, aimed to close the Jesuit schools; rejected in the Senate, it was followed by the decrees of 29–30 March 1880 expelling the religious congregations. Jules Ferry’s school laws then made primary education free, obligatory, and secular — the Republic’s great constructive act in the religious field. Sabatier stresses that in 1882 the laic school “was far from being anticlerical”: it was a new incarnation of a secular religious effort, an attempt by the nation to form its own citizens, not merely a war on the Church. Yet the conservative parties preached a crusade against it, and the school became the field of a long and bitter struggle over the soul of French childhood.
The Separation of Church and State (1905)
The culmination of the anticlerical programme was the law of 9 December 1905 separating the churches from the state, ending the Concordat regime that had governed the relations of the Church and the state since Napoleon. The measure completed the laic project: the state would no longer recognise, endow, or regulate any religion; the churches were to organise themselves through the associations cultuelles (“worship associations”) that the law provided. Sabatier, writing six years later, treats the Separation as a fact to be understood rather than fought: he notes with some irony the “Cultuelles, attempted toward 1905,” the new church launched with the favour of the ministry and the great newspapers — a sign of the religious experiments the age produced. His analysis of the post-Separation situation stresses not a simple decline of religion but a profound re-orientation.
The religious re-orientation
Sabatier’s central argument is that the laic movement and the Separation were not the death of religion in France but the condition of its transformation. He distinguishes free thought from anticlericalism, warning against confounding the two, and observes the “rapid progress of indifference and an unexpected awakening of religious aspirations — often to be observed in one and the same individual.” The Church, he holds, retains “a unique, incomparable place” in the conscience of the coming generation because alone it has taken consciousness of the unity and eternity of its life — even as its political power has been broken. The current religious orientation is “essentially French,” a movement of reconstitution in which the sentiments of the present generation — the sense of the mystery, of unity and solidarity, of tradition, of disinterested duty — are of undoubted Catholic origin though no longer bound to the clerical order. The Separation thus ended the Concordat’s political entanglement and opened, in Sabatier’s hopeful reading, a new epoch of religious liberty and revival.
The moral and spiritual stakes
Péguy’s Notre jeunesse adds a further dimension. He insists that the de-republicanisation of France and its de-Christianisation are one and the same movement of “demystification,” by which the people no longer believes in the Republic or in God — the sterility of the modern world that “prospers against all culture.” He observes how “clerical politics” has made of the Christian mystique what “radical politics” has made of the republican mystique, comparing the degradation of the saints by the clergy to that of the heroes by the parliamentarians. For Péguy the struggle over the Church and the Republic was at bottom a struggle over faith itself, and the laic school — by separating the spiritual from the political in a single movement of unbelief — risked drying up both the political and the Christian city. Anticlericalism, in this reading, was never merely a political programme but a spiritual event, and its legacy was ambiguous: it broke the Church’s power while carrying forward the very faith it thought it had abolished.

concepts/ausgleich-1867.title: The Ausgleich (Compromise) of 1867
concepts/ausgleich-1867.content:
The Ausgleich of 1867
The Ausgleich (“compromise,” in Hungarian kiegyezés) of 1867 was the constitutional settlement by which the Austrian Empire was transformed into the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary. Concluded between the Crown and Hungary in the aftermath of the defeats of 1866, it restored Hungarian self-government, established the common affairs and the Delegations, and created the dualist structure that endured until 1918. Its central enactment in Hungarian law was Act XII of 1867, and its architect was Ferenc Deák. The settlement remains one of the most contested acts of the century: Beksics defends it as the restoration of Hungarian statehood, while Sosnosky condemns it as a work that carried the germ of strife within it.
The constitutional arrangements
The Compromise rested on the historical Hungarian constitution and the Pragmatic Sanction. By Act XII of 1867 Hungary recognised the inseparable and indivisible possession of the kingdoms and the common defence, while receiving back its own responsible government, parliament and administration. The Austrian half, the kingdoms and lands represented in the Reichsrat (Cisleithania), was constituted in parallel by the December constitution of 1867, while the Hungarian half (Transleithania) comprised the lands of the crown of St. Stephen. The two states shared the person of the ruler and the common affairs: foreign policy, the army, and the finance for these, administered by three joint ministries and controlled by the Delegations drawn from the two parliaments. The customs and economic union, with a common tariff, currency and commercial policy, was a separate part of the settlement renewed periodically. Within Hungary, Croatia-Slavonia was bound to the kingdom by the nagodba (“settlement”) of 1868, which gave it a measure of autonomy.
Deák’s work and the army question
The negotiations of 1866–1867, resumed after Königgrätz, were conducted for Hungary by Deák, who asked nothing less than the conversion of the old unitary empire into a double state. The Crown’s first serious scruples concerned the unity of the army. In the drafting of § 11 of the Hungarian act, Deák refused to recognise a separate Hungarian army, declaring that such a course “would be personal union,” and that a Hungarian army “has never existed, neither in law nor in practice.” Andrássy supported him against the opposition, reminding it that with two legislatures and two governments a modern state could not also have two armies. Yet Deák was finally induced, to satisfy the demand of the subcommittee, to weave the “Hungarian army” into the wording of the paragraph — an inconsistency that Sosnosky calls fatal, since it kept the dispute over the common army alive for decades. The act was adopted by the Hungarian lower house on 30 March 1867 by 257 against 117 votes, and shortly after by the Magnates.
The acquiescence of the Reichsrat
A notable feature of the settlement was that the Austrian parliament was never asked to consent to the state-legal transformation of the whole monarchy. The Hungarian parliament had decided the matter over the heads of the Austrian deputies. Sosnosky calls this a demand such as had hardly ever been made of a representative body — that the Reichsrat assent to a remodelling of the entire monarchy arranged without its participation. Yet the Reichsrat did not resist: it gave no formal consent, but tacitly acquiesced, sending a deputation to Ofen for the coronation of Franz Joseph as King of Hungary, which amounted to a formal recognition of the Hungarian decision, and refraining from asserting its parliamentary rights against Hungary. The German-liberal party then at the helm in Cisleithania, and the leading press, hailed the Ausgleich as the end of the “long pernicious quarrel” and the beginning of a prosperous development for the new double state.
Two judgements
The verdicts of the two chief contemporary sources diverge sharply. Beksics, writing a generation after the event, defends the Compromise as the restoration and guarantee of Hungarian statehood: the dualism was no new creation but “gave form to a centuries-long historical development,” and Deák’s work could not be destroyed “because it answers the interests of both Hungary and Austria.” Sosnosky, on the eve of 1914, rejects this: he writes that the Ausgleich was not a successful work, that “success was not granted to the work of Deák and Andrássy,” and that it “already carried in itself the visible germ of strife.” Yet even Sosnosky concedes the good faith of the makers, and both agree on the scale of the change: the Compromise of 1867 created the frame within which the monarchy’s politics — the national struggles, the Magyarization policy, the Balkan policy, and at last the war — were all conducted down to the dissolution of 1918.

concepts/autocracy-russia.title: Russian Autocracy
concepts/autocracy-russia.content:
Russian Autocracy
The Russian autocracy — samoderzhavie (самодержавіе, “self-rule”) — is the political principle by which the Emperor of All the Russias held his power in his own person, owing it to no constitution, no parliament, and no elected body, but directly to God alone. Within the frame of this corpus it is the central institutional fact of Russian politics from the reaction that opened after 1866 to the collapse of the throne in the february-revolution-1917: the object of the Great Reforms’ cautious experiments, the creed that the reactionary counter-reformers reaffirmed with a new militancy, the thing the constitutional movement sought to limit, and the foundation whose undermining Denikin traced through the ruin of the army and the state. It is not merely a form of government but an ideology — an idea of Russia’s fitness for monarchical rule defended with the fullest seriousness by its great spokesman konstantin-pobedonostsev and, at the very end, restated by loyal churchmen as a religious faith.
Definition: power by the grace of God
Autocracy is the principle that the supreme legislative and executive power is vested, without limitation, in the person of the monarch. Unlike a constitutional monarchy, in which the sovereign rules within a law that stands above him, in Russia the emperor was held to be himself the source of law, answerable to God and his own conscience rather than to any earthly body. The conception rested on the idea, as Zhevakhov restated it in the monarchy’s last years, that Russian autocracy was “not a political but a religious” idea — the people’s faith in the anointed tsar as the anointed of God being the true basis of power. In this view the tsar was not one authority among many but the personal embodiment of the state, and to divide his power was to strike at the religious foundation of Russia itself. This is the doctrine in its purest form; and it is the standard against which all the compromises of the last reigns must be measured, for each concession — the zemstvo, the courts, the Duma — was resisted precisely as a breach of the sacred unity of power.
The reactionary reaffirmation, 1866–1881
Kornilov dates the reassertion of the autocratic principle in its aggressive modern form from the reaction that followed the Karakozov attempt of 4 April 1866. The shot that narrowly missed alexander-ii turned the temper of the highest governing circles: the reform programme of the 1860s was not repealed, but it was increasingly hemmed in by ministers convinced that it had gone too far. Count D. A. Tolstoy at the Ministry of Public Instruction pressed the classicism that was meant to discipline the young against sedition; the zemstvo found its field of activity narrowed; the new courts were gradually brought under the procuracy’s hand. The philosophy behind this policy was the conviction that representative and self-governing institutions, however harmless in appearance, were hostile to the autocratic state. The reaction reached its decisive moment in 1881. When the assassins of the narodnaya-volya killed Alexander II on 1 March, in the very hour when Count Loris-Melikov was about to lay before him a project of representative participation, the question of Russia’s future course was thrown open; and it was settled by the reactionaries’ triumph.
Pobedonostsev and the manifesto of 29 April
The man who settled it was Pobedonostsev, Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod and former tutor of the new emperor alexander-iii. At the conference of 8 March 1881 he denounced the whole course of the previous reign — the zemstvos, the new courts, the press — as the work of “talking-shops” (govorilni), and warned that the proposed representative commission would be a “supreme talking-shop” preparing the ruin of Russia. Autocracy, in his teaching, was the only form of government fitted to the Russian people; elected institutions imported from the west could only breed discord. With the Moscow publicists Katkov and Aksakov he worked on the young emperor’s instincts, and in secret, behind the backs of the reforming ministers, obtained the commission to draft a manifesto. On 29 April 1881 it was issued: the emperor announced that he was summoned by the voice of God to stand firmly to the work of government, in the trust of the strength and truth of autocratic power. The words were the programme of a reign; the whole of the following counter-reform — the land captains, the zemstvo statute of 1890, the restriction of the courts and the press — flowed from this reassertion that the emperor governed of himself and for himself, unbounded by the representative principle.
The limits of concession: the constitutional experiment
The autocracy so reaffirmed proved, in the generation that followed, the stubborn obstacle to every attempt to give Russia a share of western constitutional order. Under alexander-iii the principle was held intact and even hardened, in the conviction that the reforms of the father’s reign had been a mistake. Under nicholas-ii the strain became unbearable. The industrialization of the 1890s, the russo-japanese-war-1904-05, and the revolution-1905 at last forced concession: the october-manifesto-1905 granted civil liberties and a legislative Duma, and the empire seemed to pass from autocracy to duma-constitutionalism. Yet even this was made as little real as possible. The Fundamental Laws of 1906, framed under Witte’s premiership, preserved to the emperor the supreme autocratic power alongside the new Duma; and when the Second Duma proved refractory, Stolypin dissolved it by the coup of 3 June 1907 and rewrote the electoral law to secure a pliant chamber. The constitutional experiment was real in form, but the autocratic principle survived beneath it, and by 1914 the emperor had recovered the personal rule his grandfather had surrendered on paper. It was this unresolved contradiction — a state that could neither be fully autocratic nor become fully constitutional — that Denikin saw collapsing in 1917.
Current state: the collapse of the principle
In the frame of this corpus the autocracy is a principle already under siege through the whole period and finally destroyed. Denikin’s first volume, The Collapse of Authority and the Army, takes its title from the process by which the three pillars of the old order — “faith, tsar, and fatherland” — gave way in the months of 1917. The emperor had undermined his own throne by taking the supreme command in 1915 under the influence of the Empress’s circle; the February revolution swept away the dynasty almost without resistance; and the attempt to rebuild the state on new foundations ended in the october-revolution-1917. The White movement that Denikin chronicles was in a real sense a last defence of the old autocratic order, though its generals knew the throne could not simply be restored. The concept stands in the corpus as the negative image of everything the constitutional and revolutionary movements sought: the fixed principle against which zemstvo-great-reforms, the duma-constitutionalism, and the revolutions of 1905 and 1917 were all, in their different ways, directed. Related to it stand konstantin-pobedonostsev, its great apologist; alexander-iii and nicholas-ii, its bearers; and the assassination-alexander-ii-1881 that set its reactionary form in stone.

concepts/balkan-policy-austria.title: Austria-Hungary's Balkan Policy
concepts/balkan-policy-austria.content:
Austria-Hungary’s Balkan Policy
Austria-Hungary’s Balkan policy — die Balkanpolitik of the Habsburg Monarchy — is the specifically Habsburg programme within the wider eastern-question: the share the Dual Monarchy sought in the declining Ottoman inheritance from the catastrophe of 1866 down to the world war. Where the Eastern Question is the problem of Europe as a whole, the Balkan policy is the national, Habsburg answer to it — the policy that led from the occupation of Bosnia in 1878, through the annexation crisis of 1908, to the rivalry with Serbia and the road to sarajevo-assassination-1914. It is the concept under which the Monarchy’s whole eastern course in this period is best understood, and Sosnosky devoted his two-volume work to recounting it.
Definition: the Habsburg programme in the east
After Königgrätz (1866) drove the Monarchy out of Germany and Italy, the Balkan was, as Sosnosky writes, the only field left to its political activity; from that moment the Monarchy’s future lay in the east. The policy it pursued was at first the conserving one of Metternich’s inheritance — to keep the Turkish Empire alive as long as possible and to wait patiently for its death-hour, in order then to come forward and take a share of the inheritance. This was the programme of Gyula Andrássy, who after the disastrous Beust intermezzo took the helm and steered the new course to the east. Its decisive act was the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, undertaken by virtue of the mandate of the congress-of-berlin-1878, which planted the Monarchy among the South Slavs. The policy thereafter was a long sequence of accommodations and half-measures with the other Balkan and European powers — the alliance with Germany, the Dreikaiserbund entente with Russia, the watch over the Sandjak of Novi Pazar — all directed to the single end of keeping the Monarchy’s position in the peninsula without risking a general war.
The character of the policy: willing and power
Sosnosky’s closing retrospect draws the character of the whole policy with a historian’s severity. He discerns in it three abiding marks: a striking disproportion between the aims of the leading statesmen and the means of power at their disposal — between their Wollen and their Können; a frequent misreading of decisive political moments and the neglect of favourable opportunities; and a fatal inclination to half-measures. Every statesman of the period illustrates the pattern. Andrássy let the chance to annex Bosnia slip and contented himself with occupation, even secretly promising the Porte to hold the conquered lands only provisionally. His successors Haymerle, Kálnoky and Goluchowski carried the policy into a progressive paralysis, until under Goluchowski the will vanished altogether and the Monarchy knew only the desire to keep the peace at any price — the “good-natured universal uncle” who made way for everyone. Aehrenthal woke the Monarchy from its lethargy but used its recovered strength only passively: he bought Bosnia and Herzegovina from Turkey with money and, worse, surrendered the key to the Aegean, the Sandjak of Novi Pazar; and when the moment was ripe, with Russia powerless and the army waiting, he let the chance to settle accounts with Serbia pass and proclaimed that the Monarchy was satiated. Sosnosky calls that declaration the death-sentence of the Monarchy’s future in the east.
Berchtold and the crisis of the status quo
The policy reached its crisis under leopold-berchtold in the balkan-wars-1912-13. Berchtold had to pay for the sins of all his predecessors back to Andrássy: he was to make Balkan policy and dared take no step forward, bound as he was by the status-quo theory, by the alliance with Italy which claimed compensation should he advance, and by the reluctance of Berlin to be drawn into a Balkan war. When the Balkan League reduced the status quo to a bloody absurdity, he had to look on while the allies divided the Turkish inheritance, and let the opportunity to settle with Serbia slip past as Aehrenthal had done. His two positive acts — the creation of the truncated state of Albania, and the protest against the Peace of Bukarest that was not followed by deeds — were, in Sosnosky’s phrase, half-measures in the old style. The july-crisis-1914 was the last, forced application of the policy: the moment at which the Monarchy at last made serious demands upon Serbia, but, as Sosnosky lamented, again with half-measures — a punitive expedition that left Serbia in possession of its territory, which could only begin the old game anew.
The Serbian question as the heart of the policy
In its last phase the Balkan policy was above all the Serbian question. The occupation-of-bosnia-1878 and the annexation had fed the national movement among the South Slavs and their desire for territorial union; the large successes of Serbia in the Balkan Wars had given it a seductive glamour and drawn the eyes of the South Slavs from Vienna to Belgrade as the future capital of a South-Slav state. The great Serbian propaganda, conducted with the connivance of the Serbian government, ate into the Monarchy’s southern lands. Sosnosky judged the Serbian question a Lebensfrage — a question of life — for the Monarchy, cutting as it did into its very organism through the South-Slav problem, and he concluded that only the disappearance of Serbia from the map could give the Monarchy rest. This was the conviction that underlay the policy of the general staff and of the war party, and it was the answer the Monarchy finally gave in the July crisis. The Balkan policy of Austria-Hungary thus runs, in one unbroken line, from the conserving conservatism of Andrássy to the ultimatum of Berchtold and the mobilisation of conrad-von-hotzendorf.

concepts/bonapartism.title: Bonapartism
concepts/bonapartism.content:
Bonapartism
Bonapartism is the political tradition of Napoleonic authority — a plebiscitary Caesarism that joins democracy to authoritarian rule, claiming to embody the sovereignty of the people through the will of a single man. Rooted in the first Napoleon and revived by the Second Empire of Napoleon III, it offered France the promise of order, glory, and national greatness in exchange for the abdication of parliamentary liberty. In the decades after 1870, Bonapartism survived as a party of the fallen dynasty, a recurrent menace to the nascent Republic, and a temptation that the Republic’s founders explicitly rejected.
Plebiscitary Caesarism and the imperial idea
The core of Bonapartism was the appeal from the assemblies to the people directly — the plebiscite. Hanotaux, describing the constitutional theory that preceded the Republic, writes of the “advent of democratic Caesarism” in the nineteenth century, the form in which the Emperor rested his title not on divine right but on the repeated consent of universal suffrage. This was the essence of the régime personnel: the sovereign as the popular tribune invested with absolute power, standing above parties and parliaments, deriving his legitimacy from the nation rather than from any intermediary body. It was a democratic doctrine turned against democratic liberty.
Delord’s republican history treats the Second Empire as this doctrine in action. The imperial cult — the centenary of Napoleon I celebrated in 1869, the pictures restored to the Louvre, the Saint-Mandé banquet — renewed the family’s appeal to glory and to the memory of the first Emperor. Ollivier, who ultimately broke with the system, portrays the authoritarian Emperor as caught between the logic of his own plebiscitary title and the demand of an increasingly self-conscious public opinion for constitutional guarantees.
The Bonapartist party in the Republic
After the fall of the Empire, Bonapartism did not vanish. Hanotaux’s volumes on the early Republic return again and again to the “Bonapartist peril” as a shadow over the National Assembly and the monarchy’s failure. The appel au peuple group — the name itself a Bonapartist formula for the referendum — agitated for a return to the imperial system; Bonapartist manifestations broke out around the majority of the Prince Imperial; the parliamentary inquiry on Bonapartist manœuvres was ordered in 1874. In the constitutional struggle of the Assembly, the Bonapartists formed one of the three monarchical parties whose divisions saved the Republic, refusing fusion with either Bourbon branch and keeping alive the hope of the imperial restoration.
Hanotaux stresses how the Bonapartists’ presence fragmented the monarchical right and thereby unintentionally cleared the way for the Republic. In the electoral politics of 1873–1876 the Bonapartists recur as a permanent, active element — campaigning, propagandising, and allying now with the extreme right, now even with the left, in the intricate combinations of the Assembly. The Prince Imperial, the heir of the dynasty, stood at the centre of these hopes until his death in 1879; thereafter the imperial party faded into the background of French politics, surviving as a tradition rather than a threat.
The Republic’s rejection of the Napoleonic inheritance
The Third Republic defined itself precisely against Bonapartism. Its hatred of personal power — Hanotaux’s theory of the Constitution of 1875 emphasises the “hatred of personal power” as a governing sentiment of the constituents — was the direct antithesis of the Napoleonic doctrine. The parliamentary Republic built assemblies, ministerial responsibility, and a ceremonial presidency precisely so that no single man could again place himself above the law as the embodiment of the people. The fall of the Second Empire, the Prussian war and the Commune, and the long consolidation of the Republic were read by contemporaries as the definitive judgment on Bonapartism’s promise of order and glory: order had ended in defeat, glory in national disaster.

concepts/culturkampf.title: The Kulturkampf (1871–c. 1879)
concepts/culturkampf.content:
The Kulturkampf
The Kulturkampf (“culture struggle”) was the conflict between the government of otto-von-bismarck and the Catholic Church in Prussia and the new German Empire in the 1870s, fought over the limits of the state’s authority against the claims of Rome. The term, meaning literally “culture struggle,” was applied to the battle Bismarck and his Liberal allies waged against the influence of the clergy in the life of the state — a battle waged through a series of laws, known after their May enactments as the Maigesetze (May Laws), that brought the training, appointment, and discipline of the clergy under state control. The struggle opened in 1871, reached its height in the middle years of the decade, and ended, without victory, in Bismarck’s retreat after the turn toward protectionism and the break with the Liberals. For this corpus it is the German expression of the wider anti-clerical conflict that runs through the period, comparable to the anticlerical politics of France and the liberal empire.
The enemy within the new Reich
Lenz’s account of the Kulturkampf treats it as the great inner crisis that followed the founding of the Empire, the opposition that arose “out of the nation itself, which had just gone out unanimously against the hereditary enemy of the German name.” An opposition formed, so stormy in attack, so unshakable in defence, and so fundamental in its hostility to the newly created state, that all the opponents Bismarck had previously met shrank before it. It was split into two camps — the clerical and the social-democratic — which differed in origin, aim, and character but were bound by “the common hatred of the new Reich and the internationality of their policy,” a hatred great enough to bridge the gulf between them. Even their leader of the social democrats, August Bebel, had risen as an agitator of the Catholic journeymen’s associations, so closely did the two oppositions touch at the root.
The clericals were the first and best armed. Gathering even while Germany’s finest sons still fought in France, they entered the first Reichstag in March as a firmly closed band of fifty-seven deputies. Their ranks joined Poles and Guelphs, Prussians and Rhenish confederationists, feudal lords and democrats — “the vanquished, the subjugated, who gathered round the banner of the church militant.” At their head stood, beside Reichensperger and Mallinckrodt, the old Guelph minister, the Prussian diplomat who in June 1866 had delivered the letter of defiance to the German Confederation and its Catholic leading power — Bismarck’s own youth-friend, Charles Savigny, of Huguenot and Brentano blood, driven by wounded ambition into the arms of his country’s mortal enemies. They were a party that denied even its own name — “We are not confessional,” their leader declared — while their programme, colourless and many-hued, could have been claimed by other parties too.
Bismarck’s reluctance
Bismarck did not seek the struggle, and entered it only when he saw no other way. Lenz insists that “Bismarck never thought of renewing the battles of the confessional age”: his counsel had always been to avoid unnecessary concessions, never to give the impression of needing help, and otherwise to wait for the attack behind the bulwarks of the state, resolved to defend every inch of possession even against seemingly reasonable demands. Through the years in which the war with France was preparing, and even when the ghibelline spirit threatened to break into the church itself, he resisted the temptation to influence the course of the Council through which the Pope sought to lead the opposing elements of his church to victory. He turned back the request of his Roman envoy, Count Harry von Arnim, to send plenipotentiaries of the governments to Rome — partly because the measure was impractical, but chiefly because such an interference in the life of the church would contradict “the Protestant character of Prussia itself.”
It was only when Rome itself laid down binding norms for the relation of state and church without admitting the interested state as an equal factor, or when the German bishops sought help, that Bismarck was resolved to bring the power of the state to bear. And so it happened: while Germany flung itself into its war for freedom and greatness, Rome proclaimed the dogma that gave the last consecration to the theocratic absolutism of the Tiber — the dogma of papal infallibility. The German bishops dared not leave their Roman root, and their inner resistance shattered against the “ruthless offensive of the Jesuit-led Curia.” Academic Germany protested loudly against the new dogma as a falsification of the old and true Catholicism; religious teachers in the Catholic gymnasia and the theologians in the faculties refused to obey their bishops. In Bavaria the movement was even stronger than in Prussia: the greatest scholar of the Catholic world, Ignaz von Döllinger, turned away from the church and placed himself at the head of its opponents. “As a Christian, as a theologian, as a historian, as a citizen,” he declared on 28 March, “I cannot accept this doctrine.” He was excommunicated, but his university elected him rector, and the minister and King Ludwig himself showed him sympathy.
The struggle breaks out
Even then Bismarck hoped at first to avoid the war. He tried the Curia directly, and it almost seemed Rome might side with the victor; the negotiations that Ledochowski conducted at Versailles in November were followed in March by a letter of congratulation from the Pope to the Kaiser expressing the hope of friendship between Reich and Church. But the antagonisms to be reconciled were far too great for diplomacy to help. The Curie followed its own interest and the spirit of the church over which it ruled: it wanted help against the “robber-king” who had made the Holy Father a prisoner in his own house, and demanded the undoing of the Italian conquest of Rome. Bismarck could not give what the Curia wanted, any more than he could grant the Centre party’s demand to transfer the vague provisions of the Prussian constitution on church and state to the Reich — both contradicted the principles on which the new Reich rested.
And Prussia’s government could not refuse its own subjects’ requests for protection against their ecclesiastical superiors, in their consciences and their rights. Before the end of 1870 the cultus minister, von Mühler — himself anything but a liberal — met the archbishop of Cologne’s edicts against the Bonn theologians with a rescript insisting that the legal position of professors of Catholic theology was to be measured only by the statutory provisions the state itself had erected. The minister stood by the contested teachers at Breslau and Braunsberg too: the pupils must accept the instruction their teachers offered or leave the school, since the withdrawal of the missio canonica had no effect in state law. In that the sum of the conflict already found expression.
When battle became unavoidable, it was not Bismarck’s way to let his opponents strike first. Already in April he announced that the aggressive tendency of the new fraction might force the government, for the sake of effective defence, to become aggressive in turn; in June the moment seemed to him to have come. On 8 July, four days after the bishop of Ermland had pronounced the great excommunication over one of the resisting teachers, came the first blow: the abolition of the Catholic department in the ministry of cultus. Respect for public opinion was never Bismarck’s strength, and he had proved that he did not shrink from conflict with it; but he had never wanted to make the conflict a regular state institution. He had taken up the struggle because he could reach his goal no other way.
The May Laws and the height of the fight
The war was fought, in Lenz’s account, not by Bismarck alone but by Bismarck at the head of an alliance he did not love. “Had the Conservatives remained true to him, he would certainly have entered it with a gladder heart — he would have had the ground that was agreeable to him.” But the party of the old friends left its former leader in the lurch and forced upon him the alliance or, as Roon called it, the mésalliance with the Liberals. The Liberal influence found its expression in a part of the May Laws, from the school supervision law down to the requirement of a three-year course of study for Catholic theologians at German universities and their submission to a state examination in the historical sciences. Bismarck’s own aims were not set so far — not because he stood nearer the Roman spirit, but because they lay too far off for his realist eye, and because he feared the liberal flood might reach further and overflow his own field. He would later complain that the liberal jurists had spoiled his concept, and almost disowned his share in the laws; but Lenz is firm that he gave the direction, that “Falk set the pace that Bismarck prescribed him.” The individual details may have been worked out by Falk and his counsellors, but the goals were set by their master and lord. Some laws he regarded, like his allies, from the first only as weapons of war (Kampfgesetze). “For a generation,” he announced at the height of the conflict, he had calculated the struggle.
The consequences were terrible. The shepherds of the Catholic flock — a whole series of bishops and many hundreds of priests — were deposed or went to prison; their pulpits stood empty, their faithful were left orphaned, and ever higher swelled the flood of hatred and accusation against the “diocletian” persecution of the church. Law hung upon law; ever deeper the political power pressed into the fabric of the Catholic church, its dogma, cult, and constitution; and ever more defiant, more unbending became the force it met. It availed nothing to repeat a thousand times that government and majority of the Reichstag did not want to touch the faith, that Catholic subjects stood as near to the Kaiser’s heart as the evangelical, that his chancellor claimed nothing but the right of the state to draw its own boundary and to secure itself against arbitrarily begun attacks. It was no tolerance anymore, Lenz writes, and had never been, and could not be. It was the inner contradiction between the political power that had united Germany and the Roman Catholic world of ideas that had been subjected to it, breaking forth with elemental force: “the spirit of the Counter-Reformation remained alive in our people, and it was this that rose up against the heretic-state that the weapons had made victor.” Ever more clearly the Protestant character of the struggle came to light.
The crumbling of Bismarck’s world
The war cost Bismarck his old friends. Already in December 1872 he wrote to Roon, almost in despair, of a trade “in which one gains many enemies but no new friends — rather loses the old ones if one carries it on honestly and fearlessly for ten years.” The shield-bearers of his first campaigns as minister — men like Kleist, Blanckenburg, and the old Thadden — joined the long-since fallen Gerlach and Senfft-Pilsach. Twice, at the end of 1872 and again a year later, Blanckenburg refused to join the ministry; “Bismarck,” he wrote to Roon in November 1873, “has broken every bridge in Pomerania that I might have rebuilt.” It was the Prussian particularism that spoke from these words, the “junker spirit” to which the German idea had always been foreign and uneasy. Roon himself and even the Kaiser grew uneasy; the Kaiserin, once the patroness of liberal interests, drifted into the catholicizing current, and Bismarck’s own health broke, driving him into the long seclusion of Varzin — yet he remained chained to his office, “carrying his Promethean fate,” for the work he had created demanded its master.
On the other side the Liberal allies sought to turn the wave to their own advantage. They were themselves among the vanquished, but the glory of 1870 had served them better than any other party; their strength lay in Prussia’s new provinces and in the federal states, from which came their most brilliant leaders. In the elections to the first two Reichstags the National Liberals held an overwhelming majority, still carrying in their programmes a remnant of the ideals of 1848 — a Reich ministry, the guarding of popular rights, the enlargement of parliamentary power. They wanted to support the chancellor but also to force him into their direction, and the friction began again immediately after the war. In the summer of 1873 came a violent clash when Lasker, the eloquent, spoke of popular rights in the debate on the military law; Bismarck answered this “declamatory digression” — “These are speeches from a past time, which I am entitled to call declamatory” — under stormy protests. In 1874, at the great military debate, the two sides came close to the “crash”; the breach was patched by the compromise that fixed the strength of the army for seven years, but the alliance was already far loosened. “Bismarck wants to be rid of the Liberals,” Blanckenburg reported to Roon in the autumn.
An unavailing struggle
Lenz’s verdict on the Kulturkampf is that it was, in the end, a failure — “a war that at last ran into the sand.” He asks directly: has Bismarck suffered his first defeat in it? Did he achieve what he wanted? “The answer will differ according to whether one asks what Bismarck, and what the parties that stood in battle with him, expected of it.” The leaders of the national movement, the Liberals of every shade, hoped from the outset for more than the chancellor: that “the destruction of the two Catholic great powers” would be followed by the demolition of the Roman spirit in the fatherland of Martin Luther. None wished to rob Catholic countrymen of the form of their worship and faith, but they hoped to reshape the spirit of German Catholicism and subject it to the high ideas that had fructified the German mind for centuries. Bismarck’s own aims were more modest and more political: he wanted to remove “the foreign body that had lodged itself in his work,” to break the fraction that contrasted more sharply than any other party with the Prussian state-idea and with the principle of the new Reich itself. That the time would come when precisely that fraction would possess the decisive power in national politics — even that he would one day have to treat with it — he certainly did not expect when he summoned the national genius to battle against it.
The struggle thus failed of every aim. The state neither destroyed the Roman spirit nor broke the Centre party; it emptied pulpits and filled prisons, but the resistance it met only stiffened. When Bismarck turned, after the crisis of the later 1870s, to protectionism and the new economic policy, he abandoned the Liberal alliance and with it the Kulturkampf, moving toward a settlement with Rome. The Kulturkampf thereby closes a chapter: it had been the first great inner test of the new Reich, the moment when the anti-clerical energy that in France and the liberal empire shaped politics found its German and Protestant form — and, like its French parallels, it ended in retreat, leaving the church embattled but unbroken.

concepts/dualism-austria-hungary.title: The Dual Monarchy (1867–1918)
concepts/dualism-austria-hungary.content:
The Dual Monarchy
The Dual Monarchy (Doppelmonarchie, in Hungarian dualizmus, “dualism”) was the constitutional system created by the Compromise of 1867 by which Austria and Hungary existed as two separate, self-governing states joined by the shared person of the Habsburg ruler and by a limited set of common affairs. It was the political frame within which the whole Austrian and Hungarian history of this wiki’s period unfolded, from 1867 to its dissolution in 1918. The umbrella concept covers the Ausgleich itself, the common ministries, the Delegations, the customs and economic union, and the standing of Croatia and the nationalities within the Hungarian half.
The dynastic foundation
The basis of the dualist system was the dynasty and the Pragmatic Sanction. Redlich explains that Austria was “the creation of a dynasty” which for more than six centuries had joined almost unmeasured authority to the satisfaction of the needs of many tangled peoples — the hereditary lands, the lands of the Bohemian crown, and the whole territory of the ancient Hungarian crown of St. Stephen. The dynastic idea was that all these, while keeping their historical-political individuality, formed from the standpoint of the head of the House of Habsburg one great condominium. Within this frame Hungary always stood apart: even after the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 was adopted into Hungarian law in 1723, the kingdom’s constitutional position remained fundamentally different. Beksics rests the whole subsequent relation of Hungary to Austria on that Sanction, by which the succession of the House of Habsburg and the inseparable and indivisible possession of the kingdoms was settled.
Two states, one ruler
The essential structure of the dualism was the identity of the ruler. Beksics, in his chapter on the personal union (personál-unió), insists that the tie binding Hungary and Austria was the identity of the ruler’s person, and that the union of the two mutually independent states existed for mutual defence and for that alone. As long as the ruler’s person was common to Hungary and Austria this personal union and its consequences would stand; only in the single case of the cessation of the identity of the dynasty would new arrangements follow — an eventuality, he wrote in 1892, “entirely outside the range of political possibility.” The common affairs (közös ügyek, “common matters”) — foreign policy, war, and the finance for these — were managed jointly. The Austrian half was the Reichsrat-represented kingdoms and lands (Cisleithania); the Hungarian half was the lands of the crown of St. Stephen (Transleithania), including Croatia-Slavonia under the settlement of 1868.
The common machinery
The common affairs were administered by three joint ministries — for foreign affairs, for war, and for the common finances — responsible to the two states through the Delegations (delegációk, “delegations”). The Delegations were the joint parliamentary bodies, drawn from the two parliaments, by which the common affairs were managed and controlled. Beksics devotes a chapter to them and to the common army. The army was the keystone of the Austrian position within the dualism: Sosnosky calls it “the last bulwark” of the crown’s authority against the Magyar drive for independence. The customs and economic union bound the two states in a common commercial and monetary system, renewed periodically, while each retained its own finances, government and parliament for internal matters. Hungary kept, besides the common army, its own home-defence force, the honvédség, and the extraordinary levy.
A contested settlement
The dualism was from the first a subject of bitter dispute. Beksics’s whole treatise is a Hungarian defence of the Compromise against the claim, then beginning to be taught in the schools, that between Hungary and Austria there was a real union and that Hungary’s statehood had been impaired by the dualist system. He argues that the Compromise preserved, and did not impair, the statehood of the Hungarian state, and that Deák’s work answered the interests of both Hungary and Austria. Sosnosky, from the German-national side, condemns it: he compares the monarchy to “a wagon drawn by two horses that do not agree and pull apart,” holds that the dualism in its present form had become untenable, and writes that “a higher and quite unprejudiced judge has given the verdict — history.” Both writers, however, treat the dualism as the inescapable frame of the monarchy’s politics: Sosnosky’s four possible futures — revision of the dualism, a greater Hungary, trialism, and a federal “Greater Austria” — were all variations on or departures from it. The system endured until the war, when, as Redlich shows, the very structure of the two states — Hungary’s refusal to accept the Austrian war-surveillance office, its economic isolation of Austria — became one of the forces of the monarchy’s collapse, ending formally with the October Manifesto of 1918.

concepts/duma-constitutionalism.title: The Duma and Constitutionalism
concepts/duma-constitutionalism.content:
The Duma and Constitutionalism
The Duma and constitutionalism describe the short-lived experiment in representative government that Russia attempted after the revolution-1905: the State Duma (Государственная Дума), the elected legislative chamber created by the october-manifesto-1905, the Fundamental Laws that surrounded it, and the constitutional order that survived — in form — until 1917. Within the frame of this corpus it is the moment when the autocracy-russia of the Romanovs seemed at last to yield to the western principle of a share of power, and the demonstration of how little of the concession was meant or made real. The story runs from the granting of the manifesto through the four Dumas, and its turning-point is the coup of 3 June 1907, when pyotr-stolypin dissolved the Second Duma and rewrote the electoral law to secure a submissive chamber — the act that Witte, from exile, bluntly named a state coup (государственный переворот).
Definition: the representative experiment
The Duma was the chamber of elected deputies that Nicholas II was forced to grant by the revolutionary upheaval of 1905. The October Manifesto promised civil liberties and a legislative Duma — a body that would not merely advise but take part in legislation — and the empire was, on paper, transformed from an autocracy into something like a constitutional monarchy. The earlier Bulygin Duma, projected in the summer of 1905 as a purely consultative body, had been swept away by the October events and the creation of a legislature with real powers. The change was the central fact of the new political order: for the first time in Russian history the emperor would share his legislative power with an elected parliament. The question that divided the next decade was how far that sharing would go — whether the Duma would be a genuine parliament or a screen behind which the autocracy continued to govern as before.
The First and Second Dumas
The experiment began badly and worsened. The First Duma, elected in 1906 on a wide franchise, was dominated by the liberal Constitutional Democrats and proved refractory from the start: it demanded a responsible ministry, pressed the radical solution of the land question, and refused to work within the narrow limits the government allowed. Witte, who had presided over the granting of the manifesto, called it a “Duma of popular retribution” (Дума народного гнева); the government answered its demands by dissolving it after barely two months and by the agrarian legislation framed over its head. The Second Duma, elected in early 1907, was even more radical — its left flank swollen by the revolution’s aftermath — and the confrontation with the new minister of the interior and then premier, Stolypin, grew acute. The Fundamental Laws of 1906, framed under Witte, had already preserved to the emperor the supreme autocratic power alongside the Duma, reserving to him the sole right to amend them and to govern by emergency decree when the Duma was not sitting. The stage was set for a decisive trial of strength between the elected chamber and the crown.
The coup of 3 June 1907
The trial was decided by force. Accusing the Social Democratic deputies of conspiracy, the government on 3 June 1907 dissolved the Second Duma and simultaneously issued a new electoral law, altering the franchise by imperial decree without the consent of the chamber it had abolished. The act violated the letter of the Fundamental Laws, which had made the electoral law subject to the Duma’s concurrence, and for that reason Witte — who had by then left the premiership — flatly called it a state coup. It was, he observed, deliberately prepared so that the public might “more easily digest” a change that struck at the representative principle: a bogus plot was manufactured to justify a dissolution that was really meant to remodel the parliament. The new law, framed by the reactionary Kryzhanovsky and approved under Stolypin’s direction, heavily weighted the franchise toward the gentry and the propertied, cut the representation of the peasants, workers, and the national borderlands, and secured the government a chamber of landowners and moderates.
The Third and Fourth Dumas: the constitutional limits
The Third Duma, elected under the new law in 1907, was a different body — conservative, submissive, and willing to work with Stolypin, who governed through it the last years of his life until his assassination in 1911. The Fourth Duma, elected in 1912, continued in the same spirit. This was the “constitutional” Russia that went to war in 1914: a parliament existed, elections were held, legislation passed through it, but the supreme power remained with the emperor and his ministers, responsible to him and not to the chamber. The constitutional experiment, in Witte’s judgment, had been hollowed out: the empire had accepted the forms of a representative monarchy while keeping the substance of autocratic government. The Duma’s weakness was the weakness of the whole edifice — an institution that could protest and obstruct but could not rule, and that found itself brushed aside when the war and the revolution came.
Current state: the collapse of the experiment
In the frame of this corpus the Duma stands as the incomplete constitution that neither saved nor served the monarchy. It gave Russia the forms of parliamentary life and trained a generation of politicians, but it never acquired real power, and the tension between its existence and the survival of autocracy was one of the running complaints that fed the revolution-1905’s aftermath and the growing estrangement of educated society. When the war overwhelmed the empire, the Duma was powerless to arrest the collapse of authority that Denikin chronicles; the Provisional Government that followed the february-revolution-1917 grew out of a Duma committee, and the october-revolution-1917 swept both it and the whole constitutional experiment away. The concept stands between the autocracy-russia that resisted it and the revolutions that destroyed it, the proof that Russia could neither remain fully autocratic nor become truly constitutional. Related to it stand pyotr-stolypin and sergei-witte, the october-manifesto-1905 and revolution-1905 that created it, and the white-movement that, after 1917, fought — ambiguously — for some part of the order the Duma had represented.

concepts/eastern-question.title: The Eastern Question
concepts/eastern-question.content:
The Eastern Question
The Eastern Question — die orientalische Frage — is the European problem of the decline of the Ottoman Empire and the disposition of its territories, above all in the Balkans: the great standing issue of European diplomacy from the eighteenth century down to the world war. It is the umbrella concept of this period’s eastern history, the thread that runs unbroken from the Turkish wars of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, through the Crimean War and the Congress of Berlin, to the annexation crisis of 1908 and the balkan-wars-1912-13 that set Europe on the road to 1914. Within its frame the Powers of Europe, and above all the Habsburg Monarchy and Russia, contended for the inheritance of the sick man of Europe — a struggle that the Austrian historian Sosnosky took as the very subject of his account of the Monarchy’s Balkan policy.
Definition: the problem of the sick man of Europe
The Eastern Question arises from the circumstance that the Ottoman Empire, which once menaced Vienna itself, had for centuries been in retreat before the two empires that pressed it from the north, Austria and Russia. Its European provinces — the Balkans — were inhabited by Christian peoples increasingly conscious of their nationality and restive under Turkish rule; its government was weak, its finances broken, its hold on its lands precarious. The problem for Europe was what was to become of these lands. No single Power could be suffered to divide them alone: the whole history of the Eastern Question is the history of the efforts of the other Powers to prevent Russia, in particular, from seizing Constantinople and the Straits, and to keep the Ottoman state alive as the least of evils. Sosnosky’s first volume opens with the Turkish wars in this exact frame — the age of Turkish attack to 1718, the age of Turkish defence from 1719 to 1792, and the century of Austrian policy from Kaunitz to Beust — establishing that the question of the Balkans is as old as the standing of the house of Austria.
The Habsburg share: from the Turkish wars to Berlin
The Monarchy’s part in the Eastern Question was peculiar. Thrown back by Königgrätz in 1866 out of Germany and Italy, it was left, as Sosnosky put it, only the Balkan as a field for its political activity; henceforward the Eastern Question was the Monarchy’s question, the one great issue on which its future hung. Under Andrássy it held to a conserving policy, keeping the Ottoman Empire alive as long as possible and waiting for the hour of its death to claim a share of the inheritance. When Russia’s victory in the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–78 threatened to partition Turkey at San Stefano, Andrássy intervened, saved the Porte from destruction, and carried the congress-of-berlin-1878 which gave the Monarchy the mandate to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina. That settlement was the pivot of the Eastern Question in the century’s last quarter: it acknowledged the principle that the disposition of the Turkish lands was a matter for the European concert, and it planted the Monarchy firmly in the South-Slav world.
The new century: the question comes to a crisis
Through the decades that followed, the Eastern Question passed through the crises that Sosnosky’s second volume chronicles — the Bulgarian crisis of 1885, the annexation crisis of bosnian-annexation-crisis-1908, and the balkan-wars-1912-13. Each marked a further step in the decay of the Ottoman power and of the concert that had policed its decline. The annexation of Bosnia by Aehrenthal broke the letter of the Berlin settlement and embittered Serbia; the Balkan Wars completed what the congress had postponed, driving the Turks almost wholly out of Europe and doubling the size of Serbia. The old conserving answers of the Powers — the status quo, the concert, the keeping of the sick man alive — were exhausted, and the Eastern Question resolved itself into the Serbian question, which the Monarchy could no longer escape. When the shots of Sarajevo fired in 1914, the Eastern Question had become the world war.
Current state: the question at the outbreak of war
In the frame of this corpus the Eastern Question is the governing problem of the years 1866–1919 in the east. Its solution, in the sense of a peaceful settlement, never came; what came instead was the violent liquidation of the Ottoman power in Europe and the collision of Austria-Hungary and Russia that ignited the world war. The concept is the wide circle within which the specifically Habsburg programme — the balkan-policy-austria — is the smaller, national ring: the Eastern Question is the problem of Europe as a whole, of which the Monarchy’s rivalry with Serbia, and its confrontation with Russia, are the decisive expression. Related to it stand the congress-of-berlin-1878, the occupation-of-bosnia-1878, the bosnian-annexation-crisis-1908, and the balkan-wars-1912-13, with the july-crisis-1914 as its terrible conclusion.

concepts/german-question.title: The German Question (1848–1871)
concepts/german-question.content:
The German Question
The German Question (deutsche Frage, “the German question”) was the central political problem of central Europe in the middle of the nineteenth century: who was to unite Germany, and on what terms — by which state, under what constitution, and embracing which territory. From the collapse of the old German Confederation through the wars of unification it was the question of whether the many German states and lands should be drawn into a single national state, and whether the lead should fall to the Habsburg monarchy of Austria or to the Hohenzollern kingdom of Prussia. The answer, settled by war in 1866 and completed in 1871, was the kleindeutsch (“little German”) solution — a Prussian-led Germany from which Austria was excluded. The concept underlies the founding of the north-german-confederation and the german-empire-proclaimed-1871.
A question of the century
The German Question was not born in 1866 but reached back to the era of the French Revolution and Napoleon, when the thousand-year old Holy Roman Empire dissolved and the German lands were reorganized into a loose bundle of sovereign states. After the Congress of Vienna these states were bound only in the German Confederation, a defensive league of more than thirty members presided over alternately by the two great powers, Austria and Prussia. It was a structure of princes, not of peoples, and its loosening only sharpened the underlying question: whether the German nation, whose national idea had been kindled in the struggle against Napoleonic France, could ever find a single political home.
Lenz, writing the biography of the statesman who finally answered the question, frames it as the inheritance of 1848. The revolutionaries of that year, he recalls, had set the goal of gathering “the strength of the nation in one centre” — of founding a united fatherland. Yet the Frankfurt Parliament failed, and its failure left the German Question open and unresolved through the 1850s. The Confederation remained, in effect, a diplomatic holding pattern, while underneath it two rival conceptions of unity competed for the loyalty of the German public.
Two answers
These two answers, the kleindeutsch and the grossdeutsch, defined the field of debate. The grossdeutsch (“greater German”) solution would have brought all the German-speaking lands, including the German provinces of Austria, into a single state under Habsburg leadership — a Germany that stretched from the Alps to the Baltic and the North Sea. The kleindeutsch (“lesser German”) solution would have built a smaller German state under Prussian leadership, deliberately excluding Austria so that its non-German millions could not dilute the national character of the new state. (See kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch.)
Lenz observes how profoundly the question divided even those who agreed on the goal. All the German parties, he notes — “even the Kleindeutschen” — stood with their front toward the Rhine rather than toward the Danube; they saw France rather than Austria as the enemy. The peculiarity of Bismarck was that he alone located the decisive adversary in Austria, and dreaded above all that Prussia might be drawn into a war against France that would leave the Habsburg power intact. While the conservative friends of the Kreuzzeitung preached the duty of defending Austria’s “legitimate rights,” and Moltke wanted to strike against France, Bismarck saw that the German Question could only be resolved against Austria, on the battlefield or in its shadow.
The Confederation proves unworkable
By the 1860s the German Confederation had become the chief obstacle to every solution. The project of the Frankfurter Fürstentag (the Frankfurt Congress of Princes) of 1863 showed the futility of reform through the old order. There the Austrian minister Schmerling, urged on by the emperor, put forward a plan to reorganize the Confederation with an imperial presidency, a house of princes, and a delegated parliament — a scheme that would have entrenched Habsburg predominance. Bismarck, then Prussia’s minister-president, treated the whole enterprise with contempt, calling it “a foam-wave” arranged more for the inner politics of Austria than as a serious move, and urging the king simply to efface himself and let the Bundestag friends make what they could of their own new building. The Congress collapsed, proving that the German Question could not be answered within the existing Confederation, because Austria and Prussia could not share a lead that each claimed for itself.
Settlement by war
The resolution came through force. In the austro-prussian-war-1866 Prussia defeated Austria at Königgrätz, dissolved the old Confederation, and excluded Austria from Germany. The Peace of Prague left the German Question, for the moment, with the kleindeutsch answer enforced by arms. Bismarck then erected the north-german-confederation over the states north of the Main, a Prussian-led federal state with a directly elected parliament, and — crucially — framed it from the outset as the foundation that could later be extended to the south. Lenz emphasizes that the constitution Bismarck drafted in December 1866 was “in its outlines already the constitution which Bismarck gave the North German Confederation and, after the victory over France, transferred to the German Empire.” In it there was no longer any place for Austria.
The South and the completion
The German Question was not yet fully closed, for the four south German states — Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden, and Hesse-Darmstadt — remained outside the northern federation, left by the Peace of Prague a merely international position that neither prescribed nor forbade their union with the North. This was the great question of the years 1867–1870. Bismarck himself wished to postpone its answer, for he saw clearly that as soon as the southern states entered, the international crisis — the great European war that had been happily avoided in the German conflict — would break. He wanted the foundations of his power to rest secure in German soil before he challenged the fate that was gathering on every horizon.
The completion came with the franco-prussian-war-1870-71. The French Emperor Napoleon III, in whose calculations the perpetuation of German division had been a pillar of French greatness, challenged Prussia, and the resulting war drew the south German states into a common cause with the North. At the german-empire-proclaimed-1871 the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles, and the German Question received its final answer: a Prussian-dominated kleindeutsch empire under the Hohenzollern crown, with the Habsburg lands forever outside. What the revolutionaries of 1848 had demanded, Lenz concludes, was achieved by the very power whose ministry Bismarck directed — “the strength of the nation gathered in one centre,” but a centre fixed by Prussian might rather than by the national assembly of Frankfurt.

concepts/industrialization-witte.title: Witte's Industrialization
concepts/industrialization-witte.content:
Witte’s Industrialization
The industrialization of the 1890s and early 1900s is the programme of state-directed economic transformation associated with sergei-witte, minister of finance from 1892 to 1903: the gold currency, the spirits monopoly, the great railway-building, the harnessing of foreign capital, and the protectionist tariff system that together remade the Russian economy in a single generation. Within this corpus it is the bridge between the reactionary Russia of alexander-iii and the revolutionary Russia of nicholas-ii — the economic dynamism that modernized the country, that financed the railways and the treasury, and that at the same time piled on the population a burden of taxes and debt which the critics of the age, above all Granat’s financier Bogolepov, laid bare as the price of the “brilliant period” of state finances. It is the material foundation beneath the political story: the transformation that created the industrial working class, swelled the cities, and prepared the strains that burst forth in the revolution-1905.
The state-directed programme
Witte inherited and carried to its height the state’s leading role in the economy. His predecessors — Bunge and Vyshnegradsky under Alexander III — had already begun the fiscal centralization and protectionism that his system perfected. Witte’s conviction was that Russia, coming late to industry, could not wait for the slow organic growth of the western countries but must build its factories and railways rapidly by the deliberate action of the state. The treasury was the engine: state spending, state-guaranteed loans, state-ordered railway construction, and a tariff wall that shielded Russian industry from foreign competition while drawing in the foreign capital needed to build it. The programme was inseparable from the political order — it was the work of an autocratic ministry that could plan over the heads of the nation — and it expressed the belief that economic strength was the foundation of the empire’s greatness, the premise of its standing among the Powers.
The gold standard and the monetary reform
The centrepiece of the financial system was the monetary reform that made the ruble convertible on a gold basis. Laid down in its preparation still under Alexander III, it was carried through under Nicholas II by the ukases of 1897. The credit ruble, which had floated with the fortunes of the treasury, was stabilized at a fixed rate against gold; a new gold ruble was established by a kind of devaluation, fixed at the most stable existing rate of the paper ruble; and the State Bank was charged with the unfailing conversion of its notes into gold. The effect was to give Russia, for the first time, a hard and trusted currency on the western model, and to make it attractive to the foreign investor. Bogolepov’s essay in Granat is critical even here: the gold currency “cost the country” heavy sacrifices, and the reserve that underwrote it was supplied above all by foreign loans — the great French loans that bound Russia to her creditor and financed the system. Yet the reform worked: Russia’s money became as good as any in Europe, and the capital that had shunned an unstable paper currency now flowed in to build the railways and factories.
The spirits monopoly and the railways
To feed the treasury and the programme, Witte turned to indirect taxation and to the state’s own monopoly. The spirits monopoly (vinnaya monopoliya), reorganized from 1896, made the state the sole seller of drink — one of the largest and steadiest revenues of the empire, financing a great part of the state’s new expenditure. Alongside it stood the excises on tobacco, sugar, matches, and the raising of customs duties, and the state’s protectionist care of industries like sugar that it had chosen to favour. The other great engine was the railway. Witte, coming to the finance ministry from the South-Western Railway, knew the railways as no other minister did; under him the state built and bought lines on a scale unknown before, and above all pushed forward the greatest monument of the programme, the Trans-Siberian Railway, which carried the empire’s ambition into the Far East. The railways, the gold currency, and the monopoly formed one connected system: the state borrowed and taxed to build, the railways earned and opened the country, and the convertible ruble drew the foreign capital that paid for it all.
The cost of the “brilliant period”
The other face of the programme is the indictment that the Granat volume sets against it. Bogolepov’s running thesis is that the “brilliant period” of Russian state economy was purchased at the price of extreme strain on the taxable capacity of the people, irregularities of state economy, and the ruin of the propertyless. The state’s finances grew brilliant while the mass of the population bore the burden: indirect taxes pressed hardest on the poor, the redemption payments of the emancipated peasants hung over the village, and the famine of 1891–92 had shown how fragile the peasant economy was. The industrialization created its own social facts — the industrial boom of 1894–99 drew hundreds of thousands into the factories of Petersburg, Moscow, the Donbass, and the South, and the economic crisis of 1899–1903 threw them into unemployment and strikes. Martov’s essay in the same volume chronicles the growth of the mass labour movement that the Witte years called forth, and the government’s uneasy combination of factory legislation, repression, and the police experiments of Zubatov. The system had modernized Russia, but it had also created the industrial proletariat and the strained, indebted village that would carry the revolutions of the new century.
Current state: the foundation of the new Russia
In the frame of this corpus Witte’s industrialization stands as the economic transformation that made the Russia of Nicholas II. It provided the treasury with its revenues, the state with its railways and its Far Eastern reach, and the empire with the financial strength to fight the russo-japanese-war-1904-05 — whose defeat and cost, with the great foreign loan of 1906 that liquidated its legacy, closed the era. It created the industrial working class and the swollen cities that the revolution-1905 and the february-revolution-1917 were to shake. And it left a legacy of taxation and debt that Granat’s essayists judged the ruin of the propertyless and the seed of revolution. Related to it stand sergei-witte its architect, the duma-constitutionalism that the social strains of his economy helped to force, and the revolution-1905 that marked the political reckoning of the economic change.

concepts/irredentism.title: Irredentism (Italia irredenta)
concepts/irredentism.content:
Irredentism (Italia irredenta)
Irredentism — from Italia irredenta, “unredeemed Italy” — was the nationalist claim of the Italian state and its partisans to the Italian-speaking lands that unification had left under foreign, principally Austrian, rule: the Trentino (Trent and its Alpine valleys), Trieste, and the Istrian and Dalmatian littoral of the eastern Adriatic. Born in the years immediately after 1860–70, when the peninsula was united but its frontiers still ran along the old Austrian boundary, irredentism supplied the emotional and ideological motor of Italian nationalism in the decades before the First World War, and it was one of the forces that carried Italy into the war against Austria-Hungary in 1915. It was a concept of the incomplete nation: the Risorgimento had made the Kingdom of Italy, but it had not redeemed all Italians, and the unredeemed lands — le terre irredente — became the permanent, unfinished business of the national idea.
The unfinished unification
The ground of irredentism was laid by the incompleteness of unification. The war of 1866, in which Italy fought beside Prussia against Austria, delivered the Veneto to the kingdom — but by a diplomatic gift, the cadeau du Veneto, transmitted through Napoleon III after Prussia’s victories, rather than by an Italian military conquest. Tivaroni records the ironies and disappointments of that settlement: the attempt to include the Trentino in the treaty failed because Bismarck refused, and even the victorious general Garibaldi, who had pressed into the Trentino with his volunteers toward Riva and Trento, was held back from Trento itself. The frontier drawn in 1866 thus left the Italians of the Trentino, of Trieste and of Istria under the Austrian crown, across a boundary that ran through Italian-speaking country. For the nationalists this was a scandal and a call to arms; the country had achieved unity but not completion, and the phrase Italia irredenta named precisely what was missing.
The nationalism of the redeemed and unredeemed
Irredentism grew into a political force in the decades after 1870. It drew on the Mazzinian and democratic tradition of the Risorgimento, on the memory of the martyrs, and on the grievance of the boundary fixed at Vienna and then at the Congress of Berlin; and it was sharpened by the policy of the Habsburg monarchy toward its Italian subjects. The Austro-Hungarian state that issued from the austro-hungarian-compromise-1867 treated the Italians of the Trentino and the Littoral as a minority within its other nations, and the irredentist agitation in Italy answered with the claim that those lands belonged to the Italian nation by language and by right. Within Italy the movement was at once patriotic and subversive — a reproach to the governments that had accepted the frontiers of 1866, and a standing threat to the good relations of the kingdom with its great neighbour.
The war of 1915
Irredentism was a chief instrument of Italy’s intervention in the First World War. When war broke out in Europe in 1914, the neutral Italy of 1914–15 was courted by both alliances, and the interventionists built their case on the redemption of the unredeemed lands: the war against Austria-Hungary was presented as the fourth war of independence, the completion of the Risorgimento, the deliverance of Trento and Trieste. The soldiers who crossed the frontier on 24 May 1915 carried the irredentist hope onto the Isonzo and the Trentino fronts, and the isonzo-battles-1915-17 were fought in good part for the possession of the Julian marches toward Trieste. Cadorna’s plan of operations, aiming at the Austrian boundary and the Adriatic littoral, was in its strategic shape an irredentist design — the drive to reach and redeem Trieste by breaking the Austrian line.
The redemption of 1918
The victory of battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918 in October–November 1918 realised, at the war’s end, what irredentism had demanded for half a century. The Comando Supremo’s official account of the battle closes with the occupation of Trento and the landing at Trieste — the two cities that had been the supreme symbols of Italia irredenta — as the Austrian army was annihilated and Austria sued for the armistice. Trento and Trieste, together with the Trentino and the Istrian littoral, passed under Italian sovereignty in the peace that followed. Irredentism thus achieved its object at the very close of this corpus’s frame; the movement that had animated Italian nationalism since the frontier of 1866 was consummated in the victory of 1918, even as the settlement of the Italian frontier on the eastern Adriatic would leave new disputes behind it.
