concepts/kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch.title: Kleindeutsch and Grossdeutsch (c. 1815–1871)
concepts/kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch.content:
Kleindeutsch and Grossdeutsch
The terms kleindeutsch (“lesser German”) and grossdeutsch (“greater German”) name the two rival solutions to the german-question — the two answers to the question of how, and over what territory, Germany should be united. The grossdeutsch (“greater German”) solution would have gathered all the German-speaking lands, including the German provinces of the Habsburg monarchy, into a single national state, ideally under Austrian leadership. The kleindeutsch (“lesser German”) solution would have united Germany under Prussian leadership, deliberately excluding Austria — because Austria, with its millions of Slavs, Magyars, and Italians, could never be absorbed into a German nation-state without dissolving its national character. The distinction was the central axis of German politics between the failure of 1848 and the wars of unification; the german-question was finally resolved in 1866–71 on kleindeutsch lines.
The two programmes
The grossdeutsch programme rested on the ideal of a Germany co-extensive with the German language and culture, embracing Austria as its historical heart. It was the natural programme of the Austrian government, of the Catholic and clerical south, and of all those for whom German unity was inseparable from the greatness of the house of Habsburg. In its most ambitious form it would have transformed the Austrian Empire itself into the leading power of a great all-German confederation.
The kleindeutsch programme, by contrast, was the programme of Prussian hegemony. It accepted the sacrifice of Austria’s German provinces — and therefore of millions of Germans — for the sake of a compact, powerful, Protestant-led state that the non-German peoples of the Habsburg lands could not corrupt. Its partisans were found above all among the liberal nationalists of Prussia and the north, the heirs of the failed Frankfurt Parliament of 1848, who had come to see that the German Question could only be solved by Prussian power.
The nation against the Danube
Lenz repeatedly stresses how far the kleindeutsch sentiment ran through the whole national movement, even before it was forced to a decision. “However the German parties might conceive their goal,” he writes of the 1850s, “they were all, even the Kleindeutschen, with their front toward the Rhine rather than toward the Danube” — that is, they all saw France as the enemy and Austria as at best a rival. This shared orientation was precisely what made Bismarck’s policy exceptional: while the nation feared France, Bismarck alone identified Austria as the power that had to be broken. He dreaded nothing more than a Prussian war against France that would spare the Habsburg monarchy, and he aimed instead to let Austria fall in Italy while Prussia gathered strength at home. His difference from his own conservative friends, the Kreuzzeitung party who preached the defence of Austria’s “legitimate rights,” was total: for him the German Question could not be answered while Vienna remained within the German body politic.
The pressure of the South
The division between the two programmes ran directly through the German states, and nowhere more sharply than south of the Main, where the grossdeutsche cause was strong. Lenz describes how, in the years before the decisive struggle, the Bavarian chamber, “in which the Grossdeutschen ruled,” passed resolutions on the Zollverein that came close to dissolving it in favour of a south German special league joining Austria. The clerical and Catholic south gravitated to Vienna, while the Protestant and liberal north leaned to Berlin. “That in the nation itself the Grossdeutschen, whether stamped liberal or clerical, were one and all in Habsburg’s camp needs no words,” Lenz observes — “but even the ranks of the kleindeutsche party felt themselves shaken” by the pressure of the Austrian programme, fearing they might be left to face the darkest reaction on their own.
The Austrian counter-programme
The grossdeutsch cause was most openly and formidably advanced by the Austrian government itself in the early 1860s. The reform plan of Schmerling, presented at the Frankfurt Congress of Princes in 1863, was in effect a grossdeutsch programme: a reorganized Confederation with an imperial presidency under the Habsburg emperor, a house of princes, and a delegated parliament. It was drawn up with the assistance of the old radical Julius Fröbel, and it aimed to reconcile legitimacy with liberty, the claims of Austria with the demands of the national state, and to found “the new Germany” peaceably at a congress of princes in the city of the old Bundestag under the presidency of the heir of the last imperial dynasty. For Prussia this was an attempt at “the violent coercion of Prussia” through the use of the majority in the Bundestag — and Bismarck met it with contempt and studied inaction, “effacing” Prussia and letting the scheme collapse of its own hollowness. The failure of the grossdeutsch programme at Frankfurt marked the last serious attempt to solve the German Question on the greater-German basis by agreement.
The kleindeutsch victory
The decision was reached by war. In the austro-prussian-war-1866 Prussia defeated Austria, and the kleindeutsch solution was imposed upon Germany by force: Austria was expelled from German affairs, the Confederation dissolved, and the north-german-confederation founded under Prussian leadership with no place left for Vienna. What remained was to draw the south German states — among whose populations the grossdeutsch sentiment still ran strong — into the Prussian system, which the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 and the german-empire-proclaimed-1871 accomplished. Lenz’s account of the constitution Bismarck drafted in December 1866 makes the kleindeutsch character of the whole construction explicit: it was “in its outlines already the constitution which Bismarck gave the North German Confederation and, after the victory over France, transferred to the German Empire,” and in it Austria had no place.
The kleindeutsch solution was thus a compromise that satisfied neither pure ideal — it excluded Austria but kept a directly elected Reichstag and a parliament of the nation, elements that had been demanded by the revolutionary and liberal movements of 1848. The grossdeutsch dream did not die, but it passed from the realm of the possible into that of nostalgia and grievance, surviving in the Catholic and particularist south and resurfacing, transformed, in the revanchist and pan-German politics of later decades. For the purposes of this corpus, the distinction matters as the frame within which otto-von-bismarck and wilhelm-i carried out the foundation of the Empire.

concepts/liberal-empire.title: Liberal Empire (Empire libéral, 1869–1870)
concepts/liberal-empire.content:
Liberal Empire (Empire libéral, 1869–1870)
The Liberal Empire (Empire libéral) was the transformation of the Second Empire in its last two years — from the senatus-consult of September 1869 and the letter of 19 January 1869 through the Ollivier ministry of 2 January 1870 — whereby the authoritarian regime turned toward parliamentary government while preserving the imperial crown. It is the central subject of Émile Ollivier’s great memoir L’Empire libéral, whose very title makes the claim that the liberal transformation was not a betrayal of the Empire but its fulfilment. The experiment died within months, engulfed in the Franco-Prussian War.
The road to parliamentary government
The liberalisation began in measured steps. The letter of 19 January 1867 had conceded a regulated right of interpellation and promised press and meetings laws; these came fully into force in 1868. But the decisive turn came in 1869. After the elections of that year — which Ollivier reads as a defeat of the authoritarian Empire represented by Rouher and a victory for the liberal programme — the Emperor yielded the ground. The senatus-consult of 8 September 1869 replaced the irresponsible regime with a system of ministerial responsibility, giving the Corps législatif a genuine share in government.
Ollivier’s Le 19 janvier, published in March 1869, supplied the doctrine: the Empire must either advance into responsible, parliamentary government or perish as an anachronism. In Ollivier’s telling the Emperor, who had said he would not go back but would not go forward, finally accepted the necessity of moving forward. The negotiations that produced the ministry of 2 January 1870 are recorded by Delord in the Préface de l’Empire libéral: the approaches between Ollivier and the Emperor through Clément Duvernois, Ollivier’s conditions and programme, his disguised journey to Compiègne, and the final formation of a ministry drawn from the liberal centre under his presidency.
The ministry of 2 January 1870
The Ollivier ministry marked the inauguration of the Liberal Empire proper. It was a cabinet of the constitutional centres — Daru, Buffet, and their friends entering with conditions — and it presented itself as a government of the parliamentary majority, responsible before the Chambers. Ollivier, who had spent years as the advocate of liberal reform within the Empire, now became its president of the council, seeking to make the imperial crown compatible with a fully constitutional regime. The ministry’s programme, in his telling, was to complete the edifice of liberty within the frame of the dynasty.
The task was formidable. Ollivier’s own memoir emphasises the contradictions: the Empire was still a personal, plebiscitary power at its base, and the Emperor retained the reserve of his own authority; the liberal ministry had to govern with an assembly that contained both an intransigent republican left and a Bonapartist right hostile to parliamentary government. The prophecies of misfortune, Ollivier records, came from all sides — Thiers, the irréconciliables, and the opposition press alike foretold disaster for a hybrid regime that satisfied neither the partisans of absolute authority nor the partisans of liberty.
The fate of the liberal experiment
The Liberal Empire governed for barely eight months. It had to confront the European crisis that broke over the Hohenzollern candidature and the Ems affair, and in July 1870 Ollivier, against his pacific instincts, led France into the war with Prussia. The catastrophe of Sedan, the capture of the Emperor, and the revolution of 4 September 1870 swept away both the Empire and its liberal ministry together. The experiment — an attempt to reconcile the Napoleonic tradition of authority with the nineteenth-century demand for parliamentary government — was never given the chance to mature.
For Ollivier the Empire libéral remained his great historical vindication, the subject of a multi-volume memoir composed in the decades after the fall. For the Republic that followed, the failure of the Liberal Empire demonstrated the impossibility of reconciling personal power with liberty — a lesson the Third Republic’s founders took to heart. The term itself, however, continued to be used: Hanotaux, writing of the “liberal Empire” in the constitutional theory preceding 1875, treats it as one more episode in the nineteenth century’s circuit between democracy and authority.

concepts/magyars-magyarization.title: The Magyars and Magyarization
concepts/magyars-magyarization.content:
The Magyars and Magyarization
The Magyar national policy, and the linguistic Magyarization (magyarizálás, “Magyarizing”) that accompanied it, was the attempt to consolidate the Hungarian kingdom as a Magyar national state within the lands of the crown of St. Stephen, pressing its subject peoples — Germans, Romanians, Slovaks, Ruthenians, Serbs and Croats — toward the Hungarian language and nation. Two contemporary witnesses frame the question from opposite sides. Gusztáv Beksics, the Hungarian publicist, wrote to defend and advance the Magyar national consolidation; Theodor von Sosnosky, the German publicist in Vienna, wrote to condemn the Magyar national state and its treatment of the non-Magyar peoples. Together their works give the fullest contemporary account of the theory and practice of Magyarization, and of the nationalities question that strained the Hungarian half of the monarchy toward 1914.
The Magyar national state
Sosnosky opens his account of Hungarian politics with a portrait of the “Magyar political nation” — its passionate, domineering temper, its self-absorption, and its attitude toward the non-Magyar peoples of the kingdom. The conception of the “Magyar national state” (magyar nemzeti állam) was, he argues, the short-sighted, perverse and intolerant idea that governed all of Hungary, standing in the sharpest contrast to the far-sighted, wise and tolerant view that had originally prevailed. He recalls that the founder, St. Stephen, ruled on the maxim that a kingdom of one language and one custom is weak and fragile, and had encouraged the immigration of foreign, chiefly German, elements to bring culture into the land; the successors and even the later dynasties had done the same. Only toward the end of the eighteenth century did an expressly national movement arise in Hungary, and the irony of history, as Sosnosky notes, was that the Germanising measures of Kaiser Joseph II strengthened the Magyar national feeling — whereupon the same Magyars who had resented the attempt to rob them of their nationality began to do to their non-Magyar fellow-citizens exactly what had been done to them.
The instruments of Magyarization
The pressure operated through the school, the courts, the electoral system, and the administration. The Nationalities Law (Act XLIV of 1868) had, in Sosnosky’s phrase, subjected the non-Magyars of Hungary to an “arbitrary lumping together of the five peoples of Hungary into one indivisible unitary Hungarian nation,” an “assault on their national individuality.” It provided some hope of a dam against the Magyar flood; but the dam proved not tight enough, and the Magyar high flood, seeping through slowly but irresistibly, “washed away one national possession after another.” The Magyars, with the “artful petifogging” that was their habit in national questions, reinterpreted and circumvented the inconvenient law, or where that was impossible violated it. In the schools the non-Magyar languages were pressed back in favour of the Magyar; officials ignorant of the languages they served had to sign the most important documents in Hungarian; pastors who had grown grey in their German or Slav service had to issue baptismal and other certificates in a language they did not understand, while Magyar priests were set over German or Slav congregations whose tongue they did not know, and every attempt at resistance was punished in a truly barbarous fashion. The result was that Hungarian patriotism degenerated into a “linguistic monomania.” Those who had only imperfectly acquired the Magyar tongue — the half-Magyarized, whom Sosnosky calls the Talmi-Magyaren (from the gilded imitation gold) — he numbers at about a million. The principle of the identification of nation with language governed the whole policy.
Beksics and the agrarian foundation
Beksics, writing from within the Hungarian national camp in 1896, approached the question from a different and striking direction. His A magyar faj terjeszkedése (The expansion of the Hungarian race) argued that linguistic assimilation had failed: “linguistically we are incapable of assimilating the nationalities,” he declared — three decades of constitutional rule and a national cultural policy had produced, so far as linguistic absorption was concerned, very poor results, and in places there had even been positive regression. The national consolidation, in his view, could not be achieved through language alone; it must rest on the free expansion of the Hungarian race, and above all on agriculture and the creation of a Hungarian peasant proprietorship. He pointed to the alarming phenomenon that in the very counties that showed the tremendous force of the race the number of births was now falling or stagnating, and argued for the division of the great estates to create a numerous landed peasantry as the means of expansion. The two works thus represent the two poles of the question: the language-policy that the national state had pursued, and the demographic and agrarian foundation that a reformer within the national camp believed was the true basis of survival.
The working of the national state
Sosnosky treats in turn each of the subject peoples — the Germans, the Romanians, the Slovaks, the Ruthenians, and the Serbs — and the working of the Magyar national state upon each, together with the position of Croatia-Slavonia under the nagodba of 1868. He insists that the Magyarizing system, by the measureless hatred it had roused in the peoples who suffered under it, had prepared the downfall of the very Magyar domination it was meant to secure: “at the day when Hungary tore itself loose and won its full independence, its ruin would also begin,” for the peoples would seize the favourable moment to free themselves. It was, he wrote, a tragicomic spectacle to see the Magyars “desire nothing more hotly, strive after nothing more vehemently than their own downfall.” Redlich, writing after the war, echoed the judgement from the Austrian side, describing the perpetual keeping-down of the nationalities by the Magyar gentry and the “complete political helotisation” that the Romanian people of Transylvania had learned to regard as its permanent fate, and judged that only an unsuccessful war or the dynasty’s own action could have broken the supremacy of the Magyars — a supremacy the war itself at last dissolved.

concepts/military-dictatorship-conrad.title: Conrad's Military Dictatorship and the Doctrine of Preventive War
concepts/military-dictatorship-conrad.content:
Conrad’s Military Dictatorship and the Doctrine of Preventive War
The doctrine of preventive war as it was developed and pressed by the chief of the Austro-Hungarian general staff, conrad-von-hotzendorf: the conviction that the salvation of the Dual Monarchy lay in an early, decisive war against its enemies — above all Serbia, and behind Serbia Russia, and in due course Italy — fought before the odds grew irrecoverably worse. It is at once a military doctrine and a programme of political action, and it stood in chronic tension with the civilian leadership of the Monarchy. The name by which contemporaries and historians have known it, the military dictatorship of Conrad, captures the ambition of the general staff to bend the state’s policy to the demands of the army and the clock of mobilisation.
Definition: war as the continuation of policy
The doctrine rests on the maxim, which Sosnosky also quotes from the first page of the general staff’s tradition, that war is nothing but the continuation of politics by other means. Conrad drew the conclusion that the root of all evil for the Monarchy was the relation to Serbia and to the Russia that stood behind Serbia, and that “at this root the evil had to be seized; everything else was secondary.” He recognised two roads to the goal: first, the attainment of a lasting, confederal union of Serbia with the Habsburg Monarchy in a peaceful manner; but if Serbia declined the union and continued its hostile aspirations — and this, he held, was the case that existed — then a warlike settlement at the suitable moment. The suitable moment was, in his view, always passing. Already in 1906, on his appointment as chief of the general staff, he had pointed to this; in 1908–09 he had declared the moment come to make clear conditions with Serbia, foreseeing that the chances of this unavoidable settlement would only grow worse; and in 1913 he held the last moment to have come to carry it out at all with hope of success. If that moment too were neglected, he believed, the Monarchy would drift without a rudder to the doom that threatened it from Serbia and Russia.
The preventive war against Serbia and Italy
The doctrine embraced, besides Serbia, the other enemies of the Monarchy. Conrad pressed the case for war not only against Serbia but against Italy, whose irredentist agitation and whose renunciation of the alliance, in his reading, made it a foe that must be settled before it could strike. His advocacy was grounded in the very character of the alliance system: the Monarchy was encircled, its opponents arming visibly, and only an early war fought on its own terms could prevent a later war fought at the enemy’s convenience. The most famous formulation of the idea is the memorandum of the Monarchy’s own minister at Bukarest, Count ottokar-czernin, of 11 March 1914, preserved among Conrad’s papers: that one must “have done with the present Serbia” if there were to be peace in the Balkan; and that a warlike preventive measure must not be judged only from the standpoint of consuming the prey — Serbia had been called the europäischer Blinddarm, the European appendix, and one operates on the appendix not to keep it but to have done with it. The analogy expressed exactly the preventive logic: war against Serbia was to be fought not for conquest but for relief, to end the perpetual source of infection at the Monarchy’s flank.
The tension with the civilian leadership
The doctrine brought Conrad into open conflict with the Monarchy’s civilian statesmen. Against Baron alois-aehrenthal the divergence over the military requirements of the exposed position grew into a running feud; Conrad pressed for the reinforcement of the army and came into conflict with the minister of foreign affairs over the means he held the situation to demand, until on 30 November 1911 the Kaiser removed him from the post of chief of the general staff and appointed him army inspector. The conflict with the civilian Ballplatz was not one of mere procedure but of principle: where Aehrenthal and, after him, leopold-berchtold strove to keep the peace and to localise the Balkan crises, Conrad insisted that peace was the road to ruin and that the diplomatic half-measures of the state were wasting the last chances of a successful war. The rupture extended even to the heir, franz-ferdinand, with whom Conrad quarrelled over policy in the manoeuvres of 1913, though the archduke, who had engineered Conrad’s reinstatement, remained convinced that the man who had prepared all the plans of war should command the army should war come.
The outcome: reinstatement and the coming of war
The vindication of the doctrine, as Conrad saw it, came with the war it had prophesied. Reinstated as chief of the general staff on 12 December 1912, in the midst of the Balkan crisis, Conrad watched the last moments pass unused while the policy of the Monarchy let itself be taken prisoner by side-issues — to the joy of its enemies, as he put it. When the sarajevo-assassination-1914 came in June 1914, he greeted it as the war-declaration of Serbia, the hour that at last summoned every man to his place; and in the july-crisis-1914 he threw the whole strength of the army into the war he had so long urged. Yet the sequel was the demonstration of the limits of the doctrine. In the battle-of-galicia-1914 the war that was to save the Monarchy opened in disaster, and Conrad’s own closing reflection held that the decision of the war lay in the failure of the agreed first action — the plan whose maker he had been. The military dictatorship of Conrad thus stands as the apotheosis and the bankruptcy of preventive war: the doctrine that brought the Monarchy to the sword it thought it must draw, and to the catastrophe that the sword could not avert.

concepts/mystique-politique.title: Mystique and Politique (Péguy)
concepts/mystique-politique.content:
Mystique and Politique (Péguy)
“Mystique and politique” is Charles Péguy’s famous distinction, drawn in Notre jeunesse (1910), between the spiritual faith of the Dreyfusards and its degeneration into political calculation. For Péguy, every great cause begins in mystique — a lived, disinterested faith for which men are willing to die — and ends in politique — the parliamentary, calculating language of parties that translate and betray what was done in the name of faith. His distinction became one of the defining ideas of the French intellectual tradition and the key to his own reading of the Republic and the modern world.
The faith of the Dreyfusards
Péguy’s essay is an “examen de conscience” of the generation that had fought for the revision of the Dreyfus trial. The Dreyfusard cause, in his account, was a mystique: a faith held for its own sake, without calculation. The Dreyfusards refused to accept an official injustice because — in a deep Christian movement — “a single injustice, a single crime suffices to break the whole social pact, the whole social contract.” They spoke the language of eternal rather than temporal salvation, refusing that France should be “constituted in a state of mortal sin.” Péguy opposes the hommes du salut éternel to the hommes du salut temporel: the adversaries spoke the language of reason of state, that one must not sacrifice a whole people for one man; the Dreyfusards answered that the honour of a people is “of a single piece.” Bernard-Lazare, whom Péguy honours as the prophet of the affair, embodied this faith — defending the returned captain even in his imperfections, for “he is innocent, that is already much.”
The affair, Péguy writes, was “the last of the operations of the republican mystique,” the supreme surge of the heroism of his generation. His own, he says, is “the last of the generations which possess the republican mystique” — the rear-guard of the republican faith, its tradition borne by ordinary families, the “tissue of the Republic.”
The degeneration into politique
The distinction that gives the essay its fame is the passage from faith to calculation. “The republican mystique — that was when one died for the Republic; republican politique — that is now when one lives from it.” The political parties, Péguy holds, can speak only the political, parliamentary language, and they translate — betray, traducunt, tradunt — everything that is done for the mystiques. Since the degradation of the Dreyfusard mystique into Dreyfusard politique, he and his collaborators have known fifteen years of poverty defending Christian consciences and republican liberties, only to find reactionary politicians forbid them being republicans and republican politicians forbid them being Christians.
Péguy’s maxim is universal: “Everything begins in mystique and ends in politique. Everything begins with mystique, with one’s own mystique, and everything ends in politique.” The question is not whether a given policy is good or bad but whether it springs from a living faith or from calculation. He compares the degradations — what “clerical politics” has made of the Christian mystique, what “radical politics” has made of the republican mystique, what the clergy has made of the saints, what the parliamentarians have made of the heroes — and insists that one must compare like with like, mystique with mystique and politique with politique, never a mystique with a politique.
The modern world against culture
The source of the degeneration, for Péguy, is what he calls le monde moderne — those who believe in nothing and glory in it, “not even in atheism.” The de-republicanisation of France is the same movement as its de-Christianisation, a single movement of “demystification,” by which the people no longer believes either in the Republic or in God. This is “modern sterility,” which dries up equally the political and the Christian city. The modern world, he writes, opposes not only the old régime but every old culture together: “it is the first time in the history of the world that a whole world lives and thrives, appears to thrive, against all culture.”
Yet Péguy does not despair: “this race has seen many others.” The Republic has ceased to be lived and has become a thesis — “when a regime, from organic, has become logical, and from living historical, it is a regime that is on the ground.” But he hopes the following generation will be “at last a mystical generation,” and that the two mystiques, republican and Christian, will flower again together in a single deep movement. Against the royalists of the Action française, he concedes that the only force of a traditional monarchy is that the king is loved — “the only force, the only value, the only dignity of everything is to be loved” — and finds in their “we would be ready to die for the king” the one thing that speaks to him, for it is a truth of faith rather than an argument. Yet one founds no culture on derision and sarcasm. The essay closes with the word that the royalists are but “a vague and theoretical menace,” and “the day they become a real menace they will see what we are still capable of doing for the Republic.”
The distinction in the corpus
The mystique/politique distinction runs beneath the other texts of this corpus. Sabatier’s L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle, which cites Péguy among the French authors shaping the religious movement, shares his sense of a present mystique — a religious aspiration awakening amid indifference, seeking the foundations of a new temple in sentiments of Catholic origin. And the distinction illuminates the whole arc of the Third Republic: the republican mystique of the founders and its degeneration into the politique of the party men, the transformation of a lived faith into a set of propositions. Péguy’s idea thus became, for the generation before the war, the means by which contemporaries understood the passage of their own great causes from heroism to calculation — and the criterion by which they judged every institution, party, and faith of the modern world.

concepts/narodnaya-volya.title: Narodnaya Volya (The People's Will)
concepts/narodnaya-volya.content:
Narodnaya Volya (The People’s Will)
Narodnaya Volya (Народная Воля, “The People’s Will”) was the Russian revolutionary terrorist organization of the late 1870s and 1880s that made the assassination of the emperor the centre of its programme. Breaking out of the populist movement of the intelligentsia that had gone “to the people” in the hope of raising the peasants, the party concluded that the autocratic state was the sole obstacle to the people’s welfare and that the revolutionaries, who could not command the masses, must strike at the state through its head. Its campaign of bombs and mines against alexander-ii culminated in the catastrophe of 1 March 1881, when the emperor was killed on the eve of the very reform he seemed about to grant. Within this corpus the party stands as the answer of despair to the reaction that followed 1866, the direct cause of the reaffirmation of autocracy-russia under alexander-iii, and the archetype of the revolutionary terrorism that runs through Russian history to 1917.
The revolt against the peasant-based movement
The party grew out of the failure of the earlier populism that Kornilov’s lectures chronicle. Through the 1870s the radical intelligentsia — the Chaikovtsy, the followers of Bakunin and Lavrov, the society Zemlya i Volya (“Land and Freedom”) — had put its faith in the peasantry, going “to the people” to preach socialism and raise the village against the state. The movement ended in disillusion: the peasants did not rise, the propaganda of the intellectuals met indifference or hostility, and the police, as Pahlen’s memorandum recorded, rounded up the agitators in droves. The conviction spread among the revolutionaries that the state, not the people, was the true enemy, and that a small, disciplined, conspiratorial organization could by violence shake the autocracy that the masses could not or would not move. Out of this reasoning, by the end of the 1870s, Zemlya i Volya split, and from its terrorist wing arose the party that set the assassination of the tsar as its first and governing task.
The campaign against Alexander II
The party’s central committee — the Ispolnitelny komitet (“Executive Committee”) — organized a series of attempts on the life of Alexander II. The record is one of audacity and near-misses. There were shots and plots on the emperor’s routes; there was the celebrated attempt of the young nobleman who fired in the Palace Square; and there was the spectacular explosion in the Winter Palace itself, when a bomb planted by a carpenter named in the palace stores blew up a dining-room that the emperor, by a change of plan, had not entered. The campaign threw the highest circles into confusion and vacillation. The emperor, warned repeatedly by his ministers, was kept from his customary Sunday outings; the government answered with the establishment of the Supreme Administrative Commission under Count Loris-Melikov, who combined the repression of the terrorists with an approach to the liberals — the beginnings of the constitutional movement that pointed toward a share of representative government. The revolutionaries watched this, and their design matured: they had determined not merely to strike, but to strike at the very moment that would make the blow decisive.
1 March 1881
The plot that closed the reign was prepared with the greatest care. The Executive Committee stationed its agents along the route the emperor would take through the capital to the Winter Palace: the conspirators Zheliabov and Perovskaya directed the bomb-throwers, and mines were laid under the streets against a possible escape. On 1 March 1881 the emperor, who had been persuaded to drive out again after a long confinement, was returning from the Mikhailovsky Palace when the first bomb was thrown, wounding the escort and stopping the carriage. As the emperor lingered over the wounded — the fatal hesitation — a second assassin hurled the grenade that struck him down. He was carried to the palace to die that same day. The party had achieved its aim, and had achieved it with terrible irony: at the very hour of his death, Alexander II was on the point of accepting Loris-Melikov’s project for a representative commission — the constitution that the terrorists, by killing the reformer, did more than anything else to destroy. The assassination of the Tsar-Liberator closed an era and opened the era of reaction.
The myth of regicide and its cost
The act that was meant to free Russia bound it faster. The death of Alexander II handed the throne to alexander-iii, resolved against the liberalism of his father, and to his tutor konstantin-pobedonostsev, who had already prepared the counter-reform. In the days after the catastrophe the revolutionaries found that the people did not rise to welcome the regicide; the peasantry, as Witte records in his account of the reaction, was horrified rather than liberated, and the “Holy Brotherhood,” a league of loyalists formed to oppose the revolutionary conspiracy, gathered the support of the propertied classes. The party itself was destroyed by the police in the years that followed, its leaders hanged or imprisoned. But the myth of regicide outlived the organization: the image of a handful of devoted revolutionaries striking down the tyrant at the centre of his power passed into the legend of the Russian revolutionary movement, and the tactical question the party had raised — whether a bold blow could shatter the autocracy — haunted the revolutionaries of the next generation. The revolution-1905 and finally the february-revolution-1917 completed, by mass movement, the destruction that Narodnaya Volya had hoped to achieve by the assassin’s bomb.
Current state: the archetype of revolutionary terror
In the frame of this corpus Narodnaya Volya appears as the hinge between the populism of the 1870s and the revolutionary politics of the new century. It is the subject of the assassination-alexander-ii-1881 and the moving cause of the reactionary reign that followed; its terrorist method was the seed of the strike of violence that runs through the later revolutionary movement; and its tragic logic — that the autocracy would yield only to a blow at its head — stands in sharp contrast to the social-democratic and mass movements that the industrialization of the 1890s called forth. Related to it stand the assassination-alexander-ii-1881 it accomplished, the autocracy-russia and zemstvo-great-reforms it shaped and undid, and the revolution-1905 and october-revolution-1917 that inherited, by different means, its aim of overthrowing the autocratic state.

concepts/nationality-question-habsburg.title: The Nationality Question of the Habsburg Monarchy
concepts/nationality-question-habsburg.content:
The Nationality Question of the Habsburg Monarchy
The nationality question (Nationalitätenfrage) was the fundamental internal problem of the Habsburg monarchy: how a state composed of some ten or twenty nationalities could be governed and held together in an age when, as Sosnosky puts it, the national principle had become “the governing force of the age.” Within the Austrian half (Cisleithania) it pitted Germans against Czechs, Poles, Ruthenians, Slovenes and Italians; it fed the movements of pan-Germanism, pan-Slavism and Italian irredentism; and it strained the monarchy increasingly toward the war of 1914. It is the Austrian counterpart to the Magyarization question of the Hungarian half, and together the two form the internal history of the Dual Monarchy.
The national principle and language
Sosnosky compares the Habsburg monarchy, after Helfert, to “a settled-down migration of peoples.” In Cisleithania lived not fewer than ten nations — Germans (about 35.8 per cent), Czechs, Poles, Ruthenians, Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, Italians and Ladins, and Romanians — to which the whole monarchy added several more. Given this national motley, frictions and even collisions between the peoples were “not strange, indeed almost inevitable”; but the permanent national quarrel that had raged through the monarchy for more than half a century was neither founded nor justified, for several nations could live together in peace, as Switzerland and the United States proved. What was needed, Sosnosky writes, was “only the honest will; but that is wanting, at least in those who have the power to exercise it.” The identification of nation with language — Nationalität und Sprache — was the deepest cause: each nation made a monstrous cult of its own nationality and demanded of the others recognition of a precedence it had usurped, while the press and parliament, far from extinguishing the consuming fire, fanned it as their chief political task.
The national currents
The national principle broke into distinct currents. Pan-Germanism (Alldeutschtum), in the broad sense of the whole German-national movement in Austria, was the attempt of the German element, which had once held constitutional power, to defend its leading place against the other nationalities. Pan-Slavism (Panslawismus) found its principal exponents in turn among the Czechs, the South Slavs, the Poles and the Ruthenians; within the Austrian state it appeared above all as the Czech national movement, which demanded the recognition of the Czech language and resisted what it saw as German overlordship, and it shaded by the end of the period into a neo-Slavism. The Italian irredenta (Irredenta) in the littoral and Tyrol looked across the frontier to the kingdom of Italy, which claimed the unredeemed lands. Sosnosky sets out the symptoms and causes of the national malady: the symptoms were the ceaseless parliamentary obstruction and street violence — the Czechs’ obstruction of the Reichsrat, the riots and clashes over language; the causes lay in the very structure of a state whose peoples each believed itself the first, in which no single nation could claim the hegemony that the Germans had once exercised and had lost “through their own fault.”
The system and its failure
The Austrian half was governed within the frame of the Reichsrat and the December constitution of 1867. Redlich’s account of the pre-war system shows how far the nationality conflict had already corroded it: the ministry in Vienna long exercised the legislative power in practice through the emergency-notification provision (Article 14) by imperial decree, and the Reichsrat had been sent home in the spring of 1914 on the renewal of obstructionist tactics among the Slav parties. The universal suffrage of 1907, expected to heal the national discord, had disappointed; the government sat as “officials’ ministries” before a house elected under it, and Redlich describes “the unceasing accession of national radicalism among the Czechs, South Slavs and Ruthenians,” the growth of an anti-parliamentary mood at court and among the generals, and the reflux of all this upon the separatist and dissolving currents among the South Slavs, Poles and Ruthenians. The nationality question, in short, was not solved but deepened by the parliamentary system itself.
The possible solutions
The nationality question was at the root of the alternative futures that Sosnosky surveyed on the eve of 1914. The most radical was the “Greater Austria” (Groß-Österreich) of Aurel Popovici, who proposed to dissolve the monarchy on the basis of its ethnographic map into some fifteen national states under a common emperor and a central government for the common affairs, with German as the mediating language of the Reich — a fusion of the old centralist unitary state with the modern idea of national autonomy, which Sosnosky calls “a juster solution of the apparently insoluble nationality question than can be imagined,” though he notes the conservative and Magyar resistance it provoked. Trialism, the addition of a South Slav unit, was the more practical proposal; the revision of the dualism and a greater Hungary were the others. All these, Sosnosky argued, were variations of one goal, which for so many-peopled a realm could be no other than “to attain unity through multiplicity,” and so to embody the watchword of its ruler — viribus unitis, “with united forces.” The war dissolved the question not by solution but by dissolution: the national states that replaced the monarchy, as Redlich shows, took up their ready-formed officials and organs from the last legal act of the dynasty.

concepts/north-german-confederation.title: The North German Confederation (1867–1871)
concepts/north-german-confederation.content:
The North German Confederation
The North German Confederation (Norddeutscher Bund, “North German league”) was the federal state created by Prussia after the austro-prussian-war-1866 out of the German lands north of the river Main, and the constitutional form through which the kleindeutsch solution was first given institutional shape. Founded in 1867 (see the event north-german-confederation-1867), it united Prussia and the smaller north and central German states under a Prussian federal presidency, a Federal Council (Bundesrat), and a directly elected parliament (Reichstag). It was designed from the outset as the permanent shell of the future German nation-state: when the southern states joined after the franco-prussian-war-1870-71, the Confederation’s constitution was carried over almost unchanged into the German Empire. The concept therefore describes not merely an interlude but the constitutional grammar of the Reich that followed.
A Prussian construction
The North German Confederation was the work of otto-von-bismarck above all. Lenz’s account of its founding is emphatic that, whatever the forms of consultation, the constitution was a personal creation. When the drafts of the privy counsellors Hepke, Lothar Bucher, and Max Duncker were laid before him, none found his approval; with their “centralizing, federal-state tendency” they reminded him too much of the constitutions of Frankfurt and Erfurt. He insisted instead on keeping to the ground of the memorandum of 1861: to hold to the form of a Staatenbund (a league of states) while giving it practically the nature of a Bundesstaat (a federal state), “with elastic, inconspicuous but far-reaching expressions.” He had no scruple in applying the accustomed nomenclature — even the name Bundestag — to the new federal forms. The draft that became the foundation of both the North German Confederation and the German Empire itself he dictated in a few hours on the afternoon of 13 December 1866; Lothar Bucher worked out the sketch that same night, and on 15 December it was laid in print before the plenipotentiaries of the allied governments.
The federal structure
The Confederation rested on a division of authority between the federal presidency, the Federal Council, and the Reichstag. The presidency, held by the Prussian king in his capacity as head of the union, was endowed with the strongest rights: the full representation of the union abroad, the power over war and peace, the supervision of the execution of federal decisions, the appointment of all federal officials, the executive power against recalcitrant members, and the supreme command in peace and war over a federal army organized on the Prussian model; the fleet was placed directly under Prussian command. Yet the constitution still granted the allied governments that measure of influence which corresponded to their power, and above all it guaranteed them the full security of their existence, both against the foreigner and against the national storms that had once threatened them with destruction.
Against the ministries and houses proposed by the privy counsellors — which would have fostered the particularist elements — Bismarck set “with a truly bold stroke” the Bundesrat directly in the place of a Reich ministry. This council, so named as the central authority, was to fill the individual offices of the federal service with expert commissions drawn from its own midst and to present its phalanx of forty-three seats to the Reichstag. It was the collective organ of the state governments, and Lenz observes that, despite repeated temptations that powerful governments such as Bavaria might lead a Catholic Fronde, the unity of the supreme council of the nation was never shaken, and the governments have ever since stood unanimous against the Reichstag.
The popular element
The other pillar was the directly elected Reichstag, the expression of the national will, in which Bismarck deliberately placed the “counterweight” to dynastic ambition and particularist strivings. It was here that the statesman joined hands, against his own instincts, with the liberal and democratic forces he distrusted. He adopted the universal, equal, and direct suffrage on the model of the Reich constitution of 1849 — in part to outbid the Austrian and reactionary governments before the war, in part because he believed the lower classes more conservative and monarchical than the middle ones, and that the propertied employers would keep their social power over their workers even under universal suffrage. He rejected as “the most contemptible, the most senseless of all electoral systems” the Prussian system of indirect election by classes, wishing to drive liberalism from the stronghold it had built in Prussia through the class suffrage. As a counterweight he insisted that no pay (Diäten) ever be given to the deputies.
The liberal leaders, seeing in universal suffrage the strongest and most legitimate weapon against particularism, could not resist it. Miquel’s argument carried the day: universal suffrage might have its doubts, but they must not reject it, for it was the summons to all classes and stations to join the national union and renounce the “dull separatism.” The most acute liberal leader, Heinrich von Sybel — who had returned to parliament and joined the new National Liberal party under Bennigsen’s leadership — warned of the inner dangers of unchaining the masses; but even he did not foresee that universal suffrage would one day subject the army of workers to socialist utopias and raise the clericals to power in the new Reich.
A federal economy
The Confederation’s parliament legislated the framework of a national economy. Unanimously the first Reichstag passed the law of freedom of movement (Freizügigkeit), which permitted every member of the union to reside and settle anywhere in the union and gave everyone the capacity to acquire landed property and to carry on a trade; the removal of restrictions on interest (Zinsbeschränkung) broke one of the strongest clamps on commerce and industry; and laws followed on the post, on passports, on federal debts, and on universal military service. These measures extended and deepened the economic unity already prepared in the Zollverein, whose reform in 1867 was handled through the new Federal Customs Council and its parliamentary counterpart, the Zollparlament, which met twice from 1868 onward.
The frame of the Reich
The North German Confederation was explicitly a provisional form designed to admit the South. The Peace of Prague had given the southern states an international position that neither prescribed nor forbade their joining the northern power, and the question of their entry dominated the years 1867–70. Bismarck himself wished to postpone it, knowing that its coming would bring the international crisis — the great war happily avoided in 1866. When that war came, with France, the Confederation provided the ready-made instrument: after the victory, its constitution, “in its outlines already the constitution of the German Empire,” was transferred almost entire to the new Reich, so that the Empire of 1871 was the North German Confederation enlarged and crowned. The concept thus stands at the hinge between the german-question and its final kleindeutsch answer.

concepts/ordre-moral.title: Ordre moral (1873–1874)
concepts/ordre-moral.content:
Ordre moral (1873–1874)
L’ordre moral (“moral order”) was the policy of the conservative-moralist ministries under President Mac-Mahon after the fall of Thiers — the two first Broglie cabinets of May 1873 to May 1874 — which sought to govern France in the name of God, the family, and order, against the revolutionary and republican spirit. Hanotaux’s second volume is organised around this policy and its failure: the attempt to restore a monarchical and clerical order, defeated by the divisions of the royalists and by the republican movement of the country.
The politics of 24 May and the formula of order
After the fall of Thiers on 24 May 1873, Marshal Mac-Mahon was elected president — 390 votes, with the left abstaining — accepting with a soldier’s word to continue the liberation of the territory and to restore ordre moral. Hanotaux notes the foreign alarm calmed by the Marshal’s name, the reaction of a country weary of revolution and war, and the character of the new president: a soldier of honour, loyal, but no politician. The ministry of 25 May, under the presidency of the duc de Broglie, adopted the formula of “moral order” as its programme: the defence of religion, property, and social order against the democratic and revolutionary currents that had destroyed the Empire.
The religious character of the policy was explicit. Hanotaux’s chapter “L’« ordre moral »” records the resumption of the Assembly session after 24 May, the interpellations, the religious question, the pilgrimages, the cult of the Sacré-Cœur, and the project of the votive church of Montmartre. The ordre moral presented itself as the reconciliation of France with its religious and monarchical traditions after the disasters of the Empire, the war, and the Commune — a moral restoration of the country under the authority of God and the head of state.
The monarchical campaign and its failure
The ordre moral was bound up with the attempt to restore the monarchy. The monarchical parties, encouraged by their victory of 24 May, pursued the fusion of the two branches of the Bourbon house — the reconciliation of the Orléanists and legitimists around the comte de Chambord. Charles Chesnelong was delegated by the commission des Neuf to Chambord at Salzburg, where he received verbal declarations on the constitution and the flag; the campaign seemed on the point of success. But Chambord’s letter of 27 October 1873, refusing to abandon his conditions and his flag, broke the enterprise. The monarchical past, Hanotaux concludes, was liquidated; the Republic’s place was cleared.
After the failure of parliamentary restoration, the Assembly granted Mac-Mahon the Septennat (20 November 1873), and Broglie formed a second ministry, seeking to consolidate around the Marshal a “government of the middle classes.” It failed in turn: the majority of 24 May disaggregated, the mayors’ law and the constitutional projects divided it, and on 16 May 1874 the duc de Broglie fell. The ordre moral had lasted barely a year, destroyed both by the impossibility of restoring a king and by the divisions among its own supporters.
The meaning of the failure
For Hanotaux, the failure of the ordre moral was the failure of the old France — of the privileged classes and the monarchy — to re-establish themselves after the catastrophe. The right had won the election of February 1871, but it could not turn its victory into a durable order; it was defeated less by the republicans than by its own divisions and by the refusal of the country to abandon the Republic that had made peace and begun reconstruction. The ordre moral stood for a conception of order imposed from above, religious and monarchical; its defeat prepared the way for the Constitution of 1875, for the republican conquest of the executive, and for the eventual passage from the clerical-conservative Republic to the laic, anticlerical Republic of the Ferry years. The cry that Gambetta had raised at Grenoble in 1872 — that clericalism was the remaining enemy — pointed toward the struggle that would define the Republic’s later decades.

concepts/republicanism-france.title: Republicanism in France
concepts/republicanism-france.content:
Republicanism in France
French republicanism was the ideology of the Republic — the doctrine that sovereignty resides in the people and that no man, no family, and no dynasty may stand above the law. In the decades after 1870 it passed from a persecuted opposition faith to the governing ideology of the state, and its internal tensions — between moderate and radical strands, between the mystique of the founders and the politique of their successors, between the promise of liberty and the demands of the laic school — defined the character of the Third Republic.
The radical and moderate strands
Republicanism was not a single doctrine but a family of doctrines held together by a common hatred of monarchy and of personal power. Hanotaux’s constitutional theory distinguishes the elements that survived into the Constitution of 1875: popular sovereignty, the law of majorities, universal suffrage, the rights of minorities, national unity, and the conciliation of unity and liberty. Against the memory of the Empire and of democratic Caesarism, the republicans set the representative regime and the parliamentary Republic. The moderates — the centre gauche around Thiers and then the “opportunists” — sought a conservative, reassuring Republic of order and liberty; the radicals — heirs of the old revolutionary tradition — demanded the full programme of social and political transformation, universal suffrage used boldly, and the destruction of clerical influence.
The radical tradition surfaced in the elections and agitations of the Second Empire’s last years: Gambetta’s Belleville programme of 1869, with its demands for civil liberties and its hostility to the Empire, and Jules Ferry’s “necessary destructions” were the republican programme in opposition. Under the Republic, Gambetta — the great tribune of the movement — embodied the union of the two strands: the orator who spoke for the “new social strata” (nouvelles couches) at Grenoble in 1872 and who led the campaign against the Seize Mai, yet who could be charged, as a statesman, with moderating the radical impulse into the practical politics of consolidation.
Gambetta and the Republic of the republicans
Gambetta was the central figure of republican consolidation. From his prodigious plea in the Baudin trial of 1868, through his provincial campaigns, his leadership of the union of the 363 against the Seize Mai, and his cry that Mac-Mahon must “submit or resign,” he was the incarnation of republican energy. Hanotaux treats the twelve-year heroic age of the Republic’s foundation as in large part Gambetta’s work, and its close with his death in 1882 as a brutal conclusion after which “figures and the aspect of things change.” Gambetta’s republicanism was the republicanism of the nation and of the people — a faith in universal suffrage and in the regenerative power of the Republic to heal the wounds of defeat and civil war.
The anticlerical and school-building programme
The distinctive achievement of republican consolidation — the programme that most sharply defined the regime — was the laic reform of education and the reduction of clerical influence. Jules Ferry’s school laws made primary education free, obligatory, and secular; the expulsion of the congregations followed the decrees of 29–30 March 1880; the phrase that Gambetta had coined at Grenoble — “clericalism, that is the enemy” — became the watchword of the republican majority. Sabatier treats the laic school as “the new incarnation of a secular religious effort,” a movement by which “our country has sought to conquer itself” — not a mere anticlerical negation but a constructive attempt to give the citizen a moral formation. The anticlerical and school-building programme thus belonged to the republicans’ positive vision of a regenerated, unified nation, even as it divided France between clerical and laic camps for a generation.
Mystique and politique
Beyond its institutions and its programme, republicanism carried a moral and spiritual content that Péguy articulated with unmatched force in Notre jeunesse. For Péguy, the republican faith of his fathers was a mystique — “when one died for the Republic” — a lived instinct borne by ordinary republican families, of which his own generation was the last to possess the tradition. The Dreyfus affair was “the last of the operations of the republican mystique.” But by 1910 the Republic, he wrote, had become a thèse: the intermediate generation had lost the instinct of republican mystique, the Republic had passed from organic to logical, and the mystique républicaine had degenerated into politique républicaine — “everything begins in mystique and ends in politique.” Péguy’s lament testifies both to the depth of the republican faith and to the Republic’s later loss of that faith, as the party politicians succeeded the founders. Republicanism was thus never merely a doctrine of state; it was a form of secular faith, and its decline into political calculation was itself a central theme of the generation before the war.

concepts/risorgimento.title: The Risorgimento
concepts/risorgimento.content:
The Risorgimento
The Risorgimento — “the resurrection” — is the Italian name for the movement of national revival and unification that, across the first three-quarters of the nineteenth century, transformed a peninsula of separate and foreign-ruled states into the Kingdom of Italy. As the corpus’s sources treat it, the Risorgimento was both an event and a narrative: a lived history of revolutions, wars and annexations running from the failed uprisings of 1821 and 1831 and Mazzini’s Giovine Italia, through the revolutions of 1848–49, the war of 1859, the Expedition of the Thousand and the annexation of the South in 1860, the war of 1866 that brought the Veneto, and the capture-of-rome-1870 that completed unification — and a national idea, a story the Italians told themselves of how a people that had been divided and ruled by foreigners came to be one nation. Tivaroni’s three volumes, L’Italia degli Italiani, are explicitly a history of the movement as the culmination of the national idea; Garibaldi’s Memorie tell the same story from within, as the autobiography of its most famous soldier; and Oriani’s La lotta politica in Italia reads the whole of Italian history as the long preparation for the nation that the Risorgimento at last achieved.
The idea and its makers
The Risorgimento began as an idea before it was a fact. In the restored absolutisms of the years after 1815, and against the legacy of the Napoleonic age, the national idea took form in secret societies and in the thought of its prophets. Tivaroni’s retrospective on “lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale” (the development of the national thought) traces the strands: the height of Mazzini’s prestige and his doctrine of republican regeneration, the germs of monarchical unity in Vincenzo Gioberti’s vision of an Italian federation under the Pope, the murattismo that dreamed of a liberal Napoleonic kingdom in Naples, and the Società Nazionale Italiana that eventually brought the monarchists and the revolutionaries together on the ground of unity under the House of Savoy. From the failed revolutions of 1821 and 1831 and the youth of Giovine Italia through the climacteric of 1848–49 — the Sicilian rising, the Milanese Five Days, the Roman Republic that giuseppe-garibaldi defended — the movement built its martyrology and its language. The Risorgimento, as Tivaroni presents it, was carried by the partito d’azione, the party of action, and by the moderates who finally supplied it a state.
The wars and the conquests
The Risorgimento was accomplished by a combination of war, revolution and diplomacy. The war of 1859, prepared by camillo-cavour at Plombières and fought beside Napoleon III, drove Austria out of Lombardy; the revolutions of 1859–60 in Florence, Modena, Parma and Bologna, and the annexation of central Italy, extended the kingdom to the centre; and the expedition-of-the-thousand-1860 of Garibaldi, carrying the revolution into Sicily and Naples, delivered the South to the national cause. Oriani divides the work between the “royal conquest” of the north and centre and the “revolutionary conquest” of the South, and Tivaroni’s decisive year 1860 binds them together: the plebiscites of October 1860 and the fall of Gaeta made the Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed in 1861 under victor-emmanuel-ii. The two wars that followed completed the map — the italian-war-1866 that added the Veneto (though by the diplomatic cadeau rather than by victory, with the defeats of battle-of-custoza-1866 and battle-of-lissa-1866) and the capture-of-rome-1870 of 20 September 1870, which breached Porta Pia, ended the temporal power of the Pope, and gave the kingdom its capital, followed by the law-of-guarantees-1871.
The unfinished nation
Even completed, the Risorgimento left the nation unfinished, and its aftermath belongs to this corpus’s years. The annexation of the South brought the problem of the southern-question-italy — the brigandage reaction of the 1860s, the tributary burden, and the economic backwardness that Fortunato would spend his life exposing. The frontier fixed in 1866 left the Italians of the Trentino, Trieste and Istria under Austria, and from that incompleteness grew irredentism, the claim of the Italia irredenta that would help carry Italy into the First World War in 1915 and be consummated in the victory of battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918. And the politics of the new kingdom, with its trasformismo and its colonial misadventures, tested whether the national idea could survive the nation’s existence. The Risorgimento thus frames the whole Italian story of this corpus: the movement that made the state supplies the lens through which every later Italian figure — the soldier Garibaldi, the statesmen Cavour and Crispi and Depretis, the meridionalist Fortunato, the generals of the world war — understood and justified his action.
The interpretations
The sources of this corpus offer two great readings of the Risorgimento. Tivaroni, writing at the close of the century as the historian of the national movement, treats unification as the happy culmination of the Italian people’s history, judging the actors by how far they advanced the national goals of Venice, Rome and the completion of the state. Oriani, the philosopher of the nation, reads the whole of Italian history backward to the Risorgimento as its consummation, and is more critical: the new monarchy, in his account, was historically insufficient, the parties were corrupted, and the national achievement was shadowed by the mediocrity of the men who followed Cavour. Garibaldi’s Memorie stand between them, the testimony of the soldier who made the revolution and then lived to see the state he had served become the prison of his last aspirations. Between the celebrant and the critic, the Risorgimento emerges as the central event and the central idea of the Italian century — the act by which a people, in Tivaroni’s closing image, made itself a nation.

concepts/roman-question.title: Roman Question (1866–1870)
concepts/roman-question.content:
Roman Question
The Roman question (questione romana) is the conflict between the Italian Kingdom’s claim to Rome as its capital and the Pope’s temporal power over the city — kept open through the 1860s by the French garrison under Napoleon III, and resolved only by the breach of Porta Pia in 1870. In this corpus’s frame (1866–1919) the question moves from the frustrating impasse of Mentana (1867) to its violent solution and its long constitutional aftermath in the Law of Guarantees.
Two claims on one city
Unitary Italian writers treat Rome as the necessary capital of the nation and the temporal monarchy as a medieval residue to be swept away; papal and Catholic legitimist speech treats temporal power as the guarantee of the Pope’s independence from any national cabinet. Tivaroni’s third volume narrates the whole contest from the Syllabus through the ministries of Rattazzi, Menabrea and Lanza-Sella, the conspiracy in Rome, and Mentana — the knot that bound Italy’s claim to the presence of the French regiment.
The French guarantee and its withdrawal
The guarantee of the Pope’s temporal power rested on the French troops in Rome. After Mentana (3 November 1867) the position seemed secure — until the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 forced Napoleon III to withdraw the garrison. Tivaroni and Oriani both present the war’s collapse as the moment the Roman question passed from the hands of diplomats into the power of Italian arms, as the fall of the French Empire removed the one protector who had held the city for the Pope.
The breach of Porta Pia and the Law of Guarantees
With the French gone, the Italian government’s hesitation yielded to the demand for Rome. The breach of Porta Pia on 20 September 1870 took the city; the Law of Guarantees of 13 May 1871 sought to regulate the Pope’s position — the inviolable person, the Vatican palaces, the freedom of the conclave — while the Pope, refusing to recognise the seizure, confined himself to the Vatican as the self-styled prisoner. The question thus entered its long “Vatican” phase, unresolved for the rest of the century.
Beyond pure diplomacy
The Roman question is simultaneously diplomatic, military and moral. It structures French domestic politics as much as Italian foreign policy, and it binds the church thread of the corpus (the Pope’s refusal of the Non expedit, the Roman Syllabus) to the secularising story of the new Kingdom.

concepts/second-empire-france.title: Second Empire, France (1852–1870)
concepts/second-empire-france.content:
Second Empire, France (1852–1870)
The Second Empire was the regime founded by Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte after the coup of 2 December 1851 and proclaimed empire in 1852, overthrown by the catastrophe of the war with Prussia in September 1870. For the Republic that followed it, the Empire was the negative term against which the whole of the new regime defined itself: a dictatorship of personal power, of plebiscitary appeals to the people, and — in its last years — of a liberal transformation that came too late to save it. Taxile Delord’s opposition Histoire du second empire and Émile Ollivier’s L’Empire libéral memoir record the regime from inside its arc of authoritarian strength and liberal decay.
The authoritarian Empire and its contradictions
The Empire inherited the Napoleonic name and, with it, the promise of the first Napoleon’s glory. Hanotaux, writing of the Emperor on the eve of the Prussian war, calls Napoleon III “a reduced copy of the first Bonaparte” — the dynastic heir who ruled by a mixture of plebiscitary democracy and personal authority, appealing over the heads of assemblies directly to universal suffrage. The authoritarian system rested on the Corps législatif as a docile instrument, on a controlled press, and on the figure of Eugène Rouher, whom Ollivier’s republican enemies and even Ollivier himself dubbed the vice-empereur. The Senate was a conservative counterweight; the ministries answered to the sovereign rather than to the Chamber.
Delord’s account of the years 1867–1869 shows the system beginning to crack. The universal Exhibition of 1867 brought the sovereigns of Europe to Paris in a display of imperial splendour, yet the same season brought the failure in Mexico, the execution of the Archduke Maximilian at Querétaro, and the first shots of a resurgent opposition. The regime’s foreign-policy reverses — the Luxembourg neutralisation after Sadowa, the retreat from Rome’s guarantee challenged at Mentana — combined with financial and food crises to produce what Delord calls the first symptoms of the Empire’s decadence. A new “party of action” rose among republican youth, the revolutionary Commune of the Paris workers was styled in the agitation, and Henri Rochefort’s pamphlet La Lanterne sold on the boulevards at ten centimes, prosecuted, condemned, and succeeded by an ever-wider hostile press.
The authoritarian Empire’s liberal turn
The years 1867–1869 were marked by a measured liberalisation that the Emperor hoped would reconcile the educated middle classes without surrendering real power. The letter of 19 January 1867 replaced the unvarying address with a regulated right of interpellation and announced the press and public-meetings laws, which came fully into force in 1868. The new press regime abolished discretionary control and let loose the torrent of hostile journalism; the public-meetings law opened the first political meetings of the Second Empire. In the session of 1868–1869 Thiers demonstrated, as Ollivier records, “the need to restore the constitutional regime,” while Rouher protested and resisted every advance.
It was precisely the half-conceded liberties that exposed the regime’s dilemma. Delord presents the election of 1869 as a condemnation of the authoritarian Empire represented by Rouher and a victory for the programme of the liberal Empire associated with Ollivier; the complementary elections of late 1869 and the extraordinary session at the Louvre saw the dissolution of the government majority and the collapse of the authoritarian system. The Empire could no longer stand still: it had to recede into pure authoritarianism or advance into parliamentary government. Out of that impasse came the negotiations between the Emperor and Ollivier through Clément Duvernois, the disguised journey to Compiègne, and the ministry of 2 January 1870 that inaugurated the Liberal Empire.
The Republic against the Empire
When the Empire fell after Sedan and the revolution of 4 September 1870, the Republic that rose from the ruins defined its legitimacy in opposition to the Bonapartist practice of personal power. The Third Republic’s founders insisted on a regime of assemblies, of ministerial responsibility, and of a presidency reduced to a figurehead — precisely the inverse of the imperial régime personnel. Hanotaux’s history of the Republic is framed throughout as the liquidation of the Bonapartist past and the erection, in its place, of the parliamentary Republic. The Republic’s consolidation through Thiers, through the failure of the monarchical restoration, and through the Constitution of 1875 was, in this reading, the definitive answer to the Second Empire’s promise of order and glory through one man.

concepts/socialism-in-france.title: Socialism in France (1870s–1900s)
concepts/socialism-in-france.content:
Socialism in France
Socialism in France in the last decades of the century passed through the divisions the corpus documents from within: parliamentary and ministerial socialism on one side, the autonomous workers’ movement (mouvement ouvrier) of revolutionary syndicalism on the other. The question posed by Lagardelle’s essays of 1898–1908 is whether socialism should seek power through democracy and the Republic or constitute itself as an independent class force against the state.
The parliamentary question
Lagardelle’s first part examines socialism’s relation to democracy: the formation of the socialist party and its entry into republican politics, the case of Millerand and the Waldeck-Rousseau ministry, the Dreyfus affair’s pull on the socialists, and the meaning of ministerialism. The split is between those who would carry the Republic forward from within the parliamentary game and those who held that the working class must act on its own, in its own organs, without compromising with a bourgeois state.
Syndicalism and the workers’ movement
The second part advances the syndicalist answer: the labour syndicate, not the party, as the autonomous and creative force of the future; the general strike and direct action as the means; the political and agricultural policy of the syndicalist movement. This is the doctrine of the CGT and of the theorists who made France the homeland of revolutionary syndicalism before 1914.
The mystical counter-current
Péguy, in the same years, supplied the moral and religious temper of the same quarrel: his Notre jeunesse defended the “mystique républicaine” and the Dreyfusard faith against its degeneration into “politique,” and reserved its deepest contempt for the “monde moderne” that prospers against every culture. Together Lagardelle and Péguy map the spiritual and organisational crisis of the French Left in the years before 1914 — the Republic that could not hold its own revolutionaries.

concepts/southern-question-italy.title: The Southern Question (questione meridionale)
concepts/southern-question-italy.content:
The Southern Question (questione meridionale)
The Southern Question — in Italian the questione meridionale — is the term under which the post-unification Italian state and its intellectuals confronted the economic and social backwardness of the Mezzogiorno (the “South”) as opposed to the centre and north of the peninsula. Born in the decades after 1860, when the Kingdom of Italy annexed the Two Sicilies and the Papal states and found itself governing regions of enormous diversity, the question was the running indictment of unification as a merely political act: the South had entered the national state by plebiscite and annexation, but its peasant agriculture, its communal tenures, its malaria, its emigration, and its crushing fiscal burden had not been integrated into a common prosperity. No single figure articulated the question more fully than giustino-fortunato, the deputy for Melfi whose collected speeches, Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano (1880–1910), gave the problem its classic statement in parliament; and the brigandage of the 1860s, described by alfredo-oriani, supplied the violent first chapter of the Southern story.
The tributary system and the burden of the South
At the centre of Fortunato’s analysis stood the finances of the state. The unified kingdom adopted the Piedmontese fiscal and administrative system, and applied it to the South with a uniformity that the South’s poverty could not bear. Fortunato devoted a famous discourse of 21 January 1882 to the leggi d’eccezione nel sistema tributario, the “exception laws in the tributary system” by which the taxation of the Southern provinces exceeded both their capacity and the services they received; and his appendix to the discourse Il dovere politico (9 October 1898) documented the tributary burden of the Mezzogiorno before and after unification, arguing that the South paid to the state more than it drew from it. The central government, with its seat in the north, spent on the army, the navy, and the administration, while the poor provinces of the South furnished the money without receiving the roads, the schools, the irrigation, or the credit that might have raised them.
Brigandage and the demanial lands
The first and most violent form of the Southern problem was brigandage. Oriani, describing the reaction that followed the annexation of the South, records how the “bandit habit” of the camorra and the mafia favoured the organisation of the brigands, how the fallen Bourbon clergy and aristocracy encouraged them, and how the Papal state was a refuge and arsenal for the bands — a revolt that combined regional hatred of the new conquerors, feudal reaction, and the misery of the countryside. Fortunato, writing of the demanial lands, exposed the deeper cause: the great common and feudal domains of the South, the demanio “feudal or universal,” had never been divided among the peasantry, and the new legislation kept them locked or sold them in ways that served the speculators rather than the peasants. The reduction of the local magistracies, the neglect of credit, and the ruin of the grain banks (monti frumentari) completed the picture of a countryside denied the instruments of improvement.
Malaria and emigration
Two further themes round out the question as Fortunato posed it in the closing years of his collection. Malaria, the endemic fever of the lowlands and coasts of the South, wasted the population and the land; Fortunato’s last published discourse, Malaria e chinino (30 June 1910), argued for the campaign of quinine and drainage as among the few remedies the state could bring to the Mezzogiorno. And emigration, the great current of the last decades of the century, was treated in L’emigrazione meridionale (30 June 1909) as an economic necessity rather than a moral evil — a natural exodus of the poor to the Americas and beyond, which relieved but did not solve the South’s distress, and which Fortunato refused to blame or forbid. The question, in his telling, was structural: it would yield only to the reform of the state’s finances, credit, and public works in the South, and not to colonial adventure or military glory abroad.
The Southern Question in the state’s politics
The Southern Question was also a political question. It framed the relationship of the South to the parliamentary regime, the trasformismo that turned southern deputies into courtiers of the premier, and the colonial policy that diverted the nation’s strength to Africa while the South starved — the policy Fortunato opposed after the disaster of battle-of-adua-1896, urging “absolute recollection” in Eritrea and reform at home. For Fortunato and the meridionalist school, the South was not a separate land to be annexed or punished but the measure of the state’s failure: a unified Italy that left its poorest provinces tributary, malarial and depopulated had not truly become one nation. The question, first posed in these parliamentary decades, would outlast the period and become one of the permanent themes of Italian public life.
