concepts/stab-in-the-back-legend.title: The Stab-in-the-Back Legend
concepts/stab-in-the-back-legend.content:
The Stab-in-the-Back Legend
The claim, proclaimed aloud by Germany on the morrow of its defeat in 1918, that its army had suffered no military defeat in the field, that its soldiers had not been vanquished by enemies from without but had been stabbed in the back by the triumphant revolution from within. The German name for it is the Dolchstoßlegende, the dagger-stab legend. Recouly records and rebuts it in his closing chapter on war and peace, as the state of mind of Germany at the moment of the armistice and as the seed of the sombre prospect of a new war. It is the doctrine by which a defeated nation denied its defeat, transferred the responsibility for the catastrophe to its own internal enemies, and prepared the ground for the revisionist politics of the years that followed.
The inscription on the tomb
The legend found its lapidary expression in the inscription that the celebrated scholar Wilamowitz-Moellendorff composed for the tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Berlin: INVICTIS VICTI VICTURI — “to the unconquered soldiers, today’s conquered who will be tomorrow’s conquerors.” This phrase illustrated in a striking manner the state of mind of Germany immediately after its defeat. Germany proclaimed loudly, to the face of the world, that it had suffered, militarily speaking, no defeat at all. It affirmed — contrary to all truth, in Recouly’s judgement — that its soldiers had not been conquered on the fields of battle by the enemies from without, but solely by the enemies from within: that they had been stabbed in the back by the triumphant revolution. Without that revolution they would have been victorious; their momentary failure was a simple accident, an anomaly that imminent and certain victories would cause to be forgotten.
The assertion of the undefeated army
The whole legend rests on the assertion that the German army, in the field, was never beaten. Its soldiers, the claim ran, were undefeated — invicti — for the defeat that brought Germany down was the work not of foreign arms but of the internal revolution that rose in the rear. The revolution, that is, had struck the army a blow from behind, a coup de poignard dans le dos, a dagger-thrust in the back, at the very moment when its front was still holding. The armistice-11-november-1918 came not because the army had been broken by the enemy but because the homeland had collapsed behind it. This was the sense in which the soldiers of the trenches were regarded as unconquered, their defeat in November 1918 as an accident that the victories of tomorrow would efface. The formula INVICTIS VICTI VICTURI united the three tenses of the legend: the soldiers unconquered in the past, the Germans conquered today, the victors of tomorrow.
The legend thus took on the colour of a betrayal — of the soldiers by the civilians, of the front by the home front, of the faithful by the revolutionary. It pointed to no foreign enemy as the author of the German collapse but to an enemy of another kind, hidden within: the revolution that had risen in the rear and cut the army down while it fought. In this it was the most complete expression of the refusal of the German people, or of those who spoke in its name, to accept that its armies had been vanquished in a fair and open contest of arms.
The betrayal and the German pride
Recouly sets the legend against the larger moral of the war, which his whole history had been concerned to draw. Germany, for all its marvellous military preparation, was finally defeated because, too sure of its warlike superiority and committing its habitual sin of pride, it entered the conflict in bad diplomatic conditions and ranged too many enemies against itself. This was the background against which the legend had to be judged: a nation that had overreached itself, and that, rather than confess its miscalculation and its defeat, chose to throw the blame upon an internal betrayal. The claim of the undefeated army was in this light an act of the same pride that had entered the war believing victory certain — a pride that survived the catastrophe and refused to learn from it.
The legend was further sustained by the circumstances of the war’s close. The armies of the Central Powers had stood, for long years, upon the soil of the enemy, in occupation of vast territories; the fighting in the west, after the failure of Ludendorff’s offensives of the spring of 1918 and the counter-offensives that followed, had turned against them, but the retreat was a German retreat, and the illusion could be maintained that the soldiers had not been broken but merely abandoned. The revolution that rose at home in the closing weeks of the war gave the legend its ready-made author. It was easier, and more flattering, to say that the army had been stabbed in the back than to acknowledge that it had been beaten in the field.
The decision was won in the field
Recouly’s rebuttal rests on the true course of the war, which he had narrated from beginning to end. The decision of the war was won and lost upon the battlefield, by the merit or failure of the chiefs and the troops, and not delivered by any dagger from behind. At the battle-of-the-marne-1914 the skill and sang-froid of the French generalissimo, and the errors that excess of confidence made the German generalissimo commit, turned the situation, dismantled the German machine, and transformed a war that was to have been short into one of long duration. In 1918 the failure of Ludendorff’s offensives of July, followed three days later by a still graver failure, marked the beginning of the descent that became ever more rapid and soon vertiginous; and it was Foch’s counter-offensives, the hundred-days-offensive-1918, that broke the German army.
Nor was the German collapse a sudden accident of the last weeks. The war had been lost step by step, on the field, from the very first battles. The grave blunder of the German military chiefs — ignorant of politics — in deciding on unrestricted submarine warfare had provoked American intervention and added one more enemy; and with the defection of Russia the German advantage had been won and lost again as the power of the West was concentrated against it. The army that the legend called undefeated had been defeated, over four years, by the weight of a war it had itself called down. The revolution at home was in truth the consequence, not the cause, of that defeat — the fruit of the exhaustion, the hunger and the disillusion that years of war had sown, not the sudden blow that felled a still-victorious army.
The consequences of the legend
For Recouly the legend mattered above all for what it portended. It revealed Germany’s true face on the morrow of its defeat, and it raised the question that tormented him: how those who had vanquished it with such difficulty, France first, could have committed the folly of not taking more solid precautions against it. A Germany that proclaimed its soldiers unconquered, that inscribed on its tomb the promise that today’s conquered would be tomorrow’s conquerors, was a Germany that had not accepted the verdict of the war and was preparing to reverse it. The treaty of peace, badly conceived and still worse executed, had done nothing to remove the danger; on the contrary, by the lightness and imprudence of a policy that rested on appearances and not on realities, it had left the legend to grow unchecked.
The sombre perspective of a new war, only sixteen years after a war that had nearly laid France low, was the direct consequence. The legend was not merely a false account of the past; it was the bridge by which the past defeat was converted into the expectation of future victory, the soil in which the next conflict was to take root. It is thus, in Recouly’s telling, the central doctrine of the German refusal to accept the peace — a doctrine at once military, political and moral, by which a defeated and overreaching nation denied its defeat and armed itself, in spirit, for the day of its return.

concepts/syndicalism.title: Revolutionary Syndicalism
concepts/syndicalism.content:
Revolutionary Syndicalism
Revolutionary syndicalism was the doctrine of the autonomous workers’ movement (mouvement ouvrier) that arose in France in the decades around 1900 and found its most systematic theorist in Hubert Lagardelle. It held that the working class must emancipate itself through its own organisations — the trade unions, or syndicats — by direct action and the general strike, independently of parliamentary democracy and of the bourgeois state. Lagardelle’s Le socialisme ouvrier (1911), a collection of essays written from 1898 to 1908, documents both the formation of the movement and the ideas that defined it.
The movement independent of parliamentary democracy
The starting point of syndicalism was the refusal to identify socialism with democracy. Lagardelle poses the question directly — “Socialism or Democracy?” — and argues that the working class, having won political citizenship, finds itself excluded from economic power: as citizens the proletarians may administer the state’s budget, but as workers in the workshop they remain “a passive multitude” with no part in the direction of enterprises, dominated by a class that makes them pay dear for a tutelage at once useless and arbitrarily prolonged. The irresistible tendency of the proletariat, he writes, is to carry into the economic order the democracy partially realised in the political order — to possess and direct in common the means of production as they possess and direct the political power. But this emancipation was to be the work of the class itself, through its unions, not of the parliamentary parties.
The political experience of the 1890s confirmed the syndicalists’ distrust of parliamentarism. Lagardelle recounts the Dreyfus affair, the amnesty, and the socialists’ entanglement in ministerial politics — the ministry of Waldeck-Rousseau with Millerand as the first socialist minister — and the phenomenon of “ministerialism” by which socialism was absorbed into democratic government. Against this, the syndicalist current insisted on the autonomy of the workers’ movement, its separation from the parties, and its refusal to surrender the class struggle to electoral combinations.
Anti-statism and direct action
The central ideas of syndicalism, as Lagardelle expounds them in “Les idées syndicalistes,” were anti-statism, revolutionary evolution, the syndicate and the class struggle, direct action, and the general strike. The state was the great enemy: “the state is the greatest of all” the adversaries of the workers, watching the syndical organisation with an administrative and police eye, seeking to restrict the autonomy of all groupements and to extend indefinitely its own activity. Against the encroachments of the state and the temptations of “state socialism,” the syndicalists set the autonomous organisation of labour and the direct action of the workers themselves. The working class is “the revolutionary class par excellence,” and its revolution must be effected by revolutionary means — “not by democratic means” — through the class struggle preparing the triumph of the organised proletariat.
The general strike held a central place in the doctrine as the instrument of this revolution. Direct action — the strike, the boycott, the sabotage of the workshop — replaced the ballot as the workers’ means of making their power felt, and the general strike was conceived as the culminating act by which the organised working class would take possession of production. Lagardelle’s syndicalism was a “revisionism of the left,” insisting that the crisis of socialism was due to the divorce of theory and practice and that the syndicate, rather than the party, was the true organ of the working-class movement.
The CGT and the politics of the movement
The doctrine was embodied in the French general confederation of labour, the Confédération générale du travail (CGT), and the syndical congresses — notably Bourges in November 1904 — recorded the formation of the movement’s collective consciousness. Lagardelle’s later essays, written to 1908, address the relation of the socialist party to syndicalism. He argues that the party, carried by the idealism that issues from the syndicalist working masses, must present itself before the non-working masses as “the only party of political cleanliness and of anti-statist action,” making its own the essential claims and fundamental ideas of syndicalism — a programme of reduction of the state and of financial morality. The movement, in this vision, was the seed of a new society: the workers’ organisations themselves, the future organs of a self-governing economy, prefigured within the old order the free association that was to replace it.

concepts/third-republic-france.title: Third Republic, France (1870–1940)
concepts/third-republic-france.content:
Third Republic, France (1870–1940)
The Third Republic was the French regime proclaimed on 4 September 1870 after the fall of the Second Empire and the disaster of Sedan, finally consolidated by the Constitution of 1875, and lasting until the defeat of 1940. Its founding was a twelve-year “heroic age” — in the phrase Hanotaux attributes to Gambetta — spanning the German war, the Commune, the failure of the monarchical restoration, the Constitution of 1875, the Seize Mai crisis, and the establishment of the parliamentary Republic. This corpus documents that founding through the four volumes of Hanotaux’s Histoire de la France contemporaine, and its later meaning through the essays of Péguy and Sabatier.
From the fall of the Empire to the government of Thiers
The Republic was born of defeat and civil war. With the Emperor captured at Sedan, the revolution of 4 September 1870 proclaimed the Republic in Paris, but the war continued until the armistice and the elections of 8 February 1871, dominated by the great question of war or peace. The National Assembly, meeting at Bordeaux, turned to Adolphe Thiers — elected in twenty-six departments with nearly two million votes as, in Hanotaux’s phrase, “administrator of the national misfortune” — and named him chief of the executive power. Under Thiers the Republic made the peace, signed the Treaty of Frankfurt, crushed the Commune, and began the work of paying the indemnity and liberating the territory.
Thiers governed under a provisional title, the Rivet constitution of 31 August 1871 making him President of the Republic responsible before the Assembly. He sought a Republic that would be “conservative” and that would reassure the country — at first sparing even the name of Republic — while the monarchical majority in the Assembly, unable to agree on a single pretender, let the provisional regime continue. By his message of 13 November 1872 Thiers pronounced explicitly for the Republic, and by the great speech of 23–24 May 1873 he had “taken his party on the Republic.” On 24 May 1873 a coalition of the right put him in a minority, and he resigned; Marshal Mac-Mahon succeeded him, pledged as a soldier to continue the liberation and to restore ordre moral.
The failure of the monarchy and the Constitution of 1875
The National Assembly, elected with a monarchical majority, failed to restore a king. Hanotaux’s second volume tells the double failure of the monarchical restoration: the fusion of the two branches of the Bourbon house and the comte de Chambord’s letter of 27 October 1873, which insisted on his conditions and broke the campaign. After the Septennat of 20 November 1873 gave Mac-Mahon seven years of power, and after the fall of the duc de Broglie on 16 May 1874, “the monarchical past of France is liquidated. There is a clear place for the Republic.”
The Constitution of 1875 was voted by a majority of one voice on the Wallon amendment of 30 January — an anonymous, improvised work, as Hanotaux stresses, of three constitutional laws (Senate, 24 February; public powers, 25 February; relations of the powers, 16 July) and two organic laws. It established a parliamentary Republic: two chambers with preponderance to the popularly elected one, a presidency, a cabinet, and ministerial responsibility. Hanotaux’s theory of the constitution emphasises the sovereignty of the people, universal suffrage, the rights of minorities, national unity, the conciliation of unity and liberty, and a governing hatred of personal power — the whole erected against the memory of the Empire and of democratic Caesarism.
The Republic of the Republicans
The parliamentary Republic was consolidated through a series of crises and ministries chronicled in Hanotaux’s fourth volume. After the elections of 20 February 1876 gave the Republic a majority, President Mac-Mahon’s attempted coup of the Seize Mai (the letter of 16 May 1877) — the dissolution of the Chamber and the Broglie ministry — was answered by the union of the republican deputies, the famous “363,” and by the republican victory in the elections of 14 October 1877. Gambetta’s cry, that the Marshal must “submit or resign,” set the terms of the struggle. Mac-Mahon’s resignation in January 1879 and the election of Jules Grévy as President completed the republican conquest of the executive; Grévy, Hanotaux judges, conceived the presidency as the ideal of France ought to be, though his election was a fault.
Under Waddington, Freycinet, and above all Jules Ferry, the Republic turned to the work of consolidation and laicisation: the amnesty, the “purification” of the administration, the return of the Chambers to Paris, the first 14 July festival, the Ferry school laws making primary education free, obligatory, and secular, the expulsion of the religious congregations, and the colonial expansion into Tunisia. Gambetta’s “grand ministry” of 1881–82 — the ministry of the man who had been the incarnation of republican energy — failed in a few months, cut short in 1882 by the Chamber’s rejection of constitutional revision, and Gambetta himself died the same year. Hanotaux closes the Republic’s heroic age there, with the parliamentary Republic established and tested.
The Republic as a lived faith and as a regime
Beyond the institutional history, the Third Republic carried a moral and spiritual meaning that Péguy and Sabatier articulate in this corpus. For Péguy, writing in Notre jeunesse (1910), the Republic had once been a mystique — “when one died for the Republic” — borne by ordinary republican families, and the Dreyfus affair was its last surge of heroism. By his own day, he laments, the Republic had ceased to be lived and become a thesis; the intermediate generation had lost the instinct of republican mystique, and the Republic, from organic, had become logical. Sabatier, in L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle (1911), treats the Republic’s laic school as a new incarnation of a secular religious effort — “by the laic school our country has sought to conquer itself” — and reads the Republic’s religious orientation as essentially French, a movement of religious reconstitution rather than of mere anticlerical negation. The Third Republic was thus both a constitutional regime and a faith: the durable political form that answered the century’s demand for liberty, unity, and the reconciliation of the citizen with the state.

concepts/total-war-economy.title: The Total War Economy
concepts/total-war-economy.content:
The Total War Economy
The Kriegswirtschaft, the war economy — the immense system of state direction and organisation of production, consumption and trade into which the belligerent nations of the First World War transformed their economic life. Recouly and the other observers of the war recognised the mass war as a new phenomenon, one that drew into itself the whole material and spiritual strength of the peoples; and the Austrian administrator and scholar josef-redlich gave the concept its sharpest form in his study of the war government. The war economy, he wrote, was the inevitable consequence of the modern popular war, and the scientific description of it was the true centre for the understanding of the modern phenomenon of the mass war. In Austria-Hungary it took the double shape of a state food administration and a network of industrial war organisations, bound together into what contemporaries came to call the state socialism of the war, and it issued, at the close, in the doctrine of the Übergangswirtschaft, the transitional economy, that must carry the state from war to peace.
The war economy as the consequence of the mass war
At the opening of the war the peaceful system of world economy, in the first days of August 1914, was abolished. In its place arose a wholly peculiar condition, first of all Europe and soon of the overseas cultural states. The Central Powers and their two eastern allies were forced from the very beginning into a system of economic autarky, whose most characteristic feature was the hard necessity imposed by the blockade conducted by the Western powers, England at their head. Austria-Hungary, like Germany, was by the blockade and by the specifically economic manner of warfare developed under its pressure in the first war year thrown into a state of complete economic isolation. It was in the face of this isolation that the whole apparatus of the war economy was constructed, as the means by which the state undertook, from month to month more extensively, the care for the feeding of the population and the direction and leadership of the whole agricultural and industrial production for the feeding of the army and the supply of all kinds of war material.
The blockade and the economic autarky
Redlich’s account insists that Austria-Hungary and Germany, blockaded from without, had no choice but to organise their economic life under state direction. The blockade and the economic warfare of the Entente, together with the neutrals morally and politically dominated by them, cut the Central Powers off from the world market and their accustomed sources of supply. Czernin, from the other side of the war, records the same fact from the standpoint of the Central Powers’ own experience: the hunger blockade of Austria was carried on throughout the war, and millions in the territories of the Central Powers perished by the blockade. It was the blockade, in Redlich’s analysis, that formed the specifically central-power character of the war economy — an autarkic, planned economy of scarcity, built on the state’s monopoly over food and raw materials.
The food administration
The care for the feeding of the people was the government’s concern from the very outset of the war, and it became, month by month, the largest of all the agendas of state administration in wartime. Austria’s position was rendered the more difficult by the conduct of Hungary, which sealed its frontier against every export of foodstuffs to Austria, reducing Austria to a state of complete economic isolation by its own ally. The decisive step came in the spring of 1915, when, with the sealing of the Hungarian frontier carried out with full severity, Vienna resolved to establish the unbroken state monopoly over grain and over the whole procedure of the production of flour and bread and their distribution to the population — the first and most eminent type of that state-economic institution which characterised the whole war economy of Austria as well as of Germany.
By some decrees armed with the force of law, together with the declaration of the blockade over all grain and flour products and the taking of stocks, the principle of the rationing of bread and flour was fixed and the institution of the bread card created. At the same time the Kriegsgetreideverkehrsanstalt, the war-grain traffic institute, was called into being as the central organ of all these measures; it had to organise and carry through the now-introduced state monopoly of the grain and flour economy. The whole burden of this new administrative task, growing out of the war economy, was laid on the state administrative authorities in the individual crown-lands and their attached provincial branch institutions of the central institute on the one side, and on the local communes, as the organs legally called to the immediate administration, on the other. The whole edifice, which lasted to the end of the war and in Austria years beyond it, was complete in 1915. Alongside it was created the Amt für Volksernährung, the office for popular nutrition, the new central authority for the food system; and new legislation over market traffic in the most indispensable articles of consumption was built up, with the duty of delivery on the part of primary producers and the fixing of maximum prices as its foundations.
The price policy and its consequences
The war economy was, in its very nature, a price-police. The principle of maximum prices was first fixed in the grain economy, then extended in Austria one after another to all agricultural produce — a policy of consumer protection that led inevitably to a continual reduction of production. This policy of fixing maximum prices, in combination with the state rationing of foodstuffs, drew after it very important, partly fateful consequences for the whole development of the war economy. For although the low price of flour and bread in favour of the masses was achieved, these prices sank after a time below the world-market price of the cereals and partly below the self-costs of the native producer of grain. The consequence was that the spur to the increase of grain production in Austria grew ever weaker, and a sinking of the agrarian production of Austria-Hungary set in. In connection with the fixing of maximum prices there were constantly ordered new economies, new aggravations of the stretching regulations — a progressive worsening of flour and bread.
The industrial war economy and the Wirtschaftszentralen
Beyond the food administration, the war economy was extended in the course of the first war year, under the pressure of the blockade, over the whole field of industrial production and trade. The same process of a peculiar nationalisation of production and of the regulation of consumption was accomplished over the whole field of industrial, mining and purely commercial activity within the entire state and imperial territory, in essentially the same form of the so-called Zentrale — the central organisation. The securing of raw materials for the war industry gave rise to an industrial war economy and the step-by-step abolition of free economic intercourse, first in the cotton industry, then in the metal industry; and to the rise of the special war associations (Kriegsverbände) of the several branches of industry and trade, with a progressive militarisation of industry through the administration of the centrales.
The great pattern of this organisation was the Wirtschaftszentrale, of which an official statistic published after the end of the war counted no fewer than ninety-one in all. Twenty of these had to do with agriculture and food; fifteen with the textile industry; eight with paper and printing; thirteen with the chemical, oil and fat industries; six with hides and leather; thirteen with the metal, machinery and technical-requirements industries; four with the industry of stones and earths; three with wood and cork; seven with trade and traffic in general; one, the Devisenzentrale, with the traffic in foreign means of payment; and finally the war organisation of the interests of the organised consumers. By their organisation, thirty-four of these were state compulsory organisations (Kriegsverbände and Wirtschaftsverbände) embracing all the members of a branch; nineteen were centrales and commissions whose members were branch representatives appointed by the government; fourteen were committees whose members were government-appointed; twenty-one were commercial companies registered and state-empowered; and the rest, including the war-grain traffic institute, the fodder-stuff office and the vegetable-and-fruit office of the Amt für Volksernährung, held a special position, combining an administrative division staffed by public officials with a business division for the commercial agendas.
The Kriegsverbände of the several industries represented state compulsory cartels, founded by ordinance, of which all undertakings processing the same raw material were compulsory members. Their tasks were the keeping of a production and consumption statistic, the use, administration and distribution of raw materials and half-fabricates, the making of applications in the fixing of prices, the advising of the central offices in the awarding of contracts, and cooperation in a whole series of economic questions — all purely administrative agendas, with the exclusion of every commercial activity. In this way the Austrian war government gradually drew to itself the direction of the whole economic life of Austria, both production and consumption, until at last the principle of freedom of economic intercourse occurred in the Austrian state territory only as a rare exception, or as a widely spread but forbidden function of the illicit trade, the Schleichhandel.
The state socialism of the war
Redlich’s culminating conception is the state socialism of the war. The middle position of the Austrian government between the army high command and the war ministry on one side and industrial production and the consuming population on the other, and the enormous extension of the whole war-economy apparatus and its capacity, produced a double organism of military and civil war-economy leadership. The war ministry created a new Kriegswirtschaftsamt (war-economy office), divided into an executing group, a scientific committee for the war economy, and a statistical group; this was the military central organ for the whole war economy, the war-economy staff, under whose influence all other departments of the war ministry had to discuss and work out the war-economy arrangements with the allied and neutral states. The whole process of the daily war economy ran as an unprecedentedly powerful giant machine that admitted no delay and no resistance — a machine which, in its never-stopping activity, subjected men and things, personal achievements, raw materials and the end products of industry, all alike, to the commanding behest of the endlessly continuing war, and which at its height might be compared to a mechanism in which the army in the field was the great motive power, transmitting itself through the wheel-work of the war ministry to the civil governments of both states of the Monarchy — in Austria through the two great wheels of the ministry of commerce and the Amt für Volksernährung.
The theory of the war economy, developed in Germany and Austria, rested on an older Austrian tradition: the bureaucratic state socialism that had been built up in the later nineteenth century, in the years of the Taaffe regime, through the productive employment of the impulses coming from Germany, and which the war now extended enormously. What was new in the war was the principle that the state must direct the whole economic life for the ends of the war, and the confidence that the new machinery, once created, could be preserved and turned to the service of the peace.
The Übergangswirtschaft
From the theory of the war economy there was developed, as the war drew on, the doctrine of the necessity of a transitional economy, the Übergangswirtschaft, at the coming of peace. It was recognised that the war had wrought such deep changes in the whole economic life of the peoples that one must reckon, after the close of the war, with a shorter or, in all probability, longer period of transition from the war economy to a newly established system of free economy. In this period of transition the state would have to reserve to itself, if not all the powers of wartime, then most of them, in the interest both of the state and of a healthy renewal of the peaceful economic life and the preservation of the social peace between the different classes of the population.
From this standpoint Richard Riedl in 1916 drew up a great plan of provision for the tasks of the transitional economy, laid down in his Denkschrift über die Aufgaben der Übergangswirtschaft, the memorandum on the tasks of the transitional economy. Its governing idea — adopted by the Austrian government — was that the complete reorganisation of industry brought about by the war economy should, so far as possible, be maintained for the purposes of the restoration of civil economic life after the war, and be made serviceable for the adaptation of industry and trade to the new conditions of returning to peaceful work. Above all, it was argued, the state power must continue to intervene regularly in price formation even after the war: in the war the free price formation of trade had been in wide measure replaced by official price-fixings, and from the foodstuffs outward, maximum prices had been decreed for an ever-growing number of articles, which the defects of this kind of price-determination then drove on to the seizure of stocks, the regulation of production and a uniform administration under the points of view of the public interest, until the whole system converged upon the goal of the transfer of ever-greater parts of economic life into a state of planned, regulated administration.
The high point of this intellectual development in Austria was the creation of the Generalkommissariat für Kriegs- und Übergangswirtschaft, the general commissariat for the war and transitional economy. The ideas developed in it were connected, as Redlich notes, with the movement founded by Friedrich Naumann for the creation of a Mitteleuropa — a central Europe resting on a political and economic unity under Prussian-German leadership, in which the war-economy organisation was to be preserved and extended into a permanent union of the Central Powers. The whole conception was set out in the Denkschrift of the ministry of commerce of 1917, which surveyed the rise and development of the war economy and proposed its continuation.
The failure of the war economy
Yet the war economy in Austria ended in failure. Its collapse was the consequence of the overstraining of the physical, moral and spiritual forces of the population and of the excessive length of the war. The war loans, which the government raised with a wholly new mechanism of subscription drawn up in the widest possible extent, through the collaboration of the government with communes, chambers of commerce, insurance institutions, savings-banks, cooperative associations and above all the banks, and promoted by the whole apparatus of propaganda and agitation — ever more imposing subscription results being brought up to the last war loan of 1918 — drew after them, in connection with the inflation of the currency, the heaviest economic and social damages. The state war economy, which was to have been the instrument of victory, overreached itself: the population could no longer bear the price, and the Kriegswirtschaft of Austria perished with the Monarchy that had created it.

concepts/trasformismo.title: Trasformismo
concepts/trasformismo.content:
Trasformismo
Trasformismo — literally “transformism” — was the practice of Italian parliamentary politics in the decades after unification by which the prime minister absorbed deputies of the opposition into his government majority, dissolving the distinction between government and opposition and reducing the parties to a shifting mass gathered around the premier. Its master was agostino-depretis, who led the Left to power in 1876 and then governed by attracting to his side the moderates and conservatives of the defeated Right; and its name was taken from a famous jibe that Depretis had “transformed” or “converted” his opponents — that the fierce enemies of yesterday became the supporters of today. The practice was at once the lubricant of the young kingdom’s constitution and, in the eyes of its critics, the corruption of its parliamentary life; giustino-fortunato, speaking from the South, made the fight against trasformismo one of the recurring themes of his parliamentary career, and the very title of his discourse of October–November 1882, Il «trasformismo» e le elezioni del 29 ottobre 1882, marks the moment when the word passed into general use.
The dissolution of the parties
Trasformismo grew out of the particular structure of the Italian state. The kingdom had been created by an act of annexation and plebiscite, not by the victory of a party; the Right and the Left that divided the Chamber after 1861 were not classes or ideologies but parliamentary groupings formed around the politics of unification, and neither could claim a social base in the regions it governed. When the Left, under Depretis, took office in 1876, it found that it could not rule as a disciplined party of the sort that governed England or France. Instead Depretis governed by concession and absorption: he offered ministries and favours to deputies of the Right, drew them into the government majority, and so made the Chamber a court gathered around himself rather than a contest of principles. Oriani, judging the post-Cavour generation, wrote that Depretis “conserved of Cavour the parliamentary dexterity and the practice of all the portfolios,” and that legislative action was reduced to “legislative empiricism” — a continuous improvised innovation by which the state was kept running without any consistent doctrine.
The elections of 1882 and the politics of the court
The practice reached its fullest expression in the elections of 29 October 1882. In the discourses of that year — I partiti storici e la XIV Legislatura (2 September 1882) and Il «trasformismo» e le elezioni del 29 ottobre 1882 (22 and 7 November 1882) — Fortunato gave the word its canonical definition and denounced the practice as the ruin of the parliamentary regime. Where a healthy constitution rested on the conflict of parties and programmes, trasformismo rested on the personal ascendancy of the premier and on the corruption of individual deputies; the old “historical parties,” Fortunato argued, had been levelled into a single undistinguished mass, and the Chamber had lost every fixed line of principle. The reform of the electoral law that enlarged the suffrage, he contended, was being used not to strengthen the representation of the nation but to multiply the deputies who could be bought into the government’s majority.
Trasformismo and the Southern question
For Fortunato the politics of trasformismo had a particular bearing on the South. The southern deputies, elected by small and dependent colleges, were the most vulnerable to absorption into the government majority, and the South’s needs — its tributary burden, its credit, its public works — were precisely those most easily sacrificed to a politics of favour and survival. His whole career as deputy for Melfi was a standing protest against the transformation of the Southern representation into a clientele of the premier. The critics of trasformismo saw in it the cause of the kingdom’s political stagnation: the absence of real parties meant the absence of real alternatives, and the state drifted from crisis to crisis — the financial scandals, the African disasters of battle-of-adua-1896, the repression of the Left — without ever putting before the country a genuine choice.
The inheritance of trasformismo
Trasformismo did not end with Depretis. The practice outlived him and became the ordinary method of Italian government, carried to its highest development by Giovanni Giolitti in the early twentieth century, who governed by the same art of absorbing the opposition and holding a shapeless majority together. In this sense trasformismo is the distinctive politics of the post-unification Kingdom, as much a feature of the Italian state as its constitution and its annexations — the way in which a country of incompatible regions and interests, governed without strong parties, held itself together by the personal skill of its premiers. It stands in this corpus as the negative image of the strong state sought by francesco-crispi, the flexible parliamentary method that Crispi’s authoritarian temper rejected, and against which the meridionalist criticism of the southern-question-italy was partly directed.

concepts/trialism.title: Trialism
concepts/trialism.content:
Trialism
Trialism (Trialismus) was the proposal to reorganise the Habsburg monarchy from a dual into a triple state by adding a third unit to the two of Austria-Hungary — in its common form, a South Slav unit embracing the South Slav lands of the monarchy together with Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was the alternative future most discussed on the eve of 1914, associated with the circle of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and treated by Sosnosky in his survey of the possible futures of the monarchy as one of the four paths open to it. Its very name was a new, public-law-precise word for an old aspiration, the “Illyrism” of Ljudevit Gaj.
The proposal
Sosnosky defines trialism as the conversion of the monarchy “from a double state into a triple state,” in which the third in the alliance would be the South Slav lands of the monarchy — those belonging to Austria as much as those belonging to Hungary — together, naturally, with Bosnia-Herzegovina. As an idea it had been at first belittled as a fantasy of over-heated South Slav exaltados; but, Sosnosky observes, “an idea behind which seven million passionate adherents stand cannot be laughed away and cannot be talked away — it forces for itself a hearing and attention.” The shots on Cuvaj, the Croatian ban, had already shown this, and the events of the Balkan wars made a longer “overhearing” of the question impossible: both Vienna and Budapest, whether they wished or not, would very soon be obliged to occupy themselves with this “supposed utopia.”
Its attractions and its dangers
For Austria, Sosnosky argues, the trialist idea had real merits. It rested on the natural ethnographic principle; the number three “fits a leading whole far better than the number two — tres faciunt collegium”; and the South Slavs would form a real counterweight to the preponderance of the Magyars. Above all, he writes, if the wishes of the South Slavs were not regarded, if Croatia remained longer exposed to the Magyar pressure, then among the South Slavs of the monarchy the empire-friendly great-Croatian movement might give way to the empire-hostile great-Serbian one, whose goal lay outside the monarchy — a possibility brought into dangerous proximity by the fresh victor’s nimbus that the Serbs of the kingdom had recently won in the Balkans. The monarchy was thus confronted with the choice: either to transform dualism into trialism, or to bring about the erection of a hostile South Slav state on its borders. Yet trialism also carried grave dangers. The principal difficulty lay in Hungary, which would resist its realisation with all its force, and with right from the Magyar standpoint: the erection of a South Slav state would cost Hungary the loss of Croatia-Slavonia and thereby of its only access to the sea — “an amputation which no land and no people would allow itself to suffer willingly” — and probably also the Serb-inhabited districts of the Bácska and the Torontal, together with Hungary’s claims on Bosnia-Herzegovina and Dalmatia. On the Austrian side the obstacles were scarcely smaller: Dalmatia, with its rich coast, was Austria’s principal share of the Adriatic, and the loss of Triest was quite out of the question. Nor was it certain that a new Illyrian kingdom would remain with Austria rather than gravitate from Vienna toward Belgrade — that the great-Croatian realm would not become a great-Serbian one. Lacking any security against a South Slav–Magyar coalition, the leading authorities of the monarchy, Sosnosky judged, would hardly be inclined to risk so high a stake as the existence of the Habsburg realm on so doubtful a political experiment.
Trialism and Franz Ferdinand
The trialist idea was most closely associated with the heir to the throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand. His known hostility to the Magyar supremacy, his championship of the armed forces, and his personal concern with the South Slav question — Conrad records that the archduke asked his views on the South Slav problem and that Conrad urged a settlement favourable to the Croats — made him the natural patron of a reorganisation that would relieve the South Slavs of the Hungarian crown. Redlich, writing after the catastrophe, judged that it was the death of Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo that “removed, to all appearance forever,” the possibility of breaking the Magyar supremacy from within the monarchy. The war that followed, however, dissolved the question in a different way: the South Slav lands passed not into a trialist third unit of the monarchy but into the new kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and the monarchy itself ceased to exist.

concepts/triple-alliance.title: Triple Alliance (1882)
concepts/triple-alliance.content:
Triple Alliance
The Triple Alliance (Dreibund / Triplice) of 1882 bound Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy in a defensive pact that became the axis of the “assurance-policy” (Rückversicherungspolitik) of the Central Powers against France and Russia. In this corpus it is the framework of Habsburg diplomacy from the Congress of Berlin to 1914, and the source of the rivalry with the Triple Entente that shaped the road to the Great War.
The German and Austrian guarantee
Sosnosky’s survey of Habsburg politics presents the alliance as the German assurance that freed Austria-Hungary’s hand in the Balkans — the sense that behind the Monarchy stood the German Reich, and beyond the German Reich the Italian ally. The annexation crisis of 1908 and the Bosnian question were conducted under this assurance, with Germany’s backing (through Tschirschky and Bülow) the decisive element that carried Vienna through the international storm of 1908–09.
Italy, the weakest partner
Italy’s membership was the anomaly: formally allied to Austria-Hungary, Italy nevertheless nursed irredentist claims against it and drifted in the 1910s toward the Entente. Conrad von Hötzendorf’s memoirs, which treat Italy as the potential enemy of the Monarchy, register the alliance’s fragility — the military chief who planned against his own ally. The Triple Alliance held through the Libyan war and the Balkan wars, but it was already unravelling when Italy chose neutrality in 1914 and entered the war against the Central Powers in 1915.
The diplomatic frame of 1914
For this knowledge base the Triple Alliance is one of the two great alliance systems whose mobilisation locked in the July crisis of 1914: the German-Austrian-Italian (in practice German-Austrian) bloc against the Franco-Russian-Entente bloc. It is the institutional hinge between the Eastern Question, the Balkan policy, and the outbreak of the Great War.

concepts/war-plans-1914.title: The War Plans of August 1914
concepts/war-plans-1914.content:
The War Plans of August 1914
The strategic schemes of concentration and attack with which the great powers of Europe entered the war in the summer of 1914: the German plan of the great wheeling offensive against France through Belgium, the French Plan XVII, the double deployment of Austria-Hungary against Serbia and against Russia, and the reluctant Russian general mobilisation that set the whole machinery in motion. Together they defined the first weeks of the war — and, in the judgement of the soldiers who lived them, its very decision. For the decision of the war lay, as the chief of the Austro-Hungarian general staff conrad-von-hotzendorf put it, in the success or failure of the agreed first action; what followed was only a stubborn struggle to make good the consequences of that first action. The plans were thus not merely technical arrangements for the movement of armies but the instruments by which the war was, almost automatically, set loose upon Europe.
The German problem of the two fronts
Germany, wedged between France and Russia, faced the problem of a war to be conducted on two fronts, east and west, almost from the founding of the Empire. Almost on the morrow of the victories of 1870 the elder Moltke, the victor, had reflected on it, seeing in it the most formidable test that could threaten the existence of the new German Empire. But the military weakness of France — which, despite the miraculous speed of its recovery, took a long time to reconstitute its forces — and the close friendship uniting the two empires, Russian and German, made the risk of a double war appear at first very light, almost non-existent. As soon as France had rebuilt its strength, and above all after the conclusion of the Franco-Russian alliance, the problem had to be taken up again and solved.
Germany was not strong enough to attack on both sides at once, east and west, and so must confine itself to the defensive on one front while seeking a rapid decision on the other. Moltke had first foreseen the defensive against the French and the offensive against the Russians, on whom important successes could be won quickly; his successor Waldersee kept that plan. When Schlieffen took direction of the great general staff the data of the problem had changed. The strength of the French army had grown, and the Russian army appeared difficult, if not impossible, to surprise and put out of action by a sudden attack. For these two reasons Schlieffen resolutely reversed the earlier conceptions: one would defend in the east and attack in the west, violently, irresistibly.
The Schlieffen plan
Schlieffen, the type of the Germanic staff officer with his qualities and defects, steeped in military history acquired by methodical and obstinate labour, joined audacity and daring of design to a certain automatic rigidity. The ideal battle he meant to deliver and win against the principal adversary — the Vernichtungsschlacht, the battle of annihilation — he conceived on the model of Cannae, the victory of Hannibal over the Romans. The great Punic general, though his army was inferior in numbers, enveloped the Roman troops on both wings by the rapidity of his movements and cut them to pieces. This model seduced the German staff; its spirit was literally obsessed by the prestige of that famous day, regarded as the ideal victory, capable of ending the war in a single stroke. In these conceptions there was a certain dose of pedantry and even of puerility: what relation, after all, between an episode of war more than twenty centuries old, fought with very reduced forces, and the battles fought by millions of men that were to mark a modern war?
The offensive thus decided in the west, what form was it to take? The fortresses with which France had covered its eastern frontier appeared an obstacle difficult to overcome quickly, so Schlieffen decided to turn them, to carry his principal attack toward the north, where there were no fortresses, where the great plains of Flanders offered an excellent terrain for the deployment of armies, and where the rivers converging in the direction of Paris marked the natural, historic road of invasions. The German armies would cross Belgium from side to side and, by a vast enveloping movement as wide and overflowing as possible, would bring down all enemy resistance. France must be regarded as a great place of strength, he wrote in 1905, whose outer enceinte, the sector Belfort–Verdun, is almost impenetrable; the front Mézières–Maubeuge–Lille–Dunkirk is certainly fortified, but with breaches, and at present almost unoccupied. It is there that we must attempt the irruption into the fortress.
For the plan to succeed, the German right wing had to be as powerful, as formidable as possible. This was obtained by confining the whole extent of the front to a strict defence, so as to assign the maximum of forces to the right armies charged with the decisive blows. The forces provided for the right wing stood in the ratio of seven to one with those destined for the left wing in Alsace-Lorraine. Schlieffen desired to give the greatest possible extension to his enveloping movement, pushing his manœuvre, if necessary, to outflank Paris to the west, to cross the Seine downstream of its confluence with the Oise, and so to encircle the capital not only from the west but from the south. The plan was characterised by the hardiness, the audacity, of its conceptions — a hardiness perhaps too great, the ratio of one to seven appearing excessive, for it supposed an almost complete inertia on the part of the enemy in Lorraine.
The German method and its fateful assumptions
The conception rested on a psychology drawn from Prussia’s own past. Prussia had acquired its prestige in the Seven Years’ War, in 1866 against Austria, in 1870–71 against France, and in each of these three wars it had to do with adversaries almost entirely passive. From these successive experiences, always turning to its advantage, its staff had drawn certain habits of mind leading it to believe that the enemy would always be as inert. The German method, moreover, was that of the elder Moltke, which consisted in giving the executants general directives derived from an over-all plan and then letting them fend for themselves as best they could — a method that Foch had condemned in his lectures at the École de Guerre, demonstrating its errors and dangers as leading to a disordered, incoherent battle not directed by its chief. The German strategy makes bankruptcy, Foch said, in one of his lapidary phrases; it is saved only by the tactics.
Moltke the nephew, who in 1914 applied the same principles and methods on a far greater scale, let the bridle slip to his lieutenants, who soon came to do as they pleased — above all the most enterprising of them, von Kluck, charged with the essential mission of turning and beating the left wing of the French armies. There was, in the German spirit, something mechanical, automatic, frozen, that accommodated itself ill to the complex and shifting realities of life. The application of these methods would lead to the same errors as in 1870, on a far vaster scale. Only then, whereas in 1870 the French high command had been incapable of profiting by the German errors through its own insufficiency and mediocrity, in 1914, on the contrary, it profited by them and drew victory out of them. The whole moral, the whole explanation, the whole contrast of the two wars lay there.
The French Plan XVII
On the French side the plan bore the name of Joffre, who as generalissimo was its author. Invested in the summer of 1911, during the Agadir crisis, with the two functions of chief of the general staff and vice-president of the superior council of war, he had carried responsibility for the strategic plan entirely when the war broke out. The plan XVII, so called after the series that preceded it — plan XVI, plan XV, and so on, as with the kings of France — did not, as the public supposed, regulate the operations and the offensive of the armies, but almost exclusively their mobilisation first, their concentration afterwards. From 1870 to 1914, as France increased its military power, the plans felt the direct effect of this increase. Purely defensive at first, they took on an ever more offensive character, especially after the conclusion of the Franco-Russian alliance; and from 1900 to 1911, under the impulse of Foch at the École de Guerre, the partisans of a reasoned, reflective offensive won the day over those of the defensive.
All the efforts of the high command since 1870 had borne on the rapidity of mobilisation, permitting the concentration to be made as close as possible to the frontiers, in order to avoid, from the very beginning of hostilities, the invasion of the national soil. Joffre, an engineer by mind and temperament, an excellent organiser who possessed to the full the handling of railways, attached himself to rendering mobilisation more rapid still, to carrying the concentration forward, and above all to better preparing the rapid use of the reserves. These considerations led him to propose, on 18 April 1913, a new plan — plan XVII — which, approved by the superior council of war and by the government, came into force in the spring of 1914. It provided, in its great lines: on the right a mass (the First and Second Armies) between the Vosges and the Hauts-de-Meuse; a central army (the Third) in the region of the Hauts-de-Meuse; on the left a mass (the Fifth Army, extended eventually by the British) in the region of Rethel and Mézières; and a second-line army (the Fourth), concentrated initially toward Bar-le-Duc, called upon to reinforce, as circumstances dictated, the mass of the Ardennes or the mass of Lorraine.
The intention of the French commander-in-chief was to take up the offensive when all forces were gathered. But he took no definitive decision as to the zone of the principal effort; the modalities of the offensive were to be fixed according to the information that came in on the disposition realised by the enemy and the intentions of his high command. Thus the offensive conception of Joffre — reserved and opportunist — contrasted in striking fashion with the audacious and imperative schema of Schlieffen.
The French knowledge of the German plan
The invasion of Belgium was perfectly foreseen by the French high command. Indeed, from 1904 an officer of the German great general staff, the Vengeur — the name by which he signed his letters — had sold the German strategic plan, providing for the passage of the German armies across Belgian territory, to the French for sixty thousand gold francs. The episode was dramatic: the plan was bought for cash from a traitor of the German staff. The violation of Belgium was therefore foreseen; what was debated was how far the enveloping movement would extend — whether it would stop at the Meuse or overflow beyond it.
The French staff did not believe that the Germans would extend their movement beyond the Meuse. The forces at their disposal from the beginning, it was thought, did not permit them to give so great an extension to their front. Nor did the French staff take into account the German reserve corps, estimating that the enemy would not use them immediately, on the same footing as the active corps, of which they had neither the training nor the power in artillery. Wilhelm II had once said: No fathers of families in the front line! The French staff had excellent arguments for not believing in the immediate use of the German reserve corps — though the use presented inconveniences as well as advantages, and the Germans themselves were not all agreed on the point. They decided finally to employ them from the first days, which struck the calculations of the French staff with error. It was this that Joffre, a good loser if ever there was one, himself acknowledged, writing in his memoirs: It must be confessed: the use the Germans made in August of their reserve army corps was a surprise for us, and this surprise is at the origin of… — the sentence breaking off at the very point where the consequences of the error began.
The Austro-Hungarian deployment against Serbia and Russia
For Austria-Hungary the plans were complicated by the two-fold object of the war. The diplomatic action aimed only at the war against Serbia; for this, mobilisation and the deployment against Serbia and Montenegro, the full mobilisation B, had to be ordered. Yet the danger existed that Russia would fall upon the Monarchy, threaten it with war and itself wage that war. Militarily it would have been the most desirable to meet this danger initiative-ly, to treat the war against Serbia as a side-issue and to open that against Russia; but to do this on the bare possibility of Russian intervention was impossible, for in such a course Austria-Hungary would have forfeited the duty of its allies to participate, and would have drawn upon itself the grave reproach of unleashing the world war, whereas the war against Serbia was only an act of brutally provoked self-defence.
For the diplomat the position was clear; not so for the chief of the general staff, who must have in view a war quickly and decisively conducted against Serbia, and yet be ready suddenly to turn everything to the war against Russia. It was a dilemma that carried the most oppressive responsibility and created the operationally most unfavourable position, all the more as the anxiety arose that the drawing-out of the diplomatic action, and with it of the beginning of the war, would give Serbia time for extensive preparations. To all this was joined the complete uncertainty over the attitude of the allies: it was cleared up favourably as regards Germany, but as to the behaviour of Italy and Rumania there were grave doubts. The changes made to the originally fixed deployment against Russia recorded the effect of this double object: the army had first to be strong against Serbia, then, with the turn of events, to face the Russian mass in Galicia. It was this double plan, and the later obligation to carry the main strength to the Russian front while the war against Serbia went on with reduced forces, that Conrad held to have vitiated the agreed first action from the outset.
The Russian mobilisation
The Russian mobilisation, upon which the German historians made all their efforts bear, could not and must not, in all justice, be separated from the events that preceded and provoked it. It was only one fact in a complex web of facts, only one part in a whole. On the afternoon of 29 July the tsar, yielding to the reiterated demands of his general staff, justly alarmed at the military preparations of Austria and Germany, let the order for general mobilisation be torn from him, informing his ally France at once. That measure decided, he returned in the course of the evening on his resolution and ordered it to be postponed, following a personal telegram from Wilhelm II that seemed to leave him some hope of peace. The next day, 30 July, in the presence of the very bad news arriving from Vienna and Berlin, all his hopes vanished and he consented to sign, at four o’clock, the order for general mobilisation.
But was it then Russia that had begun, as the German historians would have it believed, the series of military decisions? Not at all. The Austrian government, fully in agreement with Germany, had sent to Serbia on 23 July an ultimatum of an unusual stiffness and brutality, leaving the Serbs only forty-eight hours to reply, although they had accepted on all points save one all the demands of Austria, however hard. The Austrian minister left the Serbian capital and diplomatic relations were broken off. After mobilising eight army corps without delay, the Austrian government declared war on Serbia two days after its minister left Belgrade — a declaration decided by Berchtold, the minister of foreign affairs, against the advice of the military, who wished to wait a little longer until their preparations were complete. Berchtold would not wait: he wished to put Europe as soon as possible before an accomplished fact, fearing that if he delayed he would no longer be able to evade the increasingly pressing demands for mediation from London, Paris and even St Petersburg.
The chain of the plans
It was not the Russian mobilisation — dated only 30 July — but the Austrian declaration of war on Serbia, dated the 28th, that in the succession of events leading to the general conflagration marked the important, capital fact. Austria, deliberately rejecting all mediation and all pacific arrangement, meant to settle its quarrel with Serbia by arms alone, and Germany did nothing to hold it back but gave it, on the contrary, its full support, knowing of and approving both the ultimatum and the declaration of war. And it was this declaration of war that decided Russia to mobilise. Russia, a partial mobilisation presenting almost insurmountable technical difficulties because of the immense extent of its empire and the insufficiency of its railways, chose general mobilisation. The German plan, the French Plan XVII, the Austro-Hungarian double deployment, and the Russian mobilisation were thus not independent schemes but links in a single chain: each assumed and answered the other, and the clash of their timetables produced the war of masses that none of them, in the event, had calculated correctly. The war that was to have been short, by the exact calculation of the plans, instead embarked upon a long duration from the moment the German machine was half-dismantled at the battle-of-the-marne-1914.

concepts/white-movement.title: The White Movement
concepts/white-movement.content:
The White Movement
The White movement (Бѣлое движеніе) is the armed resistance to the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War of 1917–20, of which the Volunteer Army (Добровольческая армія) of the South, raised by Generals mikhail-alexeyev, lavr-kornilov, and anton-denikin, was the first and archetypal form. Within the frame of this corpus the movement is chronicled by its own commander: Denikin’s Essays on the Russian Troubles carry it from the collapse of the old army and authority in 1917, through the Kornilov rising and the imprisonment at Bykhov, to the raising of the volunteer host on the Don, the terrible ice-march-1918 of the First Kuban March, and the death of Kornilov at Ekaterinodar. The White movement was the counter-revolution in arms — the attempt of the officer corps and the patriot public to reverse the ruin of the state by force, to save Russia from what the Whites called the “red scourge,” and to fight on when the army and the monarchy that had been their world were already gone.
Definition: counter-revolution in arms
The White movement was born of the failure of the old order and the advent of the Bolsheviks. Its leaders were the officers and generals of the imperial army who could not accept the collapse of the state and the peace at any price of october-revolution-1917. The term “White” — set against the “Reds” of the Bolsheviks — was not a party or a programme so much as a negative: everything that was not Bolshevism, everything that stood for the defence of Russia against the revolution. The movement was, Denikin insists, no mere restoration: its generals knew that the old autocratic order could not simply be brought back, and they hesitated over every political slogan, torn between the “all-Russian” scale of their task and the local business of holding the South against the Red armies. At its heart was a soldier’s patriotism — the faith, as Denikin’s first volume puts it, in the old pillars of “faith, tsar, and fatherland,” shaken but not extinguished by the catastrophe of 1917.
From the collapse of the army to Bykhov
The movement’s prehistory is the ruin Denikin chronicles in the first volume of his Essays. The old army, demoralized by the war and dissolved by the revolution — above all by Order No. 1 and the collapse of discipline — ceased to be an instrument of the state. The February revolution swept away the throne almost without resistance; the Provisional Government proved powerless to command the army or the country; and by the autumn of 1917 the idea of a military dictatorship was already being canvassed among the command, who saw in it the only hope of saving Russia from the soviets. The abortive rising of Kornilov in August 1917 — the “Kornilov affair,” in which the Supreme Commander, trusting in the officers and the Allies, moved against the revolutionary government only to be denounced as a mutineer by Kerensky and arrested — was the first open act of the counter-revolution, and Denikin treats Kerensky’s “victory” over it as the prelude to Bolshevism. The Bykhov prisoners — Kornilov, Denikin, and their comrades — were the nucleus of the future White command.
The birth of the Volunteer Army on the Don
With the Bolshevik coup the scattered officers and patriots turned toward the Don, where the Cossack ataman Kaledin still held a refuge. General Alekseev arrived at Novocherkassk on 2 November 1917 and began the “Alekseev organization,” the small armed nucleus “destined,” as Denikin writes, “to play so considerable a role.” Through the winter of 1917–18 the volunteers gathered on the Don — officers, junkers, students, the remnants of the old army’s best — under a loose “triumvirate” of Alekseev, Kornilov, and Kaledin, united by the single resolve to fight the Bolsheviks. The tasks of the army were as yet undefined, its means scarce, its political ground uncertain; but the first volunteers had a spiritual quality Denikin honours — men who came to the Don knowing they might die, in the name of Russia. When the Don itself fell and Rostov had to be abandoned before the advancing Red Guard, the army took to the steppe and became a wandering host.
The First Kuban (“Ice”) March
The first campaign of the Volunteer Army, the march from Rostov into the Kuban in the early months of 1918, is the epic that gives the movement its legend. Leaving Rostov in February, the small army — a few thousand men against the surrounding Bolshevik forces — marched south in the winter mud and cold, fighting every step of the way. Denikin records the cruelty of the retreat from the Don — the plunder, the murder of the wounded, the fear for families — and the courage that answered it. The crossing of the Laba, with the junkers wading through the icy water; the running battles at Lezhanka, at Ust-Laba, at Filippovsky; and above all the fight of 15 March at Novo-Dmitrievskaya, the “Ice March” itself, the glory of General Markov’s officer regiment. The army turned toward Ekaterinodar, joined by the Kuban volunteers, and laid siege to the city — and there, on 31 March 1918, a shell struck down Kornilov. The death of its founder nearly broke the movement. Denikin, called by the dying man’s staff, assumed the command; the army lifted the siege and marched back through the Kuban to the Don, its strength spent but its legend made.
Current state: the legend of the first rising
In the frame of this corpus the White movement appears at its origin and its purest form: the small army of the First Kuban March, not yet the mass fronts of the later Civil War that Denikin’s later volumes (not in this wiki) would chronicle. The movement that the Essays portray is the counter-revolution in its moment of extremity — a handful of men who rose “first in defence of Russia against the red scourge,” in Denikin’s closing words, and whose struggle outlived them by two and a half years before the scattering of the survivors across the world. It stands in the corpus as the armed opposite of the october-revolution-1917, the loyalist counterpart to the religious and monarchist devotion of the autocracy-russia (though its generals could not simply restore it), and the last defence of the duma-constitutionalism and old imperial order that 1917 had destroyed. Related to it stand lavr-kornilov and anton-denikin, its founders; the ice-march-1918 that made its legend; and the february-revolution-1917 and october-revolution-1917 against which it fought.

concepts/zemstvo-great-reforms.title: The Zemstvo and the Great Reforms
concepts/zemstvo-great-reforms.content:
The Zemstvo and the Great Reforms
The Great Reforms (Великія реформы) are the complex of measures carried through by alexander-ii in the 1860s that transformed the old Russia of serfdom and seigneurial autocracy — above all the emancipation of the serfs (1861) and the creation of local self-government in the institution of the zemstvo (земство, “land assembly”). Within the frame of this corpus they are the given starting-point of Russian internal history after 1866: the works of the reforming era against which the reaction of the last reigns was directed, the institutions through which educated Russia learned the habit of public life, and the seedbed of both the constitutional movement and the medical and educational work that bound the intelligentsia to the people. Their character is double — at once a genuine grant of self-government and a strictly circumscribed one, and the story of the period is largely the story of how the government first created and then fought its own creation.
Definition: local self-government in the reforming era
The zemstvo institutions, established by the statute of 1864, were elected local assemblies — provincial (gubernskie) and district (uezdnye) — entrusted with the economic and social business of the countryside: roads, public charity, education, medicine, statistics, and the raising of local rates and dues to pay for them. Together with the new judicial statutes, the reformed municipal government (the Municipal Statute of 1870), and the military reform of Miliutin (universal military service, 1874), they formed the institutional edifice of the Great Reforms. Their significance lay less in the power they held — which was narrow — than in the principle they embodied: that a part of the public business of the empire was to be conducted by elected representatives of local society rather than by officials of the crown. This was, in embryo, a breach in the autocratic monopoly of government, and it was the reason both the reformers cherished the zemstvo and the reactionaries distrusted it.
The sphere of zemstvo activity and its limits
Kornilov’s lectures on the zemstvo institutions of 1866–1878 lay out both the work and its boundaries. The zemstvos were given a sphere of activity and the means to pursue it — the right to levy dues on land and, increasingly, their own budgets — but their competence was confined to local economic matters and expressly excluded the political. From the outset a collision arose over money: the zemstvos, needing funds, sought to tax trade and industry, and here they ran headlong into the government, which would not see the state’s fiscal monopoly invaded by elected bodies. The class character of the zemstvos was marked — the landowners dominated, and the peasant members were few and overshadowed. Yet within their sphere they were active: the zemstvo school spread elementary education across the countryside against the resistance of the Ministry of Public Instruction, and the zemstvo physicians built the public medicine that Granat’s essay in this corpus chronicles. It was this productive activity, and the public spirit it fostered, that made the zemstvo at once the government’s most useful auxiliary and its most dangerous rival.
The government’s struggle with the zemstvo
The reaction that opened in 1866 and hardened under alexander-iii was in large part a struggle against the zemstvo. The government distrusted the zemstvos’ claim to tax trade and industry, restricted their field of activity, and fought the spread of the zemstvo school, which the Ministry of Public Instruction feared as a nursery of sedition. When the zemstvo movement, stirred by the russo-turkish-war-1877-78 and the Eastern Question, began to address the government with demands for reform, the breach widened: the zemstvo addresses of 1878–79 were answered with displeasure rather than concession. Under Alexander III the reaction turned to reconstruction. The statute of 12 June 1890 recast the zemstvo to secure the preponderance of the nobility and tighten the governor’s supervision over its proceedings; the peasants were reduced to indirect election through their own bodies; and the zemstvo, while it kept its name and much of its work, lost much of the independence that had made it the school of the constitutional movement. The land captains (zemskie nachalniki) of the law of 1889 carried the government’s hand still deeper into the village, subjecting the peasantry to the supervision of officials appointed from above. The reforming creation of the 1860s had been bent to the service of the order it was meant to leaven.
Current state: the seedbed of reform
In the frame of this corpus the zemstvo appears as the enduring institution through which the reform era lived on into the age of reaction. Though its political voice was suppressed, its practical work continued and grew — the zemstvo medicine that Granat’s Kanel praises as the foundation of Russian public sanitation, the schools, the statistics, the famine relief of the disastrous early 1890s. And it remained the natural home of the educated society that, denied the political institutions of the west, found in local self-government the one arena of legitimate public action. From the zemstvo movement grew the constitutional agitation that in 1905 forced the october-manifesto-1905 and the duma-constitutionalism; many of the men who sat in the Dumas had learned their politics in the zemstvo assemblies. The Great Reforms and their zemstvo stand, then, as the positive achievement of the period that the reaction could curtail but never undo — the foundation on which the liberal and constitutional Russia of the new century was built. Related to it stand alexander-ii, the Tsar-Liberator who created it; its opposite and adversary, the autocracy-russia; and the duma-constitutionalism that at last gave Russian society a central representative body.
