concepts/zollverein.title: The Zollverein (1834–1871)
concepts/zollverein.content:
The Zollverein
The Zollverein (“customs union”) was the German customs union, founded in 1834 under Prussian leadership, by which the greater part of the German states abolished their internal tariff frontiers and adopted a common tariff toward the outside world. It was the great economic foundation of German unity, and it ran as a parallel and preparatory track to the political unification that this wiki follows: long before the north-german-confederation and the german-empire-proclaimed-1871 gave Germany a political form, the Zollverein had already made it an economic unit. The concept covers the union’s role in economic unification, its reorganization after 1866, and the federal organs — the Federal Customs Council (Zollbundesrat) and the Zollparlament (“customs parliament”) — through which it was integrated into the new federal state.
The economic foundation of unity
Lenz presents the Zollverein as one of the two institutions, along with the army reform, by which Prussia “developed institutions which Emperor Wilhelm and Bismarck could take up as constituent elements” in their work. It had been built up against Austria, and in the years of reaction it had been deliberately used by the Berlin government to bind the German states to Prussia. Prussia’s possession of the Zollverein gave it, in the view of contemporaries, its one secure position in Germany: as Lenz notes the point that Prussia’s constitution was “the only recruiting means Prussia had in Germany,” while “in all other directions — Zollverein, material advantages, and so on — Austria would run Prussia a close race.” The Zollverein thus stood as the economic counterweight to the Austrian political programme, and it was a chief field on which the kleindeutsch and grossdeutsch programmes contended long before the armies met.
Austria’s counter-policy
Because the Zollverein was the engine of Prussian influence, Austria repeatedly sought either to enter it or to break it. Lenz recounts how, in the 1850s, Austria had hoped to create a rival “seventy-million empire” that would “outshine the old Zollverein and drive Prussia from one of its surest positions,” and how a treaty of 7 September 1851 bound the Habsburg government to join the old union on 1 January 1854. The Austrian ambassador Arnim was sent to negotiate a commercial treaty with Austria in place of the Zollverein, and the Austrians hoped to force their way into the union on the basis of the old tariff. Prussian policy resisted this, preferring the compact, Prussian-led union to a wider Austria-dominated one. The Bavarian chamber, in which the Grossdeutschen ruled, at one point passed resolutions on the Zollverein that came close to its dissolution in favour of a south German special league joining Austria. The union was thus a constant battlefield between the two great powers for the economic allegiance of Germany.
Reform after 1866
The victories of 1866 transformed the Zollverein along with the German Question. With Austria expelled from German affairs, the way was open to reorganize the customs union as an instrument of the Prussian-led federal state. Sybel’s sixth volume, covering the years 1866–67, treats this reorganization in detail under the heading of the “new Zollverein treaties” (neuen Zollvereinsverträge): the economic integration of the territories annexed to Prussia, the pressure put upon the southern German states to accept the new terms, and the deliberate linking of economic unity to political unification. A second set of chapters on the “consolidation of the Zollverein question” (Befestigung der Zollvereinsfrage) describes how the Customs Union was consolidated as an instrument of Prussian policy through the Federal Customs Council (Zollbundesrat), while particularist interests in the south continued to resist.
The Zollparlament
The parliamentary arm of the reformed union was the Zollparlament, the customs parliament, which drew together elected deputies from across the union, including the southern states that remained outside the north-german-confederation. The idea of such a body was old in Bismarck’s mind — Lenz records that, in the memorandum he drafted in 1861, he proposed a Zollparlament as a “surrogate” for the federal institutions that were lacking, since the existing order could only be completed through “voluntary and terminable associations beside the Confederation.” After 1866 the Zollparlament gave institutional form to this notion, meeting twice from 1868 onward. Lenz observes that within it, and in the Reichstag, there were “heated debates, and the particularists of north and south clashed sharply,” yet the interests themselves were “all by nature related and came to an accommodation through discussion and vote.”
The customs union and the Reich
The Zollparlament was a transitional device that bridged the gap between the economic unity of Germany and its incomplete political unity — for the southern states, inside the customs union but outside the northern federation, were bound to Prussia economically while still politically separate. When the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 drew the South into the Reich, this economic seam was stitched shut, and the Zollverein was absorbed into the tariff and financial system of the unified Empire. The concept thus illustrates a wider theme of this corpus: the economic integration of Germany, prepared over decades by the Zollverein, ran ahead of and ultimately helped to compel its political integration. What the tariffs had bound together, the armies and constitutions of 1866–71 completed.

entities/achille-bazaine.title: Achille Bazaine (1811–1888)
entities/achille-bazaine.content:
Achille Bazaine (1811–1888)
François-Achille Bazaine was a marshal of France and the commander of the French Army of the Rhine in the war of 1870. His name is bound to the greatest disaster of the campaign after Sedan: the siege of Metz, into which the largest intact French army allowed itself to be shut, and the capitulation of that army in October 1870 while France still hoped for relief. He is the most contested figure in the corpus’s account of the war, because on him converged the accusations of the generals, of the parliamentary opposition, and of the postwar courts — a controversy that is itself one of the sources’ recurring themes, with Ollivier weighing the evidence for and against him.
Command of the Army of the Rhine
After the defeats at Wissembourg, battle-of-woerth-1870 and Forbach in the first days of August 1870, the French high command was thrown into confusion, and Marshal Bazaine emerged as the central figure of the army assembled at Metz. Ollivier records that the Emperor, whose health had broken and whose personal command had proved disastrous, was stripped of his authority and the command imposed on Bazaine, who had at first refused it; on 5 August the Emperor had met Bazaine at Boulay and taken no decision, and by mid-August Bazaine held the 2nd, 3rd and 4th corps under his orders as commander-in-chief. The plan of concentrating the army at Metz was Bazaine’s, and it was there, before the fortress and the surrounding German armies, that the fate of the campaign would be decided.
The question of responsibility at Forbach
Ollivier’s analysis of the opening battles turns on the question “Qui est responsable: Frossard ou Bazaine?” — who was responsible, Frossard or Bazaine. General Frossard, beaten at Forbach on 6 August, tried to cover his failure by charging that Bazaine had not succoured him in time. Ollivier examines whether Bazaine was bound to come onto the field, weighing Frossard’s claim that the combat was going in the French favour until four in the afternoon and that timely reinforcements would have turned the reverse into a victory. The episode established a pattern: Bazaine’s slowness, his careful dispositions, and the accusation that he let an opportunity slip for lack of decision. Mac-Mahon, by contrast, “accused no one” and silently accepted full responsibility for his own defeat — a contrast Ollivier draws to the discredit of the Metz command.
The siege of Metz, August–October 1870
After the defeats, the Emperor and the army fell back toward Châlons and Metz. Hanotaux records the fateful decision of the war of movement: Mac-Mahon’s army, marching to the northeast to effect its junction with Bazaine, was forced into the funnel of Sedan by the speed of the Prussian armies and destroyed there on 1 September, while the Army of the Rhine remained shut up in Metz. From that point Bazaine commanded the last great intact French force, besieged by the Germans through September and October while Paris itself was invested. Hanotaux notes that Bazaine announced a sortie toward Montmédy, and that it was partly the hope of this junction that drew Mac-Mahon into the trap; but the promised breakout never decisively relieved the army, and the siege wore on. The surrender of Metz — a whole army laying down its arms — was, in the French reading the sources record, a catastrophe of the same order as Sedan, for it delivered the strongest fortress and the largest force to the enemy and left the national defence, after Sedan and the fall of the Empire, with almost nothing.
Capitulation and the postwar trial
With the capitulation of Metz in October 1870, Bazaine passed into German captivity. After the war and the restoration of order, the Republic pursued him. Hanotaux records that at the apogee of Thiers’s government, in the session of 1872, the National Assembly opened an inquiry on the capitulations and Marshal Bazaine was sent before a court-martial. The trial became a national reckoning over the disaster: the court found him guilty of surrendering an army and a fortress to the enemy in a manner contrary to honour, and condemned him. He was then a prisoner on the Île Sainte-Marguerite off the Mediterranean coast, from which, as the sources’ frame implies, he escaped — condemned in his absence and spending his remaining years in exile, dying in Spain in 1888. The controversies of his command — his disputed slowness, his intentions, the question of what he owed Frossard and what the army owed France — remained a live wound in French politics, the theme that the participant sources (Ollivier) and the later national history (Hanotaux) both return to as they assign the blame for the fall of the Empire.

entities/adolphe-thiers.title: Adolphe Thiers (1797–1877)
entities/adolphe-thiers.content:
Adolphe Thiers (1797–1877)
The little man with the spectacles who governed France through its deepest humiliation since the First Empire — and who alone had the authority to make peace, crush the Commune, pay the indemnity, and free the territory before the monarchical majority toppled him. Thiers, called by the elections of February 1871 “administrator of the national misfortune,” was head of the executive power from February 1871, then President of the Republic under the Rivet law of 31 August 1871, until his overthrow on 24 May 1873. His triple task — peace, repair, and a durable political form — defined the opening years of the Third Republic.
The statesman of 1830
Thiers was not a man of the new France but of the old: a Marseillais of modest birth, author of the Histoire de la Révolution française, journalist of the National who had helped make the July revolution of 1830. Hanotaux’s portrait sets him directly against Napoleon III — prudence, experience, foresight against adventure; short stature, spectacles, imperturbable aplomb. Where the Empire had gambled on glory, Thiers offered the continuity of a cautious administrator. It was this reputation that made him, in the disasters of 1870–71, the natural rallying point of a country that wanted peace and order rather than either guerre à outrance or a king it could not agree upon.
Chief of the executive power
Elected in twenty-six departments with nearly two million votes, Thiers met the National Assembly at Bordeaux and was named chief of the executive power. His cabinet of 19 February 1871 organized the new authority and won recognition from the foreign powers. Against the republicans of the Left who demanded war to the last, Thiers carried the peace: he negotiated the preliminaries at Versailles, sat with Bismarck (21 February), and defended the claims of the country even as the German chancellor held the armed hand. The question of Metz and Belfort divided the two; Thiers saved Belfort for France and struck a milliard from the original demand. He bound himself to the country’s desire for peace, and made that peace the foundation of his authority.
Peace and the Commune
The Assembly’s shift to Versailles and its measures against the armed population of Paris detonated the insurrection of 18 March 1871. For two months Thiers and the Versailles government fought the paris-commune-1871 — the siege of the capital by the army under Marshal Mac-Mahon, the provincial risings put down, and finally the Bloody Week. Thiers, like the Assembly, regarded the suppression as the indispensable condition of national recovery. At the same time he completed the peace: the definitive treaty-of-frankfurt-1871 of 10 May 1871 ceded Alsace and part of Lorraine and fixed the five-milliard indemnity. When Bismarck offered German financiers to carry the debt, Thiers refused and staked the payment on France itself — the loan of two milliards of June 1871, subscribed 381,906 times, proved his confidence. The conventions of 12 October 1871 began the evacuation of the German troops.
The apogee and the ‘libérateur du territoire’
The session of April–August 1872 was the apogee of Thiers’s government: peace signed, the Commune defeated, reconstruction under way. Under the Rivet law he had become President of the Republic, yet remained responsible before a hostile Assembly. His message of 13 November 1872 finally pronounced the word “Republic,” and the right recoiled. Negotiating for the anticipated evacuation of the remaining German soldiers — Gontaut-Biron, Saint-Vallier, Arnim, Bismarck — Thiers secured the convention of liberation of 15 March 1873, and the Assembly declared that he had deserved well of the country. He became the libérateur du territoire, the man who paid the milliards and sent the occupying armies home.
The fall of 24 May
The very success undid him. Having secured liberation, Thiers had spent his usefulness in the eyes of the monarchical majority, which now wanted a president it could control and a king it still hoped to crown. The pact of the three monarchical parties, the resignation of Grévy, the election of Barodet at Paris, the resignations of Jules Simon and de Goulard — all preceded the decisive sittings. On 24 May 1873 Thiers made his great speech: peace signed, Commune defeated, indemnity paid, evacuation decided. “I have taken my party on the Republic,” he told the Chamber. Put in the minority, he resigned. Mac-Mahon was elected president in his place. Hanotaux’s judgment is that the right toppled Thiers before he could found the Republic, and that both conservatives and republicans misread the act — the Republic was not killed, only postponed. Thiers, the libérateur du territoire, lived to see the Republic he had prepared emerge from the ruins of the monarchical attempt, dying in 1877 just as the parliamentary Republic was being born.

entities/agostino-depretis.title: Agostino Depretis (1813–1887)
entities/agostino-depretis.content:
Agostino Depretis (1813–1887)
Agostino Depretis, leader of the parliamentary Left and prime minister of Italy through most of the 1880s, was the master of the political practice that his own era named trasformismo — the absorption of opposition deputies into the government majority and the dissolution of clear party lines. Born in 1813, a veteran of the Risorgimento and of the first parliaments of the kingdom, he governed the new Italy for a decade, presided over the African conquest that ended in the disaster of Dogali, and died in 1887, leaving the stage to francesco-crispi. Where Crispi was the strong man and the author, Depretis was the adroit parliamentary manager; Oriani, who judged the post-Cavour ministries harshly, wrote that Depretis “conserved of Cavour the parliamentary dexterity and the practice of all the portfolios, yet like all the merely able was small.”
The parliamentarian of the Left
Depretis’s rise was through the Left of the Italian Parliament, the party that had opposed the long dominance of the Right since unification and that finally came to office in 1876 with the “advent of the Left.” Oriani’s ninth book, “Le due monarchie,” records the exhaustion of the Right, the fall of the last Minghetti ministry, and the accession of the Left under Depretis — a change of government rather than of constitution, which nevertheless gave the country a new political generation. Depretis brought to the premiership the habits of the old parliamentary world: flexibility, patience, and a genius for holding majorities together by concession rather than by force. He was the incarnation of the practice Oriani describes as legislative empiricism — the continuous, improvised innovation by which a government that had to innovate in order to conserve kept the machine running.
Trasformismo
Depretis’s distinctive contribution to Italian politics was trasformismo itself. Rather than rule through a disciplined party, he drew deputies of the Right and of every nuance into his government majority, so that government and opposition ceased to correspond to any stable principle and the Chamber became a shifting mass around the prime minister. Fortunato, who fought against the practice from the South, recorded it in his very first speeches: the “dissidence” that broke the Depretis majorities in 1880, and the elections of 29 October 1882 in which trasformismo reached its fullest expression — the absorption of old enemies, the levelling of the historical parties, and the confusion of every line of political principle. For Fortunato, Depretis’s method was the ruin of the parliamentary regime, dissolving the parties into a shapeless court of the premier; for the state’s defenders it was the necessary art of governing a country of incompatible regions and interests. Either way, it was the politics of Italy for a generation, carried on after Depretis by Giolitti.
The African conquest and Dogali
Depretis’s last years were occupied with the extension of Italian power into Africa, in the wave of European colonial expansion that Oriani treats as “la conquista africana.” The kingdom took the Red Sea port of Massawa in 1885 and pushed inland, and on 24 January 1887 an Italian column was cut to pieces by the Ethiopians at Dogali — a defeat that Oriani’s account places at the climax of the volume, the first great humiliation of Italian imperialism. The disaster fell at the end of Depretis’s career, when his health was failing; he died in 1887, before the consequences could be pursued, leaving the colonial question and the government to Crispi. Fortunato, looking back from the aftermath, saw in the whole colonial turn the origin of the calamities that followed, and his speeches are a running indictment of the policy that Depretis had launched and Crispi would carry to catastrophe.

entities/albrecht-von-roon.title: Albrecht von Roon (1803–1879)
entities/albrecht-von-roon.content:
Albrecht von Roon (1803–1879)
Albrecht von Roon, Prussian minister of war, was the author of the army reorganization that made the Prussian victories of 1866 and 1870 possible and the central figure of the constitutional conflict that shook Prussia in the early 1860s. In this corpus’s frame his story is inseparable from that of the crown he served: he was the man who gave wilhelm-i the instrument — a strong, professional standing army — that helmuth-von-moltke used to win Königgrätz and Sedan, and he was the friend and patron who, in the crisis of 1862, summoned otto-von-bismarck into the ministry to break the deadlock between crown and parliament. He is one of the three figures — the organizer, the strategist, and the statesman — whose combined arts carried Prussia through the wars of unification.
The army reform
Roon rose with the accession to the regency in 1858. In July of that year he submitted to the Prince Regent a memorandum on the army constitution that, as Lenz records, “opened his way into the ministry.” The core of his argument was a critique of the Landwehr — the territorial militia that was the second line of the Prussian army. The Landwehr, Roon contended, made one not master in one’s own house. At every conflict of opinion between the government and the governed, one would have to calculate and estimate the effect that contested measures of external as well as internal policy might have on the armed part of the people, on the Landwehr; its existence therefore bound the government’s hands, exposed it to the harassment of party scribblers, made it dependent on the wind of public opinion, and rendered any free political action impossible. The remedy was to reduce the militia element and build up the regular, professional army, bound to the crown.
Lenz presents Roon as “a man after Wilhelm’s heart,” obedient so long as the regent kept to a liberal course, but more capable and willing to hold him upright in conflict. He looked with contempt and anger on the “Democrats”; he called himself a reactionary at his first meeting with Gerlach; and from the first hour he was the wedge in the liberal ministry. The reform was carried through in the interest of the old military families and the Junker class: the Landwehr officers and the bourgeois officer candidates were pushed back, and the upper classes of the cadet houses were emptied to secure the new posts for the sons of military families. Crown and nobility, drawn together again by the shock of revolution, stood joined; the army became, in the famous phrase the sources echo, the rocher de bronze, the bronze rock, of the throne. Roon himself acknowledged that the king, if advised to give way, would do so — “but,” the passionate minister wrote, “I hope to God that He will paralyse my tongue before it agrees.” He set everything on spurring on his royal master against the liberal claim to limit the rights of the crown.
The constitutional conflict
The reform required money, and the liberal Chamber of Deputies, the bearer of the constitutional movement, refused to vote it. There followed the constitutional conflict of the 1860s, in which the crown governed without a lawful budget. It was Roon who sought a way out. In the crisis of June 1861, when the question whether the new king should mark his accession by an homage in the old ständische forms set the cabinet against the crown, Roon acted. He was isolated in the ministry, and his object was first of all to strengthen his own position in it — above all to remove Graf Schwerin, the true bearer of liberal policy, from the king’s council. On 26 June 1861 he wrested from the king, after long resistance, the commission to look about for other ministers; and on the same day he wrote to President von Möller and Herr von Selchow, and on the next day also to Bismarck at Petersburg. It is uncertain, Lenz notes, whether the letter to Bismarck went out directly on the king’s order, but Wilhelm seems to have spoken of him and to have given permission to enquire of him.
Bismarck’s reply set out the program that he would carry into office: to hold firm in the military question, to break with the Chamber over it, to dissolve it, and then to show the nation how the king stood with the people. But that first crisis ended in compromise — the homage was given up for a solemn coronation, and the liberal ministers kept their places. When Bismarck arrived in Berlin, he found Roon absent; and the plan came to nothing for the moment.
The summons of Bismarck and the victory
The final break came in September 1862. In the extremity of the conflict over the military budget, when the crown could find no minister willing to govern against the parliament, it was Roon who at last prevailed on the king to take the step that decided Prussia’s future: he called Bismarck from Petersburg to the ministry. Lenz’s later reflection on the fall of 1890 marks the significance of that act: “King Wilhelm then seized Bismarck’s hand, because he alone of all his servants promised him help in the matter most sacred to his life, and it was done for his salvation.” The hand that the king seized had been reached to him by Roon, who had built the army and then brought in the statesman to defend it.
Roon’s army reform, once freed from parliamentary obstruction by Bismarck’s government, became the instrument of Prussian victory. The reorganized army, commanded on campaign by the General Staff of Moltke, overthrew Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–71. The victories of battle-of-koniggratz-1866 and Sedan, which founded the north-german-confederation and then the german-empire-proclaimed-1871, were won by the troops that Roon had organized and the system he had built. He stands, with Moltke and the King, among the founders of the Empire — the organizer whose work made possible what the strategist directed and the statesman guided.
Roon died in 1879, in the first decade of the German Empire his army had helped to create.

entities/alexander-ii.title: Alexander II (1818–1881)
entities/alexander-ii.content:
Alexander II
Alexander II (1818–1881), Emperor of All the Russias from 1855, enters this wiki’s frame already the Tsar-Liberator (Царь-Освободитель) — the author of the emancipation of the serfs (1861) and of the whole complex of zemstvo-great-reforms that reshaped Russian life in the 1860s. In the years 1866–1881, which Kornilov’s course treats as one long reactionary period, his story is that of a reformer caught between the consequences of his own work and a revolutionary movement that answered reform with terror. The arc runs from the Karakozov attempt of 4 April 1866, through the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–78 and the rise of the narodnaya-volya (“People’s Will”), to the catastrophe of 1 March 1881, when the emperor was assassinated on the very eve of the constitutional experiment he seemed at last ready to grant. His reforms before 1866 belong to the preceding wiki of 1800–1865; here the emphasis falls on the reaction that followed the first shot and on his death.
The Karakozov attempt and the onset of reaction
Kornilov dates the reaction precisely: it opened with the attempt on the emperor’s life by Dmitry Karakozov on 4 April 1866, and thereafter coloured the whole remaining fifteen years of the reign. The shot did not halt the gradual development of Russian internal life after the reforms of the 1860s — the peasant reform was extended to the appanage and state peasants, the Municipal Statute of 1870 and Miliutin’s military reforms with universal military service (1874) were carried through, the new judicial institutions opened and the zemstvo spread. But it turned the temper of the highest governing circles. Two men came to stand for the two opposite sides of Alexander II’s reign: Count D. A. Tolstoy, minister of public instruction, who after 1866 pressed the reactionary line of classicism in the schools, the restriction of the universities, and the struggle against the zemstvo school; and D. A. Miliutin, the reforming war minister, who in Kornilov’s reading represented the reforming side of the same emperor. Tolstoy’s allies were the publicist Mikhail Katkov and, behind both, the conviction that the programme of the previous decade had gone too far.
Zemstvo, court, and press under reaction
The reaction touched every institution the Great Reforms had created. The zemstvo, which had been granted a sphere of local activity and its own budgets in the 1860s, found itself fighting the government over the right to tax trade and industry, and watched its field of activity steadily narrowed as the ministry struggled with it. The new courts, opened with such promise, were slowly hemmed in: Count Pahlen’s procuracy reasserted control, special procedures were devised for state crimes, and cases were gradually withdrawn from the jury. The press, which the 1860s had loosened, was subjected again to the censor’s hand, and the principal organs of opinion hardened into their camps — the reactionary papers of Katkov on one side, the populist journals on the other. The mood of society soured with the reaction, and the gap between the reforming promise of the early years and the closing bureaucracy of the later ones became the underlying complaint of educated Russia.
The popular masses and the populist movement
Beneath this struggle of government and society lay the unresolved peasant question. Kornilov’s account of the economic condition of the peasantry in the 1860s–1870s is sombre: pauper allotments, the otrezki (“cut-offs”) of land taken from the peasants at the emancipation, rising lease prices, arrears of taxes and redemption payments, and the famines of 1868 and of Samara in 1872–1873. The peasants’ insufficiency of allotments and the burden of payments became the standing subject of zemstvo investigations and of the populist literature. From this soil grew the movement of the intelligentsia “to the people” — the student disturbances of 1869, Nechaev and his conspiratorial methods, the Chaikovtsy circle, the theories of Bakunin and Lavrov, and ultimately the revolutionary society Zemlya i Volya (“Land and Freedom”), which by the end of the 1870s had given way to the terrorist party narodnaya-volya that set its sights on the person of the emperor himself.
The Eastern Question and the war of 1877–78
Foreign affairs meanwhile carried Russia into the russo-turkish-war-1877-78. The Eastern Question, the rivalry of Russian and English interests in Asia, the conquest of the Caucasus and the Central Asian khanates, and above all the troubles of the Balkan Slavs under Turkish rule — the Bulgarian massacres, the Serbian war — drove the government to war with Turkey. Russia’s victory brought the Peace of San Stefano, only to be revised at the Congress of Berlin (1878) before the other great powers, and the economic and financial cost of the war, with the resignation of Finance Minister Reutern, added to the discontent at home. The war stirred the Slavophiles and revived the zemstvo movement; the government, appealing for society’s support, met instead with zemstvo addresses demanding reform. The revolutionary movement, far from quieting, organized into the party that would make the assassination of the emperor its central aim.
Loris-Melikov and the catastrophe of 1 March 1881
After a series of attempts on his life — including the explosion in the Winter Palace itself — the emperor established the Supreme Administrative Commission headed by Count Loris-Melikov, who sought to combine the repression of the terrorists with concessions to the liberals: senatorial inspections, attention to the peasant question, the beginnings of a rapprochement with the constitutional movement, and finally a report proposing a special preparatory commission of elected representatives. Revolutionaries and liberals alike watched him warily. Kornilov records that Loris-Melikov, confident of his system’s success, misjudged the revolutionaries’ strength. On 1 March 1881, while the emperor, who had twice been kept from Sunday outings by Loris-Melikov’s warnings, drove back through the capital to the Winter Palace, the Narodnaya Volya struck. The conspiracy of Zheliabov and Perovskaya, the bomb-throwers stationed along the route, the mines laid under the streets — all came together as the first bomb wounded the emperor and the second, thrown as he lingered over the wounded, killed him. The assassination of Alexander II not only cut short the possible reform of Loris-Melikov but handed the throne to a son resolved on autocracy, and so closed the reign of the Tsar-Liberator with the reaction that would mark the age of alexander-iii.

entities/alexander-iii.title: Alexander III (1845–1894)
entities/alexander-iii.content:
Alexander III
Alexander III (1845–1894), Emperor of All the Russias from the assassination of his father on 1 March 1881 to his own death in 1894, was the autocrat of the counter-reforms. Where his father had been the Tsar-Liberator, he was, in the language of the age, the mírotvorets (“peacemaker”) — a title his contemporaries bestowed on the emperor who kept Russia at peace for thirteen years and won the French alliance. Yet at home his reign meant the deliberate undoing of much of the reforming impetus of the 1860s: the tightening of autocracy under the influence of konstantin-pobedonostsev, the zemstvo captains and the counter-reform of local institutions, the reaction in education and the press, and the elevation of finance — under Vyshnegradsky and then the young sergei-witte — into the instrument of a rearmed and protected state. Witte, who served him, calls him a great emperor undervalued by contemporaries; Kornilov, a liberal historian, treats him as the embodiment of the reaction that closed the century.
The unready heir and the first steps
Witte stresses that Alexander III, as the second son of Alexander II, was never prepared for the throne: his elder brother Nicholas was the heir, and when that brother died the future emperor found himself upon it with little of the education reserved for a crown prince. He came to power on 1 March 1881 convinced of the justice of autocracy. In the highest governing circles the first weeks of the reign saw a struggle between the constitutional tendencies of Loris-Melikov and the reactionaries gathered around Pobedonostsev. At the conference of 8 March 1881, called to consider Loris-Melikov’s project of a representative commission, the emperor heard his old tutor konstantin-pobedonostsev denounce the plan as the culmination of the “talking-shops” — the zemstvos, the new courts, the licentious press — and Pobedonostsev had his way. On 29 April 1881, to the surprise of the ministers, the manifesto appeared declaring the firm resolve to uphold and defend the samoderzhavie (“autocracy”) against all encroachments. Loris-Melikov resigned, and the reaction had found its direction.
The counter-reforms
The reaction unfolded through the 1880s. Under the ministry of N. P. Ignatiev and then, after his fall, under the decisive hand of Count D. A. Tolstoy, the government set itself against the institutions of the preceding reign. The guiding idea, as Kornilov records the phrase of the ruling circles, was to create in the localities a “strong authority close to the people” — an administrative tutelage that would also restore the nobility to an honored and influential place. This found its clearest expression in the law of 12 July 1889 on the land captains (zemskie nachalniki): men drawn from the landed nobility, armed with wide powers of tutelage over the peasants and their self-government and courts. The Statute on zemstvo institutions of 12 June 1890 followed, drawing the zemstvo into the system of state institutions and cutting back the independence it had enjoyed since 1864; the justices of the peace were abolished, their functions divided between the circuit courts and the new land captains. In the schools the reaction reigned under Delianov and Tolstoy, in the press under the new law of 1882, and against the non-Orthodox and the Jews the government moved to persecution. The nobility’s jubilee of 1885 and the programme of Pazukhin gave the reaction its social programme: the defence of the nobility as the chief support of the throne.
Finance: Vyshnegradsky and the beginning of the Witte system
On the financial side the reign belongs first to I. A. Vyshnegradsky. After the humane and democratic-minded Bunge had been hounded from the finance ministry at the start of 1887, Vyshnegradsky — a technologist, professor, and speculator rather than a theorist — took the direction sharply rightward. Kornilov describes his system: the accumulation of large cash reserves in the treasury, intervention in foreign exchange markets to support the credit ruble, and the extreme development of protectionism, carried to its height in the new tariff of 1891. The economic policy strained the taxable capacity of the people and subordinated the factory legislation of Bunge’s years to the wishes of large industry. At the same time the groundwork was laid for the monetary reform that sergei-witte, who followed Vyshnegradsky in the ministry, would carry through under the next reign — the gold standard toward which the finance ministers of the century had all in some measure striven. Witte, brought by Alexander III from the South-Western railways to the department of railway affairs and then, after the catastrophe at Borki (which his own warnings had nearly prevented), to the ministry of ways of communication and the finance ministry, was the emperor’s own discovery; the two men’s relationship, as Witte tells it, was one of mutual regard, and the emperor’s death in 1894 cut short a minister’s service he had come to value.
Foreign policy: the Franco-Russian alliance and the Far East
In foreign affairs the reign was marked by the pursuit of peace and the reorientation of Russia’s alliances. The conquest of Turkmenia and the check on English rivalry in Central Asia were accomplished, and the Balkan complications with Bulgaria managed. Most importantly, when the new German Emperor Wilhelm II proclaimed the existence of the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria, and Italy directed in effect against Russia, Alexander III answered by announcing his own alliance with France. The French fleet’s visit to Kronstadt and the Russian reply at Toulon, the French crowds’ enthusiasm — Kornilov records these as the outward signs of a new European system. The Franco-Russian rapprochement, in his judgment, put an end to Bismarck’s design of a final blow against France and for a comparatively long time secured the European peace; it was for this that some called Alexander III the peacemaker. In the last years of the reign the same emperor’s diplomacy turned increasingly to the Far East, and the building of the Siberian railway — begun on his initiative and pushed forward — prepared the ground for the new policy that would draw Russia into collision with Japan under his successor, nicholas-ii. Kornilov ends his course at this point, on the threshold of the Far Eastern crisis and the great events of 1904–1906.

entities/alexander-kerensky.title: Alexander Kerensky (1881–1970)
entities/alexander-kerensky.content:
Alexander Kerensky
Alexander Fyodorovich Kerensky (1881–1970) was the head of the Provisional Government of Russia in 1917, the man who presided over the empire’s brief, fateful passage from the fall of the monarchy to the fall of the republic itself. A lawyer and a leader of the Trudovik and then the Socialist-Revolutionary movement, he rose in the february-revolution-1917 as minister of justice, then of war, and finally, in July 1917, as prime minister. His dilemma was the war: the obligation to keep Russia in the total-war-economy and honor the Allied cause against the rising demand of the army and the people for peace. Denikin, who watched him from Stavka and then from Bykhov, treats him as the man whose “victory” over the Kornilov movement cleared the road for Bolshevism, and whose final overthrow in the october-revolution-1917 ended the only alternative to both the old autocracy and the new dictatorship.
The minister of the revolution
From the first days of the revolution Kerensky was its most prominent figure — the spellbinding tribune who, as Denikin notes, drew his name, his position, and his power from “revolutionary democracy,” the socialists of the soviets and the parties of the left. He held the war portfolio in the first Provisional Government, and it fell to him to carry the army through the collapse of discipline that followed Order No. 1 of the Soviet. Denikin’s first volume records the corrosion of the army under the committee system and the impossible position of a minister who had to hold the loyalty of the revolutionary soldiers while the officers, whom he could not fully trust, watched the ruin of their command. In the war, Kerensky’s dilemma was the central question of the summer: the Provisional Government’s declaration of its determination to defend the country and the Allied cause, which Denikin dismisses as “phrases” masking the reality of an army that would no longer fight. The failed June offensive, which the revolution had been expected to revive, broke the last hope of a military solution.
The struggle with Kornilov
The crisis of the summer brought Kerensky and the commander-in-chief, lavr-kornilov, into open collision. Denikin analyses the mutual suspicion: Kornilov distrusted the premier and feared arrest; Kerensky, for his part, saw in Kornilov’s demand for the restoration of discipline a threat to the revolution and to his own supremacy, and he feared that the “strong hand” would displace the socialists. Savinkov, the war minister’s agent, moved between them. When the Kornilov movement came to its head in late August, Kerensky declared the supreme commander a mutineer and crushed the rising — with the aid, Denikin points out, of the very forces, the soviets and the revolutionaries, that would next turn against him. Denikin’s verdict is the volume’s title theme: Kerensky’s “victory” over Kornilov was the “prelude to Bolshevism.” By destroying the only organized force that could have restored order, the premier left the state defenseless before the one party, the Bolsheviks, that had a will to power.
The finale: October
After August, Denikin shows Kerensky ruling in growing isolation. The command was disarmed, the administration was “leaders without an army,” and the soviets advanced steadily upon the government. The prime minister’s own position became a personal dictatorship without force behind it — a solitude that the Bolshevik seizure of power in October exposed. The capture of Petrograd found the Provisional Government almost unresisted, and Kerensky’s attempt to rally troops at Gatchina came to nothing. He fled Russia and spent the rest of his long life in emigration, his name fixed in history as the man who, by refusing to choose between the revolution and the state, lost both. Zhevakhov’s hostile sketch of the “hysterical Kerensky” of the February days — the premier “casting lightning glances about him” at the release of the arrested dignitaries — and Denikin’s cooler analysis together frame the paradox of a tribune of the revolution who ended by serving neither the revolution nor the state.

entities/alexandra-feodorovna.title: Empress Alexandra Feodorovna (1872–1918)
entities/alexandra-feodorovna.content:
Empress Alexandra Feodorovna
Alexandra Feodorovna (born Princess Alix of Hesse-Darmstadt, 1872–1918), wife of the last Emperor Nicholas II and Empress of Russia from 1894, appears in the ecclesiastical court memoirs of Nikolai Zhevakhov as a figure of intense religious devotion whose piety drew her into the shadowy circles of the Imperial court on the eve of the revolution. Her reign as consort coincides almost exactly with the closing generation of the Russian autocracy that this corpus documents from within.
The Empress and the Church
Zhevakhov, a deputy ober-procurator of the Holy Synod and a loyalist witness of the Imperial household, presents Alexandra as a sincerely and deeply religious woman whose Orthodox faith was the governing impulse of her private life. Her audiences with churchmen, her interest in the affairs of the Synod, and her support of pious foundations run through his recollections of the war years, 1915–1917. In the same pages she is inseparable from the figure of the starets Grigori Rasputin, whose spiritual influence over the Tsarina was a scandal that the court could neither silence nor explain. Zhevakhov’s account is that of an insider who reveres the Empress yet cannot conceal the entanglement that discredited the dynasty.
The war years and the fall
In the months of the war the Empress’s authority at Tsarskoye Selo grew as the Tsar was away at the Stavka; her letters and her interventions, always cast by her defenders as maternal concern for her son’s health and for the dynasty, were read by contemporaries as the hand of a woman governed by the starets. The February Revolution of 1917 put an end to the monarchy she embodied; she was arrested with her family in March, and the corpus’s sources close with the household’s overthrow rather than its fate. The last glimpse is the Empress as a figure of the old court at the moment of its dissolution.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Alexandra is the female pole of the Rasputin question and the most intimate emblem of how the religious life of the Imperial court, in the years 1915–1917, had come to appear both fervent and fatally compromised. Her story binds the church-ecclesiastical thread of Zhevakhov’s memoirs to the collapse of the monarchy narrated by Denikin and Witte.

entities/alfredo-oriani.title: Alfredo Oriani (1852–1909)
entities/alfredo-oriani.content:
Alfredo Oriani
Alfredo Oriani (1852–1909) was an Italian novelist, historian and political thinker whose sweeping interpretation of Italian history, La lotta politica in Italia (1892), is one of the founding syntheses of Italian nationalism. Written at the very end of his life and long neglected, the work became, after his death, a touchstone for the generation that claimed to complete the Risorgimento.
The loner of Cardello
Oriani lived as a reclusive writer on his small estate of Cardello in Romagna, publishing novels and historical essays that found few readers in his lifetime. His vision was aristocratic, pessimistic and fiercely national: he saw the history of Italy as a long struggle in which the democratic principle had repeatedly failed and only strong national will could give the peninsula its due place. La lotta politica in Italia, cast as an “origins of the present struggle,” carried this reading from the fall of Rome through the communes, the signorie, the French Revolution and Napoleon, and the Risorgimento.
The three volumes
The three volumes of the corpus trace a single arc: the municipal federalism of medieval Italy and the age of the signorie; the democratic era from the French Revolution through the Restoration and the Risorgimento proper (Mazzini, 1848–49, Cavour); and finally the unification and the first decades of the Kingdom, from the war of 1859 and the Thousand through the war of 1866, the taking of Rome and the Law of Guarantees, the advent of the Left in 1876, and the African conquest closing on Dogali (1887). Throughout, Oriani’s judgment is the historian-polemicist’s: the revolution of the South is weighed against the moderation of Piedmont, the democratic ideal against the practical state-building of Cavour and his successors.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Oriani is the interpretive counterpart to the participant and contemporary narratives — the solitary thinker who turned the events Garibaldi and Tivaroni describe into a national philosophy. His third volume carries the Italian thread from 1870 through the 1880s with a synthesis that no other source in the corpus attempts.

entities/alois-aehrenthal.title: Count Alois Aehrenthal (1854–1912)
entities/alois-aehrenthal.content:
Count Alois Aehrenthal (1854–1912)
Alois Lexa von Aehrenthal, Austro-Hungarian minister of foreign affairs from 1906 to his death in 1912, was the author of the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the decisive act of the monarchy’s Balkan policy in the years before the First World War. His story in this corpus’s frame is the effort to reassert the Habsburg position in the East by a bold stroke — the tearing up of Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin — and the international crisis that stroke set off, together with his long rivalry with the chief of the general staff, conrad-von-hotzendorf, over the question of war against Serbia. Sosnosky’s survey of the monarchy’s politics opens its account of foreign policy on the road “from Schwarzenberg to Aehrenthal,” and closes its chapter on the annexation with an assessment of “Ährenthal’s annexation policy,” marking him as the figure on whom the Eastern orientation of the monarchy converged.
The making of the foreign minister
Aehrenthal came to the Ballhausplatz in 1906 as the heir of a tradition of Austrian policy that had, since the withdrawal from Germany after 1866, shifted the weight of the monarchy toward the East. Sosnosky’s account of the monarchy’s foreign affairs reviews this road from the age of Prince Felix zu Schwarzenberg and the reaction after 1848 down to Aehrenthal’s chancellorship, and presents the annexation of October 1908 as the culmination of the shift toward the Balkans. Aehrenthal’s instrument was the settlement of Berlin: the monarchy had occupied and administered Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1878 under the mandate of the congress-of-berlin-1878, but the two provinces remained under the nominal sovereignty of the Sultan, and the legal condition of the occupation was provisional. To give the administration a secure constitutional footing and to end the ambiguity, Aehrenthal conceived the plan of annexing the provinces outright.
The annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina (1908)
The act of annexation was accomplished on 6 October 1908 — a day, Sosnosky notes, of ominous association in Austrian history, for it was the date of the murder of Field Marshal Count Latour by the Viennese mob in 1848. The Kaiser’s hand-written letter to the minister of the exterior, dated at Budapest on 5 October 1908, declared that the cultural and political purposes for which the monarchy had undertaken the occupation and administration of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the successes of the existing administration bought with heavy sacrifices, could be durably secured only by the granting of constitutional institutions, for which the creation of a clear and unambiguous legal standing of the two lands was the indispensable prerequisite; he therefore extended the rights of his sovereignty over Bosnia and the Herzegovina, set the succession order in force for them, and, in token of his peaceful intentions, ordered the evacuation of the Sandjak of Novi Pazar. A proclamation to the inhabitants followed, promising constitutional institutions and a share in the decisions over the affairs of their homeland. The formal announcement appeared in the Wiener Zeitung of 7 October, while the daily papers printed the text in their morning editions of the preceding day.
The annexation tore up Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin and provoked an international crisis. There followed, as Sosnosky recounts, the crisis with the Porte, the storm in Serbia and Montenegro, and the stand of the great powers. In Belgrade the extra sheet of the Politika announced the annexation, and the Serbian foreign ministry, as Conrad recorded, demanded immediate mobilisation and war to the death against the monarchy. But the crisis was weathered: Austria-Hungary asserted itself, the war preparations of 1909 were completed, and the storm subsided.
The Friedjung trial
The annexation crisis carried with it a celebrated internal trial. The historian Dr. Heinrich Friedjung, who had been in communication with Count Aehrenthal and had used documents supplied to him in an attack on the South-Slav leaders, was confronted in the course of 1909 with the charge that these documents were forgeries, and the libel proceedings that followed — the Friedjung trial — became a scandal of the crisis. Sosnosky, who knew Friedjung and used his writings, records the affair and its bitter effect on Friedjung’s judgment, observing that Friedjung’s own opinion of Aehrenthal was by no means turned by his painful experience with him. The trial, in which the forged character of the documents against the South-Slav leaders was exposed, damaged the moral standing of the annexationist cause and became one of the enduring embarrassments of Aehrenthal’s policy.
The rivalry with Conrad
Aehrenthal’s most fateful domestic contest was with the chief of the general staff. Conrad, on entering office, sought an intimate accord with the foreign minister, writing him a courteous letter that set out his view of the connection between external policy and war preparation; the reply was formally correct and obliging, but the accord was never reached on all questions. The two men divided above all over Italy and Serbia. Conrad pressed for a preventive war against Serbia and regarded Italy as a latent enemy against whom one must prepare; Aehrenthal, pursuing a policy of diplomatic assertion that sought to avoid a general war, resisted the army’s demands. The divergence over the army budget deepened through 1911 until, in November 1911, the conflict with the minister of foreign affairs contributed to Conrad’s dismissal from the post of chief of the general staff. The clash between the soldier who urged war and the statesman who sought to win by a bold but limited stroke is one of the central tensions of the period, and it was cut short only by Aehrenthal’s death early in 1912, shortly before the outbreak of the Balkan wars that vindicated, in Conrad’s eyes, his warnings.

entities/anton-denikin.title: Anton Denikin (1872–1947)
entities/anton-denikin.content:
Anton Denikin
General Anton Ivanovich Denikin (1872–1947) was a commander of the Russian army in 1917, the successor to General lavr-kornilov at the head of the Volunteer Army in 1918, and the author of the Ocherki Russkoi Smuty (“Essays on the Russian Troubles”) — the great staff memoir-history of the collapse of authority and the army. His testimony frames this wiki’s account of the Russian revolution from the side of the command: as a general on the Romanian front in February 1917, as quartermaster-general at Stavka under Alekseev through the spring, as a prisoner of Bykhov with Kornilov in the autumn, and as the man who took up Kornilov’s work and led the white-movement after his death.
Stavka and the collapse of the army
Denikin came to the revolution as a corps commander on the Romanian front, absorbed in local concerns and isolated from the capital. The February revolution and the abdication of nicholas-ii he learned of “afterward”; his first volume records the slow ruin of the army under the new order. The decisive blow was Order No. 1 of the Soviet, which set up soldiers’ committees and broke the authority of the officers; Denikin’s account of the supplementary Order No. 2 and of the whole committee system shows the discipline of the ten-million-strong army dissolving within months. Arriving at Stavka on 25 March, he was made quartermaster-general by General Alekseev on the frank understanding that he would speak his mind. His impressions of Petrograd at the end of March, the “trifles of life at Mogilev,” and his portrait of General Markov — the second quartermaster-general, bound to him “inseparably” until his “glorious death” at the head of the Markov division — give the reader the texture of the command that tried, and failed, to hold the army together.
The Kornilov affair and Bykhov
In the struggle of the summer of 1917, Denikin was drawn wholly into the orbit of Kornilov. His second volume — The Struggle of General Kornilov — is at once a defence of the Kornilov movement, an indictment of alexander-kerensky, and a participant’s account of the rising. He was arrested with the other commanders after the collapse of the kornilov-affair-1917 and imprisoned at Bykhov, where the general staff of the coming White movement passed the autumn in confinement. His account of Kerensky’s “victory” — the solitary premier, the soviets’ growing power, the army without leaders — is among the sharpest analyses in the whole source. When the Bolsheviks took power in October and the old army dissolved, the Bykhov prisoners escaped to the Don and found their way into the Volunteer Army that Alekseev and Kaledin were forming.
Successor to Kornilov
At Ekaterinodar in the ice-march-1918, when Kornilov was killed on 31 March 1918, Denikin — his chief of staff — was asked whether he would take command. His answer, recorded in the memoir, is terse: “Yes.” He lifted the siege of Ekaterinodar, led the army back through the Kuban to the Don, and there, joined by the Drozdovtsy and with the Germans already appearing on the Don, began the longer war that his later volumes would carry beyond this wiki’s sources. His speech at Ekaterinodar in 1919, printed as the preface to the second volume, is the emblem of his cause: a curse on those who in Kornilov’s lifetime awaited his execution and promised flowers on his grave, and a tribute to the general “who loved Russia more than himself.” Denikin survived the White defeat to die in exile in America in 1947, his Essays remaining the indispensable record of the Russian Troubles from the side of those who fought to hold the state together.

entities/armando-diaz.title: Armando Diaz (1861–1928)
entities/armando-diaz.content:
Armando Diaz (1861–1928)
Armando Diaz, born in 1861 at Naples, was the Italian general who succeeded luigi-cadorna as Chief of Staff after the disaster of battle-of-caporetto-1917 and who carried the Italian army through the defensive victory of the Piave in June 1918 to the offensive of battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918 in October–November 1918 — the battle that ended the war on the Italian front. Where Cadorna had been the general of the grinding offensive, Diaz was the general of the recovery: appointed on 8 November 1917, in the middle of the retreat to the Piave, he rebuilt the broken army into a defensive instrument, repelled the Austrian attempt to cross the Piave in June 1918, and then launched the final offensive that annihilated the Austro-Hungarian army and drove it from the field. The official account of the battle, published by the Comando Supremo itself in 1918, is the principal source for his crowning victory, and Frescura’s Diario di un imboscato records the same events from the rearguard.
The succession after Caporetto
Diaz took command at the darkest hour of the Italian war. Cadorna was dismissed on 8 November 1917, with the army in retreat from the Tagliamento toward the Piave after the Austro-German breakthrough at Caporetto on 24 October. The task that fell to Diaz and his new Chief-of-Staff team was to arrest the retreat, hold the defensive line of the Piave and the Monte Grappa, and rebuild the shaken army — a work of reorganisation, reinforcement and moral restoration that Frescura’s chapter “Cadorna” sets against the reformation of the Supreme Command. Diaz chose a defensive strategy for the winter of 1917–18, husbanding the army’s strength rather than repeating the costly offensives of his predecessor, and preparing, in the months after the crisis, the “powerful offensive organism” that the official account of the final battle describes.
The Battle of the Piave (June 1918)
The first test of the new command came in June 1918, when the Austro-Hungarian army launched a great offensive to break the Italian line and settle the war in the south. The attack was arrested, in the official account’s words, “nettamente sull’altipiano e quasi nettamente sul Grappa”; where it broke through, on the Montello and the lower Piave, the enemy found itself on the same day attacked and thrown back across the river. The effect of the Italian reaction was such, the account records, that the Austrian official reports lost all hope of revenge — “così ebbero principio sul Piave le nuove sorti della guerra del mondo,” the new fortunes of the world war began on the Piave. Frescura’s La battaglia del Piave (June 1918) treats the same struggle from within the rearguard and the shelters, and the victory proved that the army which Caporetto had seemed to destroy was whole again.
Vittorio Veneto and the end of the war
In October 1918 Diaz struck. The offensive of battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918, from 24 October to 4 November 1918, was prepared on the conviction — set out in the Comando Supremo’s preface — that the fastest dissolution of the world conflict would be obtained by putting the Austrian army out of action, and so isolating Germany militarily. The Italian army forced the Piave, broke the enemy front, collapsed the Grappa front, and reached the Livenza; then came the pursuit, the recovery of the highlands, the occupation of Trento, and the landing at Trieste. “L’esercito austriaco era così annientato,” the official account concludes — the Austrian army was thus annihilated — and Austria sued for the armistice of 3 November 1918, with operations ending on all fronts on 11 November 1918. Frescura’s closing chapters, “Dal Piave alle Alpi Giulie” and “Chiuso il libro della guerra,” trace the final advance and the close of the war. The victory made Diaz a national hero, a duke and a marshal of Italy; he served as minister of war and died in 1928, remembered as the general of the redemption — the man who, taking command after the greatest disaster in Italian military history, ended the war with a total victory.

entities/benedetto-cairoli.title: Benedetto Cairoli (1825–1889)
entities/benedetto-cairoli.content:
Benedetto Cairoli
Benedetto Cairoli (1825–1889) was an Italian statesman of the Risorgimento, prime minister of the Kingdom of Italy in the years 1878–79, and a leading figure of the parliamentary Left that took power in 1876. In the corpus’s frame he appears as a survivor of the heroic age of the national movement carried into the prosaic work of governing — a veteran of the revolutionary wars, brother of the Cairoli brothers who fell as volunteers, and the head of the Left whose irredentist leanings and whose conduct of foreign policy toward Tunisia and the colonial question defined the second period of the monarchy. His premiership marked the moment when the generation of the unification, having risen on revolutionary enthusiasm, had to confront the realities of a poor, newly united state.
A revolutionary family
The name Cairoli belonged, in the memory of the Risorgimento, to a family of heroes. Oriani, evoking the volunteers of the Thousand and the national wars, recalls “intere famiglie di fratelli come i Cairoli” — whole families of brothers like the Cairolis — and numbers among the legionaries the Cairoli brothers who were to die in the ventures of the movement. The family was one of those “ultimi” — the last of the line — who went to their deaths in the republican expeditions; at the tragic enterprises of the later ‘sixties the last Cairoli brothers “dovevano morirvi,” were to die there. It was out of this world of the partito d’azione, of Mazzinian volunteers and Garibaldian legionaries, that Benedetto Cairoli came, as one of those political men, long unknown, who were to become ministers. In 1867 he was president of the central committee of the party of action at Turin, which, at the moment of the attempted insurrections, “titubò malgrado tutte le istanze di Mazzini” — hesitated despite all Mazzini’s urgings.
The advent of the Left
After the taking of Rome in 1870 and the law of the Guarantees, the older generation of the national movement passed from revolution into the state. The advent of the Left in 1876, which closed the long supremacy of the Right under Cavour’s successors, brought to power the men of the partito d’azione — Cairoli, Depretis, Crispi, the radicals of the historical Left. Oriani treats this as the opening of “il secondo periodo monarchico,” the second monarchical period, in which the Left, the party of the men who had once been Garibaldians and conspirators, took the direction of the kingdom. Cairoli stood among the principal leaders of this new ruling group, the survivors of the heroic generation now charged with the government of a state that had emerged from the Risorgimento exhausted and poor.
The premiership
Cairoli became prime minister in March 1878, at the head of a Left ministry. The succession of ministries in these years was rapid and confused — Fortunato’s list of the Thirteenth Legislature records the alternation of Depretis and Cairoli ministries: the first ministry of Depretis (1876–77), a second of Depretis (1877–78), then “1° Min. Cairoli, dal marzo al dicem. ‘78,” the first Cairoli ministry from March to December 1878; then a third Depretis ministry, a second Cairoli ministry from July to November 1879, and a third Cairoli ministry from November 1879. This was the era of unstable parliamentary majorities that Fortunato, as a young deputy of the dissidence, criticised — the era in which the Left, having broken the Depretis majorities, could not itself hold power steadily. Cairoli’s own tenure was short and embattled, caught between the factions of his own party.
Irredentist leanings
Cairoli’s politics carried the mark of his revolutionary past. As a leader of the Left he was associated with the irredentist tendency — the current of opinion, strong among the men of the partito d’azione, that looked to the redemption of the “unredeemed” Italian lands still under Austrian rule, Trentino and Trieste. Fortunato, addressing the electors of Melfi, invoked Cairoli and Zanardelli by name in the context of the national cause and the Italian “fratelli” beyond the frontier, praying that the state would not “togliere con una mano ciò che diamo con l’altra” — take away with one hand what it gives with the other. The irredentist sympathy was a source of difficulty for the monarchy, straining its relations with Austria-Hungary and complicating the very alliances on which Italy’s security rested.
The colonial reverses
The great failure of Cairoli’s years in office lay in the colonial and foreign field. The “conquista africana” — the African conquest — which Oriani treats as the theme of the second monarchical period, led Italy into the Red Sea and toward the colonial adventures that ended in the disaster of Dogali (24 January 1887). The reverses in Tunisia — where France established her protectorate in 1881, to the chagrin of the Italian colonial party — and the subsequent African reverses fell upon the governments that followed the Left’s advent, and the irredentist-cum-colonial policy with which Cairoli’s name was linked contributed to the mood of disappointment that Fortunato chronicled. The defeat at Dogali, closing Oriani’s narrative, marked the bitter end of the African phase begun in the years of Cairoli and the Left.
Legacy
Cairoli died in 1889, at the end of the decade that had seen the Left in power and the beginnings of the African and colonial disappointments. He stands in this corpus as the representative of the revolutionary generation turned statesman — the Garibaldian and party-of-action veteran who took his place among the leaders of the Left, whose irredentist sympathies and whose ministries of 1878–79 marked the passage from the Risorgimento to the mundane politics of the new kingdom, and whose name was linked to the colonial reverses that Oriani recorded. He embodies the tension between the heroic ideal of the national movement and the difficult realities of the Italian state that Fortunato, from the South, so persistently lamented.

entities/camillo-cavour.title: Camillo Cavour (1810–1861)
entities/camillo-cavour.content:
Camillo Cavour (1810–1861)
Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, was the Piedmontese statesman who engineered the unification of Italy, and he stands at the very edge of this corpus’s frame: born in 1810, he died on 6 June 1861, weeks after the kingdom he had created had come into being, and therefore just before the 1866 starting-point of this wiki’s survey. He is included here as the indispensable predecessor — the architect whose death left the new Kingdom of Italy to be governed by his successors, and whose methods, in Oriani’s judgment, were never again equalled. Tivaroni, in the gallery of the men of the Risorgimento with which he closes his history, devotes to Cavour the fullest of his portraits — the youth, the journalist, the deputy and minister, the judgements upon him, his mind, and the judgement of posterity — and Oriani treats him as the mind of the “royal conquest” that complemented Garibaldi’s popular one.
From journalist to minister
Cavour came late to politics, as a journalist and economic reformer of Piedmont before he entered the ministry. Tivaroni’s portrait traces his youth in the conservative Piedmontese world, his turn to English-style liberalism, and his establishment as the leading parliamentary figure of the constitutional monarchy. After the defeat of 1849 and the accession of victor-emmanuel-ii, Cavour rose through the ministries to become prime minister, and from 1852 governed Piedmont in the interest of a national policy that the other Italian states could not pursue. His instruments were the Statuto, a free parliament, a modernized administration, and a diplomacy that lifted the little subalpine kingdom into the councils of the great powers — most strikingly by joining the Crimean war in 1855 to secure a seat at the peace table.
The war of 1859 and the annexations
Cavour’s decisive stroke was the alliance with France. At the secret meeting of Plombières he and Napoleon III agreed on a war against Austria, and in 1859 the Franco-Sardinian armies won the battles of Magenta and Solferino and drove the Austrians out of Lombardy. The peace of Villafranca, which Napoleon III concluded behind Cavour’s back and which left the Veneto still Austrian, provoked his furious resignation; but the revolutions of central Italy in 1859–60, which overthrew the old regimes in Florence, Modena, Parma and Bologna, and the cession of Nice and Savoy to France as the price of the annexation of the centre, restored him to office to complete the work. The year 1860 saw the expedition-of-the-thousand-1860 conquer the South under Garibaldi, and Cavour — fearing a revolution he could not control — sent the royal army through the Marches to meet it, so that the plebiscites of October 1860 delivered the whole peninsula to Victor Emmanuel’s crown.
The last months and the death of 6 June 1861
In the spring of 1861 the first Italian Parliament assembled, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed with Victor Emmanuel II as its king and Rome as its nominal capital. Cavour’s last months were occupied with the consolidation of the new state — the finances, the unsettled South where brigandage was already rising, and the vain negotiations with the Holy See over Rome. He died on 6 June 1861, before any of these tasks was resolved. Tivaroni’s account of his death — “La morte del conte di Cavour” — frames it as the moment at which the state lost the mind that had made it; the ministries that followed, those of Ricasoli, Rattazzi, Farini-Minghetti and Lamarmora, would govern the peninsula until 1866 without his commanding intelligence. Oriani’s verdict is that none of his successors ever showed his greatness: the mediocre show of the first ministries is for Oriani the proof of how much the new kingdom owed to a single man, and how uncertainly it could steer itself without him. Cavour thus belongs to this corpus less as an actor within its years than as the foundation with which every subsequent Italian politician — and above all the parliamentary men of the post-unification decades — had to reckon.

entities/carlo-tivaroni.title: Carlo Tivaroni (1826–1898)
entities/carlo-tivaroni.content:
Carlo Tivaroni
Carlo Tivaroni (1826–1898) was an Italian patriot and historian, author of the monumental Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, of which the L’Italia degli Italiani volumes in this corpus form the third series. A participant in the struggles he narrated, he brought to his history the memory of the revolutionary generation and the partisan viewpoint of the moderate national movement.
A patriot historian
Born in 1826, Tivaroni belonged to the generation that made the Risorgimento. His Storia critica, published in the decades after unification, was one of the most ambitious contemporary histories of the movement, cast in a critical and narrative mode that sought to explain how Italy was made. The two volumes used here carry the story from the war of 1859 through the acquisition of the Veneto in 1866 and the taking of Rome in 1870.
The two volumes
The second Italia degli Italiani volume (1859–1866) narrates the battles of Magenta, Solferino and Villafranca; the revolutions and annexations of central Italy and the cession of Savoy and Nice; the Expedition of the Thousand, the conquest of the Two Sicilies and the fall of Gaeta; the death of Cavour (6 June 1861); and the succession of ministries of the new Kingdom under Ricasoli, Rattazzi, Farini-Minghetti and Lamarmora. The third volume (1866–1870) covers the war of 1866 against Austria, the Roman question from the Syllabus through Mentana, and the breach of Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, closing with a retrospective on the national idea and portraits of the leading figures of the Risorgimento.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Tivaroni is the contemporary consolidator narrative of Italian unification — the moderate-national historian who frames the wars, annexations and ministries as the unfolding of the national idea. He complements the first-person account of Garibaldi and the philosophic synthesis of Oriani, and provides the constitutional and diplomatic detail of the new Kingdom’s early years.
