entities/charles-peguy.title: Charles Péguy (1873–1914)
entities/charles-peguy.content:
Charles Péguy
Charles Péguy (1873–1914) was a French poet, essayist and the founder of the Cahiers de la Quinzaine, the review through which he gave voice to the Dreyfusard generation of the Third Republic. Born at Orléans of modest stock, he arrived in Paris a socialist and a republican by heredity, and his public career was an unbroken argument with the France of his own time — an argument he carried on as a man of letters, editor and publisher rather than as a party man. In the corpus’s frame he stands chiefly for one idea: the distinction between a mystique and the politique into which it decays, and the conviction that the Republic of his fathers had been a thing of faith which his own generation had allowed to become a thing of office. He died on the Marne in September 1914, in the first weeks of the war that closed the period.
Founder of the Cahiers
Péguy was, above all, a man of the review. The Cahiers de la Quinzaine was not a newspaper but a continuing book, a series of pamphlets issued a dozen times a year, each devoted to a single work — often Péguy’s own, often the writings of his collaborators Daniel Halévy and Jean Variot and the circle gathered around him. It was, as he insisted, “une compagnie parfaitement libre d’hommes qui tous croient à quelque chose,” a free company of men who all believed in something. He ran the enterprise in poverty and defiance, printing what he chose regardless of the market, and in so doing made the Cahiers one of the rare organs of the intellectual Left that answered to no party discipline. Its survival through years of financial difficulty and isolation was itself, for Péguy, a profession of faith.
The mystique of the Republic
The central act of Péguy’s public life was the Dreyfus affair, which he called “our youth.” A Dreyfusard of the first hour, he treated the fight for the revision of Captain Dreyfus’s conviction not as a juridical quarrel but as the last surge of republican heroism — “le dernier sursaut, le soubresaut suprême de cet héroïsme et de cette mystique.” In Notre jeunesse (1910) he set down what the affair had meant. His generation, he held, was “l’arrière-garde,” a rear-guard a little isolated, the last that possessed the republican mystique — the lived faith for which “les républicains étaient héroïques et que la République avait les mains pures.” His fathers had possessed this faith as an organic instinct; the young had it only as a set of propositions. “La mystique républicaine, c’était quand on mourait pour la République; la politique républicaine, c’est à présent qu’on en vit” — the republican mystique was when men died for the Republic; the republican politique is when they live off it. That single sentence condensed his whole indictment of the Republic that had triumphed.
Mystique and politique
The distinction between mystique and politique was Péguy’s most famous legacy. A mystique, in his usage, was a living faith, a deep movement of the soul; politique was what the parties made of it once they took it over. The political parties, he wrote, can speak only the political, parliamentary language, and they translate — traducunt, tradunt, they translate and they betray — everything that is done for the mystiques. The corruption of Dreyfusard mystique into Dreyfusard politique was for him the emblem of the age: the generous enthusiasm of 1898 had become the spoils of office. He recalled that since that degeneration his circle had known fifteen years of poverty defending Christian consciences and republican liberties, only to find reactionary politicians forbidding them to be republicans and republican politicians forbidding them to be Christians.
Men of eternal and temporal salvation
Beneath the political quarrel Péguy found a religious one. The adversaries in the affair spoke the language of reason of state, of the temporal salvation of the people and the race — that one must not sacrifice a whole people for one man. The Dreyfusards, by contrast, spoke in a deep Christian movement: “une seule injustice, un seul crime… suffit à rompre tout le pacte social, tout le contrat social,” one injustice, one crime suffices to break the whole social pact. He drew the division between “les hommes du salut éternel” and “les hommes du salut temporel,” the men of eternal and the men of temporal salvation; the Dreyfusards did not wish France constituted in a state of mortal sin. To make the point he invoked Saint Louis, who told his clerk he would rather be a leper thirty times over than commit a single mortal sin. In the same spirit he honoured Bernard-Lazare, “né à Nîmes le 14 juin 1865; mort à Paris le premier septembre 1903,” as the prophet of the affair, the first defender of Dreyfus, whose word — “Il est innocent, c’est déjà beaucoup,” he is innocent, that is already much — he called “le mot décisif de l’affaire.”
Against the modern world
Péguy’s quarrel extended beyond the parties to the age itself. He set against his own generation “le monde moderne,” those who “ne croient plus à rien, qui s’en font gloire et orgueil,” who make a glory and a pride of believing in nothing — “pas même à l’athéisme.” He saw the de-republicanisation of France and its de-Christianisation as one single movement of “démystication,” by which the people no longer believed either in the Republic or in God, a “stérilité moderne” that dried up alike the political and the Christian city. It was, he wrote, “la première fois dans l’histoire du monde que tout un monde vit et prospère, paraît prospérer contre toute culture.” Yet he did not despair: “cette race en a vu bien d’autres,” and he hoped the coming generation would be “enfin une génération mystique.” He would not, for all his grief at the Republic’s decay, take refuge in derision — no culture is founded, he held, on sarcasm — and he closed Notre jeunesse on a note of defiant loyalty to the Republic, warning the royalists that if they ever became a real menace they would see what his company was still capable of doing for France.
Significance
Péguy stands in this corpus as the conscience of the Dreyfusard generation and the great theorist of the mystique-politique distinction. His essay Notre jeunesse is a defining text of the intellectual history of the Third Republic between the affair and the war, aligning the republican mystique with the Christian, setting the eternal above the temporal salvation of the state, and warning against a modern world that prospered against every culture. Killed on the Marne in 1914, he belonged both to the France that had come out of the affair and to the Catholic-renewal current that Sabatier surveyed on the eve of the war; his death made him one of the emblematic figures of the generation the war consumed.

entities/comte-de-chambord.title: Comte de Chambord, Henri V (1820–1883)
entities/comte-de-chambord.content:
Comte de Chambord, Henri V (1820–1883)
The legitimist pretender to the throne of France, known to his partisans as Henri V, whose refusal to abandon the white flag of the Bourbons blocked the monarchical restoration of 1873 and thereby sealed the survival of the Republic. The comte de Chambord, grandson of Charles X, was the last serious claimant of the elder line; his letter of 27 October 1873, refusing the tricolour, destroyed the fusion of the two branches of the house of Bourbon and forced the monarchical majority to fall back on the septennat-1873 that handed the Republic its foundation.
The pretender
The comte de Chambord was the posthumous son of the duc de Berry, born at the height of the Restoration in 1820, and the recognized head of the elder Bourbon line. Exiled after 1830, he had lived at Frohsdorf and the Austrian and Italian courts, the perpetual claimant of a throne France had not offered him. Hanotaux records his character as a man of principle and of the old monarchy, faithful to his faith and to his flag, who regarded himself as the trustee of the legitimacy of the Bourbons. His sense of royal honour, and of the divine right on which he believed the crown rested, was absolute.
The hopes of 1873
After the fall of adolphe-thiers on 24 May 1873 the monarchical majority of the National Assembly believed the restoration was at hand. The programme was “fusion”: the union of the two branches of the house of Bourbon, by which the comte de Paris, head of the Orléans branch, would defer to the elder pretender, and the crown of a restored monarchy would pass in time to the Orléans. The comte de Paris came to Frohsdorf; the Orléans princes were elected deputies; the three monarchical parties — legitimist, Orléanist, and Bonapartist — plotted together. Hanotaux frames the whole campaign as a high cause ruined in verbal dissension, a tragicomedy of representative illusion disposing of France without consulting her.
The mission to Salzburg
The decisive episode was the delegation of Charles Chesnelong to the comte de Chambord at Salzburg in October 1873. The monarchists, anxious to secure the pretender’s acceptance of the tricolour flag of the Revolution, sent their emissary to obtain his agreement to the constitutional conditions and above all to the flag. Chesnelong’s interviews at Salzburg seemed to promise much; he returned on 16 October believing the campaign could go forward. But the pretender’s prolonged silence, and the reports that filtered out, alarmed the monarchical chiefs who had already committed the army and the country.
The letter of 27 October
On 27 October 1873 the comte de Chambord wrote his fateful letter, refusing the tricolour and insisting on the white flag of the Bourbons. “The only sacrifice I cannot make is that of my honour,” he declared; by his unshakable fidelity to his faith and his flag, he argued, it was the honour of France itself that he upheld. The letter killed the restoration at a stroke. The comte de Paris’s unpublished letter of 15 October had already sketched the line of retreat toward the Marshal; the monarchical campaign was abandoned, and the council of ministers pronounced instead for prorogation of Mac-Mahon’s powers. The pretender’s intransigence had done what all the republicans could not: it had cleared the way for the Republic.
The man who saved the Republic
In the aftermath Chambord still contemplated a direct adventure, and he came to Versailles, where Blacas carried his cause to the Marshal — who refused to receive him. The monarchical chiefs, their plans in ruins, clung to the septennat; the extreme right was left in embarrassment, and Chambord left Versailles. Hanotaux’s conclusion is that the expectant policy once more profited the Republic: by refusing the one concession that could have crowned a king, the legitimist pretender condemned the monarchical cause and assured that the Republic would be voted — by a majority of one voice on 30 January 1875 — in a hostile Assembly. The comte de Chambord, who believed he was defending the honour of France, was in the event the unwitting founder of the Third Republic. He died in 1883, the monarchy never restored.

entities/comte-de-palikao.title: Count de Palikao (1796–1878)
entities/comte-de-palikao.content:
Count de Palikao
Charles Cousin-Montauban, comte de Palikao (1796–1878), was the French general who headed the government that succeeded Émile Ollivier’s liberal ministry after the catastrophes of August 1870, presiding over the last days of the Second Empire before the revolution of 4 September. His ministry of 9 August 1870 was the regime’s desperate final bid for survival, and his name, along with those of Bazaine and Mac-Mahon, is bound up in the sources with the responsibility for the empire’s military ruin.
The soldier
Palikao had made his reputation as a colonial and expeditionary commander — his earlier service in Algeria and the China expedition of 1860 (from which his title derived) marked him as a soldier of action rather than a parliamentary statesman. When the disasters of Wissembourg, Wœrth and Forbach in early August 1870 revealed the army’s collapse and the fall of the ministry of 2 January became inevitable, the Empress-regent and the imperial circle turned to a soldier to restore confidence.
Head of the ministry
On 9 August 1870 Palikao formed the ministry that replaced Ollivier’s, with the Emperor stripped of direct command and the new government cast as a ministry of public safety for the war. Ollivier’s memoir of the fall of his own government treats Palikao’s accession and the accounts the general gave of it with the partisan suspicion of a deposed minister. Palikao’s government proved powerless to arrest the German march on Metz and Paris; within weeks the proclamation of the Republic on 4 September swept it away. He spent the rest of his life abroad, his reputation consumed by the ruin of the empire he had failed to save.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Palikao is the terminal figure of the liberal Empire — the soldier-politician called in when the parliamentary experiment had failed and the dynasty was fighting for its life, and the last head of government before the fall. His brief ministry marks the transition from the Empire libéral of Ollivier to the Republic of the 1870s.

entities/conrad-von-hotzendorf.title: Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925)
entities/conrad-von-hotzendorf.content:
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925)
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf, chief of the Austro-Hungarian general staff in 1906–1911 and again from December 1912, was the leading soldier of the monarchy in the decade before the First World War and the man who more than any other shaped its war plans against Serbia, Russia and Italy. His story in this corpus’s frame runs from his appointment in 1906, through the annexation crisis and the Balkan wars when he pressed unceasingly for a preventive war, to his reinstatement in 1912 and his command in the opening campaigns of 1914, and ends with his relief from office in 1917. The great instrument of his memory is his five-volume memoir Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, written in the collapse after 1918 to set down — as he said, not as a general history but as purely personal records — the political and military career that the memory of the old army had come to need.
The calling to the general staff
Conrad came to the highest military post late and by reluctant steps. In the spring of 1899 he was colonel and regimental commander in Austrian Silesia; on 9 April 1899 he was appointed brigadier at Trieste and promoted major-general three weeks later, and as the senior general there soon took over the military station command when the senior admiral left the post of sea-district commander. The position imposed on him political as well as purely military duties, and from Trieste he gained an early picture of the situation whose essential conclusion, as he recorded it, was that it was a utopia to count on Italy as an ally — one had rather to be prepared to be deserted by Italy, and in all likelihood attacked, as soon as a favourable opportunity offered. His summons to the office of chief of the general staff in 1906 came against his own pleading to be excused, and he set down in his memoir the stages through which a man in an exposed official position passes — first congratulated, then observed, then criticised, then abused, and finally pelted with stones — through all of which he said he had since passed.
The governing conviction of his whole peacetime activity, he declared, was that the monarchy was threatened by dangers to its very existence that his opponents in opinion either did not estimate at their full magnitude or believed they could escape by temporising, whereas he was convinced they could be met only by preventive action. The dangers were the disintegrating national movements within, the aggressive tendencies of Serbia, Russia and Italy, and the indirect dangers flowing from Austria-Hungary’s alliance with Germany. In these he saw the determining factors for the conduct of internal and external policy, and the necessity of reckoning with war as their means. From the first he sought an intimate connection between external policy and the work of war preparation, and on entering office wrote a courteous letter to the minister of foreign affairs, Baron Ährenthal, asking his support in common working; the reply was a formally correct and obliging letter, but in time many divergences of opinion led to it that the accord he held so indispensable was not reached on all questions.
The annexation crisis and the war against Serbia
In the years of the bosnian-annexation-crisis-1908 Conrad’s view of the South-Slav question hardened into the conviction that would govern him for the rest of his career. He described the process by which the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to be proclaimed, and the friction the crisis produced between the general staff and the foreign ministry. When the extra sheet of the Belgrade Politika announced on 6 October 1908 that the annexation was to be proclaimed, the Serbian foreign ministry demanded immediate mobilisation and war to the death against the monarchy — a mood, he insisted, that was not first called forth by the annexation question but was the permanent keynote, breaking out spontaneously at the least occasion. Already in 1906, on his appointment, he had pointed to the settlement with Serbia as the root of all evil; in 1908–09 he described the moment as come to make clear conditions with the monarchy’s southern neighbour, foreseeing that the chances of this unavoidable settlement must from then on only grow worse.
Against Italy his mistrust was equally fixed. He had from Trieste concluded that Italy must be reckoned a potential enemy, and he laboured in the years of office for measures against a possible Italian war, urging that the monarchy, with its manifold frontiers and its exposed position, could not restrict its war preparations to a few limited war-cases as Spain and Italy could. His proposal of an action against Italy in 1908 foundered on the resistance of the foreign ministry, and the conviction grew on him that the moment when one might act with the back safely covered against Italy was always slipping away. It was on this ground that his conflict with Count Ährenthal deepened year by year.
Dismissal and reinstatement (1911–1912)
The divergences between the military requirements Conrad pressed and the conduct of the foreign ministry came at last to open rupture. He demanded the creation of six army inspectors as future commanders-in-chief and the reinforcement of the army, and clashed with the minister of foreign affairs and the authorities over the means the exposed position of the monarchy demanded. On the afternoon of 29 November 1911 he was told on the archduke-heir’s behalf that on the following day he was to appear in audience before the Kaiser, who would announce his dismissal from the post of chief of the general staff with simultaneous appointment as army inspector. Conrad replied that he had no thought of sulking, that he had done his service as chief as well as he could, and was glad to be rid of a post that had in any case been forced upon him and to come again nearer to the troops. On 30 November 1911 the Kaiser at Schönbrunn told him that he was obliged to remove him from his present post and appoint him army inspector; and the personal relation, the Kaiser was graciously pleased to say, had become a friendly one.
The dismissal lasted barely a year. With the outbreak of the first balkan-wars-1912-13 in October 1912 the whole situation of the monarchy was changed, and the archduke-heir franz-ferdinand charged Conrad with a mission to Bukarest to secure Rumania for the case of war against Russia, under the outward pretext of conveying the Kaiser’s condolences to King Carol on the death of the Countess of Flanders. On 7 December 1912 the archduke received him at the Belvedere, where the maps of the various theatres of war lay on the tables, and turned to him suddenly: “So, now I must tell you something more; you must become chief of the general staff again.” Conrad hesitated and objected that it would not be right to remove his successor who had been appointed barely a year before; but the archduke answered that this removal would take place with all honour for the person concerned, and that he, as presumptive supreme commander of the army, must lay weight on having at the head of the general staff, should it come to war, the man from whom all the preparations for war proceeded. On 12 December 1912 Conrad received the hand-written warrant of the Kaiser reinstating him, and took up again his activity in that office.
1913 and the last moment
Reinstated, Conrad pressed with redoubled force for what he called the last moment. In 1913 he set down his conviction with the greatest plainness: the root of all evil for the monarchy was still, as always, the relation to Serbia and to the Russia standing behind Serbia, and at this root the evil had to be seized; everything else was secondary. The ways that had always floated before him were, in the first place, the attainment of a lasting confederal union of Serbia with the Habsburg monarchy in a peaceful manner; but if Serbia declined the union and continued its hostile aspirations directed against the monarchy — and this case, he held, was present — then a warlike settlement at the suitable moment. In 1913 he held the last moment to have come to carry out this settlement at all with hope of success; if this moment too were neglected, the monarchy seemed to him to drift without a rudder toward the unavoidable doom that threatened it from Serbia and Russia. It remained unused. The policy of the monarchy, he lamented, let itself be taken prisoner by side-issues and distracted from the great goal — to the joy of its enemies.
The account of 1913 and the first half of 1914, as he rendered it month by month, carries the reader through the second Balkan war, the Skutari affair, the peace of Bucharest and of Constantinople, and his own rupture with the archduke-heir after the manoeuvres in Bohemia, down to the last audiences and the departure for Sarajevo on 23 June 1914, four days before the assassination. The war he had so long foretold came with the sarajevo-assassination-1914, and Conrad entered it as the commander whose plans he had spent his whole tenure preparing, an episode that Czernin, a critic of his conduct, recorded from the proximity of the court.
The world war and the relief
In the war Conrad commanded through the opening campaigns of 1914 — the terrible fighting of the east, the engagements that belong to the story of the battle-of-galicia-1914 — and continued at the head of the army through the exhausting years that followed, drawing ever closer to the front of the military-dictatorship that his opponents accused him of seeking. His memoir carried the account through the war years to his relief from office in 1918, when he closed his military career and withdrew into private life, at first, as he said, with no thought of writing memoirs. It was the collapse of the old fatherland and its glorious army, and the many publications and requests that reached him, that moved him at last to set down his experiences. He professed the philosophical conviction that not individual men make their time, but that the time makes its men — that the men who stand by chance at the head of great epochs act by obeying the impulses dictated by the great drift of the age, and are commonly identified with successes and failures that are in truth caused only by the great course of historical development. States and peoples, like trees in a forest, germinate, strike root, grow and spread, and when their lifetime runs out they break down to make room for new formations.

entities/emile-ollivier.title: Émile Ollivier (1825–1913)
entities/emile-ollivier.content:
Émile Ollivier (1825–1913)
Émile Ollivier was a French lawyer, orator and statesman of the liberal Opposition who became the head of the government of the liberal-empire — the “ministry of 2 January 1870” — and who, by his own account, bore the decision for the war of 1870. He is at once a protagonist of the Second Empire’s last years and the author of the great memoir-history L’Empire libéral that this wiki draws on for the crisis of July and August 1870. No other figure of the corpus is so entangled in the central question of the war’s responsibility, and no other defends himself so explicitly against the charge of having gone to war “au cœur léger” (with a light heart).
The liberal deputy who rallied to the Empire
Ollivier began as a republican and a young opponent of the Empire, but in the 1860s he moved toward the position that the dynasty could be transformed from within — that a “liberal Empire” was possible and preferable to sterile opposition. Delord, the republican historian, watches this evolution with suspicion. At the opening of the session of 1867, in the wake of the Emperor’s letter of 19 January promising interpellation and press and meetings laws, Ollivier astonished his friends by rallying to the majority. In the same session he turned on the ministry and called Rouher, the authoritarian vice-emperor, the “vice-empereur.” Delord presents the rallying of Ollivier as the emblem of a regime that bought reformers by conceding liberty piecemeal. Through the elections of 1869 and the extraordinary session, Ollivier’s star rose as the natural leader of the tiers-parti, the centre that would reconcile the dynasty and the Chambers.
The ministry of 2 January 1870
The formation of the government of 2 January 1870 was the work of long negotiation, conducted between the Emperor and Ollivier through Clément Duvernois. Delord’s chapter “Préface de l’Empire libéral” recounts Ollivier’s conditions and programme, his disguised journey to Compiègne, and the Emperor’s final acceptance; the ministry was completed only when Daru and Buffet agreed to enter, and it was Magne who was sacrificed to bring them in. With this ministry the senatus-consult of 1870 made the ministers responsible to the Corps législatif, and Ollivier, though without the formal title, stood at the head of the government. The liberal Empire, in his own conception, was the honest attempt to give the Second Empire the parliamentary institutions it had always lacked. Sybel, from the German side, treats Ollivier’s ministry as a sign of French weakness and indecision rather than of renewal — a cabinet caught between the Court, the war party and the parliamentary Left.
The July 1870 crisis and the decision for war
In July 1870 Ollivier was at the centre of the hohenzollern-candidature-1870 crisis. When Leopold of Hohenzollern’s acceptance of the Spanish crown was revealed, the ministry resolved to turn aside the candidacy by diplomacy, and Ollivier read from the tribune the ministerial declaration of 6 July. He records his despair at the trap, his efforts to confine the quarrel to the candidacy and to set aside older grievances, and his repeated attempts to keep the peace even after the demand of guarantees was forced upon the government by the Right. In his account it was Bismarck’s falsification of the ems-dispatch-1870 — the soufflet, the “slap in the face” — that made war unavoidable, and it was to this outrage that France was bound to reply. On 15 July 1870 Ollivier read the declaration of war to the Chamber of Deputies; replying to Thiers, who had argued that this was the wrong occasion to avenge Sadowa, he pronounced the words for which he was afterwards condemned: that he accepted the war “le cœur léger,” certain in his conscience that France had not wanted it. His own volume L’Empire libéral is framed from its opening as a defence of this decision and of the ministry’s conduct against the postwar verdict of a “mediocre talker whose presumptuous ineptitude lost two provinces.”
The fall of the ministry, 9 August 1870
The war opened with disaster. At Wissembourg on 4 August and at battle-of-woerth-1870 and Forbach on 6 August the French armies were beaten, and the news broke over Paris on the night of the 6th and the days that followed. Ollivier’s own memoir of these days — Le Suicide — is among the most intimate in the corpus: the false news of a victory on the balconies of the Ministry of Justice, the rising agitation in the capital, the cries of “Ollivier à la lanterne! Vive la République!” in the streets. He worked for national defence, attempted to arrest the revolutionary chiefs, and pressed for the Emperor’s return to Paris, while the Court and the Empress moved against him. On 9 August 1870 the Chamber, turned against the ministry by a coalition of the Right and Left united on the Duvernois motion, forced his resignation. Ollivier was dismissed by the Empress; the new government was formed by General Cousin-Montauban, comte de Palikao. He calls the overthrow of his cabinet a “national catastrophe,” the first act of the Empire’s suicide.
The memoirist and his verdicts
After 1870 Ollivier lived as a private citizen, and devoted his later decades to writing L’Empire libéral (published from 1895), a massive apologia-and-history in which the July crisis, the battles and the fall of his ministry are recounted in exhaustive detail with a block of documentary éclaircissements. His two volumes in this corpus — the fourteenth, La Guerre, on July 1870, and the sixteenth, Le Suicide, on the opening disasters — carry his double purpose: to vindicate the liberal Empire and its decision for war, and to fix responsibility. He is generous to Mac-Mahon, who “accused no one,” and severe on the charge against Marshal Bazaine, whose conduct at Metz he analyses at length; he attacks the German thesis that Bismarck was innocent of the war, arguing that Bismarck alone organised the candidacy and falsified the dispatch, and that serious historians of all nations place the responsibility on him. As a source he is a participant whose honesty and self-interest must be weighed together — the very debate the corpus preserves.

entities/ferenc-deak.title: Ferenc Deák (1803–1876)
entities/ferenc-deak.content:
Ferenc Deák
Ferenc Deák (1803–1876), whom his countrymen called a haza bölcse, “the sage of the fatherland,” was the Hungarian statesman who prepared and carried through the Compromise (Ausgleich) of 1867. He had been the author of the April Laws of 1848 that set up the responsible Hungarian ministry; after the failure of the revolution and the years of absolutism that followed, he became the architect of the settlement that restored Hungarian self-government within a dualist monarchy. Beksics’s A dualismus is in effect a monument to Deák and to the conception that bears his name — the work that, as Beksics concludes, “answers the interests of both Hungary and Austria” and “gave form to a centuries-long historical development.” The great creation “on which Deák’s name is written,” Beksics insists, “need not be feared from the weak breezes of internal quarrels.”
The author of the April Laws
The constitutional settlement of 1848, by which the Hungarian state acquired a responsible ministry and its own ordering of the common affairs with Austria, was Deák’s work. It was this foundation — the establishment of Hungarian statehood on the basis of the historical constitution and the Pragmatic Sanction — that the revolution of 1848–49 overran and that the reaction after Világos swept away. When the war ended in disaster and the provisorium of absolutist administration followed, Deák’s programme of legal, constitutional opposition was the alternative to the insurrectionary path of Lajos Kossuth, whom Deák condemned. In the revolutionary years, as Sosnosky notes, Deák was counted among the ministers of the settlement, and his moderation stood in contrast to the passionate self-assertion of the Magyar movement.
The architect of the Compromise
After the defeats of 1866, Deák resumed the negotiations between the Crown and Hungary. He could boast, as Sosnosky records, that even after the severe humiliation and weakening of Austria he asked no more for Hungary than before the war. His moderation was not generosity but prudence: he would not overdraw the bow, being certain he could obtain no more whatever he asked, and what he asked was already considerable — nothing less than the conversion of the old unitary empire into a novel double state. The Crown’s first serious scruples concerned the unity of the army. In the drafting of the much-contested § 11 of the Hungarian Compromise act, Deák’s first proposed wording spoke only of “the army”; the opposition in the subcommittee, led by Kálmán Tisza and Ghyczy, demanded that a separate Hungarian army be recognised. Deák answered that he too would wish for a separate Hungarian army, but that the law article of 1715 (which provided for a paid army maintained by Hungary but recruited from foreigners as well as Hungarians and at the ruler’s disposal) stood in the way. He denied the historical right of a distinct Hungarian force with the famous words: “What is that, the Hungarian army? Such a thing has never existed, neither in law nor in practice; there was only ever talk of a block of Hungarian regiments.” With these words, writes Sosnosky, “the sage of the nation,” celebrated by the Magyars themselves as their greatest statesman, deprived the Magyar demands of their historical justification, and one of their main supports collapsed.
When the opposition still refused to accept the necessity of unity, Deák spoke the momentous words: “That would be personal union! Let us say the word, and the curse will fall upon us.” Andrássy supported him. Yet Sosnosky notes a “fatal inconsistency”: Deák was strangely induced, to satisfy Ghyczy, to weave the “Hungarian army” into the wording of the paragraph after all — an inconsistency that only the pressure of the moment explains, but which kept the dispute alive. The Compromise act, with these and other modifications, was adopted by the Hungarian lower house on 30 March 1867 by 257 against 117 votes, and shortly after by the Magnates. The Austrian Reichsrat, never asked to consent to the transformation of the whole monarchy, tacitly acquiesced — sending a deputation to the coronation of Franz Joseph as King of Hungary that amounted to a formal recognition of the Hungarian settlement.
The “sage of the fatherland”
Sosnosky, though sharply critical of the Ausgleich as a work, is at pains not to wrong its creators. “Deák and Andrássy,” he writes, “were moved by the best intentions and accomplished an extremely laborious work that put their patience and their working power to a hard test”; but patience and force of will are not enough to create a great work, which requires also success, and success “was not granted to the work of Deák and Andrássy,” for it already carried in itself the visible germ of strife. Beksics takes the opposite view, defending the Compromise as the natural and indestructible outcome of centuries of development: the dualism existed before 1848, the common affairs and their management existed, and through all the centuries only one thing had proved firm and immovable — “the tie that binds Hungary to Austria through the dynasty, and its consequence, the union of the two mutually independent states for mutual defence and for that alone.” On this foundation Deák’s work rested, and against it the “weak breezes of internal quarrels” could not prevail. Whatever their difference of judgement, both writers agree on the scale of the man: the constitution-maker who stood at the head of the Hungarian nation in its settlement with the dynasty, and whose name gave its character to the Dual Monarchy that endured until 1918.

entities/francesco-crispi.title: Francesco Crispi (1818–1901)
entities/francesco-crispi.content:
Francesco Crispi (1818–1901)
Francesco Crispi, born in Sicily in 1818, was the most formidable of the Italian statesmen of the second half of the century — a republican revolutionary of the Risorgimento who became, late in life, the strong-armed prime minister of the monarchy, the author of its colonial policy, and the man who fell with the disaster of Adua in 1896. His story is the arc of the revolutionary made minister: the organizer of the Sicilian rising of 1860, the prophet of the unitary monarchy in the South, the republican republican who declared that “the monarchy unites us and the republic would divide us,” and finally the autocratic premier of the 1880s and 1890s whose African adventure ended in catastrophe. Oriani’s La lotta politica in Italia follows him from the Sicilian preparations of 1859–60 through the making of the kingdom, and giustino-fortunato’s parliamentary speeches record the ruin of his policy after battle-of-adua-1896.
The Sicilian revolutionary
Crispi began as a conspirator of the Mazzinian left. Oriani’s account shows him, in the years before 1860, repeatedly entering Sicily to introduce arms and to organize the risings, in contact with the agents of the partito d’azione and encouraged by Mazzini himself. His part in the preparation of the expedition-of-the-thousand-1860 was that of the political organizer who prepared the ground for Garibaldi’s landing; Oriani describes him as the most obstinate persuader of the enterprise, and notes that the ascendancy he had gained in the island made him the natural intermediary between the Garibaldian movement and the cautious Piedmontese government. It was to the Sicilian revolutionary tradition that Crispi belonged, and from it he carried into his later ministry the instincts of the strong state and the distrust of party.
The turn to the monarchy
The decisive turn of Crispi’s early career was his acceptance of the monarchy as the necessary form of Italian unity. In the annexed South, Oriani records, the aristocracy had been drawn into the national movement by the monarchical element, and a republic would have loosed an indomitable reaction in the Mezzogiorno. The phrase Oriani attributes to Crispi in 1864 — “la monarchia ci unisce e la republica ci dividerebbe,” “the monarchy unites us and the republic would divide us” — crystallized the policy by which the republican left reconciled itself to the Savoyard crown, and it marks the point at which the old conspirator became a pillar of the state. The remainder of the 1860s and 1870s saw him in and out of office, one of the leading men of the parliamentary Left, before the death of agostino-depretis in 1887 opened the premiership to him.
Prime minister and the strong state
Crispi was prime minister from 1887 to 1891 and again from 1893 to 1896, and he governed as a strong man in a parliamentary age — the opposite pole of the trasformismo of his predecessor, and a figure feared and hated in proportion to his energy. He carried the colonial policy beyond the Eritrean foothold toward the interior of Ethiopia, committing the kingdom to the African expansion that Oriani’s ninth book treats under the heading of “la conquista africana.” Domestically his years were marked by the repression of the socialists and of the Sicilian Fasci in 1893–94, which made him the symbol of authoritarian order against the democratic and socialist Left. His ambition was to make Italy a great power — a navy, an empire, a place in the first rank of Europe — and his methods were those of a man who believed the state could be governed only by a firm hand.
Adua and the fall
Crispi’s empire foundered in the highlands of Ethiopia. The drive to subdue the Negus, Menelik, led the Italian army deep into Tigré, and on 1 March 1896 the column was annihilated at battle-of-adua-1896 — the disaster that Fortunato calls the “immane disastro di Adua” which suddenly made the country, and the parliament born of the passions of that year, a prisoner of the consequences. The defeat brought down Crispi’s government and his political career; the colonial programme collapsed into the defence of the Eritrean foothold. In the elections that followed, Fortunato, speaking to the electors of Melfi in March 1897, urged a policy of “absolute recollection” — to restrict all military ambition to the Eritrean colony, to withdraw from the African adventure, and to repair at home the damage done abroad. The catastrophe, in Fortunato’s reading, was not the work of a single hand but the outcome of the “sciagurata” colonial policy that Crispi embodied, and it left the kingdom humiliated and its institutions shaken. Crispi died in 1901, out of office and out of power, remembered as the strongest and most dangerous of the makers of the new Italy.

entities/franz-ferdinand.title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand (1863–1914)
entities/franz-ferdinand.content:
Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand Karl Ludwig Joseph Maria (1863–1914), nephew of Emperor Franz Joseph and, after the death of his father Archduke Karl Ludwig, heir presumptive to the Habsburg throne, was at his fiftieth birthday in December 1913 the object of an extraordinary national attention — the man “who would one day be called to direct the destinies of the realm.” In the seven months that followed he was shot dead with his wife at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, and the shots set the world war in motion. In the last years of the Dual Monarchy he had become the focus of a programme of military strengthening and of a possible reorganization of the state — the circle of hope for those, like Conrad von Hötzendorf, who wished to see the monarchy gird itself for the coming struggle.
Birth and ancestry
Sosnosky, writing the biographical portrait in the Österreichische Rundschau Sonderheft, records that Franz Ferdinand was born on 18 December 1863 in the Herberstein palace in Graz, “a Christmas gift” to his parents, Archduke Karl Ludwig and Archduchess Maria Annunziata, a Bourbon of the Two Sicilies. His father, the brother of the Emperor, had withdrawn from political life two years before and lived as a private man in Graz. By his descent, as a genealogist had shown, the archduke united in his veins the blood of no fewer than a hundred and twelve ancestral houses, and in eleven generations counted over two thousand verifiable ancestors — making him one of the most richly-ancestored princes in Europe.
The soldier and inspector-general
The military essays of the Sonderheft ground the heir’s martial zeal in the traditions of the dynasty — from the founder Kaiser Rudolf, through Maximilian the knight and Charles V, to Maria Theresia. Voinovich, the general of infantry, argues that the archduke was convinced “that the foremost means to the greatness of the state lies in the sharpening of the sword,” and that he gave the chief weight of his labours to the armed power of the monarchy, labouring without rest to raise it. The marine essay recalls that it was reserved for the heir to give the navy, neglected in detail by his war-lord uncle, his more particular care. As inspector-general of the armed forces Franz Ferdinand worked for the unity of all the forces of the realm and the suppression of “all destructive tendencies and separatist strivings” — the very programme with which Conrad, as he records, found himself in agreement when the archduke sounded him out on a long carriage-drive after manoeuvres in 1901.
The traveller to the East
The world journey was, in the estimate of both Sosnosky and Rear-Admiral Koudelka, who accompanied him, the decisive turning-point of his life. Sailing from Europe on 15 December 1892 in his twenty-ninth year, he returned with rich ethnographic and natural-scientific collections and, more than that, “a direction for his later years” — a knowledge of foreign lands and peoples that, as the soldierly essay insists, only strengthened his love of the fatherland. His patronage extended to the academies of sciences of Prague and Cracow and to a series of sciences, above all botany and the study of home, while at Konopišt in Bohemia he built up, over more than twenty years, a park of some 340 hectares and collections of armour, trophies and works of art celebrated throughout Europe.
The South Slav problem and the trialist ideas
In the last years of his life Franz Ferdinand stood at the centre of the debate over the future of the monarchy. The South Slav question, Conrad records, was among the questions the heir put to him in 1901, and Conrad urged a settlement favourable to the Croats. Sosnosky, surveying the possible futures of the monarchy on the eve of 1914, sets out trialism — the conversion of the dual state into a triple state by the addition of a South Slav unit — as the idea “on the agenda,” and notes that its adherents looked to a strong hand at the head of the state to impose it against the resistance of the Magyars, who would lose Croatia-Slavonia and their only access to the sea. The heir’s reputation as a champion of military and central power made him the natural patron of such a project, even though, as Sosnosky observes, the obstacles on the Austrian as much as the Hungarian side made its realisation doubtful. Redlich, writing after the catastrophe, judged that the death of the archduke at Sarajevo destroyed the possibility of breaking the Magyar supremacy from within the monarchy — the “second possibility” of reform that vanished with him.
Sarajevo
On 28 June 1914 the heir to the Habsburg throne and his wife fell to an assassin’s bullets in Sarajevo, the capital of the annexed province of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The shots at once extinguished the one figure around whom the hopes of military and constitutional reform had gathered, and they provided the occasion for the July crisis that carried Europe into war. The Monarchy that marched to war in the summer of 1914 was thus deprived of the very man who, in the judgement of his contemporaries, had been the strongest will for its renewal.

entities/franz-joseph.title: Franz Joseph (1830–1916)
entities/franz-joseph.content:
Franz Joseph
Franz Joseph I (1830–1916), of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, came to the throne as Emperor of Austria in 1848 at the height of the Revolution and died as Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary in the autumn of 1916, in the third year of the Great War. His reign spans the whole frame of this wiki’s period: it was he who, defeated at Königgrätz and driven out of Germany, accepted the transformation of the old unitary empire into the Dual Monarchy through the Ausgleich (“compromise”) of 1867; he who for nearly half a century thereafter held together the two halves of that monarchy by the sheer force of his person; and he who carried the realm into the war of 1914. If the dynasty was the foundation of the Habsburg state, Franz Joseph was in his long age its most constant embodiment — a ruler whom Redlich would describe as the bearer of a conception of the Austrian state, and whom Sosnosky, with all his criticism of the dualist system, never ceased to treat as the living keystone of the whole.
The crown as burden
The opening essay of the Österreichische Rundschau Sonderheft on the heir to the throne sets out the peculiar condition of the Habsburg ruler that Franz Joseph for sixty-eight years endured. In this many-shaped realm, the essay argues, the crown is a heavier burden than anywhere else, “for here the dynasty itself is the foundation of a structure that is not always logically and organically articulated — elsewhere the state carries the dynasty, here the dynasty carries the state.” Redlich, writing in the first chapter of his Carnegie study, explains this in constitutional terms: Austria was “the creation of a dynasty” which for more than six centuries had combined an almost unmeasured idea of its own authority with the satisfaction of the needs of many tangled peoples — the old hereditary lands, the lands of the Bohemian crown, and the whole territory of the ancient Hungarian crown of St. Stephen. The dynastic, the family idea, was that all these, though each kept its historical-political individuality, formed from the standpoint of the head of the House of Habsburg one great condominium, a Reich unity whose political and military force flowed from the will of the hereditary lord. Within that frame, however, Hungary always stood apart: even after the Pragmatica Sanctio of 1713 was adopted into Hungarian law in 1723, the old constitutional position of the kingdom remained fundamentally different from that of the other lands.
The Compromise and the king of Hungary
It was the defeats of 1866 — Königgrätz against Prussia, and the loss of Venice to Italy — that forced on Franz Joseph the settlement which the Hungarians, led by Ferenc Deák, had for years been demanding. Deák asked nothing less than the conversion of the old unitary empire into a novel double state, and the Crown’s first “serious scruples” concerned the unity of the army. Beksics, in his defence of the dualism, insists that Deák’s work preserved rather than impaired Hungarian statehood, resting as it did on the Pragmatic Sanction and the centuries-old tie of the shared dynasty: Hungary and Austria were to remain two mutually independent states, joined “for mutual defence and for that alone.” The Hungarian parliament adopted the Compromise act on 30 March 1867 by 257 against 117 votes, and the Magnates followed; the Austrian Reichsrat, which was never even asked to consent to a state-legal transformation of the whole monarchy, tacitly acquiesced — indeed it sent a deputation to Ofen for the coronation of Franz Joseph as King of Hungary, which the Croatian diet refused to do. Sosnosky, sharply critical of the whole Ausgleich, nevertheless records what the dualism meant for the Emperor: the crown lost no part of its reality in Hungary, for the tie of the shared person of the ruler remained the one firm and immovable thing binding the two states.
The long reign amid the nationalities
For the four decades that followed, Franz Joseph presided over a monarchy beset by the national principle that Sosnosky calls the governing force of the age. Within Austria (Cisleithania) the German, Czech, Polish, Ruthenian and Slovene populations — roughly ten nations, or by some reckonings twenty nationalities counting Hungary — contended ceaselessly; within Hungary the Magyar national state pressed upon its German, Romanian, Slovak, Ruthenian, Serb and Croat subject peoples. The Emperor’s part was to hold the balance and to reconcile the divergent elements through the person of the crown. Sosnosky dwells on the proofs of “self-overcoming and of forgetting” that Franz Joseph gave toward Hungary: in 1906 he received in audience Ferenc (Franz) Kossuth, son of the very Lajos Kossuth who had declared the House of Habsburg forever deprived of the Hungarian throne, and conversed with him in Hungarian; in the same year he ordered the repatriation of the remains of Ferenc Rákóczy from Turkey, the same Rákóczy who had once conspired with the Turks and Louis XIV against the house. These gestures, Sosnosky argues, were among the strongest proofs of a self-command rare in any monarch.
The army and the Crown
The common army was the keystone of the Austrian position within the dualism — “the last bulwark,” as Sosnosky calls it, of the crown’s authority against the Magyar drive for independence, and the point on which the Hungarian opposition concentrated its attacks. It was Deák who, in the negotiations of the Ausgleich, denied the historical right of the Hungarians to a separate army, declaring that such a course would be “personal union,” and who warned: “Let us say that word, and the curse will fall upon us.” Franz Joseph, as Kriegsherr (“war-lord”), remained the head of this common force, and the archduke who was his heir took up the same cause, labouring for the reform and strengthening of the army and navy. The struggle over the language of command and the Hungarian military demands — reaching its crisis under Count István Tisza in the parliament of 1903–1904, when obstruction over the recruits’ quota pushed the realm to the brink of an ex-lex state — was in effect a struggle over how much of the crown’s last fortress the Magyars could breach.
The war and the death of the Emperor
When the war broke out in 1914 Franz Joseph was in his eighty-fourth year. The Reichsrat had been sent home in the spring of 1914 on the renewal of obstructionist tactics among the Slav parties, and the government had resolved to govern through the emergency-notification provision of Article 14 of the Austrian constitution — a system, Redlich notes, that the ministry in Vienna had long in practice exercised anyway. The war government that followed was shaped by the supremacy of the Hungarian government and of Count Tisza over a subordinated Austria, under the tenacious anti-parliamentary policy of the Austrian minister-president Count Stürgkh. Franz Joseph did not live to see the catastrophe. His death and the accession of Emperor Charles form the opening of Redlich’s “second period of the war government”: the death of the Emperor Francis Joseph, as Redlich writes, at once weakened the influence of the Army High Command on the Austrian government and on the shaping of home policy, and made way for the eventual convocation of parliament and the attempts at reconciliation that came too late. On the Emperor’s death the tie of the person common to Hungary and Austria — the very foundation of the personal union that Beksics had declared “entirely outside the range of political possibility” to dissolve — passed to his grand-nephew, and within two years the Dual Monarchy itself was gone.

entities/giuseppe-garibaldi.title: Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882)
entities/giuseppe-garibaldi.content:
Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882)
Giuseppe Garibaldi, born at Nice in 1807 of a Genoese sailor family, was the soldier of the Italian Risorgimento — the one man of the movement whose name crossed every frontier and outlived every party. In this corpus’s frame he is the veteran who, having already conquered the Two Sicilies for the national cause in 1860, fought on through the defeats of the following decade — wounded and captured in the Calabrian hills at Aspromonte, broken at battle-of-mentana-1867, and in his last campaign leading an improvised volunteer army for the French Republic in the Vosges during the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 — before returning to die quietly on the rocky island of Caprera in 1882. His own Memorie, dictated and signed at Civitavecchia in 1875 and published in their diplomatic edition by Ernesto Nathan in 1907, tell the whole story in the first person: a “stormy life, made up of good and evil,” written by a man who called himself a hater of tyranny and falsehood, a republican who yet believed a temporary and honest dictatorship necessary at the head of nations “victims of the most pernicious Byzantinism.” Tivaroni, surveying the movement in the closing volume of his history, gives him a gallery of portraits — the adventurer, the hero, the general — and judges him before history’s bar as the emblem of the armed revolution that made the kingdom.
The years in South America
The opening of the Memorie carries Garibaldi from his Genoese childhood and early voyages and service in the Sardinian navy, through his conversion to the Italian national idea and his flight into exile after the failed rising of Genoa in 1834, to a decade of warfare across the Atlantic. In South America he served the Rio-Grandense republic in its war of independence against the Brazilian Empire — the corsair voyages, the building and arming of a little fleet, the defence of the Rio Grande, and the campaigns with the gaucho republicans that brought him his wife Anita. He knew disaster on the shores of Santa Catarina, shipwreck, and flight across the Sierra. Then came the passage to Uruguay and the defence of Montevideo against the siege of Oribe and Rosas, where he formed the Italian Legion and won the soldier’s fame that carried his name home. It was from the Plata that he resolved, in 1848, to return and offer his sword to Italy, sailing with sixty-three volunteers on 15 April 1848.
The Roman Republic
The second period of the Memorie is the return and the revolutionary year. Garibaldi offered his and the Legion’s services to the Italian cause in the Lombard war against Austria, entered Rome, and took part in the defence of the Roman Republic of 1849 against the French army of Oudinot. The siege of Rome, the fighting at the gates, his wounding, and the heroic retreat with the remnants of his command across central Italy — pursued through the Romagna until the pursuit died out and the survivors dispersed — made him, as Tivaroni’s retrospective holds, the symbol of the Italian revolution. From that episode his fame ceased to be merely that of a capable commander of volunteers and became legendary; the fugitive who had defied the French before Rome was henceforward the living standard of the partito d’azione, the party of action that stood apart from the constitutional monarchists.
The Expedition of the Thousand (1860)
Garibaldi’s greatest feat, and the centre of the whole Risorgimento as his memoirists tell it, was the expedition-of-the-thousand-1860 of May–October 1860. The third period of the Memorie opens with a hymn to Sicily — “genitrice degli Archimedi,” the land of the Sicilian Vespers and of the two lads of Syracuse — the island that was to “wake the sleepers.” The account runs from the embarkation at Quarto and the landing at Marsala, through the astonishing victory at Calatafimi (15 May 1860) and the taking of Palermo (27 May 1860) and the reduction of the island, to the crossing of the Straits of Messina, the landing on the Neapolitan mainland, the assault of Reggio, and the advance on Naples; it closes with the decisive victory of the Volturno (1–2 October 1860, with Bronzetti at Castel Morrone and the fighting at Caserta Vecchia). By that campaign the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was delivered to the national cause, and the Thousand and the southern volunteers became the heroes of a whole generation. Oriani, writing from the other political pole, nevertheless treats this as the revolutionary conquest that supplied the monarchy its second half — the royal annexation of the North and centre balanced by Garibaldi’s popular conquest of the South.
Aspromonte and the Trentino
The fourth period of the Memorie (1860–1870) is one of disillusion and defeat. In 1862 Garibaldi marched again, this time against Rome, in a movement Victor Emmanuel’s government could not sanction; at Aspromonte the royal troops met him in Calabria, wounded him, and took him prisoner, and he was held at the Varignano before returning to Caprera. In the war of 1866 he led the advance into the Trentino — the only bright spot of an otherwise disastrous italian-war-1866 — threatening Riva and Trento while the main armies stumbled toward battle-of-custoza-1866. His own Memorie and Tivaroni’s history agree that the Trentino campaign showed him at his best, pressing the Alpine passes with his volunteers as far as prudence and the faintheartedness of his superiors allowed. And then came the catastrophe of battle-of-mentana-1867 (3 November 1867), where the attempt to seize Rome for the Republic was crushed at the gates of the Papal city by the Papal troops and the French reinforcements. Garibaldi ended the period a prisoner and exile of his own island.
The campaign of France and the return to Caprera
The fifth and last period is the campaign of 1870–71. Called to the service of the French Republic after Sedan, Garibaldi commanded the improvised Army of the Vosges against the Prussians: the combats of Lentenay and Autun (21–23 January 1871), the three days’ holding of Dijon, and the final retreat ordered when the enemy masses, freed by the fall of Paris and the armistice, gathered to envelop the small army. Elected a deputy to the National Assembly at Bordeaux, he took his seat “with the sole intent of carrying my vote to the unhappy Republic,” and, seeing nothing more could be done, returned to Caprera, where he arrived on 16 February 1871. His Army of the Vosges, composed of too republican elements, was dissolved by the government of Thiers. The Memorie close with his death at Caprera in 1882, and Tivaroni’s portrait of “Garibaldi at Caprera” fixes the final image of the exile-general who, having given the nation its kingdom, retired to a barren rock and the memory of a thousand battles.

entities/giustino-fortunato.title: Giustino Fortunato (1848–1932)
entities/giustino-fortunato.content:
Giustino Fortunato (1848–1932)
Giustino Fortunato, born in 1848 at Rionero in the Vulture region of Basilicata, was the voice of the southern-question-italy in the Italian Parliament — the deputy for the college of Melfi from 1880 to 1909 and later a senator, whose collected speeches make up the two volumes of Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano. Discorsi politici (1880–1910) that are the principal sources of this wiki on the South. Where others proclaimed the glories of the new kingdom, Fortunato insisted, in speech after speech, on the backwardness and the burdens of the Mezzogiorno: the tributary system that pressed hardest on the poorest provinces, the neglected credit and the ruined grain banks, the communal domains locked against the peasantry, the malaria and emigration that bled the land, and the colonial adventures that wasted the nation’s strength. He was a meridionalist, a liberal, and a pessimist — a deputy who saw his constituency with an economist’s exactness and described its misery without consolation, and whose thirty years of parliamentary eloquence defined the Southern Question as a problem of the Italian state itself.
The deputy for Melfi
Fortunato entered Parliament at the elections for the Fourteenth Legislature in May 1880, standing for the college of Melfi on a program of “dissidence” from the broken majorities of agostino-depretis. His first published discourse, La «dissidenza» e le elezioni del 16 maggio 1880, opens the collection and sets its tone: the appeal to the electors, the criticism of trasformismo, and the insistence that the South’s deputies should serve their constituencies rather than the premier. From that beginning he held the college for a generation, returning again and again to the same themes before the electors of Melfi at Potenza, Lavello, and in the Chamber itself. The speeches are dated precisely — 15 June 1880 on the grain banks, 18 October 1880 at Bologna on the credit cooperatives of the South, 2 December 1880 and 19 November 1881 on the communal domains, 21 January 1882 on the exception laws in the tributary system — and each returns the general question of the state to the particular earth of Basilicata.
The economic condition of the South
The substance of Fortunato’s work was economic. He was the parliamentarian of the grain banks (monti frumentari) that he sought to transform, of the credit cooperatives that the South lacked and the North possessed, and of the demanial question — the vast communal lands, the “feudal and universal” demanio, which had never been divided among the peasantry and which the state’s legislation kept locked. He returned relentlessly to the tributary burden: the leggi d’eccezione by which the taxation of the South exceeded both its capacity and its services, so that, as he documented in the appendix to his discourse of 9 October 1898 on Il dovere politico, the Mezzogiorno paid to the state more than it received, before and after unification alike. His statistical habit — the appendices on the economy of Basilicata, on the tributary burden, on the state’s finances — gives his speeches a documentary weight rare in the oratory of the time, and his own family’s position as a southern landowner gave him an authority the demagogues lacked.
The state, the bank, and the empire
Fortunato’s parliamentary career crossed every great controversy of the later decades. He spoke on the finances of the State (25 October 1892), on the war navy (4 May 1893), on the issuing institutes and fiduciary circulation (25 June 1893), and on the banking crisis of the 1890s (10 and 16 May 1895) — the financial collapse that shook the kingdom in the years of Crispi. On the empire he was an early and consistent opponent: after the disaster of battle-of-adua-1896 and the fall of francesco-crispi, he urged the electors of Melfi in March 1897 to support a policy of “absolute recollection” — to confine all military ambition to the Eritrean colony, to withdraw from the interior, and to refuse the “aberration, falsity, and imposture” of the African adventure. He mourned the martyrs of Adua, commemorated the fallen of the fatherland, and opposed the mounting military expenditure (23 March 1901) as a burden the poor provinces could not bear.
The last years: emigration and malaria
The closing speeches of the collection turn to the two great drains on the South. L’emigrazione meridionale (30 June 1909) treats the mass emigration to the Americas not as a moral evil but as an economic fact — “l’emigrazione non è un fatto artificiale, ma una necessità,” a natural current of population that only reform could make less destructive — while noting that Sicily, which emigrated little, suffered all the more for staying. And Malaria e chinino (30 June 1910), the last discourse in the collection, takes up the fight against the malarial fevers that ravaged the lowlands of the South, the campaign for quinine and drainage that was among the few remedies the state could apply. Fortunato died in 1932, having spent his long life as the conscience of the South in the councils of the nation — a figure whose measured, sorrowful eloquence made the Southern Question a permanent item on the agenda of the Italian state.

entities/grigori-rasputin.title: Grigori Rasputin (1869–1916)
entities/grigori-rasputin.content:
Grigori Rasputin
Grigori Efimovich Rasputin (1869–1916), the starets (“elder”) from the Siberian village of Pokrovskoe, was the peasant holy man who gained an extraordinary hold over the court of nicholas-ii and the Empress alexandra-feodorovna in the last years before the revolution. To the public of the capital he was the scandal of the age — the debauched monk whose favor was believed to decide appointments, whose name was whispered behind every ministerial change, and whose murder in December 1916 became one of the great episodes of the monarchy’s collapse. His treatment in this wiki’s sources comes almost entirely from the official and courtly side: nikolai-zhevakhov, the deputy ober-procurator, writes as a defender of the imperial family and of eldership itself, insisting that the legend of Rasputin was manufactured to destroy the dynasty; Witte, writing earlier and from outside the court, records the beginnings of the Rasputin business in the last years of his life.
The holy man and the court
Zhevakhov, who knew the religious atmosphere of Petersburg at first hand, places Rasputin in the long line of Russian “God-seekers” and holy fools — predecessors such as Archimandrite Mikhail and the “tongue-tied Mitya” had prepared the capital’s appetite for just such a figure. Rasputin appeared as the peasant who could pray for the sick, above all for the hemophiliac heir Alexei, whose illness dominated the private life of the imperial family. The Empress, in Zhevakhov’s account, believed in him with a religious conviction — when a lady of the court protested against the scandal Rasputin caused, the Empress answered that “the official Church has always crucified its prophets.” The Sovereign, too, trusted him: “if not for the prayers of Grigory Efimovich,” he is reported to have said, “I should long ago have been killed.” Around this private faith grew the public legend, and with it the machinery of the dynasty’s ruin.
The scandal and its uses
For the hostile public, every evil of the reign was laid at Rasputin’s door. Zhevakhov’s central contention is that the danger was not the man but the weapon his name became: that “talk about Rasputin was more harmful than Rasputin himself,” and that a small circle working to destroy the state used the name of the starets as one of its instruments. He records the psychosis of the capital, in which every appointment — every high position — was ascribed to Rasputin’s influence, and in which men nearest the throne were most eager to disown any connection with him, shouting his condemnation the louder to prove their loyalty. Witte, from the cooler vantage of his retirement, records the same thing with contempt: the rise of Rasputin, and the crowd of Grigori’s, of Germogen, of Iliodor, of the “dark forces” who trafficked in the favor of the court. Whether the starets truly directed the government or was merely the screen behind which others governed, the effect was the same — the monarchy, identified in the public mind with Rasputin, lost the last remnant of its prestige.
The murder
The catastrophe came in December 1916. In Zhevakhov’s account, which he sets within his scheme of the “periods” of the collapse, the murder of Rasputin marked the passage of the revolution from agitation to act. He records the killing as an act of treachery against a man he insists was not what his enemies said — “Rasputin was killed not when he was a power, but when he was already…” — and he is careful to note the strange alliance of those who struck: the aristocrat Yusupov and the monarchist Purishkevich, men who thought to save the dynasty by removing its disgrace. The murder did not save the throne; it removed the one figure whose favor had seemed to bind the Empress, and left the court, the Church, and the government more isolated than before. Two months later the February revolution swept away the monarchy that had been so fatally entangled with the name of the starets.

entities/gusztav-beksics.title: Gusztáv Beksics (1847–1906)
entities/gusztav-beksics.content:
Gusztáv Beksics
Gusztáv Beksics (1847–1906) was a Hungarian publicist, politician and national thinker of the dualist era, the author of A dualismus (1892), the classic Hungarian public-law defence of the 1867 Compromise, and of A magyar faj terjeszkedése (1896) on national consolidation. His two works in this corpus present the Hungarian side of the Dual Monarchy from within — the constitutional justification of the Ausgleich and the demographic-national programme of the Magyar ascendancy.
The defender of the dualism
A dualismus was written at the quarter-century mark of the Compromise, at a moment when the system faced challenges from both the Austrian side and the Magyar national movements. Beksics set out the history and public-law meaning of the dualist arrangement: Hungary’s independent statehood before and at the time of the Pragmatic Sanction, the common affairs of 1848, the provisional system (the provisorium) that preceded the settlement, and the origin of the dualism itself. He defended the common army and the Delegations, the ministry of common affairs and the royal household, and asserted Hungary’s international personality and financial and economic independence against the charge that the Compromise had subordinated the Magyar nation. His treatment of Croatia and the nationalities and his discussion of how Act XII of 1867 might be altered mark the fault-lines of the system he championed.
The national consolidator
The companion volume, A magyar faj terjeszkedése és nemzeti konszolidácziónk (2nd ed. 1896), turned from constitutional law to the demographic and social basis of Hungarian strength. Beksics argued that the consolidation of the nation must rest on the free expansion of the Hungarian race: the failure of linguistic assimilation, the alarming demographic phenomena of the Hungarian counties, the relation of agriculture and land tenure to population growth (against Malthus), the agrarian socialism of the alföld, and the creation of a Hungarian peasant proprietorship as the means of expansion.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Beksics is the Hungarian voice of the Dual Monarchy — the constitutional patriot who vindicates the Ausgleich against both the Austrian centralists and the Magyar nationalists. His works stand in explicit dialogue with the German liberal criticism of Sosnosky, and together they map the internal strains of Austria-Hungary before 1914.

entities/gyula-andrassy.title: Count Gyula Andrássy (1823–1890)
entities/gyula-andrassy.content:
Gyula Andrássy
Count Gyula (Julius) Andrássy the elder (1823–1890) was the Hungarian statesman who, after Ferenc Deák had prepared the ground, carried the Compromise of 1867 into being as the first Hungarian minister-president under the dualist system, and then, as joint foreign minister from 1871 to 1879, pursued the Balkan programme and concluded the alliance with Germany. Sosnosky counts him “the most significant statesman” to have directed the foreign policy of the realm since Prince Felix zu Schwarzenberg — a minister who, unlike the mere officials who usually held the office, knew what he wanted and did it. (His son of the same name, Gyula Andrássy the younger, was to be foreign minister again in 1918, in the last months of the monarchy.)
The maker of the Compromise
Andrássy stood at the side of Deák in the negotiations of 1866–1867. When the Hungarian opposition, in the subcommittee drafting the common affairs, insisted on a separate Hungarian army, it was Deák who denied the historical right of such a force and Andrássy who supported him — reminding the opposition, as Sosnosky records, that with two legislatures and two governments a modern state could not also have two armies. As the first Hungarian minister-president under the settlement he took the lead in the great transformation that Beksics describes as the restoration of Hungarian statehood within the dualist frame: Hungary became once more a self-governing state, joined to Austria by the shared person of the ruler and by the common affairs of foreign policy, war and finance, for mutual defence and that alone.
The Eastern programme and the occupation of Bosnia
As joint foreign minister from 1871 Andrássy turned the monarchy’s attention to the East. He had recognised, as Sosnosky puts it, “that for the monarchy there was nothing more to seek in Germany, that its role there was played out forever, and that its future tasks lay in the Orient, on the Balkan.” He pursued so purposeful an Oriental policy that Prince Gortschakow found it advisable to keep on good terms with him. In the conventions of Reichstadt (8 July 1876) and Budapest (15 January 1877) Austria-Hungary and Russia fixed their spheres of influence in expectation of a Russo-Turkish war, and Andrássy secured for his realm the possession of Bosnia and Herzegovina — important, above all for military reasons, as the hinterland of Dalmatia — as the compensation for Russia’s expected acquisitions.
When Russia, after defeating the Turks, imposed the Treaty of San Stefano with only a modest role allowed to Austria-Hungary, Andrássy refused to accept this breach of the earlier conventions and, with England as a powerful ally, forced the settlement to be revised on the European stage. The Congress of Berlin of 1878 restricted Russia’s claims and conferred on Austria-Hungary the mandate to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina. But the occupation proved far harder than Andrássy expected. The story was current that he said a single company of infantry with the regimental band would suffice to subdue Bosnia; whether the jest was really his or was put into his mouth, Sosnosky notes, his hope of acquiring the provinces without blood and treasure proved an “egregious error.” Not one company but a whole army corps and a division were needed, and after more than two months of costly fighting the fanaticised population was at last mastered — resistance secretly supported by the Porte, which allowed Ottoman troops to make common cause with the insurgents while the two states were officially at peace.
The alliance with Germany
Andrássy did not annex Bosnia — a “grave omission” which, Sosnosky holds, was to exact a bitter reckoning thirty years later — and he did not long remain in office after the occupation. He resigned in 1879 for reasons his biographer Wertheimer was expected to clarify. But before he left the field he bequeathed to the realm its most valuable legacy: the Schutz- und Trutzbündnis (defensive and offensive alliance) with Germany, concluded shortly before his retirement to secure both states against an attack by Russia. This, Sosnosky argues, was a deed that in part outweighed his error in the Oriental question. The Dual Alliance of 1879, as the same work shows in its survey of Austria-Hungary and the German Empire, became the foundation of the monarchy’s place in Bismarck’s and then Wilhelmine Germany’s system of alliances. Andrássy had laid the basis of the alliance “in union with Bismarck,” with whom he went together, “in defiance of all revanche-lusts.”
