entities/helmuth-von-moltke.title: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder (1800–1891)
entities/helmuth-von-moltke.content:
Helmuth von Moltke the Elder (1800–1891)
Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, chief of the Prussian General Staff, was the military architect of the victories of German unification — the man who planned and directed the campaigns that threw Austria out of Germany in 1866 and brought France to defeat in 1870–71. This page concerns the elder Moltke, the strategist of Königgrätz and Sedan, and not his nephew, the Chief of Staff of 1914 whose name became attached to the failure of the opening campaigns of the First World War. In the wars of 1866 and 1870 the elder Moltke’s planning, his system of concentration, and his disciplined delegation to his subordinates gave Prussia an advantage that outweighed numbers and that his contemporaries, in the words of the sources, could only describe as a masterpiece of operational art.
The staff system
The foundation of Moltke’s achievement lay in the institution he commanded. As chief of the Prussian General Staff he made of that body a permanent school of strategic thought and detailed planning, in which the movement of armies, the supply of troops, and the alternatives of the campaign were worked out in peacetime so that in war the execution might follow the design. Lenz’s biography shows Moltke’s place in the military order that the army reform of albrecht-von-roon and wilhelm-i had created: he was, in Lenz’s reckoning of the great organs of the state, one of the men of the military class who thought alike — “Moltke just as much as Roon and Edwin Manteuffel” — in whom the crown’s reorganized army rested. The Army Reform had filled the officer corps with the military families; Moltke, from that corps, gave the professional direction that the enlarged army needed.
The planning of 1866
The Bohemian campaign of 1866 displayed Moltke’s method at its most characteristic. Prussia disposed its field forces against Austria in three separate armies — the Elbe Army, the First Army, and the Second Army — advancing by different routes through the passes into Bohemia. The risk of such an arrangement was that the enemy might concentrate and fall on the separate parts before they could unite; the whole art lay in bringing the three masses together at the decisive point and moment. Sybel’s account emphasizes how Moltke had to judge the enemy’s dispositions, correcting the assumption that the Austrians would gather in Bohemia when in fact they concentrated far to the east in Moravia, at Olmütz. “Moltke explained to him very calmly,” Sybel writes of one such interchange, “that the enemy stood not in Bohemia but assembled in Moravia” — a knowledge that governed the whole design of the advance.
At the climax, before Königgrätz, Moltke’s instructions to the commanders showed the balance of his system: a precise statement of the great purpose, and full freedom in the choice of means. On the evening of 2 July, learning that the Austrians had crossed the Bistritz in strength near Sadowa and that a meeting with the First Army might be expected the next morning, he wrote to the Crown Prince ordering him at once to make his dispositions to support the First Army, to advance against the right flank of the enemy’s probable march, and to intervene as soon as possible. The earlier orders given “under different circumstances” were, he added, no longer binding. Sybel comments that the direction that was to decide Germany’s future was, again, entirely in Moltke’s manner — “specific statement of the great object, full freedom in the choice of means.” It was the exact opposite of the Austrian commander Benedek’s procedure.
Königgrätz
The risk of the plan was grave. The total Prussian strength, as Sybel computes it, was not greater but slightly less than the enemy’s: 221,000 men against 222,000 Austrians, the latter massed on a narrow space, the former converging on the battlefield from miles away. The Crown Prince’s divisions had four to seven hours of marching over different and everywhere bad roads before they could reach the enemy; a delay, and the First Army might be crushed by nearly double its number. What Prussia had to set against this was, in Sybel’s words, “merely an imponderable magnitude: the moral strength of the Prussian army.” And in that moment, after the victories already won, it was permitted to count on it. There was no distrust of self or of comrades; there was neither waywardness nor lack of independence among the leaders, and all looked with entire devotion to the “genial and rapid decision-power of the supreme direction.” Discipline, honour, and patriotism combined in overwhelming aggressiveness and inexhaustible endurance.
So it proved. The battle of battle-of-koniggratz-1866 on 3 July 1866 — the decisive day that Sybel says was a day of world-historical significance — began with the First Army forcing the crossing of the Bistritz and seizing the villages along the Austrian front, while the Austrians held the commanding heights of Chlum and the Swiepwald behind Sadowa. The fight was long and bloody; the weight was carried by the Prussian infantry armed with the quick-firing needle-gun, which outmatched the muzzle-loaders of the Austrians. The crisis came when the Prussian centre seemed to have exhausted itself against the Austrian line. Then, in the afternoon, the Crown Prince’s Second Army arrived on the Austrian flank and rolled up the defence; the position at Chlum, seized at the height of the battle, decided it. The Austrian army, its centre broken, streamed back toward Königgrätz in retreat. A defeat of that magnitude ended the war at a stroke.
From 1866 to Sedan
The victory of Königgrätz made Moltke’s reputation, and the same system was applied on a grander scale against France in 1870. When the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 broke out in July of that year, Moltke directed the concentration of the German armies on the French frontier and their march across it in a series of great enveloping movements. The wars against napoleon-iii’s empire were decided by the same convergence of separate armies on the decisive point: the battles of August (which Lenz invokes alongside Sedan as scenes graven on the memory) destroyed the main French armies in the field, and the encirclement at Sedan in September 1870 — the “judgment of God at Sedan,” as Lenz calls it — compelled the surrender of the Emperor himself with his whole army. The fall of Sedan ended the Second Empire and left Paris to be besieged. Moltke’s planning had carried the war to a conclusion in weeks, with a completeness that astonished Europe.
In the new German Empire, Moltke remained the symbol of the military power that had made the Reich possible. He is remembered here, with Roon and the King, as one of the three men whose separate arts — the statesman’s, the organizer’s, and the strategist’s — combined to win the victories of 1866 and 1870. He died in 1891, in the first years of the new Reich he had helped to create.

entities/hubert-lagardelle.title: Hubert Lagardelle (1875–1958)
entities/hubert-lagardelle.content:
Hubert Lagardelle
Hubert Lagardelle (1875–1958) was a French socialist publicist and the leading theorist of revolutionary syndicalism in the decade before the First World War. A collaborator of the Mouvement socialiste, the review of the syndicalist Left, he devoted his writing to a single question: whether socialism would be absorbed by democracy, or whether, while using democracy for its own ends, it would remain itself as the movement of the working class. His book Le socialisme ouvrier (1911), a collection of essays written from 1898 to 1908, marked the stages of his thought through the Dreyfus affair, the ministerialist experiment of Waldeck-Rousseau and Millerand, and the rise of the syndicalist movement. He is the corpus’s principal spokesman for the doctrine that the working class must act through its syndicates and direct action rather than through the parliamentary party.
The stages of a thought
Le socialisme ouvrier was not, Lagardelle warned, a literary work. It brought together fragments written “au jour le jour, sous le coup des événements,” day by day, under the pressure of events, following in anxiety the transformations of contemporary socialism. He did not conceal the book’s vices — its discontinuities, repetitions, disproportions — nor that many parts had grown old, nor that there were affirmations he would no longer present in so absolute a manner. His conceptions, he admitted, had modified themselves as they underwent the test of life; he meant only to mark the stages of a thought. That honesty was itself characteristic of a man who was always re-examining his own doctrine as events outran it.
Socialism or democracy
The first part of the book, written at the height of the Millerand crisis, posed the founding question of the age: Socialisme ou Démocratie? Would socialism be absorbed by democracy, or, while using democracy for its ends, would it remain itself? Lagardelle examined the democratic confusion, the programme adopted at the Congress of Tours (1902), and the conditions of a minimum programme, and set the claims of democracy and class struggle against the practical work of democratic politics and economic organisation. He treated at length the career of Millerand — his Plateforme électorale of February 1898, his entry into the ministry of Waldeck-Rousseau alongside the Marquis de Galliffet, the general of the Commune’s suppression — as the great test of whether socialism could survive ministerialism. The Dreyfus affair, the amnesty, and the work of the Waldeck-Rousseau ministry (which he called “Dreyfusism in power”) gave the question a concrete urgency: could socialists participate in a bourgeois government without ceasing to be socialists?
The function of the party
Lagardelle’s answer turned on the distinction between the action of the party and the action of the class. He analysed corporatism, syndicalism and politics as competing forms, defended socialist unity, and weighed “electoral revolutionaryism” against the patient organisation of the working class. The party, in his syndicalist scheme, could not be the true organ of the workers’ emancipation; that role belonged to the syndicate. Democracy, though it might be used, threatened to dissolve the class struggle into a purely political contest, and the parliamentary party risked becoming the means by which the workers were absorbed into the bourgeois state.
The ideas of syndicalism
The second part of the book set out the syndicalist doctrine that Lagardelle had made his own. He noted the unequal import of the congresses of Amsterdam and Bourges in 1904, and traced the formation of syndicalism as “une formation de l’histoire,” a product of history rather than of theory. In his essay on “le révisionnisme de gauche” (November 1904) he observed that there was unanimous agreement that the socialist crisis was due to the divorce of theory and practice. The syndicalist ideas he defended were anti-statism and revolutionary evolution; the syndicate as the organ of the class struggle; direct action and the general strike as the true means of emancipation; and the subordination of the party to the public services the workers controlled. Against the parliamentary path he set the autonomous, economic action of the working class.
The syndicalist policy toward the peasants
Lagardelle extended his doctrine beyond the industrial workers to the countryside. At the socialist congress of Toulouse (15–20 October 1908) he urged the party to carry its case to the small rural proprietors and the non-working popular masses. If it came to them, he argued, with a programme of the reduction of the State and of financial morality, it would penetrate the rural milieux; if it came with dogmatic programmes and abstract formulas, it would not touch them; if it offered a conservative programme, it would not seize them either. Carried by the idealism that issued from the syndicalist working masses, the party must appear as the only party of political cleanliness and of anti-statist action, making its own the essential claims and fundamental ideas of syndicalism.
Significance
Lagardelle stands in this corpus as the theorist who carried the syndicalist current of French socialism to its clearest formulation in the years between the Dreyfus affair and the war. His work marks the moment when the syndicalism of the Bourses du travail and the general strike confronted the parliamentary socialism of Jaurès and the ministerialism of Millerand, and refused to let the class movement be absorbed into democratic politics. Read alongside Péguy’s lament for the republican mystique and Sabatier’s survey of the religious orientation of the age, Le socialisme ouvrier belongs to the ferment of French ideas on the eve of 1914.

entities/josef-redlich.title: Josef Redlich (1869–1936)
entities/josef-redlich.content:
Josef Redlich
Josef Redlich (1869–1936) was an Austrian constitutional jurist, historian and politician who, as professor of public law at the University of Vienna and a former minister, wrote the culminating Carnegie study of the Habsburg state’s government and administration at war. His Österreichische Regierung und Verwaltung im Weltkriege (1925) is the authoritative account of how the Dual Monarchy governed during the Great War — from the pre-war system of emergency decrees, through the militarisation of the civil administration under the Army High Command, to the dissolution of the Reich and its legacy to the new national states. He was himself briefly minister of finance in 1918, in the last months of the monarchy, so that his history is also that of an insider who had held office at the hour of the collapse.
The constitutional jurist
Redlich’s work opens by announcing its subject: the Austrian war government as both political organ — “the bearer and expression of a particular conception of the Austrian state” — and as supreme administrative organ. He notes the peculiar pre-war condition of Austrian government: the ministry in Vienna had long in practice exercised the legislative power too, meeting the unavoidable needs of legislation through the emergency-notification provision of the constitution (Article 14) by imperial decree. The ministry had resolved to keep this system through the war, the Reichsrat having been sent home in the spring of 1914 on the renewal of obstructionist tactics among the Slav parties. Redlich frames the whole as the last chapter of three and a half centuries of Habsburg government and administration, for the state that bore it disappeared entirely with the war, “the Allied war aim of destroying the Habsburg realm having been realised in the peace treaties.”
The pre-war system
Redlich’s first chapter analyses the pre-war foundations of state power: the Emperor and the question of the monarchy, the ministries and ministerial responsibility, the Reichsrat with its upper and lower houses and the nationality struggles within them, the organs of self-government and the provincial (crown-land) administration, and the political character of the civil service. He describes an administration already working largely by Article-14 decree and marked by deepening nationality conflicts. His third chapter, on the last peace government, records the disappointment at the supposed healing effect of the universal suffrage of 1907, the influence of the annexation of Bosnia in sharpening national antagonisms, the perpetual keeping-down of the nationalities by the Magyar gentry, the growth of an anti-parliamentary mood at court and among the generals, and the unceasing accession of national radicalism among Czechs, South Slavs and Ruthenians.
The war government and its historian
The central chapters trace the war government itself: the suppression of parliament at the outbreak, the issue of the emergency decrees, the passing of civil power to the Army High Command over wide areas, the transformation of civil into military administration, the consequent permanent tension between government and army command, the war-surveillance office (Kriegsüberwachungsamt), and the system of the Austrian war government down to the assassination of the minister-president Count Stürgkh in the autumn of 1916. Redlich emphasises the supremacy of the Hungarian government and of Count Tisza, the subordination of Austria, and the “strictly bureaucratic character of the war government with its ruinous effect on the whole public condition of the state.” He treats at length the war economy and the “state socialism of the war,” the rationing of food, the central authorities for the food supply, and the war associations that militarised industry — a war economy that failed, in his judgement, “as a consequence of the overstraining of the physical, moral and spiritual forces of the population and of the excessive length of the war.”
The second period and the dissolution
The eighth chapter opens with the death of Kaiser Franz Joseph and the accession of Emperor Charles, the weakening of the army command’s influence, and the succession of ministries from Koerber through Clam-Martinitz. It traces the convocation of parliament and the appearance of separatist strivings among Czechs and South Slavs, the amnesty granted by Charles and the resentment it provoked, the October Manifesto, the paralysis of parliament and its dissolution into purely national groups, and the beginning of the catastrophe in September 1918. The ninth chapter treats the fall of the Reich and the new national states. Redlich concludes that the October Manifesto of Emperor Charles was “the formal, legally valid dissolution of the historic unitary state”: by his word the Emperor himself, exercising for the last time the right of autocratic constitutional legislation that the house of Habsburg had always claimed, called the complex of new national states into being. The dissolution went forward on a formally legal path; the last act of the dynasty gave the new states, ready formed in the person of their national officials, the organs with which to begin independent government. As minister of finance in 1918 Redlich was among the last bearers of that old-Austrian officialdom whose quiet continuance of work through the collapse he records with a historian’s detachment.

entities/joseph-joffre.title: Joseph Joffre (1852–1931)
entities/joseph-joffre.content:
Joseph Joffre (1852–1931)
Joseph Joffre, French commander-in-chief from the outbreak of the war until December 1916, was the victor of the battle-of-the-marne-1914 and the architect of the French war in its first and hardest years. Recouly’s synthesis makes him the central figure of the French high command: the generalissimo whose skill and sang-froid turned the situation at the Marne, whose robust common sense weighed the strategic problem at Chantilly in 1916, and whose “disgrace” — the removal of 1916 — Recouly bluntly numbers among the events that saved Germany. In this corpus’s frame Joffre’s story is that of the offensive-minded commander who opened the war, held the frontiers against the German wheel, won the decisive defensive battle of the war, and was then superseded in the long attrition of Verdun and the Somme.
The man of the offensive
Recouly presents Joffre as “entirely won over to the idea of the offensive,” on moral, political and military grounds alike. The offensive answered, in this conception, to the French character and temperament; and an army that had not fought in Europe for half a century could only regain confidence in itself through advance and attack. His staff work had bound France and Russia in formal military agreements obliging both armies to attack the German forces as soon as they were ready — the framework of the war-plans-1914 that governed the opening of the war. Joffre was sixty-two years old in 1914, a year younger than marshal-foch, and it was he, as generalissimo of the French armies (généralissime des armées françaises), who received the directives of the concentration and issued the orders of the opening battles.
The Marne
The great act of Joffre’s command was the battle-of-the-marne-1914 of September 1914. Recouly stresses that nothing is more complicated or confused than the battle if one tries to follow it in detail, nothing simpler or clearer if one holds to its great lines. It was the skill and sang-froid of the French generalissimo, and the mistakes that excess of confidence made the German generalissimo commit, that turned the situation. After the defeat of the frontier battles and the long retreat, Joffre prepared the counterstroke. Recouly recounts how, on the eve of the decision, he drove in his limousine through crowded roads to the château of Vaux-le-Pénil near Melun for an moving interview with the British commander-in-chief, who finally promised his cooperation; how Franchet d’Espérey, “a magnificent soldier,” declared himself ready to march; and how, the last hesitations lifted, Joffre — fully conscious of the enormity of the risk — ordered the great battle engaged for 6 September, warned the government, which had left Paris for Bordeaux, and signed for the troops his immortal order of the day. The Marne was lost for Germany, and at a stroke the German machine was half-dismantled: the short war became a long one. Yet Recouly also records that the exploitation of the victory gave not the results Joffre expected, and that his attempt to free the territory in the course to the sea collided with an analogous German manœuvre.
Chantilly and the strategy of 1916
In 1916, the third year of the war, Recouly presents Joffre examining the situation at his headquarters at Chantilly “with robust and clear common sense.” The year that had ended had marked a setback for the Allied cause, yet the failures suffered, especially in the East, were not catastrophic. It fell to Joffre to frame the Allied plan of 1916 — the coordination of the Somme offensive in the West with the pressure of Russia and the new allies in the East. But the double strain of the battle-of-verdun-1916 at Verdun and of the Somme, and the political impatience of the Third Republic, were wearing down his command.
The disgrace
The chapter of Recouly’s book that closes Joffre’s command bears a striking title: La disgrâce de Joffre et la révolution russe sauvent l’Allemagne — “the disgrace of Joffre and the Russian revolution save Germany.” For Recouly the removal of Joffre in December 1916 was one of three hard blows that the German staff, already shaken by the failure before Verdun, the attrition of the Somme, and the entry of Romania, might not otherwise have survived. Joffre’s own finest instrument, marshal-foch, was likewise set aside; Recouly notes that even Weygand, who was to become Foch’s chief of staff, “was still a choice of Joffre.” His dismissal, whatever its political motives, deprived the French command of the generalissimo who had won the Marne at the very moment the war was entering its most trying phase — and Recouly regards the succession as one of the gravest errors of the Allied war.

entities/jules-ferry.title: Jules Ferry (1832–1893)
entities/jules-ferry.content:
Jules Ferry (1832–1893)
The minister of the school laws — the laws that made primary education free, compulsory, and secular — and the republican statesman who carried the laicization of the French school into law. Jules Ferry, the austere and combative Lorrain of the parliamentary Republic, was twice president of the council in the 1880s, the author of the école laïque and of the Tunisian protectorate, and the man whose fall over Tonkin opened a new era in colonial politics. Hanotaux presents him as the representative, in power, of the doctrine of republican anticlericalism.
The republican of the centre
Ferry belonged to the generation of republicans who came to office with the triumph of the parliamentary regime after 1879. Hanotaux records that he brought to the realization of the republican programme “vigour, rudeness, realistic logic — whence his strength and the hatreds he raised.” He was a republican of the moderate centre, prepared to build the secular Republic by law rather than by revolution, and the natural colleague of Gambetta and the leaders of the Chamber. He entered the Waddington cabinet as minister of public instruction, and it was there that he prepared the great school legislation.
The school laws and article 7
Ferry’s school policy rested on a plan conceived in advance: in less than three months he deposited the series of projects that struck, in Hanotaux’s phrase, at the three teachings at once — “the famous school laws, ‘the wicked laws’” (les lois scélérates). The primary-school law introduced gratuité, obligation, laïcité — free, compulsory, secular schooling — taking up the older Barodet proposal and making it the law of the Republic. Against the teaching congregations Ferry pressed the notorious article 7, which would have forbidden the unauthorized religious orders from teaching; when the Senate rejected it, the french-constitution-1875-era ministry fell back on the decrees of 29–30 March 1880, which led to the expulsion of the Jesuits. The school, Ferry insisted, was the instrument by which the Republic would form its citizens and detach the rising generation from clerical influence — the institutional expression of the anticlericalism that Gambetta had proclaimed the enemy.
The Tunisian campaign
Ferry’s foreign policy carried the Republic into empire. At the Congress of Berlin and its aftermath the powers had tacitly offered Tunisia to France as a compensation for the acquisitions of others; Ferry, with the support of the Chamber, resolved to take it. The Kroumir incursions furnished the pretext, the expedition was launched, and the third-republic-france established its protectorate over Tunisia by the Treaty of Bardo. The venture satisfied French expansion and the need for colonial prestige after the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, though it alarmed Italy and embroiled France in the Mediterranean rivalries that would shape the coming decades.
Fall over Tonkin
Ferry’s second great colonial undertaking, the advance into Tonkin and Annam, proved his undoing. The distant war, the reverses, and the mounting cost turned the Chamber against him; defeated on the Tonkin question, he fell from power. Hanotaux’s narrative, which closes on the death of Gambetta in 1882, treats Ferry within the larger arc of the Republic’s founding ministries — the age in which the parliamentary Republic, having conquered the domestic institutions, turned to the world. Ferry, like Gambetta, embodied the confident republicanism of the “heroic age” that was passing.

entities/jules-grevy.title: Jules Grévy (1807–1891)
entities/jules-grevy.content:
Jules Grévy (1807–1891)
The third President of the Republic, from January 1879 to 1887, and the man who consolidated the parliamentary regime that Mac-Mahon had tried to resist. Jules Grévy, the austere lawyer of the Jura, was the president who made the office subordinate to the Chamber — the living proof that the Republic could govern without a strong head of state. His presidency marked the passage from the founding “heroic age” to the settled parliamentary routine, and Hanotaux treats his election with a certain irony.
The republican of 1848
Grévy belonged to the older republicanism, born before the Second Republic of 1848. He had been associated with the republican movement since his youth; Hanotaux’s portrait recalls his origins, his role in 1848, his relations with Lamartine, and his long career as a parliamentary republican. As president of the National Assembly he had shown the reserve and legalism that marked his whole career. He was, above all, a man of the constitution and of the parliamentary majority — the antithesis, in temperament, of the soldier-president Mac-Mahon he succeeded.
Chief of the republican party
When Thiers died in 1877, in the middle of the seize-mai-1877 crisis, Grévy became the leading figure of the republican party — the steady hand that could hold the union of the 363 together against the Marshal’s dissolution. He had already given his name to a celebrated constitutional amendment during the debates of the National Assembly, a motion for a purely parliamentary Republic without a strong presidency. His victory in the senatorial elections of January 1879 and Mac-Mahon’s consequent resignation opened the presidency to him.
President of the parliamentary Republic
Elected president in January 1879, Grévy at once set the tone of his presidency: he would not govern, he would let the Chamber govern. Where Mac-Mahon had asserted the independent authority of the head of state, Grévy accepted that the president stood aside, that ministries rose and fell with parliamentary majorities, and that the Republic was above all the rule of the Assembly. Hanotaux’s judgment is that Grévy’s election was in itself a fault — for the Republic, Hanotaux argues, needed a president of some authority rather than a pure spectator — yet it was precisely this self-effacement that consolidated the parliamentary regime. Under Grévy the ministries of Waddington, Freycinet, and Ferry carried through the amnesty, the school laws, and the Tunisian campaign while the president looked on.
The consolidator forced from office
Grévy’s very conception of the office made him the personification of the parliamentary Republic’s stability through the early 1880s. But the same low-key presidency could not resist the scandals and crises that the maturing regime threw up, and in 1887 he was forced to resign — the victim of the corruption affair that touched his entourage and of the political storms of the Boulanger era. His departure, coming after the death of Gambetta and the fall of Ferry, closed the generation of the founders. Grévy had shown that the Republic could survive without a powerful president; the price was the weakening of the presidency itself.

entities/jules-simon.title: Jules Simon (1814–1896)
entities/jules-simon.content:
Jules Simon (1814–1896)
The philosopher-politician of the Third Republic — the successor of Dufaure, head of the ministry whose dismissal by Marshal Mac-Mahon on 16 May 1877 touched off the seize-mai-1877 crisis. Jules Simon, a professor of philosophy and a republican of the liberal centre, governed in the difficult passage after the Constitution of 1875, caught between a conservative president and a republican Chamber. His fall at the hands of the Marshal became the decisive test of the parliamentary regime.
The philosopher and the republican
Jules Simon was that rare figure in French politics: a professor of philosophy who turned to public life. Hanotaux records his standing as a thinker and writer on education and his long career in the liberal opposition under the Empire; he had been one of the ministers who, in the last days of the liberal Empire, had accepted the office that the imperialists finally wrecked. By 1876 he was a veteran republican of the centre, a man of moderate and constitutional opinions, at once too republican for the right and too cautious for the extreme Left.
Dufaure’s successor
After the elections of 1876 delivered a republican Chamber, Dufaure governed the first parliamentary ministry of the new regime; when he resigned at the close of 1876, unable to stand between Chamber and Senate, Mac-Mahon called on Jules Simon to form the ministry. Simon took office in December 1876, the first head of government chosen by the Marshal from the republican majority. His position was delicate: he had to satisfy the republican Chamber that had placed him there and the conservative president who had appointed him. He was, Hanotaux notes, embarrassed by his past and pressed on all sides — by the extreme Left demanding reform and amnesty, by Gambetta watching from the budget commission, by the Marshal testing how far he would resist.
The religious question and ‘le cléricalisme, voilà l’ennemi’
The decisive issue was religion. Simon’s ministry had to deal with the ultramontane question — the interpellation on ultramontane manœuvres, the growing confrontation between the republican state and the Catholic hierarchy loyal to Pius IX. In the great interpellation of the spring of 1877, Jules Simon and Gambetta made common cause, and it was then that Gambetta launched his resounding phrase: « Le cléricalisme, voilà l’ennemi ! » (“Clericalism — there is the enemy!”). Simon, though himself a liberal who respected conscience, was pushed toward the anticlerical programme that the Chamber demanded. This was more than Mac-Mahon and the ordre moral party could bear: the Marshal’s ministry, it seemed, was drifting into the arms of the enemies of religion.
The letter of 16 May
Mac-Mahon, resolved to break with the Left majority, dismissed Simon on 16 May 1877 — by letter, in the brusque manner that gave the crisis its name. The president charged that Simon had not resisted the clerical-baiting of the Chamber, that he could not govern with a ministry the president could not trust. Hanotaux treats the act as the Marshal’s deliberate assertion of the presidential power over the ministry. Jules Simon’s dismissal, rather than quieting the crisis, provoked it: the republicans of the Chamber united against the Marshal, interpellated, refused the budget, and carried the country with them in the elections of 14 October 1877. Simon, the mild philosopher dismissed by a soldier, had provided the occasion on which the parliamentary Republic defeated the presidential interpretation of the french-constitution-1875. He remained thereafter a figure of the republican centre, respected but passed by the greater events of the consolidating Republic.

entities/kalman-tisza.title: Kálmán Tisza (1830–1902)
entities/kalman-tisza.content:
Kálmán Tisza
Kálmán Tisza (1830–1902) was the Hungarian minister-president from 1875 to 1890, the longest tenure in the history of the kingdom, and the principal consolidator of the Dualist settlement of 1867. In the corpus’s frame he appears through the eyes of the German publicist Theodor von Sosnosky as the builder of the “magyarische Nationalstaat” — the statesman who, coming out of the old opposition to the Compromise, made himself its most effective defender and who welded the Hungarian Liberals into the governing party that carried Magyar supremacy over the subject peoples for a generation. He was the father of Count Stephen Tisza, who would carry the same defence of dualism and of Magyar supremacy into the years of the Great War.
From opposition to the Compromise
Tisza’s political journey mirrored that of the Magyar gentry as a whole. He had sat as a member of the oppositional minority in the fifteen-man committee that drafted the Compromise act of 1867 — the committee whose deliberations turned on the interpretation of the Pragmatic Sanction and of the word “common” in the common institutions. In that committee, Sosnosky records, Tisza was among those who would allow certain “Agenden des Heerwesens” — the business of the army — to be regulated “im gemeinsamen Einverständnis” with Austria, but not “gemeinsam,” not as a truly common affair. The independence of Hungary, Sosnosky remarks, was the political ideal of all Magyars without distinction of party, and the future minister-president, as a former member of that oppositional minority, could not have stood far from that view. Yet, once in power, he felt himself obliged to uphold the settlement that bound Hungary to the Crown of Austria.
The long premiership
Tisza became minister-president in 1875, at the head of the Liberal party he had formed by fusing his own following with the Deákist supporters of the Compromise. He remained in office for fifteen years, until 1890 — a stability that gave the Dualist system in Hungary its settled parliamentary form. Sosnosky presents him as the object of the fiercest hatred of the oppositional parties, which branded him a traitor to the national cause, accusing him of connivance with Austria. But the truth, in Sosnosky’s judgement, was the reverse of the accusation: the very independence party that so passionately hated and pursued him, and that set him up as a betrayer, was in reality served by his policy better than by its own. The difficulties he made for Austria, the obstacles he placed in the way of Viennese centralising designs, worked for the cause those parties claimed to serve far more effectually than their own agitation did.
The builder of the Magyar national state
The premiership of Tisza was the period in which the “magyarische Nationalstaat” — the Magyar national state — took its definitive shape. Against the background of the passionate, domineering temper of the Magyar political nation that Sosnosky describes in his introduction to the Hungarian half of his work, Tisza’s government carried through the policies of Magyarisation that were to define the treatment of the subject nationalities down to 1918: the school, the courts, and the electoral system were all turned to the creation of a Magyar political nation, and even those who were half-Magyarised — the “Talmi-Magyaren,” the sham Magyars — were the product and the tool of this project. It was under the aegis of Tisza’s long ministry, and of the Liberal party he commanded, that the German, Romanian, Slovak, Ruthenian and Serb populations of the kingdom found themselves pressed within a state conceived as the state of the Magyars alone.
The defence of dualism
Tisza’s achievement was to reconcile the two poles of Magyar politics — the ideal of independence and the necessity of the tie to Austria — in a working system. He defended the dualist settlement against the pan-Magyar extremists who dreamed of a Hungary sharing nothing with Austria but the ruler, even as he resisted the Austrian claims that would have reduced the kingdom to a province. His long tenure gave the Compromise of 1867 the force of an established order, so that when his son Stephen came to defend the same settlement a generation later, against the renewed assault of the independence party and the cry of Los von Österreich, it was Kálmán Tisza’s consolidation that formed the ground on which the son stood. The old Tisza, Sosnosky suggests, had by his patient defence of Hungarian interests done more for the cause the extremists professed than their own intransigence ever could.
Legacy
Kálmán Tisza died in 1902, twelve years after laying down the premiership. He left behind him the Liberal party he had created, the long peace of the Dualist system, and a tradition of Magyar state-building that his son inherited and carried into the fatal confrontation with the nationalities in the years before the First World War. To Sosnosky, writing in 1913, he was the exemplar of the settled Magyar politics of the age of consolidation — the man who had made the Dual Monarchy work for Hungary, and in doing so had shaped the national state whose unresolved nationality question stood at the centre of the monarchy’s troubles on the eve of 1914.

entities/konstantin-pobedonostsev.title: Konstantin Pobedonostsev (1827–1907)
entities/konstantin-pobedonostsev.content:
Konstantin Pobedonostsev
Konstantin Petrovich Pobedonostsev (1827–1907) was the reactionary conscience of the last two Romanov reigns — Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod from 1880, the tutor of both alexander-iii and nicholas-ii, and the most influential advocate in Russia of autocracy and Orthodoxy as inseparable supports of the state. He was the man who, in the weeks after the assassination of Alexander II, turned the new emperor from reform toward the manifesto of 29 April 1881 that reaffirmed the samoderzhavie (“autocracy”); and he lived on into the reign of Nicholas II, where his successor in the Synod’s service, nikolai-zhevakhov, could look back on him as the great proponent of the very order that collapsed in 1917.
The tutor and the counter-reformer
Pobedonostsev’s influence rested on a paradox Kornilov notes: he had been one of the authors of the judicial statutes of Alexander II — a reformer by formation — yet by 1881 he had become the head of the reaction. His power came from his place as the former tutor of the emperors, who trusted him as they trusted no minister. When Alexander III hesitated in March 1881 over the constitutional project of Loris-Melikov, it was Pobedonostsev who at the conference of 8 March denounced the whole course of the previous reign as the work of “talking-shops” — the zemstvos, the new courts, the licentious press — and warned that the proposed representative commission would be a “supreme talking-shop” preparing the ruin of Russia. With the Moscow publicists Katkov and Aksakov as his allies, he worked on the emperor’s own conservative instincts, and by the end of April had obtained from him, secretly and to the surprise of the other ministers, the commission to draft the manifesto. Its words — that the emperor was summoned by the voice of God to stand firmly to the work of government in the trust of “the strength and truth of autocratic power” — set the course of the whole counter-reforming reign.
Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod
As Ober-Procurator, the lay head of the Holy Synod — the government’s eye over the Church — Pobedonostsev stood for the identification of Orthodoxy with the state and for the defense of the established order against all that threatened it. His influence extended through the Church into education and the press, and his was the voice that championed the autocracy as the one form of government fitted to Russia. Kornilov’s account of the reaction of the 1880s repeatedly marks his role — in the restriction of the zemstvo, the persecution of non-Orthodox and non-Russians, the whole narrowing of the public life that the Great Reforms had opened.
The Zhevakhov legacy
For the witness of the Synod in the last years, Zhevakhov supplies the later testimony. Writing as a loyal church official of the monarchy’s final years, Zhevakhov treats the religious and conservative ideal that Pobedonostsev represented as the true foundation of the Russian state. In the second volume of his memoirs he expounds at length his thesis that Russian autocracy was “not a political but a religious” idea — the people’s faith in the anointed tsar as the basis of power — a thesis that is in effect the Pobedonostsev doctrine restated at the moment of its ruin. By the time of the February revolution the dynasty had long outlived the strength of that idea, and the Church itself, as Zhevakhov’s account of the February days shows, no longer answered the state’s appeal for support. Pobedonostsev, who had died in 1907, had lived to see the failure of his school; it was his successors, not he, who watched the autocracy fall.

entities/lavr-kornilov.title: Lavr Kornilov (1870–1918)
entities/lavr-kornilov.content:
Lavr Kornilov
General Lavr Georgievich Kornilov (1870–1918) was commander-in-chief of the Russian army in 1917, the central figure of the Kornilov movement and the kornilov-affair-1917 of August, and the organizer and first commander of the Volunteer Army that opened the white-movement in the civil war. His death on 31 March 1918, struck down by a grenade during the assault on Ekaterinodar in the ice-march-1918, made him the martyr of the White cause. Denikin, his chief of staff and successor, wrote the volume of his Essays on the Russian Troubles devoted to “the struggle of General Kornilov” — an account both apologetic and precise, treating the affair less as a “mutiny” than as the tragic turning of the revolution against itself.
The divergence of paths
Denikin opens his second volume by insisting that the revolution had, by the summer of 1917, outgrown the simple picture of two forces — the Provisional Government and the Soviet — facing each other. By July and August it had become a many-sided struggle among government, the soviets, and the supreme command, and after the July days and the crisis of power the Third coalition government of alexander-kerensky held its authority only formally. Into this vacuum the figure of the commander-in-chief was thrust. Kornilov, in Denikin’s account, had no definite political programme before the rising; the document later known as the “Kornilov programme” was the fruit of later collective work. What he had was the conviction that the army and the state were being destroyed, and the resolution to restore discipline. His “memorandum” on army reorganization, supported by Savinkov, demanded the restoration of the commanding authority that the revolution and the committees had broken.
The Kornilov movement and the rising
The officer corps, after the failure of the June offensive, moved into opposition to the government, and around the commander-in-chief gathered the secret organizations and the public opinion of those who hoped for a strong hand. Denikin is careful with the words: “affair,” “rising,” “conspiracy,” “mutiny” are all too narrow; he prefers the Kornilov movement for the whole, and for the days of 27–31 August the Kornilov rising. By late August Kerensky still wavered, weighing whether to be with Kornilov against the soviets or with the soviets against Kornilov; Savinkov balanced between them; Kornilov had decided on a change in the structure of power but not on the methods; and General Krymov’s troops stood ready. The mission of V. N. Lvov, carrying between the premier and the commander-in-chief, issued in the declaration by Kerensky that the supreme commander was in “mutiny.” Kornilov refused to yield; Stavka, the commanders, the Allied representatives, and the Russian public took sides; and when the rising collapsed without a battle, Krymov shot himself and Kornilov was arrested. Denikin’s verdict is blunt: Kerensky’s victory was the “prelude to Bolshevism” — a strong hand rejected, a disarmed command, and the road left open to the one organized force that would take power.
Bykhov and the road to the Don
Imprisoned with his associates in the monastery-prison of Bykhov, Kornilov watched the autumn of the revolution from a cell. Denikin, himself among the prisoners, records the life of the Bykhov group, the relations of the prisoners with Stavka and Kerensky, and the elaboration of the plans and the “programme” that would govern the White cause. With the Bolshevik seizure of power in October, the fate of the prisoners hung in the balance; the murder of General Dukhonin at Stavka — who, as acting commander-in-chief, had released them — marked the end of the old army. In the chaos of the first days of Bolshevism the Bykhov prisoners escaped and made their way to the Don, where General Alekseev had already begun the organization of a volunteer force at Novocherkassk. Kornilov’s arrival completed the “triumvirate” of Alekseev, Kornilov, and Ataman Kaledin, and the Volunteer Army — the nucleus of the white-movement — came into being in the winter of 1917–18.
The First Kuban (Ice) March and death
The army’s retreat from the Don under Bolshevik pressure became the First Kuban March, the great ordeal of the White movement. Denikin’s narrative follows it from the military council at Olginskaya, through the crossing of the Kuban, the fights at Lezhanka and beyond the Laba, and the desperate passage of the “Ice March” of 15 March at Novo-Dmitrievskaya — rain, water, and mud turning to frost, the men frozen in their coats, Markov’s Officer Regiment storming the stanitsa in the dark. Joined by the Kuban volunteers, the army turned on Ekaterinodar and assaulted it. On 31 March 1918, while the army was concentrated for the final assault, a Russian shell struck the headquarters. Denikin records the order: “At 7.30 on 31 March General Kornilov was killed by an enemy shell that hit the army staff. He fell a hero’s death — a man who loved Russia more than himself and could not bear her shame.” The loss was concealed from the army for a day; then anton-denikin, his chief of staff, took command and lifted the siege. The First Kuban March — the “Ice March” — became the founding epic of the Volunteer Army, and Kornilov its eternal memory.

entities/leon-gambetta.title: Léon Gambetta (1838–1882)
entities/leon-gambetta.content:
Léon Gambetta (1838–1882)
The orator who founded the Third Republic. Léon Gambetta, son of a Genoese grocer, was the tribune of the republican opposition under the Second Empire, the proclaimer of the Republic on 4 September 1870, the animator of national defence in the provinces during the war, and for a decade the leading voice — and at the last the minister-president — of the parliamentary Republic. His death in 1882 closed the “heroic age” of the Republic’s foundation, the period Hanotaux himself called by Gambetta’s name.
The tribune of the opposition
Gambetta’s rise was the rise of democratic oratory. Hanotaux’s portrait traces his origins and intellectual formation: a provincial of modest means who came to the bar and to politics, made his name in the great trials of the Empire’s last years, notably the Baudin subscription of 1869, and was elected to the Corps législatif. He embodied the republican Left that fought the liberal Empire of napoleon-iii as an inadequate concession. When the Empire fell in the disaster of Sedan, it was Gambetta who, on 4 September 1870, proclaimed the Republic from the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville and demanded the guerre à outrance that the more prudent republicans — and above all Thiers — refused.
The war and the Assembly
During the war of 1870–71 Gambetta left Paris by balloon to direct national defence in the provinces, the incarnation of resistance to the Prussian advance. Yet the elections of 8 February 1871, held under the shadow of defeat, returned a monarchical Assembly committed to peace, and Gambetta was forced to bend to the country’s verdict. As deputy he stood for the Republic within an Assembly that had none, and by 1872 he had become, in Hanotaux’s account, the leader around whom the republican party organized itself.
The Grenoble speech and the ‘nouvelles couches’
It was at Grenoble on 26 September 1872, in the second oratorical campaign that carried him through Savoie and the Dauphiné, that Gambetta proclaimed the advent of democracy in politics — the celebrated speech on the “new social stratum” (nouvelles couches sociales), the rising middle and popular classes who were henceforth to govern France. The same campaign named clericalism the remaining enemy, and Hanotaux records the watchword that would follow the Republic for a generation: « Le cléricalisme, voilà l’ennemi ! » (“Clericalism — there is the enemy!”). The speech alarmed the right and electrified the republican Left; it fixed Gambetta as the dangerous man of the new France that the monarchists had to stop.
Leader of the republican party
After the fall of Thiers in 1873 and the failure of the monarchical campaign, Gambetta led the republican opposition through the ordre moral and the septennat. His provincial tours, his interventions in the Assembly, and his leadership of the Left made him the presumptive chief of the coming parliamentary Republic. He pressed Mac-Mahon’s ministries, demanded that the president submit to the parliamentary majority, and was the soul of the union of the 363 that resisted the seize-mai-1877 dissolution. His challenge — that the Marshal must se soumettre ou se démettre (“submit or resign”) — became the programme of the republican victory of 14 October 1877.
President of the Chamber and the ministry
With the parliamentary Republic triumphant after 1879, Gambetta became president of the Chamber of Deputies, holding the tribune he had so often dominated. Only in 1881–82 did he at last form the ministry that bore his name, the “grand ministry” of his friends and admirers. It was a disappointment: his project of constitutional revision and scrutin de liste was beaten, and the government fell after a short tenure. Hanotaux treats the failure of the Gambetta cabinet as cutting the wings of hope and disconcerting the logic of events. Gambetta died in 1882 at the height of his legend, and Hanotaux suspends his narrative at that death — a brutal conclusion after which “figures and the aspect of things change.” For Hanotaux, Gambetta was the founder of the Republic and the democratic tribune whose voice had called it into being.

entities/leon-trotsky.title: Leon Trotsky (1879–1940)
entities/leon-trotsky.content:
Leon Trotsky
Leon Trotsky (1879–1940), born Lev Davidovich Bronstein, was a leader of the Russian Bolshevik party and, in the frame of this corpus, the man who faced the Central Powers at Brest-Litovsk in the winter of 1917–18 and there negotiated the peace that took Russia out of the war. He appears in these sources as seen from the opposite camps of the Great War: the Austrian foreign minister Ottokar Czernin met him at the negotiating table and left a vivid portrait of the Bolshevik orator reckoning on world revolution, while the White general Anton Denikin, surveying the collapse of Russia, counted him among the destroyers who had laid the Russian state low. He stands beside Lenin as one of the two architects of the Bolshevik seizure of power and of the revolutionary peace.
The revolutionary and the return from America
Trotsky’s path to the revolution of 1917 ran through exile. Czernin, describing the factions of the Russian revolution for his readers, notes the group of “Internationalisten” — those who wished to restore the International, called also Zimmerwaldists or Kienthalists — under the leadership of “Trotzki (recte Bronstein),” Trotsky (rightly Bronstein), the one returned from America, along with Larin, Martow and Martynow returned from Switzerland. The years of emigration, spent in Vienna, Paris and New York, had made him a figure of the international socialist movement; the revolution of February 1917 brought him home, and by the autumn he had thrown in his lot with Lenin’s party. Denikin, in his survey of the two extremes of the Russian social order in which alone, he thought, there was a real strong will — “die leider dem Zerstören und nicht dem Aufbauen dienstbar,” unhappily a will to destruction and not to construction — names the one extreme as having already given “Lenin, Bronstein, Apfelbaum, Uritsky, Dzerzhinsky, Peters”: Lenin, Bronstein, Zinoviev (Apfelbaum), Uritsky, Dzerzhinsky, Peters. Trotsky stood in that catalogue as one of the principal names of the revolutionary camp.
The seizure of power
The Bolsheviks took power in Petrograd in October 1917, in the coup that overthrew the Provisional Government of Kerensky. Trotsky was, after Lenin, the most prominent figure of the new regime, and it was he who became the people’s commissar for foreign affairs. Denikin, from the side of the White command, saw in the advent of the Bolsheviks the culmination of the process by which the strong will of the extremes had triumphed over the weak will of the middle — the will to destruction prevailing over the will to construction. The revolutionary government’s first acts — the decree on peace, the decree on land, the appeal to the peoples to end the war — were the work of the men who had seized the state, and Trotsky, as foreign commissar, was their spokesman toward the world.
At Brest-Litovsk
The new regime’s most pressing task was peace. Russia, exhausted by three years of war and now in revolutionary disintegration, confronted the Central Powers across a negotiating table at Brest-Litovsk in the winter of 1917–18. Czernin, who had travelled there as the representative of Austria-Hungary, records the Russian delegation that first appeared under Joffe — “ein geborener Jude namens Joffe,” a born Jew named Joffe, with Kamenev, the brother-in-law of the Russian minister of foreign affairs Trotsky, and Madame Bizenko, all released from prison by the revolution. Then, at the decisive moment, Trotsky himself arrived. Czernin describes the arrival of Trotzki, the tension of the negotiations with Kühlmann, General Hoffmann and himself, the furious telegrams of Hindenburg over any “renunciation,” Ludendorff’s hourly telephone calls, and the demand of the Austrians for a free hand should the Germans break with the Russians. In the end Trotsky accepted the ultimatum, and the peace was signed.
The reckoning on world revolution
What distinguished Trotsky at Brest was his reading of the situation as a revolutionary opportunity rather than a mere surrender. While Austria starved — Czernin records the “Hungerkatastrophe in Österreich,” the famine catastrophe in Austria — and the Central Powers pressed their territorial demands, Trotsky “rechnet auf Weltrevolution,” reckoned on world revolution. He did not treat the peace as a defeat but as an episode in a larger struggle; the collapse of the old order in Russia was, for him, the beginning of a European and world upheaval that would overtake the Central Powers in turn. Czernin, who had debated with the Bolsheviks the nature of power and of rule, was struck by this conviction and by the confidence of a man who could calmly accept an ultimatum in the certainty that history was on his side.
The judgement of his adversaries
Czernin’s portrait of Trotsky is that of an enemy who commanded a reluctant respect. In his account of the peace efforts he reflects on the coming of a “world of Bolshevism” — he wrote, in his closing reflections on the war, of the danger that anarchy and Bolshevism posed to Europe, and he recalled the remark of Charlotte Corday — “nicht einen Menschen, sondern eine wilde Bestie habe ich getötet” — as a warning of what might again be done to rid the world of such men, hoping that “diese Bolschewiken” would vanish and that a Corday might be found for Trotzki. Yet even in that hostility he granted the Bolsheviks the reality of their will and their doctrine. Denikin, for his part, treated the Bolshevik triumph as the working of the destructive will that had taken hold of one extreme of Russian society, and Trotsky, under his true name Bronstein, as one of the leaders who had brought Russia to ruin. Both accounts agree on the magnitude of the man’s role: it was Trotsky who carried the peace of Brest-Litovsk through, and in doing so withdrew Russia from the Great War.
Significance
Trotsky stands in this corpus as the Bolshevik statesman who concluded the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk and thereby ended Russia’s part in the First World War — the indispensable lieutenant of Lenin in the seizure of power, and the negotiator whose confident reckoning on world revolution marked the revolutionary internationalism of the new regime. Seen through the hostile eyes of Czernin and Denikin, he is a measure of how the European order perceived the Bolshevik danger in the very year it was born. He would go on to found and command the Red Army in the civil war that followed the peace, but it is as the man of Brest-Litovsk that he enters this corpus’s story of the years 1866–1919.

entities/leopold-berchtold.title: Count Leopold Berchtold (1863–1942)
entities/leopold-berchtold.content:
Count Leopold Berchtold (1863–1942)
Leopold Graf Berchtold, Austro-Hungarian minister of foreign affairs from 1912 to 1915, presided over the monarchy’s diplomacy through the Balkan wars and into the catastrophe of 1914 — the man who, as the hand on the Ballhausplatz during the balkan-wars-1912-13 and the July crisis, dispatched the ultimatum to Serbia that opened the First World War. His story in this corpus’s frame is the attempt to hold the monarchy’s Balkan position by a policy of peace and of standing fast — the status-quo diplomacy of the Balkan wars, the creation of Albania, the securing of Rumania — that ended in the declaration of war against Serbia in July 1914. Sosnosky closes his account of the Balkan wars with a chapter on “Berchtold’s Balkan policy,” and Czernin’s memoir opens its account of the catastrophe on “Berchtold and the ultimatum to Serbia.”
The status-quo diplomacy of the Balkan wars
Berchtold came to the foreign ministry in 1912 in the shadow of the first Balkan war, when the Balkan states had formed their league and thrown themselves upon Turkey. His policy was one of the status quo and of the preservation of the monarchy’s legitimate interests in the peninsula. The watchword that the Balkan peoples advanced — “the Balkans for the Balkan peoples” — he answered with the insistence that Austria-Hungary too had legitimate interests that could not be ignored. His diplomacy sought to hold the great powers together, to prevent the war from spreading, and to secure for the monarchy a share in the settlement that its position in the East demanded.
His most important constructive act was the creation of Albania. When the Balkan war threw up the Albanian question and the rising of 1912, Berchtold championed the formation of an independent Albania as a barrier to the advance of the Balkan states and a check on the Serbian and Montenegrin ambition to reach the Adriatic. Sosnosky’s account of the struggle over Albania and of Montenegro’s attempt to seize Scutari, with the naval demonstration before that town, belongs to the story of this policy. Berchtold’s refusal to occupy the Sandjak of Novi Pazar, his championship of Albania, and his handling of the Prochaska affair were, Sosnosky judged, the elements of a policy that sought peace without surrendering the monarchy’s standing.
Rumania and the securing of the rear
A central object of Berchtold’s diplomacy was Rumania. With the Balkan war forcing Austria-Hungary to reckon with the possibility of warlike complications and with Russia, it became advisable to secure Rumania for that case while not letting the thread with Bulgaria — Rumania’s jealous rival — break. Berchtold, Conrad records, was unremittingly concerned to shape the policy of the monarchy in this sense: to bring Rumania and Bulgaria into accord and to have Rumania actively at its side with all its forces for the eventual war against Russia. It was on this ground that in mid-November 1912 the archduke-heir charged Conrad with his mission to Bukarest, to work in this sense under the pretext of conveying the Kaiser’s condolences to King Carol. The policy of securing Rumania was pursued down to the eve of the war, and its failure — Rumania’s eventual entry on the other side — belongs to the larger tragedy of the monarchy’s position.
The ultimatum to Serbia
The gravest act of Berchtold’s tenure came in the summer of 1914. After the assassination of the archduke-heir at Sarajevo, it was Berchtold who framed the demands to Serbia and dispatched the ultimatum, and Czernin’s memoir treats the catastrophe with an account of “Berchtold and the ultimatum to Serbia,” of the warning of the German ambassador Tschirschky — who, Czernin held, more than Bethmann Hollweg drew Austria-Hungary into the war — and of the opposition of the Hungarian minister-president Stephen Tisza to the sharp ultimatum. The ultimatum, Czernin observed, did not mean that war was irrevocably willed but was conceived as a diplomatic demand to be pressed to the last; when Serbia accepted it only incompletely, the ground was laid for the war that followed. Czernin, who judged the monarchy’s greatest misfortune to be the German invasion of Belgium and who regarded Austria-Hungary’s disintegration as by then irrevocable, places the responsibility for the ultimatum squarely on Berchtold’s period of office.
Resignation and legacy
Berchtold’s tenure did not survive the opening of the war. He resigned in 1915, succeeded in a foreign policy that the war had swept beyond the control of the diplomatists, and his name remained attached to the ultimatum that had set the catastrophe in motion. In the corpus he stands as the last of the Ballhausplatz statesmen of the pre-war generation — the heir of alois-aehrenthal, against whose successor conrad-von-hotzendorf again pressed the preventive war he had urged all along, and the predecessor of ottokar-czernin, who carried the diplomacy of the monarchy through the middle of the war it had helped to unleash.

entities/luigi-cadorna.title: Luigi Cadorna (1850–1928)
entities/luigi-cadorna.content:
Luigi Cadorna (1850–1928)
Luigi Cadorna, born in 1850, was Chief of Staff of the Italian army from July 1914 to November 1917 — the general who commanded the Italian front through the first three years of the Italian war, conducted the endless offensive battles of the Isonzo, and was dismissed on 8 November 1917 in the midst of the retreat that followed battle-of-caporetto-1917. His two volumes, La guerra alla fronte italiana fino all’arresto sulla linea della Piave e del Grappa (1921–23), are the official account of his own command, carried down to the moment of his removal; and Attilio Frescura’s Diario di un imboscato supplies the soldier’s view of the same years, including a chapter on the dismissal itself. Cadorna was a soldier of the old school — rigid, exacting, and unforgiving — and his name became, for the war generation, the symbol both of the terrible grinding of the Isonzo and of the disaster of Caporetto.
Italy’s war and the plan of operations
When the European war broke out in 1914, Cadorna was made Chief of Staff and charged with preparing the army that the neutrality of 1914–15 allowed to mobilise. His first volume opens with the condition of Italy at the outbreak — the army, the country, the government and parliament — and the military preparation during the period of neutrality in 1915, before the kingdom declared war on Austria on 24 May 1915. The plan of operations was the offensive on the Isonzo and the Julian front, where the boundary with Austria ran through the mountains toward the plains of the Veneto: Cadorna committed Italy to an offensive strategy that sought to break through the Austro-Hungarian lines and to drive toward Trieste, and to defend on the Alpine and Trentino fronts. It was a plan of frontal attack, and it set the pattern of the war on the Italian front for three years.
The Isonzo offensives and the Strafexpedition
Cadorna’s command was a series of offensives on the Isonzo — the First through Fourth Battles of 1915, the Battle of Gorizia (August 1916, the Sixth), and the great autumn struggles on the Carso — each a grinding assault against the Austrian entrenchments with heavy losses and limited gains. He also had to meet the Austrian counter-stroke: the Strafexpedition, the “punitive expedition” launched from the Trentino in the spring of 1916, which Cadorna’s first volume describes at length — the Austrian offensive from the Trentino against the First Army, and the Italian counter-offensive that checked it. Through 1917 he pressed on, with the offensive on the Giulia front in May (the Tenth Battle) and the battle between the Idria and the Timavo in August–September (the Eleventh Battle), in the isonzo-battles-1915-17 that were the central experience of the Italian soldier. Frescura, who served through these years, records the “infinite gradations of the shirker” and the rearguard life of a war that spent its strength in the trenches and the Carso.
Caporetto and the dismissal
The end came in October 1917. On 24 October 1917 the Austro-German attack fell on the Second Army at Caporetto, broke the front, and dissolved the line in a retreat that Cadorna’s second volume narrates in detail — the retreat to the Tagliamento, the retreat from the Tagliamento to the Piave, and the defensive line of the Piave, where the retreat was finally arrested in November 1917. The disaster cost the army hundreds of thousands of prisoners and guns, and it cost Cadorna his command: on 8 November 1917 he was dismissed and replaced by armando-diaz. Frescura’s chapter “Cadorna” describes the reorganisation of the Supreme Command that followed, and the official account of the war would henceforward be Diaz’s. Cadorna spent the rest of his life defending his record — the two volumes are in large part that defence — and he died in 1928, remembered above all as the general of the Isonzo and the casualty of Caporetto. His own narrative of the retreat insists that the line was held on the Piave, and rebuts the view that Marshal Foch came to Italy as adviser and inspirer of the retreat, arguing rather that Foch opposed it.

entities/marshal-foch.title: Ferdinand Foch (1851–1929)
entities/marshal-foch.content:
Ferdinand Foch (1851–1929)
Ferdinand Foch, Marshal of France, was the French soldier who embodied the Allied recovery of the Great War — the victor of the battle-of-the-marne-1914 in its immediate aftermath, the great captain of the Second Battle of the Marne, and from the spring of 1918 the generalissimo of the Allied forces whose hundred-days-offensive-1918 broke the German army and forced the armistice-11-november-1918. In Recouly’s synthesis, written twenty years after the war, Foch is “a soldier of genius” to whom only the threat of catastrophe compelled the Allies to confide a single command; his story in this corpus’s frame is the story of how the French and Allied supreme command was created, exercised, and crowned with victory. His name recurs from the Marne to the armistice train at Rethondes, and — as Cadorna’s appendix testifies — as the adviser sent to Italy in the darkest hour of the Italian front.
The teacher of the École de Guerre
Foch came to the war as a thinker and teacher of war as much as a field commander. Recouly recalls his conferences at the École de Guerre, where he demonstrated with luminous force the errors and dangers of the German command method — the method, as Moltke the elder had conceived it in 1870, of giving the executants general directives drawn from an overall plan and then leaving them to fend for themselves. Such a method, Foch argued, could only end in a disordered, incoherent battle not directed by its chief. He compressed the judgment into a lapidary phrase that Recouly quotes: « La stratégie allemande fait faillite: elle n’est sauvée que par la tactique » — “German strategy fails; it is only saved by tactics.” He was sixty-three years old in 1914, a year older than joseph-joffre, and he brought to the war the will and the philosophy of command that the defensive crisis of 1918 would finally make the possession of the entire Alliance.
The Marne and the war of movement
Foch was one of the principal executants of the victory of the battle-of-the-marne-1914 in September 1914. Recouly records his celebrated maxim, « Une bataille perdue est une bataille qu’on croit perdue » — “a lost battle is a battle one believes lost” — and judges that the psychological factor almost always has a preponderant weight in war as in life. The maxim was put to the test in those days of extreme strain on the French left, where Foch’s command stood in the very line of the German wheel toward Paris. He survived the test; and the Marne, which turned the short war into a long one, began his rise as the master of the battle of attrition that the war of movement had become.
The creation of the supreme command
The central theme of Foch’s later career, as Recouly frames it, is the command unique — the single, unified direction of the Allied war. From the first winter of the war Recouly marks the capital question as the commandement unique, the supreme direction of the war: a generalissimo, master of combining all operations, disposing of reserves whether French, English, Belgian, or Italian. But this ideal solution, Recouly notes, was long out of the question; to realise the single command, only three years later, required the direct menace of a defeat and even of a disaster — the German march on Paris in the spring of 1918 separating the French armies. When Foch discussed the subject he remarked, with his habitual brusqueness, that a study on unified command should begin: « Article premier: Il n’y a pas de commandement unique » — “Article one: there is no unified command.” The irony was that he himself would become its living embodiment. Only the threat of catastrophe, Recouly writes, compelled the Allies to accept the single command, confided to “a soldier of genius, Foch.”
Generalissimo of the Allied armies
Appointed generalissimo of the Allied forces, Foch conducted the defensive against the German offensives of 1918 and then turned to the counter-offensive. His method, Recouly explains, consisted in multiple attacks that harried the fragile German facade (la façade fragile) — attacks designed to shake the German army of occupation and to overwork the German army of shock, in striking contrast with the single, concentrated blows of Ludendorff. When Ludendorff’s 15 July offensive failed and was followed three days later by a graver failure, there began for the German leader the descent that would become ever more rapid and soon vertiginous. Foch’s counter-offensives broke the German army in 1918; the offensive of hundred-days-offensive-1918 that began on 8 August — which Ludendorff himself called the black day of the German army — carried the Allies to the verge of final victory. It was Foch who received the German plenipotentiaries at the little station of Rethondes in the forest of Compiègne on the night of 7 November 1918 and imposed the armistice-11-november-1918 of 11 November that ended the fighting.
Foch in Italy, 1917
Foch’s name also connects the French and Italian commands. Cadorna’s appendix, added to the second edition of his war account, treats the mission of Marshal Foch in Italy in October–November 1917, immediately after the catastrophe of battle-of-caporetto-1917. Cadorna destroys two legends at once: on one side the French legend that Foch came to Italy as a counsellor and inspirer of energy to the Italian Supreme Command, and on the other a legend, current in Italy, that Foch, arriving at the Italian headquarters at Treviso on 30 October, advised the retreat from the Piave to the Adige and the Mincio. Against both, Cadorna insists that Foch raised no objection to the sending of the first four French divisions of the 10th Army to the Montello, and that the offensive of 24 October had been foreseen, announced and awaited by the French command rather than a surprise. The exchange over Foch’s mission is thus part of the larger argument over responsibility for the Italian disaster and over the creation of the Allied command that Foch came to personify.

entities/mikhail-alexeyev.title: General Mikhail Alexeyev (1857–1918)
entities/mikhail-alexeyev.content:
General Mikhail Alexeyev
Mikhail Vasilyevich Alexeyev (1857–1918) was the professional chief of the Russian general staff who, in the collapse of 1917, became the quiet organizer of the anti-Bolshevik resistance. Anton Denikin’s Essays on the Russian Troubles treats him as the central staff figure who held the disintegrating army together through the February Revolution and then, after the October seizure of power, laid the foundations of the Volunteer Army on the Don.
The Stavka under Nicholas II
Alexeyev served as chief of staff of the supreme command (the Stavka) under Nicholas II when the Emperor took personal command in 1915. In Denikin’s account of the army before the revolution, Alexeyev appears as the responsible professional who understood the fragility of the war-worn army and the fatal effects of politics upon it. He presided at the Stavka during the revolutionary spring of 1917, when the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet competed for the loyalty of the front.
From the collapse to the Volunteer Army
After the Kornilov affair and the Bolshevik revolution, Alexeyev made his way to the Don, where he began organizing the first nucleus of what became the Volunteer Army. Denikin describes the awkward partnership — the tactful Alexeyev and the impulsive Kornilov — that constituted the leadership of the early White movement, a division of authority that persisted until Kornilov’s death in the Ice March of spring 1918.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Alexeyev is the organizational counterweight to Kornilov: where Kornilov supplied the revolutionary gesture and the soldier’s daring, Alexeyev supplied the staff discipline and the patient construction of the anti-Bolshevik army. His death of illness in October 1918 removed the one figure who might have bridged the White command’s divisions.
