entities/napoleon-iii.title: Napoleon III (1808–1873)
entities/napoleon-iii.content:
Napoleon III (1808–1873)
Charles-Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon I, President of the Second Republic and, from the coup d’état of 2 December 1851 and the proclamation of December 1852, Emperor of the French as Napoleon III. In the frame of this wiki he is the sovereign of the second-empire-france through its transformation into the liberal-empire and into the catastrophe of 1870, in which he lost his throne, his capital and his liberty. The corpus gives him a double portrait: the republican historian Taxile Delord measures him as a dynastic adventurer watched by a hostile Opposition, while Émile Ollivier, the liberal statesman who served him to the last, defends his intentions and the sincerity of his constitutional turn. Both agree that the Empire ended not merely at the hands of the Prussians but by what Ollivier calls its own “suicide.”
The Emperor at the close of 1866
Coming out of the war of 1866, in which France had stood aside while Prussia overwhelmed Austria, Napoleon III faced the immediate problem of prestige. Delord records the universal sense that Sadowa had shifted the centre of gravity of Europe and that the French Empire, founded on military glory and the “idea of nationality,” needed a success of its own. The opening of 1867 saw the Emperor announce, in his letter of 19 January, a regulated right of interpellation and the promise of press and meetings laws — the first steps of a liberal turn that would occupy the remaining years of the reign. His ministers and his Court, the parti de l’action gathered around the Empress, were not uniformly agreed on the pace of reform; Delord notes that the Emperor’s concessions were extracted under the pressure of opinion and of a parliamentary Opposition newly emboldened after 1866.
The Luxembourg crisis and the compensations question
In 1867 Napoleon sought a compensation for the Prussian aggrandisement that could be shown to the nation. Delord recounts how France, refused any cession on the left bank of the Rhine, was left by Bismarck to seek compensations in Belgium and Switzerland, and how the affair settled on Luxembourg — a Dutch possession whose fortress and garrison were under the German Confederation. A secret Franco-Dutch understanding on cession was broken, and the crisis brought France and Prussia to the edge of war before the powers agreed to a conference in London that neutralised the duchy in May 1867. The Luxembourg affair, in Delord’s telling, was a humiliation for Napoleon: he had claimed compensation and obtained only a neutralised fortress, while the European concert, with Prussia at its centre, policed the settlement. The episode set the tone of the late Empire — every French move watched, every concession parried by Berlin. See luxembourg-crisis-1867.
The Mexican adventure and Mentana
The same years darkened the imperial record abroad. The Mexican expedition, undertaken to plant an empire under the Archduke Maximilian, ended in 1867 with the French evacuation and Maximilian’s execution at Querétaro. Delord gives the episode as a study in responsibility: Napoleon III left to Washington the choice of the Mexican president and withdrew, while Maximilian’s clerical experiment collapsed before the Juarists; the French public read the death of the archduke as a moral disaster. On the other hand, in the Roman question the Emperor was drawn the opposite way. When Garibaldi invaded the Papal States in 1867, the Empress pressed for intervention and Napoleon, after hesitation, sent troops who fought the Garibaldians at Mentana in November 1867 — a success that Delord treats as a checkmate of the Empire’s own principles, since France now sustained the Pope against the very principle of nationality on which the Empire claimed to stand. See battle-of-mentana-1867 and capture-of-rome-1870.
The liberal turn and the ministry of 2 January 1870
Under the pressure of the elections of 1869 and of a resurgent Opposition, Napoleon III moved decisively toward a parliamentary regime. Delord’s last chapters describe the “Préface de l’Empire libéral”: the negotiations with Émile Ollivier, conducted through Clément Duvernois; Ollivier’s conditions and programme; the disguised journey of the Emperor to Compiègne to meet him; the hesitations; and finally the Emperor’s letter of 27 December 1869 and the formation of the ministry of 2 January 1870, in which Ollivier became the effective head of government. The senatus-consult that followed gave the Corps législatif a share in power and made the ministers responsible to the Chambers. To Delord, a republican, this was the authoritarian Empire conceding what it had suppressed; to Ollivier, it was the honest attempt to reconcile the dynasty with liberty. Sybel, writing from the German side, treats the same evolution as a weakening of France — an empire hesitating between the parti de l’action and the liberal ministries, unable to pursue a coherent foreign policy. This transformation is the subject of the concept page liberal-empire.
The foreign-policy missteps and the Hohenzollern affair
The liberal Empire inherited the Emperor’s foreign difficulties. The Spanish revolution of 1868, which toppled Isabella II, left a vacant throne that the French government feared might pass to a Prussian prince; Sybel narrates at length how Marshal Prim, at the head of the Spanish regency, sought a candidate and eventually turned to Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. When Leopold’s acceptance was revealed in July 1870, the crisis that followed — the hohenzollern-candidature-1870, the negotiation at Ems, the ems-dispatch-1870 — swept away the diplomacy Ollivier and the Emperor had been conducting. The Emperor, whose health Delord and Ollivier both record as failing and whose personal command of the army was to prove disastrous, was pushed by the war party and by his own Court toward a war for which, in Ollivier’s later judgment, the responsibility rested with Bismarck’s provocation.
The war, Sedan and captivity
In July 1870 France declared war on Prussia. Ollivier, who carried the declaration, later defended the decision as forced upon the ministry by the Prussian outrage. The opening campaigns — battle-of-woerth-1870, Forbach — went against the French; by mid-August the Emperor, ill and stripped of effective command, had resigned the direction of the army to Marshal Bazaine and retired toward Châlons. His presence with Mac-Mahon’s army of relief drew that army into the trap of the Belgian frontier, and on 1 September 1870 the whole force was encircled at Sedan (battle-of-sedan-1870). Napoleon III, seeing further resistance hopeless, ordered the white flag raised and surrendered in person to the King of Prussia. Hanotaux records that at Sedan “Napoleon III did not only make himself prisoner”: the capitulation of the emperor and of an entire army opened a governmental void — the “vacance du pouvoir” in Thiers’s phrase — that the proclamation of the Republic on 4 September filled by revolution. The dynasty had fallen with its sovereign.
Exile and death
Carried into captivity at Wilhelmshöhe, the deposed emperor was released after the armistice and took refuge in England at Chislehurst, where he lived out the defeat in company with the Empress and their son. Hanotaux notes his death on 9 January 1873, at the approach of his sixty-fifth year, a sudden event that moved French politics on the eve of the monarchical restoration crisis. He died never having reigned again, the founder of bonapartism leaving his name and cause to a son, the Prince Imperial, who would die young in Africa.

entities/nicholas-ii.title: Nicholas II (1868–1918)
entities/nicholas-ii.content:
Nicholas II
Nicholas II (1868–1918), the last Emperor of All the Russias, reigned from the death of his father Alexander III in October 1894 to his abdication in March 1917, and died with his family at Ekaterinburg in 1918. His reign is the story of an autocrat who inherited a state already under strain and watched it pass through defeat in war, revolution, a grudging and then retracted constitution, and finally the collapse of the dynasty and of Russia itself in the Great War. The three witnesses of this wiki see him from three angles: sergei-witte, who served him and who records an emperor he found unprepared, indecisive, and in his later years surrounded by men who ruined what he himself had built; nikolai-zhevakhov, the loyal synodal official, who saw the collapse as a “fateful epoch” in which the loyalties of the court and the Church were consumed; and anton-denikin, the staff general, who traces how the revolution and the army’s collapse overthrew a throne already fatally compromised.
The unprepared heir
Witte is explicit that Nicholas II came to the throne unprepared. As a boy he had been the carefree tsesarevich whom the great prince dragged about by the ears at the Kiev station; Alexander III, never expecting to die so soon, had put off the political education of a son he still thought too young. When the father died in the autumn of 1894 the young emperor, as Witte writes, “by nature a very kind man, especially toward his family,” mounted the throne without the schooling his role demanded. The first years of the reign are told by Witte in a long series of episodes — the coronation, the Khodynka catastrophe, the negotiations with Li Hung-chang and the treaty with China, the seizure of Liaodong, the visit of Franz Joseph, Wilhelm II, and President Faure to Petersburg, the illness of the sovereign. Witte’s running complaint is of the influence of an irresponsible circle around the throne and the court’s constant undermining of the ministries.
Khodynka and the Far East
The coronation of 1896 was shadowed by the disaster of Khodynka, the field outside Moscow where a vast crowd gathered for the promised distribution of gifts and, in the press that followed, some two thousand people were killed and maimed. Witte, arriving at the field, found the traces of the catastrophe already smoothed away as if nothing had happened, the bodies removed and the festivities proceeding — a memory that fixed for many the callousness of the new reign. In foreign affairs the reign opened the era of Far Eastern adventure: the treaty with China and the Chinese Eastern Railway, the occupation of Port Arthur and Dalny, and the growing influence of the “Bezobrazov clique,” the adventurers around the throne who pushed a reckless policy in Korea and Manchuria. Witte, who had made the loan and the railway his own, found himself forced out of the finance ministry in 1903, as the war party gained the upper hand — and it was this course that carried Russia into the russo-japanese-war-1904-05.
The war, Bloody Sunday, and 1905
The war with Japan ended in defeat and revolution. From Witte’s account the paralysis of the government ran through every stage: the pressure of Trepov and the great duke on the cabinet, the police despotism of Plehve and then the “spring” of Svyatopolk-Mirsky, the ukase of 12 December 1904, and the catastrophe of 9 January 1905 — Bloody Sunday, when the workers’ procession before the Winter Palace was fired upon and the image of the tsar was broken in the eyes of his people. Tsushima completed the military disaster. The revolution of 1905 — the revolution-1905 — forced the emperor to his greatest concession: on 17 October 1905 he issued the manifesto granting civil liberty, a legislative duma-constitutionalism, and responsible government, with sergei-witte as the first premier. Witte’s memoirs record with bitter irony how the court later whispered that he had “wrung” the manifesto from an unwilling sovereign. The revolution was repressed, the Fundamental Laws of 1906 framed, and the state entered its brief constitutional experiment under pyotr-stolypin.
Stolypin and the retracted constitution
Under Stolypin the emperor presided over the duma-constitutionalism of the Third Duma and the land reform, but also over the hangings and the coup of 3 June 1907, by which the electoral law was changed to produce a Duma “not chosen but picked” for the government. Witte, dismissed after his half-year premiership, watched Stolypin’s regime with a contempt he did not conceal. The murder of Stolypin in Kiev in 1911 removed the one strong minister, and Nicholas II fell back into a governing style that Witte, from a distance, described as surrounded by mediocrities and self-interested courtiers. The last years before the war saw the rise of grigori-rasputin, the starets whose hold over the empress alexandra-feodorovna and, through her, over the sovereign, scandalized Petersburg and corroded the dynasty’s prestige.
The Great War and the collapse
The war of 1914 brought the ruin. In August 1915, under the influence of the empress’s circle and Rasputin, Nicholas II took upon himself the supreme command — a step Denikin describes as taken against the fruitless representations of eight ministers, uniting in his person the headship of the state and the conduct of the war in a moment of retreat. The total-war-economy strained food, industry, and transport; the empress and the court sank into the Rasputin scandal; the Duma’s opposition, voiced by Miliukov’s speech of 1 November 1916, demanded a responsible ministry. Zhevakhov, at the Synod through the last months, watched the authority of the crown drain away. When the February revolution broke out in Petrograd in March 1917, the sovereign at Mogilev — in Denikin’s phrase “alone, without family, without intimates” — found no one able or willing to save the throne, and on the advice of the generals and the Provisional Government he abdicated. The february-revolution-1917 thus closed the Romanov autocracy. The emperor and his family were held by the Provisional Government and then by the Bolsheviks, and in 1918, as the civil war mounted, they were shot at Ekaterinburg.

entities/nikolai-zhevakhov.title: Nikolai Zhevakhov (1874–1946)
entities/nikolai-zhevakhov.content:
Nikolai Zhevakhov
Prince Nikolai Davidovich Zhevakhov (1874–1946) was a senior official of the imperial State Chancellery who became deputy ober-procurator of the Holy Synod in the autumn of 1916 and served in that post through the last months of the monarchy until his arrest in the February revolution. He is the author of two volumes of memoirs, Vospominaniya tovarishcha ober-prokurora Svyateishago Sinoda (“Memoirs of a Deputy Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod”), which record the Church, the court, and the fall of the dynasty from a loyal, monarchical, and deeply religious standpoint. He is at once a witness of grigori-rasputin and the Rasputin scandal, of the Synod in the revolutionary days, and of the Church’s fate through the civil war and emigration.
The official and the court
Zhevakhov’s first volume opens in September 1915 with his mission to deliver the Nechaian Icon of the Mother of God to the imperial headquarters (Stavka) at Mogilev — a journey that carried him to audiences with Nicholas II and alexandra-feodorovna, and into the circles of the court and the Church that the war had brought together. An official of the State Chancellery, he was close to Count Rostovtsov and the court intermediaries, and his portrait of the Sovereign is that of a pious, unassuming man whom the author defends against the calumnies of the age. His account of Metropolitan Pitirim, of the ober-procurator A. N. Volzhin (with whom he broke over the Synod’s finances), and of his own appointment as deputy ober-procurator in the autumn of 1916 gives the reader a view of the synodal establishment in its last months.
The Rasputin excursus
The heart of the first volume is an extended meditation on Rasputin and on Russian “God-seeking.” Zhevakhov, writing as an apologist for eldership and for the imperial family, insists that the danger lay not in the starets himself but in those who used his name to destroy the dynasty — that, as he put it to a court lady, “talk about Rasputin is more harmful than Rasputin himself.” He records the hysteria of the capital, in which every appointment and every high position was ascribed to Rasputin’s influence and men sought to clear themselves of the suspicion of nearness to him; he records also the faith of the Empress, and of the Tsar himself — “if not for the prayers of Grigory Efimovich, I should long ago have been killed,” the sovereign is said to have told a lady of the court. His account of the murder of Rasputin in December 1916, and of the “exposures” against the court, is written from the official side, as the record of a man who saw the attack on the starets as an attack on the dynasty. The second volume, in the same key, carries the theme into its wider historical frame.
The Synod in the February days
Zhevakhov’s narrative of the collapse is that of an insider. Returning to Petrograd on 24 February 1917, he watched the revolution gather; his account of the memorable sitting of the Holy Synod of 26 February — when he urged the hierarchy to issue a threatening pastoral appeal to the people and was refused by Metropolitan Vladimir — shows the Church, in his telling, failing to answer the state’s need at the decisive moment. Arrested on 28 February on the oral order of alexander-kerensky, he was led through the hostile crowd to the Tauride Palace and imprisoned in the Ministerial Pavilion of the Duma, where the arrested dignitaries of the old regime heard the news of the abdication. His release, the scenes of the February street, and his reflections on the “fateful epoch” close the volume.
Exile and the Church after the revolution
The second volume carries Zhevakhov through 1917–1920: the months in Kiev, the siege of the city, the murder of Metropolitan Vladimir (January 1918), the German arrival and the Hetmanate of Skoropadsky, and his movement through the South with the retreat — Pyatigorsk, Ekaterinodar, where Metropolitan Pitirim died, and Novorossiysk, whence he departed for emigration. The second half of the volume turns to publicistics: the “methods of extermination” of the Cheka and famine, the condition of the Church under the Soviet power — the Council and the restoration of the patriarchate, the election of Patriarch Tikhon, the persecutions, and the split between the Moscow Synod and the Church Abroad. His central historical thesis, developed in his chapters on the nature of autocracy, is that Russian autocracy was “not a political but a religious” idea — the people’s faith in the anointed tsar — and that the revolution marked the ruin of that faith. As a memoirist he is the wiki’s indispensable source for the Church’s side of the Russian Troubles.

entities/otto-von-bismarck.title: Otto von Bismarck (1815–1898)
entities/otto-von-bismarck.content:
Otto von Bismarck (1815–1898)
Otto von Bismarck, Prussian minister-president from 1862 and the first chancellor of the German Empire, is the central statesman of this corpus’s frame. Born in the year of Waterloo into the Prussia of Friedrich Wilhelm III, he spent a youth that Lenz’s biography opens against the background of an old, semi-feudal monarchical state, and lived long enough to overthrow Austria in 1866, to build the north-german-confederation, to turn the war with France of 1870–71 into the foundation of the german-empire-proclaimed-1871, and then to be dismissed by a young emperor on 18 March 1890. The arc of his story in this period is the creation, consolidation, and finally the breaking of the instrument he himself had forged — a state so shaped around his own genius that when the hand that guided it was removed, the structure outlived him. Lenz closes by writing that the Reich continued to praise its master, and that even the parties Bismarck had fought as mortal enemies came at last to submit to the Reichsgedanke, the imperial idea that he had made inseparable from the faith in the power of the monarchy.
The path to power: from Junker diplomat to minister-president
Bismarck came to the ministry late and reluctantly. Lenz’s account follows him through the Revolution of 1848, his service as Prussia’s envoy at the restored Frankfurt Diet, and his embassies at Petersburg and Paris, before the summons of 1862. The instrument of that summons was the constitutional conflict. Since 1858 the Prince Regent (the future wilhelm-i) and his war minister albrecht-von-roon had pursued an army reorganization that the liberal Chamber of Deputies refused to finance; the confrontation over the military budget drove crown and parliament apart. Roon, isolated in a liberal ministry and working to bring his friend into the cabinet, engineered the crisis of June 1861 over the question of whether the new king should celebrate his accession by an homage in the old ständische, or estate, forms — a move that would have flouted the constitutional state and affronted the liberal majority. On 26 June he wrested from the king the commission to look about for new ministers, and on the next day wrote to Bismarck at Petersburg.
Bismarck’s reply, quoted at length by Lenz, shows him already the man he was to be. The occasion seemed too trivial to him to justify a breach with the Chamber; what he insisted on was not the homage but the program. He demanded a full swing of foreign policy, the abandonment of the legitimist course that the king’s personal will had imposed on the conduct of Prussia’s external affairs, and — above all — the bringing of the German question into the center of action. “One must hold firm in the military question, break with the Chamber over it, dissolve it,” he wrote, “and then show the nation how the king stands with the people.” It was already the program with which he appeared in September 1862. On the decisive principle he never wavered: the crown’s power must be upheld at all costs, and he would rather fight for it than see Prussia’s strength consumed in the petty quarrels that had sapped crown and land alike.
The overthrow of Austria (1866)
For four years Bismarck governed against the budget, ruling without the approval of the Chamber while the constitutional conflict dragged on, before he turned the contest of domestic factions to the service of a German policy. The german-question — whether Germany was to be unified, and by which of the two great powers — was the field on which he chose to fight. His diplomacy from 1864 onward dismantled the old order of the German Confederation step by step. The conquest of Schleswig-Holstein from Denmark in 1864 left Austria and Prussia as joint administrators of the Elbe Duchies, and their rivalry over that inheritance, as Sybel’s fourth volume shows, poisoned relations between the two German powers throughout 1865. The Convention of Gastein (August 1865), which partitioned the administration of the Duchies as a temporary expedient, proved no remedy; it only postponed the clash that both governments were preparing.
Bismarck’s decisive stroke was the alliance with Italy. Sybel’s account of the spring of 1866 describes how he negotiated a Prussian–Italian treaty by which the Kingdom of Italy would enter the war against Austria in return for the prize of Venetia. While Vienna sought to secure the neutrality or the support of France through secret negotiations, Bismarck worked to isolate Austria and to fix the moment of war. On 14 June 1866 Prussia pronounced the federal constitution broken and ordered its armies to march against the states of the Confederation; the austro-prussian-war-1866 had begun. The northern campaign swept away Hanover, Electoral Hesse, and Saxony, and the main war was decided in Bohemia. At the battle-of-koniggratz-1866 on 3 July, the Prussian armies converged on the Austrian position behind the Bistritz, and the arrival of the Crown Prince’s Second Army on the Austrian flank turned the day. Austria was thrown back, and the preliminary Peace of Nikolsburg led to the Peace of Prague (23 August 1866), which dissolved the German Confederation, excluded Austria from Germany, and left Prussia to annex Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, and Frankfurt. The old order was gone; the road to a new Germany lay open.
The North German Confederation and the road to empire
Out of the victory Bismarck built the north-german-confederation, a federal state of the north German states under Prussian presidency, with a Reichstag and a Bundesrat. Sybel’s sixth volume traces the constitutional work of 1866–67: the drafting and revision of the federal constitution, the renewal of the zollverein treaties by which the customs union was made an instrument of Prussian policy, and the conclusion of military conventions with the southern German states that placed their armies under Prussian command in time of war. The question of the south — the great powers of Bavaria, Württemberg, and Baden stood outside the new federation — remained open, and with it the unresolved problem of the kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch division of Germany.
The breach was made by France. Sybel’s seventh volume traces the mounting tension from 1867, beginning with the Luxembourg crisis, in which Napoleon III’s attempt to purchase Luxembourg from the Netherlands collapsed before the threat of war and a London conference instead guaranteed the Duchy’s neutrality. The years 1869–70 brought the hohenzollern-candidature-1870: the offer of the Spanish crown to Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, which Bismarck promoted and then had to disavow when France protested. The crisis came to a head at Ems, where the French ambassador Benedetti pressed the old king wilhelm-i for a guarantee that no Hohenzollern would ever again seek the Spanish throne. Wilhelm’s courteous refusal, telegraphed to Berlin, was edited by Bismarck into the curt ems-dispatch-1870 that so stung French honour that Napoleon III, goaded into war, declared it on 19 July 1870. The southern German states, bound by the new national feeling and their military conventions, marched with the north. The war that followed — the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 — brought the annihilation of the French army at Sedan, the capture of Napoleon III, and the siege-of-paris-1870-71.
In the midst of it, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871, the German Empire was proclaimed. Lenz records the laborious negotiations with the South German princes that went on “until the morning of 18 January,” and the scene when, before the victorious banners, the Kaiser’s son-in-law, the Crown Prince, raised the first Kaiserhoch. Bismarck, who had shown no reluctance to brush aside German princes when it served Prussian power, now took no village more for his king. Lenz marvels at the tact with which he grasped “the positive of power,” leaving the allied dynasties the emblems and rights that gave a gentle appearance of self-rule without disturbing the real substance of the whole.
Kulturkampf and the break with the Liberals
The first task of the new Reich, as Lenz frames it, was to secure in peace what the war had won. From the turn of the 1870s Bismarck turned against the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf (“culture struggle”) — the assault on the influence of the clergy and the Centre party, which he saw as a hostile, ultramontane power within the German state. But the struggle wore him down, and by the end of the decade he executed the sharpest reversal of his career. The turning point came with the attacks on the life of the Emperor. Lenz describes how, when the news of the second attempt — Nobiling’s assault in June — reached him in the Sachsenwald, Bismarck’s first words were “Now we dissolve the Reichstag!” He seized on the wave of popular horror to carry an exceptional law against the revolutionary movement, and to break the National Liberals, who had previously refused him. Their independence was destroyed, their internal unity shattered, and the split that Bennigsen had long staved off could no longer be prevented. From 1879 Bismarck governed on a new basis: a tariff reform, a reconciliation with conservatism and the Church, and the abandonment of the liberal alliance. The Kulturkampf was abandoned, and the Centre, once his enemy, became one of the pillars of the new order.
Foreign policy and the fall of 18 March 1890
After 1871 Bismarck’s foreign policy was the maintenance of the peace that Germany’s victories had secured. Lenz’s chapter on foreign policy in the new Reich describes the alliance system by which he sought to keep France isolated and the great powers bound to Germany. He presided over the congress-of-berlin-1878, which redrew the map of the Balkans after the Russo-Turkish war. But his last years were shadowed by the rise of a new emperor. Wilhelm II, who came to the throne in 1888, was of another temper than his grandfather, and the clash of Kaiser and Kanzler grew inevitable. In the divergence of their political directions Lenz locates the “tragic solution of 18 March”: Bismarck, the convinced monarchist, was dismissed by his monarch in 1890, after the young Kaiser chose a policy of conciliation and social reform rather than the chancellor’s renewed conflict with the Reichstag.
Retirement to the forest quiet of Varzin and Friedrichsruh, which Lenz calls the havens he had freely sought and longed for, brought him no rest. He remained the fighter he had always been, unable to keep silence, meeting his enemies “with full force and the pride that a life of unheard-of victories justified.” The loneliness of his first months yielded to a growing tide of homage; the love of the nation for the founder of its unity flamed ever hotter. “And when the giant oak of the Sachsenwald fell,” Lenz writes of his death in 1898, “friend and foe bowed in admiration and reverence before the sublime shade of the man who, equal in war and peace, had opened to his people the path to power.”

entities/ottokar-czernin.title: Ottokar Graf Czernin (1872–1932)
entities/ottokar-czernin.content:
Ottokar Graf Czernin (1872–1932)
Ottokar Theobald Otto Maria Graf Czernin von und zu Chudenitz, Austro-Hungarian minister of foreign affairs from December 1916 to April 1918, was the monarchy’s last-but-one foreign minister and the author of its most sustained peace efforts in the First World War. His story in this corpus’s frame runs from his embassy at Bukarest on the eve of the war, through his elevation to the Ballhausplatz at the end of 1916, his peace feelers of 1917, the treaty of Brest-Litovsk, and the quarrel over the Sixtus affair that brought his resignation in April 1918. His memoir Im Weltkriege (1919), written in the year of the armistice, is his account of the diplomacy of the war and of the men — franz-ferdinand, wilhelm-ii, the Emperor Charles, the German generals — among whom he moved.
The minister in Bukarest
Czernin’s first great appointment was as Austro-Hungarian minister in Bucharest, from the autumn of 1913. His memoir of Rumania is a portrait of the court of King Carol, the aged pro-German sovereign, and of the Rumanian statesmen among whom the Austrian envoy moved in the months before the war. On the day of Sarajevo, and still more after the ultimatum to Serbia — “Austria has gone mad,” was the cry that passed through Rumanian society — a wave of hatred swept over the country, and Czernin, who judged that Bratianu was never truly neutral and that Queen Marie was for war, watched Rumania slip from the alliance the monarchy had laboured to secure. He was interned at the outbreak of war, recalled to Vienna, and passed in due course to the foreign ministry. His judgment of Hungarian policy in these years was that Hungary should make concessions to the Rumanians while Tisza refused — a refusal he regarded as one of the monarchy’s great mistakes.
The peace efforts of 1917
Czernin became minister of foreign affairs in December 1916, in the fourth winter of the war, and at once confronted the decision on unrestricted submarine warfare. He records the peace offer of the Central Powers, the judgment of wilhelm-ii that the Entente had slapped him in the face, and the triumph of the submarine war against which he and Prince Hohenlohe had warned; and he set down the warning of the German leaders, still optimistic even in April 1918, and the judgment that Germany had misjudged the situation.
The longest chapter of his memoir treats the peace efforts of 1917, which form the substance of his policy. In February 1917 came peace feelers from tsarist Russia; then the outbreak of the Russian revolution, and new fears on the Thames. In April 1917 he reported to the Emperor on Austria’s exhaustion, the dull grumbling of the masses, America’s intervention, and the necessity of peace. He sought to reach the German Reichstag, worked with Erzberger and Südekum, and witnessed the Reichstag peace resolution of 19 July 1917 and the fall of Bethmann Hollweg, its victim. But the demands of the German supreme command — military control of Belgium, of Liège and the Flemish coast — and the belief of Paris and London in the dissolution of the Fourfold Alliance combined to defeat the peace wish in the Entente, and the efforts failed. His Budapest speech on world disarmament and his flirtations with a separate peace were interrupted, in the autumn of 1917, by President Wilson’s Fourteen Points and the approach of Brest-Litovsk.
Brest-Litovsk and the peace of Bucharest
Czernin’s account of the peace of Brest-Litovsk is among the most vivid passages of his memoir. He travelled to Brest-Litovsk to meet the Bolshevik negotiators — Joffe, Kamenev and Frau Bizenko — and then Leon Trotsky, whose arrival he awaited and whose acceptance of the ultimatum he records. He demanded a free hand for himself in case the Germans broke with the Russians, and he watched the German generals, Hoffmann and Ludendorff, press for a harsher peace than he favoured, and the German Kaiser’s telegram demanding Livonia and Estland. He describes the peace with the Ukraine and the Brotfriede (the “bread peace”) that was to relieve the famine catastrophe in Austria. His advocacy of a peace without annexations stood against the German appetite, and the divergence between the German and the Austrian conceptions of the settlement runs through his whole account of the negotiations.
After Brest-Litovsk came the peace of Bucharest, the separate peace with defeated Rumania. Czernin treats the Rumanian and Hungarian questions of that settlement — the message of the Emperor Charles to King Ferdinand, Austria’s claim to parity, and his own constraint before the Hungarian frontier demands and Germany’s economic demands — and he describes his conversations with King Ferdinand and the ministers who made the peace. The separate treaties of the Central Powers seemed to crown his diplomacy; but they were the last successes, and they were followed swiftly by the collapse of the Austrian war effort.
The resignation
Czernin’s tenure ended in April 1918 in the “letter affair” — the public quarrel over the revelations of the Emperor Charles’s secret peace overtures, the “Sixtus letters,” which the German generals and the Austrian court could not forgive. He offered his demission, which the Emperor at first refused, and the full constitutional responsibility for the affair was, as he records with irony, afterwards claimed by a minister who had known nothing of it and had not even been in office at the time. He resigned in April 1918, and his place passed to others as the monarchy slid toward its dissolution. After his demission, he wrote, Germany stood at the height of its military power, but the possibility of a peace of understanding had already been lost.
His closing reflection on the war is fatalistic: the longer the world war lasted, he wrote, the more it lost the character of a work directed by individual men and took on that of a cosmic event that escaped the interference of even the most powerful individuals; the promises given to the peoples and the artificially bred boundless hatred made every single man a small pebble of a stone avalanche that plunges down leaderless, choiceless and aimless. The Vienna peace settlement that followed the war, he held, had destroyed what little possibility of a just order remained, and he closed on the warning that anarchy and Bolshevism were siblings and a danger to the coming generation.

entities/patrice-mac-mahon.title: Patrice de Mac-Mahon (1808–1893)
entities/patrice-mac-mahon.content:
Patrice de Mac-Mahon (1808–1893)
Marshal of France, victor of Magenta, commander of the armies that suppressed the paris-commune-1871, and second President of the Third Republic from 24 May 1873 to January 1879. Mac-Mahon was the soldier-president the monarchical majority set against Thiers, the figurehead of the ordre moral and of the attempted royal restoration, and finally the defeated champion of a presidential interpretation of the constitution who resigned rather than submit to a republican Chamber. His presidency spans the monarchical failure, the septennat-1873, the Constitution of 1875, and the seize-mai-1877 crisis.
The soldier
Mac-Mahon was the man of the army before the man of politics. A soldier of Algeria and the Crimea, he had won the day at Magenta in 1859 — from which his title of duc de Magenta — and commanded with honour in the opening disasters of 1870, wounded at Sedan. His name, Hanotaux records, calmed foreign alarm when Thiers fell: here was a marshal, a man of word and discipline, not an adventurer. His whole career had been obedience to established authority, and it was as a soldier that he entered the Élysée — a soldier’s word to continue the liberation of the territory and to restore the ordre moral.
The election of 24 May 1873
Chosen by the conciliabules of the monarchical parties as the candidate who could unite the right, Mac-Mahon was elected president on 24 May 1873 with 390 votes, the left abstaining (Laurier alone voting for Grévy). He accepted after hesitation, and after a call on the fallen Thiers. He was the instrument of the right’s design — a president of transition, under whom the monarchy might be restored. But Mac-Mahon was an honest soldier, and Hanotaux emphasizes that he entered the presidency as a neutral head of state rather than a partisan of a dynasty.
The ordre moral
Under Mac-Mahon the first two ministries of the duc de Broglie governed in the spirit of the ordre moral: the formula of moral and religious restoration, the cult of the Sacré-Cœur, the pilgrimages, the measures against republican propaganda. The Marshal lent his name to this conservative order while the monarchical campaign ran its course. When the comte de Chambord’s letter of 27 October 1873 refused the tricolour and ruined the restoration, Mac-Mahon’s seven-year presidency was fixed by the septennat-1873 law of 20 November 1873. He declined to receive Chambord at Versailles — the Marshal, having sworn to the flag, would not bargain with the pretender over it.
President under the Constitution of 1875
The french-constitution-1875 made Mac-Mahon president under a republican constitution he had not sought and did not entirely accept. He watched the elections of 1876 deliver a republican Chamber, Dufaure and then Jules Simon govern under him, and the parliamentary regime establish itself. The Marshal, faithful to a conception of the presidency as an independent authority rather than a ceremonial office, came to resent a Chamber that pushed him aside. Hanotaux treats his eventual act of 16 May 1877 as the constitutional corollary of the septennat compromise — a foreseen, deliberated assertion of the president’s power rather than a mere boutade.
Seize Mai and the defeat of the presidential interpretation
On 16 May 1877 Mac-Mahon dismissed Jules Simon and called the duc de Broglie, dissolving the Chamber in the hope of winning a conservative majority — the seize-mai-1877 crisis. The elections of 14 October 1877 returned a republican Chamber; the Marshal’s “submit or resign” challenge was answered by the country. After the second Dufaure ministry and the republican victories in the senatorial elections of January 1879, Mac-Mahon’s position was untenable: the Republic he had been set to contain had mastered him. He resigned in January 1879, the last president who seriously believed he could stand apart from the parliamentary majority. His departure left the field to jules-grevy and the consolidators of the parliamentary regime, sealing the victory of the interpretation of the constitution that leon-gambetta and the republicans had demanded.

entities/paul-milyukov.title: Paul Milyukov (1859–1943)
entities/paul-milyukov.content:
Paul Milyukov
Paul Nikolayevich Milyukov (1859–1943) was the historian and statesman who led the Russian Constitutional Democrats (the Kadets) and became foreign minister of the first Provisional Government in 1917, the parliamentary voice of liberal Russia between the Duma and the revolution. In Denikin’s account of the Russian Troubles he embodies the war-to-victory liberalism that the February Revolution could not sustain.
The Kadet leader and the Duma
A professional historian of Russia, Milyukov turned in the revolutionary decade of 1905–17 to politics, founding and leading the Kadets, the principal liberal party of the Duma era. In the State Duma he was the spokesman of constitutional opposition to the autocracy, one of the figures Zhevakhov’s loyalist memoirs single out in the assembly that confronted the Imperial government in the war years. His programme — a constitutional monarchy on the British model, civil liberty, and, after 1914, the faithful pursuit of the war against Germany — made him the leading representative of the liberal centre.
Foreign minister and the fall
With the February Revolution of 1917 Milyukov became foreign minister in the first Provisional Government. Denikin records the defining act and its consequence: Milyukov’s note to the Allies, insisting that Russia would fight to a victorious finish, unleashed the April crisis and forced his resignation. The demand for peace, coming from the streets and the soviets, overwhelmed the liberal minister who had staked everything on the war. He remained through 1917 a voice of the constitutional idea, and after the Bolshevik revolution emigrated, spending his later years as a historian of the Russian revolution abroad.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Milyukov is the emblem of liberal-constitutional Russia — the man who stood for the war and for the parliament against both the old autocracy and the coming soviet power, and who was crushed between them. His trajectory from Duma oppositionist to wartime minister to émigré historian traces the fate of Russian liberalism in a single life.

entities/paul-sabatier.title: Paul Sabatier (1858–1928)
entities/paul-sabatier.content:
Paul Sabatier
Paul Sabatier (1858–1928) was a French Protestant pastor and historian, best known for his Vie de saint François d’Assise, which earned him the Institut’s grand prix décennal in 1905. In the corpus’s frame he appears as the sympathetic observer of the religious life of the Third Republic in the years after the Separation of Church and State — the author of L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle (1911), a study of the contemporary religious movement of France written neither as an ecclesiastic nor as a polemicist but as a historian of the “mouvement social contemporain.” A friend of the Catholic Modernists and an enemy of anticlericalism as much as of clerical reaction, he sought to discern, beneath the surface of indifference and political conflict, a genuine religious orientation that France itself had created.
The historian of Saint Francis
Sabatier’s authority as an observer of the religious movement rested on his biography of Saint Francis of Assisi, the work that had made his name and won the Institut’s grand prix décennal Lefèvre-Deumier in 1905. He wrote, he insisted in the Introduction to L’orientation religieuse, not as an ecclesiastic but in the spirit of the series in which the book appeared — “faire connaître et comprendre le mouvement social, exposer les faits et les interpréter, sans jamais se substituer à eux,” to make known and to understand the social movement, to set out the facts and interpret them without ever substituting himself for them. He took up the antique formula Historia magistra vitæ and gave it an ampler meaning: history no longer gives only examples of individual conduct, it rises to the conception of the living germs that the past contains and that the present must select as the seeds of a new century.
Religion and its orientation
Sabatier distinguished “orientation religieuse” from “affaires religieuses.” The latter designated what is most exterior in religious and ecclesiastical facts, what they become when carried onto the political markets and used in the quarrels of parties — a chronicle written day by day and left to the newspapers. The book proposed instead to discover “des aspects de réalité et de vie,” aspects of reality and of life. What many simple minds sought in religion, he found, was a fundamentally moral foundation; the religious movement always worked itself out at the expense of the churches; and the Church, for all her rights to the recognition of France and her activity through organs like the Bonne Presse to conquer the direction of political opinion, had not succeeded in arresting a new religious orientation that was taking shape outside her.
The circumstances of the orientation
Sabatier located the origins of the present religious situation in the disasters of 1870. The war against Prussia dealt, in his judgement, an irreparable blow to the prestige of the Reformation in France — the conquest was turned into a moral as much as a political question — while the Church, whose individual priests had shown themselves admirable citizens, did not on the morrow of the disasters know how to rise to the height of its task. He rejected the formula that patriotism had become the religion of France, and counted among the factors that shaped the religious orientation the laic school, accused by its enemies of being a nursery of crime; the Church, he noted, by appealing ceaselessly to the limitless devotion of her children, answered alone the most powerful instinct of the human heart.
The deficits of antireligion
Sabatier was as severe toward the antireligious Left as toward the clerical Right. Free thought, he insisted, must not be confounded with anticlericalism. He observed the profound antipathy for clericalism found among peasants who yet refused to join the anticlerical organisations, and the incapacity of anticlericalism to understand what the Catholicism of the rural populations actually was — a religion that gave the sense of discipline, of solidarity, of harmony. The efforts of scientific religion had little success. He noted the negative impression produced on some spectators by the missionary zeal of certain converters, and excluded from his study the eccentric and the morbid.
The contemporary philosophy and the movement
The philosophers, Sabatier held, had not created the present religious orientation. Christianity at its origins was a popular movement, not provoked by philosophical views; the efforts of Pillon, Renouvier and Secrétan, though of high value in intellectual circles, had no appreciable practical influence. It was rather because Bergson, Boutroux and William James answered the sense of life that the present generation attached itself to them. He dwelt on Guyau’s Irréligion de l’avenir, a work of ever-growing importance, and on Boutroux, who went still further in the way of realism — seeing in the churches an effort toward the ideal and manifesting to all a sympathy at once disinterested and efficacious, very new among philosophers.
The manifestations in church, Protestantism and free thought
Surveying the movement’s workings, Sabatier found two catholicisms coexisting in the Church, and the Modernism struggling against a Roman administration he described as a committee of public safety; the diocese of Milan and the University of Fribourg were alike accused of being nurseries of modernism. In Protestantism he found rather the absence of manifestations — the Separation had permitted new schisms in the Reformed Church, while the most evolved Catholics showed themselves severe toward it. In free thought he found something not essentially anti-religious; he noted the significance of the success of the Cahiers de la Quinzaine, and the union of freethinkers and free believers. He devoted a long section to the creation of the laic school, whose soul, he argued, came from farther and higher than the war of 1870 — it was “la nouvelle incarnation d’un effort religieux séculaire,” and its course in 1882 was far from anticlerical.
Significance
Sabatier closed on two facts in appearance contradictory: the rapid progress of indifference and an unexpected awakening of religious aspirations, often to be observed in one and the same individual. France, he believed, had arrived at an epoch of reconstitution, “une époque de reconstitution, de revanche religieuse,” analogous to the origins of Christianity. Though the Roman Church appeared struck more than any other by the political and intellectual crisis, it was the Church that had sowed in the heart of the present generation the sentiments of the mystery, of unity, of tradition, of duty — and it alone, despite its failures, kept in the conscience of the elite of the coming generation a unique place. His book is a central document of the religious question of the Third Republic between the Separation of 1905 and the war, written from the borderland between Protestantism, Catholicism and free thought.

entities/philippe-petain.title: Philippe Pétain (1856–1951)
entities/philippe-petain.content:
Philippe Pétain (1856–1951)
Philippe Pétain, Marshal of France, was the defender of Verdun and the French commander-in-chief in the last years of the Great War — the general who restored the French army after the mutinies of 1917 and who commanded under marshal-foch in the victorious hundred-days-offensive-1918. Recouly’s synthesis, drawing on Pétain’s own La Bataille de Verdun among its listed sources, presents him as the master of the defensive and of the repair of the army. In this corpus’s frame his story is that of the calm, methodical soldier of the old school who held the fortress that became the symbol of French endurance, rebuilt the army when its morale cracked, and then commanded it through the final offensive of the war.
The defender of Verdun
Pétain’s name is inseparable from the battle-of-verdun-1916 of 1916, the longest battle of the war. Recouly counts the German failure before Verdun among the characteristic setbacks of the Central Powers in 1916 — three very hard blows falling on the German staff within a few months, alongside the great Somme offensive and the entry of Romania. It was Pétain who, charged with the defence of the fortress on the Meuse, held the position against the relentless German assaults that sought to bleed the French army white. His method, as the battle’s history records, was that of rotation and of the systematic organisation of the defensive line — the method that made “they shall not pass” the motto of the defence. The publication of his own account of the battle, La Bataille de Verdun, is listed among the principal memoirs on which Recouly’s synthesis rests.
The restoration of the army, 1917
The gravest trial of Pétain’s career followed the failure of the great French offensive of the spring of 1917. Recouly records that, drawing on the experience of three years of war, General Pétain succeeded, thanks to an effort in which firmness and humanity were combined, in restoring the army whose morale had been shaken by the terrible cost of the offensive. He rebuilt the confidence of the troops after the crisis of the spring of 1917, reorganising the front and the reserves and returning the army to a defensive posture that husbanded its strength for the decisive effort. It was this restored army that Foch would wield in the great battles of 1918.
Command under Foch, 1918
In 1918 Pétain commanded the French armies under the Allied generalissimo marshal-foch. Recouly shows him in the operations of the final year widening the battle in concert with Foch’s plan of multiple attacks: when the Third Army under Humbert attacked, Pétain, élargissant la bataille vers l’est, threw the Tenth Army of Mangin into the attack between the Oise and the Aisne, while Foch invited the British commander to enlarge the struggle toward the north. It is the picture of the French commander-in-chief in full cooperation with the supreme command — a marked contrast with the independent fiefs that had marked the Allied conduct of the war before the single command. In the last phase, with Foch, Pétain and Weygand gathered in the councils of the generalissimo, the restoration of the army came to its fruit in the offensive that broke the German army and forced the armistice-11-november-1918.

entities/pyotr-stolypin.title: Pyotr Stolypin (1862–1911)
entities/pyotr-stolypin.content:
Pyotr Stolypin
Pyotr Arkadievich Stolypin (1862–1911) was prime minister of Russia from 1906 to his assassination in 1911 — the strong man who carried the empire through the aftermath of the revolution-1905 and imposed upon it a hybrid regime of duma-constitutionalism and repression. In his person the two faces of the post-October state met: the reformer who broke up the peasant commune in the celebrated land reform, and the hangman of the punitive courts. He was the architect of the 3 June 1907 coup that changed the electoral law to secure a submissive Duma, the promoter of the Western zemstvo that brought him down, and — in the furious judgment of sergei-witte, whose memoirs supply this wiki’s fullest account of him — a “most honest phrasemonger” whose liberal speeches clothed an unprecedented arbitrariness.
The appearance of Stolypin
Stolypin came to the premiership through the fire of the revolution. He had been governor of Saratov province, then minister of internal affairs, and his resolution in the disorders brought him forward as the successor to Witte, who had resigned in April 1906. The First Duma — which Witte called the Duma “of popular revenge,” meeting in the summer of 1906 — was dissolved, and Stolypin governed through the summer of the punitive expeditions, the courts-martial, and the hangings. Witte, writing from retirement, draws the portrait that has stuck: Stolypin in the Duma spoke the language of liberalism, and his collected speeches read, as Witte says, like those of a liberal statesman — while no one, Witte insists, “killed so many and in the most atrocious manner, no one acted so arbitrarily, no one so spat upon the law” as Stolypin did. The gulf between the words and the deeds, in Witte’s telling, was the essence of the man.
The land reform
Against the agrarian discontent that fed the revolution, Stolypin advanced his great constructive measure: the break-up of the peasant commune and the establishment of the peasant as an individual proprietor. The measure, prepared in the years of reaction against the insufficiency of allotments that the zemstvo investigations had exposed, was designed to create a class of sturdy independent farmers as a conservative support of the state. Witte’s account of the peasant question and of the resignation of the finance minister Kutler in 1906 records the resistance the reform encountered in the councils. The land reform was carried through the Duma and into the villages in the years before the war, and its success or failure became the great question of Russian agrarian policy. In Witte’s telling the whole was vitiated by the same arbitrariness that marked the man: the means by which it was imposed on the country were those of a government that would not be bound by its own law.
The 3 June coup
The climax of the repression was the dissolution of the Second Duma and the change of the electoral law by the manifesto of 3 June 1907 — the gosudarstvenny perevorot (“state coup”), as Witte unhesitatingly calls it. By it the emperor, at Stolypin’s urging, broke the constitution that had been granted on 17 October 1905 and issued a new electoral law in violation of the Fundamental Laws. Witte’s verdict is precise: the law was artificial, founded not on firm principles but on the shakiest calculations, and its effect was to produce a Duma not “chosen” but “picked” (podobrannaya) by the government, a Duma made for the privileged and the strong. The Third Duma that followed, though more tractable, was never in Witte’s eyes a true representative chamber. The 3 June system — a loyal Duma under a strong minister — was Stolypin’s working constitution, and it held until his death.
The Western zemstvo and the assassination
The same energy that made enemies on the left made them on the right. Stolypin’s plan to introduce the zemstvo into the Western provinces, where the Polish nobility dominated, arrayed the conservative interests of the State Council against him. Witte, who had his own score to settle, records the frictions at the top that accumulated through 1909–1911. In September 1911, at Kiev, during the festivities of the unveiling of the monument to Alexander II, Stolypin was shot in the theatre in the presence of the emperor by an agent of the security police, and died a few days later of his wound. Witte’s reflection on the murder is characteristic: the killing was “revolting and cannot be justified,” yet “it can be understood,” for the thousands hanged under Stolypin’s premiership had made of state killing a commonplace — the prime minister who held the police and the whole apparatus of repression in his own hands had, in Witte’s view, the first responsibility for his own fate. With Stolypin’s death the strong-man regime of the Third Duma was over, and the succession fell to the placid Kokovtsov.

entities/sergei-markov.title: General Sergei Markov (1878–1918)
entities/sergei-markov.content:
General Sergei Markov
Sergei Leonidovich Markov (1878–1918) was a Russian general of the First World War who became one of the most celebrated field commanders of the early White movement, distinguished in Denikin’s Essays on the Russian Troubles for his conduct of the Ice March and killed in battle in the summer of 1918. His name lived on in the Markovsky officer regiment of the Volunteer Army.
In the army before the revolution
Markov appears in Denikin’s first volume, on the collapse of authority and the army, as a staff and line officer whose professional vigour stood out against the general demoralization of 1917. He belonged to the circle of commanders who looked to a firm hand to save the front, the constituency from which the Kornilov movement drew its support.
The Ice March and the Volunteer Army
After the Bolshevik seizure of power Markov joined the Volunteer Army on the Don. Denikin’s second volume, on the struggle of General Kornilov, gives him a leading place in the First Kuban (Ice) March of spring 1918, where the small White force fought its way through the Kuban steppe against the Red armies. His energy in the marches and rearguard actions became part of the young army’s legend. He was mortally wounded in battle in June 1918, and the army honoured him by naming a regiment after him.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Markov is the representative fighting general of the early Civil War — the soldier whose name, rather than a political programme, carried the Volunteer Army through its most desperate months. He gives a human face to the White movement’s first year that the more political figures of Kornilov and Denikin do not.

entities/sergei-witte.title: Sergei Witte (1849–1915)
entities/sergei-witte.content:
Sergei Witte
Count Sergei Yulievich Witte (1849–1915) was the architect of modern Russian state finance and the first constitutional premier of the empire. Rising from the railway service of the south-west to the finance ministry under alexander-iii, he carried through the monetary reform and the gold standard, the spirits monopoly, the railway programme and the Trans-Siberian line, and the protectionist fiscal system that financed the industrialization-witte of the 1890s; under nicholas-ii he negotiated the peace of Portsmouth that ended the russo-japanese-war-1904-05 and presided over the granting of the october-manifesto-1905, becoming the first chairman of the Council of Ministers. He is also the author of the three-volume memoirs that form one of the principal sources of this wiki — an extraordinary, opinionated testimony to the Russia of Alexander III and Nicholas II.
The railway man
Witte was born in Tiflis in 1849, the son of a director of state domains in the Caucasus and a mother of the Fadeev family; his uncle was the publicist and soldier Rostislav Fadeev. After a university training in pure mathematics he was turned from a professorship by his family’s sense of what was fitting for a nobleman, and entered railway service in Odessa. He made his career on the railway “kings” of the age, as the South-Western Railway company was formed from the unprofitable Odessa, Kiev-Brest, and Brest-Grajewo lines, and rose to be its manager. His memoirs abound in the portraits of this world — the concessionaires, the engineers, the governors-general. It was his practical command of the railways that brought him to the emperor’s attention: on the imperial journeys over the South-Western line he urged that the train be run at safe speeds, and when, against his warnings, the imperial train was driven at reckless pace, the catastrophe at Borki followed — a disaster that discredited the ministry of ways of communication and opened Witte’s own road to power.
Minister of finance
After the death of Alexander III Witte was already minister of finance, having succeeded Vyshnegradsky; he had served as director of the department of railway affairs and minister of ways of communication, and had even been sent by the emperor to the cholera districts in 1892. The financial system he built is the subject of the Granat volume’s opening essay, which records both its brilliance and its cost. He introduced the spirits monopoly — the state sale of drink reorganized from 1896 — which became one of the largest and steadiest revenues of the treasury. He carried through the monetary reform that had been prepared under Bunge and Vyshnegradsky: by the ukases of 3 January, 29 August, and 14 November 1897 the credit ruble was stabilized on a gold basis, a new gold ruble was established by a kind of devaluation fixed at the most stable existing rate of the paper ruble, and the state bank was charged with the unfailing conversion of notes into gold. Foreign loans, above all the great French loans, supplied the gold reserve. Bogolepov’s essay in the Granat volume is critical: the “brilliant period” of Russian state economy was purchased at the price of extreme strain on the taxable capacity of the people, a loss-making state economy, and the ruin of the propertyless. Yet the system worked — Russia’s currency became convertible, foreign capital poured in, and the railway network, including the industrialization-witte’s greatest monument the Trans-Siberian Railway, was pushed forward at a pace unknown before.
The Far East and the Japanese war
Witte’s finance and his diplomacy ran together in the Far East. He negotiated with Li Hung-chang the treaty with China of 1896, with the Russo-Chinese Bank and the Chinese Eastern Railway across Manchuria, and watched the court’s adventure take the matter out of his hands. The “Bezobrazov clique” — the adventurers around the throne — pressed the reckless policy in Korea, and in 1903 Witte was driven from the finance ministry to the empty chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers. When the russo-japanese-war-1904-05 ended in disaster, the emperor had to turn to him again. Witte was sent to America, where with President Roosevelt’s mediation he negotiated the peace of Portsmouth in 1905 — a peace that secured Russia from the worst terms of the military defeat and made Witte a popular hero for his deft bargaining. From America he returned through Paris and Berlin, and entered Petersburg amid the revolution.
The October Manifesto and the premiership
In the autumn of 1905, with the revolution at its height, Witte pressed on the emperor the necessity of concession. On 17 October the manifesto was issued granting civil liberties and a legislative Duma, and Witte became the first chairman of the Council of Ministers. His account of the half-year premiership is frank: the repression of disorders and the punitive expeditions, the amnesty, the electoral law, the great foreign loan of 1906 that liquidated the war’s financial legacy, the framing of the Fundamental Laws. He records the pressure of Trepov and the great duke on the cabinet and the intrigues of the right, and he records, with particular bitterness, how the court later spread the story that he had wrung the manifesto from the unwilling sovereign. Dismissed in April 1906, he spent the rest of his life watching the regime from outside — an ousted and embittered observer of the Stolypin years, whose memoirs, written in retirement and completed around 1911, are a running indictment of the men who undid his work. He died in 1915, in the second year of the war he had always feared.

entities/stephen-tisza.title: Count István (Stephen) Tisza (1861–1918)
entities/stephen-tisza.content:
István (Stephen) Tisza
Count István (Stephen) Tisza (1861–1918), son of the long-serving minister-president Kálmán Tisza, was the foremost champion of Magyar supremacy and of the Compromise of 1867 in the last generation of the Dual Monarchy. He was Hungarian minister-president from 1903 to 1905 and again from 1913 to 1917, and as wartime premier he carried the kingdom through the first three years of the Great War by what Redlich calls his “dictatorial will and his courage.” He embodied in the highest degree the passionate, domineering temper of the Hungarian political nation of which Sosnosky writes — a statesman who defended the dualist tie to Austria against the independence party while pursuing with relentless rigour the Magyar national state over the subject peoples. He was assassinated in October 1918, at the moment of the monarchy’s dissolution.
The champion of the Compromise
Tisza’s father, Kálmán Tisza, had been a member of the committee that drafted the Compromise act of 1867 and had argued in its deliberations that under the Pragmatic Sanction only a common defence, not a common army, was necessary — a view against which Deák and Andrássy contended. The son inherited the father’s lifelong defence of the dualist settlement, but against a more dangerous opposition. By the opening of the twentieth century the independence movement, drawing on the Kossuth tradition and the cry of Los von Österreich (“Away from Austria!”), was pressing for a personal union in which Hungary would share nothing with Austria but the ruler. Sosnosky describes how, in the struggle over the army, the common force was the key point of the Austrian position and its last bulwark, and how the Magyar attacks upon it, now in “wild assault, now through sly enveloping manoeuvres,” had already gained footholds and even breached the wall.
The crisis of 1903–1904
The struggle over the army reached its first crisis under Tisza’s own premiership in 1903–1904. The Hungarian parliament, through obstructionist tactics, withheld the annual recruits’ quota, and the military leadership had to keep the third year-class under the colours and call up the younger reserve class-years to cover the shortfall — a measure that struck the conscripts and their families bitterly. Tisza found himself attacked not only from Vienna and by the obstruction but also by members of his own party, whom the fear of unpopularity, as much as blindness to his real aims, turned against him. One of the most eminent Liberals, Count Albert Apponyi, broke with him for personal reasons, visible in repeated fierce verbal duels between the two statesmen in the session of 23 February 1904. Tisza did not flinch: he threatened to show the “strong hand” attributed to him and to propose an alteration of the parliamentary rules of procedure that would defeat obstruction. The obstruction, seeing its popularity ebb as public resentment at the resulting ex-lex state grew, drew back and on 10 March 1904 permitted the normal recruits’ quota for the current and the past year — a truce that closed the first and longest act of what Sosnosky calls the sensational drama of the “defence bills.”
The Magyar national state
It was in this second premiership that Tisza’s policy toward the nationalities of the Hungarian kingdom found its most ruthless expression. Redlich, surveying the last peace government before the war, writes that under Tisza’s regime, “the last Hungarian minister-president appointed by Kaiser Franz Joseph, in whom the shortsighted and embittered national hatred of the Magyar noble against the Slav and Romance peoples of the Hungarian state territory once more, before the catastrophe, embodied itself in the most ruthless way,” the misfortune for the dynastic Reich idea in the south and south-west of the Hungarian state developed irresistibly. In Croatia the long struggle took a dangerous turn under the administration of Khuen-Héderváry and worsened under Tisza; in Transylvania the Romanian intelligentsia, solidly at one with the Romanian peasant masses, had learned to regard the complete political helotisation of their people as its permanent fate so long as the supremacy of the Magyars created in 1867 was not broken. This, Redlich notes, could be undone only by an unsuccessful war or by the dynasty thrusting back the Magyar preponderance from within — the second possibility which the death of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo seemed to remove forever.
Wartime premier
In the war Tisza’s supremacy was, in Redlich’s judgement, the decisive fact of the Austrian as much as the Hungarian war government. He refused from the very first day of mobilisation to recognise the Vienna war-surveillance office (Kriegsüberwachungsamt) as competent for Hungary, excluding the kingdom completely from its operation, while still building his own collaboration between the civil authorities and the military commands against the “unreliable” populations — the Serbs, even the Croats, the Ruthenians, Slovenes and Romanians. He was resolved, Redlich writes, “to conduct the inner war policy that he found necessary in Hungary with all his force, but without the least interference from Austrian factors, and strictly in the sense of the Magyar interests.” The Austrian minister-president Count Stürgkh was, we are told, “from the first a great admirer of the political genius and the force of Count Stephen Tisza,” and the subordination of Austria to the Hungarian government which Redlich describes as a cardinal feature of the war government was in large measure the work of Tisza’s will. Even the war economy bore the mark of the dualism: Hungary’s complete economic isolation of Austria in the matter of food exports was one of the great difficulties of the Austrian administration.
Assassination and fall
Tisza’s regime, like the monarchy itself, did not survive the fourth year of the war. Redlich notes his retirement was connected with the accession of Emperor Charles and the movement toward a political (rather than merely bureaucratic) war government, the attempt at reconciliation and the amnesty that so embittered German-Austrian opinion. In October 1918, as the monarchy dissolved into its national states, Tisza — the man who had embodied Magyar supremacy to the last — was assassinated, at the very moment when the Magyar domination he had defended was collapsing with the Dual Monarchy he had championed.

entities/victor-emmanuel-ii.title: Victor Emmanuel II (1820–1878)
entities/victor-emmanuel-ii.content:
Victor Emmanuel II (1820–1878)
Victor Emmanuel II, King of Piedmont-Sardinia and from 1861 the first King of Italy, stands in this corpus’s frame as the constitutional monarch who bound the revolutionary conquest of the peninsula to an old dynasty — the man the people nicknamed the Re Galantuomo, “the Gentleman King.” Born in 1820, he succeeded to the Piedmontese throne in 1849 on the abdication of his father Charles Albert, kept the constitutional Statuto that the revolutions of 1848 had wrung from the house, and reigned through the war of 1859, the annexation of central Italy, the Expedition of the Thousand and the conquest of the South, the disastrous italian-war-1866 that yet brought the Veneto, and finally the capture-of-rome-1870 that made him master of the Eternal City. He died in 1878, having outlived nearly every figure of the movement that made his kingdom. Tivaroni, closing his history with a gallery of the men of the Risorgimento, ends on “Vittorio Emanuele — Re Galantuomo; the good and intelligent King; the first King of Italy,” and Oriani treats him as the fixed pole of the monarchical solution to which the whole country, against the republicans, finally adhered.
The Gentleman King and the making of the Kingdom
Victor Emmanuel came to power in the year of the defeat of Novara, when his father’s abdication left the young king to salvage what he could from the collapse of the war of 1849. The saving act, in the account of both Tivaroni and Oriani, was his fidelity to the Statuto: he kept the constitution and the parliament that the revolution had won, and so furnished the conservative monarchy of Piedmont with the liberal instrument it needed. Through the ministry of camillo-cavour after 1852 he set Piedmont on the course of a national policy, entering the Crimean war to win a seat at the councils of Europe, and arranging the secret meeting of Plombières with Napoleon III in 1858 that prepared the war of 1859. The battles of Magenta and Solferino and the annexations of central Italy in 1859–60 extended his rule from the Alps to the Adriatic, and on the death of Cavour the young monarch was left to consolidate a state far larger than the little subalpine kingdom from which he had started.
The Expedition of the Thousand and the annexation of the South
The decisive year was 1860. While giuseppe-garibaldi carried the revolutionary flag through Sicily and Naples in the expedition-of-the-thousand-1860, Victor Emmanuel and his government struggled to keep control of a movement they could neither bless nor suppress. The royal army marched through the Marches and Umbria to meet the Garibaldian conquest, and the king received the South by the plebiscite of 21 October 1860. Oriani’s account stresses the necessity of the monarchy for the annexed Mezzogiorno: the aristocracy of the southern countryside was “transcinated into the movement by the monarchical element,” and had the country constituted itself a republic, “a perhaps indomitable reaction would have burst forth in the South.” The phrase that summed the policy for a generation — attributed by Oriani to francesco-crispi in 1864, that “the monarchy unites us and the republic would divide us” — was the ground on which the royal solution rested. Cavour’s death on 6 June 1861 left Victor Emmanuel to preside over the first Italian Parliament and the unquiet consolidation of the new kingdom, shadowed by the brigandage of the South and the unsolved question of Rome.
The war of 1866 and the Veneto
In 1866 the king led Italy into the italian-war-1866 in alliance with Prussia against Austria, in return for the promised cession of the Veneto. The war was a humiliation for the new kingdom: at battle-of-custoza-1866 on 24 June the army, commanded through Lamarmora, was thrown back, and at battle-of-lissa-1866 on 20 July Admiral Persano’s fleet was defeated by Tegethoff. Yet diplomacy recovered what arms had lost. Tivaroni records the irony by which Italy received the Veneto as the cadeau, the “gift” of the Emperor Napoleon III, who transmitted it after Prussia’s victory at Königgrätz had settled the continental war — so that the province was handed to the kingdom without being won by it, and the Trentino, for which Garibaldi had fought, was excluded from the treaty. The rising of Palermo in September 1866 and the continuing unrest showed how little the annexation had satisfied the country.
Rome: the Law of Guarantees and the last years
The last great act of the reign was Rome. After the failure of Garibaldi at battle-of-mentana-1867, the Roman question remained frozen between the kingdom and the Holy See while the French garrisoned the Papal city. The crisis of 1870 dissolved the obstacle: the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 drew the French troops home, and on 20 September 1870 the Italian army breached the walls at Porta Pia and entered Rome. Victor Emmanuel took up residence in the Quirinal, and in 1871 the law-of-guarantees-1871 unilaterally defined the relations of the State and the Papacy, ending the temporal power while the Pope remained in the Vatican. The annexation of Rome was the completion of unification. The remaining years of the reign, as Tivaroni’s retrospective presents them, saw the kingdom settle into its constitutional routine under the successors of Cavour, until the king’s death in 1878. Tivaroni’s closing judgment — the good and intelligent King, the first King of Italy — is the verdict of the monarchical Risorgimento that he embodied, and that Oriani, looking back across the whole struggle, concedes was the only solution under which the newly annexed South and the reluctant Papacy could be held together.
