entities/vladimir-lenin.title: Vladimir Lenin (1870–1924)
entities/vladimir-lenin.content:
Vladimir Lenin
Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, known as Lenin (1870–1924), was the leader of the Bolshevik party and the architect of the october-revolution-1917. From exile he watched the collapse of the autocracy-russia in the February revolution, returned to Petrograd in April 1917 with his famous theses calling for the transfer of power to the soviets and the end of the war, and in October led the seizure of power that established the first Soviet government, which he headed until his death in 1924. His part in this wiki’s sources is that of the decisive antagonist: Denikin, writing from the staff and White side, treats him as the one leader with the will and the organized following to inherit the ruin that the Provisional Government and the failed command left behind.
From exile to the February revolution
In 1917 Lenin was in exile abroad, isolated from the Russia whose revolution had broken out in February. Denikin notes the curious circumstance of the first months: the revolution that overthrew the tsar was made by men who did not expect Lenin’s doctrines to govern it. Lenin had himself argued in 1905, as Denikin reminds the reader, that “of a socialist revolution by open class struggle against the whole bourgeoisie there could be no question” in Russia — an admission that the leader of 1917 had himself long insisted upon. Yet the war, the breakdown of the state, and the radicalization of the army and the workers created the conditions he had not foreseen as possible. The Provisional Government’s prolongation of the war and the failure of the June offensive did the work of agitation for him, and by the autumn the ground was prepared.
The April theses and the struggle for power
Returning to Petrograd in April 1917, Lenin at once set his course against the Provisional Government and in favor of “all power to the soviets” — a break, Denikin notes, with the patriotic line of the other socialist parties and with the very notion of continuing the war. Denikin quotes the Bolshevik leader’s appeal against the government and the commanders and traces the open, almost public process by which the Bolsheviks prepared the seizure of power: the Northern Regional Congress of Soviets, the Petrograd Soviet, the whole Bolshevik press — in which the hidden Lenin wrote under his own name — calling for insurrection; the organization by Trotsky, on 16 October, of the Military-Revolutionary Committee, which claimed the exclusive right to dispose of the Petrograd garrison. Denikin’s judgment is that by October there was in all Russia no effective organization besides the Bolsheviks able to claim the heavy inheritance, and that this fact pronounced sentence on the country, the people, and the revolution.
October and Brest-Litovsk
The October revolution was, in Denikin’s account, less a secret conspiracy than a demonstration of strength — power “was to be taken not by conspiracy but by a friendly demonstration of forces,” as Trotsky declared in the Soviet a week before the rising. The Provisional Government, isolated and unresisted, was overthrown, and alexander-kerensky’s attempt to rally troops at Gatchina failed. Lenin’s government at once sued for peace, and in March 1918 concluded the treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918, by which Russia left the war and surrendered vast territories to Germany — a peace that Denikin, with the White cause in view, describes as a “bargain” and a “burning shame,” and that stands in the broader frame of the total-war-economy and the disintegration of the Eastern front. The new regime’s first measures — the decree on land, on workers’ control, on self-determination of peoples, the break-up of the old army — Denikin records as the beginning of the world the Whites would fight against. Lenin ruled the Soviet state until his death in 1924, having carried his party from exile to the mastery of Russia in the space of seven years.

entities/wilhelm-i.title: Wilhelm I (1797–1888)
entities/wilhelm-i.content:
Wilhelm I (1797–1888)
Wilhelm I, King of Prussia from 1861 and German Emperor from 1871, was the sovereign through whose reign Prussia overthrew Austria, defeated France, and founded the German Empire. In this corpus’s frame his story is that of the army monarch — the man who, as Prince Regent from 1858, made the reorganization of the Prussian army the central question of his reign, who stood through the constitutional conflict of the 1860s, and who lived to wear the imperial crown he had helped to win. The contrast with his grandson wilhelm-ii runs beneath the whole later part of the story: Wilhelm I was the monarch who took Bismarck’s hand in his hour of greatest need and kept it to the end, whereas the young Kaiser of 1890 let the chancellor fall.
The army and the throne
Wilhelm was never guided by military expediency alone. As Lenz’s biography makes plain, he was thoroughly convinced that the army — “the creation of his ancestors” — must rest in the hand of the ruler and stand at his absolute disposal; only so, he believed, was the freedom, that is the sovereignty, of the crown guaranteed. This conviction was, Lenz says, the very basis on which the idea of the reform he always rightly called his own had grown in him. When he took up the regency in 1858, he entrusted the execution of this program to albrecht-von-roon, who in July of that year submitted to him a memorandum on the army constitution that opened his way into the ministry. Roon was “a man after Wilhelm’s heart,” obedient while the regent steered a liberal course, but readier still to hold him upright in conflict — a wedge, from the first hour, driven into the liberal ministry.
The reform itself was a sharp reorientation of the Prussian military system. Roon pressed for a reduction of the militia-like Landwehr in favour of a standing professional army, precisely because, as he argued in his first memorandum, the Landwehr made one not master in one’s own house: at every conflict of opinion between government and governed, one would have to reckon with the effect of contested measures on the armed part of the people, binding the government’s hands and exposing it to the wind of public opinion. The reorganization that resulted was, as Lenz notes, carried through wholly in the interest of the old military families and the Junker class: the Landwehr officers and the bourgeois officer candidates were pushed back, and the upper classes of the cadet houses were emptied to secure the new posts for the sons of military families. Crown and nobility, drawn together again by the shock of revolution, stood joined in the defence of the throne.
The constitutional conflict
The reform required money, and the liberal Chamber of Deputies refused it. There followed the constitutional conflict of the early 1860s, in which the crown governed without a lawful budget while the parliament withheld its approval. It was the supreme test of Wilhelm’s conception of kingship. Lenz’s account of the crisis of June 1861 shows how Roon, seeking to strengthen his isolated position in the cabinet, persuaded the king to look about for new ministers and wrote to otto-von-bismarck at Petersburg. The occasion was the question whether the new king should mark his accession by an homage in the old ständische forms, as his brother had done in 1840 — in a constitutional state a palpable anomaly, and an affront the conservatives offered their constitutional opponents. The liberal ministers resisted, and the crisis for a time ended in compromise: the homage was given up for a solemn coronation, and the liberals kept their places.
But the conflict could not be staved off forever. In September 1862, in the extremity of the confrontation over the military budget, Wilhelm took the decisive step that Lenz marks as the turning of his reign: he reached out and took Bismarck’s hand, because Bismarck alone of all his servants promised him help in the matter most sacred to his life. As Lenz puts it, looking back from the fall of 1890, “King Wilhelm then seized Bismarck’s hand, because he alone of all his servants promised him help in the dearest concern of his life, and it was done for his salvation.” Bismarck governed for years without the approval of the Chamber, holding the military question firm, breaking with parliament, and dissolving it — the very program he had sketched in his letters from Petersburg.
The wars of unification
The constitutional conflict was resolved, not in the Chamber, but on the battlefield. With Bismarck as minister-president and the reorganized army under the command of helmuth-von-moltke, the chief of the General Staff, Wilhelm carried Prussia through the wars that unified Germany. In 1866, against Austria, the King — then seventy years old — rode with his troops into Bohemia. Sybel’s account of Königgrätz shows him rising at five in the morning of 3 July after three hours of rest, driving from Gitschin in an open carriage, and arriving to the jubilant hurrahs of his soldiers on the heights opposite Sadowa shortly before half past seven. The victory of battle-of-koniggratz-1866 threw Austria out of Germany and made possible the north-german-confederation; the Peace of Prague of 23 August 1866 dissolved the old Confederation and left Prussia dominant north of the Main.
Four years later the confrontation with France decided the fate of the German question. At Ems in July 1870, while the King was taking the waters, the French ambassador Benedetti pressed him to guarantee that no Hohenzollern would ever again seek the Spanish throne. Wilhelm’s courteous refusal was the kernel of the ems-dispatch-1870 that Bismarck’s editing turned into a provocation; France, stung, declared the franco-prussian-war-1870-71. Wilhelm commanded in the field, was present at the great victories, and — in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871 — was proclaimed German Emperor, the Kaiserproklamation by which the German princes placed the crown of the new Reich upon his head. Lenz describes how the crown of Germany, for all its brilliance, did not destroy the Hohenzollern crown but raised it to new meaning: the gold that gave truth to the new glory was still the old genuine gold of the Prussian crown, and the power of Prussia and the peculiar character of its monarchy were preserved.
The old Kaiser
The last years of Wilhelm’s reign were those of the consolidation of the Empire. His will, with that of his chancellor, was, as Lenz records in the Kaiserproclamation and the opening of the first German Reichstag, “to build out in peace what had been won.” He survived two attempts on his life in 1878, and the second of them — Nobiling’s assault in June — was the occasion Bismarck seized to dissolve the Reichstag and break the power of the National Liberals. Lenz notes that the Crown Prince, who took up the regency for the wounded sovereign and who still sympathised with the liberals, could not oppose measures meant to shield his father and the throne from murder and overthrow; and the rapid recovery of the Kaiser destroyed whatever hopes the liberals might have drawn from the bloody interlude.
Wilhelm I died in 1888, the year of the three Kaisers, leaving the throne in quick succession to his son Friedrich III and then to his grandson wilhelm-ii. The contrast between the two sovereigns frames the ending of Bismarck’s story: the old king, who in the deepest need had taken Bismarck’s hand and kept faith with him to the last, was succeeded by a young emperor who feared no conflict, hoped rather through a policy of conciliation and social reform to win back the masses hostile to the state, and in 1890 dismissed the man who had made his empire. Lenz, writing of that fall, sets the grandfather’s salvation against the grandson’s rupture: “King Wilhelm then seized Bismarck’s hand … and it was done for his salvation. His grandson, however, feared no conflict at all.”

entities/wilhelm-ii.title: Wilhelm II (1859–1941)
entities/wilhelm-ii.content:
Wilhelm II (1859–1941)
Wilhelm II, German Emperor and King of Prussia from 1888 to 1918, was the sovereign of the Reich through the years of its greatest power and its overthrow. Grandson of wilhelm-i, he dismissed otto-von-bismarck in 1890 and thereafter personified an assertive, restless German policy; in 1914 he led Germany into the war that destroyed his throne, and in November 1918 he fled to exile in the Netherlands as his empire collapsed. In this corpus’s frame his story is that of the Kaiser who was “a prisoner of his generals” — the ruler whose divine-right conception of kingship, whose oscillations in war aims, and whose final helplessness before the Supreme Command frame both the causes and the defeat of the Great War. Czernin’s memoir, written at the moment of the catastrophe, is the most intimate study of his character; Recouly and Lenz set him against the Germany that made and unmade him.
The heir of Bismarck’s empire
Wilhelm II came to the throne in 1888, the year of the three Kaisers, after the brief reign of his father Friedrich III. Lenz’s biography of Bismarck frames his accession as the rupture that ended the chancellor’s career: the old king wilhelm-i, who in his deepest need had taken Bismarck’s hand and kept faith with him to the last, was succeeded by a young emperor who feared no conflict, hoped rather through a policy of conciliation and social reform to win back the masses hostile to the state, and in 1890 dismissed the man who had made his empire. Lenz sets the grandfather’s salvation against the grandson’s rupture: the new Kaiser felt himself strong enough to govern without the Iron Chancellor. The dismissal marked the beginning of the personal regime of Wilhelm II, in which the monarch’s temperament — restless, theatrical, eloquent and impetuous — came to stand for the policy of the Reich.
Czernin’s study of the Kaiser
Czernin devotes a whole chapter of Im Weltkriege to Wilhelm II, drawing on his own dealings with him in 1917 and 1918. He stresses Wilhelm’s belief in the divine right of kings, his Gottesgnadentum — the conviction that his authority rested on God’s appointment rather than on any contract with his people. Czernin treats the emperor crisis of 1908 (the Daily Telegraph affair, when Wilhelm’s tactless interview exposed the isolation of the throne), his bearing before the war, at its outbreak, and at Kreuznach, his doubts about the war’s outcome, and his oscillations in war aims. He describes Wilhelm at Kiel Week, his nature, and “the tragedy of his life”: a man who combined great personal gifts with a temperament unfitted to the grim endurance the war demanded. Czernin records how the German Crown Prince became a pacifist in 1917, and how Ludendorff’s will and judgment pressed upon the throne.
Prisoner of the generals
The central judgment of Czernin upon Wilhelm II in the war is that he was from the first day “the prisoner of his generals.” The complete displacement of the political factors by the military — the German Supreme Command (Oberste Heeresleitung) seizing all the command authority in the state — was, in Czernin’s view, an unhappiness; had the political factors of Berlin been heard, there would have been neither the invasion of Belgium nor the unrestricted submarine war, and these two omissions would have saved the Central Powers. The blind faith in the invincibility of the army, like so much else, was an inheritance from Bismarck’s legacy, and the “Prussian lieutenant that nobody in Germany can imitate” became the Kaiser’s undoing. The whole German people believed in victory, and an emperor who had thrown himself across the path of his generals would have taken on himself a responsibility beyond the measure of the bearable. So Wilhelm let his generals act; when Hindenburg and Ludendorff became gods for the German people, they were far more powerful than the Kaiser, and he less than ever able to oppose them. Recouly strikes the same note: the war became nearly inevitable the day the civil chiefs of Germany, “the Kaiser first of all,” seized by a contagious collective intoxication, were persuaded that Germany had not in the world the place to which it had a right.
The failure of 1918 and the abdication
At the end, the Kaiser’s helplessness was total. Recouly recounts how, after the defeat of 8 August 1918, Ludendorff — who had lost all confidence in victory — himself offered his resignation to the Kaiser, who naturally refused it, and how the German leaders sought to hand the burden of peace to the civilians they had so long treated with contempt. The military defeat unravelled the throne: the revolution of November 1918 swept away the monarchy, and Wilhelm II fled across the frontier into exile in the Netherlands, abdicating on 28 November 1918. Czernin’s closing reflection on the German state of mind after the defeat — the assertion that the army had not been vanquished in the field but stabbed in the back by the revolution — is the legend by which Wilhelm’s empire and its generals sought to escape responsibility (see stab-in-the-back-legend). The exile of the last Kaiser closed, in this corpus’s frame, the story that had begun with the dismissal of Bismarck: the empire founded by the grandfather undone by the grandson’s war.

events/armistice-11-november-1918.title: The Armistice of 11 November 1918
events/armistice-11-november-1918.content:
The Armistice of 11 November 1918
11 November 1918
The armistice concluded at Rethondes in the forest of Compiègne on the morning of 11 November 1918, by which Germany accepted the conditions of marshal-foch and the Allied commands and the fighting ceased on all fronts at eleven o’clock. Recouly’s account carries the event through the German request for an armistice, the reception of the German plenipotentiaries, the signature at five in the morning, and the ending of operations six hours later. The armistice sealed the defeat of the Central Powers that the Allied offensives of 1918 and the collapse of the German allies had made complete.
Background
By the autumn of 1918 the war was lost for the Central Powers. The hundred-days-offensive-1918 on the western front had broken the German army; Ludendorff, after the day of 8 August, had concluded that the war could no longer be won militarily and passed the burden of peace to the civilians he had so long despised. The German allies collapsed in turn: the Bulgarian front fell in September, and the Italian offensive of Vittorio Veneto in October put the Austro-Hungarian army out of action, isolating Germany militarily — in the words of the Italian Comando Supremo, the Austrian army “was thus annihilated” and Germany forced to ask for an armistice. With the Quadruple Alliance in ruins, Germany sued for peace.
The German request
Germany made known the names of its plenipotentiaries and asked for the place where they might enter the French lines. Foch, having received on 7 November the radio asking him to let the German plenipotentiaries penetrate the lines, replied that same night, ordering them to present themselves at the outposts on the great road of Maubeuge–La Capelle–Guise. He left Senlis himself in his special train and arrived at 6.30 in the evening at the little station of Rethondes, between Compiègne and Soissons, in the forest of Laigle. The German delegates, delayed by the extraordinary congestion of the roads, were several hours late; they reached Haudroy, two kilometres from La Capelle, at nine o’clock. There an officer of the staff brought them to the army headquarters, and a special train conducted them to Rethondes, where they arrived about seven in the morning.
The signature
The German delegation, headed by a member of the government, Erzberger, comprised a plenipotentiary minister, General Winterfeld, formerly military attaché in Paris, a naval captain, and some officers. Foch received them at nine o’clock in his train and communicated the conditions of the armistice. The time allowed for acceptance was three clear days; the Germans were to make known their answer before 11 November at eleven o’clock. During those days events in Germany had precipitated: Prince Max of Baden, head of the government, had resigned, and the revolution had broken out in Germany (see the flight of the Kaiser). In the night of the 10th to the 11th, the German delegates, having received from their government the authorisation to sign, conferred in a memorable session with Foch, his staff, and Admiral Wemyss, representing the English government. The signatures were exchanged at five o’clock in the morning. Six hours later, at eleven o’clock, the operations were stopped on the whole front.
The armistice and the end of the war
In Paris, toward the end of the morning, the news that the armistice was signed ran through the capital like an electric spark — the ringing of bells, salvos of artillery, flags appearing at all the windows, and a crowd flooding the streets. The armistice of 11 November ended the fighting that had begun with the mobilisations and declarations of the summer of 1914 (see july-crisis-1914 and sarajevo-assassination-1914). For the Allies it was victory; for Germany it was the beginning of the political catastrophe in which the army sought to disown the defeat — the seed of the stab-in-the-back-legend by which the undefeated-in-the-field army claimed it had been betrayed from within. Recouly, writing sixteen years later, closes on the sombre note that the treaty that followed was “badly conceived and still worse executed,” and that the tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Berlin bore the inscription INVICTIS VICTI VICTURI — “to the unconquered soldiers, today’s conquered who will be tomorrow’s conquerors.”

events/assassination-alexander-ii-1881.title: Assassination of Alexander II (1881)
events/assassination-alexander-ii-1881.content:
Assassination of Alexander II (1881)
1 March 1881
Background
The Russo-Turkish war and the humiliation of the
Berlin Congress deepened the estrangement between the government of
alexander-ii and Russian society, and gave fresh life to a revolutionary movement that the
reaction of the 1860s and 1870s had only strengthened. From the disillusionment of the war the party
of the People’s Will took shape, finally organizing itself after the congresses
at Lipetsk and Voronezh. Its terrorist attacks were directed above all at the person of the tsar.
Against alexander-ii this small but extraordinarily energetic organization of revolutionary
terrorists carried on what Kornilov calls a systematic siege — a whole network of mines, ambushes,
and the like, in which the revolutionaries did not stop before digging tunnels, blowing up bridges,
trains, and houses in the cities, even though carrying these attempts out threatened the lives of
many dozens of people. Nothing stopped them; they sacrificed their own lives without the slightest
hesitation.
On one side stood revolutionaries convinced in their blindness that a successful attempt on the
tsar’s life would serve as the signal for a popular revolution that would radically change all the
conditions of political and social life in Russia — and no arguments of reason could shake them. On
the other stood a government at a loss, unable to find any point of support in a population whose
needs and rights it was not accustomed to consider, convulsively adopting various repressive
measures that only sharpened the life-and-death struggle and placed peaceful citizens in an
intolerable position, under martial law and the arbitrary will of coarse and unceremonious satraps
and police agents.
From Solovyov to the Winter Palace
After Solovyov’s attempt on the emperor’s life in 1879 and a series of other attempts, it became
clear to everyone that the government could not fight the revolutionaries by repressive measures
alone, and could not restore peace and order. At the same time the government saw that its
self-confident appeals to society for assistance could lead to nothing, so long as it was not
disposed to reckon with the interests and rights of that society. Doubts about the correctness of
the established policy began to appear even among some members of the government.
In the Kharkov governor-general, Loris-Melikov, who had been made one of the temporary
governors-general after Solovyov’s attempt, there appeared an experiment in a somewhat modified
policy: he tried to restrain the arbitrariness of the administration subordinate to him and to win
the sympathy and respect of the local population by a solicitous protection of their interests,
while continuing to persecute the revolutionaries energetically. In parallel, the chairman of the
committee of ministers, Count Valuev, began cautiously to suggest to the emperor the necessity of
reconciling the government with society, drawing from the archives his own project of 1863 for
giving representatives of society a part in state affairs. Grand Duke Konstantin Nikolaevich,
chairman of the State Council, likewise recalled a project composed by Prince Urusov in 1866 tending
toward some embryo of a consultative representative institution.
While these projects were being discussed, the government continued to rule by means of harsh
punishments and executions, and the arbitrariness that provoked universal irritation continued and
grew. The revolutionaries organized an explosion in the Winter Palace itself — in the tsar’s own
dwelling. The explosion occurred at the very moment when the whole imperial family was preparing to
take part in the gala dinner given in honor of the arrival in Petersburg of the Bulgarian prince
Alexander Battenberg. It took place on 4 February 1880 and failed of its aim only through purely
accidental circumstances. The revolutionaries had succeeded in bringing a sufficient quantity of
dynamite into the Winter Palace, storing it over the course of some months in the basement, inside a
stove that stood directly under the imperial dining room — a fact established from a plan of the
palace that they had procured in time. The only thing they could not see from the plan was that
between the basement and the dining room there was a mezzanine chamber, in which at the moment of
the explosion were the guards, several dozen of whom became its victims. The blast did not reach the
floor of the dining room with sufficient force. Moreover the imperial family had not yet sat down at
table, because the train bringing Alexander Battenberg happened to be late, and the dinner was to
take place half an hour later.
Had it succeeded, not only the emperor but the whole imperial family would have perished, and with
them all the lawful heirs — a catastrophe that might have raised the question, quite unexpectedly
for the country, either of electing a new dynasty or, as the revolutionaries dreamed, of completely
changing the form of government. The culprit was a young worker, Khalturin, who had lodgings in the
palace as a cleaner, lived there for six months, brought in the dynamite that Zhelyabov supplied to
him, and quietly waited for the right moment, postponing the explosion until he had in his hands
exact data that it would achieve its full purpose. The investigation revealed that this was no
accidental penetration: the revolutionaries had made a firm nest inside the palace.
It was a complete fiasco for the police system of protection. A few weeks before the explosion a
plan of the Winter Palace, marked with a cross at the place of the explosion, had been found in the
papers of a revolutionary at a search — yet the police, which made peaceful Petersburgers’ lives
impossible and imposed obligatory doorkeeper duties on the population at a cost of up to a million
rubles a year, paid no attention to so simple a fact.
The Supreme Administrative Commission
The fiasco revealed to the emperor himself the impossibility and extreme danger of the existing
position, and there occurred in the highest spheres a decisive turn in views on the tasks of
internal policy. The tsesarevich, Alexander Alexandrovich — the future alexander-iii — had
already shown at the conference held before the explosion that he was not at all on the side of
Valuev, and for the first time displayed clearly those political views he would profess throughout
his reign, declaring himself decisively against all constitutional plans. After the explosion, at a
new conference of 8 February 1880, the heir himself came forward with a definite plan: to establish
a supreme investigating commission on the model of those of 1862 and 1866, but with broader powers
covering the whole of Russia.
alexander-ii at first received the proposal negatively, but, persuaded by the insistent heir,
agreed. He declared that he considered exceptional measures unavoidable and would create a special
temporary dictatorial institution, the “Supreme Administrative Commission,” with extraordinary
powers chiefly for the struggle against sedition, but also charged with considering the intolerable
situation and finding a way out of it. At its head the emperor placed General Loris-Melikov — the
one governor-general who, together with considerable energy against the revolutionaries, had shown
the ability to attract the sympathy of ordinary people. The commission was to be obeyed by all
administrative authorities, even the ministers, including the war minister, who had previously been
Loris-Melikov’s direct superior.
Immediately upon taking office on 14 February 1880, Loris-Melikov published a proclamation to the
inhabitants of Petersburg, declaring that while firmly seeking the eradication of criminals who
tried to shake the state order, he wished to calm and protect the lawful interests of the
well-disposed part of society. “On the support of society,” he wrote, “I look as on the principal
force that can aid the government in restoring the regular course of state life, an interruption of
which most threatens the interests of society itself.”
Kornilov notes that those who knew Loris-Melikov — Dr. Belogolovy, who talked with him after he had
left office, and A. I. Koshelev in his memoirs — describe him as a sincerely liberal, thoroughly
honest man, inclined to meet the loyal social movement halfway and to satisfy the just demands of
the zemstvos and of liberal-minded people, up to granting society some participation in state
affairs. It is beyond doubt, however, that the basic tasks of his commission were above all
repressive: it was established before everything else for the struggle with the revolutionaries, and
on that struggle Loris-Melikov was prepared to concentrate all his forces. He was not, as has been
unfairly supposed, a constitutionalist; his outlook remained that of an administrator who saw his
police tasks with unusual breadth.
Under Loris-Melikov the reactionary Count D. A. Tolstoy resigned, senatorial inspections were begun,
the peasant question was taken up, and the constitutional movement gathered force. His programme
culminated in a report to the emperor proposing the establishment of a special preparatory
commission — the first step toward drawing elected representatives of society into legislation.
1 March 1881
The execution of the plan was prepared with care. The bombs were made by the talented technician
Kibalchich. When at the end of February Zhelyabov and Trigoni were arrested, Sofia Perovskaya, left
at liberty, judged it necessary not merely to continue the attempt but to bring it to completion as
quickly as possible, foreseeing that with Zhelyabov’s arrest the whole existing revolutionary
organization threatened to collapse.
On 1 March, Alexander II, not heeding Loris-Melikov’s warnings — who had already twice held him back
from his Sunday outing, sensing that something was being prepared — set out for the parade of
troops, and afterwards went to the Mikhailovsky Palace (where the Alexander III museum now stands)
to see Grand Duchess Ekaterina Mikhailovna, and from there meant to return to the Winter Palace. The
revolutionaries under Perovskaya showed such energy that, not knowing exactly which way the emperor
would go, they maneuvered their bombs through the streets, and Perovskaya repeatedly shifted the
bomb-carriers so that they would certainly fall on the sovereign’s route. The circumstances of the
catastrophe are generally known. On that Sunday the bombs struck, and alexander-ii was killed.
Consequences: the end of reform, the onset of reaction
The catastrophe was a fatal outcome for the whole system of measures projected by Loris-Melikov. The
emperor who mounted the throne, alexander-iii, had shown, at the conferences preceding the
Winter Palace explosion, that he promised to be a sovereign of no liberal inclination. So it turned
out in the sequel; but the first steps of his reign were subject to great vacillations, and the
course that finally established itself under him in the 1880s was not set at once. Two tendencies
contended in the highest governing circles. At the conference of 8 March 1881 the fate of
Loris-Melikov’s constitutional project was decided: under the influence of
konstantin-pobedonostsev, who agitated against the constitutional plans as ruinous, and with the
support of the publicists Katkov and Aksakov in a conservative vein, the project was rejected. The
manifesto of 29 April 1881 proclaimed the unshakable autocracy in terms that
left no room for a representative assembly.
Loris-Melikov and some other ministers resigned, and the ministry of N. P. Ignatiev followed — a
government that promised measures to improve the economic condition of the people, including
compulsory redemption and a reduction of redemption payments, under the finance minister Bunge, who
abolished the poll tax. But the liberal experiment was short-lived, and the reign settled into
reaction: the reactionary Count D. A. Tolstoy returned to power in the Ministry of the Interior, a
new press law of 1882 muzzled the press, the law of 12 July 1889 on land captains (земские
начальники) placed the peasantry under the control of noble officials, and the statute on zemstvo
institutions of 12 June 1890 subordinated the zemstvos to the nobility and
the government.
The death of alexander-ii thus closed the era of reform in Russia. The
Great Reforms were not overturned, but their further development was
arrested, and the hope of drawing society into government perished with the tsar. The
People’s Will had destroyed the one figure who had begun, at the end of his
life, to move toward reconciliation — and in so doing delivered Russia to the reaction it had meant
to overturn. Among contemporaries the shock was general. S. Yu. Witte, then a young railway official
in Kiev, heard the news in the theatre and wrote to his uncle, General Fadeev, comparing the “steam
hammer” of the workshops with the powerlessness of the state against anarchists; he joined the “Holy
Brotherhood,” a private society organized after the assassination to defend the autocracy.
Key participants

alexander-ii — Emperor of Russia, assassinated on 1 March 1881.
alexander-iii — Tsesarevich who pressed for the exceptional commission and then, as emperor, rejected constitutional reform.
People’s Will (Narodnaya Volya) — the terrorist party; Zhelyabov, Perovskaya, Kibalchich, Khalturin, Trigoni.
Loris-Melikov — head of the Supreme Administrative Commission, author of the abortive reform programme.
konstantin-pobedonostsev — the tutor and adviser who urged the new emperor toward reaction.

events/austro-hungarian-compromise-1867.title: The Austro-Hungarian Compromise (1867)
events/austro-hungarian-compromise-1867.content:
The Austro-Hungarian Compromise (1867)
13 February–12 June 1867
The Compromise (Ausgleich in German, kiegyezés in Hungarian) of 1867 re-founded the Habsburg lands as the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary, establishing the constitutional relation between the Hungarian kingdom and the Austrian half of the empire that governed the monarchy until 1918. The settlement, negotiated in the months after the defeat of 1866 and associated above all with the name of Ferenc Deák, rested on the Act XII of 1867 and restored Hungary’s statehood while joining it to Austria in a personal union for the common defence and the common affairs. It is the constitutional foundation of the whole 1866–1919 period of this wiki, and the frame within which the era’s Austrian and Hungarian history — the nationality conflicts, the rise of dualism, and the politics of the East — unfolded.
Background: Hungary’s statehood and the Pragmatic Sanction
The Compromise was the product of a centuries-long constitutional relation, and its defenders grounded it in the history of Hungarian statehood. As Beksics set out in his juridical defence of the dualism, the Hungarian nation was always one with its king: the nation was the source, the royal power the stream that flowed from it, and in Hungary not only political power but every right had the nation itself for its source. The German doctrine of the state, which set up kingship as an independent, primordial source of right, exerted, he held, a harmful reaction on Hungarian public-law science, for the Hungarian kingship never possessed such powers.
The constitutional tie that bound Hungary to Austria was the Pragmatic Sanction of 1723, by which the succession of the House of Habsburg and the inseparable and indivisible possession of the kingdoms was settled, and on which the whole subsequent relation of Hungary to Austria rested. The settlement of 1848 had established a responsible Hungarian ministry and ordered the common affairs between Hungary and Austria; but the failure of 1849 brought the provisorium, the period of provisional and absolutist administration that followed, and left Hungary without the restoration of its constitutional life until the negotiations that issued in 1867.
The making of the Compromise
The negotiations that produced the Compromise, carried through after the catastrophe of 1866, issued in the constitutional work associated with the name of Ferenc Deák. Beksics traced the origin of the dualism — how the dualist system came into being, the negotiations and the constitutional work that issued in the Compromise, and the sense in which the settlement preserved, and did not impair, the statehood of the Hungarian state. The central instrument was Act XII of 1867, whose public-law meaning became the subject of the endless disputes that Beksics wrote to settle: the claim, then beginning to be taught in the schools, that between Hungary and Austria there is a real union, and that Hungary’s statehood has been impaired by the dualist system, he declared to be a misunderstanding of an act whose meaning, rightly read, preserved the national sovereignty.
Deák’s achievement, in Beksics’s framing, was to bridge the gulf between the king and the nation. He defended the settlement as the form given to a centuries-long historical development: the dualism had existed before 1848, the common affairs and their management had existed, and through all the great changes — Hungary freed from the Turkish yoke, triumphant over the attempts to absorb it, its two great wars of liberty — only one thing had proved firm and immovable: the tie that binds Hungary to Austria through the dynasty, and its consequence, the union of the two mutually independent states for mutual defence and for that alone.
The constitutional arrangements
The Compromise created two independent states joined in a personal union — the tie binding them being the identity of the ruler — with a set of common affairs managed in common. Beksics examined the several parts of the arrangement in detail: the conduct of foreign affairs under the dualist system and Hungary’s standing as an international personality; the common military establishment and the army, and alongside it the Hungarian honvéd (home defence) force and the extraordinary levy; the financial and economic autonomy of the Hungarian state and the division of fiscal and economic matters between the two states; and the national royal household of the Hungarian kingdom.
The common affairs were managed by the three common ministries — of foreign affairs, of war, and of finance for the common expenditures — and by the Delegations, the joint parliamentary bodies by which the common affairs of the two states were conducted. Beksics devoted a chapter to the Delegations, their powers and their proceedings, and compared the handling of the common affairs in 1848 and in 1867. He also corrected what he called the erroneous public-law designations that distorted the true character of the dualist relation, insisting that the union was a personal union of the two crowns — a union of the two mutually independent states for mutual defence and for that alone.
Croatia and the nationalities
The internal bearings of the dualism reached to Croatia and the nationalities. The Hungarian-Croatian settlement, the nagodba of 1868, defined Croatia-Slavonia’s relation to the Hungarian kingdom, and the nationalities within Hungary found their place under the dualist state. Sosnosky, writing from the German-national vantage of the eve of 1914, treated the same ground more critically: he described the Magyar conception of the national state, the pan-Magyarism and the Magyarization of the subject peoples — the Germans, Romanians, Slovaks, Ruthenians and Serbs — and the struggle over the common army, its language of command, and the Hungarian military demands that repeatedly provoked crisis. The Compromise, in his view, had created a system whose national frictions were among the deepest malady of the monarchy.
The future of the dualism
The Compromise, Beksics concluded, could not be destroyed by the weak breezes of internal quarrels, not because it was intellectually perfect but because it answered the interests of both Hungary and Austria, not because it was a new creation but because it gave form to a centuries-long historical development. Only in the single case of the cessation of the identity of the dynasty would new arrangements follow, an eventuality he placed entirely outside the range of political possibility. But the German-national reading of the eve of the war saw the matter otherwise: Sosnosky surveyed the possible futures of the monarchy — a revision of the dualism, the greater-Hungarian solution, trialism with the South Slavs, or the federal “Greater Austria” of Aurel Popovici — and argued that the monarchy’s future lay in an inner reform that should reconcile the peoples with the state, the watchword being unity through multiplicity, viribus unitis (“with united forces”). The debate between the Hungarian defence of the Ausgleich and the German demand for reform defined the constitutional politics of the Dual Monarchy down to its end.

events/austro-prussian-war-1866.title: The Austro-Prussian War (June–August 1866)
events/austro-prussian-war-1866.content:
The Austro-Prussian War (June–August 1866)
June 14 – August 23, 1866
Background
The Seven Weeks’ War grew out of a quarrel that the great powers of the German Confederation had
been nursing ever since they had jointly torn the Elbe Duchies from Denmark in 1864. The joint
administration of Schleswig and Holstein became a running wound between the two German great powers,
and Heinrich von Sybel’s account of the years 1865–1866 describes the mounting Spannung zwischen
Österreich und Preußen — the tension between Austria and Prussia — as it rose almost to the point
of rupture. Each court suspected the other of seeking to turn the settlement of the duchies to its
own advantage, and the occupation of the conquered provinces, meant to be temporary, hardened into a
permanent grievance.
In August 1865 the two governments patched together the Gasteiner Konvention (Gastein Convention),
a temporary expedient that partitioned the administration of the duchies without settling their
final fate. Holstein went under Austrian administration and Schleswig under Prussian, in a division
that satisfied nobody. The arrangement was received without enthusiasm by the German states and the
European powers alike, and Sybel treats it as precisely what it proved to be: a stopgap that served
only to postpone the inevitable clash, while the underlying rivalry remained unresolved.
The Break and the Arming
The rupture came more quickly than most observers expected. Both sides set about preparing for war
“on all sides,” as Sybel titles one of his chapters, and the winter and spring of 1866 were given
over to mobilisation schedules, the concentration of troops, and the financial measures that a great
war required. Prussia, under King Wilhelm I and his minister-president Otto von Bismarck, and
Austria, under the Emperor Franz Joseph, each calculated that the German question could be settled
only by arms.
A last attempt at accommodation was nevertheless made in the spring of 1866. Napoleon III, the
French emperor, proposed a European congress to settle the German question peaceably, hoping to turn
the Austro-Prussian rivalry to France’s advantage. At the same time the Gablenz mission ran a final
errand of Austro-Prussian reconciliation. All of it came to nothing. Behind the scenes Vienna
entered into secret negotiations with Paris, sounding the French for neutrality or support in
exchange for territorial compensation, while Berlin looked in the opposite direction, toward Italy.
The Prussian-Italian Alliance
The decisive diplomatic stroke was Prussia’s. Through the spring of 1866, Bismarck negotiated an
offensive alliance with the Kingdom of Italy, concluded in April 1866. The terms bound Italy to
enter a war against Austria on Prussia’s side, with Venetia as the prize — the province that Italy
expected as its reward for joining the struggle against Vienna. For the Italians, who had long
coveted the Venetian lands still held by the Habsburgs, the offer was compelling enough to draw them
into a war whose other stakes were, to them, remote. The alliance gave Prussia a second front and
forced Austria to divide its strength between Bohemia and Italy, and it meant that the Austro-
Prussian struggle would be fought on both land and sea.
Opening Moves and the End of the Confederation
Hostilities opened in June 1866 with Prussia’s invasion of the territories of the German
Confederation. The Prussian armies overran Hanover, Saxony, and Electoral Hesse in short order; the
Hanoverian army, cornered at Langensalza on 27 June 1866, fought with courage but was compelled to
capitulate, and the Kingdom of Hanover passed effectively under Prussian control. These swift
campaigns in north Germany, which Sybel describes under the heading Unterwerfung Norddeutschlands
(“the subjugation of North Germany”), dismantled the Confederation piecemeal and demonstrated that
the medium German states could not stand alone against Prussian arms. One after another they were
overrun, occupied, or compelled to change sides, and with them the old federal structure collapsed.
The Two Theatres of War
Austria’s main force, the Northern Army under Feldzeugmeister Ludwig von Benedek, concentrated at
Olmütz and faced the principal Prussian invasion through Bohemia. There the war was decided. The
Prussians advanced in three separate armies — the Elbe, First, and Second Armies under Herwarth von
Bittenfeld, Prince Friedrich Karl, and Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm — and Helmut von Moltke’s plan
was to concentrate them on the battlefield. After the preliminary engagements of Gitschin (Jičín)
and Münchengrätz, the three columns converged for the climactic Battle of Königgrätz on 3 July 1866,
a decisive Prussian victory that shattered the Austrian army in a single afternoon.
The southern front went differently, and the Italian ally fared badly. At the Battle of Custoza on
24 June 1866 the Austrians under Archduke Albrecht defeated the Italians, and on 20 July the
Austrian fleet under Admiral Wilhelm von Tegetthoff routed the Italians off Lissa. Italy
nevertheless reaped the political prize: with Prussia’s victories, it occupied Venetia “without a
struggle,” as Sybel put it, crossing the provincial frontiers once Austria was beaten in the north.
Italian greed for Welschtirol (Trentino) and irritation at the five-day armistice Bismarck had
concluded without Italian consent drew only Bismarck’s dry retort that if Prussian troops rested
five days, they did no more than the Italian army had done for weeks after Custoza.
Consequences
The war was decided at Königgrätz and in the negotiations that followed. After the armistice, the
preliminaries were signed at Nikolsburg, and the definitive Peace of Prague on 23 August 1866 ended
the conflict. The German Confederation was dissolved, Austria was excluded from Germany, and Prussia
annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, and the free city of Frankfurt. The foundations of the new
Reich were laid in the North German Confederation, bringing the German question to its Kleindeutsch
resolution under Prussian hegemony and setting the stage for the war with France four years later.
The Austro-Prussian War, fought in a matter of weeks, had remade the map of central Europe.

events/balkan-wars-1912-13.title: The Balkan Wars (1912–13)
events/balkan-wars-1912-13.content:
The Balkan Wars (1912–13)
October 1912 – August 1913
The two wars that redrew the map of the Balkans on the eve of the Great War: the war of the Balkan League against the Ottoman Empire in the autumn and winter of 1912–13, and the inter-allied war of the summer of 1913 in which the victors turned upon one another over the spoils. Together they destroyed the Turkish dominion in Europe almost at a stroke and doubled the size of Serbia — the very change that set Austria-Hungary upon the road to Sarajevo and the July crisis of 1914. Sosnosky, closing his two-volume account of the Habsburg Balkan policy at the Peace of Bukarest, gave the wars their name in the historical literature of the Monarchy: die Balkan-Katastrophe, the Balkan catastrophe.
Background: the Eastern Question comes to a head
The wars were the eruption of the eastern-question in its most violent form yet. Through the nineteenth century the Powers had agreed only to keep the sick man of Europe on his feet; by 1911–12 that concert had broken down. The Italo-Turkish war over Tripoli (1911) taught the small Balkan states that the Porte could be attacked with impunity, and the Austro-Russian Mürzsteg agreement over Macedonia, long since dead in practice, had left the peninsula without a policeman. Under the chancellorship of Count leopold-berchtold the Monarchy still clung to the doctrine of the status quo — that nothing on the Balkan should be changed without the agreement of the Great Powers — while Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro prepared to change everything. Sosnosky describes the league that now took shape under the title “strange allies”: Bulgaria, the most powerful of the four, joined with its hereditary rivals Serbia and Greece, and with Montenegro, in a compact whose only real cement, as he judged it, was the appetite for the Turkish inheritance. The watchword raised was “Der Balkan den Balkanvölkern” — “the Balkans for the Balkan peoples” — the slogan under which the league resolved to exclude both the Porte and the tutelage of the Powers.
The first war: the league against Turkey
In October 1912 the Balkan League opened war upon the Ottoman Empire. The Turkish armies, shaken by the defeat in Tripoli and commanded by generals who had lost their nerve, collapsed with astonishing speed. Sosnosky records how the allied successes exceeded every expectation: the Turks were driven out of Macedonia, Thrace and Albania; Adrianople and Scutari were besieged and taken. Within a few weeks the whole Turkish position in Europe was overthrown, and only the Gallipoli peninsula and the line Enos–Midia — the line the Powers strove to impose as the limit of the allied conquest — remained to the Sultan. The Porte, whose empire had once ended at the gates of Vienna, was glad to keep a scrap of the Europe that had once trembled before it.
For Austria-Hungary the war was a catastrophe in prospect. Berchtold’s status-quo policy was struck dead by the speed of the allied victories. The Monarchy had to reckon with a vastly enlarged Serbia at its frontier and, behind Serbia, Russia; the general staff under conrad-von-hotzendorf prepared for the possibility of warlike complications. Sosnosky is at pains to defend Berchtold’s reserve in the crisis: his restraint over the Sandjak of Novi Pazar and over Albania was not, he argues, the paralysis it appeared, but a policy bound hand and foot by the alliance with Italy — which held the treaty right to demand the port of Valona as compensation should the Monarchy advance into Turkish territory — and by the reluctance of Berlin to be drawn into a Balkan war. The Monarchy, in Sosnosky’s image, walked like a somnambulist along an abyss, assured by its own press that all was well with its allies while Italy’s irredentist fever burned unquenched.
The road to the peace of London
Through the winter of 1912–13 the Powers, meeting in the ambassadors’ conference at London, strove to confine the war. The allies’ demands were so severe — the cession of all Turkish territory northwest of the Rodosto–Malatra line, the Aegean islands, Crete, a war indemnity — that the Powers refused them and countered with their own terms, leaving the disposal of Albania and the islands to the Great Powers. Berchtold pressed unremittingly for a prompt peace, and Sir Edward Grey at last lost patience, declaring that only the delegates ready to sign at once could count on England’s support. On the last days of May 1913 the preliminary peace of London was signed; the Ottoman dominion in Europe was formally ended, and the fate of Albania and the Aegean islands was reserved to the concert of the Powers.
The second war: the allies fall out
The peace of London solved nothing. The only bond that had held the Balkan allies together was, as Sosnosky put it, die Habsucht — greed — and greed turned within the camp as soon as the Turkish lands were won. Serbia, denied Albania by the Monarchy’s insistence, demanded compensation in Macedonia at Bulgaria’s expense; Greece and Serbia, distrusting Bulgaria, arranged the partition of the conquered territory behind its back; the Serbo-Bulgarian quarrel over the partition of Macedonia, and the Greco-Bulgarian collisions at Saloniki, mounted through the spring of 1913 toward a second war. The Tsar, the nominal arbiter of the alliance, pleaded for peace; his telegram of 8 June to the kings of Bulgaria and Serbia failed to reconcile them. In the last days of June 1913 Bulgaria, whether by accident or design, attacked its former allies. The second Balkan War had begun.
The second war went against Bulgaria from the outset. Serbia and Greece, joined by the Turks who reconquered Adrianople, fell upon the exhausted Bulgarians; in July Rumania, which had held back on the advice of the Monarchy at the start of the first war, at last intervened and crossed the Danube into the Dobrudscha without firing a shot. Isolated and beaten on all sides, Bulgaria sued for peace. The treaty was signed at Bukarest on 10 August 1913: Bulgaria lost the Dobrudscha to Rumania and much of Macedonia to Serbia and Greece, while the separate treaty of Constantinople of 29 September restored Adrianople and Kirkilisse to the Turks. The peace of Bukarest, in Sosnosky’s judgment, laid not the foundation of a lasting settlement but the seeds of new conflict — “a dragons-seed that would come up sooner or later as evil harvest.”
Consequences: the enlarged Serbia and the road to 1914
The Balkan Wars transformed the position that had sustained the Monarchy since the Congress of Berlin. Serbia was nearly doubled in size and territory and had won enormous prestige among the South Slavs; the Habsburg monarchy, by contrast, emerged humiliated, isolated even within its own alliance, its treaty of Bukarest unrevised despite its protest. Austria-Hungary had created, out of the wreck of the Ottoman power, the independent state of Albania — an act Berchtold had felt compelled to perform because neither he nor Italy would suffer the other to possess it — and had thereby barred Serbia from the Adriatic, earning its hatred. King Franz Ferdinand’s last attempts to secure Rumania’s adherence, and the general staff’s war preparations, came to nothing.
The consequence, as both Sosnosky and the diplomat ottokar-czernin record, was that the peace of Bukarest was generally recognised to be no peace at all. The aged franz-joseph told Czernin before he left for Bukarest that the treaty was untenable and that the Monarchy was going to a new war, hoping only that it would remain localised. The enlarged Serbia was far from satisfied and aspired to become a Great Power; the Monarchy, its prestige broken, was far from resigned. The two Balkan Wars had set the stage on which the shots of Sarajevo would fire the world war. They are the immediate prelude, in time and in temper, to the july-crisis-1914, and the decisive demonstration of the failure of the Habsburg balkan-policy-austria.

events/battle-of-adua-1896.title: The Battle of Adua (1 March 1896)
events/battle-of-adua-1896.content:
The Battle of Adua (1 March 1896)
1 March 1896
The battle of Adua (Adwa) on 1 March 1896, in which an Italian army was annihilated by the forces of the Ethiopian emperor Menelik II, the greatest disaster inflicted on a European army by an African power in the age of empire. The defeat brought down the government of francesco-crispi, whose African adventure had carried Italy into the Ethiopian highlands, and it turned Italian colonial policy toward the withdrawal and prudence that the leaders of the liberal opposition, above all giustino-fortunato, had long urged. In this corpus the event closes the African chapter of the second monarchical period that Oriani narrates from the conquest of Eritrea, and it marks the great check to Italian expansionism in the years before the entry into the world war.
Background
Italy’s entry into the African scramble followed hard upon the formation of the kingdom, and by the 1880s the young state had established a colony on the Red Sea coast around Massawa — the nucleus of Eritrea. Oriani, in the La lotta politica in Italia chapter on the African conquest, frames the enterprise as the attraction of Italian ambition into the general European movement of imperial expansion. Under francesco-crispi the colonial project grew more ambitious, seeking to extend Italian dominion from the coast into the highlands of Abyssinia. The first great reverse had come on 24 January 1887, when an Italian column was cut to pieces at Dogali; but the colonial policy pressed on, and in the mid-1890s a larger war broke out with the Ethiopian empire of Menelik II, who had consolidated his power and refused to accept the Italian protectorate that the treaty of Uccialli had seemed to confer.
The disaster
The decisive campaign of 1896 ended in catastrophe at Adua on 1 March 1896. The Italian commander, marching to force a decision against the Ethiopian host, was overwhelmed: the Italian army was surrounded and destroyed on the field, and the survivors, and the colony itself, fell into the hands of the enemy. Fortunato, writing in the months that followed, evokes the disaster as l’immane disastro di Adua — “the immense disaster of Adua” — a blow that had at a stroke made the country, in his words, ready for a great reaction. The scale of the loss was without precedent in the colonial record: thousands of Italian and colonial troops perished in the valley that the survivors, and the mothers of the fallen, would remember as the triste conca di Adua — “the sad hollow of Adua.” The event struck the country with a shock that resounded through its public life for years, and tablets to the fallen of Adua were later raised, and commemorated, across Italy.
The fall of Crispi
The political consequence was immediate. The disaster of Adua brought down the government of Francesco Crispi, the statesman whose African policy had staked the prestige of the country upon the enterprise, and who now fell with it. The national reaction against the colonial adventure delivered power to his opponents and made the disaster the decisive condemnation of the policy that had caused it. Fortunato’s address to the electors of Melfi in March 1897, delivered in the Nineteenth Legislature after the disaster and the fall of Crispi, turned directly upon this point: the country had been brought to grief by a colonial policy of expansion and prestige, and the lesson, in his judgment, was prudence and withdrawal — an Eritrean policy that would hold what could be held and renounce the conquest of the Abyssinian highlands. In his later commemorations of the fallen of Adua, he returns again and again to the same themes of the folly of imperial adventure and the burden it imposed upon the people.
Consequences
Adua fixed the limits of Italian empire in the Horn of Africa for a generation. The colony was saved only by the prompt abandonment of the war against Menelik, and the disaster chastened the colonial enthusiasm that had carried Italy forward in the 1880s and 1890s; the ambitions of the second monarchical period were forced back, and Italian expansion looked elsewhere. For the internal life of the country, the disaster discredited the statesman who had embodied the adventurous and authoritative style of the period, and it gave strength to the liberal, anti-imperial and southern voices — above all giustino-fortunato and the school of the Southern Question — who drew from it the argument that the Italian state should attend to its own misery at home rather than to glory abroad. It would not be until the twentieth century, and the wars of a later age, that Italy returned in force to the African empire that Adua had denied it.

events/battle-of-caporetto-1917.title: The Battle of Caporetto (24 October – 12 November 1917)
events/battle-of-caporetto-1917.content:
The Battle of Caporetto (24 October – 12 November 1917)
24 October – 12 November 1917
The battle of Caporetto (Karfreit), the Austro-German offensive that broke the Italian front on 24 October 1917 and drove the Italian army in a catastrophic retreat from the Isonzo across the Tagliamento to the Piave, before the line was at last arrested in November 1917. The greatest defeat suffered by the Italian army in the war, it cost the loss of the territory won in two years of the Isonzo battles, overthrew the chief of staff luigi-cadorna, and threw Italy into the gravest crisis of the war — the point from which the recovery under armando-diaz would culminate in Vittorio Veneto.
Background
After the Italian offensive of August–September 1917, the eleventh battle of the Isonzo, had carried the Italian line to the very edge of the plain, the Austrian command resolved to end the attrition of the Isonzo by a decisive stroke, and obtained German divisions for a combined Austro-German offensive. The blow was aimed at the junction of the Italian forces in the Julian Alps, in the sector about Caporetto (Karfreit) on the upper Isonzo, where the mountain front was held by troops weakened by the long summer battles. Cadorna, in his official account, describes the dispositions he had prepared to meet an Austro-German attack; but the sector was thin, the autumn of the third year of war had worn the army down, and the command underrated the force about to be flung upon it.
The breakthrough
On 24 October 1917 the Austro-German forces struck at Caporetto. The attack, launched with the overwhelming local superiority that the concentration of German and Austrian divisions supplied, broke through the Italian line at its weakest point; the use of new infiltration tactics and of the storm troops overwhelmed the defenders, and the front gave way in a widening gap. The Italian army, cut off from its bases in the mountains and taken in the flank, fell into confusion. Cadorna’s account, which gives the dispositions and the battle, records how the rupture spread faster than it could be contained: the units in the mountains, their rear turned, were compelled to abandon the positions won at such cost, and the whole front along the Isonzo collapsed. The retreat that followed was as much a rout as a withdrawal, the army streaming westward with the enemy at its heels.
The retreat to the Piave
Cadorna’s narrative traces the retreat stage by stage. Falling back from the Isonzo, the Italian army abandoned the whole of the Friulian plain and sought to rally on the line of the Tagliamento; but the enemy pressed on, crossed the Tagliamento in its turn, and the retreat had to be continued — la ritirata dal Tagliamento alla Piave, the retreat from the Tagliamento to the Piave. Behind the army, the loss of the eastern provinces and of immense stores was total, and the moral blow was even greater than the material. It was in the course of this retreat that the question of French help arose, and Cadorna records the mission of Marshal Foch to Italy in October–November 1917, rebutting the view that Foch came as the adviser and inspirer of the retreat and insisting, on the contrary, that Foch opposed it. The army was finally halted only on the line of the Piave and the Monte Grappa, where the exhausted forces and the torrent of the autumn-swollen river gave a defensible barrier, and where the retreat was at last arrested in November 1917.
Consequences
Caporetto was the greatest disaster in Italian military history up to that time — the loss of a whole frontier, of two years’ conquests, and of a hundred thousand prisoners and enormous material, with the frontier of the war moved from the Isonzo to the Piave within a few weeks. It brought the fall of luigi-cadorna, who was relieved of the command in November 1917 and replaced by armando-diaz; and it threw Italy, its army shattered and its people demoralised, into the gravest internal crisis of the war. Yet the arrest on the Piave proved to be the turning point: the defence of the river line, restored and rearmed by the new command with the help of the Allies, held, and the lesson of Caporetto — the need to husband the army for a decisive battle — shaped the strategy that would end the war. A year later the Italian army, rebuilt, would break the same Austrian front at Vittorio Veneto, and the humiliation of Caporetto would be reversed in the greatest Italian victory of the war.

events/battle-of-custoza-1866.title: Battle of Custoza (24 June 1866)
events/battle-of-custoza-1866.content:
Battle of Custoza (24 June 1866)
June 24, 1866
Background
The Battle of Custoza was the great Italian reverse of the Austro-Prussian War. Italy had entered
the war in April 1866 through the alliance that Otto von Bismarck negotiated with the Kingdom of
Italy, bound by the expectation of winning Venetia from the Habsburgs. When war came in June, the
Italian army advanced into the Venetian provinces against the Austrian forces in Italy, which were
commanded by the Archduke Albrecht, a capable and aggressive Habsburg field commander who had been
given a free hand to defend the Venetian frontier.
The Italian army was under General Alfonso La Marmora, a veteran of the Risorgimento campaigns.
Sybel’s account of the campaign is unsparing about the Italian operational failures: the army was
cumbersome in its movements, uncertain in its purpose, and poorly coordinated across its advancing
columns. The plan of operations called for the Italians to seize the initiative and overwhelm the
smaller Austrian forces in Venetia, but the execution was hesitant and the columns became separated
as they pushed toward the frontier. Against the Archduke Albrecht’s concentrated and aggressive
Austrians, these weaknesses were to prove fatal.
The Battle of 24 June
On 24 June 1866 the two armies met at Custoza, in the hills near the Venetian frontier. The
Austrians, seizing the initiative, fell upon the separated Italian columns and defeated them
piecemeal, striking each in turn before it could be supported. The Archduke Albrecht’s victory was
thorough and well-earned; Sybel records it as a decisive Austrian success that vindicated Austrian
arms in the Italian theatre even while the main war was going badly elsewhere on the map of Europe.
La Marmora’s army was thrown back with heavy losses, and for the moment it could no longer press the
invasion of Venetia. The defeat was a humiliation for the young Italian kingdom, and it exposed the
gulf between Italian national aspirations and Italian military performance. The army that had been
expected to overrun the Venetian provinces was instead routed on the first major encounter of the
war, and the Italian campaign collapsed into passivity.
Aftermath: An Army That Did Nothing
The consequences of Custoza were felt for the rest of the war. Defeated, the Italian army fell back
and did not seriously renew its offensive against the Austrians in Venetia. Sybel later underlined
the point through the mouth of Bismarck: when Italy complained that Prussia had granted Austria a
five-day armistice without consulting her, Bismarck retorted that if Prussian troops rested for five
days, they did no more than the Italian army had done for weeks after Custoza. The barb was sharp
and it was deserved; Italy had entered the war expecting to win Venetia cheaply, and instead had
been beaten in the field.
The failure fed a lasting bitterness within Italy. The Italian command had promised a swift victory
over the Austrians and had delivered a defeat, and the contrast with the Prussian triumphs in
Bohemia was galling. National pride, wounded at Custoza, would be wounded again a month later at sea
off Lissa, and the double reverse left an enduring scar on the self-image of the new kingdom.
Consequences
Custoza did not, in the end, deny Italy its prize. The great Prussian victories in Bohemia —
culminating at Königgrätz on 3 July — decided the war on the northern front, and Austria, crushed by
Prussia, was in no position to hold Venetia against Italy in the south. Italy occupied the province
“without a struggle,” as Sybel put it, crossing its frontiers once Prussia had won, and the peace
settlement that followed the war ceded Venetia to Italy. In the final distribution of territory,
Custoza proved a defeat without consequences.
Yet the memory of Custoza outlasted the war. The Risorgimento, which had reached its greatest
heights under the leadership of Victor Emmanuel II and the patriots who had united Italy, now
carried the stain of a major military humiliation at the very moment the kingdom seemed about to
complete its work. The defeat sharpened the discontent with the performance of Italian arms that
would colour the country’s politics for decades, and it fed the irredentist resentment against an
Austria that, though beaten by Prussia, had twice beaten Italy in the field and on the water.
Sources

events/battle-of-galicia-1914.title: The Battle of Galicia (1914)
events/battle-of-galicia-1914.content:
The Battle of Galicia (1914)
August – September 1914
The opening campaign of the Austro-Hungarian army against Russia in the first months of the world war: the great battles of Krasnik, Komarów and Lemberg–Rawa Ruska, fought in the plains of Galicia, which ended in the defeat of the Monarchy’s forces, the loss of Lemberg, and the retreat to the Carpathians. It was the military catastrophe that the military-dictatorship-conrad of the chief of the general staff had both predicted and laboured to forestall, and it shaped the whole eastern war. In his own account, the campaign was the first fruit of the july-crisis-1914 and the test of the war-plans-1914 agreed with Germany.
Background: the two-front deployment
The July crisis committed the Monarchy at once to war with Serbia and with Russia. Under Conrad’s direction the concentration against Russia was prepared in Galicia: the 1st Army at Niemirow–Sieniawa with parts at the lower San, the 4th Army about Lemberg, the 3rd Army about Zloczów and Zborów, the 2nd Army along the Strypa and south of the Dniester, with eleven cavalry divisions on the frontier. Of the forty infantry and eleven cavalry divisions mobilised against Russia, the whole weight was flung into the Galician theatre, while only a fraction — eight infantry divisions and some brigades — was left to the Serbian and Montenegrin front.
Conrad’s plan was offensive from the first. The 1st and 4th Armies were to advance east between the Bug and the Vistula to win freedom of manoeuvre and a tactical success, while the 3rd and 2nd Armies met the enemy coming from the Rovno–Dubno region and across the Zbrucz. He held to the offensive as the only way to break the enemy’s plans and not be crushed by numbers — a defensive stand, he was convinced, would lead to catastrophe against an enemy of Russia’s strength. The plan rested on the expectation of the German advance in East Prussia and on the support of Italy and Rumania; both supports were already doubtful. Conrad had never trusted Italy, and he scarcely hoped for Rumania, even reckoning with its hostility.
The battles: Krasnik and Komarów
The opening battles in the north-west of Galicia went in the Monarchy’s favour. At Krasnik and Komarów the Austro-Hungarian armies, attacking with assembled forces, beat the Russian armies opposed to them and won the tactical successes Conrad had sought. These victories, won against a brave and energetically led enemy, are among the episodes Conrad’s closing word recalls with pride, as a monument to the valour of the old k. u. k. army. But they were local triumphs on the right of the line; the decisive struggle lay farther east, about Lemberg, where the balance of the campaign turned.
The struggle about Lemberg and the loss of the city
The decisive action was fought by the two southern Russian armies under the generals Roussky and Brusilov, whom Recouly calls the two best generals of the Russian army — the one cold, severe, a professor’s air behind his spectacles, a stratagemist who knew how to command and be feared; the other an ardent, impetuous cavalry general who carried audacity into all ranks. This immense Russian offensive against the Austro-Hungarian armies was conducted with skill and at the same time with fury; borne on by the consciousness of superiority, the Russians attacked everywhere with vigour. The campaign became a great battle of encounter — Recouly dates the battle of Lemberg from 25 August to 15 September.
The Russians had the advantage not only in numbers but in the cohesion of the Monarchy’s polyglot army. Recouly observes the cracks already sounding in the Austrian army, the faithful image of the crumbling empire it served: while the Hungarians and some of the German-Austrian elements fought well, everything Slav fought without conviction, some not far from wishing for the defeat that would mean their liberation; whole regiments went over to the enemy. In the battle about Lemberg the Austro-Hungarian forces, though they held out to the utmost, were beaten. Lemberg, the capital of Galicia, fell to the Russians; Przemysl was invested; the army abandoned four hundred guns and a hundred thousand prisoners and withdrew upon the Carpathians, while Russian detachments, crossing the passes, came into view of the vast Hungarian plain.
Consequences: the collapse of the agreed first action
The defeat in Galicia was, in Conrad’s own judgment, the decisive event of the war’s beginning. In the preface to his fourth volume he wrote that the decision of the whole war lay in the failure of the plan agreed with Germany for the decisive first action; what followed was only a stubborn struggle to make good the consequences of that failure, and it failed before the superiority of the enemies and the failure of the means. The defeat on the Marne in the west, coming in the same month, was the signal for Italy, Rumania and the other opponents of Germany and Austria-Hungary to seek the Entente, giving the enemy side an overwhelming superiority.
For the Monarchy the loss of Galicia meant the loss of its one great ally’s confidence. Recouly notes that Germany was obliged to come quickly to the rescue of Austria, to prop its tottering ally — condemned, he writes, to carry Austria “literally at arm’s length” for the four years of the war. From the autumn of 1914 the eastern war became a struggle fought largely with German support on Austrian soil, and the defeat of Galicia was the first of the disasters that would bring the Dual Monarchy to treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918 and to its dissolution. The battle thus marks, in the military history of the period, the collapse of the Habsburg power in the east at the very opening of the war.
