events/battle-of-koniggratz-1866.title: Battle of Königgrätz (3 July 1866)
events/battle-of-koniggratz-1866.content:
Battle of Königgrätz (3 July 1866)
July 3, 1866
Background
The Battle of Königgrätz — known to the Austrians and to much of Europe as Sadowa, after the village
near the battlefield — was the decisive engagement of the Bohemian campaign and of the Austro-
Prussian War as a whole. Its prelude lay in the concentration of forces on either side through June
1866. Austria’s Northern Army, under Feldzeugmeister Ludwig von Benedek, had gathered at Olmütz;
Sybel’s account stresses the command controversies, organisational problems, and logistical
deficiencies that hampered it from the start. Benedek’s army was large and veteran, hardened in the
Italian wars, but it was badly served from the top and crippled by uncertain direction and a
defensive-minded plan.
Prussia, by contrast, was served by a general staff whose plan was precise and audacious. The
Prussian forces crossed into Bohemia in three separate columns: the Elbe Army under Herwarth von
Bittenfeld, the First Army under Prince Friedrich Karl, and the Second Army under Crown Prince
Friedrich Wilhelm, heir to the throne of King Wilhelm I. The design of Helmut von Moltke, the
Prussian chief of staff, was that these three columns, advancing on divergent roads, should be drawn
together by a common objective and unite on the battlefield rather than in a preliminary manoeuvre.
The plan was risk-laden — the columns marched separately and might have been beaten in detail before
they could join — but it was vindicated at Königgrätz.
The Advance into Bohemia
The road to the decisive battle ran through a series of preliminary engagements. The Prussians
pushed into Bohemia and met the Austrians and their allied Saxon and south German contingents at
Münchengrätz and then at Gitschin (Jičín). These actions, as Sybel recounts them, cleared the way
for the Prussian concentration and forced the Austrians back toward the fortress line along the
Elbe. Benedek’s army, already wracked by the command controversies of the preceding weeks, fell back
in some confusion, while the three Prussian columns, still separated, pressed forward on a
converging course.
By the beginning of July Moltke’s concentration was nearly complete. The Elbe and First Armies had
joined on the Prussian left, and the Crown Prince’s Second Army was approaching from the northeast.
Benedek, choosing to give battle rather than retreat further, drew up his army before the fortress
of Königgrätz, near the village of Sadowa, with the little Bistritz stream in his front and the Elbe
at his back. The position was strong defensively but offered no easy line of retreat, and it
committed the Austrians to a decisive stand on ground of Benedek’s own choosing.
The Battle of 3 July
On the morning of 3 July 1866 the Prussian First and Elbe Armies opened the battle, crossing the
Bistritz and pressing against the Austrian centre and left. The fighting was heavy, and for much of
the day the Prussian attacks made only halting progress against the Austrian artillery and infantry
fire. The day hung in the balance. Moltke’s whole conception depended on the arrival of the Crown
Prince’s Second Army on the Austrian flank, and the longer the battle continued without it, the more
precarious the Prussian position became.
The arrival came at last, and it decided the day. The Second Army fell upon the Austrian right and
flank with crushing force, and Benedek’s position collapsed under the converging pressure of two
fronts. The Austrian army was not annihilated — Benedek managed to extricate much of it across the
Elbe, sacrificing his rearguards to save the rest — but it was decisively beaten and could not
resume the campaign. The Prussians took tens of thousands of prisoners, along with guns and colours,
and the field was theirs.
The Needle-Gun and the Reasons for Victory
The Prussian victory was owed in no small part to the needle-gun (Zündnadelgewehr), the Prussian
breech-loading rifle that could be loaded and fired lying down, and far more rapidly than the
Austrian muzzle-loaders. Sybel gives the weapon a central place in his tactical analysis of the day.
The Austrian infantry, still firing the older rifled muskets in the slow manner of the muzzle-
loading age, was mown down as it advanced or held in place, while the Prussian infantry poured out a
far heavier and more continuous fire. The needle-gun was not the only cause of the victory, but it
was the technological edge that turned a hard-fought day into a rout.
Consequences
Königgrätz decided the war. Vienna at once sought an armistice, and the road lay open to the
negotiations that produced the preliminary Peace of Nikolsburg and, in August, the definitive Peace
of Prague. The victory transformed Prussia’s standing in Germany: with the Confederation’s leading
military power humbled, Prussia could annex Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, and Frankfurt and proceed
to found the North German Confederation under its own leadership.
For Europe, Sadowa was a shock. It announced a new great power at the heart of the continent and
redrew the map of Germany within weeks. France in particular was alarmed at the sudden consolidation
of Prussian power on its eastern frontier, and the humiliation of 1866 rankled in Paris — a
resentment that fed directly into the crisis and war of 1870. The way was prepared for the ultimate
reckoning with France, and for the proclamation of the German Empire four years after the guns fell
silent at Königgrätz.
Sources

events/battle-of-lissa-1866.title: Battle of Lissa (20 July 1866)
events/battle-of-lissa-1866.content:
Battle of Lissa (20 July 1866)
July 20, 1866
Background
The Battle of Lissa — named for the island in the Adriatic off the Dalmatian coast, rendered by the
Austrians as Lissa — was the one significant naval engagement of the Austro-Prussian War, and it
was an Austrian triumph. It came about because the Italian campaign, after the defeat at Custoza on
24 June, had settled into stalemate on land. With the army unable to make headway against the
Austrians in Venetia, the Italians turned to the sea, where their ironclad fleet was expected to
bring Austria to heel and to carry Italian ambitions across the Adriatic against the Dalmatian and
Istrian coasts that Italy coveted.
The opposing admirals were men whom Sybel judged to be of a kind: the Italian Admiral Carlo di
Persano and the Austrian Admiral Wilhelm von Tegetthoff are described as “völlig gleichwerthige und
geistesverwandte” — entirely equivalent and kindred spirits. Both commanded fleets built around the
new ironclad warships, the armoured steamers that had made the wooden navies of the sailing age
obsolete. Lissa would be one of the first great fleet actions of the ironclad age, a test of whether
the armoured ship had changed the nature of naval combat — and of whether the new machines could be
handled with the daring of the old.
The Fleets and the Setting
The Italian fleet, numerically superior and strongly armed with ironclads, was engaged in operations
off the island of Lissa in mid-July, bombarding the Austrian garrison and preparing an assault on
the island’s fortress. Persano’s fleet lay at anchor or in loose formation off the heights before
Lissa, intent on its siege. Tegetthoff, at the head of the Austrian fleet, resolved to break up the
Italian operations and came down upon them with a plan of the simplest aggression: to close at
speed, ram the enemy line, and throw the Italians into disorder at close quarters.
The two forces were products of a transition in naval warfare. Wooden ships-of-the-line were giving
way to armoured steamers, and Lissa was one of the first battles in which these ironclads fought a
major fleet action against one another. Ramming, which had been a forgotten art in the age of sail,
was revived as the ironclads’ chief offensive weapon, for the armoured ships had no turrets capable
of bringing heavy fire to bear ahead and astern. The battle would therefore be decided in the close,
crashing mêlée of hull against hull.
The Battle of 20 July
On 20 July 1866 Tegetthoff’s fleet came upon the Italians on the heights before Lissa, where Persano
was still engaged in the siege of the island. Tegetthoff did not hesitate: he launched a kräftigen
Angriff — a vigorous attack — falling upon the Italians with his armoured squadron in a wedge
formation that broke into their line. Sybel records the result as a thorough defeat for Persano, who
was “gründlich geschlagen” (“thoroughly beaten”).
The Austrians rammed and broke the Italian line, sinking the ironclad Re d’Italia, which went down
with great loss of life, and disabling other Italian vessels; Persano’s fleet was thrown into
confusion and compelled to withdraw. The victory was won against a numerically and materially
formidable enemy, and it was achieved by the sheer aggression of the Austrian attack and the
superior handling of the Austrian ironclads. Lissa was a stunning demonstration that Austrian arms,
humbled on land at Königgrätz a fortnight before, could still prevail at sea.
A Victory Without Fruits
Lissa entrenched the Austrian reputation as the premier naval power of the Adriatic and established
Tegetthoff as one of the most celebrated admirals of his generation. It was the first great fleet
action of the ironclad age and set the pattern for the close-quarters, ramming tactics that would
characterise armoured naval combat in the decades that followed. For the Austrians it was a point of
pride in an otherwise disastrous year.
Yet, like Custoza, Lissa had no ultimate effect on the distribution of territory. Austria, crushed
by Prussia on land, was forced to cede Venetia to Italy in the peace, and the Adriatic settlements
were not altered by Tegetthoff’s triumph at sea. Italy, though beaten twice, still received Venetia,
and the fleet’s humiliation changed nothing in the final terms.
Consequences
The battle’s significance lay rather in what it signified for the future. It fixed the ironclad as
the decisive instrument of naval war, and the revival of ramming tactics that it demonstrated would
shape the construction and doctrine of the world’s navies until the battleship and the torpedo came
to dominate. The Austrian victory at Lissa was studied by every naval power in Europe.
For Italy, the double reverse of Custoza and Lissa left a lasting scar on military and naval pride.
The navy that was meant to complete the work of the Risorgimento by extending Italian power across
the Adriatic had instead been driven off in confusion, and the resentment rankled. The defeats
sharpened the discontent with the performance of Italian arms that would colour the country’s
politics for decades, and fed the irredentist longing for the lands Austria still held — a longing
that would one day draw Italy back into war against the Habsburg monarchy.
Sources

events/battle-of-mentana-1867.title: The Battle of Mentana (3 November 1867)
events/battle-of-mentana-1867.content:
The Battle of Mentana (3 November 1867)
3 November 1867
The battle of Mentana on 3 November 1867, in which the Garibaldian volunteers marching on Rome were crushed at the gates of the Papal city by the Papal troops and the French reinforcements, equipped with the new chassepots. The defeat ended the last great revolutionary attempt to seize Rome by the force of the volunteers, and it demonstrated once more that the Roman question could not be solved by the partito d’azione but only, in the event, by the monarchy and the collapse of the French protectorate. It stands in this corpus as the decisive reverse that closed the revolutionary road to Rome, which the annexation of 1870 would then achieve by other means.
Background
Since the establishment of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861, Rome had been the great unfinished business of the risorgimento. The September Convention of 1864 between Italy and France had arranged the withdrawal of the French garrison from Rome while pledging Italy not to attack the Papal territory; but the city and the remnant of the Papal States remained under the Pope, guarded by the Papal army and by the French protection that the convention preserved. The revolutionary democrats, above all the followers of Mazzini, would not wait on diplomacy, and their restless pressure for the seizure of Rome was embodied in the person of giuseppe-garibaldi. The ministry of Urbano Rattazzi, in office from 11 April to 19 October 1867, found itself caught between the republican agitation for the attack and the French guarantee that forbade it.
The march on Rome
In the autumn of 1867 the Garibaldian movement resolved on a new attempt, determined to enter Rome in defiance of the Papal and French power. The Italian government could not sanction the expedition, any more than it had been able to sanction the march of 1862 that ended at Aspromonte; yet the volunteers gathered and advanced toward the Papal frontier, and Garibaldi himself, breaking from the restraint his cautious supporters urged, placed himself at their head. The enterprise was undertaken against the grain of the convention and of the monarchy’s whole policy of awaiting the diplomatic solution. The Papal forces, summoned to defend the Patrimony, went out to meet the intruders, and from the French side reinforcements were hurried to the scene.
The battle
The clash came at Mentana, a small town northeast of Rome, on 3 November 1867. The Papal troops, stiffened by the French reinforcements sent in support of the Pope, fell upon the Garibaldians, and the superiority of their arms told heavily: the French soldiers carried the chassepot, the new breech-loading rifle that had already given the French army its pre-eminence among the powers. The fire of the chassepots broke the thin and ill-armed volunteer columns, which had no answer to a weapon so rapid and so deadly. In Garibaldi’s own retrospective, written in his Memorie, the campaign of Mentana was the disastrous ending of his years of struggle for the city — the attempt to seize Rome crushed at the gates of the Papal capital by the Papal troops and the French reinforcements. The survivors were scattered or taken, and the revolutionary road to Rome was closed.
Consequences
Mentana was a double defeat. Militarily it destroyed the last great volunteer army that the revolutionary Risorgimento could throw against Rome, and it confirmed that the French protection of the Pope was still effective enough, while it lasted, to bar the city. Politically it discredited the revolutionary solution: Oriani, in his account of the last revolutionary revival, places Mentana at the centre of the failure of the partito d’azione and the parliamentary reaction that followed, and it forced the ministry of Rattazzi from office — the Menabrea ministry succeeding it on 27 October 1867, immediately in the wake of the disaster. The lesson of the defeat, that Rome could not be won by the volunteers against France, left the field to the monarchical and diplomatic road, which would be vindicated three years later when the defeat of France withdrew the protector and opened the way to the breach of Porta Pia. For Garibaldi, though he lived to see Rome Italian, the failure at Mentana stood as the last frustration of his revolutionary design upon the city.

events/battle-of-sedan-1870.title: The Battle of Sedan (1870)
events/battle-of-sedan-1870.content:
The Battle of Sedan (1870)
1 September 1870
The decisive battle of the franco-prussian-war-1870-71, fought on 1 September 1870 near the town of Sedan on the Belgian frontier. In it the French army of Châlons was encircled and destroyed, Napoleon III surrendered in person, and the defeat opened the “vacance du pouvoir” that brought down the second-empire-france and made way for the third-republic-france.
Background: Mac-Mahon’s march to relieve Bazaine
After the defeats at battle-of-woerth-1870 and Forbach in early August, the Emperor, Marshal Bazaine and the Army of the Rhine had been shut into Metz, besieged by the German armies. Marshal Mac-Mahon assembled a new army at Châlons to go to its relief. Hanotaux records the fateful decision: a telegram from Marshal Bazaine announcing a sortie toward Montmédy decided Mac-Mahon to march to the northeast and effect his junction. “The union of the two forces would have been formidable,” he writes; “but the Prussian armies gained on Mac-Mahon.” The German march was the faster, and the army of Châlons, instead of joining Bazaine, was driven toward the frontier and “went to be engulfed in the funnel of Sedan,” where the Belgian border closed off retreat on one side and the surrounding heights on the others.
The encirclement of 1 September
At Sedan Mac-Mahon’s army, with the Emperor accompanying it, found itself caught in a pocket hemmed by the Meuse and the Belgian frontier. The German armies closed the ring during the night of 31 August and the morning of 1 September, and the battle that followed was less a battle than a siege. Ollivier, who had left office, records the event from the distance of his memoir-history: the hopelessness of the position, the heroic resistance, and the grim certainty that the whole army would have to await its fate. Hanotaux speaks of the army “écrasée” — crushed — “after a heroic resistance.” Mac-Mahon was wounded and his command passed on; the army, cut off from Bazaine, from Paris and from the south, had no route of escape.
The capitulation of Napoleon III
Seeing that further resistance could only end in useless slaughter, Napoleon III ordered the white flag raised and surrendered in person to the King of Prussia. The capitulation of the emperor and of an entire army was without precedent in the century: never had a reigning sovereign of France been taken on the field. Hanotaux draws the political meaning sharply — “A Sedan, Napoléon III ne rendit pas seulement lui-même prisonnier”: at Sedan Napoleon III did not only make himself prisoner. The whole imperial edifice, which had rested on the glory and the person of the dynasty, was swept away with its sovereign. The capitulation handed the emperor into captivity at Wilhelmshöhe, from which he would pass into English exile.
Consequences: the “vacance du pouvoir” and the fall of the Empire
The news of Sedan reached Paris on 2–3 September; Palikao, president of the council, announced the catastrophe and the captivity of the emperor to the Corps législatif. The defeat created, in Thiers’s phrase which Hanotaux records, a “vacance du pouvoir” — a void of power. The regency conferred on the Empress had delegated only part of the authority, and the sovereign himself was a prisoner; of the assent of all, the catastrophe opened a governmental crisis. On 4 September 1870 the Republic was proclaimed in Paris and a Government of National Defence established, ending the Second Empire. The war, however, went on: Paris would be besieged through the winter, and the peace that followed — the treaty-of-frankfurt-1871 — would exact the loss of Alsace and Lorraine. Sedan thus stands as the hinge of the whole period: the single battle that destroyed a dynasty, created the Third Republic, and made possible the proclamation of the german-empire-proclaimed-1871.

events/battle-of-the-marne-1914.title: The Battle of the Marne (September 1914)
events/battle-of-the-marne-1914.content:
The Battle of the Marne (6–12 September 1914)
6–12 September 1914
The battle on the river Marne, east of Paris, in which the French and British armies stopped the German wheel on the capital and forced the German retreat, ending the German hope of a short war. Recouly calls it the decisive turn: “the skill and sang-froid of the French generalissimo, and the mistakes that excess of confidence made the German generalissimo commit, turned the situation; the battle of the Marne was lost, and at a stroke the German machine was half-dismantled — the war that was to have been short instead embarked on a long duration.” Conrad, from the other side, judged that the defeat on the Marne was the signal for Italy, Rumania and the other opponents of Germany and Austria-Hungary to seek to join the Entente, and thereby an overwhelming superiority came to the enemy side.
Background
The battle grew out of the war-plans-1914 and the opening campaign. The German plan — the Schlieffen plan — had flung the mass of the German army at the French left, through Belgium, intending a great enveloping battle (Vernichtungsschlacht, the battle of annihilation) against the principal adversary while the East was held defensively. The first battles of the frontiers (August 1914) seemed to give the Germans reason for the confidence that had brought them to the edge of Paris. But the German command, in the person of the younger Moltke, was already in difficulty. Recouly describes a command that was “much less a principle of direction than a resultant”: Moltke, directed more than directing, let his army commanders — above all the Crown Prince of Bavaria, “the most egoistical, the most demanding” of them — press their own local triumphs at the expense of the plan of the whole. After the frontier victories the German leaders shouted cries of triumph, mistaking their adversaries for far more beaten than they were.
The German march on Paris
The German right wing, under von Kluck and von Bülow, pursued the retreating French and British toward Paris. Recouly stresses how Moltke, believing wrongly that the main mass of the French armies was massed on his right, shifted the balance of his forces — drawing divisions toward the East and toward the secondary theatre of East Prussia, which his plan had always meant to sacrifice to the principal one. Meanwhile, at the German headquarters, a more precise and reflective vision of the facts succeeded the first exaltation: on 27 August Moltke wrote to his armies that one could not yet say what capacity of resistance the Franco-British army possessed. Kluck and Bülow, set in a temporary and badly borne subordination of one to the other, engaged in frictions and clashes; certain decisions of Bülow, disapproved by Kluck, were executed only grudgingly and with delay. The left wheel that should have closed on Paris instead left a gap between the two armies toward which the Allied counterstroke was directed.
The decision of the French command
On the French side it was joseph-joffre, the generalissimo, who turned the retreat into the counter-offensive. Recouly recounts the decisive days: Joffre, decided to risk all though fully conscious of the enormity of the risk, drove to the château of Vaux-le-Pénil near Melun for a moving interview with the British commander-in-chief, who finally promised his cooperation; Franchet d’Espérey, “a magnificent soldier,” declared himself ready to march; and the last hesitations lifted, Joffre ordered the great battle engaged for 6 September and signed for his troops his “immortal order of the day.” Foch, commanding on the left, was among the principal executants, and it was his maxim — « Une bataille perdue est une bataille qu’on croit perdue » — that Recouly cites to capture the psychological factor that carried the day. The French reserves that had been drawn toward the East were the very forces whose absence, Recouly notes, might have changed the result had they been present behind the German right wing during the battle.
The battle and its consequences
The battle, fought from 6 to 12 September, was a confused and chaotic struggle along the Marne — Recouly compares following it in detail to the hero of La Chartreuse de Parme wandering blind across the plain of Waterloo. Its great lines were simple: the German right wing, checked and threatened on its exposed flank, drew back; the whole German army fell back from the Marne, and the attempt to reach Paris had failed. The consequences were immense. The war that was to have been decided in a few weeks on the western front instead settled into the long struggle; the two sides raced to the sea and entrenched in the trenches that would hold for four years. Conrad’s retrospective gives the strategic meaning of the Marne in the whole war: the decision lay in the failure of the plan agreed between Germany and Austria-Hungary for the decisive first action, and the defeat on the Marne was the signal for Italy and Rumania to seek the Entente. The short war had failed, and the war of attrition had begun.
Key participants

events/battle-of-verdun-1916.title: The Battle of Verdun (February–December 1916)
events/battle-of-verdun-1916.content:
The Battle of Verdun (21 February – 18 December 1916)
21 February – 18 December 1916
The battle of Verdun, the longest battle of the First World War, in which the German army attacked the fortified region on the Meuse and the French army, under philippe-petain, held the fortress that became the symbol of French endurance. Recouly, writing within the frame of 1916, counts the German failure before Verdun as one of the characteristic setbacks of the Central Powers that year — one of “three very hard blows” falling on the German staff, alongside the great Somme offensive and the entry of Romania. The battle’s length and cost bled both armies; its name passed into the language as the type of the war of attrition.
Background
At the beginning of 1916, the third year of the war, the western front had long since settled into the trenches. joseph-joffre, examining the situation from his headquarters at Chantilly “with robust and clear common sense,” confronted the third year of the war on two fronts. The German command, and above all the German chief of staff Falkenhayn, sought a way to break the deadlock by attacking the French army at a point it could not abandon — the fortress of Verdun on the Meuse, held as a matter of national honour. The German calculation was less to take Verdun than to bleed the French army white by forcing it to defend the fortress at any cost. The battle thus opened in February 1916 as a deliberate attempt to bring the war of attrition to its sharpest point.
The defence
The German offensive opened on 21 February 1916 against the Verdun salient. The French defence fell to philippe-petain, who organised the fortress’s defence with the method that made his name — the systematic rotation of divisions, the organisation of the line in depth, and the maintenance of the road by which the defenders were fed and reinforced, the voie sacrée. The defence’s motto, “they shall not pass,” came to sum up the whole resistance. Recouly notes that Pétain later published his own account of the battle, La Bataille de Verdun, which stands among the principal sources on which his synthesis draws. The fighting was ferocious and continuous, the fortress and its surrounding heights the scene of repeated German assaults and French counter-attacks through the spring, summer and autumn of 1916.
The failure of the German plan and its place in 1916
The German attack did not achieve its object. Recouly’s judgment on Falkenhayn and on the German failure before Verdun is explicit: the fortress held, the French army was not destroyed, and the attempt to bleed France white recoiled on the Germans themselves. Recouly places the German failure before Verdun among the setbacks that, with the great Somme offensive which subjected the German armies to “a most disquieting attrition,” on Ludendorff’s own admission, and the entry of Romania into the war on the Allied side, struck the German staff within a few months. The cost of the longest battle of the war was enormous on both sides; by December 1916 the French had won back the ground the Germans had taken, and the front returned more or less to the line from which the battle had begun, with the fortress intact.
Consequences
Verdun’s consequences reached beyond the western front. The attrition of 1916, at Verdun and the Somme, wore down the German army while the Entente gathered new strength; and the very course of the year, in which the German hope of a decisive stroke failed, prepared the strains that would break the German and Austro-Hungarian command in 1917–1918. On the French side, the defence of Verdun made the reputation of philippe-petain and confirmed the place of the fortress in the national memory. The battle, with the Somme and the Romanian entry, marked for Recouly the moment when the Central Powers’ failure of 1916 was such that “yet the disgrace of Joffre and the Russian revolution were to save Germany” — the counterpoint that frames the turn of the war toward the revolution of 1917 and the coming offensives.
Key participants
philippe-petain · joseph-joffre · marshal-foch

events/battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918.title: The Battle of Vittorio Veneto (24 October – 4 November 1918)
events/battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918.content:
The Battle of Vittorio Veneto (24 October – 4 November 1918)
24 October – 4 November 1918
The battle of Vittorio Veneto, the decisive Italian offensive of 24 October to 4 November 1918 that broke the Austro-Hungarian army and ended the war on the Italian front, opening the way for the armistice that ended the whole conflict. Fought under the supreme command of armando-diaz, it reversed the disaster of Caporetto and completed the Italian war aims of irredentism — the recovery of the Trentino, of Trieste and of the Italian lands — a year to the very day after the retreat to the Piave had begun. In the official account of the Italian Comando Supremo it stands as the culmination of the whole Italian war, the revenge for the events of October 1917.
Background
The arrest of the Italian retreat on the Piave in November 1917 had left the front fixed on the river and on Monte Grappa, and the new supreme command under Armando Diaz had rebuilt and rearmed the army in the months that followed. In June 1918 the Austrians made their last great offensive on the Italian front, the battle of the Piave, and were repulsed with heavy loss; the Italian line held, and from that repulse the initiative passed finally to the Italians. The Comando Supremo’s preface sets out the strategic conception: the conviction that the most rapid dissolution of the world conflict would be obtained by putting the Austrian army out of action and so isolating Germany militarily — the concentration of effort against the weaker adversary. The preparation for a decisive offensive, projected and perfected through the summer and autumn of 1918, was now complete.
The offensive
The offensive programme and strategic plan of the battle, as the official account sets them out, aimed at breaking the Austrian front along the Piave and the Asiago highland. On 24 October 1918 — the first anniversary of the Caporetto attack — the Italian army struck. The preparatory action was followed by the forcing of the Piave, the crossing of the river against the enemy’s defence, and the breaking of the enemy front; the collapse of the Grappa front followed, and the Italian forces, pouring through the ruptured line, reached the Livenza and beyond. On the Asiago highland the attack carried the high country that had threatened the Italian flank since the beginning of the war. The Austrian army, which had held the Isonzo and the Carso for three years, broke at last; the pursuit swept the Italians forward in the recovery of the highlands and the advance upon the Trentino.
Trento, Trieste and the armistice
The pursuit carried the Italian forces to their war aims. The occupation of Trento delivered the Trentino into Italian hands, and a landing at Trieste raised the Italian flag over the Adriatic city that irredentism had claimed since the first days of the entry into the war; the cavalry led the pursuit through the defeated enemy’s columns. The Austrian army was annihilated as a fighting force — the official account’s phrase is l’esercito austriaco era così annientato, “the Austrian army was thus annihilated.” With its principal ally out of the war, Germany was forced to ask for an armistice, and on 11 November 1918 operations ceased on all the fronts of the world war. The Italian official account contrasts, pointedly, the Austrian report of October 1917 with the Italian recovery of 1918 — the completion of the revenge, one year after Caporetto.
Consequences
Vittorio Veneto ended the war on the Italian front and, by knocking Austria-Hungary out of the war, hastened the collapse of the Central Powers and the armistice of 11 November 1918. It completed the territorial programme of Italian unification and of irredentism, delivering the Trentino, Trieste and the Julian lands to Italy — the lands for whose recovery Italy had entered the war in 1915 and had suffered the ordeal of the Isonzo and Caporetto. The victory, won by the army that Diaz had rebuilt, crowned the Italian war with success and gave the young kingdom a place among the victor powers of the peace; and the Comando Supremo’s closing tribute — the “glorious list” honouring the infantry, the artillery, the engineers and the aeronautics — celebrated the authors of a victory that stood, in the Italian memory, as the redemption of the war.
Key participants
armando-diaz · luigi-cadorna · victor-emmanuel-ii

events/battle-of-woerth-1870.title: The Battle of Wörth (1870)
events/battle-of-woerth-1870.content:
The Battle of Wörth (1870)
6 August 1870
The defeat of Marshal Mac-Mahon’s French army at Wörth — called by the French also Frœschwiller or Reichshoffen — on 6 August 1870, the second great engagement of the opening days of the franco-prussian-war-1870-71. Fought in Alsace two days after the action at Wissembourg, it broke the French right wing, opened the road into Lorraine and, together with the simultaneous defeat at Forbach, decided the first act of the war in favour of Prussia and the German armies.
Background: the invasion of Alsace
War had been declared in July 1870, and the German armies, mobilised on the machinery of the north-german-confederation and its military conventions with the southern states, had crossed the Rhine into France within days. The French forces, divided into two great bodies, had taken position to receive them: on the left Marshal Bazaine about Metz, and on the right Marshal Mac-Mahon in Alsace, with his headquarters at Strasbourg. Ollivier’s account of the campaign records the dispositions of these first days — how Mac-Mahon, his army extended about the northern frontier, hurried reinforcements toward the line of the Wissembourg positions, where the division of General Abel Douay was posted, and how the German advance fell upon it. On 4 August the action at Wissembourg gave the Germans their first victory of the war and left the French position in Alsace uncovered.
The battle of 6 August
Two days later the collision came in full. Mac-Mahon had drawn his army up to meet the German advance, and the two forces met on the field of Wörth on the heights of Frœschwiller. The French held their ground with the tenacity for which Ollivier’s sources give them credit, and the battle was among the severest of the opening campaign — an engagement in which the Marshal himself was wounded and his army, pressed in front and turned upon its flanks, was at length broken. The issue was a decisive Prussian and German victory. Sybel, writing from the German side, records the battle and its aftermath in the phrase that passed from hand to hand — the “dissolved flight of Wörth,” the rout of Mac-Mahon’s army in disorder across the field. The defeat was total: the corps of the French right was shattered, and Mac-Mahon’s army, no longer able to hold Alsace, fell back in retreat, abandoning the province to the invader.
The consequences of the defeat
The effect of Wörth reached far beyond the field. It completed, in the first week of the war, the destruction of the French line in the east: Mac-Mahon’s army, driven out of Alsace, could no longer join hands with Bazaine’s army in Lorraine, and the German advance into the heart of France was left open. The news of the double defeat of 6 August — Wörth and Forbach on the same day — fell upon France as a calamity. Sybel’s narrative shows how the intelligence of the “Schlacht von Wörth” reverberated through the courts of Europe: it reached the King of Italy, victor-emmanuel-ii, in the night of 6–7 August and finally resolved his hesitation over the alliance with France, convincing him that the French had no generals and that nothing was to be done for the Emperor; the September Convention, the compact that had bound Italy to France, was thereby rendered void, and the road to Rome lay open. Within France the defeat of Mac-Mahon threw the government into crisis and set the stage for the disasters that followed — the fall of the second-empire-france and, two days after Sedan, the collapse of the imperial régime in the battle-of-sedan-1870.

events/bosnian-annexation-crisis-1908.title: The Bosnian Annexation Crisis (1908–1909)
events/bosnian-annexation-crisis-1908.content:
The Bosnian Annexation Crisis (1908–1909)
5–6 October 1908 – spring 1909
The annexation crisis of 1908–09 was the greatest international storm of the Habsburg monarchy’s Balkan policy in the decade before the First World War. On 5–6 October 1908 the foreign minister Count Aehrenthal announced the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, tearing up Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin that had left the two provinces under the nominal sovereignty of the Sultan; the stroke threw Serbia and Montenegro into fury, brought Austria-Hungary and Russia to the brink, and was resolved only when the monarchy, backed by Germany, compelled the powers to accept the accomplished fact. The crisis was the sharpest manifestation of the monarchy’s new assertiveness in the East and the immediate predecessor of the Balkan wars.
Background: the thirty-year ambiguity
Since the occupation of 1878, Austria-Hungary had administered Bosnia-Herzegovina under the mandate of the Congress of Berlin, but the two provinces remained legally under the sovereignty of the Ottoman Sultan, and the occupation had been declared provisional. Thirty years of administration had built the monarchy’s position in the country and bought, as the annexation proclamation was to put it, successes bought with heavy sacrifices; but the legal ambiguity stood in the way of the constitutional institutions that the country’s needs demanded. In the years before 1908 the projected railway through the Sandjak of Novi Pazar — the Sandschakbahn — and the reform questions had kept the Eastern Question alive, and the ground of the Eastern Question was everywhere contested. It was Aehrenthal’s design to end the ambiguity by a bold stroke: to annex the provinces outright, secure their legal standing, and stake the monarchy’s prestige on the acceptance of the act by the powers.
The act of annexation
The annexation was proclaimed on 6 October 1908 — a day, Sosnosky notes, of ominous association in Austrian history, since it was the date of the murder of Field Marshal Count Latour by the Viennese mob in 1848. The Kaiser’s hand-written letter to Aehrenthal, dated at Budapest on 5 October 1908, declared that the cultural and political purposes for which the monarchy had undertaken the occupation and administration of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the successes bought with heavy sacrifices, could be durably secured only by the granting of constitutional institutions, for whose enactment the creation of a clear and unambiguous legal standing of the two lands was the indispensable prerequisite; he therefore extended the rights of his sovereignty over Bosnia and the Herzegovina, set the succession order in force for them, and, in token of his peaceful intentions, ordered the evacuation of the Sandjak of Novi Pazar. A proclamation to the inhabitants followed, promising constitutional institutions and a voice in the decisions over the affairs of their homeland. The formal announcement appeared in the Wiener Zeitung of 7 October, while the daily papers printed the text in their morning editions of the preceding day.
The international crisis
The reaction was immediate and violent. In Belgrade the extra sheet of the Politika announced the annexation, and the Serbian foreign ministry, as Conrad recorded from his post on the general staff, demanded immediate mobilisation and war to the death against the monarchy. That mood, Conrad insisted, was not first called forth by the annexation question but was the permanent keynote, breaking out spontaneously at the least occasion. Russia, humiliated by the sudden reversal of the arrangements it had helped prepare, protested; England, France and Italy took up the cry against the violation of the Berlin treaty; and the monarchy stood almost alone against the European concert, its only sure support being Germany.
The crisis developed through the autumn and winter of 1908 into the spring of 1909. The monarchy, having asserted the annexation, refused to retreat; the powers demanded a European conference that Aehrenthal refused to attend on terms that would reopen the annexation; and the tension mounted until the brink of war between Austria-Hungary and Serbia, with Russia behind Serbia, was reached. The military preparations of the monarchy for 1909 were completed, the war-case against Serbia was studied on the general staff, and Conrad, who had all along urged a preventive war, saw the moment approach for which he had prepared.
The settlement
The crisis was resolved in the spring of 1909 when Germany threw its weight decisively behind the monarchy. Backed by Berlin — a support that belonged to the working of the alliance — Austria-Hungary compelled the powers to accept the annexation as an accomplished fact, and Russia, unwilling to face a war it could not win, counselled Serbia to yield. Serbia was forced to abandon its demand for the restoration of the status quo, the European conference was dropped, and the annexation stood. The monarchy’s assertiveness had triumphed; but the settlement left Serbia embittered and unreconciled, and the Russo-Serbian humiliation of 1909 became a permanent memory that poisoned the relations of the powers down to the catastrophe of 1914.
The crisis was not confined to foreign affairs. At home it produced the Friedjung trial, in which the historian Dr. Heinrich Friedjung, who had used documents supplied from Aehrenthal’s circle in an attack on the South-Slav leaders, was confronted with the proof that they were forgeries, and the libel proceedings that followed exposed the falsity of the material and damaged the moral standing of the annexationist cause. The crisis also completed the rupture between Aehrenthal and Conrad, who had pressed for war against Serbia and regarded the peaceable settlement as a wasted opportunity — a divergence that was to end in Conrad’s dismissal in 1911 and his reinstatement in 1912, when the Balkan wars vindicated, in his eyes, his warnings.
Consequences
The annexation crisis redrew the political map of the monarchy’s relations. It destroyed the Austro-Russian understanding in the Balkans and pushed the monarchy into almost complete dependence on Germany; it left Serbia, Russia’s protégé, humiliated and determined on revenge; and it showed how far the powers would go to preserve the Berlin settlement — a settlement the monarchy itself had now torn up. The crisis was the direct predecessor of the Balkan wars of 1912–13, in which the Balkan states, no longer restrained, fell upon Turkey and redrew the peninsula, and it set the stage for the Sarajevo assassination of 1914 and the world war. The road from the annexation to Sarajevo runs through the whole of the remaining history of the period, and the crisis stands as the moment when the monarchy committed its fortunes to the Balkans.

events/boulanger-crisis-1886-89.title: Boulanger Crisis (1886–1889)
events/boulanger-crisis-1886-89.content:
Boulanger Crisis (1886–1889)
1886–1889
The Boulanger crisis was a wave of populist, militarist agitation around General Georges Boulanger that threatened the parliamentary Republic in the later 1880s before collapsing. This corpus’s assigned sources treat it only at the edges — the volumes of Hanotaux’s history end at the death of Gambetta in 1882, before the movement reached its height — and the event is here recorded lightly, as the crisis of the maturing Republic that Grévy’s resignation closed.
Background
The Republic that entered the 1880s had passed through its founding “heroic age” and settled into parliamentary routine. Gambetta’s death in 1882, followed by the fall of Ferry’s ministry, closed the generation of the founders and left the regime to the play of shifting parliamentary majorities. Hanotaux’s fourth volume suspends the narrative at Gambetta’s death, treating it as a brutal conclusion after which “figures and the aspect of things change.” Into this unsettled scene — a Republic of ministries rising and falling, of opportunist governments without a commanding leader — the Boulanger agitation erupted as a challenge to the parliamentary system itself.
Narrative
The sources available here do not trace the movement’s rise in detail. What they establish is that the agitation came to a head in the later 1880s, that it was bound up with the political storms and scandals of the era, and that it forced the resignation of President Jules Grévy in 1887 — the victim, as the record of his presidency puts it, of “the corruption affair that touched his entourage and of the political storms of the Boulanger era.” The movement combined a glorification of the army and of national revenge with a populist appeal to the discontents of the parliamentary regime, and it momentarily seemed capable of overturning the Republic.
Consequences
The crisis passed. The Republic withstood the Boulanger agitation, and the regime’s consolidation survived the collapse of the movement. Grévy’s departure, coming after the death of Gambetta and the fall of Ferry, closed the generation of the founders: the parliamentary Republic had shown that it could survive without a powerful president, and the presidency had been correspondingly weakened. The Boulanger episode belongs to the class of crises by which the maturing Third Republic tested and hardened its parliamentary institutions before the moral-political ordeal of the Dreyfus affair that followed in the next decade.
Key participants

jules-grevy — President forced to resign in 1887 amid the corruption affair and the Boulanger-era storms
General Georges Boulanger — the minister and agitator around whom the movement gathered (not separately documented in this corpus’s sources)

events/brusilov-offensive-1916.title: The Brusilov Offensive (June–September 1916)
events/brusilov-offensive-1916.content:
The Brusilov Offensive (4 June – September 1916)
4 June – September 1916
The great Russian offensive in Galicia in the summer of 1916, launched by the Russian general Brusilov, which broke through the Austro-Hungarian front, captured hundreds of thousands of prisoners, and reduced the Austro-Hungarian army to dependence on its German ally. Recouly calls it “the last flaring-up of the energy, of the military force of the Russians”: after it the Russian front was to fall asleep, awaiting its collapse. In this corpus’s frame the offensive is the decisive demonstration both of Russia’s power and of the fundamental weakness of the Austro-Hungarian army that the war had exposed.
Background
The offensive of 1916 grew out of the Allied plan concerted at Joffre’s headquarters, which bound the Allies to attack the Central Powers as soon as they were ready. The Austro-Hungarian army had opened a great offensive against Italy in May 1916 — the attack between the Val Sugana and the Lake of Garda, on a front of about forty kilometres, which drove about ten kilometres into the Italian line before the Italians, clinging to the last mountain spurs, made their situation critical. The Italian high command therefore asked to be relieved by a Russian offensive. It was planned by the inter-Allied plan; the Russian attack, begun on 4 June in Galicia, preceded it by some ten days.
The offensive
Recouly’s account is compact and vivid. Brusilov — “the most enterprising, the most mordant of their generals” — launched on 4 June in Galicia four armies that struck against four Austro-Hungarian armies and one German army. The offensive developed with full success through June and July: the Russians captured more than 200,000 prisoners and hundreds of cannons. The zone of attack, between the Pripet and the Rumanian frontier, presented a development of some 500 kilometres. The Russian successes were especially marked on the two wings, where the advance quickly passed fifty kilometres: in the south the battle of Czernowitz won the Bukovina, and in the north the battle of Lutsk carried the Russians through Volhynia, though a German counter-attack halted their advance on that side. Toward the south, on the Austro-Hungarian frontier, the progress continued.
The consequences for Austria-Hungary
The strategic meaning of the offensive lay in what it did to the Austro-Hungarian army. Recouly frames the whole eastern war with the judgment that the German army, even with relatively reduced forces, almost always beat the Russian army, which was clearly inferior in high command, manœuvre, instruction and material — but that the Russian army, in return, “almost always beats, without any difficulty, the Austro-Hungarian army,” over which it affirmed its superiority from the very beginning. The reason, Recouly insists, was national: “only a vigourously organised nation, perfectly united and coherent, can have an excellent army”; Austria was “an empire made of distinct races, of heterogeneous peoples,” not properly a nation. The summer of 1916 brought this weakness to its crisis. The Austrians in peril resigned themselves to accept, or rather to suffer, the unity of command: from that point Hindenburg alone was master over the whole extent of the eastern front, and the Austro-Hungarian army passed into dependence on the German. The unexpected Russian successes, which put Austria in danger again, provoked among the Allies the happiest surprise.
The exhaustion of Russia
Yet the offensive, for all its success, was also the summit of Russian power. Recouly marks it as “the last flaring-up of the energy, of the military force of the Russians.” The enormous losses of the campaign, the strain of a war of three years, and the failing cohesion of the empire’s own institutions left the Russian army exhausted after the summer of 1916; the front was to fall asleep in expectation of its collapse. The offensive thus looks two ways in the story of the war: it wrecked the Austro-Hungarian army and brought the Central Powers to the edge, but it also spent the last great reserve of Russian strength, preparing the collapse that the revolutions of 1917 would complete (see february-revolution-1917 and october-revolution-1917). With the Somme on the western front and the Italian relief, the summer of 1916 was, for Recouly, the moment of the Allied “redressement” — yet the relief of pressure on Italy and the ruin of Austria-Hungary were bought at the price of the Russian army that had delivered the blow.

events/capture-of-rome-1870.title: The Capture of Rome (20 September 1870)
events/capture-of-rome-1870.content:
The Capture of Rome (20 September 1870)
20 September 1870
The breach of Porta Pia and the occupation of Rome by the Italian army on 20 September 1870, which completed the territorial unification of Italy and put an end to the temporal power of the Papacy over the city and the Patrimony of St Peter. The event — the fourth and last act of the risorgimento in the making of the kingdom — dissolved the remaining Papal States into the Kingdom of Italy and made Rome the capital, closing the roman-question as a territorial problem even as it opened a new one between the Italian state and the Holy See.
Background
Since 1861 the city of Rome had stood outside the Kingdom of Italy, the seat of the Pontiff and of the remnant of the temporal dominion that the popes had governed for more than a thousand years. The September Convention of 1864 between Italy and the France of Napoleon III had arranged the transfer of the Italian capital from Turin to Florence and provided for the withdrawal of the French garrison that protected Rome; but the same convention, in the compromise of the day, bound Italy not to attack the Papal territory, and France remained the guarantor of the Pope’s independence. In the years that followed, as Oriani records in his La lotta politica in Italia, the question was for a time resolved within a monarchical frame — the solution that looked to Rome coming by the hand of the monarchy rather than by revolution, as the failure of Mentana in 1867 had made plain. The kingdom waited on the disappearance of the French protectorate.
The fall of the French protectorate
The opportunity came with the franco-prussian-war-1870-71. With the outbreak of war between France and Prussia in July 1870, Napoleon III was obliged to recall the garrison that shielded the Pope, and the French troops guarding Rome were drawn away to the German front. Oriani’s chapter on the taking of Rome is framed precisely as the rivalry of France with Prussia: the end of the temporal power came about through the defeat of its European guarantor. The catastrophe of Sedan in September destroyed the imperial government of the French, and with it the last external support of the Papal state. Italy, long the ally of France by the convention, found its hands freed; the monarchy, in Oriani’s account, hesitated, reluctant to seize the city that its treaty obligations had pledged to leave untouched, yet the collapse of France removed the obstacle.
The breach of Porta Pia
The ministry of Giovanni Lanza and Quintino Sella had come into office on 15 December 1869, charged above all with the settlement of the Roman question. In the second half of September 1870 the Italian army moved upon Rome. On 20 September the artillery opened fire on the walls at the Porta Pia, and the breach was made; Tivaroni’s phrase is of the soldiers battendo sulla breccia di Porta Pia — “beating upon the breach of Porta Pia.” The Papal forces, too weak to resist, laid down their arms after a brief bombardment, and the Italian troops entered the city. The temporal power of the Popes, which had lasted over the centuries of the Papal States, came to an end that day. On 2 October 1870 a plebiscite of the Roman population ratified the annexation, and Victor Emmanuel II entered the city to take possession of his capital.
Consequences
The capture of Rome completed the risorgimento’s territorial programme: Italy was now one state from the Alps to Sicily, with its ancient capital restored to it. The territorial chapter of the roman-question was closed. But the settlement of the Pope’s position in a city now under Italian sovereignty remained, and within months the government addressed it in the law-of-guarantees-1871. The Pope, refusing to accept the loss of his temporal dominion, would withhold his recognition and withdraw from public life in protest. In the same autumn, with Rome taken and Italy at peace, giuseppe-garibaldi — the veteran of the long struggle for the city — turned to the service of the embattled French Republic and led his improvised Army of the Vosges against the Prussians, ending his military career on a foreign field. For Italy, the taking of Rome closed the heroic age of unification and opened the decades of a united kingdom, with the capital fixed at last on the Tiber.

events/congress-of-berlin-1878.title: The Congress of Berlin (1878)
events/congress-of-berlin-1878.content:
The Congress of Berlin (1878)
13 June–13 July 1878
The Congress of Berlin, which sat in the German capital through the summer of 1878, revised the Treaty of San Stefano imposed by Russia on the defeated Ottoman Empire and redrew the map of the Balkan peninsula. Its most fateful provision for this wiki’s story was Article 25, which gave Austria-Hungary the mandate to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina — the legal foundation of the monarchy’s Balkan position and the point of departure for the occupation of 1878 and the annexation crisis of 1908. Presided over by otto-von-bismarck, the Congress is the hinge of the period’s Eastern Question, and its settlement stood as the framework of Balkan politics until the annexation tore it up.
Background: from Reichstadt to the Congress
The Congress was the outcome of the great crisis that followed the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–78. The Habsburg monarchy, whose Balkan policy had since 1866 been shaped by the chancellor gyula-andrassy, had secured its position beforehand by the agreement with Russia at Reichstadt, which had defined the spheres of influence of the two powers in the Balkan lands, and by the diplomacy at Constantinople that followed. Sosnosky traces the whole road from Reichstadt to the Congress — the Austro-Russian rivalry and understanding, Andrássy’s Balkan programme, and the attempts at appeasement — and presents the occupation of Bosnia as the culmination of a policy long prepared.
The monarchy’s claim to Bosnia rested on the condition of the provinces themselves. Under Turkish rule, Sosnosky wrote, Bosnia and Herzegovina lay in a state of anarchy, agrarian misery and confessional hatred; the insurrection that had shaken them, the Sturmboten (the “portents of the storm”), and the failure of the Turkish administration to hold the country together all strengthened the case that the monarchy, as the power responsible for the peace of the eastern frontier, should take the provinces in hand. Andrássy’s Balkan programme envisaged the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the means by which Austria-Hungary would secure its position and prevent a Russian domination of the peninsula.
The Berlin mandate
At the Congress the powers revised the Treaty of San Stefano, cutting down the great Bulgaria it had created and rearranging the settlement in favour of Austria-Hungary and the other interested states. The decisive provision for Austria-Hungary was Article 25 of the Berlin treaty, which declared that the provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be occupied and administered by Austria-Hungary. The Austrian negotiators, under Andrássy, also secured the right to hold the Sandjak of Novi Pazar — the territory lying between Serbia and Montenegro, stretching in a south-eastern direction beyond Mitrovitza — where the Ottoman administration would continue but where Austria-Hungary reserved the right to keep garrisons and to occupy the military and commercial roads, so as to guarantee the freedom and security of the routes and the continuance of the new political state of affairs.
The legal character of the mandate was deliberately provisional, as a last-moment exchange at the Congress made plain. On the morning of 13 July 1878, the day the Congress was to be closed after exactly a month’s duration, the Turkish representatives appeared before the Austrian delegation and repeated their demand that the sovereignty rights of the Sultan over the provinces not be impaired by the fact of the occupation. Andrássy, placed in an extremely difficult position — to sign was to make a concession of great import, not to sign was to put the whole work of the Congress in question — chose the lesser evil and signed a protocol declaring that the sovereignty rights of His Imperial Majesty the Sultan over Bosnia and Herzegovina were in no way to be affected by the fact of the occupation, that the occupation was to be regarded as provisional, and that a preliminary agreement on the details would be concluded immediately after the Congress. This reservation of Turkish sovereignty was the legal ambiguity that the annexation of 1908 was to dissolve.
The consequences
The Congress of Berlin reshaped the Eastern Question and fixed the monarchy’s course in the Balkans. Austria-Hungary received the mandate that led directly to the military occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the late summer of 1878, undertaken with heavy fighting against the insurgent population. The Dual Alliance with Germany and the “insurance policy” of the monarchy followed in the settlement’s wake, as Andrássy and Bismarck bound the two empires together against a Russia that resented the truncation of its San Stefano gains. The Berlin settlement also left Austria-Hungary as the power of the eastern frontier, whose right to occupy and administer Bosnia under a Turkish sovereignty that still formally stood would become, thirty years later, the very issue of the annexation crisis, when Aehrenthal tore up Article 25 to end the ambiguity. The Congress thus stands as the origin of both the monarchy’s greatest Balkan acquisition and of the crisis that set the course toward the catastrophe of 1914.

events/dreyfus-affair-1894-1906.title: Dreyfus Affair (1894–1906)
events/dreyfus-affair-1894-1906.content:
Dreyfus Affair (1894–1906)
1894–1906
The Dreyfus affair was the crisis that convulsed the Third Republic for a decade — the 1894 treason conviction of Captain Alfred Dreyfus, the long campaign to prove his innocence, and the eventual vindication and rehabilitation that divided France between the defenders of the army and the state and the defenders of a single man’s justice. It was the defining moral-political crisis of the Republic, the last surge of the republican mystique in Péguy’s phrase, and the event that reshaped the alignment of French politics, religion, and socialism.
Background
The affair arose from the espionage climate of the 1890s, when France, defeated in 1870, lived in suspicion of Germany and of internal betrayal. Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer of the general staff, was convicted in 1894 of treason — of delivering military secrets to the Germans — by a court-martial on evidence that was, in reality, thin and partly forged. He was degraded and deported to Devil’s Island. For the army and for much of public opinion the verdict was a settled fact; to question it was to question the honour of the institution that embodied the nation.
Narrative
The campaign for revision began almost at once. Péguy, in Notre jeunesse, honours Bernard-Lazare — “born at Nîmes, 14 June 1865; died at Paris, 1 September 1903” — as the prophet of the affair, “the first to defend Dreyfus,” the one whose word he calls “the decisive word of the affair.” Even as some Dreyfusards grumbled at the returned captain’s imperfections, Bernard-Lazare defended him “with that admirable voluntary blindness of those who truly love”: “He is innocent, that is already much.”
The affair was transformed into a national crisis by the intervention of the intellectuals. Émile Zola’s open letter J’accuse (1898) threw the question into the open, accusing the army’s leaders of a judicial crime; his prosecution and conviction turned the Dreyfusards into a movement. The affair divided France into two irreconcilable camps: the anti-Dreyfusards, who held that the honour of the army and the reason of state must not be sacrificed for one man, and the Dreyfusards, who held that “a single injustice, a single crime suffices to break the whole social pact.” The Dreyfusard cause enlisted the new intellectuals and the republican left; the anti-Dreyfusard cause drew together the army, the clerical and nationalist right, and much of the Catholic hierarchy. The passions it unleashed — including anti-Semitic agitation — convulsed French society.
For Péguy, the affair was above all a spiritual event. The Dreyfusards, he writes, spoke “in a deep Christian movement,” refusing that France should be “constituted in a state of mortal sin”; the true division of the affair was between “the men of eternal salvation” and “the men of temporal salvation.” He calls it “the last of the operations of the republican mystique,” the supreme surge of the heroism of his generation. Sabatier, likewise, treats “the true significance of the Dreyfus affair” as one of the keys to the religious orientation of contemporary France. The affair, in this reading, was the moment when the Republic’s conscience was tested — and the moment that redefined what the Republic and its institutions stood for.
Consequences
The affair was resolved by the eventual vindication of Dreyfus. A second court-martial at Rennes in 1899 again found him guilty but with extenuating circumstances, an outcome that satisfied no one and prolonged the struggle; it was only in 1906 that the verdict was finally quashed and Dreyfus fully rehabilitated. By then the affair had permanently reshaped French politics. It discredited the anti-Dreyfusard alliance of army, Church, and nationalist right and delivered a decisive reinforcement to the republican and anticlerical cause — clearing the way for the republican governments that followed to complete the laic programme. For the socialists, as Lagardelle records, the affair and its aftermath tested their relation to the Republic: the ministry of Waldeck-Rousseau, with Millerand as the first socialist minister, marked the entanglement of socialism in parliamentary politics that the syndicalists would denounce.
Péguy’s own conclusion was darker. The affair, he held, had begun in mystique and ended in politique: the Dreyfusard faith degenerated into Dreyfusard calculation, and the party men of both sides turned against those who had fought from conviction. The degradation of the mystique into politique, the triumph of the “modern world” that believes in nothing, and the loss of the republican and Christian faiths in a single movement of “demystification” — these, for Péguy, were the enduring legacy of the affair, which proved to be the last surge of the heroism of his generation.

Bernard-Lazare — the prophet of the affair, first defender of Dreyfus
Émile Zola — author of J’accuse

events/ems-dispatch-1870.title: The Ems Dispatch (1870)
events/ems-dispatch-1870.content:
The Ems Dispatch (1870)
13 July 1870
The telegram sent by King Wilhelm I of Prussia from the spa town of Ems to his chancellor Bismarck on 13 July 1870, and — above all — the shortened, sharpened version in which Bismarck published it. In the French reading of the corpus it is the Emser Depesche as reworked by Bismarck — the soufflet, the “slap in the face” — that transformed a settled incident into an unbearable national insult and precipitated the French declaration of war.
Background: the King at Ems and the Hohenzollern affair
After the withdrawal of the Hohenzollern candidacy on 12 July (see hohenzollern-candidature-1870), the French government, at the Emperor’s prompting, had decided to demand guarantees for the future. The French ambassador Benedetti was sent to the King at Ems, where Wilhelm was taking the waters, to press the demand. In Ollivier’s account the King, a constitutional monarch, would not order Prince Leopold’s renunciation but had sought to obtain it by hint; the French instructions throughout asked only that the withdrawal be secured. Benedetti handled the negotiation at Ems with flexibility, and the King, though irritated at being pressed on his promenade, remained courteous. The demand of guarantees, however, was the work of the French Right, lacking serious grounds, and Ollivier himself advised confining it to the present rather than hardening it for the future.
The King’s refusal and the report to Berlin
On 13 July, after Benedetti’s interview, the King refused to give the guarantees demanded and, in Ollivier’s account, had already resolved to receive the French ambassador no more. The King caused two reports of the interview to be drawn up and sent the official account to Berlin through the councillor Abeken, who was with him at Ems. Ollivier insists that it was not the report of the ambassador Werther, and not any genuine French provocation, that set Bismarck to work — it was the poisoned narrative of Abeken’s telegram, which he says authorises Bismarck’s “perfidious disclosure.” Sybel, writing from the German side, gives the same facts in the national frame: the King’s correct but firm refusal, and the dispatch of the report to the chancellor.
Bismarck’s reworking of the telegram
Bismarck, who had earlier despaired at the renunciation and even offered the King his resignation, now searched in vain in Werther’s report and in the French declaration for a pretext for war, and found it in the telegram from Ems. Ollivier describes how Bismarck reworked Abeken’s dispatch until the falsified telegram became an unbearable outrage for France — a soufflet. The essence of the change was compression: from a fuller account of a polite but firm refusal, Bismarck produced a terse text in which the King was made to declare that he would receive the French ambassador no more and had nothing further to communicate — a form that read as a deliberate rebuff of France. He had the text posted and published. All Germany, in Ollivier’s words, treated war as inevitable from that moment.
The “soufflet” and its effect in Paris
The published dispatch reached Paris and fell upon the French government like a blow. Ollivier, who on the morning of 14 July believed peace secure, learned from Gramont of Bismarck’s soufflet; a council met at the Tuileries, and the ministers, who had been seeking a pacific issue, were confronted with a public insult that could not be borne. In Ollivier’s framing the grievance that finally decided the war was precisely the public outrage of the posted telegram — not Prague, not Luxembourg, not the refusal of future guarantees as such. The demand of guarantees had made war possible; the soufflet made it inevitable. On 15 July 1870 Ollivier read the declaration of war to the Chamber of Deputies, and the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 began.
The controversy over the 13th
The Ems dispatch is at the heart of the historiographical war that the sources preserve. Ollivier argues that historians who make Bismarck innocent of the war diminish him, and that those who restore his premeditation enlarge him; he cites Lorenz, Delbrück, Scherr and others for the responsibility of Bismarck, and attacks the German thesis that Prussia needed no war because France was herself preparing one. He is at pains to correct what he calls the erreur des mémoires d’Abeken sur le 13 juillet — the claim, which he rejects, that Abeken’s account of the 13th exculpates the chancellor or changes the sequence of responsibility. For Ollivier, Bismarck alone organised the Hohenzollern candidacy and falsified the Ems dispatch, and without that falsification there would have been no war. Sybel, by contrast, presents the affair within the Prussian national story as the correct response of the King and the necessary concentration of German energies against France. Between these two, the whole question of the war’s guilt is fought out.

events/expedition-of-the-thousand-1860.title: Expedition of the Thousand (1860)
events/expedition-of-the-thousand-1860.content:
Expedition of the Thousand (1860)
In May 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi and his roughly one thousand volunteers (i Mille) sailed from Genoa and invaded Sicily, conquering the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and handing the South to the nascent Kingdom of Italy. The event is the hinge of Italian unification and is treated in this corpus by Garibaldi’s own Memorie and by the contemporary national histories of Tivaroni and Oriani, which narrate it from Calatafimi to the fall of Gaeta.
From Quarto to Palermo
The expedition began at Quarto near Genoa on 5–6 May 1860, with Garibaldi defying the Piedmontese government’s official disapproval. Landing at Marsala in western Sicily, the Thousand met the Neapolitan army at Calatafimi (15 May), where the outnumbered volunteers broke the royal troops and opened the road to Palermo. The capture of Palermo and the subsequent battles of Milazzo and the Volturno extended the conquest across Sicily and onto the mainland.
The conquest of the South and the fall of Gaeta
The revolutionary momentum carried the Garibaldians through the South; Naples fell almost without resistance as the Bourbon king fled. The campaign ended with the siege of Gaeta, where the last Bourbon resistance was crushed by the Piedmontese regular army under Cialdini — the fusion of the Garibaldian conquest with the Piedmontese state. The whole operation, in Tivaroni’s reading, was the working of the national idea that geography, race, language and custom seemed to indicate.
Annexation and the meeting with Victor Emmanuel
The South voted for annexation to Piedmont by plebiscite; Garibaldi’s famous surrender of his conquest to Victor Emmanuel II at the meeting near Teano (October 1860) subordinated the revolutionary conquest to the monarchy. Cavour and the moderates absorbed the Thousand’s revolution, converting a republican adventure into the territorial base of the unified Kingdom.
Place in the corpus
The expedition is the founding revolutionary event of the unified Italy this wiki covers: it created the Southern question’s map, made Garibaldi the national hero, and set the pattern — revolution in the streets, annexation by the state — that the Kingdom followed through the war of 1866 and the taking of Rome. Its full 1860 detail sits in the 1800–1865 wiki; here it is the remembered foundation of everything from Crispi’s Sicilian pride to the irredentist and southern-question debates that followed.
