events/february-revolution-1917.title: The February Revolution (1917)
events/february-revolution-1917.content:
The February Revolution (1917)
February – March 1917
The fall of the Russian monarchy in the winter of 1917: the disorders of the Petrograd streets, the mutiny of the garrison, the abdication of nicholas-ii, and the establishment of the double authority — двоевластие (“dual power”) — of the Provisional Government and the Soviet of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies. Denikin, writing from the Staff of the Supreme Commander, saw in it the “inevitable historical process” that “led to the collapse of Russian statehood”; no one, he judged, had expected the elemental force to sweep away so quickly the supreme power, the intelligentsia, and the ten-million-strong army.
Background: the collapse of authority
Denikin traced the ruin of the old order to its roots in the preceding decades. The autocracy-russia of the Romanovs rested on “faith, tsar and fatherland,” but the defeat in the russo-japanese-war-1904-05 had left a bitterness among the military youth and a paralysis at the top of the War Ministry and the General Staff. The world war that began in 1914 had then made the state’s frailties mortal. In August 1915 nicholas-ii assumed the supreme command — in Denikin’s judgment under the influence of the Empress’s circles and of grigori-rasputin, over the fruitless representations of eight ministers. From then the sovereign dwelt at Stavka in Mogilev “alone, without family, without intimates,” while the capital slipped into the grip of ministers seen as captives of the Duma and the press.
Zhevakhov, writing from within the Holy Synod, registers the same decomposition from the church’s side. He describes the corruption of the “mechanism” of power at the top, ministers in captivity to the Duma and the newspapers, and the contrast with the still-holding lower police. The murder of grigori-rasputin in December 1916 — the subject of his long excursus — he treats as the break toward catastrophe, the act that removed the last personal support of the imperial family while doing nothing to restore its authority. By the winter of 1916–17 the state presented the paradox of a government that could neither govern nor be changed by ordinary means: the Duma’s speeches, above all Miliukov’s famous attack of 1 November 1916 with its refrain “stupidity or treason,” had exposed the court to the educated public, while the war’s burdens had turned the mass of the people against the regime.
The February days
The collapse came quickly and, to the great majority, unexpectedly. The winter of 1916–17 brought a food crisis to Petrograd: the supply of the capital broke down, the factories stopped, and the queues lengthened in the streets. On 23 February (8 March) strikes and demonstrations, prompted above all by the women’s day and the bread queues, swelled into a general movement; by 26–27 February the garrison, called upon to fire on the crowds, instead refused and went over to them. The government of the aged interior minister Protopopov at first treated the movement as “popular disturbances” to be met by “decisive measures” — machine-guns were readied for Khabalov and a punitive detachment prepared under General Ivanov — but the troops of the capital melted into the revolution. The members of the State Council telegraphed on the night of 28 February of the disruption of transport, the factory stoppages, the food crisis, and the hatred of the government.
Zhevakhov, returned from a journey to the Caucasus on 24 February, records the “first steps of the revolution” — “the next day was still more terrible than the previous.” On 26 February the Holy Synod held its memorable sitting at the very moment of the street’s breaking; on 27 February came the round-ups, “the genuine picture of the revolution”; on 28 February “the triumph of the boor,” as the author calls it, with the cabinet almost in full caught by events. On that day Zhevakhov himself was arrested and confined in the Ministerial Pavilion of the Duma with the other captured dignitaries of the fallen power. He describes the cross-section of the overthrown authority gathered there — ministers, senators, churchmen — and the rising fear of the prisoners as the revolution ran beyond all limits.
The abdication
The fall of the dynasty was sealed at Pskov. The generals and the political leaders alike had concluded that the abdication was inevitable — “in all, a clearly conscious inevitability of abdication.” Through the night the telegraph wires carried the conversations that decided the fate of the country: Ruzsky with Rodzianko and Alekseev, Stavka with the commanders-in-chief, Lukomsky with Danilov. On the morning of 2 March General Ruzsky laid before the sovereign the opinions of Rodzianko, the chairman of the Duma, and of the military commanders; the emperor listened calmly, his face as if frozen, and declared that the act of abdication in favour of his son was already signed, handing over the telegram. He had first hesitated on the report that the Duma delegates Guchkov and Shulgin were coming to Pskov, and then, in the evening, he changed the terms.
Guchkov, arriving among deep silence, drew the picture of the abyss toward which the country was moving and pointed to the only way out — abdication. The sovereign replied that he had made his decision, that he had been ready that afternoon to abdicate in favour of his son, “but then I understood that I am incapable of parting with my son. You will understand that, I hope. Therefore I have decided to abdicate in favour of my brother.” The delegates, taken by surprise, did not protest: Guchkov out of the feelings of a father, unwilling to press the tsar to part with his son, and Shulgin on political grounds, doubting whether a regent could swear fidelity to a constitution on behalf of a minor emperor. Denikin dwelt on the thirty minutes that changed the course of events — a prosaic, everyday episode had altered the fate of the dynasty. The act was signed, and with it the three hundred years of the Romanovs and the whole frame of autocracy-russia came to an end.
Dual power: the Provisional Government and the Soviet
In the place of the monarchy rose a divided authority. The Duma, seeing itself as an institution of the old order, did not formally reconvene; from its committees emerged the Provisional Government, headed by the liberal Prince Lvov, while the Petrograd Soviet of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies, born in the same days in the Tauride Palace, claimed the allegiance of the workers and of the mutinous garrison. Denikin quoted the characterisation of the Duma committee itself: the seizure of the rights of state power by irresponsible organisations, the creation of “dual power in the centre and anarchy in the country.”
The Soviet, through its leading socialists, explicitly declined to take power itself. Its spokesman Tseretelli insisted that the moment had not come for the proletariat, that this was a bourgeois revolution whose final tasks were not yet to be attempted; rather than seize the state, the democratic leaders chose to press the government by constant organised pressure. Yet the Soviet would not relinquish its hold on the army and the workers, and from the first days it exercised a power that overlapped and undercut the government’s. This unresolved contradiction, the двоевластие, defined the whole interval between the fall of the monarchy and the Bolshevik seizure in the autumn: no decree of the Provisional Government could command obedience against the will of the Soviet, and no power of the Soviet could govern the country.
Consequences: the army and the road to October
The most fateful consequence for Denikin, a commander at the front, was the dissolution of the army. The garrison’s mutiny was generalised by Order No. 1 of the Soviet, which subordinated the armed forces to the revolutionary committees and struck a blow at discipline from which the army never recovered. Denikin learned of the events far from the capital, on the Romanian Front where he commanded the 8th Army Corps, “absorbed in its local cares,” preparing a winter offensive. The news of the revolution and the abdication filtered through to men who had not been prepared for such a sudden denouement; “only here and there in the ranks” was the abdication known. Order No. 1, with its committees and its elected authority over the officers, completed what the revolution had begun: the ten-million-strong army dissolved into a debating society, and the front with it.
The Provisional Government, torn between the Soviet and the command, proved unable to restore either authority or supply. By spring the cities and the army were starving — Denikin records the official norms of bread that were never met — and the soldiers’ committees paralysed the officers. Prince Lvov’s government, and then that of alexander-kerensky, wavered between the Allies’ demand for an offensive and the army’s refusal to fight; the “rusty, notched sword,” Denikin wrote, was still swinging, but it could no longer strike. The failure of the promised June offensive and the collapse of the front in the summer would discredit the government and open the way first to the kornilov-affair-1917 and then to the october-revolution-1917. Zhevakhov, released from arrest by Kerensky after the abdication, carried away the verdict of the Synod’s circle — that what had swept the throne away was not so much a revolution as a soldier’s mutiny — but the monarchy was gone beyond recall, and with it the last formal anchor of the old order.

nicholas-ii · alexander-kerensky · mikhail-alexeyev · paul-milyukov · alexandra-feodorovna

events/franco-prussian-war-1870-71.title: The Franco-Prussian War (1870–71)
events/franco-prussian-war-1870-71.content:
The Franco-Prussian War (1870–71)
15 July 1870 – 10 May 1871
The war between the French Empire and the German states under Prussian leadership, opened by the French declaration of 15 July 1870, decided by the defeats of August and the capitulations of Sedan, Metz and Paris, and closed by the treaty-of-frankfurt-1871 of 10 May 1871. It destroyed the second-empire-france, proclaimed the german-empire-proclaimed-1871, and ended with the birth of the third-republic-france under the shadow of defeat.
Background
The war grew out of the hohenzollern-candidature-1870 and the ems-dispatch-1870. France, whose liberal ministry under emile-ollivier had gone to the brink over the Spanish candidacy, declared war on Prussia on 15 July 1870 — in Ollivier’s famous and subsequently condemned phrase, “le cœur léger,” a war he believed forced upon France by Bismarck’s provocation. Hanotaux, writing the national history, gives the deeper cause: the imperial policy of nationalities, which had humiliated Prussia’s neighbours but now confronted Prussia itself, led France into a war for which her army and her diplomacy were unprepared, while Prussia enjoyed the military conventions that had placed the armies of the southern German states under her command.
The opening battles, August 1870
The war opened disastrously for France. On 4 August the Crown Prince’s army beat the French at Wissembourg on the Lauter; on 6 August came the double defeats of battle-of-woerth-1870 in Alsace, where Marshal Mac-Mahon’s army was broken after a heroic resistance, and of Forbach near the Saar, where Frossard’s corps, though not beaten on the field, panicked and fled toward Sarreguemines. Ollivier’s memoir of these days is a study in the confusion of the French command: Mac-Mahon had resolved on a retreat and was drawn back into battle by the cannon; Frossard “constituted himself as beaten”; and the Emperor, whose health had collapsed, lost effective direction of the war. On 9 August the Chamber, turned against his ministry, forced Ollivier’s resignation, and the government passed to General Cousin-Montauban, comte de Palikao.
Sedan and the fall of the Empire
The decisive stroke of the campaign was the encirclement of Mac-Mahon’s army of Châlons, marching to relieve Marshal Bazaine at Metz. At battle-of-sedan-1870 on 1 September 1870 the whole army was caught in the funnel of the Belgian frontier and destroyed; Napoleon III, who had accompanied it, ordered the white flag raised and surrendered in person. Hanotaux stresses the political consequence: at Sedan “Napoleon III did not only make himself prisoner” — the fall of the emperor and of an army opened a void of power, the “vacance du pouvoir,” filled on 4 September by the proclamation of the Republic in Paris. The Empire was finished with its sovereign.
The siege of Paris and the close of the war
The war continued under the Government of National Defence, with Paris besieged from September 1870 and the armies of Bazaine capitulating at Metz in October. Hanotaux records how Paris let itself be reduced to famine, how the ardor of Gambetta in the provinces prolonged a hopeless struggle, and how the armies of the East and the Loire successively collapsed. Paris, reduced to famine, surrendered; its fall, in Hanotaux’s words, was the fall of France. An armistice was concluded, and the nation went to the polls.
The elections, Bordeaux and the peace
The elections of 8 February 1871 — dominated by the great debate of War or Peace, with republicans calling for guerre à outrance and the departments voting for peace — returned a National Assembly that met at Bordeaux and turned to adolphe-thiers, elected in twenty-six departments, as “administrator of the national misfortune” and chief of the executive power. Thiers negotiated the preliminaries of peace with Bismarck at Versailles in February 1871, accepting the loss of Alsace and part of Lorraine while retaining Belfort and reducing the indemnity. The definitive Treaty of Frankfurt of 10 May 1871 fixed the five-milliard indemnity and the occupation schedule (see treaty-of-frankfurt-1871). Even as the peace was being ratified, Paris rose against the Assembly in the paris-commune-1871, crushed by the Versailles army under Mac-Mahon in the Bloody Week of May 1871. The war ended with France dismembered, republican by accident of defeat, and with the German Empire proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871.
Key participants

events/french-constitution-1875.title: Constitution of 1875 (February–July 1875)
events/french-constitution-1875.content:
Constitution of 1875 (February–July 1875)
February – July 1875
The three constitutional laws by which France at last organized the Republic, voted in the spring and summer of 1875 by a National Assembly that had spent four years refusing to choose a form of government. The Constitution of 1875 — the Senate law of 24 February, the law on the organization of the public powers of 25 February, and the law on the relations of the powers of 16 July — was the anonymous, improvised foundation of the third-republic-france, adopted almost by accident, and yet it proved durable for sixty-five years.
Background
Four years after Bordeaux the National Assembly had made peace, repressed the Commune, overthrown Thiers, and voted the septennat-1873, but it still had given no constitution. Its monarchical majority was torn among the three royal houses; the Republic survived by their divisions. After the fall of the duc de Broglie in May 1874 and the failure of the Cissey cabinet, the question of the constitutional organization of the state could no longer be postponed. The republicans, growing with each by-election, demanded the Republic; the right, unable to crown a king, clung to the septennat and to delay.
The Republic voted by one voice
The decisive session came in January 1875. The commission of the Trente, charged with preparing a constitutional project, worked under presidential pressure from the Marshal and the conferences at the Élysée. The debate turned on the form of the executive and the creation of a Senate. In the great sittings of 28–30 January the Assembly rejected the Laboulaye amendment after Louis Blanc’s intervention and then came to the amendment of the deputy Wallon, which proposed that “the President of the Republic is elected by a plurality of the votes of the Senate and of the Chamber of Deputies.” The Wallon amendment, the only one that pronounced the word “Republic,” was carried by a majority of one voice. Hanotaux records the sense of the hour: the Republic had been founded almost by accident, on a single vote, in an Assembly hostile to it. The majority of one voice proved decisive — the monarchy, in effect, was never to return.
The three laws
The consequence of the Wallon vote was the elaboration of the full constitutional settlement. The law on the organization of the Senate was voted (24 February), then the law on the organization of the public powers (25 February), and finally the law on the relations of the public powers (16 July), together with the organic laws on senatorial and legislative elections. The Constitution of 1875 established a President of the Republic, a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies, and a responsible ministry; it created a two-Chamber parliamentary system with a strong presidency — the Marshal, who had hoped for a conservative Senate, retained the power to dissolve the Chamber with the Senate’s consent, and the seat of the powers remained at Versailles. Hanotaux stresses the improvised, unplanned character of the whole: three constitutional laws and two organic laws, viable despite the disdain of many of their authors, a work of equilibrium and transaction.
Consequences
The Constitution of 1875 founded the Republic on the very hesitations of its enemies. The septennat had kept a king possible; the one-vote Republic made it impossible. The new institutions were immediately put to the test: the Senate’s composition, the powers of the president, and the responsibility of the ministry became the ground of the struggle between Mac-Mahon and the republican majority that exploded in the seize-mai-1877 crisis. Yet the settlement held: the parliamentary Republic, once voted, proved stronger than the monarchists who had voted it by accident. The Constitution of 1875 was the durable frame of the Third Republic, surviving until 1940 — the improvised work that the founders themselves had despised.
Sources













SourceTreatmentHanotaux, Tome III (La Constitution de 1875)Full narrative of the session of January 1875, the Wallon amendment and the one-vote majority, the three laws, and the theory and character of the Constitution.

events/german-empire-proclaimed-1871.title: Proclamation of the German Empire (18 January 1871)
events/german-empire-proclaimed-1871.content:
Proclamation of the German Empire (18 January 1871)
18 January 1871
The founding act of the German nation-state: the proclamation of the German Empire in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, in the midst of the siege-of-paris-1870-71, by which the King of Prussia, Wilhelm I, was acclaimed German Emperor and the unification of Germany under Prussian hegemony was announced to the world. The ceremony, staged at the very seat of the defeated French monarchy, sealed the reversal of European power that the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 had effected — a humiliation and a warning to France in a single act.
Background
The war of 1870–71, provoked by the hohenzollern-candidature-1870 and the ems-dispatch-1870, had drawn the South German states to Prussia’s side against France. The victories of the German armies — battle-of-woerth-1870, battle-of-sedan-1870, the capture of Napoleon III — had made the unification of Germany, long debated in the german-question, a practical achievement of the battlefield. The German princes and free cities rallied to the Prussian king; the terms of the new Empire were settled in the conquered territory, with Paris under siege and France prostrate.
The ceremony at Versailles
On 18 January 1871 — the anniversary, significantly, of the coronation of the first King of Prussia — the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the palace of Louis XIV and the emblem of the French monarchy that had once dominated Europe. Hanotaux records the scene as the Germans themselves framed it: the King of Prussia acclaimed German Emperor by the princes, generals, and soldiers of the German armies assembled in the conquered capital’s shadow. The choice of place was deliberate — a declaration that the new Germany inherited the European primacy that France had held since the seventeenth century.
Consequences
The proclamation transformed the European order. Germany, united under Prussian leadership and the crown of Wilhelm I, replaced France as the strongest power of the continent; otto-von-bismarck became the arbiter of Europe. For France the act was a double wound — the loss of pre-eminence and the spectacle of the German Emperor enthroned at Versailles while Paris starved. It fed the demand for peace under adolphe-thiers and the resentment that the treaty-of-frankfurt-1871 would soon make permanent in the form of the ceded provinces. The Empire proclaimed at Versailles on 18 January 1871 would, until its own proclamation in reverse in 1919, stand as the symbol of German unity and German power — and as the answer to the French question of who was now first in Europe.

events/hohenzollern-candidature-1870.title: Hohenzollern Candidature (1870)
events/hohenzollern-candidature-1870.content:
Hohenzollern Candidature (1870)
1 July – 12 July 1870
The offer of the vacant Spanish throne to Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, and the diplomatic crisis it provoked between France and Prussia in the first days of July 1870. It was the match that lit the franco-prussian-war-1870-71, and the two great national histories of the corpus — Ollivier’s French memoir and Sybel’s German chronicle — recount it from opposite sides of the same events.
Background: the vacant throne of Spain
The Spanish revolution of 1868 had driven Isabella II from the throne and left Spain in search of a king. Sybel recounts how the regency of Marshal Serrano and the government of Marshal Prim, both monarchists, sought a candidate across the courts of Europe; Prim successively explored a Portuguese candidate, the duc de Montpensier of the House of Orléans, and princes of Italy before turning, with growing impatience, to the German houses. Ollivier records the same search from Paris, where every rumour of a candidate hostile to French interests was watched with alarm. The prize was the strategic fact that a prince of the Prussian royal house seated at Madrid would place a Hohenzollern on both flanks of France. See spanish-revolution-1868.
Prim and the German negotiations
The decisive turn came when the Spanish emissary Salazar, with Prim’s permission, carried the offer to Germany and, as Sybel narrates in detail, the candidacy of Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen took shape under the influence of Bismarck and the Prussian King. Sybel stresses the secrecy of the whole plan: it was arranged that the Cortes should be packed for an immediate vote so that France should be confronted with an accomplished fact. Leopold’s acceptance was telegraphed from Madrid late in June 1870, and Prim, who had judged the plan already compromised by the delay, tried to recover it by diplomacy.
The revelation and the French reaction
The secret broke in the last days of June and the first of July 1870. Ollivier describes the news bursting on Paris “like a bomb” on 3 July: the acceptance was revealed in Madrid through Zorrilla to la Época before the Cortes could vote, and the French ambassador Mercier telegraphed the intelligence to Paris. The foreign minister Gramont informed the Emperor, and the government, in Ollivier’s account, resolved at once to turn aside the candidacy. Indignation was universal in France — Ollivier lists Doudan, Jules Favre, Jules Simon, Thiers and Gambetta among those who condemned the Prussian move — and mirrored among foreign statesmen. The ministry, whose head Ollivier was, decided to confine the quarrel strictly to the Hohenzollern candidacy and to seek its withdrawal by diplomacy, rather than to reopen the older grievances of the Luxembourg and Rhine questions.
The crisis unfolds
Against Prim’s plan to have the Cortes elect Leopold on 20 July, the French cabinet acted on several fronts: a ministerial declaration read from the tribune on 6 July, the negotiation at Ems with King Wilhelm through the ambassador Benedetti, approaches to the powers and to the Spanish regency, and finally the intervention of the prince’s own family. On 11 July Leopold’s father, Prince Anthony of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, renounced the candidacy on his son’s behalf, and on 12 July Leopold himself, after violent scenes with his father and under pressure from Prim’s envoy, handed his own renunciation to the admiral. The candidacy was withdrawn. For Ollivier and the French ministry the affair appeared at that moment settled: the cause of quarrel had been removed, and the incident declared finished.
Consequences
The withdrawal did not end the crisis but set the stage for its climax. In Paris the war party, discontented at having been robbed of its pretext, pressed for guarantees against the repetition of such an affair; the Emperor and Gramont, without Ollivier, decided on 12 July to demand them, and on 13 July Bismarck’s falsification of the Ems telegram — the ems-dispatch-1870 — turned the retreat of the candidacy into a public affront to France. The demand of guarantees and the soufflet together made war inevitable, and on 15 July France declared it. The Hohenzollern candidature thus ended where it had begun: not in the quiet withdrawal of a prince, but in the franco-prussian-war-1870-71 that destroyed the second-empire-france and proclaimed the german-empire-proclaimed-1871. On the question of who had staged the affair, the sources divide — Ollivier holds Bismarck personally responsible for organising the candidacy; Sybel presents it as the convergence of Spanish search, Prussian dynastic interest and Bismarck’s policy.
Key participants

events/hundred-days-offensive-1918.title: The Hundred Days Offensive (August–November 1918)
events/hundred-days-offensive-1918.content:
The Hundred Days Offensive (8 August – 11 November 1918)
8 August – 11 November 1918
The final Allied offensive on the western front, conducted under the supreme command of marshal-foch, which broke the German army after the failure of Ludendorff’s offensives of the spring and forced Germany to ask for the armistice-11-november-1918 of 11 November 1918. Recouly’s chapter on the offensives of Foch opens with the observation, drawn from Casanova, that a man climbs only up to a certain moment; from that point he begins to descend, and in a descent the more rapid the nearer he approaches the end — motus in fine velocior. The failure of Ludendorff’s 15 July offensive, followed three days later by a graver failure, marked for Ludendorff the beginning of that descent.
Background
The winter of 1917–1918 had seen the military collapse of Russia and the defeat of Romania; by the peace treaties signed with Russia and Romania in February–March 1918, Germany obtained what it sought (see treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918). Germany could be said to have won the war three-quarters of the way on the eastern front. Freed from the East, the German command under Ludendorff threw its last strength into the spring offensives of 1918 on the western front, seeking a decision before the growing weight of American intervention could be brought to bear. The first of these offensives carried the German armies deep toward Paris. But the effort exhausted the German army, and the Allies, compelled at last by the direct menace of a defeat and even of a disaster — “the march of the Germans on Paris, separating the French armies” — created the single command under Foch.
The turn of the tide
Recouly dates the turn to the second battle of the Marne. The failure of Ludendorff’s 15 July offensive, followed three days later by a still graver failure, marked the beginning of the German descent. Foch, commanding the Allied forces, seized the initiative. His method, Recouly explains, consisted of multiple attacks harrying “the fragile facade” of the German front — attacks designed to shake the German army of occupation and overwork the German army of shock, in striking contrast with Ludendorff’s single, concentrated blows. On 8 August the Allied offensive opened on the western front; Ludendorff himself called it the day of mourning of the German army, « Der 8. August ist der Trauertag der deutschen Armee » — the day on which German divisions let themselves be completely broken through, tanks surprising divisional staffs in their headquarters, six or seven of the most particularly resistant German divisions cut to pieces, and troops crying to a fresh division marching bravely to the attack: « Streikbrecher und Kriegsverlängerer » — “strike-breakers and war-prolongers!” The French offensive broadened under Foch and philippe-petain: the Third Army under Humbert attacked, Pétain threw the Tenth Army of Mangin into the attack between the Oise and the Aisne, and Foch invited the British commander to enlarge the struggle toward the north with Byng’s army toward Bapaume.
The collapse of the German army
The psychological effect on Ludendorff was sudden and total. After the events of 8 August, Recouly records, he lost all confidence in victory: the war, in his view, could no longer be won militarily. “Our combat army no longer has its full value,” he said. He concluded that peace must be sought as quickly as possible, and the military handed over to the civilians they had so long treated with contempt. Ludendorff offered his resignation to the Kaiser, who naturally refused it; but the German command was broken. Recouly judged Ludendorff’s sudden collapse a sign of a character neither very balanced nor very solid, and the resort to the diplomats — on whose shoulders the crushing burden was suddenly laid — an act of considerable naivety, since the first and only thing to attempt was to save the army, or what could still be saved of it, by drawing it back behind the Meuse, perhaps behind the Rhine.
The pursuit and the armistice
The Hundred Days carried the Allies from the Marne across the old battlefields of 1914–1916 to the frontier. The offensive on the western front coincided with the collapse of the other fronts: the Bulgarian front fell in September (see the Italian account of the Salonica offensive in the Comando Supremo volume), and the Italian offensive of Vittorio Veneto in October put the Austro-Hungarian army out of action, isolating Germany militarily. Germany, faced with the ruin of the Quadruple Alliance, asked for an armistice. Foch received the German plenipotentiaries at the little station of Rethondes in the forest of Compiègne on 7 November; the armistice of 11 November ended the fighting on all fronts. In Recouly’s frame the Hundred Days were the descent motus in fine velocior — the swift, vertiginous fall of the German army once its last offensive had failed, completed by the collapse of its allies.

events/ice-march-1918.title: The First Kuban (Ice) March (1918)
events/ice-march-1918.content:
The First Kuban (Ice) March (1918)
February – April 1918
The retreat and forced march of the Volunteer Army from the Don into the Kuban in the winter–spring of 1918, the “first Kuban campaign” — the Ледяной поход (“Ice March”) — that carried lavr-kornilov’s little army through snow and mud to the assault on Ekaterinodar, cost the life of its leader, and passed the command to anton-denikin. It was the founding ordeal of the white-movement in the south, and the act by which the volunteers first rose “in defence of Russia against the red scourge.”
Background: the army and the Don
After the october-revolution-1917 the southern generals and the officers imprisoned at Bykhov had made their way to the Don. On 2 November mikhail-alexeyev reached Novocherkassk and began an armed force “destined to play so considerable a role”; there followed the arrival of Kornilov, the organisation of the Volunteer Army, and the attempt of the “triumvirate” of Alekseev, Kornilov and the ataman Kaledin to establish a Russian authority in the south. The volunteers were few — a handful of generals, officers and junkers, joined by some Cossacks and civilians — but they carried with them the whole moral weight of the officers’ refusal to accept the revolution.
But the winter brought the collapse of the Don. The end of the old army and the beginning of the Red Guard transformed the region; the peasants and many of the Cossacks turned against the volunteer cause, and the Soviet armed forces pressed upon Rostov and Novocherkassk. The treaty of treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918 and the German advance in the west had drawn away the attention of the world, leaving the south to its own war. Denikin described the madness left in the wake of the retreat — the plunder, the murder of the wounded, the terror of the families — and the “new tragedy of the Russian officer corps” who had staked everything on the struggle. Kaledin, despairing, shot himself as the Don collapsed; the volunteers, driven from their bases, chose to march into the unknown rather than surrender.
The march into the Kuban
The decision was taken at the military council at the stanitsa of Olginskaya: the army would abandon the Don and march south into the Kuban, the “promised land” of the Cossacks. On 23 February the volunteers entered the Kuban region, greeted, Denikin wrote, with bread and salt; but the promised rising of the Kuban did not come as hoped. The march was a running fight through a country already taken by the Bolsheviks. They fought at Berezanka, Vyselki and Korenovskaya, learned of the fall of Ekaterinodar to the Reds, and turned south.
The army moved by night through the flooded steppe, its column strung out along the roads and through the mud, its rear-guard under Bogaevsky pressed by the Kuban Bolsheviks, its headquarters improvised on the march. In the night of 8 March they crossed the River Laba, the junkers wading in water up to their chests, “blowing bubbles” in the cold. Day after day they threaded the encirclement of the khutors, and Denikin confessed to the “shady sides” of an army’s life in extremity. The fighting was continuous: the Red forces surrounded them on every side, and each day brought its skirmish or its stand. Yet the army held together, bound by the discipline of its officers and by the sheer necessity of survival, and through it all the news of the fate of Ekaterinodar and of the Kuban detachment coloured their hopes.
The Ice March
The ordeal earned its name on 15 March, in the fight at Novo-Dmitrievskaya — the “Ice March,” the “glory of Markov and the Officer Regiment, the pride of the Volunteer Army, and one of the most vivid memories of every veteran of the first campaign.” All the night before the rain had poured, and it continued into the morning; the army marched through stretches of water and liquid mud, on roads and off them, lost in the thick fog that lay over the land. The cold water soaked every garment and ran in sharp, piercing streams down the collars; the men went slowly, shuddering with cold and dragging their feet in swollen, water-logged boots. Toward noon came thick flakes of sticky snow and a wind that filled the eyes and nose and ears and took the breath.
Ahead of them a river barred the road, its far bank held by the Bolshevik outposts; the bridge was broken, and horsemen went to seek fords, some plunging with their horses into the icy water. The column crowded to the bank; the huts of a small farmstead beckoned with the smoke of their chimneys, and the men pressed into the steaming, crowded rooms to warm their frozen limbs. The crossing secured, the army pressed on, and at Novo-Dmitrievskaya the Officer Regiment under Markov won the fight that gave the whole march its name. There the treaty was concluded with the Kuban volunteer detachment, which joined its strength to the Volunteer Army, and the combined force turned on Ekaterinodar. The Ice March had become the badge of the first volunteers, the emblem of their endurance and their cause.
The assault and the death of Kornilov
By 27 March the volunteers had reached the approaches of Ekaterinodar, where the Red defenders had gathered in force. Kornilov called a military council — the first since Olginskaya — and resolved on a decisive assault, though the enemy outnumbered them many times over and the army was exhausted, its units intermixed, its commander strength shattered by four days of battle, its shells and cartridges gone, and more than fifteen hundred wounded in the lazaret. At the council the generals drew a sad picture of the position; only Markov, weary from two sleepless days, dozed through it. Kornilov did not try to soften the picture, and was unmoved by the argument for withdrawing: “There is no other way out, Anton Ivanovich. If we do not take Ekaterinodar, I will have to put a bullet in my head.”
On the morning of 31 March, while the army prepared the assault, the farmstead where the headquarters lay came under artillery fire. Kornilov was urged to move; “It is not worth it now; tomorrow the assault,” he replied. In the shelling he was struck down. Denikin wrote in the volume’s dedication: “On 31 March 1918 a Russian grenade, directed by the hand of a Russian man, struck down a great Russian patriot.” The army that had lost its leader had also lost the chance of the city; the assault, launched without him, failed.
Consequences: Denikin’s command
The death of Kornilov left the army in crisis, but the struggle did not end. The chief of staff asked Denikin whether he would take command of the army, and he answered yes. He lifted the siege of Ekaterinodar and led the volunteers away through the fights at Gnachbau and Medvedovskaya, where the feat of General Markov — a sudden, bold counter-stroke that saved the column — passed into legend. Turning north and east, the army marched from Dyadkovskaya to Uspenskaya, bearing its wounded with it, living on the bread and salt of the stanitsa, before swinging back toward the Don amid the risings that had begun to break out against the Bolsheviks in the Cossack country.
By late April, with the arrival of the detachment of Colonel Drozdovsky and the appearance of the Germans on the Don, the volunteers were back in the Don country, the siege of Novocherkassk relieved and the army given a breathing-space. The struggle was not over but had been given a new form: the little army that had marched through the ice had become the nucleus of a movement. Denikin closed the account with the scale of what the first march had meant: “Two and a half years more their struggle lasted,” and the survivors were scattered across the Slavic lands, the Allied camps, and the night shelters of the Old and New World — but the memory of those “who first rose in defence of Russia against the red scourge” would be kept while peace rested over the country.

events/isonzo-battles-1915-17.title: The Battles of the Isonzo (1915–1917)
events/isonzo-battles-1915-17.content:
The Battles of the Isonzo (1915–1917)
23 May 1915 – 1917
The twelve battles of the Isonzo, the long series of offensives fought by the Italian army under luigi-cadorna against Austria-Hungary along the river Isonzo and on the barren plateau of the Carso, from Italy’s entry into the First World War in May 1915 until the catastrophe of Caporetto in October 1917. The Isonzo front was the principal theatre of the Italian war, the road by which Italy sought to break through toward the “unredeemed” lands of Gorizia, Trieste and the Adriatic that irredentism demanded; and it was the scene of the most costly and least decisive warfare of the Italian front, a grinding struggle against a defensive line that Cadorna’s repeated offensives could rarely move.
Background
When Italy crossed the frontier on 24 May 1915, the line of battle ran along the eastern frontier of the Veneto, where the river Isonzo flows south out of the Julian Alps toward the Adriatic, and where the Austro-Hungarian army, its chief of staff Conrad long having feared and expected Italy’s defection, had fortified the passes and the high ground. The Italian war aim — the recovery of the Trentino, Gorizia, Trieste and the Adriatic coast — pointed directly at the Isonzo and the Carso, the barrier behind which lay the coveted coast. Cadorna’s strategy, as he sets it out in his account, was the offensive: to break the enemy’s line by repeated frontal assaults, forcing the river and carrying the heights that commanded the way to Trieste. The ground favoured the defence, and the first battles, in the summer and autumn of 1915, gained little at heavy cost.
The years of the offensives
Through 1915 and 1916 the Italian army mounted a series of offensives against the same fortified sector, each numbered in the Italian reckoning as a battle of the Isonzo. In the summer of 1916 the front was violently shaken from another quarter when the Austrians, seeking to relieve the pressure, launched the offensive against the Trentino that Cadorna records as the Strafexpedition — the Austrian “punitive” counter-offensive on the Asiago plateau, which threatened the Italian rear and was only arrested by the concentration of the reserves. The autumn of 1916 brought a renewed Italian effort: Cadorna’s seventh, eighth and ninth battles of the Isonzo, the offensive operations on the Carso which at last wrested Gorizia from the enemy and carried the Italian line to the threshold of the plateau. The struggles on the bare Carso, where every advance was bought in blood over a shattered limestone wilderness, became the emblem of the war’s futility and cost.
The climax of 1917
In the spring of 1917 the Italian command renewed the offensive: the tenth battle of the Isonzo, opened in May 1917 on the Julian front, pressed the enemy in the direction of the frontier, and was answered, as in previous years, by an Austrian counter-offensive and renewed action on the Trentino. Then, in August–September 1917, Cadorna fought his eleventh battle of the Isonzo — la battaglia fra l’Idria e il Timavo, the battle between the Idria and the Timavo, as he entitles it — the most powerful Italian effort of the whole war, in which the army at last broke across the last of the Carso and looked upon the edge of the plain. The twelfth battle was impending in October 1917 when the whole calculus was overturned: the Austrians, reinforced by German divisions, struck at the junction of the Italian line near Caporetto and broke it, and the eleven battles of the Isonzo were swallowed up in the great retreat to the Piave.
Consequences
The Isonzo offensives exacted an enormous price — repeated months of frontal warfare against the strongest part of the Austrian line, yielding Gorizia but never Trieste, and exhausting the Italian army that had mounted them. They bled the Austro-Hungarian army too, whose repeated defence of the Isonzo and counter-strokes on the Trentino consumed the strength of the monarchy, and the very success of the eleventh battle prepared the Austro-German decision to end the stalemate by a decisive stroke at Caporetto. That stroke, breaking the line that twelve battles had failed to move, threw the Italian army back across the Tagliamento to the Piave and brought the fall of Cadorna. The Isonzo thus stands as both the central ordeal of the Italian war and the prelude to its darkest hour — the point of departure for the recovery that would culminate, a year later, in Vittorio Veneto.

events/italian-war-1866.title: The Italian War of 1866
events/italian-war-1866.content:
The Italian War of 1866
June – August 1866
The Italian theatre of the third war of independence, fought in alliance with Prussia against Austria in the summer of 1866 — the campaign that closed the austro-prussian-war-1866 on the Italian side. It was a war in which Italy lost every pitched engagement — on land at Custoza and on sea at Lissa — and yet, because the Prussian victory in the north decided the whole struggle, ended by acquiring the Veneto. The contrast between the glory of giuseppe-garibaldi’s volunteers in the Trentino and the humiliation of the army and fleet left a bitter mark on the new kingdom.
Background: the Prussian alliance and the quest for the Veneto
Since 1859 the national programme of the Risorgimento had held Venice and Rome as the two goals still to be won. The war of 1866 offered the occasion to take the first of them. When Prussia prepared to strike at Austria over the German question, Italy, under the ministry of General Lamarmora, concluded a treaty of alliance with Prussia: the two powers were to make war together, and Italy, in return for joining, was to obtain the Veneto from Austria. Tivaroni’s account records the negotiations that attended the treaty — the Austrian diplomacy, even on the eve of war, still probing whether the Veneto could be ceded peacefully; the efforts of the Prussian alliance to gain a better price; and the flat refusal to admit the Trentino into the bargain, Bismarck answering that he could not do it because the Trentino was not his to give. In the end Italy entered the war bound to Prussia, and the fate of the Veneto — as the sequel showed — was to depend less on Italian arms than on Prussian.
The battle of Custoza
War was declared in June 1866, and the Italian army crossed the Mincio to take the offensive against the Austrians in the Veneto. On 24 June the two armies met at Custoza, on the hilly ground about the Garda. Tivaroni gives a searching account of the battle and its mismanagement. The Italian plan, which looked to roll up the Austrian centre, failed in execution; the divisions were thrown separately upon the enemy, the movements of the several corps were not co-ordinated, and while the Austrian plan under the Archduke Albert did not succeed completely, the Italians were compelled to recross the Mincio with two divisions broken and two more disordered. It was, Tivaroni observes, the first time in fifteen hundred years that the soldiers of all Italy had stood united against a common enemy — and the irony was that their commander, General Lamarmora, did not know how to use them. The defeat was not a rout, but it was a reverse, and its effect on the army and on public spirit was deep.
Inaction and the Trentino: Garibaldi’s volunteers
After Custoza the Italian army stood still. Tivaroni records the long inaction between 25 June and mid-July — the recriminations among the generals, the failure to press the war, the government’s growing despair — while the Prussians advanced in the north. In the mountain theatre, however, the war took another shape. The corps of volunteers, some 38,000 nominal under giuseppe-garibaldi, had been posted on the extreme left about the Garda, charged with distracting the Austrians and cutting the line of retreat through the Trentino. Ill-armed and ill-supplied, Garibaldi himself crippled by rheumatism and compelled to move about in a carriage, the volunteers nevertheless carried the war into the mountains, forcing the passes of the Chiese and the Ledro, storming the forts one by one and pressing upon the line toward Trento. At Bezzecce they won the victory that, in Tivaroni’s words, softened the grief of the nation for the outcome of Custoza and Lissa. The whole Trentino lay occupied, and Trento itself was about to fall, when the armistice arrived: Lamarmora’s order to evacuate the Trentino reached Garibaldi on 25 July, and the general, against every entreaty of his men, obeyed it with the single word obbedisco — “I obey.”
The battle of Lissa
At sea the war was decided on 20 July. The Italian fleet, commanded by Admiral Persano, had been built at heavy cost — Tivaroni reckons it at 127 million lire by the end of 1866 — and was the stronger of the two, with more ironclads and more guns than the Austrian fleet under Admiral Tegethoff. Yet the campaign had been one of hesitation: the fleet lay idle at Ancona, refused battle when the Austrians appeared, and finally, urged on by the minister Depretis, sailed not against the enemy fleet but against the island of Lissa in the Adriatic. There the Austrian squadron came out to meet it. In the battle that followed, Tegethoff, driving his ships in a compact mass, rammed and sank the ironclad Re d’Italia with most of its crew, while the Palestro blew up with three hundred men after her commander, Cappellini, refused to abandon her. The Italian fleet, though it remained on the waters after the enemy withdrew, had been defeated; Persano, who had transferred his flag during the action, was afterwards tried before the Senate and condemned for incapacity and negligence. Lissa cost Italy two ships and eight hundred men, and, coming after Custoza, completed the military humiliation of the war.
The cadeau du Veneto and the Peace of Vienna
The decisive events were passing in the north. The Prussian victory over Austria at Königgrätz in July decided the war, and in the armistice of Nikolsburg Austria conceded the German settlement. Italy, which had sought to obtain the Veneto by its own arms and had failed, now received it as a gift. Tivaroni describes the bitter comedy of the cadeau du Veneto: the preliminary peace transferred the Veneto to the Emperor napoleon-iii, and France then handed it over to Italy. For the Italian government and army the thing was a humiliation — Lamarmora wrote that to receive the Veneto as a present from France was dishonouring and that all the world would think Italy had betrayed Prussia; the romantic Ricasoli would rather have gone on fighting alone than accept the province as a charity. But to continue the war was impossible: the whole Austrian army of Sadowa was now free to descend upon Italy, and the government, against the advice of Ricasoli, accepted the armistice and evacuated the Trentino. On 12 August the armistice was signed at Cormons; Austria ceded the Veneto to France in the last days of August, and the transfer was completed through Napoleon’s commissioner. The Peace of Vienna, closing the Italian war, registered the acquisition of the Veneto by the Kingdom of Italy — the completion of the union of the peninsula except for Rome and the irredentist lands of the Trentino and the eastern shore.
Consequences
Italy emerged from 1866 with the Veneto — the object for which it had entered the war — but without military honour. Custoza and Lissa had shown the army and the fleet unequal to their task, and the province had been won not on the Mincio or the Adriatic but by Prussia at Königgrätz and by the good offices of the French Emperor. The government of Ricasoli, which had so fiercely desired to fight on, was discredited; a rising at Palermo in September 1866 showed the discontent of the south; and the very success of the Veneto purchase left the Roman question untouched, for France still garrisoned Rome. The Trentino, evacuated by order at the very moment of victory, remained in Austrian hands and entered the stock of Italian irredentism — the claim to the unredeemed lands of the north-east which was to recur again and again down to the Great War. The war of 1866 thus closed the chapter of the Veneto while opening that of Rome, and it is the humiliated rather than the triumphant Italy of 1866 that the sources of the Risorgimento carry forward into the struggle for the capital, which ended at capture-of-rome-1870.

events/italy-ww1-entry-1915.title: Italy's Entry into the First World War (May 1915)
events/italy-ww1-entry-1915.content:
Italy’s Entry into the First World War (24 May 1915)
24 May 1915
Italy’s entry into the First World War on the side of the Entente, announced by the declaration of war of 22 May 1915 and carried across the frontier on the night of 23–24 May, which opened the Italian front against Austria-Hungary along the Isonzo and the frontier of the Trentino. The event ended Italy’s long neutrality and transformed the war into the struggle on a fourth front that would last until Vittorio Veneto. In this corpus’s frame it is the culminating act of the irredentism that had stirred Italy since unification — the recovery of the unredeemed lands of the Trentino and the Adriatic coast.
Background
Italy had entered the war years as a member of the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary, but the alliance had never satisfied Italian ambitions. Conrad, who had commanded at Trieste, had from the first counted it a utopia to rely on Italy as an ally: one had rather, he judged, to be prepared to be deserted by Italy, and in all likelihood attacked, as soon as a favourable opportunity offered. When the Great War broke out in 1914 Italy declared neutrality, watching the balance of the struggle. The Marne and the whole turn of the war, in Conrad’s retrospective, was the signal for Italy and Rumania to seek the Entente — the moment the overwhelming superiority came to the enemy side. The war was not yet a year old when the neutrality drew to its close.
The crisis of the country
Cadorna’s account of Italy at the outbreak of the European war paints a country in ferment. He dwells on what he called the growing spirit of revolt in Italian society — the decline of religious restraint, the universal talk of rights and the neglect of duties, the open preaching of anti-militarism. And he notes pointedly that among those who made themselves the banner-bearers of this disorder were the very men who provoked Austria with irredentist demonstrations — as if they could then hold their own against a great military power, solid in its ancient discipline. The campaign for intervention, that is, was bound up with the demand for the “unredeemed” lands (terre irredente) of the Trentino, Trieste, Istria and Dalmatia, still under Habsburg rule. The diplomacy of the winter of 1914–15 moved toward the Entente, and on 26 April 1915 the Pact of London bound Italy to enter the war on the Allied side, promising in return the Trentino, South Tyrol to the Brenner, Trieste, Görz and Gradisca, Istria, Dalmatia, Valona and the Dodecanese — the very terms that Czernin’s appendix prints as the London decisions. The Italian chief of staff, Cadorna, complained that he was not even consulted about the territorial stipulations, which implied grave military questions.
The entry
Cadorna’s plan was that the declaration of war, the order of mobilisation and the crossing of the frontier should be three nearly simultaneous acts, to secure the surprise indispensable to success. So it was done: the war was declared on 22 May 1915; the order of general mobilisation went out at the same time; and in the night of 23–24 May the troops already gathered in the Veneto — an enormous force of about 400,000 men — crossed the frontier and occupied important positions beyond it on nearly the whole front. Had Italy waited for the completion of the mobilisation, Cadorna judged, the enemy would have forestalled her, by invading the territory or at least occupying the exits of the valleys. The surprise was at least in part achieved. Italy had entered the war on the side of the Entente, and the Italian front against Austria-Hungary was opened.
Consequences
Italy’s entry opened the fourth great front of the war and bound Austria-Hungary to a war on yet another frontier. The front along the Isonzo and the Trentino would become the scene of the long and sanguinary isonzo-battles-1915-17, the Austrian counter-offensive of the Strafexpedition of 1916, and the catastrophe of battle-of-caporetto-1917 before the final victory of battle-of-vittorio-veneto-1918. For the Central Powers the entry of Italy and of Rumania, as Conrad insisted, helped to give the Entente the overwhelming superiority that decided the war. For Italy, the war that had begun with the promise of the unredeemed lands would end, after years of terrible cost, with the recovery of Trentino, Trieste and the Adriatic — the fulfilment of irredentism at the price of the war itself.

events/july-crisis-1914.title: The July Crisis (1914)
events/july-crisis-1914.content:
The July Crisis (1914)
28 June – early August 1914
The five weeks between the shots at Sarajevo and the outbreak of the world war — the diplomatic storm in which Austria-Hungary’s ultimatum to Serbia, the German assurance of support, Russia’s mobilisation, and the cascade of declarations of war carried Europe from a Balkan dispute to a general conflagration. It is the culminating event of the period’s eastern crisis, the point at which the balkan-policy-austria of the Habsburg Monarchy and the eastern-question as a whole detonated into the battle-of-galicia-1914, the battle-of-the-marne-1914 and four years of war. Both the diplomat ottokar-czernin and the chief of the general staff conrad-von-hotzendorf left retrospective accounts, written from the inside and at close distance.
Background: the ultimatum and the German assurance
The murder of franz-ferdinand on 28 June supplied the Monarchy with the occasion it had long sought. The conviction at Vienna, voiced by Conrad on the very day, was that the crime was the war-declaration of Serbia and could only be answered by war; the decision to press Serbia to account was taken, and Count leopold-berchtold prepared an ultimatum. Behind it stood the assurance of Germany. Czernin records that Berchtold was fortified through the German ambassador, Heinrich von Tschirschky, in the belief that a war against France and Russia would end victoriously — the blank cheque of Berlin, as the phrase ran — and that Berchtold himself, as Czernin judged, hoped to the last to win a diplomatic success without war, “to win the victory with the pen,” while reckoning on Germany’s backing if Serbia refused. The Hungarian minister-president, Count stephen-tisza, opposed the sharp ultimatum outright, foreseeing a war he did not want; but the current ran against him.
The ultimatum and the partial acceptance
The ultimatum was delivered to Belgrade in the last week of July, demanding satisfaction for the Sarajevo crime in terms no sovereign state could accept in full. Serbia’s reply, in Czernin’s summary, accepted the ultimatum only incompletely. On 25 July — the date Conrad gives for the outbreak against Serbia — the Monarchy broke off diplomatic relations and prepared to move; the declaration of war against Serbia followed, and the Serbian war had begun. Russia, as everyone had foreseen, did not stand aside. Czernin insists that Berchtold can have had no doubt that a Serbian war would draw in Russia: his own brother’s reports from Petersburg had left none. With the Serbian war declared, Russia mobilised and intervened by arms.
Grey’s mediation and the failure of the last hour
In the final days of July the Powers struggled to arrest the avalanche. On 30 July the German ambassador laid before Berchtold a telegram from the German ambassador in London, Lichnowsky, conveying Sir Edward Grey’s proposal of a four-power mediation, on the assumption that Austria-Hungary, after occupying Belgrade, would state its terms. Grey warned privately that an Austro-Russian war would permit England’s neutrality, but that the situation would change if Germany and France were drawn in; England’s public opinion, so favourable to Austria after the murder, was beginning to turn at Austria’s obstinacy. On the 31st came the telegram of King George V to Prince Henry of Prussia, urging that Austria be persuaded to content itself with the occupation of Belgrade and neighbouring territory as a hostage for a satisfactory settlement. Vienna accepted these proposals only on conditions of military caution, and that conditional acceptance did not satisfy London. The hours slipped by unused; events outstripped the diplomats.
Russia’s mobilisation and the outbreak of the war
The turning point, in Czernin’s account, was Russia. A powerful party in Petersburg was at work to force the war at any price; the Russian entry created a fait accompli, and Vienna, in the last moment, dared not stop its own mobilisation for fear of arriving too late in its own defence. Hostilities, Czernin notes, had begun without the will of the Tsar, and Russia, having created the Zwangslage, the compulsion, had “unleashed the world war.” On the evening of 30 July the order for the general mobilisation of the Monarchy was to be laid before the Emperor; once Russia had moved, Austria’s own mobilisation and the German entry followed as a chain. Czernin, writing after the catastrophe, held that the war was unleashed by Russia, and counted Austria-Hungary’s greatest misfortune the German invasion of Belgium, which gave England its ground to enter — the decision that on the night of 4 August settled England’s part in the war.
For the general staff the crisis was above all the hour of decision against Russia. Conrad records the extension of the Danube line as a fortified central zone, the deployment of the army against Serbia and Russia, and the farewell audience with franz-joseph on 15 August before the army high command left Vienna for the Russian theatre. The war that had been dreaded and prepared for a generation had come, and the machinery of the war-plans-1914 — the Austro-German deployment, the expected decision in the west — now began to move.
Consequences: the two-front war
The July crisis ended in the general war. The Monarchy’s forces were committed at once on two fronts — against Serbia, where the opening operations were launched, and against Russia in Galicia, where Conrad’s armies marched to the disastrous battle-of-galicia-1914. In the west the German advance met the French and British at the battle-of-the-marne-1914, whose failure, as Conrad argued in his Vorwort, was the true decision of the war: it was the signal for Italy and Rumania to seek the Entente. The failure to localise the conflict, which franz-joseph had so anxiously hoped for, had plunged the Monarchy into the struggle that would end in its dissolution. The July crisis thus marks the transition from the age of Balkan crises to the age of world war.

events/kornilov-affair-1917.title: The Kornilov Affair (1917)
events/kornilov-affair-1917.content:
The Kornilov Affair (1917)
27 – 31 August 1917
The attempt of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief lavr-kornilov to impose order on a disintegrating Russia by a march of loyal troops on Petrograd at the end of August 1917, and its sudden collapse in the space of a few days — the episode Kerensky branded a “mutiny,” and which Denikin preferred to call, for 27–31 August, the kornilovskoe vystuplenie (“Kornilov rising”), reserving the wider name kornilovskoe dvizhenie (“Kornilov movement”) for the whole of the summer’s gathering of the officer corps against the revolutionary disorder. It was the decisive rupture between the Provisional Government and the command, and its failure cleared the road to the october-revolution-1917.
Background: the divergence of paths
By the summer of 1917 the revolution had split into a many-sided struggle. Denikin generalised the forces of the revolution into two resultants — the Provisional Government and the Soviet — but by July and August this simple division no longer held. After the July days and the crisis of power, Kerensky formed a third government, formally emancipated from the soviets; but power itself was slipping. The poles of the struggle were three: the government, the central executive committee of the Soviet, and the supreme command.
The June offensive had failed, and the army was dissolving under the pressure of the soldiers’ committees and the reforms of the revolutionary command. The officer corps, humiliated and disarmed, had moved into opposition to a power that could neither win the war nor restore the front. Denikin insisted that in the struggle between Kerensky and Kornilov there was an “absence of direct political and social slogans” that would divide the two sides; the conflict was not one of programs but of wills and of the desperate question of who should save the country. He stressed that the terms later used — “affair,” “rising,” “conspiracy,” “mutiny” — were all too narrow, and that the events were far more complex than a mere plot, embracing wide circles of the Russian public.
The Supreme Commander
On 19 July lavr-kornilov was appointed Supreme Commander-in-Chief, and at his appointment he demanded of the government recognition of his responsibility “only before his own conscience and the whole people” — an extraordinary, almost sovereign scheme of military command. He saw in dictatorship the only way out of the situation created by the spiritual and political prostration of the power. Denikin insisted that Kornilov had no definite political program before the rising; the “Kornilov program” circulated under that name was, in his view, the fruit of later collective work. But the movement gathered the secret organizations of the officers, the “political encirclement,” and a good part of the Russian public — a “three-sided conspiracy,” Denikin called it, between the command, the organized right, and the Allied representatives, all pressing toward a “strong power.”
Through August Kornilov pressed the “memorandum” on army reorganization — the restoration of the disciplinary authority of the officers, the subordination of the committees — while Kerensky wavered, now against the soviets with Kornilov, now with the soviets against Kornilov. The agent and intermediary between them was Savinkov, the former terrorist who served the government, weighing on both sides. Krymov, the general whose troops stood nearest the capital, had no doubt that force of arms would settle the matter; Kornilov himself, Denikin records, had decided on a change in the structure of power, though not yet on the methods.
The rupture and the march on Petrograd
The explosion came through the mission of V. N. Lvov, a former member of the Duma and of the Provisional Government, who carried to Petrograd Kornilov’s demands for the transfer of full military and civil power, on which he would form a new government. Kerensky, whatever the real tenor of the message, chose to read it as a demand for the overthrow of the government and declared the Supreme Commander a traitor. His communique began: “On 26 August General Kornilov sent to me the member of the State Duma V. N. Lvov with the demand that the Provisional Government transfer to him the whole of military and civil power.”
Through the 27th, amid a fever of appeals, the government and the revolutionary organizations branded the movement “mutiny,” “treason to the fatherland and to the revolution,” “baring of the front,” and set about stopping the advance of the troops General Krymov had brought toward the capital. Denikin catalogued the outrage of the appeals, above all the socialist manifesto of Chernov that invited the “peasants in grey soldiers’ greatcoats” to remember “the accursed name of the man” who wished to strangle freedom and take from them the land — a mobilisation of the rank and file against their own commanders. In all these appeals, Denikin noted, there was no true, factual and legal basis; they reflected rather the choleric temper of their authors. The government also acted: Kerensky ordered first Lukomsky and then Klembovsky to assume the supreme command, and both refused. The new military governor of Petrograd, meanwhile, and the committees of the railway junctions worked to halt Krymov’s echelons.
The collapse
The rising foundered without a battle. Krymov’s troops, halted by the railway workers and turned back by the committees and the soviets’ agitation, refused to march; the officer corps, though sympathetic, could not overcome the general disintegration. Kerensky ordered first Lukomsky and then Klembovsky to assume the supreme command, and both refused. Stavka was liquidated by a detachment sent for the purpose, and Kornilov was arrested and imprisoned in the town of Bykhov together with his chief associates — Denikin among them, sent from the “Berdichev group” of arrested officers. Krymov himself shot himself, unable to bear the disgrace of the episode. Denikin’s chapter heading gave the verdict in a phrase: Kerensky’s victory was the “prelude to Bolshevism.” For by destroying the command and the last instrument of authority, Kerensky had disarmed the only force that might have resisted vladimir-lenin’s party; the government had won against Kornilov only to fall a few weeks later to the october-revolution-1917.
Consequences
The Kornilov affair completed the ruin of the army and the prestige of the command. The officers emerged from it humiliated and hunted, the soldiers’ committees and the Bolsheviks greatly strengthened, and the authority of Kerensky — who had seemingly defeated his own general — left solitary and dependent on the very soviet democracy he had sought to escape. At Bykhov the prisoners lived under guard, watched by Stavka and the government, while the investigative commission of Shablovsky examined the “Kornilov program” and the plans for the future. Through September and October the empire drifted: Kerensky’s military reforms under the war minister Verkhovsky, the German occupation of the Moonsund islands, and the gathering strength of the soviets. When the october-revolution-1917 came, the Bykhov prisoners were set free amid the collapse of the old Stavka, the murder of the last supreme commander Dukhonin, and made their way to the Don, where mikhail-alexeyev and the volunteers were already gathering. The idea that had moved Kornilov — a military dictatorship to save Russia — did not die at Bykhov; it passed into the white-movement that would take the field against the Bolsheviks in the following year.

events/law-of-guarantees-1871.title: The Law of Guarantees (13 May 1871)
events/law-of-guarantees-1871.content:
The Law of Guarantees (13 May 1871)
13 May 1871
The Italian law of guarantees — la legge delle guarentigie — enacted on 13 May 1871 to regulate the position of the Pope after the loss of Rome, defining the status of the Holy See and of the Papacy within a city that had become the capital of the Kingdom of Italy. The measure answered the problem that the occupation of Rome had raised: how the spiritual head of the Catholic Church could live and govern under Italian sovereignty. It was framed unilaterally by the Italian parliament and never accepted by the Pontiff, whose refusal to treat with the new order kept the roman-question alive for another half-century.
Background
The taking of Rome on 20 September 1870 had stripped the Papacy of its temporal dominion and left the Pope resident in a city under the authority of the Italian crown. The problem was acute: the Holy See had enjoyed, as a temporal sovereign, the independence that a head of a universal Church requires, and the new kingdom had to decide what standing the Pope should hold within its own territory. The ministry of Giovanni Lanza and Quintino Sella, which had carried out the occupation, was charged with the settlement. Oriani treats the measure as the necessary sequel of the annexation — the completion, in law, of the monarchical solution of the Roman problem that he narrates in La lotta politica in Italia from the September Convention onward.
The terms of the law
The Law of Guarantees, enacted on 13 May 1871, was a unilateral law of the Italian state, not a treaty with the Holy See. It conceded to the Pope the inviolability of his person, the honours of a sovereign, and the right to maintain his own diplomatic representatives, while reserving to the kingdom the general law of the land. It granted the Pope an annual allowance in compensation for the revenues of the Papal States, and secured the extraterritoriality of the Vatican, the Lateran and the papal residence at Castel Gandolfo — the buildings of the Holy See left outside the ordinary operation of Italian law. The idea was to preserve for the Papacy the freedom and independence of a sovereign power without the territorial dominion it had lost, in a kind of personal and spiritual sovereignty over a limited, guaranteed space within the capital.
The refusal of the Pope
The law was never accepted by the Holy See. The Pope refused to recognise the Italian seizure of Rome and to treat the unilateral Italian statute as a sufficient or legitimate guarantee of his independence, holding that the loss of temporal sovereignty could not be repaired by a concession of the very state that had despoiled him. In the years that followed this refusal took institutional form in the Pope’s rule of Non expedit — “it is not expedient” — by which Italian Catholics were counselled against participation in the political life of the kingdom that had taken Rome. The practical effect was that the roman-question, though solved as a territorial matter by the capture of the city, remained an open wound in the relations between the Italian state and the Church throughout the period that this corpus covers, down to the very threshold of the twentieth century.
Consequences
The Law of Guarantees settled in law the Pope’s position inside Italy but left the moral and religious question unresolved, for the Pope’s refusal made the statute a dead letter in the eyes of the Holy See. The division it embodied would persist as a standing feature of Italian public life — a church standing apart from the state, an anti-clerical current in politics, and a population whose devout loyalty to the Pope was set against the claims of the kingdom. In the longer run the guarantees prepared the ground on which a later settlement would have to be built, but within the years of this wiki the law stands as the Italian state’s answer to the roman-question — an answer that the Pope, by his Non expedit, declined to accept.

events/luxembourg-crisis-1867.title: The Luxembourg Crisis (1867)
events/luxembourg-crisis-1867.content:
The Luxembourg Crisis (1867)
January – May 1867
The abortive attempt of napoleon-iii to buy the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg from the Netherlands, and the war scare that followed until the London Conference of May 1867 neutralised the duchy and ordered the dismantling of its fortress. It was the first great collision between France and the new north-german-confederation after the war of 1866, and — like the Hohenzollern candidature three years later — it sprang from the same unsettled question of French compensation on the Rhine.
Background: France and the compensations of 1866
In the months after the austro-prussian-war-1866 the French Emperor, who had expected to profit from the German war, found himself confronting a Prussia grown strong beyond the Main. Sybel records how Napoleon’s diplomacy sought to recover the lost balance by proposing a grand exchange: a famous triple alliance by which France would receive Luxembourg and, further on, Belgium, Prussia the South German states, with Italy joining as a third partner — a scheme by which, in Sybel’s words, the glory of the Napoleonic name would be restored without the shedding of blood. The Prussian negotiation over this plan dragged on. In December suspicion seized the Emperor that Prussia would not merely refuse the alliance but confront him as an open adversary over Luxembourg; he ordered his war minister to prepare a reform of the army that would double its strength. In January 1867 the failure of the Prussian plan and of the understanding with Italy was finally clear. “I have no ally in Europe,” Napoleon told his ministers; “I can rely only on my own people.” His resolve was taken to enter the liberal path — to win the gratitude of the people by free concessions and so to secure the throne and the succession. It was in these very days, as Sybel notes, that the Luxembourg affair entangled itself ever more dangerously.
The purchase and its denouement
The crisis turned on the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg. Though the duchy belonged to the King of the Netherlands, its fortress had been garrisoned since the Congress of 1815 by Prussian troops, as a stronghold of the German Confederation; in 1866 the Confederation had dissolved and the question of the garrison stood open. Napoleon proposed to buy Luxembourg from the King of the Netherlands. For a time his policy found a degree of favour in Berlin, and Bismarck encouraged the purchase — the transaction, from the German standpoint, would detach from Germany a point of which Prussia had no further need. The plan then miscarried. When the sale became known, German national feeling rose against the cession of a German fortress to France, and Bismarck, confronted with the storm, denounced the project he had at first countenanced. The bargain collapsed; the purchase was abandoned; and the two powers stood face to face over a question of honour and security, each convinced the other had sought to humiliate it.
The London Conference and the neutralisation
The quarrel mounted until the mediation of the powers was invoked, and the crisis was referred to a conference of the European states which met in London in May 1867. There the solution was found in the neutralisation of Luxembourg. By the arrangement the Grand Duchy was placed under the collective guarantee of the powers as a permanently neutral state; the Prussian garrison was to be withdrawn and the fortress, the object of so much contention, was to be dismantled. The conference thus removed the immediate danger of war, but at the cost of satisfying neither party. France gained no territory and no compensation on the Rhine; Germany kept Luxembourg out of French hands, but at the price of abandoning a German fortress that Prussia had garrisoned for half a century. The settlement proved, in the estimate of the French sources of the corpus, a lasting grievance — the Luxembourg affair joined the stock of injuries which France laid to Prussia’s account, to be reopened at the crisis of 1870.
Consequences
The Luxembourg crisis set the pattern of the following years. It taught Napoleon the isolation of France: the failure of the triple-alliance scheme left him without a continental ally, and the events of 1867 confirmed his turn toward internal liberal reform — the beginning of the transformation toward the liberal-empire which Ollivier records from within. For Prussia the crisis revealed both the strength and the limits of the new north-german-confederation: German national sentiment had rallied against the cession, but the Bund had not been able to keep the fortress without yielding to a European conference. The affront of the neutralisation rankled in France, where the loss of Luxembourg was felt as a humiliation, and the memory of 1867 fed the bellicose current that in 1870 seized upon the hohenzollern-candidature-1870 and the ems-dispatch-1870 as the occasion for settling the account with Prussia in the franco-prussian-war-1870-71. In that sense the Luxembourg crisis was a first rehearsal of the war — the same powers, the same grievance of compensation, the same appeal to a conference — that ended, three years later, very differently.
