events/north-german-confederation-1867.title: Founding of the North German Confederation (1867)
events/north-german-confederation-1867.content:
Founding of the North German Confederation (1867)
1866–1867; constitution in force from July 1867
The Norddeutscher Bund (North German Confederation) was the federal state which Prussia erected over Germany north of the Main in the year after its victory over Austria in the austro-prussian-war-1866. It gave a permanent constitutional form to Prussian hegemony in the North, created a federal parliament, and — by binding the northern states into one military, economic and political order — stood as the middle step between the shattered German Confederation and the German Empire proclaimed in 1871.
Background: the new order after 1866
The war of 1866 had dissolved the old German Confederation and placed the Prussian state, as Sybel’s national chronicle presents it, at the head of a reordered Germany. The Peace of Prague, closing the war, excluded Austria from the German body and drew the line of the Main across the middle of the country: to the north lay the states that Prussia proposed to unite under its leadership, to the south the four states — Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse-Darmstadt — that for the moment remained outside the new Bund. The northern annexations of 1866 had rounded out the Prussian territory that was to be the weight of the new construction. It was out of this settlement, and on the basis of the kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch decision taken in the war, that the constitutional work of the Confederation proceeded under otto-von-bismarck.
The framing of the federal constitution
The constitutional text took shape in the winter of 1866–67. Sybel describes how the original draft, associated with the name of Augustenburg, was reworked under Bismarck’s hand to secure the predominance of Prussia. The central organs were two. At the head stood the Bundespräsidium (federal presidency), which rested inalienably in the King of Prussia, who was to exercise the office of the Confederation through his chancellor; beside it sat the Bundesrat (federal council), composed of the representatives of the several member states, in which the votes were distributed so that the larger members could not outvote Prussia. The whole device was, as Sybel’s analysis of the balance between presidency and council makes plain, an instrument for reconciling the formal equality of the German states with the real supremacy of Prussia — the same device which Bismarck had already made familiar in the Zollverein and which he now applied to the political federation.
The constituent Reichstag and the Indemnity Bill
The constitution was submitted to a constituent Reichstag, elected by manhood suffrage across the northern states, which met and debated it in 1867. Sybel records the first session of the North German Reichstag and the debates over the federal constitution, the military budgets and the fiscal basis of the new state. A leading act of the session was the Indemnity Bill, by which the federal parliament regularised the expenditure which the government had incurred before parliamentary sanction. In the same months the Reichstag went on to the legislative work of the new state — the military laws that placed the contingents of the member states under a common federal military system, and the fiscal and legal harmonisation which slowly drew the separate states together. In Sybel’s framing this first federal parliament, elected by a suffrage wider than that of most of the member states, was the national organ that gave the Confederation its political life.
The reform of the Zollverein
Parallel to the political constitution ran the recasting of the Zollverein (Customs Union), the economic union of the German states whose treaties the war had thrown open. Sybel’s account of the new Zollverein treaties describes the economic integration of the annexed territories and the pressure brought on the southern German states to accept the new terms, linking economic unity with the political unification proceeding in the North. The Zollbundesrat (federal customs council) consolidated the union as an instrument of Prussian policy, while the particularist interests of the South resisted the encroachment. This double movement — a political federation above, a customs union beneath — meant that even the southern states that stood outside the Bund were drawn into a tightening German economic order. In 1868 the first Zollparlament (customs parliament) brought deputies of the North German Confederation and of the southern states together in one assembly, giving the Reichstag of the Bund a forum that reached across the Main, as Sybel records in the opening of the following volume.
The military conventions
A final and decisive strand of the new order was military. Secret conventions between Prussia and the southern German states — Baden, Bavaria, Württemberg and Hesse-Darmstadt — placed their armies under Prussian command in time of war. These arrangements, concluded outside the constitutional frame of the Bund, completed the military unity of Germany and were, as the German and French sources alike recognise, the step that would prove decisive when war came in 1870.
Consequences
The North German Confederation answered the Norddeutsche Frage that the war had posed, but it left the German question unfinished. To the South it reached only through the customs union and the military conventions; the southern states remained sovereign, their union with the North still pending. The Confederation thus embodied the Kleindeutsch programme in an intermediate form — a permanent Prussian-led federation of the North, holding the South in economic and military dependence without having absorbed it politically. That incomplete settlement set the terms of the next decade: the german-question remained open across the Main, the Zollverein and the conventions bound the South ever more tightly, and the European powers — above all napoleon-iii and the second-empire-france — watched the new German power with alarm. When the crisis of 1870 came, the machinery of the Bund, its Reichstag and its railways and armies, stood ready to be enlarged into the German Empire, german-empire-proclaimed-1871.

events/occupation-of-bosnia-1878.title: The Occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina (1878)
events/occupation-of-bosnia-1878.content:
The Occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina (1878)
Late July–November 1878
The Austro-Hungarian military occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, undertaken in the late summer and autumn of 1878 under the mandate of the Congress of Berlin, was the monarchy’s first great act on the Balkan stage of the period. Under the terms of Article 25 of the Berlin treaty Austria-Hungary was to occupy and administer the two provinces, but the task proved to be a hard campaign rather than a peaceful entry: the Austro-Hungarian army, advancing in several columns, met armed resistance from the local population, fought a series of engagements, and took the provincial capital Sarajevo only after heavy fighting on 19 August 1878. The occupation gave the monarchy its principal Balkan acquisition, laid the foundations of thirty years of administration, and opened the road that led to the annexation of 1908.
Background: the mandate and the eve of the entry
The occupation followed directly upon the Berlin settlement, which had given Austria-Hungary the mandate to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina while the Sultan’s formal sovereignty was reserved. The diplomacy of gyula-andrassy had prepared the ground: the monarchy’s Balkan programme, the agreement with Russia at Reichstadt, and the last-moment protocol at Berlin all pointed to the entry. The condition of the provinces strengthened the case — Bosnia and Herzegovina lay under Turkish rule in a state of anarchy, agrarian misery and confessional hatred, and the Austro-Hungarian claim rested on the responsibility of the monarchy to restore order and security on its eastern frontier.
Sosnosky’s account of the eve of the entry (Vor dem Einmarsch) describes the military preparations of the monarchy and the theatre of operations. The task was not expected to be easy: the two provinces, mountainous and difficult of access, were peopled by a population that regarded the coming of foreign troops with mistrust, and the Austro-Hungarian command prepared for resistance. The occupation troops — whose order of battle Sosnosky appends for the beginning of August 1878 — were organised to advance into the country and to overcome whatever opposition the country might offer.
The campaign
The campaign was fought as a series of columns converging on the interior. Sosnosky’s account of the occupation divides the operations into the several columns — the central, the right and the left — and the separate theatres: the operations in Herzegovina, the march on Sarajevo, the operations in the Posavina and the Župa, the renewed fighting in Herzegovina, the operations in southern Bosnia and in northwestern Bosnia, and finally the return home. The resistance was more serious than the monarchy had allowed: the insurgent forces, the Streitkräfte der Insurgenten, met the Austro-Hungarian army with determined opposition, and the occupation required a real war rather than a ceremonial entry.
The decisive moment was the capture of Sarajevo on 19 August 1878. The march on the provincial capital and its storming were the climax of the campaign, and after the fall of the city the Austro-Hungarian forces regrouped, pursued the remaining resistance in the outlying districts, and gradually reduced the country to submission. The fighting in Herzegovina, in the Posavina and the Župa, and in the south and northwest of the country dragged on through the autumn, and the final return home of the occupation troops came only after the whole country had been brought under the monarchy’s control.
The cost and the meaning
Sosnosky closes his account of the occupation with a summing-up of the campaign, its cost and its meaning. The occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was bought with real losses — the fighting had been sharp and the country difficult to subdue — but it gave the monarchy the prize that its Balkan policy had sought since the crisis of 1875–78. The provinces became an Austro-Hungarian acquisition administered from Vienna, and the monarchy, which had retired from Germany after 1866, found in the East the field of its renewed greatness. The occupation was the origin of the Dual Monarchy’s most lasting Balkan commitment: thirty years of administration followed, and the provisional character of the mandate — the Sultan’s sovereignty reserved at Berlin — carried within it the ambiguity that Aehrenthal resolved by the annexation of 1908. The road from the occupation of 1878 to the annexation crisis is the central thread of the monarchy’s Eastern policy in the period, and the occupation stands as its beginning.

events/october-manifesto-1905.title: The October Manifesto (1905)
events/october-manifesto-1905.content:
The October Manifesto (1905)
17 October 1905
The manifesto “On the Improvement of the State Order” (Об усовершенствовании государственного порядка), issued by nicholas-ii on 17 October 1905, which granted the empire’s population the unshakable foundations of civil liberty and promised the broad participation of the people in the work of the State Duma. For all that was to follow, Witte judged it a document that “will constitute an epoch in the history of Russia,” and it marks the hinge between the old autocracy-russia of the Romanovs and the experiment of duma-constitutionalism that ran, through every limit and evasion, to the eve of the world war.
Background: the year of troubles
The manifesto was the culminating act of the revolution-1905 that had convulsed the empire through the year. In Witte’s account the sovereign and his government were pushed step by step from one concession to the next. The catastrophe of “Bloody Sunday” on 9 January, when workers marching to the Winter Palace to present a petition were fired upon, had broken the tsar’s hold on the loyalty of the labouring masses. The defeats of the russo-japanese-war-1904-05 and the annihilation of the fleet at Tsushima had discredited the state before the army and the nation. The assassination of the interior ministers, the attempt on the life of Bogolepov and then of Sipyagin, and the harsh course of Plehve had left the government without able men. After Plehve’s death the “spring” of Svyatopolk-Mirsky promised concessions, and the ukase of 12 December 1904 spoke of the establishment of legality. In February 1905 came a manifesto on disorders and troubles and the ukase to Bulygin on drawing in “the best people” to a consultative assembly.
The autumn of 1905 was the breaking point. The peace of Portsmouth, concluded with the mediation of the American president in September, had been Witte’s own triumph, and he returned to Petersburg at the height of his prestige. But the war’s end did not quiet the country; instead the revolutionary movement surged forward, crowned by the great political strike of October that paralysed the railways, the factories and the universities. The government had to choose between the fullest repression, which threatened civil war, and a grant of constitutional liberties. Witte, who had for years urged the necessity of a constitutional order as the only alternative to revolution, carried the day. It was in this atmosphere of strike and uncertainty that the decision for the manifesto was made.
The eve and the drafting
Witte’s own account dwells on the confused and half-secret preparation. On the eve of 17 October he conferred with the moderate figures of Petersburg society — the conversations of the Naryshkina circle and others — sounding out the ground for a constitutional reform. The sovereign hesitated at Peterhof, weighing the competing counsels of the conservatives, who saw in any concession the end of the monarchy, and of those, like Witte, who insisted that a constitution alone could save the dynasty and the state. Witte prepared a report as chairman of the Committee of Ministers, setting out the necessity of civil liberty and of a legislative assembly, and pressed it upon the emperor. The report was submitted with the imperial inscription “accept for guidance,” and the manifesto was drawn in its spirit. In Witte’s telling the whole thing moved with extraordinary speed: the decision once taken, the text of the manifesto was issued on 17 October, and the report was published alongside it.
The text of 17 October
The manifesto opened with the sorrow of the sovereign before the смута — “the disorders and troubles in the capitals and in many parts of the empire fill our heart with great and heavy grief.” The good of the Russian sovereign, it declared, was inseparable from the good of the people, and the people’s grief was his own. From the troubles that had arisen might come a deep disorder of the nation and a threat to the integrity and unity of the all-Russian realm; the great vow of the tsar’s service commanded the sovereign to strive with all the forces of reason and power toward the speedy ending of so dangerous a disorder. It then laid down three imperatives upon the government:

To grant the population the unshakable foundations of civil liberty, “on the basis of real inviolability of the person, freedom of conscience, speech, assembly and association.”
Without halting the projected elections to the State Duma, to draw into participation in the Duma those classes of the population which were then wholly deprived of electoral rights, leaving the further development of universal suffrage to the newly established legislative order.
To establish as an unshakable rule that no law could take force without the approval of the State Duma, and that the people’s representatives should be secured a real share in supervising the legality of the acts of the authorities.

The manifesto closed by calling on all faithful sons of Russia to remember their duty to the fatherland and to help end the unheard-of смута, straining with the sovereign to restore tranquillity and peace to the native land. It was a document that acknowledged the reality of revolution while invoking the sacred bond of tsar and people — the voice of autocracy trying to speak in the language of the constitutional state.
The new government
The manifesto alone did not establish the new order; that required the machinery of a responsible government, and here Witte took the decisive step. On 19 October, two days after the manifesto, was published the law “On Measures to Strengthen the Unity of the Activity of the Ministers and Chief Administrations,” which created a true Council of Ministers, and on the same day Witte was appointed its first prime minister — a cabinet premier with a right of influence over all the ministers, save only the war, naval and, in some degree, the interior ministries. The published report set out the programme of the new cabinet: the consolidation of the empire, the conduct of elections, the establishment of the Duma and of the civil liberties promised. For a half-year Witte was, in effect, the first constitutional prime minister of Russia, the man called upon to reconcile the promise of 17 October with the survival of the monarchy.
Consequences: the half-year premiership
The manifesto split the liberal and revolutionary camps. For the Constitutional Democrats and the moderates it was the threshold of a constitutional order, the “constitution” they had demanded; for the socialists and much of the street it was an evasion to be carried further by force. The revolutionary movement, far from disarming, redoubled in the weeks that followed: Witte governed amid “complete confusion” of the empire, the disorders of the countryside and the punitive expeditions of the winter of 1905–06, while the Social Democrats and the Socialist-Revolutionaries held to the call for a constituent assembly and the abolition of private property in land. The government answered with both repression and concession: the amnesty, the electoral law, and the preparation of the Fundamental Laws of 1906, which defined the powers of the new Duma within the framework of an autocracy that still claimed the title of “supreme self-rule.”
To liquidate the costs of the war and to restore the finances shaken by the revolution, Witte raised the great foreign loan of 1906 — the loan that, in his own estimate and that of his critics, enabled the monarchy to survive its first constitutional crisis. He also presided over the resumption of orderly government: the settlement of the Finnish question, the beginnings of the electoral machinery. In April 1906, worn down by the right’s hostility and the left’s intransigence, he resigned. The First Duma met that spring under his successors as a “Duma of popular retribution” or of inexperience, and was dissolved within months; after the Second Duma came the state coup of 3 June 1907, which altered the electoral law under pyotr-stolypin and narrowed the franchise. Yet the structure the manifesto had set — an elected legislature with a voice over the law and the budget — outlived Witte’s fall. Strained, limited, and repeatedly evaded, it endured through the Stolypin years as the fragile constitutionalism that the world war would finally break.

events/october-revolution-1917.title: The October Revolution (1917)
events/october-revolution-1917.content:
The October Revolution (1917)
25 October 1917
The seizure of power in Petrograd by the Bolsheviks of vladimir-lenin on the night of 25 October (7 November) 1917, the overthrow of the Provisional Government of alexander-kerensky, and the establishment of the government of the Soviets — followed within months by the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly and the beginnings of one-party rule. Denikin, a prisoner at Bykhov through these weeks, recorded both the strange ease of the coup and the fatal consequences of the “non-resistance” that had preceded it.
Background: the drift to the coup
The kornilov-affair-1917 had been the turning point. In destroying the Supreme Commander and the command, Kerensky had disarmed the state; Denikin’s verdict was that the “victory” over Kornilov was the “prelude to Bolshevism.” By the autumn the government was left solitary — “an army without leaders, administration without an army,” he wrote — while the soviets, step by step, gathered the real power into their hands. The failure of the summer, the collapse of the front before the German occupation of the Moonsund islands, the starvation of the cities and the ruin of transport, all discredited the Provisional Government. The condition of the army in September and October, undermined by the soldiers’ committees and by the war ministry’s “adaptation to soviet moods,” left no force on which the government could rely.
The Bolsheviks, alone among the parties, had drawn the lesson of the summer. In the first period of the revolution, to October, their aim had been to break the “bourgeois order” and to disorganise the army; now they turned to the seizure of power itself. Their two great slogans — peace and land — and their demand for the transfer of all power to the soviets carried them into the ranks of the garrison, the workers and the peasantry. Lenin, returned from exile in April, had set the party on this course; his theses on arrival, quoted by Denikin, marked the break with the moderate socialists. The soviet democracy, which had declined power in February, found itself outflanked by a party that would take it.
The coup
The coup itself was almost bloodless. In the early hours of 25 October the Bolshevik committees, the Red Guards and the revolutionary garrison seized the key points of the capital — the stations, the bridges, the telegraph, the banks; the Winter Palace, where the Provisional Government sat, was taken that night with the arrest of the ministers. Kerensky fled Petrograd to raise troops, but the garrison refused to fight, and the “Gatchina” episode — the last attempt of his dictatorship — ended in his flight abroad and the final collapse of his authority. Denikin stressed the causes of the astonishing “non-resistance”: the universal fatigue, the seduction of the slogans of land and peace, and the discipline of a small, organised minority against a disorganised majority. Lenin himself, Denikin recalled, had earlier quoted the 1905 lesson of the impossibility of immediate socialism; yet now the party seized the state. At Stavka and at Bykhov, where the Kornilov officers lay under arrest, the reaction was one of fatalism and disarray; the command, like the government, had no answer to a coup born of the very disorder it had been powerless to cure.
The new regime and the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly
In the first days the new government of the Soviets — the Sovnarkom, the Council of People’s Commissars, under Lenin — issued a torrent of decrees: the armistice and the call for peace, the nationalisation of the land, workers’ control, and the self-determination of peoples. Many, even among its own opponents, believed the regime would not last two weeks; Denikin recorded that general expectation of ephemerality. But the soviets, and the committees, proved unexpectedly tenacious. The old army dissolved into the countryside as the soldiers answered the land decree and the call for peace, and the regime, far from collapsing, consolidated its hold on the capital and then on the provinces.
The decisive test came with the Constituent Assembly, for which elections had been held in November and which was to decide the constitution of Russia. The Bolsheviks had won only a minority of the seats; rather than surrender power to a body dominated by the Socialist-Revolutionaries, they dispersed the Assembly by force when it met in January 1918 — the suppression of the one body in which the democratic revolution had placed its hopes, and the moment that made clear the coup was not a revolution of the people but the rule of a party. The assassination of the former supreme commander Dukhonin, murdered by the mob when the new government turned against the old Stavka, marked the same abandonment of the forms of the fallen order. From Bykhov the imprisoned officers watched these events with a growing conviction that the regime would neither fall of itself nor be removed by any legal means.
Consequences
The October coup transformed the character of the Russian revolution and of the whole war. In foreign policy it led directly to the separate peace of the treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918, which took Russia out of the world war and released German divisions for the west; in internal affairs it began the suppression of all rival parties and the concentration of power in the Bolshevik Central Committee. The decrees on land, on workers’ control and on national self-determination dissolved the old bonds of the empire and set the borderlands into motion, beginning the civil conflicts of the south and the west.
For the officers imprisoned at Bykhov, the coup was the signal for escape: released amid the collapse of the old Stavka, Kornilov, Denikin and their comrades made their way to the Don, where mikhail-alexeyev had already begun the “Alekseev organisation” that would become the white-movement’s Volunteer Army. The February revolution’s promise of a democratic duma-constitutionalism had ended; in its place arose the dictatorship of the proletariat, and with it the civil war that was to consume Russia for three years. The ice-march-1918 was the first fruit of that struggle, and the whole of the White resistance its prolongation.

events/paris-commune-1871.title: Paris Commune (18 March – 28 May 1871)
events/paris-commune-1871.content:
Paris Commune (18 March – 28 May 1871)
18 March – 28 May 1871
The insurrectionary government of Paris that defied the National Assembly of Versailles after the defeats of 1870–71, and that was suppressed in the Bloody Week of May 1871. The Commune — at once a municipal revolt, a social revolution, and a reassertion of the revolutionary tradition of Paris — posed the most dangerous challenge to the nascent third-republic-france and was crushed with a ferocity that left a deep mark on French politics. Hanotaux recounts it as a civil war within the defeat.
Background
Paris, which had endured the siege-of-paris-1870-71 and had been starved and bombarded by the Germans, found the peace of the new National Assembly intolerable. The Assembly, elected by a rural France resolved on peace, sat at Versailles and treated the republican capital with suspicion; the city was garrisoned by a National Guard armed and enraged, and the war’s suffering had radicalized the working districts. Hanotaux traces the explosion to the Assembly’s measures and to the attempt to seize the guns of Montmartre on 18 March 1871. The attempt to disarm the capital detonated the insurrection; the government and the regular army withdrew to Versailles, and the Commune proclaimed itself master of Paris.
The Commune
For two months there existed a dual power: Versailles and the Commune. Hanotaux describes the composition and factions of the revolutionary government — the Central Committee, the International, the Blanquists and Jacobins, the old revolutionary currents revived in a new context. The Commune was a municipal and social experiment, a government of the working city asserting its autonomy and its revolutionary heritage against a conservative Assembly. Meanwhile the national government under adolphe-thiers regrouped the regular army at Versailles and prepared to retake the capital.
The suppression and the Bloody Week
The military operations of the civil war followed: the siege of Paris by the Versailles army under Marshal patrice-mac-mahon, the provincial risings put down one by one, and finally the assault of May 1871. The Bloody Week (la semaine sanglante), the last days of the Commune’s resistance and its crushing, was one of the bloodiest episodes in modern French history. The communards, their barricades overwhelmed, were executed in large numbers as the army reoccupied the city; the vengeance of the victorious Versailles troops matched the fury of the insurrection. Hanotaux records the repression and its legal and political aftermath — the courts-martial, the transportations, the years of mourning that followed.
Consequences
The Commune fixed the terms of French politics for a generation. For the conservative Assembly and for Thiers it justified the restoration of order; the suppression confirmed Versailles as the seat of national authority and made possible the completion of the peace and the payment of the treaty-of-frankfurt-1871 indemnity. For the French Left the Commune became a founding martyrdom — the proof of the Republic’s capacity for slaughter and the seed of the revolutionary socialist tradition. The blood of the Bloody Week separated the bourgeois Republic from the workers of Paris and fed the socialism that would return, in different forms, through the Boulanger years, the dreyfus-affair-1894-1906, and the twentieth century. In the immediate present, the defeat of the Commune allowed the National Assembly to turn from civil war to the constitutional struggle over the form of the state.
Sources

events/peace-of-prague-1866.title: Peace of Prague (23 August 1866)
events/peace-of-prague-1866.content:
Peace of Prague (23 August 1866)
August 23, 1866
Background
The Peace of Prague was the treaty that ended the Austro-Prussian War. It was the culmination of a
rapid sequence of negotiations that began immediately after the decisive Prussian victory at
Königgrätz on 3 July 1866. Vienna, its army broken and the road to its capital laid open, sought
peace at once; the preliminary terms were agreed at Nikolsburg, where the negotiations opened in the
days after the battle, and the definitive treaty was then concluded and signed in Prague on 23
August 1866.
Throughout these weeks Napoleon III hovered over the settlement as a would-be mediator. He had
proposed a European congress in the spring and now sought to limit Prussia’s gains and to win
compensation for France, but his intervention proved ineffective. Sybel observes of France’s
passivity that by declining to take part in the settlement, Paris surrendered any right to object to
changes in a treaty whose conclusion it had not shared — a pointed comment on the French position,
and a warning of the resentment that was already gathering in Paris at the sudden consolidation of
Prussian power.
The Terms
The Peace of Prague settled the German question decisively in Prussia’s favour. The German
Confederation was dissolved and never revived; Austria was excluded from the political life of
Germany, ending centuries of Habsburg primacy in German affairs and leaving the future of Germany to
be shaped by Prussia alone. The terms, as Sybel’s final book, Grundlagen des neuen Reichs
(“Foundations of the new Reich”), records them, also provided for Prussia’s annexation of Hanover,
Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, and the free city of Frankfurt, sweeping away the medium states that had stood
in the path of Prussian hegemony.
The settlement was, in essence, the Kleindeutsch programme realised by force of arms. Prussia had
fought the war, won it, and now imposed on Germany a structure from which Austria was excluded
entirely. The older vision of a Germany that might include the Habsburg monarchy in a Grossdeutsch
union was dead, buried at Königgrätz and Prague.
The Italian Settlement
Italy, Prussia’s ally, also made peace. Though beaten at Custoza and Lissa, Italy received Venetia —
occupied “without a struggle” once Prussia had won — and an uneasy Italian claim to Welschtirol
(Trentino) was refused. The Italian government, irritated at the five-day armistice that Bismarck
had concluded without its consent and disappointed at being denied Trentino, chafed under the
settlement, but had little choice but to accept what Prussia had won for it.
Bismarck, unruffled by the Italian complaints, held firm that Prussia had neither made armistice nor
peace without Italy’s being consulted, only granting a cessation of hostilities in order to
negotiate; and if Prussian troops rested five days, he observed, they did no more than the Italian
army had done for weeks after Custoza. Italy, in the end, took Venetia and made its peace, and the
Italian theatre was closed.
Consequences
The Peace of Prague transformed the map and constitution of Germany. With Austria excluded and the
Confederation gone, Prussia proceeded to construct the North German Confederation, the Prussian-led
federal state that became the scaffolding of the eventual German Empire. The foundations of the new
Reich, as Sybel titles his final book, were laid directly upon the peace, and the work of Prussian
unification that Bismarck had begun in 1862 reached its constitutional fulfilment.
The peace also left Austria humiliated but intact. Excluded from Germany and stripped of Venetia,
the Habsburg monarchy turned inward to rebuild its internal structure, and the task of reconciling
the empire to its expulsion fell to the Ausgleich of the following year — the Compromise with
Hungary that rebuilt the monarchy as Austria-Hungary. The settlement of 1866, moreover, created the
very conditions of the next great war: Prussia’s new pre-eminence in Germany, sealed at Prague, was
the challenge that brought the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 and, with it, the proclamation of the
German Empire at Versailles.
Sources

events/revolution-1905.title: Russian Revolution of 1905
events/revolution-1905.content:
Russian Revolution of 1905
1905
Background
The revolution of 1905 was the explosion of long-accumulated social and political tensions under the
impact of the disastrous war with Japan. In S. Yu. Witte’s analysis,
the rule of nicholas-ii through a “court-noble camarilla” had denied the people the economic and
social reforms they demanded; and when the government systematically refuses such demands, he
argued, the people come to the conviction that their wishes cannot be satisfied under the existing
regime, their economic and social demands are pushed aside, and political demands ripen as the means
of obtaining transformation. If the government does not wisely regulate this current, and especially
if it commits some madness such as the Japanese war, revolution breaks out. The war proved that
madness.
The ground had also been prepared by the police-created workers’ organizations introduced by
Interior Minister Plehve and known as “zubatovshchina,” in which the priest Gapon was invited to act
as leader of the workers. Witte had predicted that these organizations, designed to keep the workers
in police hands, would in time shake off their police direction and take up, in one degree or
another, socialist principles of struggle with capital — not only by peaceful means but by force.
When in 1903 the vague revolutionary ferment began, all the workers’ organizations absorbed the
revolutionary spirit, and the wave of assassinations that struck the ministers of the reaction —
Bogolepov in 1901, Sipyagin in 1902, Plehve himself in 1904 — signaled the collapse of the police
system.
The “spring” of Svyatopolk-Mirsky and the ukase of 12 December 1904
After the murder of Plehve, the new minister of internal affairs, Prince Svyatopolk-Mirsky,
attempted a policy of conciliation — a “spring” of good will toward society. His course culminated
in the ukase of 12 December 1904, which promised various measures toward the “establishment of
legality.” But the concessions came too slowly and too late to satisfy the demand for a
representative assembly, and the defeats of the war continued to inflame opinion. The government,
Witte recalled, was caught between reaction and concession, issuing measures that were at once “the
most retrograde and cruel, and at the same time madly liberal by their untimeliness.” The emperor
and the empress, Witte noted, believed that the whole people stood behind the autocracy and only the
“intelligentsia” against it — a conviction that led the government to appeal over the head of
educated society to the peasantry.
Bloody Sunday (9 January 1905)
The crisis of the old order came on 9 January 1905. The immediate occasion was a traditional
ceremony: on 6 January, at the Epiphany procession when the emperor stood with the clergy and
brilliant suite at the blessing of the water, one of the cannon firing from the Peter and Paul
Fortress across the Neva turned out to be loaded with a live, if very antiquated, charge. The shot
could have caused a great catastrophe had it reached the pavilion, but the investigation showed a
simple blunder and a mere accident; nicholas-ii treated the men who had made the mistake with
great kindness. Yet in many strata of society the incident was treated as an attempt on the tsar’s
life or at least on his peace.
Less than three days later came the well-known procession of workers under the leadership of the
priest Gapon. The workers prepared a petition to the emperor, containing demands touching their
existence — one-sided, exaggerated, not without a certain coloring of revolutionism, though written
in a fairly seemly form. Gapon was to lead many thousands of workers to the Palace Square to bow
before the emperor; they imagined that they would see his majesty, hand him their request, and
quietly depart. The police chief, General Fullon, who had trusted Gapon entirely, treated the
movement as nothing serious.
On the evening of 8 January the government met to decide what to do. Witte, as chairman of the
Committee of Ministers, was deliberately not invited, at the request of Kokovtsov, so that he would
not support the workers’ interests. Instead a delegation came to him — including the honorary
academician Arsenyev, the writer Annensky, and Maxim Gorky — begging him to take measures so that
the emperor should appear before the workers and receive their petition, or else bloodshed would
follow. Witte, whose office gave him no authority in the matter, declined to intervene; the
delegation left dissatisfied.
On the morning of 9 January Witte saw from his balcony a great crowd of workers with banners, icons,
and flags — many women and children among them, and many curious onlookers — moving toward the
Trinity Bridge. As he watched, a shot was fired, several bullets flew past, and then a systematic
series of shots followed. Within ten minutes a large crowd streamed back along the Kamennoostrovsky
Prospekt, many carrying wounded and dead, adults and children. The decision taken on the evening of
the 8th had been that the demonstrating workers should be allowed up to certain limits near the
Palace Square but not onto the square itself. When the workers approached, troops met them and
demanded they go no further or turn back, warning that otherwise they would be fired on. The
workers, not believing they would be shot, did not withdraw; everywhere volleys followed, and, as
Witte recalled, more than two hundred people were killed and wounded.
The event, he wrote, was the first blood shed in considerable quantity, and it seemed to inaugurate
the broad current of what was called the Russian revolution of 1905. It was used by those who led
the unrest to inflame the people further; exaggerated reports that thousands had been killed spread
over the whole of Russia. Even among prudent people the affair made a very bad impression, and it
produced confusion not only in society but in the ranks of the government itself, which criticized
the weak-kneed minister Svyatopolk-Mirsky. Gapon disappeared and fled. “Bloody Sunday,” as it came
to be called, marked the irreparable breach between the autocracy and the people it had once
commanded.
From Bloody Sunday to the Bulygin Duma
Through the spring and summer of 1905 the unrest widened into strikes, agrarian disorders, mutinies
in the fleet, and assassinations of officials. The government, attempting to answer the demand for
representation, issued in February 1905 a manifesto on disorders and a ukase to Bulygin “on drawing
in the best people,” and on 6 August published a law on a consultative Duma — the Bulygin Duma —
based, on the insistence of the empress, the tutor Pobedonostsev, and
State Controller Chobko, on giving the decisive voice to the peasantry, whom the court believed
loyal to the throne. The electoral law rested on the belief that the Duma should be predominantly a
peasant assembly, and that this was the historical foundation of conservatism. The law satisfied no
one, and the failure of the war, crowned by Tsushima, and the continued denial of real reform drove
the movement on. Witte’s verdict on the peasantry’s supposed conservatism was blunt: the first two
Dumas returned “the most extreme left elements and a mass of revolutionaries.”
The general strike and the soviets
In October the unrest became a national general strike. On 8 October 1905 the movement on the
railways converging on Moscow ceased; on the 10th the Kharkov railway junction stopped, on the 12th
the Petersburg junction, and in the following days movement on all the other railways, with the
telegraph, died away. By 17 October almost the whole railway network was at a standstill. Nearly all
the factories and mills of the large industrial centers had stopped work; in Petersburg the
factories began to strike on 12 October, and by the 15th the business life of the capital had
entirely ceased.
It was in this atmosphere that the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies (Совет рабочих депутатов) arose in
Petersburg. The idea of instituting it took shape at the beginning of October and was propagated by
the press. Its first meeting was held on 13 October at the Technological Institute, which issued an
appeal to the workers calling for a strike and for extreme political demands; a second meeting
followed on the 14th, at which the chairman elected was Nossar (Khroustalev), an assistant of a
sworn attorney of Jewish origin who had entered a factory as a weaver for the purpose of propaganda.
Almost all the Petersburg workers began to obey the Soviet’s decisions unquestioningly. At its
meeting of 17 October, held in the hall of the Free Economic Society, the number of members already
exceeded two hundred, and an executive committee of thirty was elected; on the same day the Soviet’s
newspaper, the Izvestiya of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies, a purely revolutionary organ, began
to be printed in the various printing-houses. The Soviet’s control over the printers, Witte noted,
placed the daily press in a certain dependence upon it, so that the newspapers hung on the will of
the workers even for their very appearance.
The Manifesto of 17 October
Under the pressure of the general strike, and after long hesitation, nicholas-ii on 17 October
1905 issued the Manifesto “On the improvement of the state order” — the
October Manifesto — granting civil liberties and promising a legislative
Duma elected by a widened franchise, and appointing Witte chairman of the Council
of Ministers. Witte’s account is explicit that the manifesto was the work of the sovereign, pressed
upon him by events; Witte himself had urged the safer course of a rescript setting out a programme
rather than a manifesto read aloud in all the churches, precisely so that responsibility would fall
on his ministry and not bind the emperor.
The manifesto, however, did not immediately quiet the country. On 18 October the Soviet of Workers’
Deputies met and resolved to propose a general strike, since the manifesto did not satisfy the
working masses. Yet by 19 October the strike in Moscow and elsewhere began to subside and the
railways resumed movement, and the Soviet itself resolved on the same day to end the strike from 21
October. In the days after the manifesto there were clashes on the streets between revolutionaries,
troops, police, and counter-revolutionaries, in which several people were killed and, among others,
the Petersburg professor Tarle was wounded in the head near the Technological Institute. The
government permitted calm processions in honor of 17 October but suppressed any that aimed at
disorder, and within a few days quiet was restored in the capital.
Consequences
The revolution of 1905 forced the transformation of the autocracy into a
constitutional monarchy on paper. The Manifesto of 17 October, the
Fundamental Laws of 1906, and the convening of the State Duma were the
institutional fruits of the upheaval. The government of Witte lasted only about
half a year as a “cabinet”; he resigned in April 1906, to be succeeded by the ministries of
Goremykin and then Stolypin. The regime survived the immediate crisis through a combination of
concession and repression — Witte described the empire as descending into “complete confusion,” with
punitive expeditions against the disorders — and through the great foreign loan of 1906, which
liquidated the war expenditures and stabilized the shaken finances.
But the revolution was not wholly suppressed. Witte’s bitter retrospective judgment was that the
opportunity was thrown away: had the emperor made the peasant and other reforms himself after
Portsmouth, there would have been no 17 October; and because, after the revolution was put down, the
government “played to the right and to the left,” the country slid toward anarchy. The first
experiment in constitutionalism, the First and Second Dumas, ended in the “state coup” of 3 June
1907, which altered the electoral law to secure a conservative majority. The revolution of 1905
established the soviets as a form, foreshadowed the revolution of 1917, and left unresolved the very
conflicts — over land, labor, nationality, and political power — that had produced it.
Key participants

nicholas-ii — Emperor, who conceded the October Manifesto and appointed Witte.
sergei-witte — Chairman of the Council of Ministers after the manifesto; author of the programme of concession.
Father Gapon — priest who led the 9 January procession.
Svyatopolk-Mirsky — liberalizing interior minister discredited by Bloody Sunday.
Nossar (Khroustalev) — chairman of the Petersburg Soviet of Workers’ Deputies.

Sources













SourceTreatmentWitte — Memoirs, Vols. 2–3Vol. 2 treats the ukase of 12 December 1904, 9 January (ch. 41), the Bulygin Duma (ch. 49), and the eve of October (ch. 51); Vol. 3 treats the Manifesto of 17 October (ch. 52), the general strike, the Petersburg Soviet (ch. 56), the Duma, and the aftermath.

events/russo-japanese-war-1904-05.title: Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905)
events/russo-japanese-war-1904-05.content:
Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905)
1904–1905
Background
The war with Japan grew out of the Far Eastern policy pursued by Russia in the reign of
nicholas-ii. The impulse that drove Russia into the Pacific, S. Yu. Witte later traced to a
fatal divergence. As finance minister, Witte had concluded the treaty with China,
secured a loan guarantee, and built up the Russo-Chinese Bank and the Chinese Eastern Railway as the
instruments of a Russian sphere in northern China and Manchuria. The object of the new course was an
outlet to the open sea in the Far East — a scheme that Witte connected with the late
Alexander III’s attraction to the Russian North and his own advocacy of a naval
base on the Murman coast, a plan Nicholas II failed to adopt. In 1897 the government
seized the Liaodong Peninsula with its naval base of Port Arthur and the adjoining Dalny. From that
step, in Witte’s retrospective judgment, everything followed: “if we had not sought an outlet to the
open sea in the Far East,” he wrote, “there would have been no such ill-fated step as the seizure of
Port Arthur, and then, as we went ever downward, step by step, we should not have reached Tsushima.”
The conduct of the policy fell increasingly into the hands of an adventurer group around Bezobrazov,
and into conflict with the finance ministry that had built the railways and banks of the new sphere.
Witte, who pressed the view that Russia’s strength lay in the peaceful economic development of the
Far East and in agreement with Japan, found himself opposed by a court circle that sought expansion
on the cheap. In 1903 the influence of the Bezobrazov clique grew, and Witte, who opposed its rash
course, resigned as finance minister, remaining as chairman of the Committee of Ministers — a change
of position he came to regard as the moment when the emperor passed into the hands of the
adventurers. War Minister Kuropatkin remained in the government, and the negotiations with Japan
over Korea and Manchuria were conducted through the viceroy of the Far East, Alekseev, and dragged
on in a fashion that exasperated the Japanese government.
The road to war
Witte’s memoirs preserve the immediacy of the slide into conflict. The Japanese envoy in Petersburg,
Kurino — a clever man whose whole aim as envoy was that there should be no war — warned Witte that
the negotiations were being conducted so that Russia evidently wanted war. Japan gave answers
immediately, Russia only after weeks or months. Count Lamsdorf, the foreign minister, referred
questions to Alekseev; Alekseev and Rosen referred them to the emperor, who was away. In July 1903,
a month before Witte’s resignation from the finance ministry, Kurino presented to him and to
Lamsdorf a draft agreement between Japan and Russia on Far Eastern affairs which, had it been
accepted, would have removed the resolution of the Far Eastern question by means of war. Witte found
the agreement perfectly acceptable and insisted on it, but his insistence came to nothing: the draft
was sent to the viceroy Alekseev for his opinion and there it stuck. Endless negotiations dragged on
from July to January and ended in nothing.
In mid-January, at a court ball, Kurino approached Witte to warn him that he should urge the foreign
ministry to give a speedier answer to Japan’s last declaration; that a whole week had passed without
a reply, the negotiations being evidently deliberately slowed down; and that Japan had been driven
beyond patience — if no answer were given within a few days, war would break out. No timely answer
was given. On 26 January Japanese ships attacked the Russian squadron near Port Arthur and sank
several of the vessels; on 27 January the manifesto of war followed. The next day there was a solemn
thanksgiving service in the Winter Palace, and Witte notes the gloomy, oppressive mood. When the
emperor passed General Bogdanovich, who shouted “hurrah,” only a few voices joined in. The war,
Witte insists, was extremely unpopular from the first; the people did not want it, and most cursed
it. The administration organized a series of street demonstrations, but they met with no sympathy
whatever; from this alone, he wrote, no good results from the war could be expected.
Character of the war
Witte’s account is a portrait of miscalculation at the top. Interior Minister Plehve, when
Kuropatkin reproached him as the only minister who had wanted the war and had joined the band of
political adventurers, answered: “Alexei Nikolaevich, you do not know the internal position of
Russia. To hold back the revolution we need a little victorious war.” Witte comments acidly on this
“state wisdom and perspicacity.” nicholas-ii himself, he says, was deeply convinced that Japan,
though perhaps with some effort, would be beaten to pieces, and that there was nothing to fear over
money, since Japan would repay everything by means of an indemnity. In his early resolutions the
emperor’s usual expression for the Japanese was “these macaques,” a name taken up by the so-called
patriotic newspapers maintained on public money.
The command was as ill-conceived as the policy. The commander-in-chief was first the viceroy
Alekseev, who had never been a soldier, had had nothing to do with land forces, and had made his
naval career more by his diplomacy than by naval service. He was later withdrawn from Mukden and
replaced by Kuropatkin. The war was, in Witte’s verdict, “the unhappiest of unhappy wars,” and its
natural sequel was the revolution long prepared by the police-noble regime. He pitied the tsar, “a
good and not unintelligent man, but without will,” on whose weakness of character developed his
vices as an autocratic and unlimited ruler.
The war was fought at sea and on land across Manchuria and the approaches to Port Arthur, and step
by step the Russian position collapsed. The seizure of Port Arthur proved to be the fateful step
that dragged Russia from one defeat to the next, until the fleet was lost at Tsushima — the disaster
that gave its name to the chapter of Witte’s memoirs on the oscillation of opinion. The defeats at
the front ran parallel with the growth of domestic unrest, and the longer the war continued the less
confidence the government commanded. A reserve army was raised and held under arms, and the
prolonged employment of troops in police service at home “in considerable degree demoralized” the
forces that remained inside the empire — an element of the coming collapse.
Tsushima and the approach of peace
Witte frames the defeats as both military and political. The revolutionary unrest gathered strength as the war went badly, and the reverses in the Far East, by exposing the
weakness of the autocracy, fed the demand for internal change. By the summer of 1905 Russia, beaten
at sea and failing on land, and menaced even at home, had reached a point where continuation of the
war threatened the loss of Vladivostok, Kamchatka, and the adjacent islands, mastery over which had
passed wholly into the hands of the Japanese.
The disaster of Tsushima, and the impossibility of retrieving the position, brought the government
to seek peace. President Theodore Roosevelt of the United States offered his mediation, and
Witte was dispatched to America to conduct the negotiations at Portsmouth. His
mission succeeded where the war had failed: the peace concluded at Portsmouth — in Witte’s phrase,
“a peaceful victory” — stopped the senseless and unsuccessful bloodshed with relatively
insignificant sacrifices, saving Vladivostok and Kamchatka and ending a war that threatened to crown
Russia’s misfortunes with the loss of its remaining Far Eastern possessions. The immediate cost was
high: the lease of Port Arthur and the Liaodong Peninsula passed to Japan, together with the railway
line of South Manchuria, and the position in Korea was given over to Japanese preponderance. Yet the
peace restored at least the outward integrity of the empire, and the public, under the impression of
this act of “belated state wisdom,” breathed easier; the name of the man who had won an external
peace naturally came to mind for the task of internal pacification. For his services Witte was
raised to the rank of count.
Consequences
The Portsmouth peace came too late to save the government at home. The revolution of 1905 had already broken out, and the war had been one of its principal causes: it had drained
the treasury, discredited the autocracy, and left a reserve army whose men, held under arms after
the peace, began to ferment against an order that kept them from home. The failures of the war
discredited the old ministerial system and opened the way for the internal transformation of the
empire — the concessions that culminated in the Manifesto of 17 October 1905 and the institution of the Duma.
In Witte’s retrospective judgment the war was the great “madness” that, on top of the refusal of
necessary reform, precipitated revolution. Had the emperor himself, after the Portsmouth peace, on
his own initiative carried out a broad peasant reform in the spirit of Alexander II
and granted the long-overdue freedoms — had he, for example, freed the Old Believers from their
restraints and stood on the principle of religious toleration and the removal of unjust restrictions
on the non-Russian peoples — there would have been no need of 17 October. The Russian Revolution, he
wrote, was “long prepared by the police-noble regime”; the war brought it to the surface.
Key participants

nicholas-ii — Emperor of Russia, who carried the responsibility for the Far Eastern policy and the conduct of the war.
sergei-witte — Finance minister who opposed the adventurist course, then as envoy concluded the Portsmouth peace.
Kuropatkin — War minister, then commander-in-chief in the field.
Alekseev — Viceroy of the Far East, first commander-in-chief.
Plehve — Interior minister, advocate of the “little victorious war.”
Theodore Roosevelt — American president, mediator at Portsmouth.

Sources













SourceTreatmentWitte — Memoirs, Vols. 2–3Vol. 2 covers the Far Eastern policy, the treaty with China and the Chinese Eastern Railway, the seizure of Port Arthur, the negotiations with Japan, the war itself (ch. 38), Tsushima (ch. 44), and the Portsmouth peace (ch. 45); Vol. 3 treats the aftermath.

events/russo-turkish-war-1877-78.title: Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)
events/russo-turkish-war-1877-78.content:
Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)
1877–1878
Background
The war of 1877–1878 was the crisis in which the eastern-question — the long-standing question
of the fate of the Ottoman Empire’s European provinces and of the position of its Balkan Slavs —
finally brought Russia into open conflict with the Porte. In the account of A. A. Kornilov’s lecture
course, the ground had been laid over the preceding years by a policy that pressed outward on every
side. Government policy in the borderlands tightened: there were pressures in Little Russia and
Poland, and a foreign policy of expansion that set Russian and English interests at odds in Asia,
where the conquest of the Caucasus and of the Central Asian khanates extended the empire far beyond
its old frontiers.
Within Turkey itself troubles multiplied. The movement of the Balkan Slavs grew into insurrection,
and the Serbian war and the Bulgarian massacres turned the grievances of the South Slavs into a
cause that excited Russian society. The great powers entered a round of negotiations over the
condition of the Christian provinces of European Turkey, but these repeatedly failed to arrest the
drift toward war. The revolt of the South Slavs gave the Russian government both an opportunity and
a pretext for intervention in the affairs of the Ottoman Empire, and when the diplomatic path failed
the empire of alexander-ii resolved upon war.
Kornilov treats the war as one of the decisive episodes of Alexander’s reign, bound up with the
reaction at home and with the disillusionment that was soon to turn society against the government.
The war itself, and still more the peace that followed it, became a turning-point in the internal
history of Russia no less than in the Eastern Question.
The state of preparation
Kornilov is scathing about the military preparation. When war actually began, it emerged that the
state was not ready in any respect. The government was obliged to make mass issues of paper money,
which destroyed the plans of Finance Minister Reutern for restoring the exchange rate of the paper
ruble and undermined the careful financial edifice he had built through the reform era. The reforms
of War Minister Miliutin — above all the replacement of conscription by universal military service,
carried out only in 1874, two years before the mobilization of 1876 — were so new and had so
overturned the old structure of the army that carrying out a full mobilization proved far from easy.
The administrative authorities on whom the correctness and speed of mobilization depended proved to
be beneath all criticism, so that in the course of six months only an inadequate body of troops
could be brought to the Turkish frontiers.
Part of the blame Kornilov lays on Count Ignatiev, the Russian ambassador at Constantinople, who
asserted that the Turks could be beaten very easily, that Turkey was decaying, and that only very
small forces were needed to strike her a decisive blow. In reality there were not only too few
troops but an extremely badly chosen army staff. The commander-in-chief was the emperor’s brother,
Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaevich, a man entirely without the necessary strategic talents. As chief of
staff he chose General Nepokojchitsky, who in youth might have been capable, especially as a writer
on military questions, but was now quite out of date, distinguished by complete lack of
resourcefulness, and had no campaign plan whatever.
The first campaign and Plevna
Immediately after the brilliantly executed crossing of the Danube came complete disorganization. In
the absence of any general plan, the commanders of the separate detachments began to undertake
highly risky actions on their own initiative. The enterprising and brave General Gurko rushed
straight beyond the Balkans and, meeting no significant obstacles, was carried almost as far as
Adrianople. Meanwhile Osman Pasha, commanding several tens of thousands of Turkish troops, occupied
the unassailable position of Plevna in the rear of the Russian forces that had crossed the Balkans.
The storming of Plevna was repulsed, and it soon became clear that this was a place so unassailable
that Osman could not be driven out, and one had to think of a prolonged siege — for which there were
not enough troops to invest Plevna from all sides.
The position was dire. Had Suleiman Pasha, commanding the southern Turkish army then on the far side
of the Balkans, at once crossed the mountains as ordered and joined Osman, Gurko and the other
advanced detachments would have been cut off and destroyed. Only because Suleiman, apparently
competing with Osman, went to drive the Russians out of the Shipka Pass held by Radetsky instead of
crossing by a free pass, were the advanced detachments saved. Shipka was held, Suleiman was beaten
off by Radetsky, and Gurko was able to retreat safely while fresh Russian troops came up.
Plevna nevertheless had to be besieged for several months. The first attempt to take the Plevna
heights came in July 1877, and Osman Pasha could be compelled to surrender only in December, and
then only because the whole Guard, which could mobilize and be transported quickly, was summoned
from Petersburg to the theatre of war. It was also necessary to turn to Prince Karl of Romania, who
agreed to give his — small but well-trained and well-armed — army of thirty-five thousand only on
condition that he himself be named commander of the whole siege corps. Only with the arrival of the
engineer-general Totleben, summoned from Petersburg, did the siege of Plevna go properly, and Osman
Pasha at last had to lay down his arms after an unsuccessful attempt to break out.
The advance and the Adrianople armistice
The campaign thus dragged on through all of 1877 and part of 1878. After the capture of Plevna the
Russians crossed the Balkans once more, occupied Adrianople, which was not then a fortress, and
approached Constantinople in January 1878. At this point alexander-ii received a telegram from
Queen Victoria begging him to stop and conclude an armistice. Although the emperor had promised
England before the war that he would not seek to occupy Constantinople, Lord Beaconsfield had in
support of this telegram already got Parliament to vote six million pounds for war preparations, and
war with England seemed almost inevitable.
Turkey, however, was utterly exhausted and was compelled to sue for peace without waiting for
English support. In mid-January 1878 (new style) the Adrianople armistice was concluded, based on
the sultan’s promise to satisfy the demands of the great powers and to give a proper order — partly
in the form of semi-independent principalities, partly in the form of territories with Christian
governors-general — to the Christian provinces of European Turkey.
San Stefano and the Treaty of Peace
Shortly after the armistice diplomatic negotiations opened at San Stefano, conducted on the Russian
side by Ignatiev with complete success. In March the peace treaty was signed, satisfying all
Russia’s demands. Not only were Serbia and Montenegro enlarged, but Bulgaria became a
semi-independent principality with territory reaching to the Aegean Sea. In Asia the Russians had
waged war with far greater success than on the Balkan peninsula, taking Kars, Erzerum, and Batum. By
the peace treaty it was established that, in exchange for part of the war indemnity of 1,400 million
rubles which Turkey was to pay, she would cede to Russia, in the region of Asiatic Turkey and out of
the occupied territory, Kars and Batum with their districts. As an indispensable condition of peace,
the emperor Alexander also demanded the return of that strip of Bessarabia which in 1856 had been
separated from Russia and given to Romania; Romania, which had fought in alliance with Russia, was
greatly offended by this, and in compensation was given Dobruja.
The Congress of Berlin
No sooner did England learn of these conditions than Lord Beaconsfield protested against any
alteration of Turkish territory without the participation of the great powers that had taken part in
the Paris Congress of 1856. Alexander II therefore, in the end, under threat of a heavy war with
England and Austria, had to agree to a congress of representatives of the great powers at Berlin,
under the presidency of Bismarck. At this congress the conditions of peace were substantially
altered: the acquisitions of Serbia, Montenegro, and especially Bulgaria were cut down. From the
latter a whole region was detached south of the Balkans — Eastern Rumelia — which remained a Turkish
province with a Christian governor-general. Beaconsfield also protested against Russia’s territorial
acquisitions; he could not destroy them, but he succeeded in insisting that Batum be changed from a
military port into a peaceful harbor, open to all states.
In this way the conditions of peace were changed to Russia’s disadvantage. This, together with the
conduct of the war — which had produced a series of failures — and with the thievery that once again
was exposed in the supply of provisions (for the investigation of which a special committee was
appointed), created extraordinary indignation and embitterment of feeling in wide circles of Russian
society. As Kornilov emphasizes, it was not only the radical and revolutionary strata who were
indignant, but even the most loyal circles, with the Slavophiles at their head. When the rumors of
the concessions made at the congress-of-berlin-1878 reached Moscow, Ivan Aksakov spoke at a
public meeting of the Slavonic Society in thunderous terms of the “shameful tidings” of Russian
concessions carried daily from Berlin by the press into the knowledge of the whole people, and
declared that he refused to believe such acts of Russian diplomacy could be approved and
acknowledged by the “supreme authority.” The reputation of the empire among the Balkan Slavs, the
position of the southern part of Bulgaria, the independence of the remaining Slav peoples, the
political preponderance of the hated Austria — all, Aksakov insisted, had been given away.
Consequences
The war had serious economic and financial consequences. The mass issue of paper money undermined
Reutern’s financial programme, and the finance minister resigned. The war exhausted the treasury at
the very moment when the government had been struggling, in Reutern’s system, to raise the country’s
general productivity and especially its export trade and to build the railways. The
eastern-question was not settled but merely deferred; the settlement at Berlin left Russia’s
prestige among the Balkan Slavs diminished and Austria’s influence correspondingly enhanced.
At home the disillusionment of the war, the discovery of corruption, and the anger over Berlin fed
the growing gulf between the government and society. The zemstvo movement
gathered strength, the government appealed to society for support, and the zemstvos responded with
addresses that pressed for participation in government. The revolutionary movement, hardened by the
years of reaction, turned toward systematic terrorism, and the party of the
People’s Will took shape in the aftermath of the war. The war and the peace that
followed thus marked a step on the road that led to the attempts on the life of alexander-ii and
to the catastrophe of 1881 (see assassination-alexander-ii-1881).
Key participants

alexander-ii — Emperor of Russia, who imposed the Bessarabian condition on the peace.
The Ottoman commanders — Osman Pasha (defender of Plevna) and Suleiman Pasha (the southern front).
Russian commanders — Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaevich (commander-in-chief), Generals Gurko, Radetsky, and the engineer-general Totleben.
Count Ignatiev — Russian ambassador at Constantinople, negotiator of the San Stefano treaty.
Bismarck — president of the congress-of-berlin-1878.

Sources













SourceTreatmentKornilov — Course of Russian History, Part 3Lecture XXXVI treats the Eastern Question, the war of 1877–1878, its course and outcome, the Berlin Congress, and the economic and financial results of the war.

events/sarajevo-assassination-1914.title: The Sarajevo Assassination (1914)
events/sarajevo-assassination-1914.content:
The Sarajevo Assassination (1914)
28 June 1914
The murder of the heir to the Habsburg throne, Archduke franz-ferdinand, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, by the young Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip on the streets of Sarajevo — the pistol shots that, within five weeks, set Europe alight. The act itself was a single day’s violence in a Bosnian capital; its consequences were the july-crisis-1914 and the outbreak of the world war, and it is the hinge upon which the whole period turns. Both the chief of the general staff, conrad-von-hotzendorf, and the diplomat ottokar-czernin, who knew the heir and the monarchy, left accounts of the crime and of its meaning.
Background: the archduke’s journey to Bosnia
The assassination grew out of the settlement of the balkan-wars-1912-13. The Monarchy had barred the enlarged Serbia from the Adriatic by creating the state of Albania, and the South-Slav agitation, fed from Belgrade, burned against the Habsburg rule in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Into this tinder walked the heir. Franz Ferdinand had announced his intention to travel to Bosnia in the spring or summer of 1914, to attend the army manoeuvres of the 15th and 16th corps and to visit the capital. It was a gesture of sovereignty over the annexed province, and it was timed, as contemporaries noted, for Vidovdan, the Serbian national day of mourning for the battle of Kosovo.
The archduke travelled by sea to Metković and then by rail through Mostar into the Herzegovina; the Duchess came overland by way of Bosnisch-Brod. The pair lodged at the spa of Ilidže, nine kilometres west of Sarajevo, where the general staff chief Conrad, with his officers Metzger and Kundmann, had arrived on 24 June for the manoeuvres. Conrad records the ease of those days — the informal suppers, the archduke’s charm, the imperial couple’s joy at news of their eldest son’s examination results — and the extensive measures taken for the safety of the guests, an infantry detachment mounting the guard. The manoeuvres of 26 and 27 June passed without incident; on the evening of the 27th Conrad took his leave, the archduke bidding him “auf Wiedersehen bei den Manövern” — words, Conrad wrote, that were the last he was ever to address to him.
The day: Appelkai and the Lateiner bridge
The 28th of June was set aside for the ceremonial visit to Sarajevo, the seat of the government of Bosnia. The archduke’s motor car, with the Duchess, was followed by a second car carrying Count Harrach and other members of the suite, and by a third in which sat Colonel Bardolff and his officers; Field Marshal Potiorek, the governor and army inspector, rode with the imperial couple. As the procession drove along the Appelkai quay toward the town hall, a young man hurled a bomb at the archduke’s car. It struck the folded roof, rolled off, and exploded beneath the following car, wounding Colonel von Merizii in the head and several other officers; the imperial couple, save for a graze on the Duchess’s neck, were unhurt. The first assassin, Cabrinović, was seized across the Miljačka river.
The archduke was deeply shaken. At the town hall, receiving the mayor, he complained of the attack and asked Potiorek whether the drive should continue, and whether it would go on like this with bombs. Potiorek assured him nothing more would happen, and the party — against its own fixed decision to avoid the town centre and drive straight along the quay — was led by the leading cars into the Franz Joseph Street. As the archduke’s car turned the corner, the youth Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb student from Belgrade, fired from point-blank range. One bullet struck the Duchess in the lower body, another the archduke in the throat. The car reversed over the Lateiner bridge and reached the Konak, the governor’s residence, in two minutes, but the wounds were mortal. The archduke, streaming blood, lost consciousness and died within the quarter hour; the Duchess was already dead on arrival. The last rites were administered; Archbishop Stadler came with the clergy and prayed over the bodies.
The aftermath: a burial without honour
The double murder threw the Monarchy into an agony of grief and indignation. Conrad, hearing the news at Agram on his way to a generals’ journey, was summoned back to Vienna by the Emperor. He read the crime as no single fanatic’s act but the work of an organised plot — “the war-declaration of Serbia against Austria-Hungary,” he wrote, which could only be answered by war; the long chain of the Balkan antagonism had found its last link. Czernin, minister at Bukarest, saw the sudden turn of opinion: the whole world, its sympathies briefly with the Monarchy after the murder, was swept by a wave of hatred once the ultimatum followed.
The obsequies themselves were a study in the hierarchy of the court. The Emperor ordered that the imperial couple should not be separated even in death; but the etiquette of the Capuchin crypt, the burial place of the Habsburgs, would not admit the morganatic Duchess of Hohenberg, and so the heir to the throne was laid to rest at his own estate of Artstetten in Lower Austria, without the customary honours and without the attendance of foreign princes. The bodies were brought by rail from Sarajevo to Vienna and, in a dark and silent night procession, to the West station and thence to Artstetten. Czernin, who had known the archduke as a friend, judged him no warmonger but a man who would have reconstructed the Monarchy — a “more a patron than an adversary of the Serbs,” in his phrase, and no partisan of a closer attachment to Germany. The shots of Sarajevo removed the one figure of the dynasty whose authority might have weighed against the war party in the weeks that followed.
Consequences: the road to war
The assassination was the immediate cause of the july-crisis-1914. Within a month the Monarchy had addressed its ultimatum to Serbia, Russia had mobilised, and the localisation of the conflict — Franz Joseph’s fondest hope, as Czernin recalled his words after Bukarest — had failed. The heir’s death did not, of itself, make the war; but it supplied the pretext and the passion. It also removed, as Czernin insisted, the most powerful advocate of a different course, leaving the direction of the Monarchy in the hands of the aged franz-joseph, the cautious Berchtold, and the generals who had long argued that the Serbian question must be settled by the sword. The murder of the heir of the house of Habsburg thus stands at the head of the world war of 1914.
