events/seize-mai-1877.title: Seize Mai crisis (16 May 1877)
events/seize-mai-1877.content:
Seize Mai crisis (16 May 1877)
16 May – 14 October 1877
The great constitutional crisis of the early Third Republic, begun on 16 May 1877 when Marshal Mac-Mahon dismissed the ministry of jules-simon and, later, dissolved the republican Chamber. The Seize Mai — the sixteenth of May — was the decisive confrontation between the presidential and the parliamentary interpretation of the french-constitution-1875, and it ended with the victory of the republican majority in the elections of 14 October 1877 and the defeat of the Marshal’s conception of the presidency.
Background
The Constitution of 1875 had left ambiguous the respective powers of the president and the Chamber. Marshal patrice-mac-mahon, elected under the septennat-1873 and holding a conservative conception of the presidential office, had watched the elections of 1876 deliver a Chamber solidly republican. Dufaure and then Jules Simon governed as the heads of ministries drawn from that majority; Mac-Mahon came to regard himself as a president who might stand apart from, and even against, the Chamber. Hanotaux treats the coming conflict as the constitutional corollary of the septennat compromise — a foreseen act of authority rather than a mere whim.
The letter of 16 May
The occasion was the religious question. The republican Chamber, with leon-gambetta thundering « Le cléricalisme, voilà l’ennemi ! » (“Clericalism — there is the enemy!”), pressed the ultramontane question upon the ministry. Jules Simon, a liberal who yet depended on the republican majority, was unable to resist the Chamber’s anticlerical temper. On 16 May 1877 Mac-Mahon wrote to dismiss him, charging that Simon could not govern with the president’s confidence. The letter of 16 May was the act of a president asserting his power to choose and dismiss the ministry — a deliberate challenge to the parliamentary regime.
Dissolution and the 363
After the dismissal, the Marshal called the duc de Broglie to form a ministry of resistance and, on the advice of the Senate, dissolved the Chamber. The republican deputies, united against the Marshal’s attempt, became the “363” — the body that refused to accept the dissolution and rallied the country. The campaign of the summer of 1877 was fought with ferocity: official candidature, administrative pressure, prosecutions of Gambetta, the clerical question inflamed by the Vatican, and the Marshal’s own tour of the provinces. Hanotaux records the death of Thiers during the crisis and the leadership of jules-grevy over the republican party. The Marshal’s manifesto of 19 September and his challenge to the country set the terms: the nation itself would decide.
The elections of 14 October
The elections of 14 October 1877 decided the crisis. The government was beaten: the country returned a republican Chamber, confirming the vote of 1876. The Marshal’s ministry remained briefly, but the Chamber refused the budget and pursued an inquiry into the Seize Mai; the Broglie ministry fell, the interlude of Rochebouët could not govern, and Mac-Mahon was forced to recall Dufaure. The presidential attempt had failed before the national movement that had already imposed itself on the National Assembly. Hanotaux frames the outcome as the defeat of “the politics of the president.”
Consequences
The Seize Mai settled the nature of the Third Republic. It established that the president could not govern against a parliamentary majority — that the Chamber, not the president, controlled the ministry. Gambetta’s challenge, that the Marshal must se soumettre ou se démettre (“submit or resign”), was answered in the Marshal’s own fate: after the republican victory in the senatorial elections of January 1879, Mac-Mahon resigned, and jules-grevy succeeded him. The parliamentary interpretation of the french-constitution-1875 triumphed definitively; the president became the ceremonial head of a regime governed by the Chamber. The Seize Mai was the last great assertion of the presidential power in the founding generation — and its failure consecrated the parliamentary Republic.

events/separation-church-state-1905.title: Separation of Church and State (1905)
events/separation-church-state-1905.content:
Separation of Church and State (1905)
9 December 1905
The Separation of Church and State, enacted by the French law of 9 December 1905, ended the Concordat regime that had bound the Catholic Church to the state since Napoleon and set the churches free to organise themselves outside the public power. It was the culmination of the anticlerical programme of the Third Republic and the event around which Paul Sabatier’s L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle (1911) is organised — the moment at which the religious question in France was posed anew.
Background
The Separation closed a long republican struggle. Since Gambetta’s cry that clericalism was “the enemy” and the Ferry school laws of the 1880s, the Republic had progressively reduced the Church’s hold on public life — the closing of the congregational schools, the expulsion of the religious orders, the secularisation of the state school. The laic programme, as Sabatier stresses, was never a mere anticlerical negation: “by the laic school our country has sought to conquer itself,” a new incarnation of a secular religious effort. The Separation of 1905 carried this programme to its logical conclusion, ending the concordat and the state’s endowment and regulation of the clergy, and declaring the Republic neutral in matters of religion.
Narrative
The law of 9 December 1905 separated the churches from the state. It abrogated the Concordat and the other religious laws of the old regime; the state would no longer recognise, endow, or regulate any religion. The churches were to organise their own affairs through the associations cultuelles — the “worship associations” that the law provided for the administration of religious property and worship. The Catholic Church refused, for a time, to accept the associations, and the new regime was contested and difficult; Sabatier records with a certain irony the “Cultuelles, attempted toward 1905,” the efforts to found new religious institutions under the law, born with the favour of the ministry and of the great newspapers.
The Separation was not, in Sabatier’s analysis, a mere political decree. It belonged to a wider religious re-orientation of France, a movement that the war of 1870, the laic school, and the crisis of the Church had shaped. He distinguishes free thought from anticlericalism and warns against confounding the two: the Republic’s laicism, in the better sense, was an effort to give the citizen a moral formation rather than a war upon religion. The event of 1905, in this reading, ended the political entanglement of the Concordat and opened a new epoch in which religion would be a free matter of conscience.
Consequences
The Separation completed the laic Republic and marked the definitive end of the Concordat regime. It was the culmination of the anticlerical program that ran from the Ferry school laws and article 7 through the decrees of 1880, and it stood as the settled achievement of the republican governments that followed the Dreyfus affair. For Sabatier, writing six years later, the result was not a decline of religion but a re-orientation: the “rapid progress of indifference and an unexpected awakening of religious aspirations,” often in one and the same individual, an epoch “of reconstitution, one might say of religious revenge, somewhat analogous to the origins of Christianity.” The Church, though stripped of its political power, retained “a unique, incomparable place” in the conscience of the coming generation.
For Péguy, writing in 1910, the religious question had a more sombre reading. The de-republicanisation of France and its de-Christianisation were one and the same movement of “demystification” — the modern world that believes in nothing and “appears to thrive against all culture.” The Separation, in his eyes, belonged to that movement which dried up equally the political and the Christian city. Yet even Péguy hoped that the republican and Christian mystiques would flower again together, in a single deep movement, in the generation to come.
Key participants

The republican governments of the early 1900s — the authors of the Separation law
paul-sabatier — the historian who recorded the post-Separation religious re-orientation
charles-peguy — the critic who read the Separation within the movement of demystification

events/septennat-1873.title: The Septennat (20 November 1873)
events/septennat-1873.content:
The Septennat (20 November 1873)
20 November 1873
The law by which the National Assembly conferred on Marshal Mac-Mahon a personal seven-year presidency, adopted on 20 November 1873 after the failure of the monarchical restoration. The Septennat was the monarchical majority’s fallback when comte-de-chambord wrecked the restoration with his letter of 27 October 1873 — a provisional expedient intended to keep a king possible that in fact cleared the way for the Republic.
Background
The National Assembly elected in February 1871 had made peace, repressed the paris-commune-1871, and overthrown adolphe-thiers on 24 May 1873, but it still could not agree on a form of government. Its majority was monarchical, but divided among legitimists, Orléanists, and Bonapartists — a monarchical majority without a single candidate. The hope was “fusion,” the union of the two branches of the house of Bourbon under the comte de Chambord; the campaign of autumn 1873 was staked on the pretender’s acceptance.
The failure of the restoration
The decisive blow was Chambord’s letter of 27 October 1873, refusing the tricolour flag and clinging to the white flag of the Bourbons. The monarchical chiefs — the Nine, the commission that had delegated Charles Chesnelong to Salzburg — abandoned the campaign; the comte de Paris had already sketched the “line of retreat” toward the Marshal. With the restoration impossible, the right needed a way to keep power without a king and to postpone the question of the form of the state. Their answer was to prolong the presidency of the soldier they had installed at the Élysée.
The vote of 20 November
The Assembly, on the proposal of the duc de Broglie and the governmental right, voted on 20 November 1873 to confer on Marshal Mac-Mahon the exercise of the presidential power for a term of seven years — the septennat. Hanotaux records the embarrassment of the extreme right, the attitude of the Orléans princes, the proposals of Changarnier, and the comte de Chambord’s presence at Versailles, where Mac-Mahon, through Blacas, refused to receive him. The vote established a provisional regime: the septennat was “personal” to the Marshal, a tenure that left the future open. It was, Hanotaux writes, the expectant policy once more profiting the Republic.
Consequences
The Septennat shaped the whole settlement of the next years. It gave France a president for seven years without deciding whether the regime was a monarchy or a republic; Broglie’s second ministry and the ordre moral governed under it, and Broglie would declare the septennat “incommutable.” But a personal, provisional presidency was a holding position that could not last: it prepared the constitutional settlement of 1875, which the Assembly would be forced to make as the septennat expired into permanence. By keeping the throne empty and the Marshal seated, the Septennat — designed to preserve the monarchy’s chances — in fact made the Republic inevitable. It stands with the french-constitution-1875 as the hinge between the monarchical majority and the parliamentary Republic.
Sources

events/siege-of-paris-1870-71.title: The Siege of Paris (1870–71)
events/siege-of-paris-1870-71.content:
The Siege of Paris (1870–71)
19 September 1870 – 28 January 1871
The investment of Paris by the German armies during the autumn and winter of 1870–71, in which the capital of France was cut off, reduced to famine, and finally compelled to capitulate. It was the last act of the war after the catastrophe of battle-of-sedan-1870, and its grim months of hunger and humiliation prepared the bitterness that exploded in the paris-commune-1871 the following spring.
Background: the war after Sedan
After the fall of the Empire and the proclamation of the third-republic-france on 4 September 1870, the Government of National Defence resolved to continue the war. Hanotaux records the paradox of that decision: the country, in its patriotic anger at the disaster, refused to accept the loss of territory, yet the army was destroyed and the capital exposed. The German armies, having taken Sedan and forced the capitulation of Metz, closed upon Paris. The investment of the capital began in mid-September 1870, and by the end of the month Paris was surrounded, its fortifications ringed by the besieging armies and its communications with the rest of France cut.
The famine of the capital
The siege became a contest of endurance. Hanotaux describes how Paris, isolated, “let itself be pushed to famine” — Paris se laisse acculer à la famine. The provisioning of a city of two million was impossible over a closed ring; food ran short through the autumn and the winter cold of 1870–71, and the population endured the slow starvation of the capital. Meanwhile the armies of the provinces, animated by the ardor of Gambetta, attempted to break the ring — Hanotaux records the “admirable ardor” that revived courage in the provinces and threw every available force against the blockade, but the armies of the Loire and of the East were successively beaten and driven back. The hope of relief faded as the winter wore on.
The surrender of Paris
With famine at its last extremity and the provincial relief defeated, Paris was reduced to surrender. Hanotaux gives the summing judgment: “Paris, enfin, réduit à la famine, doit se rendre. Sa chute est celle de la France” — Paris, finally reduced to famine, must surrender; its fall is the fall of France. The capitulation of the capital was signed at the end of January 1871, and with it came the armistice that ended the fighting. The siege was the effective conclusion of the franco-prussian-war-1870-71: once Paris had fallen, Hanotaux writes, the opinion spread that peace was inevitable, and the country turned from war to the elections and the negotiation of peace.
Aftermath: capitulation, elections, and the Commune
The surrender of Paris was followed by the national elections of 8 February 1871, in which the departments, exhausted and desiring peace, returned an Assembly that met at Bordeaux and entrusted the peace to adolphe-thiers. Thiers was at pains, as Hanotaux records, to keep the negotiation of the peace separate from the capitulation of Paris — “It is Paris that is reduced, not France” — the better to save what could be saved. But the capital itself, humiliated by the siege, outraged by the surrender and by the entry of the German armies into a city that had held out so long, and radicalised by the working-class agitation of the war years, would not accept the Assembly’s peace. The distrust between armed Paris and the conservative, royalist-leaning Assembly ripened through the spring of 1871 into the insurrection of 18 March and the paris-commune-1871. The second siege of Paris that followed — the siege of the Commune by the Versailles army under Mac-Mahon — was fought in the streets the German armies had just abandoned, and the capital that had resisted the invader was taken by its own government in the Bloody Week of May 1871. The four months of the German siege thus fed directly into the civil war that dismembered France after the peace.

events/spanish-revolution-1868.title: The Spanish Revolution (1868)
events/spanish-revolution-1868.content:
The Spanish Revolution (1868)
September 1868
The revolution that, in the third week of September 1868, drove Queen Isabella II from the Spanish throne, and thereby opened the vacancy which the courts of Europe spent the next two years trying to fill. It is in the frame of this corpus the decisive European event of 1868: the flight of the Bourbons at Madrid left a throne without a king, and the search for a successor — pursued across Portugal, France and finally the German houses — led directly to the hohenzollern-candidature-1870 and the franco-prussian-war-1870-71.
Background: the unpopular Queen and the generals
Ollivier’s memoir-history gives a full portrait of Isabella II and of the causes of her ruin. A queen whose reign had been a long alternation of courts and pronunciamientos, she had worn out the loyalty of the army and of the political factions alike. The two great liberal leaders, Marshal Prim and Marshal O’Donnell, had successively raised their revolts under the conservative governments of Narváez and O’Donnell; the death of O’Donnell, the reactionary ministry of González Bravo, the arrest of Marshal Serrano and the exile of the duc de Montpensier completed the alienation. Prim’s ambition — a republican of convenience who had served every government in turn — was to place the country under a new régime of which he should be the master. By 1868 the conspiracy against the Queen had been long in the making.
The September rising and the battle of Alcolea
The revolution broke out in the fleet and spread to the land. Ollivier recounts how the conspiracy of the admiral Topete, joined by Prim, raised the navy at Cadiz in September 1868; the rising, once begun, carried the revolutionary generals with it, and on the march toward Madrid the forces of the Queen were met and beaten at the battle of Alcolea. Isabella, abandoned, fled across the frontier into France. Marshal Serrano entered Madrid at the head of the revolution, and Prim, in the words of the cry that gave the movement its temper, raised the slogan ¡Abajo los Borbones! (“Down with the Bourbons!”). The dynasty was dethroned; the throne stood empty.
The search for a king
The revolutionaries, though united against Isabella, were divided over what should replace her. As Ollivier records, the democrats would not give up their republic, while the Unionists and the Progressives insisted on a monarchy — but of whom? The Unionists had a candidate ready in the duc de Montpensier, husband of the Infanta Luisa and himself a liberal prince in disgrace at the court; the Progressives looked elsewhere. The search ranged over the princes of Europe. Ferdinand of Portugal was first approached and refused; the duc de Montpensier was pressed but could not carry the unanimity of the movement; princes of Italy were explored. As the months passed without a king, the provisional governments of Marshal Serrano and of Marshal Prim, both monarchist, grew more importunate. It was in the course of this hunt that the first hints of a Hohenzollern candidacy appeared — a suggestion which Prince Anthony of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen at first rejected, because, as he is reported to have said, France would not tolerate it. Prim’s patience was running out.
France, Napoleon and the vacant throne
From Paris the revolution was watched with uneasiness and then with a policy of wait-and-see. Ollivier records Napoleon III’s declared abstention: the Emperor would recognise any government born of popular election — even one dominated by Montpensier — and inclined rather to the restoration of Alfonso, the Queen’s son, as the reasonable solution. But the abiding French anxiety was that a hostile prince on the throne of Madrid would place a foreign influence on both flanks of France. Europe, Ollivier notes, attributed a hidden hand in the Spanish revolution to otto-von-bismarck — a suspicion which the Prussian statesman, in a conversation with the English statesman Clarendon, disclaimed. Prussia had drawn the line at the Main, and Napoleon had reiterated that Prussia would not be allowed to cross it; but the Spanish vacancy offered a field in which that line could be turned. The ultimate irony of the whole affair, which the sources preserve from opposite sides, is that the candidate who finally emerged — a prince of the Hohenzollern house, seated at Madrid through Prussian influence — was precisely the danger that French policy had feared from the start.
Consequences
The Spanish revolution left a monarchy without a king, and that vacancy became the fuse of the greatest war of the century. The search which Prim and the provisional governments pursued so impatiently ended, in the summer of 1870, in the acceptance of Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen — the hohenzollern-candidature-1870 — whose revelation in July 1870 precipitated the French declaration of war and the franco-prussian-war-1870-71. What began as the fall of an unpopular queen in September 1868 thus issued, through the empty throne of Spain, in the destruction of the second-empire-france and the proclamation of the german-empire-proclaimed-1871. In the Spanish frame itself the revolution opened the interregnum that ended only with the election of King Amadeo of Savoy in 1870 and, after his abdication, the short-lived First Republic — but the decisive consequence for the rest of Europe lay in the candidacy to which the vacant throne gave rise.

events/treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918.title: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (1918)
events/treaty-of-brest-litovsk-1918.content:
The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (1918)
3 March 1918
The peace concluded at Brest-Litovsk between the Central Powers and the Soviet Republic, signed on 3 March 1918, by which Russia withdrew from the world war at the price of enormous territorial and economic concessions in the west and south. It was the first great settlement of the war, the fruit of the German eastern victory, and — from the standpoint of the Austrian minister ottokar-czernin, who negotiated it, and of the Russian generals who refused it — a document of deeply contested character: for one the deliverance of the starving Central Powers, for the other a “burning shame.”
Background: the collapse of the Russian front
The treaty grew out of the ruin of the Russian front after the february-revolution-1917. Czernin, the Austro-Hungarian foreign minister, dated the possibility of peace with Russia to the summer of 1917, when reports from the neutral world described the disintegration of the Russian army and the bitter struggle within the Russian parties over the Allied-urged offensive. The army at the front was no longer willing to fight; the infantry in particular refused the offensive, while only the officers, the cavalry and the Cossacks remained for the war. The soldiers’ committees had paralysed the command, and the front was dissolving into the countryside. Kerensky’s June offensive collapsed, and the front dissolved into revolutionary chaos.
After the october-revolution-1917 the Bolsheviks of vladimir-lenin, who had promised peace and land, took power and at once sued for an armistice. On 22 December 1917 negotiations opened at Brest-Litovsk between the Central Powers and the delegation of the Soviet government. For the Central Powers, exhausted by three and a half years of blockade, the prospect of the eastern peace was the prospect of survival; for the Allies it was a betrayal of the common war. The German high command, confident of victory in the east, saw in the negotiations the means of detaching Russia and of turning the mass of the army against the west.
The negotiations
Czernin himself went to Brest-Litovsk and left a vivid record of the proceedings. The German negotiator was the state secretary Kühlmann, supported by the soldier-diplomat General Hoffmann; the first Russian delegations were led by Joffe, with Kamenev and others, and later by leon-trotsky. The Central Powers professed an “annexationless peace” (annexionsloser Friede) — peace without forcible annexations, on the basis of the self-determination of peoples — while the Germans in fact pressed for the detachment of the border provinces of Poland, Courland and Lithuania.
Through January the talks dragged on, complicated by the Ukrainians, who claimed a separate voice and concluded their own peace, and by the looming famine of the Central Powers, above all of Austria. Czernin was harassed by the German high command — Hindenburg’s furious telegrams over any “renunciation,” Ludendorff’s hourly telephone calls — and at one point demanded a free hand for himself in case the Germans broke with the Russians. The Bulgarians threatened, the Germans feared that the Entente might accept a general peace, and the Russian delegation, for its part, tried to play for time, counting on the revolution to spread. The whole was a tangle of ambitions, suspicions and necessities in which the fate of millions was decided.
Trotsky’s defiance and the ultimatum
In January leon-trotsky arrived to lead the Soviet delegation, and the tone changed. He was greeted with demonstrations for peace at the stations on the way; but he proved an extremely skilled and at first courteous negotiator, who sought to use the proceedings as a platform for world revolution. He was, in Czernin’s phrase, the leading spirit of the “Internationalists,” those who wished to restore the International and to refuse a separate peace with the imperialists. Czernin, under the pressure of the Austrian famine and the demands of the allies, concluded that the peace must be had at once.
The Germans finally presented an ultimatum, backed by the threat of a renewed advance; Hoffmann, the old staff officer, wished to “give the Russians a good beating.” On 10 February Trotsky, refusing both peace and war, broke off the negotiations and returned to Petrograd, declaring “no war, no peace” and counting on a German revolution. The German high command answered by resuming the offensive, which met almost no resistance from the dissolving Russian army. The Soviet government, under Lenin’s insistence on peace at any cost, bowed to the ultimatum, and the treaty was signed at Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918. A separate peace with the Ukraine had already been concluded in February — the Brotfriede (“bread peace”) on which Austria, starving, had pinned its hopes of grain.
The terms
By the treaty Russia renounced Poland, Courland, Lithuania and Livonia and Estland, whose future Germany was to determine, withdrew from Finland and the Ukraine, ceded the districts of the west, and conceded to Germany and Austria-Hungary economic and financial advantages. In the south the Ukraine passed under German influence, and Russia lost the line of the old front. From the standpoint of the white-movement, Denikin condemned the settlement as the “bargaining between the Central Powers and their soviet agents,” a memory evoking “burning shame and pain”: never, he wrote, had European statesmen thrown off with such shamelessness every covering of honour and justice. He noted that the Sovnarkom, linked by financial relations to the German staff, yet observed the outward decorum, and that even the Bolsheviks’ own military council had voted against signing, with only Lenin, the commander-in-chief Krylenko and a minority for peace at any cost. The separate peace took Russia out of the war and released the German armies for the final offensives in the west, one of the critical events of 1918.
Consequences
For the Central Powers the treaty was a triumph — the fulfilment of the eastern war aims and the prospect of relief from the blockade — but its fruits were soon poisoned. The expected grain and oil of the Ukraine did not end the Austrian famine, and the Brotfriede proved a delusion; Czernin, who had staked his policy on the eastern settlement, resigned in April 1918 amid the failure of his peace hopes in the west. For Russia the treaty was the price of the survival of the soviet regime, won at the cost of vast territories and of the moral authority of the revolution; it confirmed the Bolsheviks in power while the white-movement and the Allies denounced them as the betrayers of Russia.
The collapse of the Central Powers in November 1918 annulled the treaty in fact, but its legacy endured: the borderlands of the west and south passed through years of war and reorganisation, and the German occupation of the Ukraine and the Baltic drew into the conflict both the volunteers of the south and the forces of the new states. The Brest settlement stands as the first great act of the peacemaking that the war’s end would complete at Versailles, and as the demonstration, for all of Europe, of what a peace of force could mean. For the ice-march-1918, unfolding in the same weeks in the south, it was the shadow in which the White resistance began.

events/treaty-of-frankfurt-1871.title: Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871)
events/treaty-of-frankfurt-1871.content:
Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871)
10 May 1871
The definitive peace that closed the franco-prussian-war-1870-71, signed at Frankfurt, by which France ceded Alsace and part of Lorraine and undertook to pay an indemnity of five milliards of francs. The Treaty of Frankfurt fixed the humiliation of defeat in permanent form — the loss of the eastern provinces and the burden of the indemnity that France would spend years and a national effort to discharge. It was the foundation upon which the government of adolphe-thiers built its authority, and the wound from which the French sense of revanche would spring.
Background
The armistice concluded during the siege-of-paris-1870-71 had been followed by the election of the National Assembly on 8 February 1871, returned under the shadow of defeat to make peace. At the preliminaries of Versailles, Thiers sat with Bismarck (21 February) and bargained under the double pressure of a Paris still armed and already insurgent and of a country resolved on peace. The questions of Metz and Belfort divided the negotiators; the fate of Alsace and Lorraine, and the size of the indemnity, were the crux of the whole settlement.
The negotiation
Thiers’s negotiation was conducted in the shadow of the coming paris-commune-1871 — the capital was in open insurrection from 18 March even as the peace was being completed. Hanotaux records the debate over whether Metz might have been saved and whether the London conference was neglected; in the event Belfort was retained for France and a milliard struck from the original demand. The definitive treaty was signed at Frankfurt on 10 May 1871. Its territorial clauses ceded Alsace and part of Lorraine; its financial clauses fixed the indemnity at five milliards, with a schedule of payment and occupation; commercial and transit stipulations bound the two countries. It was, Hanotaux writes, the Germanic wehrgeld — the war-price exacted from French savings and French future.
The indemnity and the liberation
The Treaty of Frankfurt thus set France two tasks: to pay the five milliards and to recover its territory from the occupying German armies. Thiers refused Bismarck’s offer to bring in German financiers and staked the payment on France itself; the loan of two milliards of June 1871, subscribed 381,906 times, began the discharge. The conventions of 12 October 1871 began the evacuation of the German troops, and the negotiations for anticipated evacuation — Gontaut-Biron, Saint-Vallier, Arnim, Bismarck — bore fruit in the convention of liberation of 15 March 1873. When the last payment was completed and the evacuation finished (16 September 1873), Thiers had already been toppled, but the libérateur du territoire had done his work.
Consequences
The Treaty of Frankfurt shaped the Europe of the following half-century. It left France dismembered and diminished in European weight, while Germany, triumphant, became the arbiter of the continent under otto-von-bismarck. The loss of Alsace-Lorraine created a permanent grievance — the protest of the annexed provinces against German rule, the pressure of revanche on French politics — and the indemnity, paid so surprisingly fast, testified both to French wealth and to the efficiency of the new Republic. The treaty of 10 May 1871 was the point of departure for the Republic’s recovery and for the armed peace that dominated Europe until 1914.
Sources

events/unrestricted-submarine-warfare-19.title: Unrestricted Submarine Warfare (1917)
events/unrestricted-submarine-warfare-19.content:
Unrestricted Submarine Warfare (February 1917)
February 1917 – 1918
Germany’s declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917, by which the German navy was authorised to sink without warning the merchant shipping of neutrals as well as of enemies in the war zones, and which brought the United States into the war on the side of the Entente. Recouly numbers the decision among “the grave blunders of its military chiefs — ignorant of politics” that defeated Germany: the political defection of Russia brought victory within two fingers of Germany, but the unrestricted submarine war, by provoking American intervention, added one more enemy to the list. Czernin, who as Austrian foreign minister opposed it, records the decision and its fatal consequences in detail.
Background
The war had reached the point where Germany, unable to break the Entente on land, turned to the submarine as the weapon that could sever the sea-borne supplies of Britain. The temptation was immense: the U-boat offered the prospect of strangling the island power that was the heart of the blockade. But the instrument could only be used ruthlessly, against all shipping in the war zones, and that meant sinking the vessels of neutrals — above all of the United States, whose trade and lives would be caught in the net. Recouly sets the decision in the frame of the German command’s fatal over-confidence: the German military chiefs, convinced of their superiority over all adversaries, resolved to conduct the war henceforth “impitoyably, with the maximum of violence,” regardless of the neutrals they might drive into the enemy camp. Ludendorff had no care for the risk of bringing the United States into the conflict.
The decision
Czernin, newly elevated to the Austrian foreign ministry, treats the decision as the capital error of the war. He records that he and Prince Hohenlohe warned against it; that the German leaders, State Secretary Zimmermann and Admiral Holtzendorff, came to Vienna to press it; and that Holtzendorff gave a guarantee of success. The German leaders still in April 1918 remained optimistically convinced that the war would be ended before America had time “to come.” Czernin records the judgment that the calculation was false — “that we all know today.” The German generals’ psychology was governed by a “victory psychosis”: convinced that their army was invincible, they believed the submarine war would bring Britain to her knees in a few months. The decision was taken against the warnings of the political factors; Czernin insists that had the political men of Berlin been heard, there would have been no unrestricted submarine war, and that this one omission would have saved the Central Powers. Wilhelm II, “a prisoner of his generals,” let the Supreme Command have its way. Hindenburg and Ludendorff — “gods for the German people” — were far more powerful than the Kaiser, and he less than ever able to oppose them.
The American entry
The consequences followed with the swiftness the warning had predicted. The unrestricted submarine war, sinking American ships and citizens, drove the United States into the war on the side of the Entente in the spring of 1917. Recouly marks the entry of America as the decisive addition of one more enemy that made German victory impossible: it was a measure that risked displeasing the neutrals and making them enter the conflict, and Ludendorff “has no care for it.” Where the Russian revolution had seemed to save Germany by removing the eastern enemy, the American intervention replaced the balance on the other side. Czernin records how England, at least from the summer of 1917, was resolved to shatter Germany, and how the fiasco of the submarine war revealed the false calculation of its authors: the construction of further U-boats had to be restricted in the course of the war, and Germany misjudged the whole situation.
Consequences
The unrestricted submarine war thus stands as one of the turning points of the war — the decision that brought the manpower and wealth of the United States to the Entente just as the collapse of Russia (see february-revolution-1917 and october-revolution-1917) had freed the Central Powers in the East. For Recouly it is the capital illustration of his thesis: Germany, too sure of its warlike superiority and committing its habitual sin of pride, ranged too many enemies against itself. The submarines, far from ending the war, helped to condemn the Central Powers to the defeat that the armistice of 1918 sealed. Czernin, writing from the Austrian side, sums up the decision as a grave blunder of the military leaders “ignorant of politics” — the blunder that added the decisive weight against the Central Powers.
Key participants
wilhelm-ii · ottokar-czernin · joseph-joffre
Sources

index.content:
Rest of Europe 1866–1919 Wiki

A narrative-research knowledge base on continental European history from the Austro-Prussian War through the First World War and its immediate aftermath. The United Kingdom is treated separately in its own wiki.
Last updated: 2026-08-16 | Total pages: 157 (62 entities · 57 events · 38 concepts) over 52 sources

The Arc of the Corpus
In 1866 Prussia defeated Austria and expelled it from Germany; by 1871 a German Empire proclaimed at Versailles stood where the German Confederation had been, while Italy, made in the wars of 1859–70, was completing its own unification. The middle decades saw the consolidation of these new states — the Kaiserreich under Bismarck until his fall in 1890, the Third Republic founded in France between the Commune and the constitution of 1875, the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary working out the 1867 Compromise against its nationalities, and Tsarist Russia lurching from the emancipation era through the reaction of Alexander III to the upheaval of 1905. The corpus then follows the alliances and crises of the pre-war generation — the Eastern Question, the Triple Alliance, the annexation of Bosnia and the Balkan wars — into the July crisis of 1914 and the Great War itself, closing with the collapse of the Habsburg, Romanov and Hohenzollern dynasties and the Russian revolution and Civil War. It is built from the memoirs and contemporary histories of the people who made it: Sybel and Lenz on Bismarck; Delord, Ollivier and Hanotaux on France; Garibaldi, Tivaroni, Oriani and Fortunato on Italy; Beksics, Sosnosky, Conrad and Czernin on Austria-Hungary; Kornilov, Witte, Zhevakhov and Denikin on Russia; and Recouly on the war.

sources/beksics-a-dualismus-1892.title: Beksics — A dualismus
sources/beksics-a-dualismus-1892.content:
Beksics — A dualismus
Gusztáv Beksics (1847–1906), A dualismus. Története, közjogi értelme és nemzeti törekvéseink. Budapest: Az Athenaeum R. Társulat Kiadása, 1892. A Hungarian constitutional-juridical treatise of some three hundred and forty pages, drawn from the scan preserved in the Harvard Law School Library (University of California/Google-digitized copy, oclc 14025910) via Anna’s Archive; the raw text in this wiki was taken from the already-OCR’d page texts of that scan (Hungarian). Beksics, a Hungarian publicist, lawyer and politician, wrote to settle the public-law disputes that “incessantly agitate” opinion and parliament over the meaning of the Compromise — in particular the claim, then beginning to be taught in the schools, that between Hungary and Austria there is a real union, and that Hungary’s statehood has been impaired by the dualist system.
Dominant years in the text are 1867–1868 (with the long constitutional history that produced the Compromise).
Preface — Előszó
Public-law questions incessantly agitate public opinion and parliament; heated debates turn on the dualism, especially on the content and public-law meaning of Act XII of 1867. Is it true that the meaning of that act is uncertain, so that the nation’s sovereign rights are in doubt? Beksics declares the book’s method: the 1867 Act can only be correctly interpreted by examining what Hungary’s statehood consisted in before and after the Pragmatic Sanction, in 1848, and what it consists in since 1867 — requiring the study of all the sources of Hungarian constitutional history and public law, above all the Corpus Juris, which few now consult.
I. Király és nemzet — King and nation
The Hungarian nation was always one with its king. The nation was the source, the royal power the stream that flows from it. The Hungarian people existed before Hungarian kings; it completed its formation into a nation and a state by placing the crown on its leader’s head. Hungarian kingship was a consequence, not an antecedent; in Hungary not only political power but every right had the nation itself for its source. The German doctrine of the state, which set up kingship as an independent, primordial source of right with sovereign powers over legislation and judicature, exerted a harmful reaction on Hungarian public-law science; the Hungarian kingship never possessed such powers.
II. Magyarország államisága a pragmatica sanctio előtt — Hungary’s statehood before the Pragmatic Sanction
The examination of what Hungary’s statehood consisted in before the Pragmatic Sanction — the character of the medieval Hungarian state and the constitutional relations that preceded the Compromise.
III. Magyarország államisága a pragmatica sanctio idejében — Hungary’s statehood at the time of the Pragmatic Sanction
Hungary’s statehood in the age of the Pragmatic Sanction (1723), by which the succession of the House of Habsburg and the inseparable and indivisible possession of the kingdoms was settled, and on which the whole subsequent relation of Hungary to Austria rested.
IV. A magyar állam és a közös ügyek 1848-ban — The Hungarian state and the common affairs in 1848
The constitutional settlement of 1848, the establishment of the responsible ministry, and the manner in which the common affairs between Hungary and Austria were then ordered — the antecedents of the dualist arrangement.
V. A provisorium — The provisorium
The period of the provisional arrangement and absolutist administration that followed the failure of 1849, and the condition of Hungary in the interval before the Compromise.
VI. A dualismus keletkezése — The origin of the dualism
How the dualist system came into being — the negotiations and constitutional work that issued in the Compromise of 1867, associated above all with the name of Ferenc Deák.
VII. A magyar államiság és a dualismus — Hungarian statehood and the dualism
The relation between Hungary’s restored statehood and the dualist system; the sense in which the Compromise preserved, and did not impair, the statehood of the Hungarian state.
VIII. Külügy és Magyarország nemzetközi egyénisége — Foreign affairs and Hungary’s international personality
The conduct of foreign affairs under the dualist system and the standing of Hungary as an international personality — in what degree Hungary figures as a subject in the international order.
IX. Hadügy és hadsereg — Defence and the army
The common military establishment and the army under the Compromise; the organisation of the joint armed forces of the two states.
X. A honvédség és a rendkívüli véderő — The home defence and the extraordinary levy
The Hungarian honvéd (home defence) force and the extraordinary levy established alongside the common army.
XI. Delegáczió — The Delegations
The Delegations, the joint parliamentary bodies by which the common affairs of the two states are managed, and their powers and proceedings.
XII. A közös ügyek miniszteriuma 1848-ban és 1867-ben — The ministry of common affairs in 1848 and 1867
A comparison of the handling of the common affairs in 1848 and in 1867 — how the common ministries were constituted in each settlement.
XIII. Nemzeti királyi udvartartás — The national royal household
The national royal household (nemzeti kir. udvartartás) of the Hungarian kingdom within the dualist arrangement.
XIV. Magyarország pénzügyi és gazdasági függetlensége — Hungary’s financial and economic independence
The financial and economic autonomy of the Hungarian state under the Compromise, and the division of fiscal and economic matters between the two states.
XV. Personál-unió — Personal union
The character of the union as a personal union of the two crowns — the tie that binds Hungary and Austria being the identity of the ruler — and the consequences that flow from it.
XVI. A dualismus belső vonatkozásai — The internal bearings of the dualism
The internal relations of the dualist system: (1) Horvátország — Croatia and the Hungarian-Croatian settlement (the nagodba of 1868); (2) Nemzetiségek — the nationalities within Hungary and their place under the dualist state.
XVII. Mikép változtatható meg az 1867: XII. t.-czikk? — How can Act XII of 1867 be altered?
The question of how the Compromise act could be changed, and the position of a hypothetical third factor in the monarchy alongside Hungary and Austria.
XVIII. Hibás közjogi elnevezések — Erroneous public-law designations
The correction of erroneous public-law terms and usages that distort the true character of the dualist relation.
XIX. A dualismus és nemzeti törekvéseink — The dualism and our national aspirations
The relation of the dualist system to Hungarian national aims: (1) whether the dualism can be developed, and (2) the Hungarian national state — how national aspirations are to be pursued within the framework of the Compromise.
XX. A dualismus jövője — The future of the dualism
Since the Compromise the internal relations of Austria have passed through significant transformations; the German element, which had seized constitutional power, lost its leading role through its own fault, and the federalist tendency won a partial triumph. Beksics does not pronounce on the chances of Austrian politics, still less preach intervention in it; yet conditions might arise in Austria incompatible with the Hungarian national interest that would move Hungarian statesmen to interpose. His closing argument: such is the grand conception of the Compromise of 1867 — years and decades may pass, new relations may arise out of events at home and abroad, but they cannot destroy Deák’s work, not because it is intellectually perfect but because it answers the interests of both Hungary and Austria; not because it is a new creation but because it gave form to a centuries-long historical development. The dualism existed before 1848; the common affairs and their (though unwritten) management existed; and through all the centuries and great changes — Hungary freed from the Turkish yoke, triumphant over the attempts to absorb it, its two great wars of liberty — only one thing proved firm and immovable: the tie that binds Hungary to Austria through the dynasty, and its consequence, the union of the two mutually independent states for mutual defence and for that alone. As long as the ruler’s person is common to Hungary and Austria this personal union and its consequences will stand; only in the single case of the cessation of the identity of the dynasty would new arrangements follow — an eventuality entirely outside the range of political possibility. The great creation on which Deák’s name is written, the historical dualism which the storms of centuries could not destroy, need not be feared from the weak breezes of internal quarrels.
Series note
This volume sits at the constitutional foundation of the 1866–1919 period covered by this wiki: the Compromise of 1867 created the Dual Monarchy, the political frame within which the era’s Austrian and Hungarian history unfolded. Written by a Hungarian participant in the public-law debates of the time, it is a contemporary Hungarian account (rather than a retrospective) of the settlement, and stands beside the German and other works of the period as the Austrian–Hungarian constitutional thread. It is chronologically prior to the works of Theodor von Sosnosky on the politics of the Habsburg realms in the same wiki.

sources/beksics-a-magyar-faj-terjeszkede.title: Beksics — A magyar faj terjeszkedése és nemzeti konszolidácziónk
sources/beksics-a-magyar-faj-terjeszkede.content:
Beksics — A magyar faj terjeszkedése és nemzeti konszolidácziónk
Gusztáv Beksics (1847–1906), A magyar faj terjeszkedése és nemzeti konszolidácziónk, különös tekintettel a mezőgazdaságra, birtokviszonyokra és a népesedésre. Második kiadás. Budapest: Az Athenaeum Részvénytársulat Kiadása, 1896. A Hungarian national-political and demographic treatise of some one hundred and thirty pages, drawn from a scanned edition of the second issue (page 1 carries the Barcode 3 1761 08137940 6) obtained via Anna’s Archive; the raw text in this wiki was obtained by OCR of the scanned images (the PDF carries no embedded text layer; Hungarian). The book examines the means and prospects of Hungarian national and state consolidation at a moment — three decades after the Compromise of 1867 — when the linguistic assimilation of the nationalities was visibly failing and the Hungarian population’s growth in the purely Hungarian counties was stagnating.
Dominant years in the text are the 1890s, with the three decades since 1867 as its constant point of reference.
Preface — Előszó a második kiadáshoz
Beksics declares the book’s two fundamental theses. First: linguistically we are incapable of assimilating the nationalities — even counting those, from among the peoples of Hungary other than the Germans, who have acquired the Hungarian tongue, their number dwindles to insignificance. Three decades of constitutional rule, self-determination and a cultural policy directed by the nation itself have produced, so far as linguistic absorption is concerned, very poor results; if the towns had not grown into Hungarian cultural points, one would have to say that the cultural means of national and state consolidation had failed. The language frontiers have not been pushed forward; in places there has been positive regression — at the borders, in Upper Hungary and in Transylvania, the Slovak and Romanian tongues have defeated Hungarian at the points of contact; in Árva, Trencsén and Liptó the small Magyar population is on the verge of extinction. Second: the relation of agriculture and of landed property to population growth. The dependence is not simple but complicated, crossing society and the most different regions of the country; but where industry is not yet developed enough to complicate it, the effect of agriculture on population is everywhere clearly visible. The demographer finds no more favourable field for uncovering the relation between population and agriculture than the Hungarian Dunántúl and Alföld, where industry as yet plays the least part. The generalisation of English conditions was the greatest error of Malthus’s theory; the study of agriculture as the chief cause of population, though attempted by Lavergne in the sixties, remained neglected for want of data. Against Malthus, Carey, Ricardo, Wappäus and the syncretic Oettingen, Beksics maintains — on statistical grounds — that in certain circumstances agriculture and the division of land are the first-rank factor in promoting or hindering population growth. Up to a certain point of development agriculture is the most powerful multiplier of population (in Austria itself the agricultural Galicia and Bukovina multiply faster than the industrial Czech provinces); beyond a certain density industry takes over the leading role. When the land needed for expansion is wanting, population growth stops; and here the difference between races is decisive — the same economic conditions see different races expand in different proportions, a racial propagative force that science and practice alike have unduly neglected. The preface also notes that, contrary to the Western view that Catholics multiply less than Protestants, in Hungary the Catholics show almost the greatest growth.
I. Fejezet — Nemzeti konszolidácziónk és eszközei (National consolidation and its means)
The national policy — if it is not mere phrase — must be founded on the recognition that consolidation cannot be achieved through language alone. The examination of what national consolidation requires and of the true means by which the Hungarian nation can consolidate itself and expand within the lands of the Crown of St. Stephen.
II. Fejezet — A magyar faj terjeszkedésének bizonyítékai (The proofs of the expansion of the Hungarian race)
The great rate of expansion of the Hungarian race is made indubitable by the older and the newer data alike. From the Turkish conquest onward the proofs of Hungarian expansion are marshalled — where the Magyar has advanced and at what rate, and the regions in which the race has shown its greatest force.
III. Fejezet — Aggasztó jelenségek a magyar faj terjeszkedésében (Alarming phenomena in the expansion of the Hungarian race)
In the very twenty-five counties that display the tremendous force of the Hungarian race and stamp their character on the country — the phenomenon that made Hungary one of the most multiplying lands of Europe — the number of births is now falling, or with few exceptions stagnating. This is not the effect of the agricultural crisis; low grain prices have no influence upon it. The chapter weighs these alarming symptoms against the record of expansion.
IV. Fejezet — Mezőgazdaság és nemzeti politika (Agriculture and national policy)
Agriculture as an instrument of national policy. The cultivation of the soil and the conditions of the countryside as a means of strengthening and expanding the Hungarian element against the nationalities.
V. Fejezet — Népszaporodás és agrikultura (Population growth and agriculture)
What effect has agriculture upon population growth? The relation is examined statistically — how the agricultural character of a region governs the multiplication of its inhabitants, and the stages at which agriculture gives way to industry as the chief agent of growth.
VI. Fejezet — Népszaporodás és földbirtok (Population growth and landed property)
The relation of population growth to the ownership of the land — how the distribution and tenure of landed property promote or hinder the multiplication of the race, and the demographic consequence of the great estate.
VII. Fejezet — Az alföldi agrár-szoczializmus (The agrarian socialism of the Alföld)
Twice in Sicily the agrarian revolt broke out in arms — first in September 1866, when the insurgents held Palermo for seven and a half days; again at the end of 1893 and the beginning of 1894, when a whole army had to be mobilised against the rebels. Both outbreaks took the Italian official circles and public opinion by surprise, and a whole literature grew up about the woes of the Sicilian peasant. Beksics turns from the Sicilian to the Hungarian Alföld: the agrarian socialism that has stirred the great plain of Hungary, its causes in the land-hunger of the peasantry, and the danger it poses to the national and state order.
VIII. Fejezet — A magyar parasztság (The Hungarian peasantry)
The condition of the Hungarian peasantry — the survivors of the Hungarian race upon the soil, their relation to the land they till, the history of their emancipation, and the forces that make them conservative holders or restless aspirants after land.
IX. Fejezet — Bérlet vagy tulajdon (Tenancy or property)
The alternative between tenancy and ownership as the basis of the peasant economy and of Hungarian expansion: whether the peasant should hold the land he works as a tenant or as a proprietor, and which arrangement best serves both the multiplication of the race and the national consolidation of the country.
X. Fejezet — A népszaporodás gátjainak megszüntetése (The removal of the obstacles to population growth)
Before passing to the remedies for the causes that hinder the multiplication of our race, Beksics briefly recapitulates what has been said, then sets out the means by which the obstacles to population growth are to be removed — chiefly through the division of the great estates and the creation of a numerous landed peasantry.
XI. Fejezet — Az uj földbirtokviszonyok és az uj Magyarország (The new land-tenure relations and the new Hungary)
The connection between the new distribution of the land and the regeneration of the nation. Beside agriculture the population can no longer multiply as it should; the chapter draws the national consequences of the new land-tenure relations and the new Hungary that they are to call into being.
Befejezés (Conclusion)
To what has been said Beksics has little to add. He declines to repeat himself, but closes by pointing once more to the fundamental considerations. The future of the Hungarian nation, its state and national consolidation, can only be assured if the forces latent in the race unfold freely and every obstacle is removed from before the expansiveness of the Magyars; otherwise the nation will be compelled to lower its national ideal and the level of its existence. In the expansion of the Hungarian race alarming phenomena appear. In the twenty-five counties that show the tremendous force of the race the number of births is falling, or with few exceptions stagnates. This phenomenon is not the effect of the agricultural crisis; low grain prices have no influence upon it; the data adduced are, he believes, completely convincing. As applied to Hungarian conditions, the Malthusian doctrine — that the proletariat must be allowed to starve, that relief only multiplies the poor — proves erroneous; the land-hunger of the peasant and the division of the great estates, far from increasing a menace, are the very means by which the race multiplies and the national consolidation is secured.
Series note
This volume sits within the 1866–1919 period covered by this wiki, at the point where the Austrian–Hungarian thread turns from the constitutional settlement (the Compromise of 1867) to the national and demographic question of the Hungarian kingdom in the last decade of the century. Written by a Hungarian publicist in the 1890s, it is a contemporary Hungarian account of the nationality and land question — the internal counterpart to the constitutional theme of Beksics’s own A dualismus (1892) in the same wiki. Chronologically it precedes the works of Theodor von Sosnosky on the politics of the Habsburg realms.

sources/cadorna-la-guerra-alla-fronte-it.title: Cadorna — La guerra alla fronte italiana, Vol. I
sources/cadorna-la-guerra-alla-fronte-it.content:
Luigi Cadorna — La guerra alla fronte italiana fino all’arresto sulla linea della Piave e del Grappa (24 maggio 1915 – 9 novembre 1917), Volume I
General Luigi Cadorna (1850–1928), Chief of Staff of the Italian army from July 1914 to November 1917, La guerra alla fronte italiana fino all’arresto sulla linea della Piave e del Grappa (24 maggio 1915 – 9 novembre 1917), Volume I, Nuova edizione con l’aggiunta di un’appendice sull’intervento del Maresciallo Foch in Italia, Fratelli Treves, Milano, 1923 (Nono migliaio). The volume carries three chorographical maps. The text of this wiki is the HathiTrust full-text scan (University of Michigan copy), 332 pages.
This is Volume I, containing Chapters I–VI. Its dominant years are 1914–August 1916, from Italy at the outbreak of the European war to the capture of Gorizia in the Sixth Battle of the Isonzo.
Chapters
Capitolo Primo. L’Italia allo scoppio della guerra europea — the condition of Italy when war broke out in Europe in 1914: the army (L’Esercito), the country (Il Paese), and the government and parliament (Governo e Parlamento). Capitolo II. La preparazione militare della guerra durante la neutralità — the military preparation during the period of neutrality, 1915. Capitolo III. Il disegno di operazioni — the plan of operations. Capitolo IV. Le operazioni militari nell’anno 1915 — the operations of 1915, in three parts: the operations of spring and summer (Operazioni della primavera e dell’estate), the operations of autumn (Operazioni dell’autunno), and observations on the operations of 1915 (Osservazioni sulle operazioni del 1915) — the First through Fourth Battles of the Isonzo. Capitolo V. L’offensiva austriaca nella primavera del 1916 — the Austrian offensive of spring 1916 (the Strafexpedition against the Trentino): events to mid-May, the period before the offensive, measures taken to reinforce the First Army, the Austrian offensive from the Trentino, and the Italian counter-offensive. Capitolo VI. La battaglia di Gorizia — the Battle of Gorizia (August 1916), in two parts: the dispositions before the battle (Disposizioni anteriori alla battaglia) and the course of the offensive action (Svolgimento dell’azione offensiva), which opened the Sixth Battle of the Isonzo and the capture of Gorizia.
The volume closes with the appendix on the intervention of Marshal Foch in Italy, added in this new edition.

sources/cadorna-la-guerra-alla-fronte-it.title: Cadorna — La guerra alla fronte italiana, Vol. II
sources/cadorna-la-guerra-alla-fronte-it.content:
Luigi Cadorna — La guerra alla fronte italiana fino all’arresto sulla linea della Piave e del Grappa (24 maggio 1915 – 9 novembre 1917), Volume II
General Luigi Cadorna (1850–1928), Chief of Staff of the Italian army from July 1914 to November 1917, La guerra alla fronte italiana fino all’arresto sulla linea della Piave e del Grappa (24 maggio 1915 – 9 novembre 1917), Volume II, Fratelli Treves, Milano, 1921 (Settimo migliaio). Copyright by General Luigi Cadorna, 1921. The text of this wiki is the HathiTrust full-text scan (University of Wisconsin copy), 298 pages.
This is Volume II, containing Chapters VII–XIII and the conclusion. Its dominant years are autumn 1916 – November 1917, from the autumn operations on the Carso to the arrest of the retreat on the Piave after Caporetto.
Chapters
Capitolo VII. Le operazioni militari nell’autunno del 1916 — the military operations of autumn 1916: the first, second, and third offensives on the Carso (the Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Battles of the Isonzo), the offensive action on Monte Pasubio, the operations between the Avisio and the Vanoi-Cismon, and observations on the military events of the year 1916. Capitolo VIII. Le operazioni militari nella primavera del 1917 — the military operations of spring 1917: the period before the offensive on the Giulia front, the offensive on the Giulia front in May 1917 (the Tenth Battle of the Isonzo), the Austrian counter-offensive, and the action on the Trentino front. Capitolo IX. La battaglia fra l’Idria e il Timavo (agosto–settembre 1917) — the battle between the Idria and the Timavo, August–September 1917 (the Eleventh Battle of the Isonzo): the dispositions given before the battle and the battle itself. Capitolo X. Caporetto — Caporetto, 24 October 1917: the preparations for meeting the Austro-German attack (Predisposizioni per fronteggiare l’attacco austro-tedesco) and the battle (La battaglia). Capitolo XI. La ritirata fino alla linea del Tagliamento — the retreat to the line of the Tagliamento. Capitolo XII. La ritirata dal Tagliamento alla Piave — the retreat from the Tagliamento to the Piave. Capitolo XIII. La linea difensiva della Piave — the defensive line of the Piave, the arrest of the retreat in November 1917.
The volume closes with a Conclusione (268). In the course of Chapter XII Cadorna discusses the mission of Marshal Foch in Italy (October–November 1917), rebutting the view that Foch came as adviser and inspirer of the retreat and arguing that Foch opposed it.

sources/comando-supremo-la-battaglia-di-.title: Comando Supremo — La battaglia di Vittorio Veneto (24 ottobre–4 novembre 1918)
sources/comando-supremo-la-battaglia-di-.content:
Regio Esercito Italiano, Comando Supremo — La battaglia di Vittorio Veneto, 24 ottobre–4 novembre 1918
La battaglia di Vittorio Veneto, 24 ottobre – 4 novembre 1918, published by the Comando Supremo of the Regio Esercito Italiano, 1918 (OCLC 10783357). The text of this wiki is the HathiTrust full-text scan (University of Michigan copy, 60 pages, a gift of the Italian Military Attaché).
The volume is the official account of the final Italian offensive, written at the moment of victory. Its Premessa (Preface) sets out the conviction of the Supreme Command that the most rapid dissolution of the world conflict would be obtained by putting the Austrian army out of action and so isolating Germany militarily — the concentration of effort against the weaker adversary, the plan for an action on the Asiago highland in spring 1918, and the preparation, in the months after the crisis of 1917, of a powerful offensive organism.
Structure
Parte I. La preparazione — the preparation: the situation after the enemy offensive of June 1918 (the Battle of the Piave), the offensive programme, the strategic plan of the battle, the dispositions, and the opposing forces. Parte II. La battaglia — the battle (24 October – 4 November 1918), in four movements: (1) the preparatory action; (2) the breaking of the enemy front — the forcing of the Piave, the crisis, the delineating success, the collapse of the Grappa front, the reaching of the Livenza, and the action on the Asiago highland; (3) the pursuit — the recovery of the highlands, the occupation of Trento, the last resistances of the enemy, the landing at Trieste, and the cavalry in the pursuit; (4) the armistice — “L’esercito austriaco era così annientato” (The Austrian army was thus annihilated), with Germany forced to ask for an armistice and the end of operations on all fronts on 11 November 1918. The part closes by contrasting the Austrian official report of October 1917 with the Italian recovery and the completion of the revenge a year later. Parte III. Gli artefici della vittoria — the authors of the victory: “Un elenco glorioso” (A glorious list), honouring the infantry (the Fante d’Italia), the artillery and bombardiers, the engineers and the pontieri of the 4th Regiment, the cavalry in the pursuit, and the aeronautics. Appendice. Le truppe italiane sugli altri campi della guerra mondiale — Italian troops on the other fields of the world war: France (the II Corps on the Ardre in July 1918, the Chemin des Dames and the pursuit, the taking of Rozoy-sur-Serre), Albania, Macedonia (the Cerna and the offensive that brought down the Bulgarian front, the taking of Krusevo, the armistice of Salonicco), and Palestine.
The volume ends with an INDICE (table of contents) followed by a fold-out map of the theatre.

sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd1.title: Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band I: Die Zeit der Annexionskrise 1906–1909
sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd1.content:
Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band I: Die Zeit der Annexionskrise 1906–1909
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925), Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918. Erster Band: Die Zeit der Annexionskrise 1906–1909. In zwei Teilen, mit einem Anhang und einer ethnographischen Karte. Wien, Berlin, Leipzig, München: Rikola Verlag, 1921. The memoirs of the chief of the Austro-Hungarian general staff from his appointment in 1906 to his relief from office in 1918. This first volume, published in 1921, covers the period from autumn 1906 to the end of 1909, the years of the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the crisis that followed; the raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of Michigan library; Rikola Verlag 1921, oclc 656540), 694 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order.
Einführung
Conrad explains the origin and character of the work. He recalls that on his appointment as chief of the general staff in 1906 he answered a comrade’s congratulations with the remark that whoever attains an exposed official position is first congratulated, then observed, then criticised, then abused, and finally pelted with stones — stages through which he has since passed. He had never kept a diary; only where official need required a precise dating of events did he employ his wing-adjutants as trustworthy confidants to take down what passed at the more important conferences, dictating to them the essentials afterwards where their presence was excluded. After his removal from office in July 1918 he had closed his military career and withdrawn into private life, at first with no thought of writing memoirs; the collapse of the old fatherland and its glorious army, and the many publications and requests that reached him, moved him at last to set down his experiences. The work bears, as its title says, not the character of a general historical work but of purely personal records. He sets out his philosophical conviction — that not individual men make their time, but that the time makes its men; that the men who stand by chance at the head of great epochs act by obeying the impulses dictated by the great drift of the age, and are commonly identified with successes and failures that are in truth caused only by the great course of historical development. States and peoples, like trees in a forest, germinate, strike root, grow and spread, and when their lifetime runs out they break down to make room for new formations.
Erster Teil
1. Allgemeine Lage Österreich-Ungarns
Conrad opens with the view that governed his whole activity in peacetime: his whole work as chief of the general staff was shot through with conflicts arising from the fact that his fundamental views on policy and its conduct stood in contradiction to those of the decisive personalities. He saw the monarchy threatened by unmistakable dangers to its existence; his opponents in opinion either did not estimate these at their full magnitude or believed they could escape them by temporising, whereas he was convinced they could be met only by preventive action. The dangers were the disintegrating national movements within, the aggressive tendencies of Serbia, Russia and Italy, and the indirect dangers flowing from Austria-Hungary’s alliance with Germany. In these he saw the determining factors for the conduct of internal and external policy, and the necessity of reckoning with war as their means. He gives a sketch of the complicated internal structure of the monarchy for the foreign reader, and of the deliberate misleading by which Austria-Hungary’s hostile agitators deceived foreign opinion.
2. Die Berufung zum Chef des Generalstabes
Conrad recounts his path to the highest military post. In spring 1899 he was colonel and regimental commander in Austrian Silesia; on 9 April 1899 he was appointed brigadier at Trieste, promoted major-general three weeks later, and soon, as the senior general there, took over the military station command when the senior admiral left the post of sea-district commander. The position imposed on him political as well as purely military duties. From Trieste he gained an early picture of the situation whose essential conclusion was that it was a utopia to count on Italy as an ally; one had rather to be prepared to be deserted by Italy, and in all likelihood attacked, as soon as a favourable opportunity offered. He traces the development of his views and the circumstances of his summons to the office of chief of the general staff.
3. Die Vorgeschichte der Annexion
Conrad turns to his official activity as chief of the general staff. The first and most important thing on entering office was to establish accord with the minister of foreign affairs, Baron Ährenthal, because he considered the intimate connection between external policy and the work of war preparation incumbent on the chief of the general staff the essential thing. He wrote to Ährenthal a courteous letter setting out this view and asking his support in common working; the reply was a formally correct and obliging letter. But in time many divergences of opinion led to it that the accord he held so indispensable was not reached on all questions. He sets out the considerations he urged — for a state, as the example of Spain and Italy showed, could restrict its war preparations to its few limited war-cases, whereas the monarchy, with its manifold frontiers and its exposed position, was differently placed — and the memorial of 30 December 1907 which he laid before the Kaiser.
4. Die Entwicklung der Annexionskrise
For the development of the annexation crisis the conditions in the South Slav lands and on the Balkans were chiefly determining. Croatia was united with Hungary by the Ausgleich of 1867/68; at its head stood a banus, but the Croatian questions were represented and decided in Budapest, and the banus was named by the emperor only with Hungary’s consent. The aim of the leading Hungarian politicians was to restrict Croatia’s already narrowly measured special rights and gradually to extend the sphere of power of the Hungarian state over Croatia and Slavonia, and also over Dalmatia, Bosnia and the Herzegovina, for which they invoked long-faded historical rights. All this met resistance not only from the Croats but from the remaining South Slavs, all the more as the Hungarian government provoked it by administrative measures — Magyar speech on the Croatian railways, exploitation of the forests, hindrance of railway building favourable to Croatia, one-sided finance whereby some fifty million crowns a year were said to flow from Croatia to Hungary, the Magyarising of Fiume, school policy and the like. Conrad describes the party struggles within Croatia, the pure Croatian Starčević party against the Hungarian-oriented National party and against the Serbs, and the whole process by which the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to be proclaimed.
5. Der Verlauf der Annexionskrise
Conrad narrates the course of the crisis through its phases and the friction it produced, not shunning apparently irrelevant detail, for the picture must be clear. He quotes the telegrams that came in on 6 October 1908, when the extra sheet of the Belgrade Politika announced that the annexation of Bosnia was to be proclaimed, and the Serbian foreign ministry demanded immediate mobilisation and war to the death against the monarchy. That mood, he notes, was not first called forth by the annexation question; it was the permanent keynote, breaking out spontaneously at the least occasion. He recounts the diplomatic and military measures, the attitude of Russia and of the other powers, the war preparations for 1909, and the receding of the crisis as the monarchy asserted itself.
Zweiter Teil
Politischer Abschnitt
The political section of the second part treats the political side of the period, the relations with the ministry of foreign affairs, the party conditions and the intrigues, and the political frictions of Conrad’s tenure as they bore upon the army and upon the conduct of the monarchy.
Militärischer Abschnitt: Einführung, I. Entwicklung der Wehrmacht
The military section treats the development of the armed power of the monarchy during Conrad’s years of office. The introduction is followed by an account of the organic development of the Wehrmacht and the system of defence, of training, manoeuvres and regulations, of the spirit of the army, of personal matters, of the general staff, and of the war navy; of concrete preparations for war; of fortifications; of the means of communication; and of the intelligence service. Conrad dwells on the inadequacy of the means granted the army and on his unceasing labour to raise it to the level the exposed position of the monarchy demanded.
Schlußwort
Herewith, Conrad concludes, closes the account of the events in the time from autumn 1906 to the end of 1909. For the following period down to the outbreak of the world war the occurrences that concern him are to be related year by year and within each year in their chronological succession, so that the reader may have the picture of the gradual development. He welcomes it if the reader has gained the impression that many statements in these pages repeat themselves wearily; that impression may make clear over how long periods the execution even of the most insignificant measures was drawn out, and how many of these measures, despite unceasing admonition, remained unfulfilled.
Anhang (Anlage 1 bis 42)
The appendix contains forty-two documents from the two parts: the studies on South Tyrol and on the war preparations (Studien I–IV), the memorial of 6 April 1907 with its additions, the proceedings of the Skupština at Sarajevo in November 1907, the conferences with Baron Ährenthal in November and December 1907, the memorial of 31 December 1907, the exchange of letters with the archduke-heir Franz Ferdinand and with Baron Ährenthal through 1908 and 1909, the audience of 16 December 1907, the conversation with King Carol I of Rumania at Sinaia on 22 June 1908, the correspondence with General von Moltke, chief of the German general staff, the bases of the concrete war preparations for 1909, the memorial of 6 March 1909 on the war-case against Serbia, the data for orientation on Austria-Hungary’s Wehrmacht in 1906, and the revelations from the Serbian side.

sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd2.title: Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band II: Die Zeit des libyschen Krieges und des Balkankrieges bis Ende 1912
sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd2.content:
Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band II: Die Zeit des libyschen Krieges und des Balkankrieges bis Ende 1912
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925), Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918. Zweiter Band: Die Zeit des libyschen Krieges und des Balkankrieges bis Ende 1912. Wien, Berlin, Leipzig, München: Rikola Verlag, 1922. The second volume of the memoirs of the chief of the Austro-Hungarian general staff carries the account from 1910 through the end of 1912, treated year by year: the receding of the annexation crisis, the army budget conflict and Conrad’s dismissal in November 1911, the outbreak of the Italian war over Tripoli, his years as army inspector, the first Balkan War, and his reinstatement as chief of the general staff in December 1912. The raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of California, Berkeley library; Rikola Verlag 1922), 484 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order.
1910
Allgemeine Lage
Conrad characterises 1910 as, on the one hand, the outward calming of the annexation crisis and the appearance of peaceful conditions, on the other hand the increasing thickening of the ring closing around Germany and Austria-Hungary, the visible war preparations of their opponents, and the demand this raised to bring one’s own forces to the greatest possible height. This it was his business to promote. The diplomacy of the Central Powers was chiefly concerned with plastering over the cracks; the diplomacy of the Entente powers, and of Italy, seized upon the great moving forces and used them for their own ends. In Germany Bethmann Hollweg had on 14 July 1909 followed Prince Bülow as imperial chancellor, after the passage of the great imperial finance reform. Conrad traces the political and military position of the monarchy in this year, the normal work of the general staff, the organic development of the Wehrmacht, and his personal employment.
1911
Normale Arbeiten, Ausbau der Wehrmacht, Konflikt in der Budgetfrage
The account of 1911 treats Conrad’s normal work, the development of the armed power of the monarchy, and the conflict over the budget.
