He pressed for the creation of six army inspectors as future commanders-in-chief and for the reinforcement of the army, and came into conflict with the minister of foreign affairs and with the authorities over the means he held the exposed position of the monarchy to demand.
Ausbruch des libyschen Krieges (Tripolis)
The action against Tripoli ripened in the summer of 1911. Conrad quotes the correspondence of the Austro-Hungarian military attaché in Rome, Lieutenant-Colonel Mietzl, on the position of the Italian minister of foreign affairs, San Giuliano, who in the debate on the foreign budget was attacked for his weakness and in particular over Tripoli, gave himself the credit that Italy had a claim to a special position there, but set right the exaggerated and invented reports which the Italian press had for months been putting into the world about Tripoli, about the treatment of the Italians by Turkey and about the penetration of the other states, in order to work up public opinion. Whether that speech answered to San Giuliano’s conviction or only served to veil Italy’s intentions might be left open; the signs multiplied that military preparations were in train in Italy for an action abroad, with the participation of the fleet, starting from southern Italy — whether against Albania or against Tripoli was at first doubtful.
Der Konflikt mit Graf Ährenthal
Conrad recounts the deepening of his conflict with Baron (by then Count) Ährenthal, minister of foreign affairs. The divergences between the military requirements he pressed and the conduct of the foreign ministry led to growing friction, which he set down at length and which finally brought about his dismissal.
Meine Entlassung von der Stelle des Chefs des Generalstabes
On the afternoon of 29 November 1911 the new wing-adjutant of the archduke-heir, Lieutenant-Colonel Dr. von Bardolff, told Conrad on the archduke’s behalf that on the following day he was to appear in audience before the Kaiser, who would announce his dismissal from the post of chief of the general staff with simultaneous appointment as army inspector. Conrad replied that he had no thought of sulking, that he had done his service as chief as well as he could, and was glad to be rid of a post that had in any case been forced upon him and to come again nearer to the troops. On 30 November 1911 he appeared at Schönbrunn. The Kaiser said it grieved him, but after mature reflection he was obliged to remove Conrad from his present post and appoint him army inspector; the reasons were known to him. The Kaiser spoke appreciative words, and had the grace to say that their personal relation had become a friendly one and that he had had Conrad called to tell him of his dismissal himself, because his upright manner had won his respect.
1912
Rein militärische Tätigkeit als Armee-Inspektor
Conrad divides his professional activity in 1912 into his purely military activity as army inspector and his politico-military activity in that office. As army inspector he had been assigned the command of the 3rd army in case of war. He describes the application of the army manoeuvres and instructional journeys, and his concrete proposals for the reinforcement of the forces in the light of the threatening situation.
Ausbruch des Balkankrieges
With the outbreak of the first Balkan War in October 1912 the whole situation of the monarchy was changed. Conrad describes the military and political position, the concentration of the armies of the Balkan states against Turkey, and the considerations that the monarchy had to weigh in the face of the possible involvement of Russia.
Meine Mission in Rumänien
The difficult situation created by the Balkan War, which forced Austria-Hungary to reckon with the possibility of warlike complications, and also with Russia, made it advisable to secure Rumania for this case. It was a question, however, of not letting the thread with Bulgaria — Rumania’s jealous rival — break, that is, of smoothing out the differences between Bulgaria and Rumania and offering one’s good offices for this. Count Berchtold was unremittingly concerned to shape the policy of the monarchy in this sense: to bring Rumania and Bulgaria into accord and to have Rumania actively at its side with all its forces for the eventual war against Russia. In mid-November 1912 Conrad was charged by the archduke-heir to prepare himself for a mission to Bukarest to work in this sense. As an outward pretext, he was to convey to King Carol the condolences of the Kaiser on the death of the Countess of Flanders, the king’s sister. From Berchtold he received his instructions; he met the king and the leading Rumanian statesmen, and sought to secure Rumania’s adherence to the monarchy.
Meine Wiederernennung zum Chef des Generalstabes
On 6 December 1912 Conrad received through the head of the military chancellery of Archduke Franz Ferdinand the written order to present himself in audience with the archduke on 7 December. The archduke received him at the Belvedere; on the tables lay the maps of the various theatres of war with the concentration plans for the several war-cases. The archduke declared that he wished to go over all this once more with him, since the plans had remained almost wholly unchanged since Conrad’s time as chief of the general staff, and that with the present situation one must be prepared for surprises. When the discussion was ended, the archduke turned to him suddenly: “So, now I must tell you something more; you must become chief of the general staff again.” Conrad was astonished, hesitated, and made objections, in particular that it would not be right to remove again his successor who had been appointed barely a year before. The archduke replied that this removal would take place with all honour for the person concerned, but that he, as presumptive supreme commander of the army, must lay weight on having at the head of the general staff, should it come to war, the man from whom all the preparations for war proceeded. The Kaiser, he added, was in agreement and would receive him in audience that very day. On 12 December 1912 Conrad received the hand-written warrant of the Kaiser reinstating him as chief of the general staff, and he took up again his activity in that office.
Anhang
The appendix contains the extracts from the chief of the general staff’s audience of 13 February 1911, the memorial of 23 April 1911, and the memorial of 15 November 1911 with its appendices.

sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd3.title: Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band III: 1913 und das erste Halbjahr 1914, bis zum Fürstenmord in Sarajevo
sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd3.content:
Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band III: 1913 und das erste Halbjahr 1914, bis zum Fürstenmord in Sarajevo
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925), Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918. Dritter Band: 1913 und das erste Halbjahr 1914. Wien, Berlin, Leipzig, München: Rikola Verlag, 1923. This third volume, the last of the three dedicated to the events before the outbreak of the world war, covers the year 1913 and the first six months of 1914, and ends with Conrad’s departure for Sarajevo on 23 June 1914, four days before the assassination of the archduke-heir. The raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of California, Berkeley library; Rikola Verlag 1923), 828 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order.
Charakteristik der politisch-militärischen Lage (1913)
Conrad states his governing conviction with the greatest plainness: the root of all evil for the Austro-Hungarian monarchy was still, as always, the relation to Serbia and to the Russia standing behind Serbia. At this root the evil had to be seized; everything else was secondary. The ways that had always floated before him were, in the first place, the attainment of a lasting confederal union of Serbia with the Habsburg monarchy in a peaceful manner; but if Serbia declined the union and continued its hostile aspirations directed against the monarchy — and this case was present — then a warlike settlement at the suitable moment. Already in 1906, on his appointment as chief of the general staff, he had pointed to this, and in 1908–09 he had described the moment as come to make clear conditions with Serbia, foreseeing that the chances of this unavoidable settlement must from then on only grow worse. In 1913 he held the last moment to have come to carry out this settlement at all with hope of success; if this moment too were neglected, the monarchy seemed to him to drift without a rudder toward the unavoidable doom that threatened it from Serbia and Russia. In this conviction he did everything to see that this last moment did not pass unused. It remained unused. The policy of the monarchy let itself be taken prisoner by side-issues and distracted from the great goal — to the joy of its enemies.
1913
The account of 1913 is given month by month. It opens with the political and military situation from the beginning of the year to the resumption of hostilities against Turkey on 3 February 1913, with the audiences and political conferences of this period, the military agreements between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy and the fleet agreement, and the military measures down to 2 March. Conrad then treats the period from the resumption of hostilities to the rupture of the Balkan league on 28 May 1913, with the particulars of the events, the documents and the conferences, and the Skutari affair; then the period from the rupture of the Balkan league to the intervention of Rumania on 10 July 1913; then the period from Rumania’s intervention to the peace of Bucharest (10 August 1913) and that of Constantinople (29 September 1913). He records his presence at the German imperial manoeuvres at Schweidnitz (6 to 10 September), and the manoeuvres in Bohemia with his rupture with the archduke-heir Franz Ferdinand. The year closes with the events from the peace treaties of Bucharest and Constantinople to the end of the year, the consecration of the memorial of the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig, and a retrospective. In the chapters on the essential military measures abroad and in Austria-Hungary, and the concrete war-preparation work of 1913, he surveys Rumania, Turkey, Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro and Russia, and the state of the armed forces of the monarchy.
Das erste Halbjahr 1914
Jänner, Feber, März
The first half of 1914 is likewise treated month by month, with a foreword and surveys of Albania, Epirus, Germany, Italy, the concrete war-preparation work, additions on the general situation, the events at home, the development of the Wehrmacht, the training, manoeuvres and generals’ conference, and the audiences with the archduke-heir and the Kaiser.
April, Mai, Juni
For the spring months Conrad treats Rumania, Turkey, Serbia, Montenegro, Germany — including his visit to General Moltke at Karlsbad — Russia, France, England and Albania; the general situation; the development of the Wehrmacht; the meetings of Kaiser Wilhelm II with Archduke Franz Ferdinand; the audience with the Kaiser on 4 June; and the instructional journey, manoeuvres and departure for Sarajevo.
Übungsreise, Manöver, Abreise nach Sarajevo
The archduke-heir had told Conrad, on the occasion of the army manoeuvres in Bohemia in 1913, of his intention to travel to Bosnia in spring or summer 1914 and on that occasion to attend manoeuvres of the troops of the 15th and 16th corps, to be held by order and under the direction of the chief of the land and army inspector, Feldzeugmeister Potiorek. Conrad asks leave for his plan to lead the generals’ journey in Croatia, and fixes his own programme accordingly. He is informed that he is to arrive at Bad Ilidže (near Sarajevo) on 24 June and may leave again on the evening of 27 June. On 8 June he travels to lead the great general-staff journey through Graz, Marburg, Pettau and Nagykanizsa, combining with it the intention of learning the terrain intended for the army manoeuvres of autumn 1914. From 9 to 18 June he leads the great general-staff journey; on 19 June he is again in Vienna; on 23 June he travels with Colonel Metzger and Major Kundmann from Vienna to Sarajevo — four days before the assassination at Sarajevo.
Schlußwort
With this, Conrad writes, he closes the three first volumes dedicated to the events before the outbreak of the world war. The reader may have found it laborious to work through the many particulars; but if he has undergone this labour, he will have gained a true picture of the situation as it existed in Austria-Hungary when the great struggle for existence broke over the old empire. For the creation of this picture the form of the mosaic seemed to him more appropriate than a carefully painted, sensational canvas; he thought it more stimulating for the reader to draw the conclusions himself from the material laid before him than to accept a subjectively coloured summary ready-made.
Anhang (Anlage 1 bis 10)
The appendix contains ten documents and maps: sketch A of the situation on the Balkan theatre of war in January 1913 and sketch B of July 1913 (as supplements in a pocket at the end of the volume), the prospect of an Austro-Russian war and Rumania, the changes in the relative strength of the armed forces in consequence of the projected increases (March 1913), the report on the observations at the manoeuvres in Germany in 1913, the protocol of the council of ministers for common affairs of 3 October 1913, the verbal note to the Serbian government of 17 October 1913, political and military news from Rumania, the letter of the Italian chief of the general staff Lieutenant-General Pollio of 28 November 1913, and the further supplements.

sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd4.title: Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band IV: 24. Juni 1914 bis 30. September 1914
sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd4.content:
Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band IV: 24. Juni 1914 bis 30. September 1914
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925), Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918. Vierter Band: 24. Juni 1914 bis 30. September 1914. Wien, Berlin, Leipzig, München: Rikola Verlag, 1923. This volume carries the account from Conrad’s arrival at Ilidže near Sarajevo on 24 June 1914, through the assassination, the outbreak of war, the declaration against Serbia and the deployment and first operations against Serbia and Russia, down to 30 September 1914. The raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of Michigan library; Rikola Verlag 1923), 970 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order.
Vorwort
Conrad observes that although this fourth volume embraces only the time from 24 June to 30 September 1914, it nevertheless contains the history of the war from its beginning to its decision; for this decision lay in the failure of the plan agreed between Germany and Austria-Hungary for the decisive first action. What followed was only a stubborn struggle in the endeavour to make good this decision and its consequences. It failed because of the superiority of the enemies, the failure of the means, and the social, or rather national, disintegration within. The defeat on the Marne was the signal for Italy, Rumania and the other opponents of Germany and Austria-Hungary to seek to join the Entente, and thereby an overwhelming superiority came to the enemy side.
Erster Teil — Der Fürstenmord in Sarajevo, der Kriegsausbruch und die politischen Vorgänge bis zum Abgehen des Armeeoberkommandos auf den Kriegsschauplatz
The first part opens with the assassination of the archduke-heir at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Band III had closed with Conrad’s departure from Vienna on 23 June for Bosnia, to the manoeuvres between the 15th and 16th corps. He records the political events up to the outbreak of war, the declaration of war against Serbia on 25 July 1914, and the political events from the outbreak of the war against Serbia to the departure of the army high command for the Russian theatre of war on 16 August 1914, closing the part with a retrospect.
Zweiter Teil — Die Anfangsoperationen in Serbien und Rußland bis zum 15. August 1914
The second part, on the opening operations in Serbia and Russia down to 15 August 1914, opens with the chapters “Kriegskritiker und Propheten”, “Die k. u. k. Wehrmacht”, “Das k. u. k. (erste) Armeeoberkommando”, “Befehls- und Machtbereich des Armeeoberkommandos”, “Das Verhältnis zu den Verbündeten”, “Gemeinsamer Oberbefehl”, and “Wesen der Kriegführung — Kriegsausgang — Geschichtsschreibung”. Conrad then treats the military events from 23 to 31 July 1914, the general questions concerning the war case against Russia, the changes in the originally fixed deployment against Russia, the summarized data on the deployment against Russia and Serbia-Montenegro, and the deployment against Serbia and against Russia, with a retrospect. He records the military events from 1 to 15 August (to the departure of the army high command from Vienna for the Russian theatre of war), the extension of the Danube line as a fortified central zone, a summary of the events on the Balkan theatre of war from 12 to 15 August, the general picture of the situation on 15 August, his farewell audience with Kaiser Franz Joseph on 15 August, and the departure of the army high command for the Russian theatre of war.
Dritter Teil — Der Kriegsverlauf vom 16. August bis 30. September 1914 und die politische Entwicklung in dieser Zeit
The third part treats the course of the war from 16 August to 30 September 1914 and the political development of this time, in a day-by-day narrative, with a foreword, a retrospect, and a closing word.
Schlußwort
Conrad writes that where in this volume, in the description of the war events, he has unreservedly and truthfully cited individual cases of the failure of k. u. k. troops and leaders, the reader should yet keep before his eyes the high measure of valour, endurance and fighting ability that was required to fight the victorious battles of Krasnik and Komarów in the stubborn struggle with a brave, energetically led and finally numerically superior enemy, and to hold out to the utmost in the battle of Lemberg–Rawa Ruska. The weeks-long struggles of this war period set a lasting monument of honour to the heroism of the old k. u. k. army. All participants may remember this with pride, and it is a duty to think with gratitude of those who sank on the battlefields “faithful unto death”, not only for the existence of the old empire but also for the protection of the nearer homeland. He hopes that a generation may again flourish for Austrians that accomplishes the like. In the open and unreserved setting forth of the events he saw the most correct and worthy form of meeting the tendentious, spiteful attacks that were levelled at the old k. u. k. army and its leaders by their adversaries; the objective reader will know how to separate light and shade.
Anhang
The appendix contains 27 documents and the map supplements A to D (9 leaves). The supplements 1a, 1b, 2, 6, 22a, 22b and 22c are bound into this volume; the remaining supplements and the 9 leaves of map supplements lie in a separate pocket.

sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd5.title: Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band V: Oktober, November, Dezember 1914
sources/conrad-aus-meiner-dienstzeit-bd5.content:
Conrad von Hötzendorf — Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918, Band V: Oktober, November, Dezember 1914
Franz Graf Conrad von Hötzendorf (1852–1925), Aus meiner Dienstzeit 1906–1918. Fünfter Band: Oktober, November, Dezember 1914. Wien, Berlin, Leipzig, München: Rikola Verlag, 1925. This final volume carries the account from 1 October 1914 to the close of the first war year. The raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of Michigan library; Rikola Verlag 1925), 1022 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order.
Vorwort
Conrad explains that, ill for more than a year, he had been unable to complete the manuscript of Band V as he wished in the autumn of the previous year, and the volume therefore appears late. Its predecessor, Band IV, ends with the preparation of the Austro-Hungarian armies and the German eastern army for the renewed offensive against Russia and with the first events of the recommenced offensive against Serbia, closing with 30 September 1914. Band V continues the account of events in direct succession, beginning therefore with 1 October, and reaches to the close of the first war year 1914. Like the others, this volume claims to be only a single, rough-hewn building stone, a small part of the great material out of which future historians will have to erect the structure that may be called an objective representation of the world war. He hopes so. But should they set the one-sided, chauvinist-propagandist purpose of historiography, under the cloak of patriotic duty, higher than scientific objectivity, nobility and dignity, and should they deliberately turn the torch of truth to the ground and stifle it, then the hope of a great objective work will remain in vain and posterity will be richer in many a delusion. He has kept, in Band V as in Band IV and for the same reasons, to the day-by-day rendering of events, which alone can give the reader a halfway accurate picture of the progress of the military action. The supreme leader in war must be ready to act at every hour of day and night and be prepared to see everything he has planned and ordered frustrated. His memoir work is meant to leave the historian an ordered, intellectually connected document material, and also to offer the professional soldier the possibility of coming to know the war and its conduct at the highest point in its innermost connections and often decisive details.
The renewed offensive in Galicia and Poland; battles at the San and on the Vistula
The volume’s principal subject is the renewed offensive in Galicia and Poland; the battles at the San and on the Vistula; the retreat of the allies in Poland and Galicia; the breaking forth of the Russian masses over the Vistula; the battles at Łódź–Lowicz, Krakau and Limanowa–Łapanów; the advance of the allies; the fighting in Poland; the battles at the San and near Sambor; the fighting in the Carpathians; the renewed advance of the Russians; the limitation of both sides’ advance; and the temporary position warfare from the Baltic to the frontier of Rumania.
The second offensive and the setback in Serbia
The volume also covers the second offensive and the setback in Serbia, month by month for October, November and December, closing with a retrospect on the battles of Łódź, Krakau and Limanowa–Łapanów.
Charakteristik der Lage am Jahresschluß
Conrad summarizes the situation at the close of the year. Against Russia: Group Pflanzer in stubborn, energetic small war on the forest-Carpathian wall, holding the important Uzsok Pass, with Przemysl in active defence binding strong forces of the besieger; the 3rd Army’s eastern group not only checking the enemy’s advance but itself in successful attack, while the main body of the army gave way before the strong pressure of the superior enemy; the 4th and 1st Armies stubbornly holding their fronts; the German 9th Army thrown into the defensive and expecting reinforcements. On the Balkan front, the Balkan forces drawn together in the 5th Army were, after the failed offensive, recovering behind the Save and Danube; Bosnia was secured by special groups, and the small war against Montenegro was successfully in progress. On New Year’s Eve he drove with Lieutenant-Colonel Kundmann to Berlin, departing by special train from Teschen at 10 in the evening, toward the new year.
Rückblick auf das erste Kriegsjahr und dessen Vorgeschichte
Under the headings of war guilt (Kriegsschuld) and the causes of the war (Kriegsursachen), Conrad insists that this retrospect can only touch the most essential in a fleeting reference. To grasp the thousandfold connections that in their final result led to the world war, the laborious path remains of following, in strict objectivity and on the basis of far-reaching historical knowledge, the rich and ever-growing material that the literature has offered. A complete connection will only be researchable until the archives of the enemies also open. Whoever goes this way unprejudiced, guided only by the drive for truth, will soon come to the insight that there can be no question of war guilt, and that the world war, too, is to be valued as one of those unavoidable transformations that spring from the developmental drive of states and peoples and from the resulting struggle for existence. Once one reaches this height of conception, every seeking of a guilt for the war appears an idle, even petty undertaking. Only the fathoming of the causes of the war can form the field of historical research; it must proceed from the struggle for existence as the world-dominating principle. This is not, he adds, an excuse for the means employed by statesmen, politicians and regents to reach their goals: the whole Great-Serbian policy, bloody and murder-stained in its procedure, must always be regarded with disgust and contempt. A politics that aims only at preserving peace must in the end lead to ruin and defeat; only a politics with positive goals, resolved on struggle when chances offer and skilled in creating, bringing about and exploiting those chances, makes it possible to survive the struggle for existence victoriously. Aging monarchs and statesmen resting on inherited laurels commonly lack the inner force for this; but nature sees to it that young opponents arise who reach actively over them into the wheel of history. So, he writes, was the policy of our opponents. Setting against the conservative, merely preservative foreign policy of Kaiser Franz Joseph and the no less peace-loving Kaiser Wilhelm II the busy policy of a Poincaré, the aggressive policy of a Pašić, the sly policy of a Bratianu, the faithless far-reaching policy of a Salandra, San Giuliano and Sonnino, the coldly calculating policy of England, and finally the deed-hungry policy of the Russian Panslavists who went their own ways over the head of the weak Tsar, one may find the connection that led to Germany’s and Austria-Hungary’s isolation and defeat. The shots fired on 28 June 1914 against the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary tore the trustful out of this deception; it was too late. After the Berlin Congress (1878), Bismarck thought to drive Europe from the box, but already forces were stirring around him that pressed toward a transformation of the world situation. Even at the end of the nineteenth century a transformation of the grouping of the powers in Europe had begun that could be called the encirclement of Germany and Austria-Hungary, whose aim was to paralyse and shatter these two powers.
Schlußwort
Conrad closes by defending the k. u. k. army against the belittlements that had come to it from the German side during the war, stating that as the oldest general of the old army, in which he served forty-seven years in war and peace, he felt the duty to correct legends of which it was to be feared they would be stamped as facts and taken over as such into history. He wished in particular to protect the k. u. k. army against those lightly thrown, spiteful phrases hurled at it by men who wandered in the labyrinth of arrogance. He was not blind to the defects of the old army, as numerous passages of his work show; but in his defence he was also guided by the wish not to let irritations arise between the Germans and Austrians, which would be the more misplaced as, surrounded on all sides by enemies, they were more than ever dependent on keeping their concord.
Anlagenverzeichnis
The appendix (Anlagen and maps A–E and 1–35) lies in a separate pocket given with this volume. It includes plans of the fortresses of Przemysl and Krakau, the order of battle and strength of the k. u. k. armies on the Russian theatre of war (early October, mid-November, early December 1914), and a series of situation documents for the own and the presumed enemy positions on the Russian and Serbian theatres of war through October, November and December 1914.

sources/czernin-im-weltkriege-1919.title: Ottokar Czernin — Im Weltkriege (1919)
sources/czernin-im-weltkriege-1919.content:
Ottokar Czernin — Im Weltkriege
Ottokar Theobald Otto Maria Graf Czernin von und zu Chudenitz (1872–1932), Im Weltkriege. Berlin und Wien: Ullstein & Co, 1919 (21.–30. Tausend). The memoir of Austria-Hungary’s foreign minister from December 1916 to April 1918, published in the year of the armistice. The raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of Michigan library), 452 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order. The narrative runs through a Vorwort, twelve chapters, and a final Schlußbetrachtung, followed by an Anhang of seven documentary appendices and a Namen- und Sachregister.
Vorwort
Czernin opens by disclaiming any intention to write the history of the war exhaustively — impossible in a small book and not its purpose. Its purpose is rather to portray single events and single personalities, which he saw from closer proximity and therefore more clearly than the public, to deliver individual moment-photographs of the great drama; out of these individual pictures a whole will nonetheless emerge that in many respects may deviate from the still so fragmentary war histories known until then. Every man sees men and events from his personal angle — that is unavoidable. He speaks of men who stood near him, of others who crossed his path without leaving a personal impression, and of still others with whom he had grave conflicts, and he tries to judge all of them objectively. He depicts men and things as he saw them; where the depiction appears false, the ground lies not in preconceived opinion but in a perhaps existing lack of judgment. Not everything was to be said; much was not explained though it could be explained, for the time separating him from the events is still too short to draw the veil from every occurrence. But what is suppressed changes nothing in the total picture, which he portrays as it mirrors itself in his head. Signed O. Cz.
I. Einleitende Betrachtungen
Czernin’s introduction to the war’s causes. Just as a thunderstorm is preceded by the separation of electricities and an atmosphere no longer bearable, so the political barometer of the foreign ministries had stood at storm for years. The visible beginnings of the European tension reach back to the time of Edward VII: on the one side England’s fear of the gigantically growing Germany, on the other the Berlin policy that had become the terror of the Thames and the belief that in Berlin the thought was taking root of seizing world dominion. He holds that France and England did not want the war in 1914, and describes the moral coalition against Germany, the mad armaments fever, and Czernin’s last conversation with Franz Ferdinand. He treats the catastrophe, Berchtold and the ultimatum to Serbia, a Lichnowsky dispatch (Grey’s mediation attempt), the telegram of King George to Prince Heinrich, the English proposal conditionally accepted, the war as unleashed by Russia, Tisza against the sharp ultimatum, and Tschirschky’s own démarches — he, not Bethmann, for drawing Austria-Hungary into this war. He recounts his audience with the Emperor at Ischl, Rumania and Italy confronted with accomplished facts, and calls Austria-Hungary’s greatest misfortune the German invasion of Belgium. On the evening of 4 August came the decision on England’s neutrality at Germany. He marks the first fateful victory of the German military men and judges Bismarck’s heritage a curse for Germany, Wilhelm II a prisoner of his generals. The Entente was never for a peace of understanding; he cites the London Pakt of 26 April 1915, Austria-Hungary’s military inferiority, and the question of a separate peace for Austria as war with Germany. He closes with the politics of Stephan Tisza and the judgment that Austria-Hungary’s disintegration was irrevocable.
II. Konopischt
Czernin’s portrait of the heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, framed by his estate at Konopischt. Konopischt has become the cradle of many legends, and the role the heir played before the war is subject to many and partly false commentaries. The Archduke-thronfolger was a quite peculiar nature: the main trait of his character was a great lack of balance — he knew no middle line, was as hot in hatred as in love, pursued nothing as other men do but did all he did in superhuman dimensions; his buying and collecting fury for antiquities was proverbial and bordered on the fantastic, and a first-rate shot, he hunted only on the greatest scale. Czernin treats the park of Konopischt, the Archduke’s lack of linguistic talent, his embitterment, his antipathy to everything Hungarian, his aversion to cringers and flatterers, Franz Ferdinand and Aehrenthal, the great-Austrian program, the cooling of his relations with Franz Joseph, his approach to Kaiser Wilhelm, and his refusal of the role of warmonger. He writes of the Duchess of Hohenberg, the Archduke’s personal fearlessness and his great qualities, the old Emperor, Franz Ferdinand’s end, the planned reconstruction of the Monarchy, army and fleet, a three-emperors alliance against revolution, and the judgment that the Archduke was more a patron than an adversary of the Serbs and no partisan of a closer attachment to Germany.
III. Wilhelm II.
Czernin’s study of the German Emperor. He treats Wilhelm’s belief in the divine right of kings (Gottesgnadentum), the emperor crisis of 1908, and his own dealings with Wilhelm II in 1917 and 1918. He writes of Emperor Charles’s faith in his own popularity, of Byzantinism, of Emperor Charles and Conrad (von Hötzendorf), and the reinstatement of Joseph Ferdinand. He describes Wilhelm at Kiel Week, his nature, and the tragedy of his life. He examines his bearing before the world war, at the outbreak of war, at Kreuznach, his doubts about the war’s outcome, and his oscillations in war aims. He recounts how the German Crown Prince became a pacifist in 1917, Czernin’s visit to the Western front, a letter of Emperor Charles to the Crown Prince proposing territorial sacrifices in Alsace-Lorraine, Austrian renunciation of Galicia, and the attachment of Poland to Germany; and Ludendorff on the pacifist Crown Prince and Ludendorff’s will.
IV. Rumänien
Czernin’s account of his time as minister in Bucharest from autumn 1913. He describes King Carol, the secret alliance as a scrap of paper, Bratianu, and Rumanian society. He recounts the day of Sarajevo, Take Jonescu, the sudden turn after the ultimatum — “Austria has gone mad” — and a wave of hatred. The King was full of grief; he writes of Carmen Sylva (Queen Elisabeth), and judges that Bratianu was never truly neutral. Queen Marie was for war. Czernin was interned; he recounts the Zeppelin raids on Bucharest and his return journey through Russia. He distinguishes three phases of the relations, holds that Hungary should make concessions while Tisza refused, and closes with reflections on diplomacy and on the Russian ruble’s influence.
V. Der verschärfte U-Bootkrieg
Czernin on his elevation to minister of foreign affairs and the decision for unrestricted submarine warfare. He recounts the peace offer of the Central Powers, Wilhelm II’s judgment that the Entente had slapped him in the face, Tirpitz, the ruthless U-boat war, and Bethmann on the iron pressure of the military. He gives the warnings of himself and of Prince Hohenlohe, the visits of Zimmermann and Admiral Holtzendorff to Vienna, and Holtzendorff’s guarantee of success; the optimistic posture of the German leaders still in April 1918; Hindenburg and Ludendorff; Ludendorff’s judgment that the dynasty could not survive a peace of renunciation; his correspondence with Tisza; and the judgment that Germany misjudged the situation, the construction of further U-boats being restricted in the course of the war.
VI. Friedensversuche
The longest chapter, on the peace efforts of 1917. Czernin sets out Austria-Hungary’s foreign policy and Hungary’s interference, Tisza, and a letter of Tisza. In February 1917 came peace feelers from tsarist Russia; then the outbreak of the Russian revolution, and fears on the Thames. In April 1917 he reported to Emperor Charles on Austria’s exhaustion, the dull grumbling of the masses, America’s intervention, and the necessity of peace. He gives Bethmann’s answer, his attempt to reach the German Reichstag, Erzberger and Südekum, the Reichstag peace resolution of 19 July 1917, and Bethmann its victim; Michaelis’s “as I understand it” and his letter demanding that Belgium, Courland, Lithuania and Poland be brought into close economic and military connection with Germany and that Longwy and Briey be made economically useful for Germany. He gives the demands of the German supreme command — military control of Belgium, Liège and the Flemish coast — and his own judgment that Belgium was a grave obstacle to peace. He treats the indiscretions and interferences, the belief of Paris and London in the dissolution of the Fourfold Alliance, the decline of the peace wish in the Entente, and the flirtation with a separate peace. He writes of England’s fear of German militarism, the Stockholm socialist conference, the failure of the peace efforts, his Budapest speech on world disarmament, the fiasco of the U-boat war, Austria and the London dictate, England and Germany, the dead point, the misleading double policy behind the backs of the responsible men, Clemenceau for Germany’s annihilation, and the intransigence of the Entente.
VII. Wilson
On President Wilson in autumn 1917: his Fourteen Points, the national world problem, the President on Czernin’s policy, and the interruption of the attempts at understanding by Czernin’s resignation.
VIII. Eindrücke und Betrachtungen
Short chapter of impressions and reflections: the defeat of the victors, Europe’s self-laceration in 1917, and Hertling.
IX. Polen
On the Polish question: Tisza against the Austro-Polish solution, Germany’s demand for the evacuation of the part occupied by Austria, the Polish tactics, the German wishes for frontier rectification and Ludendorff’s resistance, and the exchange of Poland for Rumania. He treats Czernin and the Poles, and Mitteleuropa.
X. Brest-Litowsk
Czernin’s account of the peace of Brest-Litowsk. He covers Kerensky’s offensive and the Russian parties, the Bolsheviks, his journey to Brest-Litowsk, General Hoffmann, Joffe, Kamenev and Frau Bizenko, Kühlmann, and the annexionless peace. He gives the threats of the Bulgarians, the Germans’ fear that the Entente might accept a general peace, Hoffmann on the border provinces, Hindenburg’s furious telegrams over the “renunciation” of everything and Ludendorff’s hourly telephone calls, the Russian contradiction and protest strike, the Ukrainians, the arrival of Trotsky, Czernin’s demand for a free hand for himself in case the Germans broke with the Russians, Trotsky’s acceptance of the ultimatum, Hoffmann’s wish to “give the Russians a good beating,” and his unlucky speech. He describes the famine catastrophe in Austria, Trotsky’s reckoning on world revolution, Czernin in Berlin with Hertling and Ludendorff, Kaiser Wilhelm’s telegram demanding Livonia and Estland, the peace with the Ukraine, and the Brotfriede (bread peace).
XI. Der Friede von Bukarest
On the peace of Bucharest. Czernin treats Rumania and Hungary, the message of Emperor Charles to King Ferdinand, Austria’s parity, Kühlmann informed by Czernin of the accomplished fact, and the judgment that without the King only an illegitimate peace with Rumania was possible. He writes of the Averescu ministry, his conversation with King Ferdinand, the Dobrudscha question, Marghiloman, his own constraint before the Hungarian frontier demands, Germany’s economic demands, Germany’s wish for occupation for five or six years after the general peace, and the Bulgarian-Turkish conflict.
XII. Schlußbetrachtung
Czernin’s closing reflection. The further the world war progressed, the more it lost the character of a work directed by individual men and took on that of a cosmic event that escaped the interference of even the most powerful individuals. The coalitions’ agreements chained the cabinets to certain war aims; the promises given to the peoples, the whipped-up hopes of the advantages of final victory, the artificially bred boundless hatred, the increasing barbarization of the world, all created a situation that made every single man a small pebble of a stone avalanche that plunges down leaderless, choiceless and aimless and can no longer be directed by anyone. The Versailles Four-Power Council tried for a time to make the world believe it possessed the power to rebuild Europe according to its ideas — but these were four fundamentally different ideas, for Rome, Paris, London and Washington saw four different worlds, and the four representatives, “the big four,” were each a prisoner of his programs, his promises and his peoples. At home one cursed and derided Wilson for abandoning his program; certainly there is not the least resemblance between the Fourteen Points and the peace of Versailles and St. Germain, but one forgets that Wilson no longer had the power to enforce his will against the other three. Clemenceau, the antipode of Wilson, was likewise not free: if he had tried to make a “Wilson peace,” all the great and small rentiers of France would have risen against him, for they had been told for five years “que les boches payeront tout” — he did what he did with relish, but he had to do it, or France drove him away. He treats Italy’s abyss of revolution and Lloyd George, concluding that the historical moment in which Wilson lost power and imperialism seized it was the year 1917. The Entente, which did not let the war be ended and continued the hunger blockade for months after the close of hostilities, made anarchy a world danger; anarchy and Bolshevism are siblings — Bolshevism is the most frightful grimace of state institutions, its father the war, its mother the famine, its patron despair. Versailles is no end of the war, only a phase of it; the war continues, if in changed form. Coming generations will not call the great drama that has dominated the world for five years the world war but the world revolution, and will know that this world revolution only began with the world war. Neither Versailles nor St. Germain will create a lasting work; in this peace lies the dissolving germ of death. Slowly, under unspeakable torments, a new world will be born; other generations will arise and build up what war and revolution have destroyed — to every winter follows spring, and to death resurrection. Signed, Juli 1919.
Anhang
The seven documentary appendices: I. the decisions of the London Conference of 26 April 1915 (the text of the London Pact with Italy — the military convention, the promised Trentino, South Tyrol to the Brenner, Trieste, Görz and Gradisca, Istria, Dalmatia, Valona, the Dodecanese, the war loan of 50 million pounds sterling, and the exclusion of the Holy See from the peace — signed by Grey, Cambon and Imperiali); II. Count Czernin’s note to the American government of 5 March 1917; III. State Secretary Helfferich on the U-boat war; IV. Count Czernin’s speech in the Austrian Delegation of 24 January 1918; V. the protocol on the peace negotiations at Brest-Litowsk; VI. the protocol on the peace negotiations at Bucharest; VII. the Fourteen Points of Wilson. Followed by the Namen- und Sachregister (index of names and subjects).

sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t4.title: Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome IV
sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t4.content:
Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome IV
Taxile Delord (1815–1877) — Histoire illustrée du second empire. — Tome quatrième. — Nouvelle édition. — Paris: Librairie Germer Baillière et Cie, 108, boulevard Saint-Germain, 1880 (printer: Coulommiers, Typographie Paul Brodard). 59 gravures dans le texte.
Republican journalist and deputy (Siècle), Delord writes a contemporary opposition history of the Second Empire as a continuous narrative, not memoir. This is the illustrated edition (Baillière [1880–83]) of the same multi-tome work originally published 1869–75. The present volume opens with the 1864 legislative session (Thiers and Rouher debating the “liberties necessary”, Ollivier separates from the opposition) and carries the narrative through the Mexican expedition (1864–1865), the Algerian voyage, the climactic 1866 war between Prussia and Austria (Sadowa, Custozza, Treaty of Prague), the close of the Mexican expedition, and a long chapter on the clergy in France (1863–1867: the Syllabus, Encyclical, Protestant internal struggles).
Core chronological span is 1864–1867 — the liberal Empire’s middle years, the Austro-Prussian War as the European watershed, the winding-down of the Mexican adventure, and the religious conflicts (Ultramontane Syllabus versus liberal Catholicism, the Protestant orthodox-liberal schism).
OCR from local Anna’s Archive scan set (OCLC 7058591; Baillière [1880–83]). Cleaned raw keeps title-page through table of contents; internal double-spaces collapsed; front blank library leaves dropped.
Chapters
Chapitre I — La Session de 1864
Opening of the 1864 session; Emperor’s discourse. Senate address: petition on publicity of municipal council sessions, petition on irreligious writings, Renan before the Senate. Corps législatif verification of powers: election of Casimir Périer (Thuillier discourse), Lavertujon. Jurisprudence of the majority. The 300-million loan; Berryer’s discourse. Address debate: amendments of the Left and Centre-Left. Thiers’s discourse; Rouher’s reply — the “liberties necessary”. Jules Favre’s discourse; amendment against official candidacies; Thiers ripostes to Rouher. Abrogation of the coalition law. Pelletan and the municipal regime of Paris and Lyon. Trial of the Thirteen. Foreign policy debate: Schleswig-Holstein and Mexico. Election of Bravay. Alliance of Morny and Ollivier. Ollivier separates from the opposition. Jules Simon’s amendment. Jules Favre and Émile Ollivier. Thiers on the budget. Berryer’s discourse; Rouher’s reply. Ernest Picard and Pelletan.
Chapitre II — L’Expédition du Mexique (1864–1865)
Ball given by General Bazaine in honour of the Emperor and Empress. Coldness of relations between Maximilian and the French. Maximilian at odds with the clergy; he is not sure of the army. Maximilian seeks financial resources; French claims; the Jecker bonds. Maximilian’s programme; formation of the Bureau de l’Esprit public. Maximilian requests a police personnel from Paris. Military situation: French occupation confined to a few points. Colonel Dupin’s exploits. Maximilian undertakes an interior journey. Hostility of the Holy See; arrival of the nuncio at Vera-Cruz. Roman court’s demands. Financial mission of two Mexican bankers to Paris; de Germiny. The Mexican loan patronised by Rouher. Napoleon III’s letter to Bazaine. Bazaine exercises a real dictatorship. Maximilian adopts the grandson of Iturbide. Cruel position of his government. Bazaine’s marriage. Juarez crosses the border. Maximilian’s letter to Napoleon III. Seward’s note on the Mexican Empire and French occupation.
Chapitre III — L’Année 1865
State of opinion at the beginning of 1865. Receptions at the Tuileries. Death of Proudhon. Prohibition of the Barthélemy hall conferences. Duruy’s report on primary instruction; he is disavowed. Death of Morny. Publication of Napoleon III’s Histoire de César (volume I). Death of Cobden. Death of Lincoln. Voyage of the Emperor to Algeria; Prince Napoléon’s discourse at Ajaccio; emotion caused in official circles. The Montmorency trial; the Sandon affair. Prince Napoléon resigns all his functions. The coachmen’s strike. Municipal elections. Death of Palmerston. The Berne congress; the Liège congress. Death of Leopold, king of the Belgians. Death of Lamoricière. Death of Dupin. The committee of Nancy. Imperial letter to Prince Napoléon.
Chapitre IV — L’Algérie (1830–1868)
Projected imperial voyage to Algeria. Retrospective glance at the history of Algeria. State of the colony under the 1830 monarchy, under the 1848 Republic, under the presidency of Louis-Napoléon. Algeria after the coup d’état. General Randon named governor-general. Expedition against the Kabylie of Djurjura. Prince Napoléon minister of Algeria. Maréchal Pélissier governor-general. Imperial letter of 6 February 1863. Senatus-consult of 2 April of the same year. Insurrection of the Saharan tribes. Civil power and military power. Decree of 7 July 1864. The Emperor sails for Algiers; he visits the provinces. Return to France; results of the voyage.
Chapitre V — Session de 1865
Opening of the legislative session. Imperial discourse. Senate: address discussion. Troplong and de Boissy. Relations between Church and State; discourses of Rouland, Mgr de Bonnechose, and Bonjean. Statistics of religious associations. The 15 September Convention. Rouher’s discourse. The Mexican question. Adoption of the address. Petition discussion: transfer of Charles X’s ashes; the hereditary Senate; prostitution; homeopathy; Dupin’s discourse. Close of the Senate session. Corps législatif: formation of the bureau; verification of powers. Address debate: Ollivier takes another step toward the government. Latour-Dumoulin. 28 March séance: Thiers’s discourse; Thuillier’s diatribe in reply. Election in the 3rd circonscription of the Gard. Article-by-article discussion of the address. Opposition amendment; Jules Favre forced to renounce the floor; Ollivier secures adjournment. The Left decides to refrain from further debate; evening meeting of the Left reverses the decision. Law on press offences; electoral liberty. Electoral questions; financial questions. Amendment on the right of testament; election of mayors. Ernest Picard and the city of Paris. Mexico; Algeria; the Italian question. Closure of the address debate. Reading of the address to the Emperor; his reply to the deputation. Provisional liberty. Secondary instruction. The contingent. The budget.
Chapitre VI — La Politique Extérieure pendant l’Année 1865
Retrospective glance at foreign affairs. Difficult situation of Prussia. Austria’s embarrassments. Note of the Moniteur du soir. Salzburg interview. Rupture of the European equilibrium. Convention of Gastein. Prussia’s anxieties. Bismarck’s voyage to Biarritz. Napoleon III’s dream — at what price will he sell his neutrality between Prussia and Austria? 1 January 1866 reception. Revolution in Spain. Restoration of the tribune in the Corps législatif. Election in the Bas-Rhin; Laboulaye candidacy. The Auxerre discourse. Napoleon III’s double policy. Death of Flocon. Fermentation of spirits. Senatus-consult of 6 July.
Chapitre VII — Session de 1866
Opening of the session; Emperor’s discourse. Senate address: Boissy and President Troplong. Mexico; the 15 September Convention. Rouher’s declaration. Persigny’s discourse. Vote of the address; Emperor’s reply to the Senate deputation. The Luxembourg garden and the Senate. Petition discussion. Corps législatif: opening discourse by Walewski. Verification of powers; discussion of election. Thiers and Jules Favre. Schism in the majority. The agricultural inquiry; the Crédit foncier and Brame; the financial question. Berryer takes the floor. Discussion of the address’s final paragraph. Will the Left vote the Tiers-parti amendment? The opposition amendment. Granier de Cassagnac and the press; Jérôme David’s reply; Martel attenuates. Rouher takes the floor; Ollivier replies. Vote of the address; Emperor’s reply. Resignation of de Bussière (Bas-Rhin). Law on the merchant marine; the military contingent. German affairs debate: Thiers’s discourse; enthusiasm of the majority. Discussion of the law on conseils généraux. Law on literary property. Law on offences committed abroad. Imperial letter to Drouyn de Lhuys. Mexico. Law on Sunday observance. Secret funds; press independence; protest of Guéroult and Havin. Tactical error. Thiers and Larrabure attempt to return to foreign affairs. Jules Simon and the Paris works. Paris city finances. Closure of the session. New situation of the parties.
Chapitre VIII — L’Année 1866
Prussia and Austria in the first months of 1866. Prussia’s threatening dispatch to Austria. War council at Berlin. Napoleon III’s attitude. Discouragement of the friends of peace. The small German states incline indirectly toward Austria. Bismarck tries to make Napoleon III declare his intentions. Difficulties raised by the king of Prussia. Bismarck fears French intervention. Vienna cabinet proposals to Berlin. Prussian army put on war footing. Prussian army enters Saxony, Hanover, and Electoral Hesse. Wilhelm I sides with his minister. War council of 7 March at Vienna. Austrian military preparations. The Bamberg conferences. Austria wrongly believes she can count on the small states. Bavaria’s decision. Military convention between Austria and the Confederate states. Bismarck launches his plan of federal reform. State of the Prussian army. The Austrian army and its heterogeneous composition. Hanover and Hesse in Prussian hands. Benedek’s errors. Position of Austrian forces. Combat of Munchengraetz. Crown Prince of Prussia enters Bohemia. Engagements through daylight into the night of 27 June. Clam-Gallaz abandons the Iser line. The Crown Prince debouches onto the Nachod plateau. Moral effect of Nachod. Wilhelm I and Bismarck join the army.
Chapitre IX — Sadowa
Benedek wants to retake the Iser line. Clam-Gallaz, with the 1st Corps and the Saxons, establishes himself at Gitschin. Attack on Gitschin; Clam-Gallaz ordered to rejoin the main army. Silesian army repulsed. Critical situation of the Prussians. Benedek fights partial combats instead of a general action. He falls back on Königgrätz. The armies of the Crown Prince and Prince Frederick-Charles effect their junction. Benedek withdraws his army. Benedetti joins the king of Prussia at army headquarters. Prussian HQ orders the attack. The king’s anxiety. Appearance of the Royal Guard. Capture of Chlum by the Guard. Benedek’s general offensive fails. Prince Frederick-Charles advances and pushes the Austrian army back toward Sadowa. Benedek’s disorderly retreat on Königgrätz. The Prussian army is forced to halt for a day. Sadowa, one of the bloodiest battles of the century.
Chapitre X — Custozza
Relations of Prussia and Piedmont. Rupture between Prussia and Austria. Italy joins Prussia in asking Napoleon III to remain neutral. Gastein Convention. The Venetian question. Bismarck and Italy. Francis Joseph and the grand council at Berlin. General Govone’s mission to Berlin; Prussian proposed treaty. Count Arèse’s mission to Paris. Napoleon III’s discontent. Useless proposition of a congress. Opening of hostilities. Formation of the two armies. Archduke Albert concentrates his army on the Adige. Victor-Emmanuel enters the Quadrilateral. Sudden Austrian attack. General La Marmora directs his reinforcements on Custozza, the centre of the battle. Italian defeat; retreat of the Italian army.
Chapitre XI — Le Traité de Prague
Benedek withdraws on Olmütz. Francis Joseph accepts Napoleon III’s mediation. Prussia presses its march on Vienna. Benedetti at Prussian army headquarters. The Prussians within two leagues of Vienna. Five-day truce. Prussia and the federal army. General Vogel von Falkenstein’s mission. Combat of Kissingen. Capture of Frankfurt. General Manteuffel concludes an armistice with the secondary states. End of the war. Bismarck preoccupies himself with possible French compensations. Austria makes double integrity of its territory and Saxony’s a sine qua non of peace. Nikolsburg preliminaries. Signature of peace at Prague. Political results of the war.
Chapitre XII — Les Suites de Sadowa
Moniteur note announcing mediation. Enthusiasm of brokers and journalists. The Empire not ready for war. First overture regarding Belgium. Napoleon III’s double game. Drouyn de Lhuys replaced by Moustier. Draft treaty of which Benedetti imprudently leaves the outline in Bismarck’s hands. Bismarck turns toward Russia. Optimistic circular of La Valette. Napoleon III at Vichy. The Luxembourg question. Arrival of the Empress of Mexico at Paris. Ratification of the treaty between Austria and France for the cession of Venetia. The Geneva congress. The new military organisation. Fould’s report on the financial situation. Manifesto of the comte de Chambord.
Chapitre XIII — Fin de l’Expédition du Mexique
Unanimous press complaints against the prolongation of the intervention. The United States gives Napoleon III one year to evacuate Mexico. Arrival of Baron Saillard at Mexico bearing a letter from Drouyn de Lhuys; Maximilian refuses to receive him. Disastrous situation of the Mexican Empire; Maximilian’s discouragement. Lack of understanding between Maximilian and Bazaine; Maximilian requests Bazaine’s recall. Capture of Matamoros by the republicans. Almonte’s useless mission to Napoleon III. Maximilian wants to abdicate; his wife prevents him and departs for Paris. Clerical plot discovered at Mexico. Republican troop advances. The United States insists on the departure of the French army. General Castelnau sent to Mexico. Maximilian and Father Fisher. Bazaine’s extraordinary conduct. Fould’s confidential report. Interview of Maximilian and Castelnau. Bazaine’s double game revealed.
Chapitre XIV — Le Clergé en France (1863–1867)
Polemic between Bishop Dupanloup and Edgar Quinet. The cult of the Virgin. Publication of the Vie de Jésus. Efforts of Lyonnais Catholics to preserve their liturgy. The Malines congress. The Encyclical and the Syllabus. Government prohibits publication of the first part of the Encyclical. Letter of the Bishop of Montpellier. Grief of the liberal Catholics; the Encyclical commented by the Bishop of Orléans. The Emperor authorises Donnet to convoke the provincial synod at Poitiers. Changes in the Protestant Church: universal suffrage applied to consistory elections. Liberal Protestants and Orthodox Protestants. Foundation of the Union protestante libérale. Struggle between the Presbyteral Council and Pastor Martin Paschoud. Elections of 1865: Guizot elected only on the second ballot with a weak majority. The liberal Protestants in vain demand a second Presbyteral Council. The minister of cults takes sides against the liberal Protestants.
Notes

Series: Histoire illustrée du second empire by Taxile Delord; this is the Tome quatrième of the illustrated edition (Baillière [1880–83]), corresponding to the fourth volume of the original 1869–75 Baillière set (OCLC 6266334). Delord’s Tome V (1874; 1867–1869) continues the series in this wiki. Tome III (1857–1864) and Tome II sit in the 1800–1865 wiki.
Placement: Rest of Europe 1866–1919 wiki — the narrative’s centre of gravity is the 1866 Austro-Prussian War (Sadowa, Custozza, Prague) and its aftermath (Venetian cession, Luxembourg question, Mexican evacuation). The volume also covers the 1864–1865 sessions and continues into religious politics down to 1867, but the decisive watershed of Sadowa anchors it in this wiki.
Voice: Contemporary republican narrative history; represent what Delord states, without modern scholarly reframing.
Illustrations: 59 wood engravings in the text (not preserved in this raw OCR).
Related in corpus: Sybel Die Begründung des deutschen Reiches (vols III–IV covering the same Austro-Prussian crisis from a Prussian-nationalist perspective) sits under the German Unification shelf in this wiki. Delord’s French republican viewpoint complements the German sources.
Raw: delord-histoire-second-empire-t4.txt

sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t5.title: Delord — Histoire du second empire, Tome V
sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t5.content:
Delord — Histoire du second empire, Tome V
Taxile Delord (1815–1877) — Histoire du second empire (1848–1869). — Tome cinquième. — Paris: Librairie Germer Baillière, rue de l’École-de-Médecine, 17, 1874. Printer: Imprimerie de E. Martinet, rue Mignon, 2.
Republican journalist and deputy (Siècle), Delord writes a contemporary opposition history of the Second Empire as a continuous Histoire, not memoir. The series band on the half-title is 1848–1870. This volume carries the running title L’Empire (suite) and is the fifth tome of the set. Body text runs through printed p. 632 (Fin du cinquième volume); table of contents follows (to Fin de la table des matières du cinquième volume).
Core chronological span is 1867–1869: from the letter of 19 January 1867 and the legislative session through the Luxembourg crisis, the Exposition, Maximilian’s death, Mentana, Rochefort’s Lanterne, the Baudin subscription and trial, the elections of 1869, the extraordinary session, the formation of the Ollivier ministry (Préface de l’Empire libéral), and the preliminaries of the Vatican Council (opening 8 December 1869).
OCR from local Anna’s Archive scan set (OCLC 6266334; Baillière 1869–75). Cleaned raw keeps title-page through end of table; internal double-spaces collapsed; front blank library leaves dropped. Tome II (authoritarian Empire through early 1860) sits in the 1800–1865 wiki.
Chapters
Chapitre I — La Session (1867)
Letter of 19 January, legislative session, press and meetings bills, foreign affairs and Luxembourg, fall of Walewski.
Opening of 1867: Café de la Renaissance students’ trial; Jules Favre’s candidacy at the Academy; death of Victor Cousin. The imperial letter of 19 January replaces the address with a regulated right of interpellation and announces press and meetings laws. Senate: Troplong, senatus-consult of 7 February, primary-instruction law, Sainte-Beuve’s speech and the storm it raises. Corps législatif: Walewski; Jules Favre and Rouher; Émile Ollivier rallies to the majority and astonishes his friends; foreign-affairs interpellation (Thiers, Favre, Garnier-Pagès, Ollivier, Rouher); Rouher evokes 2 December; Walewski resigns; Schneider president, Jérôme David vice-president. Luxembourg affair; Moustier’s declaration; municipal-councils law; pension to Lamartine; Berryer and Mexico; budget; Ollivier attacks the ministry and calls Rouher vice-empereur; the Emperor answers by sending Rouher the diamond plaque of the Légion d’honneur. Close and summary of the 1867 session.
Chapitre II — La Neutralisation du Luxembourg (1867)
Post-Sadowa compensations, Benedetti talks, Dutch cession project, London conference, neutralization.
Need to restore imperial prestige after Sadowa; territorial compensations claimed from Prussia; dilatory reception; Prussia refuses any left-bank cession; Bismarck leaves France free to seek compensations in Belgium and Switzerland; the Benedetti treaty draft. Diplomatic situation at the end of 1866; Holland denounces the 1839 treaty; secret Franco-Dutch understanding on cession; the secret breaks; Prussian anger and Bismarck’s reply in the Berlin parliament; circular of 15 April; conference announced; neutralization of Luxembourg accepted as a truce; press exaltation and democratic division on war; Berlin students’ reply to Strasbourg students.
Chapitre III — L’Exposition de l’Industrie (1867)
Universal Exhibition, sovereigns in Paris, Berezowski attentat, Rome on the horizon.
Preparations and inauguration; real opening in early May; King of the Belgians; the Tsar’s hesitations calmed by Piétri; King William I of Prussia arrives reluctantly; false position of Napoleon III and his guests; review in the Bois; Berezowski attentat, trial, and condemnation; Tuileries ball; departure of Alexander II and William I; Viceroy of Egypt; the Sultan; sudden departure of the Empress; King of Italy expected in vain (General Dumont’s mission to Rome); the Roman question reappears; Paris transformed; the Frenchman and Frenchwoman of 1867; Emperor and Empress; prizes and closure; impression on foreigners.
Chapitre IV — Mort de Maximilien (1867)
Evacuation of Mexico, Querétaro, execution of the archduke.
Imperial dispatch of 10 January 1867 to General Castelnau; Napoleon III leaves to Washington the choice of a Mexican republican president, excluding only Juárez; Bazaine’s talks with Porfirio Díaz; French evacuation and Bazaine’s return to Toulon without military honours. Maximilian’s clerical attempt to hold the empire; march on Querétaro; siege and capture by the Juarists; Escobedo announces the capture; defence before the court-martial; condemnation; letter to Juárez; execution; effect on opinion; diplomacy and the question of responsibility.
Chapitre V — Le Congrès de la Paix (1867)
International Workingmen’s Association, peace leagues, Geneva congress, Garibaldi.
IWA in France and its hesitation to enter politics; Geneva and Lausanne congresses; Ligue de la paix (Passy, Michel Chevalier, Arlès-Dufour, Père Gratry, etc.); English peace society; Phare de la Loire call for an international peace congress; adhesions across Europe; presidency offered to Garibaldi; his arrival at Geneva; he proclaims the fall of the papacy; congress slides into mysticism and revolutionary tendency; Genevan government unease; dissolution and results.
Chapitre VI — Entrevue de Salzbourg (1867)
Dumont at Rome, Salzburg meeting, Moustier circular, Bismarck reply, Fleury at Vienna.
General unease; General Dumont’s mission to Rome; elections of conseils généraux; departure of Emperor and Empress for Germany; Salzburg interview and its consequences; speeches at Arras, Lille, and Amiens; Moustier circular; Bismarck’s reply; court to Biarritz; General Fleury’s journey to Vienna; Italian manifestations; death of Fould; state of minds; Emperor’s return to Paris (16 October).
Chapitre VII — Mentana (1867)
Garibaldian invasion of the Papal States, French intervention, battle of Mentana.
Garibaldi organizes a new expedition against Rome after leaving Geneva; Italian army on the Roman frontier; volunteers enter papal territory; first encounters with pontifical troops; Florence’s difficulty stopping the invasion; will the imperial government intervene? Empress for intervention; Emperor hesitates; Persigny and then Rouher rally; mixed occupation rejected; riot in Rome; French troops at Civitavecchia; battle of Mentana; General de Failly’s cruel mot; Garibaldi arrested; Spanish intervention negotiated between Queen Isabella and the Empress.
Chapitre VIII — Crise dans le gouvernement (1867)
Austrian emperor in Paris, Montmartre manifestation, financial and food crisis, Pinard ministry.
Arrival of the Emperor of Austria; Hôtel de Ville banquet; Italian crisis and state of minds; results of the Geneva congress; manifestation of 4 November at the Montmartre cemetery; workers’ summons to the Paris deputies; war fears; financial and food crisis; “grève du milliard”; seditious placards; government feels weakened; Magne at Finance; choice of interior minister; Rouher’s report on candidates; Pinard named under the Empress’s influence.
Chapitre IX — Session de 1868
Opening 18 November 1867, Roman question, Rouher’s « jamais », military law.
Throne speech; Roman question in the Senate (Moustier) and Corps législatif (Rouher’s famous jamais); German affairs; Buffet amendment on interpellation; Kerveguen–Guéroult–Havin incident; talk of dissolving the Corps législatif; military law; majority’s unease.
Chapitre X — Décadence de l’Empire (1867)
Parti de l’action, Montmartre, “Commune révolutionnaire,” first symptoms of decline.
New party of action; manifestation of 2 November; conspiracy styled the revolutionary Commune of the Paris workers; girls’ education; end of the year; bad business situation; grève du milliard; general discontent; Emperor’s illness; first symptoms of the Empire’s decadence. Pinard installed 15 November finds the Montmartre manifestation the first fruit of the Geneva alliance between militant republican youth and the proletariat.
Chapitre XI — La Lanterne (1868)
Recognition of the North German Confederation, press prosecutions, Rochefort’s Lanterne.
Tuileries receptions; recognition of the Confederation of the North German States; Château-d’Eau slides; arrests and condemnations; ten papers prosecuted for illicit reports; petition against higher education; Dupanloup brochures; Odéon manifestation; Manin exhumation and blocked Italian commission; fat dinner on Good Friday; Emperor at Rouen; force disperses a private electoral meeting at Nîmes; troubles at the École de médecine; election of Jules Grévy; first political meetings in Paris; La Lanterne.
Chapitre XII — Session de 1868
Press law, public meetings, Sainte-Beuve in the Senate, finances and Haussmann.
Senate: Chaix-d’Est-Ange on liberty of teaching; press-law debate; Rouher fails to close discussion; Sainte-Beuve’s speech and the snub the Senate gives him; popular libraries. Corps législatif: interpellations on newspaper trials and Paris cemeteries; general discussion of the press law (Pelletan, Jules Simon, Jules Favre, Thiers); weak reply by Pinard; article 1 carried; stamp; Guilloutet amendment; Berryer additional articles; accounts question and Thiers; Granier de Cassagnac’s coarseness toward Favre; public-meetings law voted; Brame and Pouyer-Quertier on the economic regime; Rouher–Ollivier dispute; Haussmann’s report and apology; finance laws; Mexican-bond indemnity; moral chastisement inflicted on Rouher; Thiers’s speech; Emperor at Troyes.
Chapitre XIII — La Souscription Baudin (1868)
Troyes and Châlons, Walewski’s death, Baudin’s tomb, monument subscription.
Emperor at Troyes and at the camp of Châlons; King of Prussia’s allocution alarms the Bourse; Berne congress; International at Brussels; elections of the Var, Moselle, and Nièvre; death of Walewski; Emperor returns from Biarritz; Baudin’s tomb at Montparnasse; manifestation around the tomb; subscription for a monument; numerous adhesions; letter of Berryer.
Chapitre XIV — Le Procès Baudin (1868)
Trial of the Avenir and Réveil, Gambetta’s speech, Berryer’s death.
Political importance of the prosecution opened over the Baudin subscription; choice of counsel — Léon Gambetta, Laurier, Emmanuel Arago, Leblond, Hubbard; opening; second sitting; Gambetta’s prodigious plea; judgment; second trial of Avenir and Réveil with Temps and Journal de Paris; death of Berryer; public meetings; general agitation; rumours of conspiracy; start of electoral agitation; threatened Montmartre manifestation and useless police measures. Delord presents the trial as a democratic opportunity to put the coup of 2 December back on the stage.
Chapitre XV — Session législative (1869)
Last session of the 1863 legislature, press law effects, Paris–Crédit foncier, budget.
Rumours of new liberal reforms; opening of the Chambers; Emperor’s speech. Senate: Maupas interpellation on the new press law; petitions; Paris–Crédit foncier treaty. Corps législatif: chamberlains question; half-defeat of the government; interpellation on the Réunion riot and press law; Paris finances and danger of the discussion; government act of contrition; Haussmann and Frémy; Rouher poses the cabinet question; strong opposition minority; general budget debate; Thiers on electoral corruption of 1863; budget voted; end of the 1869 session and of the 1863 legislature; glance over that legislature.
Chapitre XVI — Les Élections générales (1869)
Centenary of Napoleon I, campaign, Gambetta–Carnot, Rochefort, white blouses.
New Year speech; pictures restored to the Louvre; Magne’s financial report; Belgian question; Muséum revolution; Saint-Mandé banquet; centenary of Napoleon I; Emperor at Chartres; abstention and blank votes; failure of the Union libérale; red spectre; remaniement of electoral circumscriptions; campaign opens 3 May; Bancel and Ollivier; Châtelet meeting and troubles; Ollivier’s profession of faith; 1st circumscription Gambetta vs Carnot; Gambetta’s electors’ cahier; Thiers, Raspail, Guéroult; Rochefort’s candidacy; results and second ballot; Thiers, Jules Favre, Garnier-Pagès, Jules Ferry elected; troubles in Paris; the blouses blanches.
Chapitre XVII — Session extraordinaire (1869)
Ricamarie, Schneider crisis, tiers-parti interpellation, Rouher to the Senate presidency.
Persigny’s letter to Ollivier; rumours of liberal concessions denied in a letter to Mackau; Ricamarie affair; Franco-Belgian railway conference; Solferino anniversary; Châlons camp allocution; Beauvais speech; Schneider’s resignation and withdrawal; opening of the extraordinary session; Pyrénées-Orientales election; rastels; left and tiers-parti interpellations; Rouher’s manœuvre; right interpellation; new ministry formed; Rouher president of the Senate; effect on the Chamber; left protest project; senatus-consult discussion; Devienne report; Prince Napoléon’s speech.
Chapitre XVIII — Les Élections complémentaires (1869)
Emperor’s health rumours, convocation decree, Ledru-Rollin candidacy, left manifesto.
Alarming rumours on the Emperor’s health officially denied; threat of inquiry; Basel congress; Gorchakov in Paris; calls to convoke the Chambers (Kératry, Gambetta); decree of 3 October convoking Chambers for 29 November; abandoned manifestation project; Ferry’s collective left protest dropped; Aubin strike; complementary elections; unsworn candidates; Ledru-Rollin candidacy offered, profession of faith, hesitation, Rochefort’s journey to London, final refusal; election results; left manifesto.
Chapitre XIX — Reprise et fin de la session extraordinaire de 1869
Louvre inauguration, left interpellations, collapse of the majority, end of the authoritarian Empire.
Session inaugurated at the Louvre; imperial speech; public admitted to Senate sittings. Corps législatif: four left interpellations; left bill on constituent power; bureau; Rochefort’s proposal; centre left and centre right; dissolution of the majority and difficulty of forming one; Raspail demands indictment of the ministry; verification of powers; Raspail–Rochefort proposal; rastels; elections of Girault and Clément Duvernois; debates lose interest; end of verification and of the extraordinary session; last days of the authoritarian Empire.
Chapitre XX — Préface de l’Empire libéral (1869)
Ollivier–Duvernois negotiations, disguised visit to Compiègne, ministry of 2 January 1870 prepared.
Negotiations resume between the Emperor and Émile Ollivier through Clément Duvernois; grave embarrassments — the government must recede or advance; can the Empire transform itself? Ollivier offers to attempt the trial; his conditions and programme; disguised journey to Compiègne; Emperor hesitates and makes his will; Ollivier returns to Saint-Tropez then is summoned back to Paris; he accepts the ministry; ministerial negotiations; Daru, Buffet; Girardin’s discontent; Magne blocks Duvernois; rupture between the two founders of the liberal Empire; Emperor’s letter of 27 December; Ollivier communicates it to the two centres; Segris and Talhouët will enter only with Daru and Buffet; Magne sacrificed; definitive formation of the ministry; effects on public opinion.
Chapitre XXI — Préliminaires du Concile (1867–1869)
Infallibility propaganda, liberal Catholics, Hyacinthe, Dupanloup polemics, opening 8 December 1869.
Announcement of the council; propaganda for papal infallibility; new devotion; league of infallibility encouraged by Pius IX; alarms of some bishops; Malines congress; Bishop of Orléans, professional schools, and the teaching league; episcopate and Duruy; clergy and the imperial family; Deguerry chaplain to the Prince imperial; Sorbonne incident; Father Schrader’s book and attacks on Bossuet approved by bishops and Pope; Pope’s letter to the archbishop of Paris; Civiltà cattolica article; infallibility assured in advance; liberal Catholics and the council; dogmatization of the Syllabus; Assumption dogma; episcopal mandements; episcopate and the 1869 elections; Montalembert’s letter to German Catholics; Mgr Maret’s book; Father Hyacinthe’s protest and excommunication; imperial government and the council; polemics between Dupanloup and Manning / Deschamps; Dupanloup’s pastoral on Veuillot; Rome ends the bishops’ polemic by refusing the imprimatur; opening of the council 8 December without special incident; Sixtine preparatory allocution — remedies for Christian and civil society’s ills: the remedy is the Syllabus.
Notes
