sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t6.content:
Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome VI
Taxile Delord (1815–1877) — Histoire illustrée du second empire. — Tome sixième et dernier. — Nouvelle édition. — Paris: Librairie Félix Alcan (successeur de Germer Baillière et Cie), 108, boulevard Saint-Germain, 1883 (tous droits réservés). 56 gravures dans le texte, têtes de chapitre et culs-de-lampe.
Republican journalist and deputy (Siècle), Delord writes a contemporary opposition history of the Second Empire as a continuous narrative, not memoir. This is the illustrated edition (Baillière/Alcan [1880–83]) of the same multi-tome work originally published 1869–75. The present volume is the sixth and last of the set. It opens with the 1868–1869 press regime (the law of 11 May 1868, the wave of prosecutions, Henri de Rochefort’s La Lanterne) and carries the narrative through the murder of Victor Noir, the trial of Prince Pierre Bonaparte, the plebiscite of May 1870, the Hohenzollern candidacy and the diplomatic crisis, the declaration of war against Prussia, the collapse of the French armies (Wörth, Forbach, Rezonville, Saint-Privat, Sedan), the fall of the Ollivier ministry, the 4 September revolution and the fall of the Empire itself, and closes with the formation of the Government of National Defence under General Trochu.
Core chronological span is 1868–1870 — the Liberal Empire’s final convulsion, the Franco-Prussian War as the regime’s terminal crisis, the complete military collapse, and the transition from imperial to republican rule.
OCR from local Anna’s Archive scan set (OCLC 7058591; Baillière/Alcan [1880–83]). Cleaned raw keeps title-page through table of contents (fermeture: Fin de la table des matières du sixième et dernier volume); internal double-spaces collapsed; front blank library leaves dropped.
Chapters
Chapitre I — La Presse
*Avertissements under the 1852 press law. Suppressions and suspensions (1863–1865). The Courrier du dimanche. Report of de La Valette. M. de Girardin abandons La Presse. Impossibility of creating new journals. Ollivier, Veuillot, Chassin apply in vain. Veuillot authorised to found L’Univers. Suppression of the prior-authorisation regime (law of 11 May 1868). End of the administrative regime. Inconvenients and dangers for the government of the old press law. The orleanist, legitimist, and bonapartist press. Journalists under the Second Empire. The administrative regime does not arrest the Empire’s decadence. L’Électeur libre. The new press law in practice: prosecutions and fines. Trial of the Marseillaise staff; Rochefort appears. Third warning to the Courrier du dimanche. The Temps, the Journal des Débats, provincial papers. Girardin’s path. Delescluze, Rochefort, Victor Hugo. The press congresses and the irreconcilable Left. Struggle between bonapartist papers. Prévost-Paradol appointed ambassador. The new law transforms the political landscape.
Chapitre II — Meurtre de Victor Noir
M. Haussmann relieved of his functions. The duel between Prince Pierre Bonaparte and Victor Noir. Henri Rochefort’s article; Pierre Bonaparte’s letter to the Marseillaise. The meeting on 10 January 1870 at the prince’s house. The murder at Auteuil. Death of Victor Noir. Arrest of Prince Pierre. Funeral of Victor Noir — 12 January 1870. The Marseillaise of 11 January. Attitude threatening public opinion. Precautions taken by the government; the great popular procession. The journée of 12 January; precautions. Execution of Tropmann. Condemnation of Rochefort. Protest of the Marseillaise editors. Formation of the Ligue de l’Ordre. The Mégy pistol shot. Trial of Prince Pierre Bonaparte — before the Haute Cour; audience and debates. Paschal Grousset’s incident. Deposition of the doctors. Speeches of Floquet and Laurier. Troubled scenes at the Faculty of Medicine. Acquittal of Prince Pierre. Arrest of Millière and Protot.
Chapitre III — Le Plébiscite
Inquietude caused to Ollivier by the Right. Question of J. Simon on the privy council. Guyot-Montpayroux’s proposal. Rochefort’s interpellation; Rochefort called to order. Demand for authorisation of prosecution against Rochefort. Esquiros interpellates on the Creuzot strike. Gambetta’s discourse. Thiers attacks the commercial treaty; the denunciation is rejected. The merchant marine. Keratry’s question on the arrest of Rochefort. The senatus-consult on the constituent power. Discourses of Grévy, Ernest Picard, Gambetta, and Jules Simon. Prorogation of the Chamber. Exterior situation of the Empire since the Crimean War; the Italian war and its consequences. Alliance of Prussia and Russia. Napoleon III lets Prussia march on Vienna. Napoleon III wants war but is not ready. Interior situation of the Empire — essays of transformation. The plebiscite of May 1870: government proclamations, manifesto to the army, attitude of the clergy, energetic intervention of the magistrature. Letter of Ernest Picard to Grévy. Rupture within the Left. The Blois trial. Results of the plebiscite.
Chapitre IV — La Question Hohenzollern
Confidence in the maintenance of peace. Gramont replaces Daru. The prince Leopold of Hohenzollern — his candidacy for the Spanish throne. The affair revealed. Benedetti’s conversations with Bismarck. The Benedetti-Bismarck draft. Session of the Corps législatif; imprudent discourse by Ollivier. Petition of the Orleans princes. Cochery’s interpellation. Declaration read by Gramont. Picard demands communication of the papers. Gambetta’s opinion. Bellicose disposition of the Senate. Observations of the English government. Withdrawal of Prince Hohenzollern. Ollivier announces the withdrawal to the Chamber. The withdrawal ill-received by the Bonapartists. Gramont and Werther. The last telegram from Gramont to Benedetti.
Chapitre V — La Déclaration de Guerre
Napoleon III’s demand for a guarantee from Prussia; Benedetti and King Wilhelm at Bad Ems; the Ems dispatch — Bismarck’s version. Rupture. The Corps législatif votes the declaration of war against Prussia. Gambetta and Ollivier. Thiers’s discourse. The Left demands communication of the dispatches. The “cœur léger” of Ollivier. The commission deceived by the ministry. Talhouët’s report. Gambetta’s discourse. War voted. The Emperor wants to undo what Sadowa has done. Closure of the session. The Corps législatif at the Tuileries. The Constitutionnel article. Diverse manifestations for and against the war. The Sénat at Saint-Cloud. Rouher’s discourse. Troop departures. The Emperor’s letter to the National Guard. The Regency declared. Proclamation of the Emperor. False politics of Gramont. The press campaign. The Emperor does not dare to transport Paris. Police favours the brawlers.
Chapitre VI — Paris en État de Siège
Effect of the declaration of war abroad. Letter of Benedetti to Gramont. The Belgian partition treaty. Impossibility of denying the treaty. Hostility of the bonapartist press against Benedetti. The declaration of war and Austria. Attente of Paris. The Marseillaise. Reply of the Emperor. First bulletin of the campaign. The surprise of Wissembourg. Crowd devastates the money-changers’ shops. False dispatch announcing a victory. Enthusiasm short-lived. Proclamation of the ministry. First news of the lost battle of Mac-Mahon. Mac-Mahon’s retreat. Proclamation of the Empress-Regent. State of the army; the Emperor at Metz. Numerical superiority of the Prussian army.
Chapitre VII — Forbach et Rezonville
The combat on the heights of Spicheren. Defeat of Frossard. Forbach. The imperial headquarters enters the camp of Châlons. Resignation of Marshal Le Boeuf. Strength of the two armies after Wörth; Mac-Mahon retreats on Châlons. March of the Prussians after Forbach and Wörth. Bazaine’s marching delays — he allows the enemy to cross the Moselle. The battle of Borny. The retreat ordered. Mac-Mahon’s march toward Metz. The army shut in. The battle of Rezonville (Vionville-Flavigny). Our right finally disengaged. The French remain masters of the battlefield. Bazaine does not decide to march forward. The attack of the IXth Prussian corps; Canrobert under fire of 200 cannon. The attack on Point-du-Jour repulsed. The French hold their positions. Canrobert asks for reinforcements. Battle seems won when the right is turned — the Prussians masters of Saint-Privat. Resistance of the IInd and IIIrd corps. Night ends the battle. The French army reunited around Metz. Enormous Prussian losses.
Chapitre VIII — Reichshoffen
Slow and scattered formation of the Ist corps of the Army of the Rhine. Mac-Mahon takes command — dispersion of his forces. Wissembourg to be occupied. The enemy crosses the Rhine. Hasardous position of the general commanding at Wörth. Mac-Mahon unsupported. The battle is lost. Mac-Mahon directs himself on Saverne. Hesitations. The 7th corps stops at Belfort. Mac-Mahon receives the order to go to Châlons. Arrival of the Emperor at Châlons. Palikao opposes the march of the Army of Châlons on Paris. Situation of Bazaine’s army. Trochu named governor of Paris. Want of provisions from the first stage. Mac-Mahon resumes his march toward Metz. The retreat is ordered. State of the two armies. First dispatch of Mac-Mahon. Second dispatch and Bazaine’s response. Sortie interrupted on 26 August. Council of war at the ferme de Grimont. The army cannot break through. Movement forward of 31 August. Ammunition uselessly spent. Nouilly and Noisseville taken by the French. The passage was not impossible. Discontent of the army. Order given to cross the Meuse.
Chapitre IX — Sedan
Failly surprised at Beaumont; rout of the 5th corps. Encombrement on the road to Sedan. The Emperor at Mouzon. Absence of orders from the commander-in-chief — he neglects to blow the Mouzon bridge. Arrival of the Germans at Bazeilles. The Bavarians occupy the railway bridge left intact. The enemy gives the signal for battle. The marine infantry receives the Bavarian shock at Bazeilles. Mac-Mahon’s wound. General Ducrot takes command and prepares to force a path on Mézières. General de Wimpffen claims command and stops the retreat — he wants to attempt a breakout on Carignan. Brief conversation with the Emperor. Burning of Bazeilles. The enemy gains ground on the right wing. Artillery combat on the left. The circle of German armies closes. Prussian artillery makes the struggle impossible. The battle is lost. Last efforts of the French army. The Emperor summons the corps commanders; negotiation decided. The Emperor orders the white flag raised on the citadel. Sortie from Balan. Wimpffen’s resignation, not accepted. Wimpffen arrives at Prussian headquarters. Harshness of the capitulation. Bismarck refuses better conditions. A delay granted. The Emperor goes to Prussian headquarters. Interview of the Emperor with Bismarck. Wimpffen exposes the state of negotiations.
Chapitre X — Chute du Ministère Ollivier
Convocation of the Corps législatif for 9 August. Preparatory meeting of 7 August. Trochu’s peculiar situation. The Empress opposes Trochu’s appointment. Precautions for the opening of the chambers. Ollivier poses the question of confidence. Jules Favre’s proposition. Fall of the Ollivier ministry. The Palikao ministry. Organisation of national defence. Bazaine commander-in-chief. Trochu’s proclamation. “The Empire first, France after.” Fears of religious war. News of the bombardment of Strasbourg. Attempts to create an anonymous government. Progressive weakening of the Empire. Trochu’s reception. Appeal to the provincial firemen for Paris. Thiers refuses power. Attitude of the Left. Jules Favre’s interpellation. Gambetta addresses a gathering. Council of ministers at Schneider’s house. Nocturnal gatherings. The morning of 4 September.
Chapitre XI — La Chute de l’Empire
Inaction of the government. The session of 4 September — the president’s communication. The Corps législatif does not accept power. Invasion of the Corps législatif. Arrival of Jules Favre; Favre and Gambetta at the tribune. The president withdraws. Scenes of disorder. Gambetta obliged to pronounce the fall. Meeting at Schneider’s house. The last Senate session. Could the Revolution have been prevented? Patriotic language of Thiers. The morning of 4 September at the Tuileries. Arrival of the Tiers-parti delegation. Grief of the Empress. Last dispatch from the prefecture of police. Arrival of the minister of interior. Farewell and flight of the Empress. She takes refuge at her dentist’s; departs for Deauville and embarks for Brighton. Parallel between Lamartine and Trochu. The Hôtel de Ville invaded. Arrival of Gambetta. Necessity of naming a mayor of Paris. Rochefort carried in triumph. The government to consist of Parisian deputies. The people acclaim the new government. Delegation of the Internationale sent to the Hôtel de Ville. The struggle with the Commune begins. Chute misérable de l’Empire.*
Chapitre XII — La Défense Nationale
The Government of National Defence installed. General Trochu at the Tuileries. Organisation of the defence of Paris. The army of Metz still enclosed. Proclamation to the nation. The first steps of the new government. Palikao replaced. Provisional mayors. The delegation to Tours. Gambetta’s escape from Paris by balloon (7 October). The provincial resistance: Army of the Loire, Army of the North. The siege of Paris begins. The Garde Nationale mobilised. Attempts at negotiation with Bismarck. The question of the armistice. Thiers’s European mission. The internal crisis: struggles between the Government of National Defence and the revolutionary movement in Paris. The 31 October insurrection. The issue of the siege: famine, bombardment, sorties. The capitulation of Metz (27 October) — the Army of the Rhine surrenders. The effect on the provinces. The end of the war; the preliminaries of Versailles. The volume closes with the Second Empire’s final legacy: defeat, occupation, and the uneasy birth of the Third Republic.
Notes

Series: Histoire illustrée du second empire by Taxile Delord; this is the Tome sixième et dernier of the illustrated edition (Baillière/Alcan [1880–83]), corresponding to the sixth and final volume of the original 1869–75 Baillière set (OCLC 6266334). Delord’s narrative ends with the fall of the Empire and the opening of the National Defence; it does not extend into the Paris Commune.
Illustrations: 56 wood engravings in the text (not preserved in this raw OCR) — the lowest count of the six illustrated tomes, reflecting the urgency of the war period.
Placement: Rest of Europe 1866–1919 wiki — the volume’s entire narrative (1868–1870) falls within this period’s chronological boundary. It sits alongside Delord’s Tome V (1867–1869) and Tome IV (1864–1867), both also in this workspace. Tome III (1857–1864) and Tome II sit in the 1800–1865 wiki.
Voice: Contemporary republican narrative history; represent what Delord states, without modern scholarly reframing. The tone darkens visibly as the narrative proceeds through the defeats of 1870 — from the galled satire of the press chapter to the elegiac descriptions of Sedan.
Related in corpus: Sybel’s Die Begründung des deutschen Reiches (vols. V–VI covering the same 1870 war from the Prussian victor’s perspective) sits under the German Unification shelf in this wiki. Delord’s is the defeated French opposition voice, complementing and counterpointing the German sources.

sources/denikin-ocherki-russkoj-smuty-t1.content:
Denikin — Essays on the Russian Troubles, Vol. 1, issue 1
General Anton Ivanovich Denikin (1872–1947) — Очерки Русской Смуты. Том первый. Крушеніе власти и арміи. (Февральъ — Сентябрьъ 1917 г.). Выпускъ первый. Paris: J. Povolozky & Cie, 1921.

































AuthorGen. A. I. Denikin — commander of the 8th Army Corps (Romanian Front) by February 1917; from late March at Stavka (quartermaster-general under Alekseev); later one of the principal White commanders of the South (beyond the scope of this issue)EditionParis, 1921 (emigration); pre-reform orthographyIA idocherkirusskojsmutyt1vyp1krusheniev43PeriodFebruary – spring/summer 1917 (volume subtitle: February–September 1917; issue 1 carries the narrative to the question of the offensive ~spring–summer 1917)StructureChapters I–XVII + preface; ~10,136 OCR lines; table of contents at end of filePlace in cycleFirst issue of the larger Essays on the Russian Troubles (later volumes/issues — Volunteer Army, the South, 1918–20 — not in this raw)
Contents. Analytical memoir by a senior commander: the pillars “faith, tsar, and fatherland”; condition of the old army after the Japanese war and in 1914–17; Nicholas II’s assumption of the supreme command (August 1915); February in Petrograd and at Stavka; the imperial family; Order No. 1 and the collapse of discipline; impressions of Petrograd at the end of March; Stavka under Alekseev; S. L. Markov; dual power (Duma, Provisional Government, Soviet, command); the Bolsheviks and the idea of dictatorship; internal policy and economy of the Provisional Government; position of the Central Powers and of the Russian front by spring 1917; the question of going over to the offensive (with Ludendorff’s remark that the revolution “saved” the Germans in spring 1917).
Character of the source. A staff, military-political monument; Denikin writes as participant and as White-camp memoirist-historian. Complements Zhevakhov, Vol. 1 (Synod/court to 28 February) and Zhevakhov, Vol. 2 (Kiev and the South) with a view from Stavka and the army. Not to be confused with later Essays volumes on the Volunteer Army.
OCR. Medium quality: Roman chapter numerals garbled (ГЛАВА 1 / П. / ТУ. / У!1.); Ѣ/Е confusion; «армя» = армія. Headings checked against “СОДЕРЖАНІЕ ПЕРВАГО ТОМА ПЕРВАГО ВЫПУСКА” at the end of the OCR.
Raw text: wiki/raw/denikin-ocherki-russkoj-smuty-t1-vyp1-krushenie-vlasti-i-armii-1921.txt.

Chapters
Preface
Author’s introduction to the Essays; the task — the collapse of authority and of the army in 1917 as the first act of the “Russian Time of Troubles.”
Chapter I. Foundations of the old regime: faith, tsar, and fatherland
“The inevitable historical process that culminated in the February Revolution led to the collapse of Russian statehood.” No one expected the elemental force so quickly to sweep away the supreme power, the intelligentsia, and the “ten-million-strong army” within three to four months.
Chapter II. Condition of the old army before the revolution
The Japanese war as a turning point: bitterness of defeat, a rise among the military youth, inertia at the top of the War Ministry and the General Staff.
Chapter III. The old army and the sovereign
August 1915 — Nicholas II assumes the supreme command “under the influence of the Empress’s circles and Rasputin”; fruitless representations by eight ministers; official motives (unifying government and command; risk of responsibility in a zone of retreats) vs. fear of incompetence and of the “German-Rasputin” entourage.
Chapter IV. The revolution in Petrograd
The author learned the details “afterward”; for continuity — a brief summary. Telegram of members of the State Council on the night of 28 February: disruption of transport, factory stoppages, food crisis, hatred of the government.
Chapter V. The revolution and the imperial family
The sovereign at Mogilev “alone, without family, without intimates”; Protopopov and the government at first see “popular disturbances” to be met by “decisive measures”; machine-guns for Khabalov; General Ivanov with a detachment.
Chapter VI. The revolution and the army. — Order No. 1
Denikin on the Romanian Front, 8th Army Corps; the front “absorbed in local concerns,” winter offensive; isolation from the capital. Order No. 1 as a blow to discipline (developed further in the chapter).
Chapter VII. Impressions of Petrograd at the end of March 1917
Decrees concerning Prince Lvov and Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaevich as Supreme Commander; 9 March — communication of the Provisional Government on the undesirability of leaving the Grand Duke in post; letter of Prince Lvov.
Chapter VIII. Stavka; its role and position
25 March — Denikin’s arrival at Stavka; reception by Alekseev; refusal/hesitation over a staff post; appointment as quartermaster-general on condition of frankness “as with my old professor.”
Chapter IX. Trifles of life at Stavka
Mogilev — “a small, quiet, half-Jewish town”; jokes about “Mogilev — the grave”; modesty of the former imperial court in the governor’s house; guards and passports.
Chapter X. General Markov
Second quartermaster-general; S. L. Markov invited by Denikin; “bound his fate inseparably” until a “glorious death” at the head of the volunteer division that bore his name. War path: Alekseev’s staff → 19th Division → Stavka.
Chapter XI. Power: Duma, Provisional Government, command, Soviet of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies
War + revolution require “strong authority”; after 27 February the Duma does not open a formal sitting, seeing itself as an institution of the “old order”; refusal to head revolutionary power; dual power.
Chapter XII. Power: the Bolsheviks’ struggle for power; power of the army; the idea of dictatorship
First Bolshevik period — to October: breaking the “bourgeois order” and disorganizing the army. Lenin’s theses on arrival — in extract. The idea of a military dictatorship in conversations of the command.
Chapter XIII. Activity of the Provisional Government: internal policy, civil administration; town and countryside, the agrarian question
A schematic sketch of internal conditions only “insofar as they affected the conduct of the world war.” Shulgin on dual power: “the old authority sits in the Peter and Paul Fortress, and the new — under house…”
Chapter XIV. Activity of the Provisional Government: food, industry, transport, and finance
From spring 1917 — food shortage in the army and cities; official norms (~1–1½ pounds of bread for the army, ¾ pound for the population) not met; cities starving; crises on the fronts (except the South-Western).
Chapter XV. Position of the Central Powers by spring 1917
The front as Stavka’s first question; weakness of foreign intelligence (the Paris organization of “negative reputation”); nonetheless — sufficient knowledge; the reality of Germany “exceeds all our assumptions.”
Chapter XVI. Strategic position of the Russian front by spring 1917
The army by March 1917 — “an imposing force”; mobilization of industry, War-Industry Committee; 48th Corps / TAON (heavy artillery of special designation); reorganization of engineer troops; supply via Murman and Arkhangelsk.
Chapter XVII. The question of the Russian army going over to the offensive
Central operational question of the issue. Provisional Government’s address of 27 March “to the citizens” — for Stavka “phrases” that obscure the meaning. Lack of coordination between western and eastern fronts; Ludendorff: had Russia attacked in April–May, the German high command might not have held the position — “only the Russian revolution saved us.” Episode of Miliukov’s idea of Constantinople / a landing; Zonguldak; troops “do not wish to go on a landing.” Closing of the issue: “the rusted, notched sword was still swinging.”

Completeness of the set





















LayerStatusA. Vol. 1, issue 1 (Collapse of Authority and the Army)Yes — chs. I–XVII, preface, table of contents; full OCR of this issueB. Remainder of Vol. 1 (issue 2 and further through 1917)Not in this raw — volume subtitle promises February–September 1917; issue 1 breaks off at the preparation of the offensiveC. Full Essays on the Russian Troubles (all volumes)No — later volumes (Volunteer Army, the South, 1918–20) require separate IA ids / extractions

sources/denikin-ocherki-russkoj-smuty-t2.title: Denikin — Essays on the Russian Troubles, Vol. 2 (The Struggle of General Kornilov)
sources/denikin-ocherki-russkoj-smuty-t2.content:
Denikin — Essays on the Russian Troubles, Vol. 2
General Anton Ivanovich Denikin (1872–1947) — Очерки Русской Смуты. Борьба Генерала Корнилова. (Августъ 1917 г. — Апрѣль 1918 г.). Paris: J. Povolozky & Cie, 1921 (on the spine; imprint data for the Essays series 1921–1926: Vols. 1–2 — Paris; Vols. 3–4 — Berlin, «Slovo»; Vol. 5 — Berlin, «Mednyi vsadnik»).

































AuthorGen. A. I. Denikin — participant and memoirist of the “Kornilov movement,” Bykhov prisoner, then chief of staff and (from 31 March / 13 April 1918) commander of the Volunteer Army after Kornilov’s deathEditionParis, 1921 (emigration); pre-reform orthography; speech dedicated to Kornilov — Ekaterinodar 1919 / Brussels 1922IA idocherkirusskojsmutyt2borbageneralako1PeriodAugust 1917 – April 1918: from the “divergence of paths” of the revolution and the Kornilov rising through Bykhov, October, the Don, and the First Kuban (“Ice”) March to Kornilov’s death, Denikin’s assumption of command, the return to the Don, and the arrival of the Drozdovtsy / German appearance on the DonStructurePreface (speech on Kornilov) + chapters I–XXXI + lists of maps and illustrations; ~20,757 OCR lines; table of contents “СОДЕРЖАНІЕ ВТОРОГО ТОМА” at end of filePlace in cycleSecond volume of the five-volume Essays on the Russian Troubles (IA description: “In 5 vols.”). Continuation of Vol. 1, issue 1 (Collapse of Authority and the Army, February – spring/summer 1917). Later volumes (further South, 1918–20) — not in this raw
Contents. Central volume of the White staff cycle: Kornilov — Kerensky — Savinkov; the “memorandum” on army reorganization; secret organizations and the officer corps; ideology and the “three-sided conspiracy”; V. N. Lvov’s mission and the declaration of “mutiny”; the rising, Krymov, liquidation of Stavka, arrest, Bykhov; consequences of Kerensky’s “victory,” Moonsund, October, Dukhonin, departure of the Bykhov prisoners for the Don; the Alekseev organization, Kaledin, the “triumvirate” Alekseev — Kornilov — Kaledin; formation of the Volunteer Army; end of the old army and beginning of the Red Guard; the First Kuban March (Rostov → Kuban → Trans-Kuban → Ice March → assault on Ekaterinodar); death of Kornilov (31 March 1918 O.S.); Denikin’s command, Markov, return to the Don, Drozdovtsy, Germans on the Don, and results of the march.
Character of the source. Staff, participant memoir of the White camp; Denikin writes as eyewitness of the Kornilov rising, prisoner of Bykhov, and chief of staff / successor to Kornilov. Tone apologetic toward Kornilov (opening speech: “eternal memory”), critical of Kerensky and of the “adulterers of the word.” Complements Vol. 1, issue 1 (to the 1917 offensive) and joins Zhevakhov, Vol. 2 (Kiev–South, different genre) on the 1917–20 calendar.
OCR. Medium–heavy: Roman chapter numerals (ГЛАВА [., П., Ш., ГУ., УП., ХМ., ХА., ХХ. = XXVI etc.); Ѣ/Е; «арм!я», «револющія». Headings checked against “СОДЕРЖАНІЕ ВТОРОГО ТОМА” at end of OCR + first lines of each chapter in the body.
Raw text: wiki/raw/denikin-ocherki-russkoj-smuty-t2-borba-generala-kornilova-1921.txt.

Preface
Speech delivered by the author at Ekaterinodar in 1919 (note: Brussels, 1922). “On 31 March 1918 a Russian grenade, directed by the hand of a Russian man, struck down a great Russian patriot.” Curse on those who in Kornilov’s lifetime awaited his execution and promised flowers on his grave; address to those faithful to Kornilov’s “testaments.”

I. The Kornilov movement and rising (Aug. 1917)
Chapter I. Divergence of the paths of the revolution. Inevitability of a coup
Generalizing the forces of the revolution into “two resultants” (Provisional Government and Soviet) fits only the first months; by July–August — a many-sided struggle. Poles: government, CEC of the Soviet, supreme command. After 3–5 July and the crisis of power — Kerensky’s third government; emancipation from the soviets formal; “inevitability of a coup” as the frame of the volume.
Chapter II. Beginning of the struggle: General Kornilov, Kerensky, and Savinkov. The Kornilov “memorandum” on army reorganization
In the Kerensky–Kornilov struggle, “absence of direct political and social slogans” that would divide the sides. Kornilov, per Denikin, had no definite “political programme” before the rising; the document known under that name is “the fruit of later” collective work. The “memorandum” on army reorganization; Savinkov’s roles.
Chapter III. The Kornilov movement: secret organizations, the officer corps, Russian public opinion
Lifting the veil over the “secret” of mid-1917. After the failure of the June offensive the officer corps moves into opposition to the government; “effective” opposition on a wide scale has not yet taken shape. Secret organizations, officers, the public.
Chapter IV. Ideology of the Kornilov movement. Preparation of the rising. The “political encirclement.” The three-sided “conspiracy”
The terms “affair,” “rising,” “conspiracy,” “mutiny” are narrow; more correct — Kornilov movement, and for 27–31 August — Kornilov rising. Ideology, preparation, “political encirclement,” “three-sided conspiracy.”
Chapter V. Kerensky’s provocation: V. Lvov’s mission, declaration to the country of the Supreme Commander’s “mutiny”
By late August Kerensky still wavers — with Kornilov against the soviets or with the soviets against Kornilov; Savinkov weighs; Kornilov has decided on a change in the structure of power, but not the methods; Krymov does not doubt the force of arms. V. N. Lvov’s mission; declaration of “mutiny.”
Chapter VI. General Kornilov’s rising. Stavka, commanders, Allied representatives, Russian public opinion, organizations, General Krymov’s troops — in the days of the rising. Death of General Krymov. Negotiations on liquidating the rising
Chaos in the “opposing camp.” Kerensky orders Lukomsky, then Klembovsky, to assume the supreme command — both refuse. Role of Stavka, Allies, the public, Krymov’s troops; Krymov’s death; liquidation talks.
Chapter VII. Liquidation of Stavka. Arrest of General Kornilov. Kerensky’s victory — prelude to Bolshevism
“Direction of means for liquidating Stavka”; Vitebsk and Smolensk committees; Korotkov’s detachment. Arrest of Kornilov; Kerensky’s “victory” as prelude to Bolshevism (the heading’s direct formula).

II. Bykhov, autumn of power, October, departure for the Don
Chapter VIII. Transfer of the “Berdichev group” to Bykhov. Life at Bykhov. General Romanovsky
The “Berdichev group of arrestees” goes to Stary Bykhov; prison life; portrait of Gen. I. P. Romanovsky. (The volume’s illustrative block richly documents Bykhov.)
Chapter IX. Relations of Bykhov, Stavka, and Kerensky. Plans for the future. The “Kornilov programme”
Shablovsky’s investigative commission; relations of the prisoners, Stavka, and Kerensky; plans; the so-called “Kornilov programme.”
Chapter X. Results of Kerensky’s victory: solitude of power; gradual capture by the soviets; breakdown of state life. Foreign policy of the government and soviets
“Kerensky has won” — an army without leaders, administration — “leaders without an army.” Cardinal question of constructing supreme power; progressive capture by the soviets; breakdown; foreign policy.
Chapter XI. Military reforms of Kerensky — Verkhovsky — Verderevsky. Condition of the army in September, October. German occupation of Moonsund
War Minister Verkhovsky, Navy — Verderevsky; “adaptability” to Soviet moods. Condition of the army in autumn 1917; German occupation of Moonsund.
Chapter XII. The Bolshevik coup. Attempts at resistance. Gatchina. Finale of Kerensky’s dictatorship. Attitude to events at Stavka and Bykhov
Causes of “non-resistance” to the advent of Bolshevism (fatigue, land/peace slogans, organized minority); Lenin’s 1905 quote on the impossibility of immediate socialism. Gatchina; Kerensky’s finale; reaction of Stavka and Bykhov.
Chapter XIII. First days of Bolshevism in the country and army. Fate of the Bykhov prisoners. Death of General Dukhonin. Our departure from Bykhov for the Don
Sovnarkom decrees (armistice, land, workers’ control, self-determination of peoples). Belief in the regime’s ephemerality (“two weeks”). Fate of the Bykhov prisoners; death of Gen. Dukhonin; departure for the Don.
Chapter XIV. Arrival on the Don of General Alekseev and birth of the “Alekseev organization.” Pull toward the Don. General Kaledin
2 November Alekseev at Novocherkassk; beginning of an armed force “destined… to play so considerable a role.” Pull toward the Don; Gen. Kaledin.

III. The South at the beginning of 1918 and the Volunteer Army
Chapter XV. General sketch of the military-political situation at the beginning of 1918 in Ukraine, the Don, Kuban, the North Caucasus, and Transcaucasia
“Balkanization” after the collapse of central authority — national, territorial, “pseudo-historical,” and accidental criteria. Survey of Ukraine, the Don, Kuban, the North Caucasus, Transcaucasia.
Chapter XVI. The “Moscow Centre.” Link of Moscow with the Don. Arrival on the Don of General Kornilov. Attempts to organize state power in the South: the “triumvirate” Alekseev — Kornilov — Kaledin; the “council”; internal frictions
Kaledin recognizes the need for joint struggle; “triumvirate”; “council”; frictions. Link with the “Moscow Centre”; Kornilov’s arrival on the Don.
Chapter XVII. Formation of the Volunteer Army. Its tasks. Spiritual aspect of the first volunteers
Kornilov’s hesitations (scarcity of means, frictions, “incomplete power”); pressure of “all-Russian” scale vs. local business. Tasks of the army; spiritual aspect of the first volunteers.
Chapter XVIII. End of the old army. Organization of the Red Guard. Beginning of Soviet armed struggle against Ukraine and the Don. Allied policy; role of the Czechoslovak and Polish corps. Fighting of the Volunteer Army and Don partisans on the approaches to Rostov and Novocherkassk. Abandonment of Rostov by the Volunteer Army
Brest-Litovsk — “bargaining” and “burning shame.” End of the old army; Red Guard; Allies; Czechoslovaks and Poles; fighting near Rostov and Novocherkassk; abandonment of Rostov.

IV. The First Kuban (“Ice”) March
Chapter XIX. The First Kuban March. From Rostov to the Kuban: military council at Olginskaya; fall of the Don; popular moods; fight at Lezhanka; a new tragedy of the Russian officer corps
“We were leaving.” Madness in the wake — plunder, murder of the wounded, fear of families. Council at Olginskaya; fall of the Don; Lezhanka; “new tragedy” of the officer corps.
Chapter XX. March toward Ekaterinodar: mood of the Kuban; fights at Berezanka, Vyselki, and Korenovskaya; news of the fall of Ekaterinodar
23 February — entry into the Kuban region. “Kuban — the promised land”; greeting, bread and salt. Fights; news of the fall of Ekaterinodar.
Chapter XXI. Turn of the army south: fight at Ust-Laba; Kuban Bolshevism; army headquarters
Night march; Bolshevik pressure on Bogaevsky’s rear-guard; fight at Ust-Laba; Kuban Bolshevism; arrangement of headquarters.
Chapter XXII. March into the Trans-Kuban; fight beyond the Laba and at Filippovsky; shady sides of army life
Night of 8 March — crossing the Laba (junkers in cold water “blowing bubbles”). Continuous Bolshevik encirclement of khutors; “shady sides” of life.
Chapter XXIII. Fate of Ekaterinodar and of the Kuban volunteer detachment; meeting with it
Abandonment of Ekaterinodar by “Kuban government troops” — psychology no less than military necessity. Kuban volunteer detachment; meeting with the Volunteer Army.
Chapter XXIV. The Ice March — fight of 15 March at Novo-Dmitrievskaya. Treaty with the Kubantsy on joining the Kuban detachment to the army. March on Ekaterinodar
15 March — the Ice March — “glory of Markov and the Officer Regiment, pride of the Volunteer Army.” Rain, water, and mud; treaty with the Kubantsy; march on Ekaterinodar.
Chapter XXV. Assault on Ekaterinodar
By 27 March — Erdeli’s cavalry and Bogaevsky’s 2nd Brigade on the right bank of the Kuban; Markov’s brigade covers the train. Bold design “not carried to its logical end”: the leader’s sense of humanity vs. tactical speed of concentration.
Chapter XXVI. Death of General Kornilov
31 March — artillery shelling of the farm district. Kornilov is asked to move headquarters: “It is not worth it now; tomorrow the assault.” Last conversation with the author; death. (The volume’s opening speech rhymes with this chapter.)

V. After Kornilov — Denikin’s command, the Don, Drozdovtsy, Germans
Chapter XXVII. My assumption of command of the Volunteer Army. Lifting the siege of Ekaterinodar. Fights at Gnachbau and Medvedovskaya. Feat of General Markov
Chief of staff: “Will you take command of the army?” — “Yes.” Lifting the siege; fights; feat of Gen. Markov.
Chapter XXVIII. March east — from Dyadkovskaya to Uspenskaya; tragedy of the wounded; life in the Kuban
Dyadkovskaya — day halt, bread and salt of the stanitsa people; plan to confuse the Bolsheviks by suddenness. Tragedy of the wounded; life in the Kuban.
Chapter XXIX. Risings on the Don and in the Kuban. Return of the army to the Don. Fights at Gorkaya Balka and Lezhanka. Liberation of Zadonye
News from Prochnookopskaya and the Labinsk department; preservation of a secret organization. Return to the Don; Gorkaya Balka, Lezhanka; liberation of Zadonye.
Chapter XXX. The Drozdovtsy march
With arrival on the Don — contact with the outside world. 23 April the Don militia of the Southern Group of Col. Denisov takes Novocherkassk. March of Col. Drozdovsky’s detachment; cautious reports of Gen. Kislyakov.
Chapter XXXI. German invasion of the Don. Contact with the outside world and three problems: unity of the front, foreign “orientation,” and political slogans. Results of the First Kuban March
Strengthening of the Don capital; marching ataman Popov; “provisional government.” Germans on the Don; three problems (unity of the front, orientation, slogans). Results of the First Kuban March: “Two and a half years more their struggle lasted” — and the scattering of the survivors across Slavic lands, Allied camps, and “night shelters” of the Old and New World. Closing of the volume: when “peace rests” over the country, the people will remember “those who first rose in defence of Russia against the red scourge.”

Volume apparatus (lists)
At the end of the OCR — a list of maps (Krymov’s echelons 29.8.1917; Moonsund; Kornilov’s march with the Tekin Regiment; situation Jan. 1918; map of the First Kuban March by dates; Kuban detachment; assault on Ekaterinodar; Drozdovtsy march) and a list of illustrations (Kornilov 1906 and 1917, Bykhov prison and prisoners, Romanovsky, Dukhonin, Markov, badge of the First Kuban March, photograph of Kornilov’s body, Drozdovsky, and others).

Completeness of the set
