sources/erzherzog-franz-ferdinand-50-geb.title: Erzherzog Franz Ferdinand, unser Thronfolger — Sonderheft der Österreichischen Rundschau
sources/erzherzog-franz-ferdinand-50-geb.content:
Erzherzog Franz Ferdinand, unser Thronfolger — Illustriertes Sonderheft der Österreichischen Rundschau, zum 50. Geburtstag
Erzherzog Franz Ferdinand, unser Thronfolger. Zum 50. Geburtstag. Illustriertes Sonderheft der Österreichischen Rundschau. Wien und Leipzig: K.u.K. Hof-Buchdruckerei und Verlags-Buchhandlung Carl Fromme; für Deutschland Georg Stilke, Hofbuchhändler Sr. K.u.K. Hoheit des Kronprinzen, Berlin. Issued 18 December 1913 (the archduke’s fiftieth birthday). Editors (Herausgeber): Leopold Freiherr von Chlumecky, Dr. Karl Glossy, Dr. Felix Freiherr von Oppenheimer; verantwortlicher Redakteur Karl Junker. Copyright 18 December 1913 by Österreichische Rundschau, Wien. A series of eight essays and illustrated plates on the heir to the Habsburg throne, drawn from the scanned copy (University of Toronto; Google scan) via tesseract Fraktur OCR (German) of the 120 scanned pages; the raw text in this wiki is that OCR.
The special issue opens by recalling that in a few days Austria-Hungary’s future emperor and king would complete his fiftieth year, and that more than ever all eyes turned upon the man who would one day be called to direct the destinies of the realm. Its several contributions, by the general, the admirals, the university professors and the chamberlain who knew him, together present the heir of the house of Habsburg as soldier, sailor, patron of art and science, hunter and collector.
Unser Thronfolger (Leopold Freiherr von Chlumecky)
Chlumecky reflects on the peculiar burden of the Habsburg ruler: in this many-shaped realm the crown is a heavier burden than anywhere else, for here the dynasty itself is the foundation of a structure that is not always logically and organically articulated — elsewhere the state carries the dynasty, here the dynasty carries the state. Austria-Hungary’s sovereign cannot confine himself within the narrow limits sometimes drawn by doctrinaire constitutional conceptions. Chlumecky sets out the theme that runs through the whole special issue: the future emperor as the bond that encircles and unites the divergent elements of the monarchy.
Erzherzog Franz Ferdinand (Theodor von Sosnosky)
Sosnosky gives the biographical portrait. Franz Ferdinand Karl Ludwig Joseph Maria was born on 18 December 1863 in the Herberstein palace in Graz, a Christmas gift to his parents, Archduke Karl Ludwig (brother of Kaiser Franz Joseph, son of Archduke Franz Karl and Archduchess Sophie, born Princess of Bavaria) and Archduchess Maria Annunziata (daughter of King Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies, of the house of Bourbon). By this descent, as a genealogist had shown, the archduke united in his veins the blood of no fewer than one hundred and twelve ancestral houses (seventy-one German, twenty Polish, eight French, seven Italian and six of various other nations), which in eleven generations counted 2047 verifiable ancestors — making the heir one of the most richly-ancestored princes in Europe. At the time of his birth his father lived as a private man in Graz, having withdrawn two years earlier from political life. Sosnosky traces the upbringing and formation of the future heir. (The world journey, which he undertook in December 1892, was a decisive turning-point in his life.)
Der Thronfolger als Soldat (General der Infanterie Emil Voinovich Edler von Belobreska)
Voinovich, a general of infantry, presents the heir as soldier, and grounds his martial zeal in the traditions of the dynasty — the founder Kaiser Rudolf, Maximilian the knight, Charles V, the devout Ferdinand II, and Maria Theresia, who though but a weak woman bore the heart of a king. On such a foundation, he argues, a lively feeling for the greatness of the dynasty and the realm fills the archduke; his wide travels taught him to know foreign lands and peoples, yet he kept his love of the fatherland — glowing even more after his great journey he loves the great, beautiful realm he is called one day to rule. Convinced that the foremost means to the greatness of the state lies in the sharpening of the sword, he gave the chief weight to the armed power of the monarchy, labouring without rest to raise it.
Der Thronfolger und die Marine (Konteradmiral Franz Mittl)
Rear-Admiral Mittl recalls that the ruling house of the Habsburgs counts many names bound up with the development of seafaring — Charles V, in whose realm the sun never set, and whose rule only a sovereign could boast in whose realm the navy held a dominating position; and later Kaiser Karl VI, Maria Theresia and Kaiser Franz Joseph I, whose names remain forever linked to the flourishing of the seafaring of the Danubian monarchy. But the manifold tasks of the head of state did not permit these bearers of the crown to enter into all the details of that peculiar machinery, so remote from ordinary life; it was reserved for the heir to the throne to give the navy his more particular care. Mittl sets out the archduke’s role in fostering the fleet.
Erzherzog Franz Ferdinand als Kunstfreund (Professor Dr. Georg Graf Mycielski)
Mycielski, professor at the university of Cracow, presents the heir as a friend of art, and dwells on the collections he built up at his castle of Konopišt in Bohemia. Three special collections are singled out. The greatest creation is the armoury in the upper storey of the castle, where the archduke placed the most precious and rarest treasures of the whole Este collection (which he was continually enriching by new purchases) — armour, cannon and old Este standards; the early and late Renaissance triumphs there in a series of complete suits of armour with the finest gold and silver inlay and extraordinarily fine reliefs and engravings of Italian and Augsburg workmanship, among them the charming work of Benvenuto Cellini, rare shields and helmets, and complete horse-armour for tournament or combat — an armoury (Armeria Areiducale in Konopišt) that is a pearl among the European collections of its kind, in its chief stock an inheritance of the famous ancestors from Ferrara, enriched and completed by the archduke with new objects, chiefly from the Renaissance period. A small but exceedingly interesting special collection fills a square chamber of the tower exclusively with powder-horns and small horns of the most varied kinds from all epochs, finely wrought. A third collection is devoted to the archduke’s hunting trophies from his travels.
Der Thronfolger und die Wissenschaft (Hofrat Professor R. von Wettstein)
Wettstein (Richard von Wettstein, botanist) treats the heir’s relation to science. The archduke had taken the protectorate of the academies of sciences in Prague and Cracow, so that the prince nearest the throne stood in intimate relation to the three highest central institutions of the realm devoted only to science. He brought a quite special interest to a series of sciences — in the first place the natural sciences, especially botany, and likewise folklore and the study of home (Volks- und Heimatkunde). His love of nature went back to the impressions of his youth in the Lower-Austrian Voralpen. After journeys through much of Europe and then to Egypt, Syria and Palestine, he undertook his great world journey in 1892, returning with rich ethnographic and natural-scientific collections, which under his continued personal participation were first housed in the upper Belvedere, then in the Modena-Palais in Vienna, and finally in the new building of the Hofburg. At the botanical exhibition of 1905 at Schönbrunn (with the international botanical congress, whose protectorate he held) and at the opening in 1913 of the Austrian Adriatic exhibition (also under his protectorate) he surprised the specialists with his detailed knowledge. His interest in natural science was intimately bound up with a love of horticulture, whose rise in Austria in these years is directly or indirectly owing to his fostering and purposeful intervention; at Konopišt he created over twenty years, under difficult conditions, a park of some 340 hectares, renowned both for the grandeur of the layout and for its artistic and loving treatment of detail.
Die Weltreise des Erzherzogs Franz Ferdinand (Konteradmiral Alfred Freiherr von Koudelka)
Rear-Admiral Koudelka recounts the world journey. On 15 December 1892 the archduke sailed from Europe to travel round the world. The journey, which he undertook in his twenty-ninth year, was a decisive turning-point in his life — it was that great journey that gave his later years their direction and set before him his task; after it he became a frequent visitor of Brioni and of the coast. Koudelka, who accompanied the heir on his voyage, describes the route and the impressions gathered on it, and the abiding effect the journey had upon the future emperor.
Erzherzog Franz Ferdinand als Jäger (Camillo Morgan)
Morgan, the master of the hunt, presents the heir as hunter. In green Styria, where the archduke’s cradle stood, the old noble chase (Edelgejaid) had ever flourished — there Duke Frederick the Belligerent had his hunting-seat Dobl, the hunting-horns of Duke Ernst the Iron and of his consort Cimburgis of Masovia, won at a bear-hunt, had rung out, and Kaiser Maximilian I, the “last knight” and “great-mighty woodman”, had thrown his hunting-knife after the swift chamois. Morgan suggests these three hunt-loving rulers may have stood by the cradle of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and begged for him the gift of St. Hubertus, that he become as true a hunter as they — and he did. His aged imperial uncle on the old Habsburg throne himself called him “much-tried huntsman”. His trophies grew to the colossal; by the thousands mounted the red-deer antlers, the falls of the fallow-deer, the chamois beards, the roe antlers, the boar’s jaws and the woodcock’s feathers and the pelts of beasts of prey; to these trophies of home game were added the elephants and tiger trophies from India (from his world journey), the bear trophies from the preserves of the Kaiser of Russia, the bison (Wisent) and so on. Morgan closes with the dedication of Austria’s huntsmen to the heir, and quotes the “Thronfolger-Hymne” set to music by the composer Tresdorn, with its invocation of the holy hunt-patron St. Hubertus, prayed by the hunters of the realm for the future bearer of the crown — “so far as the double eagle’s wings beat”.

sources/fortunato-il-mezzogiorno-e-lo-st.title: Fortunato — Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano, Discorsi politici, Vol. I
sources/fortunato-il-mezzogiorno-e-lo-st.content:
Giustino Fortunato — Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano. Discorsi politici, Volume I
Giustino Fortunato (1848–1932), Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano. Discorsi politici (1880–1910), Seconda edizione, Vallecchi Editore, Firenze, 1926. This is Volume I, containing the first nineteen discourses (I–XIX), published in order of chronology as spoken by the author in parliament and before the electors of the college of Melfi. The first edition was issued by Laterza of Bari in 1911; the preface of the second edition is dated Gennaio 1926 and is signed U. Zanotti-Bianco. The text of this wiki is the HathiTrust full-text scan (OCLC 7097481, University of Iowa copy, DG828 F6 v.1), 486 pages.
Dominant years in this volume are 1880–1896, from Fortunato’s first appeal to the electors of Melfi in May 1880 to the discourse on the Regions of 3 July 1896.
Discourses
I. La « dissidenza » e le elezioni del 16 maggio 1880 (5 e 22 maggio 1880) — Fortunato stands for the college of Melfi at the elections for the XIV Legislature; the address to the electors on the dissidence which broke the Depretis majorities. II. La trasformazione de’ monti frumentari (15 giugno 1880) — on the transformation of the grain banks in the Neapolitan provinces. III. Le cooperative di credito nel Mezzogiorno (18 ottobre 1880, Bologna) — the credit cooperatives of the South. IV. Nuove leggi su demanî comunali (2 dicembre 1880 e 19 novembre 1881) — the new laws on communal domains and the Southern demanial question. V. Scrutinio di lista (25 marzo 1881) — the list ballot. VI. Le leggi d’eccezione nel sistema tributario (21 gennaio 1882) — the exception laws in the tributary system. VII. I partiti storici e la XIV Legislatura (2 settembre 1882, Melfi) — the historical parties and the Fourteenth Legislature. VIII. Il « trasformismo » e le elezioni del 29 ottobre 1882 (22 ottobre e 7 novembre 1882) — trasformismo and the elections of 29 October 1882. IX. Commemorazione di Francesco De Sanctis (22 gennaio 1884) — the commemoration of Francesco De Sanctis. X. La XV Legislatura e i nuovi partiti (30 aprile e 6 giugno 1886) — the Fifteenth Legislature and the new parties. XI. La riduzione delle preture (17 febbraio 1890) — the reduction of the local magistracies. XII. Il problema economico e la XVI Legislatura (30 ottobre e 5 dicembre 1890, Potenza) — the economic problem and the Sixteenth Legislature. XIII. La XVII Legislatura e la finanza dello Stato (13 e 25 ottobre 1892, Melfi) — the Seventeenth Legislature and the finances of the State. XIV. Marina da Guerra (4 maggio 1893) — the war navy. XV. Istituti di emissione e circolazione fiduciaria (25 giugno 1893) — the issuing institutes and fiduciary circulation. XVI. La crisi bancaria e la XVIII Legislatura (10 e 16 maggio 1895, Melfi) — the banking crisis and the Eighteenth Legislature. XVII. L’ora presente (19 maggio 1895, Venosa) — the present hour. XVIII. Reclutamento territoriale (5 dicembre 1895) — territorial recruitment. XIX. Le Regioni (3 luglio 1896) — the Regions.

sources/fortunato-il-mezzogiorno-e-lo-st.title: Fortunato — Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano, Discorsi politici, Vol. II
sources/fortunato-il-mezzogiorno-e-lo-st.content:
Giustino Fortunato — Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano. Discorsi politici, Volume II
Giustino Fortunato (1848–1932), Il Mezzogiorno e lo stato italiano. Discorsi politici (1880–1910), Seconda edizione, Vallecchi Editore, Firenze, 1926. This is Volume II, containing the final fourteen discourses (XX–XXXIII). The first edition was issued by Laterza of Bari in 1911; as the preface of the second edition notes, this edition omits the discourses for the inauguration of the railway lines from Rocchetta to Rionero and from Rionero to Potenza and the convivial greeting to Zanardelli at Melfi (26 September 1902), which appear in the author’s own book on the Ofantine railways. The text of this wiki is the HathiTrust full-text scan (OCLC 7097481, University of Iowa copy, DG828 F6 v.2), 530 pages.
Dominant years in this volume are 1897–1910, from the discourse on the Nineteenth Legislature and colonial policy (March 1897) to the discourse Malaria e chinino of 30 June 1910, the last in the collection.
Discourses
XX. La XIX Legislatura e la politica coloniale (5 e 11 marzo 1897) — after the disaster of Adua and the fall of Crispi, Fortunato appeals to the electors of Melfi on the colonial question, urging an Eritrean policy of prudence and withdrawal. XXI. L’ordinamento dell’Esercito (4 maggio 1897) — the reorganisation of the army. XXII. Per le lapidi a’ martiri della patria (20 settembre 1898) — for the tablets to the martyrs of the fatherland. XXIII. Il dovere politico (9 ottobre 1898) — political duty, with an appendix on the tributary burden of the Mezzogiorno before and after Unification. XXIV. Per le lapidi ai Caduti di Adua (6 maggio 1900) — for the tablets to the fallen of Adua. XXV. Il regime parlamentare e la XX Legislatura (13 e 31 maggio 1900, Melfi) — the parliamentary regime and the Twentieth Legislature. XXVI. Dopo il misfatto (11 ottobre 1900, Lavello) — after the regicide of Monza. XXVII. Le spese militari (23 marzo 1901) — the military expenses. XXVIII. La XXI Legislatura e le pubbliche libertà (18 e 30 ottobre 1904) — the Twenty-First Legislature and public liberties, with an appendix on the Southern Question and the tributary reform. XXIX. In memoria di Giuseppe Plàstino (31 maggio 1905) — in memory of Giuseppe Plastino. XXX. Commemorazione di Emanuele Gianturco (28 novembre 1907) — the commemoration of Emanuele Gianturco. XXXI. I servizi pubblici e la XXII Legislatura (10 febbraio e 7 marzo 1909) — the public services and the Twenty-Second Legislature, with a statistical appendix on the economy of Basilicata. XXXII. L’emigrazione meridionale (30 giugno 1909) — Southern emigration. XXXIII. Malaria e chinino (30 giugno 1910) — malaria and quinine, the closing discourse of the collection.

sources/frescura-diario-di-un-imboscato-.title: Frescura — Diario di un imboscato
sources/frescura-diario-di-un-imboscato-.content:
Attilio Frescura — Diario di un imboscato
Attilio Frescura (1887–1943), Diario di un imboscato, Galla Editore, Vicenza, 1919. The title page bears the publisher’s device and an epigraph from Jean Jaurès. The book is prefaced by the editor, dated Vicenza, 22 August 1919, which insists that the author — whose title seems to brand him a shirker — was in fact a decorated territorial officer who fought from 1915 to 1918, winning a silver and a bronze medal for military valour and three war crosses, and who was at Asiago in 1916, at Caporetto in 1917, and on the Piave in 1918. The text of this wiki is the scan (536 pages, of which 488 carry full text).
The work is a satirical diary of the Italian front told in the first person from the persona of the “imboscato” — the man sheltered from the trenches in the rearguard, the depots, and the staffs. Its frame is set in the opening pages: “Le gradazioni dell’«imboscato» sono infinite. Il combattente ha sempre qualcuno che è «imboscato» rispetto a sè…” (The gradations of the “shirker” are infinite. The combatant always has someone who is a “shirker” relative to himself…). The diary opens with a note that the first sheets, recording the heroic exaltation of the crowd in the days of preparation and the events of the first days of the war, were lost in part when the manuscript was saved in the second half of May 1916.
The diary runs from 24 May 1915 (the first cannon shot from Fort Verena at four in the morning, the crossing of the border) to the closing of the war in November 1918.
Chapters
I. “I Terribili” — the opening of the war at Asiago: the first days at Fort Verena and the ridge, the brigades Ivrea and Brescia, the attack of 29 May 1915, the passage of the border, and the disappointed first offensive. Dated entries begin (20 July 1915). Ottobre 1915 — a section on the second autumn of waiting. II. “Battute d’aspetto” — the waiting episodes of the winter of 1915–1916. “L’offensiva austriaca nell’altopiano di Asiago” — the Austrian offensive (the Strafexpedition) of May–June 1916 on the Asiago highland, against which the author’s manuscript was saved. Luglio 1916 — the aftermath of the offensive, with the papers of the Supreme Command on the Trentino campaign. VII. Il Carso — the fighting on the Carso. IX. Pace in guerra — “peace in war,” the truces and lulls. X. Paese di qua e paese di là — the country on this side and the other. XI. Pazzi e savi — madmen and sages. XII. Smorfie e sberleffi — grimaces and taunts. XIII. Il buon giudice — the good judge. XIV. Censori e censura — the censors and the censorship. XV. Il “siluro” — “the torpedo.” XVI. Imbasciate — embassies. XVII. Caporetto — the retreat of October–November 1917. XVIII. Cadorna — the dismissal of the Chief of Staff and the reorganisation of the Supreme Command. XIX. Un generale — a general. XX. Scaramucce nelle retrovie del Piave — skirmishes in the rearguard of the Piave. XXI. La battaglia del Piave — the battle of the Piave (June 1918). XXII. Il cattivo giudice — the bad judge. XXIII. Dal Piave alle Alpi Giulie — from the Piave to the Julian Alps, the advance after Vittorio Veneto. XXIV. Chiuso il libro della guerra — “Closed the Book of War,” the close of the diary at the end of the war, closing with the same Jaurès epigraph with which the volume opened.

sources/garibaldi-memorie-1907.title: Giuseppe Garibaldi — Memorie (1907 edizione diplomatica)
sources/garibaldi-memorie-1907.content:
Giuseppe Garibaldi — Memorie
Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882), Memorie. Edizione diplomatica dall’autografo definitivo, a cura di Ernesto Nathan. Torino: Società Tipografico-Editrice Nazionale (già Roux e Viarengo), 1907. Four hundred numbered copies printed on hand-made paper. The text is the “diplomatic” edition — that is, a faithful reproduction of Garibaldi’s own definitive handwritten autograph, without the corrections or modernisations a literary editor might have imposed — issued by the editor Ernesto Nathan (1845–1921), the London-born Mazzinian who was later Mayor of Rome, with a preface dated Rome, 20 May 1907. It is an autobiography in the strict sense: the whole is written in the first person by Garibaldi himself, framed by his own Prefazione alle mie Memorie (Caprera, 3 July 1872) and Revisione alle mie Memorie (Caprera, 7 December 1871), and closes with a colophon dated Civitavecchia, 15 July 1875. This wiki’s text is the Project Gutenberg eBook edition (EBook no. 56500, released 5 February 2018, produced by Barbara Magni), 203 pages, Italian; the PDF carries a clean embedded text layer, so no re-OCR was required.
Dominant years are 1848–1871, the revolutionary and unification decades, with the opening chapters reaching back to the author’s birth in 1807.
About the Author
Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882), born at Nice of a Genoese sailor family, was the soldier of the Italian Risorgimento. A follower of Mazzini and the Carbonarist movement from his youth, he fled into exile after the failure of the Genoese rising of 1834, serving the cause of the Rio-Grandense republic and the defenders of Montevideo against the Argentine dictator Rosas, where he formed the Italian Legion and won the renown that carried him home in 1848. After commanding in the defence of the Roman Republic (1849) and the heroic retreat through the Romagna, he returned to exile in America before settling at Caprera. His greatest feat was the Expedition of the Thousand (1860), by which the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was conquered for the cause of Italian unity. He was wounded and captured at Aspromonte (1862), defeated at Mentana (1867), and in his last campaign commanded an improvised army of volunteers for the French Republic in the Vosges against the Prussians (1870–71). He died at Caprera in 1882.
The Editor’s Preface (Ernesto Nathan, Rome, 20 May 1907)
Nathan justifies the diplomatic method: the editor’s task, where the words of a great man are concerned, is not to alter but to reproduce, since any alteration of a text which has “conquered the right to be remembered by posterity” borders on sacrilege. The preface examines the divergences that arose between Garibaldi and Mazzini — disagreements of judgment over events and the attitude to be assumed, expressed in the Memorie in a “hard and hostile” manner — and the editor’s conviction that many of these differences would have been avoided had the two men’s relations always been direct and personal, untroubled by intermediaries who coloured the one’s thought with the other’s. The same applies to the relations between Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel II, clouded by “politics and petty politics,” by old-style generals and by statesmen too devoted to the Piedmontese kingdom to embrace all Italy. Whether the outcome would have differed is, Nathan writes, a task for the impartial historian, not for the editor — Rome, 20 May 1907.
Prefazione alle mie Memorie (Caprera, 3 July 1872)
Garibaldi’s own preface: “a stormy life, made up of good and evil.” He declares himself a hater of tyranny and falsehood, a republican who nevertheless believes a temporary and honest dictatorship necessary at the head of nations like France, Spain and Italy which are “victims of the most pernicious Byzantinism”; tolerant and not exclusive, he would not impose his republicanism by force. Everything he has narrated, he says, may serve history, “of the greater part of the facts I was an ocular witness.” He has been liberal in praise of the dead who fell on the battlefields of liberty, sparing in praise of the living, and ever attacked “the priesthood” most particularly, seeing in it the prop of every despotism — a theme that runs through the whole work.
Revisione alle mie Memorie (Caprera, 7 December 1871)
The revision opens with the account of his parents: his father, a sailor like his own father before him, who kept his son from the sea until nearly fifteen; and his mother, whose tenderness he honours as the source of the little good in him. He argues that a sailor must begin his career very young, “if possible before the age of eight,” the system of the Genoese and above all the English.
Contents
The Memorie are divided into five periods, each opening its own chapter-numbering.
Primo Periodo — Youth, Voyages and South America
Capitoli I–XLVIII. The opening chapters set the man in his family and his native town, then carry him across the Atlantic: his early voyages and his service in the Sardinian navy; the conversion to the Italian national idea; his flight into exile and the years of wandering. The main body of the first period is South American: his service with the Rio-Grandense republic in its war of independence against the Brazilian Empire — the corsair voyages, the building and arming of the little fleet, the defence of the Rio Grande, the campaigns with the gaucho republicans, his meeting with his future wife Anita; the disaster on the shores of Santa Catarina, the shipwreck, the flight across the Sierra; then the passage to Uruguay and the defence of Montevideo against the siege of Oribe and Rosas, where he formed the Italian Legion and won a soldier’s fame. The period closes with the decision to leave the Plata and carry his sword to Italy, and the departure of sixty-three volunteers on 15 April 1848.
Secondo Periodo — The Return to Italy and the Roman Republic
Capitoli I–XII. The voyage home and the offer of his and the Legion’s services to the Italian cause; the revolutionary year 1848, the Lombard war against Austria; his entry into Rome and his part in the defence of the Roman Republic of 1849 against the French army of Oudinot; the siege of Rome, the fighting at the gates, the wounding and the heroic retreat with the remnants of his command across central Italy, pursued through the Romagna, until the pursuit died out and the survivors were dispersed. The Secondo Periodo is the narrative of the Roman Republic — the episode from which Garibaldi emerged as the symbol of the Italian revolution.
Terzo Periodo — The Campaign of Sicily and the Expedition of the Thousand (1860)
Capitoli I–XVIII. The famous campaign of May–October 1860. Garibaldi opens with a hymn to Sicily — “genitrice degli Archimedi,” the land of the Sicilian Vespers and of the two lads of Syracuse — the island that was to “wake the sleepers.” The account runs from the embarkation at Quarto and the landing at Marsala, through the victory at Calatafimi, the taking of Palermo (27 May 1860) and the reduction of the island, to the crossing of the Straits of Messina, the landing on the Neapolitan mainland, the assault of Reggio, and the advance on Naples; it closes with the decisive victory of the Volturno (1–2 October 1860, Bronzetti at Castel Morrone, the fighting at Caserta Vecchia). The Thousand and the southern volunteers are the heroes of this period, which delivered the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies to the Italian national cause.
Quarto Periodo — 1860–1870: Aspromonte and Mentana
Capitoli I–IX. The years of disillusion and defeat. The campaign of Aspromonte (1862) — the march that Victor Emmanuel’s government could not sanction, the encounter with the royal troops in Calabria, Garibaldi’s wounding and capture, his imprisonment at the Varignano; his return to Caprera; the third war of independence of 1866 with the advance into the Trentino; and the disastrous campaign of Mentana (3 November 1867), where the attempt to seize Rome for the Republic was crushed at the gates of the Papal city by the Papal troops and the French reinforcements. The period ends with Garibaldi the prisoner and exile of his own island.
Quinto Periodo — 1870–1871: The Campaign of France
Capitoli I–IV. The last campaign. Called to the service of the French Republic after Sedan, Garibaldi commanded the improvised Army of the Vosges against the Prussians: the combats of Lentenay and Autun (21–23 January 1871), the three days’ holding of Dijon, and the final retreat, ordered when the enemy masses, freed by the fall of Paris and the armistice, gathered to envelop the small army. Elected a deputy to the National Assembly at Bordeaux, Garibaldi took his seat “with the sole intent of carrying my vote to the unhappy Republic,” and, seeing nothing more could be done, returned to Caprera, where he arrived on 16 February 1871. His Army of the Vosges, composed of too republican elements, was dissolved by the government of Thiers. The narrative is signed at Civitavecchia, 15 July 1875.
Appendice alle mie Memorie
The book closes with the appendix giving the full table of contents of the Memorie in its five periods, from the first chapters of the youth and South-American years through the return to Italy, the Sicilian and Neapolitan campaign, the years 1860–1870, and the campaign of France.
Series note
This volume sits at the head of the Italian thread of this wiki. The introduction of the knowledge base promises the unification of Italy as well as of Germany; the sources gathered so far trace the Austrian and German threads of the continental story, while the French thread carries the Second Empire and the Third Republic. Garibaldi’s Memorie supply the missing Italian side of the same decades — the revolutionary and military history of the Risorgimento as told by its most famous soldier, in the campaign that ran from Montevideo through Rome, Sicily and Naples to the Vosges. Its emphasis on the war for Italian unity complements the diplomatic and political histories of the European states that surround it in this period; chronologically its weight lies in 1848–1871, and it reaches back beyond the 1866 starting-point of this wiki to give the earlier revolutionary ground of the Italian question.

sources/granat-istoriya-rossii-xix-veke-.title: Granat — History of Russia in the 19th Century, Vol. 8
sources/granat-istoriya-rossii-xix-veke-.content:
Granat — History of Russia in the 19th Century, Vol. 8
История России в XIX веке. — St. Petersburg: Partnership of the Brothers A. and I. Granat & Co., 1907–1911. — 9 volumes. Vol. VIII. Part 4. End of the Century [1892–1900]. Section One. — 1910. — [5], 262 pp.; 15 plates.
A collective multi-volume course issued by the firm of the brothers A. and I. Granat. Vol. VIII opens the fourth part of the series (“End of the Century”) and constitutes the first section of that part. The series frame on the title page gives 1892–1900; the essays in the volume in fact carry the narrative to 1903 (the eve of the Far Eastern crisis and the Russo-Japanese War). The volume fills the gap after Kornilov, Part 3 (the reactionary period to the famine of 1891–92) and provides a systematic survey of the “end of the century”: state economy in the Witte era, industrial boom and the labour movement of the 1890s–early 1900s, and public medicine in connection with the living conditions of the people.
Composition of the volume (three principal essays):

























AuthorEssayScopeM. I. BogolepovState economy (1892–1903)finances, taxes, monopolies, railways, gold currencyL. MartovDevelopment of industry and the labour movement from 1893 to 1903boom 1894–99; crisis 1899–1903; strikes; ZubatovismV. Ya. KanelPublic medicine in connection with the living conditions of the peopleprikaz and zemstvo medicine; sanitation; factory medicine
Character of the edition. A collection of essays by different authors, not a single-author course. Bogolepov writes as a financier-critic of the “brilliant period” of state economy; Martov as a Social Democrat, with detailed strike statistics and analysis of government policy on the labour question; Kanel as a public-health physician linking medicine to economy and everyday life. Pre-reform orthography. OCR quality — medium (Ѣ/Е, І/И confusion, “XX” for “XIX”, distorted surnames and years, e.g. “Боголфповъ”, “1892—9083” / “до 1908” for 1903 in the table of contents).
Raw volume: ~1.35 MB, 27,347 lines. Internet Archive: istorijarossiivxixvekespb19071911t20 (the suffix t20 in the identifier is not the volume number; the text itself says “Vol. VIII”).

Chapter I. M. I. Bogolepov — State Economy (1892–1903)
The essay opens with the famine of 1891–92 as the starting point and is carried to the threshold of the Russo-Japanese War. The author examines the Treasury’s “free cash,” budget growth, the policy of Vyshnegradsky and especially S. Yu. Witte, railway construction and redemption, the spirits monopoly, indirect taxes and excises, customs protectionism, the sugar industry, credit, and the introduction of the gold currency. The running thesis: the “brilliant period” of Russian state finances was achieved at the cost of extreme strain on taxable capacity, irregularities of state economy, and the ruin of the propertyless; by the beginning of the 20th century the country inherited a huge debt, a loss-making state economy, an overstrained tax press, landowner agriculture amid a hungry peasantry, and factory production working for the Treasury and for an exhausted internal market. The conclusion directly links this legacy to the Russo-Japanese War and the revolution.
Thematic lines of the essay

Aftermath of 1891–92 and “free cash.” The famine and its fiscal consequences; accumulation of Treasury cash alongside growth of state debt and expenditure (including the non-military budget).
Witte and predecessors. Transition from Bunge and Vyshnegradsky to the Witte system; intensified railway construction, breakdown of the natural economy, the redemption operation, and the money economy.
Indirect taxation and monopolies. Excises (spirits, tobacco, sugar, matches, etc.); introduction of the spirits monopoly; raising of customs duties (including on cotton); the sugar industry as an example of state-protectionist policy.
Railways, credit, gold currency. The railway business and its financial return; credit as a means of mobilization; gold currency — “costing the country” heavy sacrifices in the author’s account.
Taxable capacity, mutual responsibility, land captains. Strain on taxable capacity; link of the fiscal system to mutual responsibility (krugovaya poruka) and the administrative-peasant regime; critique of unaccountability of power in state economy.
Result of the “brilliant period.” Separated from “current contemporaneity” by the Russo-Japanese War and the revolution; heavy legacy — debt, loss-making state economy, tax overstrain, agrarian and industrial weakness of the internal market.

In the raw text the essay occupies approximately lines ~170–6844 (to “CHAPTER II”).

Chapter II. L. Martov — Development of Industry and the Labour Movement from 1893 to 1903
Martov’s essay is the largest in the volume. It is built as a connected narrative of the industrial cycle of the 1890s–early 1900s and the parallel growth of the mass labour movement, with abundant strike statistics, geography of struggle (Petersburg, Moscow, Ivanovo-Voznesensk, Łódź, Baku, the Donbass, the South, Poland, the Baltic), and analysis of government tactics (factory inspection, Witte’s circulars, repression, Zubatov experiments, laws of 1886, 1897, and 1903). Three clear subdivisions:
1. Culminating industrial boom and flowering of the mass labour movement (1894–1899)
From the mid-1890s — “unprecedented industrial animation,” coordinated with the world boom. Growth of the strike movement; distinction of offensive and defensive strikes and their outcomes (on the author’s data, success of full/partial concessions is higher in defensive struggle; strikes over fines and administrative actions more often end in defeat for the workers). Economic character of mass struggle in the boom years; attitude of Social Democracy to political and purely professional tasks; in Poland and Lithuania — greater receptivity of the masses to political agitation. Mention of Witte’s 1895 line on maintaining “patriarchal” relations between masters and workers as an attempt to preserve government tutelage over the bourgeoisie. Toward the end of the subsection — accumulation of discontent while predominantly economic demands remain in the “immediate” struggle of the masses.
2. Economic crisis of the last years of the 19th century and the turning point in the labour movement
Autumn 1899 — beginning of the industrial crisis (harbinger — the stock-exchange crisis of preceding years). Fall in iron prices; closures and cutbacks in Łódź, Białystok, Ivanovo-Voznesensk, Nizhny Novgorod, Sormovo, Petersburg (Putilov, Obukhov), the Donets basin, Baku, Mariupol, Tula, and elsewhere; lengthening of the working day with falling piece rates; unemployment 1900–1901 (oil crisis in Baku 1901, etc.). The “protracted crisis of 1899–1903” is interrupted by local revivals and complicated by the agrarian crisis and village famines throwing labour onto the urban market. Against the background of crisis — politicization of the movement: demonstrations, collisions with police and troops, growth in the use of firearms against workers (1901–1903), corporal punishment of strikers, shift from administrative exile to the courts. The Rostov strike and southern strikes of 1902–1903; summer 1903 — wave of strikes (Petersburg, Kostroma, Nikolaev, Vyshny Volochyok, etc.); general strikes in the South (including Baku). The September strike marks, for the author, the end of the “Zubatov” period; with the appearance of the Far Eastern crisis, Russian public life and the labour movement enter a new phase — beyond the 19th century.
3. Government and the labour question in the early 1900s — Attempts at legal organization of workers
The emergence of the working class onto the arena of political struggle forces the authorities to combine hardened repression with experiments in “legal” organization. Zubatov and related experiments in Moscow (mutual-aid funds, professors’ “talks,” the “Council of Workers of Mechanical Production of the City of Moscow”), Odessa (the “independents,” Shaevich’s metalworkers’ union), and elsewhere; suspicion of Social Democracy and the radical intelligentsia toward police tutelage. Factory legislation as meagre “social reforms” of absolutism under pressure of the masses: laws of 1886, 1897, and 1903 (including the 1903 law on compensation for accidents — with reservations limiting liability, “gross carelessness” of the worker, calculation of “actual earnings,” etc.). Conclusion: reformist attempts within the autocracy break against the political interest of the regime, above which it cannot rise even for the sake of self-preservation.
In the raw text the essay — approximately lines ~6848–16085.

Chapter III. V. Ya. Kanel — Public Medicine in Connection with the Living Conditions of the People
The essay opens with a numbered introductory section and then proceeds in continuous prose (without subheadings as clear as Martov’s), covering pre-reform (“prikaz”) medicine, zemstvo medicine, sanitary condition of town and village, epidemics, and, at the end, factory medicine.
1. Care of public health before the introduction of the zemstvo
Before the zemstvo institutions, public healthcare was distributed among the boards of public charity (prikazy), committees of public health, medical boards, the medical council, and the departments of state domains and appanages. Formalism, clerical reporting, and “paper” medicine predominate: on paper — hospitals, doctors, feldsher, and struggle with epidemics; in fact — lack of funds, embezzlement, unsuitable premises. The prikazy (1775–1865) opened hundreds of establishments (hospitals, asylums, almshouses, feldsher schools), but they bear the stamp of fictitiousness. Committees of public health (from 1845, expanded 1852) are composed of local official notables. Rural aid to state and appanage peasants — on the departments with negligible budgets.
Zemstvo medicine and sanitation
With the introduction of the zemstvo — collision of medical demands with the estate zemstvo, stingy with medicine; role of congresses of zemstvo physicians; critique of Prince Vasilchikov’s view (On Self-Government) of the doctor as a narrow specialist without right to general direction. Zemstvo medical organizations early link morbidity and mortality with economic, legal, and social conditions and lay the foundation of public sanitation (prevention, study of epidemics, enlightenment). Themes of the essay: the district system; feldsherism; sanitary congresses; struggle with cholera (1892–1893 and the Pirogov congresses); nutrition and “famine bread”; medical-food points for migrant workers; housing conditions of the peasantry; comparison of Russian mortality with Western European (general and infant mortality; references to Erisman, Oesterlen, and others).
City and factory medicine
Urban self-government, in the author’s view, copes with sanitation even more weakly than the zemstvo: most cities have no permanent sanitary organization; work livens only during epidemics. Dwellings of the poorest layers of the capitals (Petersburg, Moscow) as foci of infection. Factory medicine — a “fragment” of the general order: interests of entrepreneurs and workers collide; the authorities in practice defend the strong. Factory medicine and labour protection arise under external pressure (labour unrest at the end of the century, epidemics); attempts at improvement are weak because of manufacturers’ resistance. Examined are the law of 1866 on hospitals at factories and its erosion by obligatory regulations of the boards (replacement of hospitals by outpatient clinics, patchwork of norms); projects of the early 1900s (including a memorandum on the 1905 draft) and the 1903 law on compensation for the maimed. Comparative tables of fatal industrial accidents show Russia ahead of Western countries. Conclusion: the 19th century leaves the 20th a heavy sanitary legacy; the health of the people is the “question of the day” against physical and spiritual degeneration of the masses.
In the raw text the essay — approximately lines ~16086–27335 (to end of file).

The volume directly continues the chronological line of Kornilov, Course, Part 3: there, reaction 1866 – famine 1891/92 and the whole reign of Alexander III; here — the “end of the century” under Nicholas II to 1903 (Witte, industrial boom and crisis, mass labour movement, Zubatovism, zemstvo and factory medicine).
