sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.title: Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome I (Le Gouvernement de M. Thiers)
sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.content:
Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome I (Le Gouvernement de M. Thiers)
Gabriel Hanotaux, Histoire de la France contemporaine (1871–1900), tome premier. Paris: Ancienne Librairie Furne, Combet & Cie, Éditeurs, 5, rue Palatine (VIᵉ); no imprint year on the scanned copy (Internet Archive metadata: n.d.; publisher field Paris, Combet). On the Internet Archive as histoiredelafran01hanouoft (University of Ottawa / Robarts–University of Toronto copy; ABBYY FineReader OCR; 678 images). The half-title names the subject Le Gouvernement de M. Thiers. Series framing (author’s Avertissement and IA description): I Le gouvernement de M. Thiers; II–III La présidence du maréchal de Mac Mahon (two volumes); IV La République parlementaire. This wiki holds Tome I, Tome II (L’Échec de la Monarchie), Tome III, and Tome IV.
In the Avertissement Hanotaux undertakes the history of contemporary France from February 1871 to the end of 1900. The present volume contains, with the government of M. Thiers, the end of the Franco-German war, the peace negotiations, the Commune, the constitutional crisis, the debates of the National Assembly, and the liberation of the territory; it stops at 24 May 1873. The second volume is to be devoted to the presidency of Marshal Mac-Mahon and the foundation of the Republic; the third and fourth will take up the history of the parliamentary Republic. Hanotaux, then of the Académie française, presents the work as a “dossier” of democracy: he had been sixteen in 1870, came to Paris a few months after the Commune, and writes as one who has seen the facts he recounts.
Dominant years in the text are 1871–1873.
Avertissement
Programme of the four-volume series; personal origins of the book in the war of 1870 and its immediate consequences; the generation that left childhood under the shock of defeat; questions of France’s past greatness, present defeat, and coming recovery; insufficiency of democratic memory of problems already posed; the book as a contemporary “dossier.”
Chapitre premier — La Guerre
France in 1870; the imperial policy of nationalities leads to war with Prussia; portrait of Napoleon III as a reduced copy of the first Bonaparte. The Government of National Defence; conclusion of the armistice; France after the war. Elections of 8 February 1871: the great debate War or Peace dominates politics; republicans for guerre à outrance; peace lists in the departments. Meeting of the National Assembly at Bordeaux; all eyes turn to M. Thiers, elected in twenty-six departments with nearly two million votes as “administrator of the national misfortune.” Portrait of Thiers: contrast with Napoleon III (prudence, experience, foresight against adventure); Marseillais origins, Histoire de la Révolution française, the National and 1830; short stature, spectacles, imperturbable aplomb. He is named chief of the executive power.
Chapitre II — L’Assemblée Nationale à Bordeaux
Constitutional crisis: four times in the century hereditary succession has failed; the principle of hereditary sovereignty itself is shaken; popular sovereignty and the law of majorities replace divine right, with the difficulties of representation. Organisation of Thiers’s government; recognition by the foreign powers; cabinet of 19 February 1871; first administrative measures. Negotiation of the preliminaries of peace and their ratification; Thiers at Bismarck’s (21 February); Bismarck’s reserved hand versus French openness and the passion for peace after Favre’s earlier mission; Alsace and Lorraine, the question of Metz and Belfort. Versailles becomes capital. Dispositions of the monarchical parties; the comte de Chambord; first steps toward fusion; Orléans princes elected deputies; the Biarritz understanding; the pacte de Bordeaux.
Chapitre III — La Commune
Origins and explosion of the Paris insurrection after the Assembly’s measures and the attempt to seize the guns of Montmartre (18 March 1871). Dual power: Versailles and the Commune; composition and factions of the revolutionary government; the Central Committee, the International, Blanquists and Jacobins. Military operations of the civil war; the siege of Paris by the Versailles army under Mac-Mahon; provincial risings and their failure. The Bloody Week; repression; legal and political aftermath. The chapter carries the narrative from the March rupture through the crushing of the Commune and the reassertion of national authority at Versailles.
Chapitre IV — Première Crise constitutionnelle
After peace and repression, the Assembly still has given no constitution. Struggle over the form of the state while Thiers governs under a provisional title. Parties and groups at Versailles; monarchical majority without a single candidate; republican minority growing with by-elections. The Rivet constitution (law of 31 August 1871): Thiers becomes President of the Republic, remaining responsible before the Assembly; provisional organisation of the public powers. First crisis over the extent of presidential authority and the Assembly’s constituent claim; Vitet’s report and the reluctance to silence “France’s incomparable orator” by message only.
Chapitre V — Le Traité de Francfort
From the preliminaries of Versailles to the definitive Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871). Territorial clauses (Alsace and part of Lorraine); the five-milliard indemnity and occupation schedule; commercial and transit stipulations. Thiers’s negotiation under the double pressure of a Paris still armed and already insurgent and of a country resolved on peace; debate whether Metz might have been saved and whether the London conference was neglected; Belfort retained for France and a milliard struck from the original demand. Ratification and the first organisation of payments and occupation zones.
Chapitre VI — Vers la libération
General balance of the war; the indemnity as Germanic wehrgeld on French savings and future. Thiers declines Bismarck’s introduction of German financiers (Bleichröder, Henckel) and stakes the payment on France itself. The loan of two milliards (law and issue of June 1871): perpetual rentes at 82 fr. 50; 381,906 subscribers; relations with the Bank of France and prior war borrowings. Pouyer-Quertier at Berlin; conventions of 12 October 1871; beginning of the evacuation of German troops. Discussion and vote of new taxes; elections to the general councils of 8 October 1871. Bismarck’s policy: rapprochement of Germany and Austria-Hungary; meetings of the two emperors at Ischl, Gastein, and Salzburg.
Chapitre VII — Le Travail parlementaire
Winter session of the National Assembly; Thiers’s message of 7 December 1871 (long, obscure, sparing the name Republic, upholding the Assembly’s sovereignty, offering to return the deposit intact). Parties and groups; Versailles as “Palais de la Pénitence”; the Orléans princes in the Chamber; Falloux and the flag question; fiscal debates. First resignation of Thiers (20 January 1872) after defeat on the raw-materials tax and the Féray–Lucien Brun resolution; emotion in all groups; Mac-Mahon joins the pressure to retain him; Batbie’s conciliation commission; Thiers withdraws the resignation. Parliamentary fusion manœuvres; Bonapartist propaganda; budget of 1872; Gambetta in the provinces, Thiers at Paris.
Chapitre VIII — L’Apogée
Session of 29 April–3 August 1872 as the apogee of Thiers’s government: fifteen months after Bordeaux, peace signed, Commune defeated, reconstruction under way. Interpellations; debate on the war contracts; inquiry on the capitulations; Marshal Bazaine sent before a court-martial. Negotiations for payment of the last three milliards; military law of 27 July 1872; convention of 29 June; budget of 1873 and new taxes; the three-milliard loan. Parliamentary situation: the centre left adheres to the Republic; attempt at a “conjunction of the centres”; Council of the Nine; the “bonnets à poil” demonstration. Vacations: Thiers at Trouville; Gambetta’s second oratorical campaign (La Ferté-sous-Jouarre; Savoie and Dauphiné; Grenoble, 26 September 1872 — the “new social stratum”; praise of Thiers at Annecy; clericalism named the remaining enemy). Alsace-Lorraine; expulsion of Prince Napoléon; Chambord and the Orléans princes; religious manifestations; elections of 20 October 1872.
Chapitre IX — La Libération du territoire
Germany after victory; Bismarck’s foreign policy and fear of French revanche (circular of Reims, instructions to Arnim); meeting of the three emperors; the Kulturkampf. Winter session; Thiers’s message of 13 November 1872 pronouncing for the Republic; protest of the right; commission of Fifteen demands ministerial responsibility; commission of Thirty; ministerial reshuffles; debate on dissolution; the government breaks with the left. Legislative work; goods of the Orléans family; death of Napoleon III; further fusion efforts; Chambord’s letter to Mgr Dupanloup (8 February 1873); the Roman question. Negotiation for anticipated evacuation: Gontaut-Biron, Saint-Vallier, Arnim, and Bismarck; the Belfort reserve and the substitution of Verdun; convention of liberation signed 15 March 1873; the Assembly declares that Thiers has deserved well of the country. Thiers yields ground to the commission of Thirty; the law of the Thirty; Thiers is edged from the tribune even as liberation is secured.
Chapitre X — Le 24 Mai
Party struggle at the height of exasperation. War-contracts commission as a combat weapon; attack on Challemel-Lacour over the Lyon markets (30 January 1873) and his three-hour defence. Municipal regime of Lyon; petition of Prince Napoléon after his expulsion; pact among the three monarchical parties. Resignation of Jules Grévy; Buffet president of the Assembly. Elections of 27 April 1873: Barodet elected at Paris; further elections of 11 May; resignations of Jules Simon and de Goulard. Conciliabules fix on Marshal Mac-Mahon as presidential candidate; Thiers reshuffles his ministry; interpellation of the right; Thiers deposits bills on the organisation of the public powers. Sitting of 23 May: duc de Broglie and Dufaure; sitting of 24 May: Thiers’s great speech (peace signed, Commune defeated, indemnity paid, evacuation decided; “I have taken my party on the Republic”); declaration of Casimir-Perier; the Target group. Thiers, put in minority, resigns. Mac-Mahon elected president (390 votes; the left abstains except Laurier for Grévy); he accepts after hesitation and a call on Thiers, with a soldier’s word to continue liberation and restore ordre moral. Conclusion: three years of French misfortune after a prosperous century; dismemberment, civil war, and the shift of European weight to a reconstituted Germany; yet the “imperishable France” of activity and radiance, the prompt recovery of the people, the dignity of the National Assembly, and Thiers’s triple task (peace, repair, durable political form) — with the judgment that the right toppled him before he could found the Republic, and that conservatives and republicans alike misread the act.
Errata
A short errata list closes the volume (raw text near the end of the file).
Series note
Tome I ends at 24 May 1873 (fall of Thiers; election of Mac-Mahon). Continuity — the two first Broglie ministries, ordre moral, the monarchical campaign and Chambord’s letter of 27 October, the Septennat, fall of Broglie (16 May 1874), and the recovery chapters — is the matter of Tome II (La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon — L’Échec de la Monarchie). The Constitution of 1875 through the letter of 16 May 1877 is Tome III; the parliamentary Republic through Gambetta’s death is Tome IV.

sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.title: Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome II (La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon — L'Échec de la Monarchie)
sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.content:
Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome II (La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon — L’Échec de la Monarchie)
Gabriel Hanotaux, Histoire de la France contemporaine (1871–1900), tome deuxième. Paris: Ancienne Librairie Furne, Combet & Cie, Éditeurs, 5, rue Palatine (VIᵉ); no imprint year on the scanned copy (Internet Archive metadata: n.d.; publisher field Paris, Combet); title page of this issue deuxième édition. On the Internet Archive as histoiredelafran02hanouoft (University of Ottawa / Robarts–University of Toronto copy; ABBYY FineReader OCR; 740 images). The half-title names the subject La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon with the band L’Échec de la Monarchie. Series framing (author’s Avertissement and IA description): I Le gouvernement de M. Thiers; II–III La présidence du maréchal de Mac Mahon (two volumes — this tome L’échec de la monarchie, the next La Constitution de 1875); IV La République parlementaire. This wiki holds Tome I, Tome II, Tome III, and Tome IV.
In the Avertissement Hanotaux explains that the presidency of Marshal Mac-Mahon required two volumes. The present tome contains the history of the two first ministries of the duc de Broglie (May 1873–May 1874) and the exposition of the double failure of the monarchical restoration attempts. The comte de Chambord is set aside after his letter of 27 October; the Septennat is organised as a provisional regime; soon afterward the National Assembly, by overthrowing Broglie at the moment when he lays a full constitutional system before it, ruins in advance the hopes of the Orléans family. “The monarchical past of France is liquidated. There is a clear place for the Republic.” Despite the Assembly’s initial dispositions, the Republic will be voted by a majority of one voice on 30 January (the matter of tome III). Chapters X–XIII form a second part: analysis of the country’s state of mind after the war and the Commune, material recovery, and intellectual activity — a retrospective national psychology spanning roughly 1871–1880. Tome III is reserved for the vote of the Constitution and the attempt of 16 May. Acknowledgments include Mme Taine (unpublished Taine correspondence), Haussonville, Costa de Beauregard, Vogüé, the duc de Magenta and the marquise de Mac Mahon (archives), vicomte Emmanuel d’Harcourt, general de Vaulgrenant, confidential material on Gambetta, and general Cuny on military questions. Printer at the close: Bordeaux — Impr. G. Gounouilhou, rue Guiraude, 9-11. Dominant years in the narrative half are 1873–1874; the recovery chapters dense through 1871–1880.
Avertissement
Two tomes needed for Mac-Mahon’s presidency; scope of the present volume (Broglie I–II, double monarchical failure, Septennat, fall of Broglie); monarchical past liquidated and place cleared for the Republic; chapters X–XIII as national psychology and material/intellectual recovery, c. 1871–1880; tome III promised for the Constitution and 16 May, completing a first whole — the history of the National Assembly and the establishment of the Third Republic; thanks for unpublished documents and interlocutors.
Chapitre premier — La politique du 24 Mai
Emotion of 24 May 1873 in Paris and the provinces as news of Thiers’s defeat, resignation, and Mac-Mahon’s election spreads from Versailles; foreign alarm calmed by the Marshal’s name. Portrait and military career of Mac-Mahon; the new president and politics; character. The cabinet of 25 May; presidential message; circular to diplomatic agents; the constitutional question; divine right and popular sovereignty. Portrait of the duc de Broglie — character and doctrines; parties in the Assembly; democratic ideas. Portrait of Léon Gambetta — origins and intellectual formation; under the Empire and during the war; deputy to the National Assembly; Gambetta the orator.
Chapitre II — L’« ordre moral »
Resumption of the National Assembly session after 24 May; Bismarck incident; the Pascal circular; Beulé; first acts of the cabinet; the formula of « ordre moral ». Interpellation Le Royer; the religious question; pilgrimages; the cult of the Sacré-Cœur; the votive church of Montmartre. Visit of the shah of Persia to Paris and the fêtes in his honour; first steps of the monarchical campaign; adjournment of examination of the constitutional laws. Measures against republican propaganda; special powers for the commission of permanence; Gambetta and the Grenoble speech; the centre left pronounces for dissolution. Summer reorganisation laws, including the general army law of 27 July 1873; prorogation from 29 July to 5 November; message of Mac-Mahon and manifesto of the Left groups. Liberation of the territory: last incidents of the German occupation; payment of the balance of the five-milliard indemnity; evacuation completed 16 September.
Chapitre III — La campagne monarchique
Hopes of the monarchical parties after 24 May; always the « fusion »; the comte de Paris at Frohsdorf; reconciliation of the two branches of the house of Bourbon; divergences between Orléanists and legitimists. The country and the monarchical campaign; meetings of the commission of permanence (25 August; 25 September); question of the duc d’Audiffret-Pasquier on the possibility of restoration; missions Merveilleux du Vignaux and de Sugny, then Combler, to Frohsdorf; note of Chambord to Ernoul and letter to de Rodez-Bénavent; decision for a meeting of the bureaux of the four Right groups on 4 October. Hanotaux frames the episode as a high cause ruined in verbal dissension — a tragicomedy of representative illusion disposing of France without consulting her.
Chapitre IV — L’entrevue de Salzbourg
Meeting of 4 October; constitution of the commission des Neuf; dinner of the quai d’Orsay; first session of the Nine; the army and the tricolour flag — « Les chassepots partiraient tout seuls »; Charles Chesnelong delegated by the Nine to the comte de Chambord. Parties and monarchical restoration; elections of 12 October; the Left organises resistance. Chesnelong at Salzburg: four interviews with Chambord; the verbal declarations of Salzburg on the constitution and the flag.
Chapitre V — La lettre du 27 octobre
Chesnelong’s return (16 October); meetings of the Nine and of the group bureaux; he reports and the campaign is to go forward; opinion. Government and restoration; preparations for the king’s return; incredulity of the country; the Lefts organise resistance; the army. Plenary meetings of the Right groups; procès-verbal of the centre droit; centre gauche refuses its concurrence; manifesto of the appel au peuple group; anxiety at Chambord’s prolonged silence; the letter of 27 October; whether Chambord meant to reign. Last meeting of the Nine; monarchical campaign abandoned; the council of ministers pronounces for prorogation of the Marshal’s powers; opinion and the parties. (The comte de Paris’s unpublished letter of 15 October already sketches the “line of retreat” toward the Marshal.)
Chapitre VI — Le Septennat
After the failure of parliamentary restoration, Chambord still contemplates a direct adventure; contact with the royalist chiefs in the Assembly is broken; they cling to prorogation prepared of long hand. Plenary meeting of the Right groups; attitude of the Orléans princes; the extreme right; prorogation to be proposed by the Rights. Resumption of the parliamentary session; Broglie proposes the septennat; presidential message; Changarnier proposition; Chambord at Versailles; Blacas with the Marshal — Mac-Mahon refuses to receive Chambord. Commission report on Changarnier; debate on prorogation; further presidential message; vote of the septennat (20 November 1873). Consequences; embarrassment of the extreme right; Chambord leaves Versailles. Hanotaux: the expectant policy once more profits the Republic.
Chapitre VII — Le deuxième cabinet de Broglie
What is the septennat? — “personal” or “impersonal”; Broglie’s circular of 25 November (firm, moderate policy; neither republic nor monarchy named). Interpellation on non-convocation of electoral colleges; pure-and-simple order of the day; resignation of the cabinet; duc Decazes; constitution of the second Broglie cabinet; its precarious situation; election of the commission des Trente. Budget of 1874; Magne’s financial system; new taxes. Trial and condemnation of Marshal Bazaine; character of the judgment; whether Bazaine “betrayed.”
Chapitre VIII — La paix armée et le kulturkampf international
Years 1873–1875 as liquidation and gestation: interior politics of the masses succeeding that of the classes; exterior politics of space soon to succeed that of nationalities. The new German Empire and Europe; Bismarck and French interior policy; the system of « paix armée »; the Kulturkampf and Germanic unity; the “white policy” and Germany. Guillaume at Saint-Petersburg; the Tsar at Vienna; Victor-Emmanuel at Vienna and Berlin; whether a quadruple entente; Germany and the monarchical campaign; Guillaume I at Vienna. Decazes at Foreign Affairs; Roman affairs and the international Kulturkampf; incident of the episcopal mandements; war fears; German military septennat; Reichstag elections in Alsace-Lorraine and protest against annexation. Fresh apprehensions from German armaments; Spanish affairs; the Austrian emperor at Saint-Petersburg; Europe and armed peace. Advent of the Disraeli cabinet; change in British policy; the Tsar’s European journey; Germany and the Eastern Question; Hohenlohe named ambassador at Paris; European situation in May 1874. First movements of “world policy”: Russia in Central Asia; Annam and Tonkin; China; Ashanti war; Great Britain and the Suez Canal; great international works.
Chapitre IX — La chute du duc de Broglie
Last struggle of royalty and the privileged classes as the old France expires; Broglie, after Chambord’s failure, tries to consolidate around the septennat a “government of the middle classes” and fails under a blow from the traditional monarchy’s faithful. Resumption of the session; the majority of 24 May disaggregates; law of the mayors and its application; the Marshal explains the duration of his powers; resistances; elections of 27 February and 1 March 1874; Bonapartist manifestations on the majority of the Prince Imperial. The republican party; Gambetta–Lepère interpellation; Challemel-Lacour; Broglie declares the septennat « incommutable »; rupture with the extreme right; Thiers; dissolution proposals; Easter recess; elections of 29 March 1874. Reorganisation laws; liquidation account; navigable ways; military administration; frontier problem — two fortified lines of defence in the East; fortifications of Paris. Summer session; Broglie’s constitutional projects — representation of “interests,” universal suffrage “expurgated,” organisation of legislative and executive power, municipal and political electorate bills, project of a second Chamber; fall of the duc de Broglie — causes and consequences (16 May 1874).
Chapitre X — Le relèvement, l’avènement de la Démocratie
Opening of the volume’s second part: the country “constitutes itself” while a neutral cabinet d’affaires holds office and the head of state has neutralised himself; the Republic will be founded by one vote in a hostile Assembly under national pressure (forward glance). Optimism of the French people after 1870; the soil of France; patriotism; national unity. Prosperous years — climate, production, harvests, industry, commerce, abundance, wages, public fortune; rapid material recovery. Population; classes of French society; bourgeoisie; the people; the « nouvelles couches »; advent of Democracy.
Chapitre XI — Les Lettres. — L’Opinion. — La Presse
Intellectual harvest after the war as a surprise to foreign opinion that had written France off. Surviving influences: Auguste Comte, Balzac, Victor Hugo, Michelet, George Sand. Realism; trouble and disenchantment after the war; Renan, Taine, Flaubert; the theatre — Dumas fils, Sardou, Bornier. The novel and naturalism — Zola, Daudet; the poets and the Parnasse contemporain — Leconte de Lisle, Sully Prudhomme, Coppée, Heredia. Literature of teaching and divulgation; foundation of the École des Sciences politiques; democratic literature; the livraison; periodicals and illustrated papers. Opinion and the press; newspaper regime; great political journals of the parties; popular press and the one-sou paper; the provincial press.
Chapitre XII — Les Arts. Les Sciences
Art as the most brilliant manifestation of humanity’s desire for survival and as first selection between the ephemeral and the durable. French art after the war; art of the cities; architecture, sculpture, painting. Music — influence of Wagner; the French school. Science — France’s scientific work; the high sciences and the principle of “Unity”; astronomy, mathematics, mechanics, physics, chemistry; organic chemistry (Berthelot); physiology (Claude Bernard); natural history; anthropology and palaeontology; the problem of life; Pasteur and microbiology; cosmic forces; Darwinism and evolutionism; medicine and hygiene.
Chapitre XIII — La crise morale
After material resources and intellectual production, the intimate holding of the social body in the crisis that purged the last consequences of the war. Moral law and society; the three risks — religious, economic, patriotic; authority and liberty; religion; interior and exterior crisis of Catholicism; Catholic France; symptoms of disaffection. Free thought; philosophical systems; philosophical opportunism; systems of morals. Economism; Saint-Simonism; the “orthodox school”; economic morals; inconveniences and benefits of economism. Morals without sanction; Descartes’s “generous man”; non-constraint; the religion of the fatherland; theory of Opportunism. Close: with Broglie gone and monarchical chances and middle-class influence spent, constitutional debates open that will lead by fatal and logical sequence to the vote of the Republic; the coming Constitution (Hanotaux here calls it of 1875/1876) as a work of equilibrium and transaction — Pascal: “La multitude qui ne se réduit à l’unité est confusion; l’unité qui ne dépend pas de la multitude est tyrannie.”
Errata
A short Errata du premier volume closes the book (corrections to tome I: Franck; Tachard; a date; Hugo title; Merveilleux du Vignaux; Janvier de la Motte). Printer line: Bordeaux — Impr. G. Gounouilhou.
Series note
Tome II ends with the fall of the first Broglie cabinet (16 May 1874) and the national-psychology second part that prepares the constitutional vote. Continuity — Cissey–Fourtou, the Constitution of 1875, Buffet, elections of 1876, Dufaure and Jules Simon, letter of 16 May 1877 — is the matter of Tome III (La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon — La Constitution de 1875). The government of Thiers through 24 May 1873 is Tome I; the parliamentary Republic from Seize Mai through Gambetta’s death is Tome IV.

sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.title: Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome III (La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon — La Constitution de 1875)
sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.content:
Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome III (La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon — La Constitution de 1875)
Gabriel Hanotaux, Histoire de la France contemporaine (1871–1900), tome troisième. Paris: Ancienne Librairie Furne, Société d’Édition Contemporaine, 5, rue Palatine (VIᵉ); no imprint year on the scanned copy (Internet Archive metadata: n.d.; publisher field also records Paris, Combet for this issue). On the Internet Archive as histoiredelafran03hanouoft (University of Ottawa / Robarts–University of Toronto copy; ABBYY FineReader OCR; 774 images). The half-title names the subject La Présidence du Maréchal de Mac Mahon with the band La Constitution de 1875. Series framing (IA description and peer volumes): I Le gouvernement de M. Thiers; II–III La présidence du maréchal de Mac Mahon (two volumes); IV La République parlementaire. This wiki holds Tome I, Tome II (L’Échec de la Monarchie), Tome III, and Tome IV.
The narrative runs from the ministerial crisis of May 1874 (fall of the first Broglie cabinet; Cissey–Fourtou) through the constitutional laws of February–July 1875, the Buffet ministry and the European “alerte” of 1875, the dissolution of the National Assembly, the senatorial and legislative elections of 1876, the first parliamentary cabinets under Mac-Mahon (Dufaure, then Jules Simon), and closes on the presidential letter of 16 May 1877. Dominant years in the text are 1874–1877.
Chapitre premier — L’Assemblée nationale et le Suffrage universel
Three years after Bordeaux: the National Assembly has made peace and repressed the insurrection, proclaimed itself constituent, yet still has given no constitution. The right is torn among the three monarchical parties; the Republic survives by their divisions. 24 May 1873 overthrows Thiers; a year later (16 May 1874) the duc de Broglie falls in turn. Failure of the Goulard combination; formation of the cabinet Cissey–Fourtou (12 May 1874); the Bonapartist peril and universal suffrage; the dissident centre droit. The Lefts accept constituent power; constitutional proposals including Casimir-Perier; municipal electoral law of 11 July 1874. The septennat bars the road to royalty; failure of the Cissey cabinet. Project of the commission des Trente; rejection of Casimir-Perier’s motion to establish the Republic; adjournment of the constitutional debate; maintenance of the state of siege; prorogation of the Assembly from 5 August to 30 November 1874. Thiers urges dissolution and appeal to the country; the right recoils from the suffrage and clings to the septennat as a term operation.
Chapitre II — Le Septennat, la France et l’Europe
Practical work of the Assembly beside the constitutional struggle: budget of 1875; resignations of Magne and de Fourtou; Mathieu-Bodet at Finance and baron de Chabaud-La Tour at the Interior; military laws; public works; the phylloxera; social questions and the parliamentary inquiry on labour; the Roussel law on protection of infants; reform of the baccalauréat. Foreign policy under German diplomacy in 1874: the Kissingen attentat and the ultramontane question; cardinal Guibert’s mandement; recall of the Orénoque; Spanish affairs and fear of German intervention; Alphonsist restoration; rivalry of Gortschakoff and Bismarck; Eastern affairs and first lineaments of a Franco-Russian understanding; British dispositions; the Suez Canal and Egypt; the Tonkin affair; the United States and international arbitration; the Brussels conference and the law of nations; international sanitary police — the policy imposed on France. Society in 1874; the Marshal’s journeys; complementary legislative and local elections; presidential message on the Assembly’s return; higher-education law in first reading; parliamentary inquiry ordered on Bonapartist manœuvres.
Chapitre III — La République fondée
The decisive session of January 1875. Initiative of the commission des Trente; conferences at the Élysée; presidential message of 5 January 1875; the government asks priority for the Senate law and is refused; ministerial resignation, then provisional maintenance. First reading of the law on the organization of the public powers; first deliberation on creation of a Senate. Second deliberation: the three sittings of 28–30 January; solemn debate on article 1; Laboulaye amendment developed and rejected after Louis Blanc’s intervention; Wallon amendment; negotiations of the Lavergne group; royalist sentiments; Desjardins sub-amendment rejected; the Wallon amendment carried by one vote and its consequences. Continuation: dissolution of the Chamber and revision of the constitutional laws; seat of the public powers remains at Versailles; second deliberation of the Senate law; Pascal Duprat amendment; declarations of the Trente and the government; dissolution projects; extreme confusion. The right offers dictatorship to the Marshal; Broglie refuses to form a ministry; the right against Buffet; the Lavergne group mediates between centre gauche and centre droit; the Marshal abandons nomination of the irremovables; agreement concluded; vote of the Senate law and of the law on the public powers.
Chapitre IV — Le Cabinet Buffet et l’Alerte de 1875
Epilogue of 25 February: Bonapartism on the bench after the constitutional votes. Parliamentary inquiry on the Bonapartists; partial elections; retirement of the de Cissey cabinet; formation of the Buffet ministry; duc d’Audiffret-Pasquier president of the Assembly; Buffet’s uncertain policy; adjournment 20 March–11 May; Gambetta’s speech at Ménilmontant. The alerte of 1875: continuation of the Kulturkampf; German press campaign against France; war fears; duc Decazes appeals to the powers; Gontaut-Biron and Radowitz; Decazes’s attempt to rally Europe; Schouwaloff’s démarche at Berlin; Hohenlohe with Decazes; a Times article; intervention of England, Austria, and Italy; change of front in Germany; the Tsar at Berlin; Russian circular — peace assured; what to conclude from the incident. Resumption of the Assembly session: suppression of partial elections; complementary constitutional projects; new commission des Trente; law on higher education; election of the Nièvre and the comité de l’appel au peuple; Buffet and the Left; vote of the organic law on the relations of the public powers and of the senatorial electoral law; budget of 1876; adjournment 4 August–4 November 1875.
Chapitre V — Théorie de la Constitution
General character of the Constitution of 1875; state of mind of the constituents; analogies with the American constitution. Precedents: French constitutions since the Revolution; the republican aspiration; precursors (Montesquieu, Rousseau, Condorcet); revolutionary experiments, direct government, power of committees, imperial dictatorship, return toward legitimacy; popular sovereignty imposed on the Restoration; electoral census and the directing classes; antinomies of 1848; advent of democratic Caesarism; the “liberal Empire”; the nineteenth-century constitutional circuit; democracy and the Republic. Doctrines: Auguste Comte, Proudhon, Tocqueville, the elder duc de Broglie, Prévost-Paradol; theorists of parliamentarism; influence of political literature on the National Assembly; “decentralization.” Theory of the constitution: sovereignty of the people; law of majorities; universal suffrage; rights of minorities; national unity; conciliation of unity and liberty; hatred of personal power; representative regime; the parliamentary Republic; two Chambers with preponderance of the popular Chamber; the presidency; the cabinet; government in office; the reign of opinion; the Constitution of 1875 before the history of France; merits and defects. Hanotaux stresses the anonymous, improvised character of the work — three constitutional laws (Senate 24 February; public powers 25 February; relations of the powers 16 July) and two organic laws (senatorial elections 2 August; deputies 30 November) — viable despite the disdain of many of its authors.
Chapitre VI — L’Agonie de l’Assemblée
With the constitution voted, the Assembly has only to yield its place. Vacations of August–November 1875; Buffet affirms a conservative policy; ministerial dissensions; Bardoux and Léon Say incidents; instructions of the comte de Chambord; Rouher’s speech; Thiers at Arcachon; Gambetta’s letter to the Lyon democracy. Last session: legislative electoral law; scrutin de liste versus scrutin d’arrondissement; Gambetta breaks with the centre droit; the Assembly chooses scrutin d’arrondissement; Buffet reconstitutes the majority of 24 May; vote of the law of 30 November 1875 and the electoral circumscriptions. Election of the 75 irremovable senators: first ballot neutralizes Lefts and right; pact among extreme right, Bonapartists, and Left; the seventy-five. Agony of the Assembly: commission of graces; amnesty proposal; state of siege and the press regime; parties take position for the legislative and senatorial elections; last days; dissolution; Hanotaux’s judgment on the National Assembly.
Chapitre VII — Le Pays et les Élections de 1876
The French people may at last, in calm and under constitutional rules, make its will known. Dispositions of universal suffrage; the nation and the parties; electoral organization; the ministry and the elections; the Marshal’s proclamation. Senatorial elections and composition of the Senate. Legislative elections: candidates and programmes; Gambetta leads the campaign — speeches at Lille, Bordeaux, and Paris; the poll of 20 February 1876 favourable to the Republic. Buffet leaves power; Dufaure charged with the interim presidency of the council; Gambetta’s “discours-ministre” at Lyon; ballottages; composition of the Chamber of Deputies; ceremony of the transmission of powers; first sittings of Chamber and Senate.
Chapitre VIII — Le premier cabinet Dufaure
From March 1876 France inaugurates the parliamentary regime: two Chambers coexist; the executive has constitutional authority. Both sit at Versailles — the Senate the National Assembly prolonged, the Chamber largely new men impatient of the royal town. Portrait of Dufaure (born 1798): character, situation, redingote and Gallican eloquence of 1830; formation of the cabinet; ministerial declaration; divisions in the majority; verification of powers; extreme Left demands amnesty; Gambetta elected president of the finance commission; Universal Exposition decreed for 1878; first republican laws. Administrative movement; death of Ricard, replaced at the Interior by de Marcère; amnesty debate; complementary elections; in the Senate, scope of the right of revision; Chamber modifies the higher-education law as to the collation of degrees; Buffet elected irremovable senator. Party excitement; mayors’ law voted in the Chamber; disagreement between Jules Ferry and Gambetta; Senate rejects the collation-of-degrees bill; conflict of the two Chambers; budget of 1877; resignation of general de Cissey, replaced at War by general Berthaut; close of the ordinary session. Vacations: partial elections; the Marshal at army manœuvres; Vatican incident; France and Italy; political speeches; Paris workers’ congress; extraordinary session of 1876; cessation of Commune prosecutions; tax reform; budget; Chesnelong irremovable senator; Senate rejects the Commune-prosecutions bill; fall of the Dufaure ministry.
Chapitre IX — Le Cabinet Jules Simon et le 16 Mai
Dufaure’s resignation letter (2 December 1876): caught between Chamber and Senate, he can no longer govern; the presidency as instituted by the law of 20 November does not fit the parliamentary regime. Last efforts toward conjunction of the centres; ministerial crisis; permanence of the Chamber; constitution of the Jules Simon ministry; Simon and the Chambers; reserved welcome of the Left; Simon and Gambetta; financial rights of the Senate; vote of the budget of 1877. First acts; administrative personnel; return of the Chambers; passing calm; politics of the centre gauche; Gambetta re-elected president of the budget commission; tactics of the extreme Left; Simon’s difficult position, embarrassed by his past; ministerial incidents; the republican programme. The religious question: Pius IX and Jules Simon; Easter recess. Interpellation on ultramontane manœuvres; speeches of Jules Simon and Gambetta — « Le cléricalisme, voilà l’ennemi ! ». The Marshal decides to break with the Left majority; municipal organization law and press law; the letter of 16 May; resignation of the ministry; “the politics of the president.” Hanotaux treats 16 May as a foreseen, deliberated act of authority — constitutional corollary of the septennat compromise rather than a mere boutade — yet imprudent and bound to fail against the national movement that had already imposed itself on the National Assembly; the letter poses the problem for the nation to resolve.
Series note
Tome III ends at the act of 16 May 1877. Continuity of the crisis — Broglie and Rochebouët cabinets, the elections of 14 October 1877, the second Dufaure ministry, Eastern Question and Congress of Berlin, Mac-Mahon’s resignation and Grévy’s presidency — is the matter of Tome IV (La République Parlementaire). The government of Thiers through 24 May 1873 is Tome I; early Mac-Mahon, the monarchical failure, and the fall of Broglie (16 May 1874) are Tome II (L’Échec de la Monarchie).

sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.title: Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome IV (La République Parlementaire)
sources/hanotaux-histoire-france-contemp.content:
Hanotaux — Histoire de la France contemporaine, Tome IV (La République Parlementaire)
Gabriel Hanotaux, Histoire de la France contemporaine (1871–1900), tome quatrième. Paris: Ancienne Librairie Furne, Société d’Édition Contemporaine, 5, rue Palatine (VIᵉ), 1903. On the Internet Archive as histoiredelafran04hano (University of Ottawa copy; ABBYY FineReader OCR). The half-title names the subject La République Parlementaire. The series leaf (as cited in the Avertissement and front matter of peer volumes) frames the four tomes as: I Thiers; II Mac-Mahon and the failure of the monarchy; III Mac-Mahon and the Constitution of 1875; IV the parliamentary Republic. This wiki also holds Tome I (Le Gouvernement de M. Thiers), Tome II (L’Échec de la Monarchie), and Tome III (La Constitution de 1875), which ends at the letter of 16 May 1877; the present volume continues from that crisis.
In the Avertissement Hanotaux presents tome IV as completing the history of the Third Republic at the time of its birth and first growth — the age of uncertainties and struggles devoted to founding a new constitutional regime and to the recovery of the country. From 1883 a more stable political period (more troubled in the moral order) will test the new institutions; he suspends the narrative at the death of Gambetta, which he treats as a brutal conclusion after which figures and the aspect of things change. Dominant years in the text are 1877–1878, with dense continuation through 1879–1882.
Avertissement
The volume closes the twelve-year “heroic age” of the Republic’s foundation. Hanotaux, writing too hastily by his own admission, records insufficiency of information, disproportion of parts, and stylistic failings, yet affirms renewed love of country and impatience, after having had to recount Bismarck’s successes, to return to France’s Richelieu. He suspends further narrative until more distance and impassibility are possible.
Chapitre premier — Le Seize Mai
Emotion provoked by Mac-Mahon’s act of 16 May 1877; plenary meeting of the Lefts; interpellation in the Chamber and Gambetta’s speech; constitution of the cabinet Broglie; presidential message and adjournment of the Chambers; manifesto of the Lefts; opinion; attitude of legitimists and Bonapartists; the government’s thesis. During the recess: ministerial circulars and administrative movements; the Marshal at Compiègne; Thiers’s role; Gambetta’s provincial speeches; the Left’s resolve to refuse the budget. Resumption of the session: second presidential message; the Marshal asks the Senate for dissolution of the Chamber; government declaration and interpellation; Fourtou; “the liberator of the territory”; union of republicans; the 363; Senate vote of dissolution; preparation of the elections.
Chapitre II — La Question d’Orient
The Seize Mai crisis is set inside European liquidation after German hegemony. New European politics; France’s importance in the European system; consequences of German hegemony; Russia’s role and the Russo-German contest over the East; Russia appeals for French concurrence; the struggle framed as Slavism versus Germanism; England intervenes as third party; tactics of Bismarck and Gortschakoff; the Pesth programme of the Three Emperors. Origins of the Eastern Question: Turkish and Christian “reform,” the Russian crusade, traditional policies of the powers, Crimean War, Treaty of Paris, Hatti-Humayoun of 1856, situation on the eve of 1870. The two chancellors; Russia opens the crisis; English attitude. Recrudescence of disorders; Turkish armaments; Berlin memorandum (England alone refuses adhesion); interview of Ems; French efforts at conciliation; Reichstadt convention; Serbia and Montenegro against Turkey; Serbian defeat; Bulgarian atrocities; English opinion and Disraeli; accession of Abdul-Hamid; Bismarck for Austria and for opposing England to Russia; Russia not ready; Constantinople conference; European ultimatum rejected by Turkey; powers “playing close”; London protocol; agreement impossible and war inevitable.
Chapitre III — Les Élections du 14 octobre 1877
Electoral campaign and official candidature; the Marshal pushed forward; republican party and union of the 363; Gambetta’s “submit or resign”; prosecution of Gambetta; quarrels among conservatives; delayed elections. The clerical question: Vatican and Seize Mai; jubilee of 1877; Crispi in France and Germany; German threats; the Left denounces the peril. Death of Thiers; Jules Grévy as chief of the republican party; the Marshal’s journey to Bordeaux and the West; manifesto of 19 September; governmental optimism. Elections of 14 October: government beaten; composition of the new Chamber; ministry remains; departmental elections and a further republican victory; uncertainties; return of parliament; parliamentary inquiry on Seize Mai; fall of the Broglie ministry. Cabinet Rochebouët; Chamber refuses the budget; Dufaure called to the Élysée, the Marshal refuses his conditions; Batbie charged to form a ministry of resistance; general excitement; Labordère incident; Batbie fails; the Marshal calls Dufaure.
Chapitre IV — Le second cabinet Dufaure et le « parti libéral »
Constitution of the second Dufaure cabinet; presidential message; changes in administrative personnel; municipal elections; ordinary session of 1878; great public works; the 3% amortizable loan; economic regime. Parliamentary work; senatorial majority; budget of 1878; liquidation of Seize Mai. Deaths of Victor-Emmanuel and Pius IX; projected interview of Bismarck and Gambetta; Gambetta’s journey to Rome; election of Leo XIII. Continuation of the 1878 session; diverse laws and proposals; the Universal Exposition.
Chapitre V — La Guerre russo-turque et le Congrès de Berlin
Russia decides on war; her interior and exterior position; Turkey’s defensive strength; the powers before the war; Anglo-Russian arrangement; Balkan populations; Romania concedes passage to Russian troops; France’s role; Austro-German entente. The war: Gourko’s raid; Russian checks and Plevna; European impression; Romania enters the campaign; fall of Plevna and taking of Kars; Russians at Adrianople; English veto; armistice; Russians at San Stefano; Bismarck’s intervention — Germany as “honest broker”; Treaty of San Stefano; Schouwaloff–Salisbury convention; programme of the congress; European missions; France accepts the invitation with reserves. The congress: Bismarck’s tactics; revival of Anglo-Russian disagreement; work of the congress in Europe and Asia; Germanic expansion in the Balkans; satisfactions distributed among the great powers; Cyprus convention and the Egyptian question; Tunisia offered to France; birth of world policy.
Chapitre VI — Démission du maréchal de Mac Mahon. — La présidence de M. Jules Grévy
(Body OCR omits the “CHAPITRE VI” heading; the chapter opens on the titled band Démission du maréchal de Mac Mahon / La présidence de M. Jules Grévy.) Socialism and beginnings of collectivism; Christian socialism; Catholic workers’ circles. Vacations of 1878; the ministry and the “old republicans”; Gambetta’s oratorical campaign in the Dauphiné; extraordinary session; invalidations; budget of 1879. Senatorial elections of January 1879 and republican success; Senart interpellation; cabinet victorious but captive; Gambetta’s difficult situation; resignation of Marshal Mac-Mahon; Jules Grévy elected President of the Republic. Portrait of Grévy: origins; 1848; Grévy and Lamartine; presidency of the National Assembly; Grévy and Gambetta; the ideal of France and what the presidency ought to be; Hanotaux’s judgment that Grévy’s election was a fault.
Chapitre VII — Le cabinet Waddington-Ferry. — L’article 7. — La Triple alliance
Grévy at the Élysée; formation of the Waddington cabinet; Gambetta president of the Chamber; vote of amnesty; beginnings of school reform; Lepère at the Interior; vote of stigma against Seize Mai. “Purification” of administrative personnel; resumption of the session; Senate votes the return of the Chambers to Paris; death of the Prince Imperial; law on higher education; law on normal schools; first 14 July festival; budget of 1880; execution of the Freycinet plan. Aftermath of Berlin: Bulgaria, Greece, Egypt; genesis of the Triple Alliance; interview of Alexandrovo and meeting at Gastein; Austro-German alliance treaty; Leo XIII and Bismarck. Leo XIII and the French bishops; Mgr Czacki nuncio at Paris; the republican party and religious policy; Jules Simon and article 7; general political situation; fall of the Waddington cabinet.
Chapitre VIII — Le premier ministère Freycinet. — Les décrets
Formation of the Freycinet ministry and its position before the Chambers; integral amnesty rejected; article 7 rejected in the Senate; promulgation of the law on higher education. The decrees of 29–30 March 1880; summer session; Constans at the Interior; French tariff policy; Léon Say’s mission to London. Difficult position of the cabinet; Senate debate on the decrees; expulsion of the Jesuits; Gambetta against the ministry; vote of the amnesty law; parliamentary work; Cherbourg festivals; resignation of Freycinet.
Chapitre IX — Le premier ministère Jules Ferry. — Les lois scolaires. — La campagne de Tunisie
Jules Ferry ministry; execution of the decrees; interpellations; discussion of the magistracy law; foreign policy. School reform and character of the Ferry laws: free primary education; obligation and laicity; the Republic’s school work and its results; right of increase; anticlericalism. The Gambetta question; Berlin conference; Greek frontiers and Dulcigno; “Gambetta means war”; the Tunisian affair; the Kroumirs; Tunisia and the powers; the expedition; Treaty of Bardo. Parties on the eve of general elections; constitutional revision and scrutin de liste; Gambetta’s journey to Cahors; Senate rejection of scrutin de liste; end of the legislature. Second Tunisian campaign; troubles in the Sud-Oranais; taking of Sfax and Gabès; electoral period; Gambetta at Belleville; results of the poll; pacification of Tunisia and occupation of Kairouan.
Chapitre X — Le Ministère Gambetta
Return of the Chambers; interpellations on the Tunisian affair; formation of the Gambetta ministry; difficult beginnings; Weiss and Miribel; Gambetta takes contact with the new Chamber. Exterior situation: Triple Alliance; Egyptian affairs; revolt of Arabi Pasha and the Anglo-French condominium; Gambetta and England. Ministerial activity and reform projects; state of opinion; triennial renewal of the Senate; project of constitutional revision and scrutin de liste; debate; government beaten; resignation of the Gambetta cabinet; second Freycinet ministry.
Conclusion
Failure of the Gambetta cabinet cuts the wings of hope and disconcerts the logic of events. Bombardment of Alexandria and end of the condominium; fall of the Freycinet cabinet; Duclerc cabinet; last projects and death of Gambetta; the democratic and social Republic. Hanotaux closes the first period of the Third Republic — the “heroic age” Gambetta himself named — spanning the fall of the Second Empire, the German war, the Commune, the failure of Bourbon royalty, the Constitution of 1875, Seize Mai, and the foundation of the parliamentary Republic.
Errata
A short Errata du quatrième volume corrects minor misprints (pages 173, 198, 368, 370).

sources/kornilov-kurs-istorii-rossii-ch3.title: Kornilov — Course of Russian History in the 19th Century, Part 3
sources/kornilov-kurs-istorii-rossii-ch3.content:
Kornilov — Course of Russian History in the 19th Century, Part 3
A. A. Kornilov (1862–1925) — Курс истории России XIX века. Часть III. — Second edition. — Moscow: M. and S. Sabashnikov Publishers, 1918.
The course is based on lectures given by the author in 1910–1912 at the Higher Women’s Courses, the Shanyavsky People’s University, and the Moscow Commercial Institute. The first edition of Part III appeared around 1914 (preface — Petersburg, 2 April 1914); this second edition — Moscow, 1918. Parts I and II of the same course (2nd ed., 1918) are in the Rest of Europe 1800–1865 wiki.
Contents of Part III. In the preface the author recalls that Part III was originally meant to cover “the internal history of Russia over the last 35 years of the 19th century.” The abundance of material and the “decisive turn in the mood of society” after the famine of 1891–92 led him to set aside the last eight years of the 19th century together with the first years of the 20th as a separate period — “a direct prelude to the great events of 1904–1906” — which might have become a fourth part of the course; in 1914 he expressed no confidence that such a fourth part would be written. The published Part III treats the reactionary period of recent internal history that began in 1866 and, with a brief clearing in 1880–1881, ran to the famine of 1891–92 — from the Karakozov attempt through the end of Alexander II’s reign and the whole reign of Alexander III. This epoch, the author notes, had until then received little systematic study.
Character of the course. Kornilov belongs to the liberal-populist school of Russian historiography. The course is attentive to socio-economic processes, the peasant question, the zemstvo, education, populism, and the revolutionary movement; the exposition is lecture-style, with discussion of sources and literature. Pre-reform orthography. OCR quality — medium, with artifacts (Ѣ/Е, І/И confusion, garbled Roman lecture numerals, etc.).
Raw volume: ~1.28 MB, 17,879 lines. Lectures XXVII–XLI (15 lectures) plus extensive bibliographic lists for the reigns of Alexander II and Alexander III and statistical appendices (population density, distribution of landownership).

Part III — Lectures XXVII–XLI
Lecture XXVII. The Karakozov attempt and the onset of reaction
The attempt of 4 April 1866. The reaction that followed; wherein it consisted. Development of Russian internal life after the reforms of the 1860s despite reaction. Continuation of some transformations. Completion of the peasant reform by extending it to appanage and state peasants. Overall picture of landownership of various groups of the population after the reforms of 1861, 1863, and 1866. Degree of land allotment security for peasants of different categories.
Lecture XXVIII. Immediate results of the peasant reform
Population growth in Russia before and after the reform. Critique of views in the literature on this subject. Settlement of the population before and after the reform. Growth of the urban population. Economic condition of Russia after the reform era. The industrial crisis and its causes.
Lecture XXIX. The financial position in the reform era and subsequent years
Tasks of financial policy under M. Kh. Reutern. Reutern’s activity. Drive to raise the country’s general productivity and especially export trade. The railway-building question; course of the matter to the mid-1870s. Concern for organizing commercial credit. Opening of private banks. Struggle with deficits in the state budget. The question of continuing internal reforms and Reutern’s report.
Lecture XXX. The Municipal Statute of 1870 and Miliutin’s military reforms
Drafting of the new municipal statute. Former urban arrangements in law and in practice. Work of the 1840s. Course of work on the statute of 1870; content and criticism. The question of army reorganization. Reforms of D. A. Miliutin. Abolition of recruitment and the statute on universal military service of 1874. Cultural and educational significance of the transformations in the War Ministry.
Lecture XXXI. The Ministry of Public Instruction after 1866
Count D. A. Tolstoy and D. A. Miliutin as exponents of two opposite sides of Alexander II’s reign. Tolstoy’s views. Tolstoy and Katkov. The question of secondary-school reform. The struggle for the introduction of classicism. Essence and significance of the reform of 1871. Tolstoy’s plans regarding the universities and the measures he took. Development of women’s education in 1866–1878. Elementary education. Statutes of 1864 and 1874. The ministry’s struggle with the zemstvo. History of the zemstvo school in 1866–1880.
Lecture XXXII. Zemstvo institutions, 1866–1878
Development of zemstvo institutions. Sphere of zemstvo activity; tasks and means. Zemstvo dues and obligations in the pre-reform period. Zemstvo budgets. Drive to tax trade and industry and collision with the government. Zemstvo expenditures and their growth. Class interests in the zemstvos. The question of natural obligations and the assessment of zemstvo dues. The tax-reform question and zemstvo projects. Government struggle with the zemstvo and restriction of its activity.
Lecture XXXIII. Judicial institutions and the press after 1866
Opening of the new judicial institutions and their first steps. Valuev’s struggle against them. Reactionary activity of Count Pahlen. Beginning of the position of the judicial statutes. Position and direction of the procuracy. Special procedure for initiating and deciding cases of state crimes. Change in the position of the bar and the question of removing various cases from jury competence. Position of the press in the post-reform period. Principal press organs and literary currents after 1866. Mood of society.
Lecture XXXIV. The popular masses and agriculture in the 1860s–1870s
Course of the redemption operation. Pauper allotments. Cut-offs (otrezki). Leases in northern and southern provinces. Rise in lease prices. Landowners’ indebtedness. Intensified ploughing up of land in view of grain export and rising grain prices. Livestock numbers among landowners and peasants. Scale of landowners’ ploughland. Conclusions on landowners’ economy in the north and south. Sale of lands; purchasers. Expansion of peasant economy at the expense of landowners’. Condition of peasant economy: insufficiency of allotments, burden of taxes and payments, inequality of assessment. Famine of 1868. Zemstvo investigations. Arrears. Peasant economy in the black-earth provinces. The Samara famine of 1872–1873. Food loans. Conclusions of Yanson and Prince Vasilchikov on the condition of peasant economy in the 1870s.
Lecture XXXV. Government, society, and the populist movement
Attitude of government and society to the condition of the popular masses. The populist current in literature. Student disturbances of 1869. Nechaev and Nechaevism. The Chaikovtsy in Petersburg; their ideas and plans. Bakunin and Lavrov abroad. Lavrists and Bakuninists. Vpered. Beginning of “going to the people.” Arrests. Pahlen’s memorandum. The society Zemlya i Volya. Development of populist ideas in legal literature.
Lecture XXXVI. The borderlands, the Eastern Question, and the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878
Government policy in the borderlands. Pressures in Little Russia and Poland. Foreign policy. The Eastern Question. Rivalry of Russian and English interests in Asia. Conquest of the Caucasus and the Central Asian khanates. Troubles in Turkey. Movement of the Balkan Slavs. The Serbian war and the Bulgarian massacres. Negotiations of the great powers. Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878: course and outcome. The Berlin Congress. Economic and financial results of the war. Reutern’s resignation. Impression of the war and congress on Russian society. Slavophiles. The zemstvo movement. The revolutionary movement. Government appeal to society. Zemstvo addresses. Formation of the party Narodnaya Volya.
Lecture XXXVII. Attempts on Alexander II, Loris-Melikov, and 1 March 1881
Organization by revolutionaries of a series of attempts on the life of Emperor Alexander II. Confusion and vacillation in the highest circles. Explosion in the Winter Palace and establishment of the Supreme Administrative Commission headed by Loris-Melikov. Loris-Melikov’s programme and its realization. Attitude of liberals and revolutionaries toward him. Tolstoy’s resignation. Loris-Melikov’s reforms. Senatorial inspections and the peasant question. The constitutional movement. Loris-Melikov’s report on establishing a special preparatory commission. The catastrophe of 1 March 1881.
Further in the volume — list of works and printed materials relating to the history of Russia in the reign of Alexander II.
Lecture XXXVIII. Emperor Alexander III — first steps
His upbringing. Attitude of society toward him before accession. His real views. First steps. Struggle of two tendencies in the highest governing circles. Conference of 8 March 1881. Vacillations. Katkov and Aksakov. Pobedonostsev’s agitation. Manifesto of 29 April 1881. Resignation of Loris-Melikov and some other ministers. Ministry of N. P. Ignatiev. His programme. Measures to improve the economic condition of the people. Compulsory redemption. Noble agitation. “Knowledgeable people.” Reduction of redemption payments. Bunge’s policy. Abolition of the poll tax. Introduction of an income tax (question and measures).
Lecture XXXIX. Peasant policy at the beginning of Alexander III’s reign
Measures to ease peasant land shortage. The Peasants’ Bank and its first steps under Bunge. Facilitation of lease of state lands to peasants. Ordering of peasant resettlement. Rules of 1881. Law of 13 July 1889. Introduction of factory inspection and the law on protection of minors and women in factories. Taxes on inheritances and on interest-bearing securities. The question of administrative peasant reform. The Kokhanov commission: participants and liquidation of its work. Collapse of the Ignatiev regime.
Lecture XL. Decisive turn toward reaction
Role of Pobedonostsev. Count D. A. Tolstoy. Reaction in the Ministry of Public Instruction. Noble reactionary policy in internal affairs. Jubilee of the Charter to the Nobility in 1885 and the noble reactionary movement connected with it. Pazukhin’s programme. Liquidation of the question of reforming peasant institutions after the closure of the Kokhanov commission. Law of 12 July 1889 on land captains (zemskie nachalniki). Statute on zemstvo institutions of 12 June 1890. Judicial novellas. New press law of 1882 and the position of the press. Persecution of non-Orthodox and non-Russians. The Jewish question. New arrangements in the army.
Lecture XLI. Finances of the second half of Alexander III’s reign and foreign policy
Financial policy. I. A. Vyshnegradsky and his system. Extreme development of protectionism in tariff policy and in railway tariff legislation. Results of this system. Foreign policy of Alexander III. Conquest of Turkmenia. Russo-English relations in Central Asia. Balkan affairs. Bulgarian complications. The Franco-Russian alliance and its significance. The Siberian railway and the beginning of a new policy in the Far East.
Further in the volume — list of works and printed materials relating to the history of Russia in the reign of Alexander III; table of contents; statistical appendices (population density by province; distribution of landownership by category of owners).

Sources

Kornilov, A. A. Курс истории России XIX века. Part III. Second edition. Moscow: M. and S. Sabashnikov Publishers, 1918.
