sources/lagardelle-socialisme-ouvrier-19.title: Lagardelle — Le socialisme ouvrier
sources/lagardelle-socialisme-ouvrier-19.content:
Lagardelle — Le socialisme ouvrier
Hubert Lagardelle (1875–1958), Le socialisme ouvrier. Paris: V. Giard & E. Brière, libraires-éditeurs, 16 rue Soufflot et 12 rue Toullier, 1911. Volume IX of the Collection des Doctrines politiques published under the direction of A. Mater (in-18, 4 fr. 50). The raw text in this wiki was taken from the Ohio State University scan (call no. HX266 L17) via Anna’s Archive; the scan carries a text layer of 464 page-files, here reassembled in numerical order. Lagardelle, the theorist of revolutionary syndicalism and collaborator of the Mouvement socialiste, warns in his Préface that this is not a literary work: the volume brings together fragments written “au jour le jour, sous le coup des événements,” following in anxiety the transformations of contemporary socialism. Many parts have aged; his conceptions modified themselves as they underwent the test of life. He means only to mark the stages of a thought.
Dominant years in the text are 1898–1908 (the book published 1911).
Préface
Lagardelle does not conceal the faults of the book: any gathering of articles presents discontinuities, repetitions, disproportions that make reading difficult. But he has not wished to make a literary work; he has simply meant to mark the stages of a thought that followed, in anxiety, the transformations of contemporary socialism. The volume has a graver vice: its fragments were written day by day, under the pressure of events; many parts have grown old, others remain uncertain; there are affirmations he would no longer present today in that absolute manner which circumstances sometimes demand but which always betrays the relative and changing reality. His conceptions modified themselves as they underwent the test of life. He feels the imprudence of gathering old pages whose tone and form hold only for the moment in which they were written.
Première partie — Le socialisme et la démocratie
I — Socialisme ou Démocratie ? (1902)
Socialism plays a decisive part. Will it be absorbed by democracy, or, while using democracy for its ends, will it remain itself? The sections trace: the democratic confusion; the programme of the Congress of Tours (1902); the conditions of a minimum programme; the characters of the Tours programme; its declaration of principles; democracy and class struggle; and democratic politics and economic organisation.
II — La démocratie sociale et le Parti socialiste
Millerand and social democracy — his Plateforme électorale, February 1898. The Dreyfus affair, the amnesty, and the socialists; the Radical-Socialists and the programme; the work of Waldeck-Rousseau — the ministry of Waldeck-Rousseau-Millerand-Galliffet; ministerialism and socialism; the school and the proletariat; from individualist democracy to social democracy; and social democracy and social Catholicism (Saint-Mandé, the “paix sociale,” Dreyfusism in power, triumphant democracy).
III — La fonction du Parti socialiste
Action of the party and action of the class; corporatism, syndicalism, politics; socialist unity; electoral revolutionaryism; eclectic socialism.
Deuxième partie — Syndicalisme et socialisme
I — La formation du syndicalisme
The syndical congress of Bourges (1904), November 1904 — the congresses of Amsterdam and Bourges of 1904 have, for the social observer, an unequal import; the evolution of the collective consciousness of social groups, which are a formation of history, offers an interest of another kind. The later sections treat the formation of syndicalism more broadly.
II — Les idées syndicalistes
“Révisionnisme de gauche” (November 1904): there is unanimous agreement that the socialist crisis is due to the divorce of theory and practice. The sections follow on the ideas of syndicalism — anti-statism, revolutionary evolution, the syndicate and the class struggle, direct action, the general strike, the socialist party and the public services.
III — La politique socialiste et le syndicalisme
The general policy of the socialist party — an intervention at the socialist Congress held at Toulouse, 15–20 October 1908, from the stenographic report. The syndicalist experience; the syndicate and the class struggle; direct action; the general strike; the socialist party and the public services. Then the syndicalist policy and the peasants — industrial and agricultural milieux, the small rural proprietors, and the policy of socialism toward the peasants. The closing argument addresses the agrarian question: let the socialist party present itself before the non-working popular masses with a programme of reduction of the State and of financial morality, and it will penetrate the rural milieux; if instead it comes with dogmatic programmes and abstract formulas, it will not touch them; if it offers them a conservative programme, it will not seize them either. Carried by the idealism that issues from the syndicalist working masses, it must appear as the only party of political cleanliness and of anti-statist action, making its own the essential claims and fundamental ideas of syndicalism.

sources/lenz-geschichte-bismarcks-1902.title: Max Lenz — Geschichte Bismarcks (1902)
sources/lenz-geschichte-bismarcks-1902.content:
Max Lenz — Geschichte Bismarcks
Geschichte Bismarcks, by Max Lenz (1850–1932), Professor of History at the University of Berlin, published by Duncker & Humblot, Leipzig, 1902 (OCLC 1158522). The text of this wiki is the HathiTrust full-text scan (University of Wisconsin copy, 472 pages).
In his Vorwort (preface, Berlin, 29 June 1902) Lenz describes the work as the almost unchanged separate edition (Sonderausgabe) of his article for the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, with which Freiherr Rochus von Liliencron, the editor of the national work, had entrusted him; the introduction and a few notes on points where he wished to point to more remote sources or had something particular to say were added. He thanks his friends Hans Delbrück and Hermann Oncken, the latter of whom followed the elaboration of the later parts of the book with penetrating criticism.
Structure
The work proceeds chronologically through Bismarck’s life:

Einleitung. Friedrich Wilhelm III. und sein Staat — the Prussia into which Bismarck was born (his birth in the year of Waterloo).
Jugendjahre — youth.
Die Revolution — the Revolution of 1848.
Frankfurt — the Frankfurt Diet.
Petersburg und Paris. Eintritt ins Ministerium — Petersburg and Paris, and entry into the ministry (1862).
Die Anfänge des Ministeriums — the beginning of the ministry.
Polnische Revolution — the Polish revolution (1863).
Der Kampf mit dem Liberalismus — the struggle with Liberalism (the constitutional conflict).
Der Frankfurter Fürstentag — the Frankfurt Congress of Princes (1863).
Schleswig-Holstein — the Schleswig-Holstein question.
Niederwerfung Österreichs — the overthrow of Austria (1866).
Norddeutscher Bund — the North German Confederation.
Hessische und deutsche Frage — the Hessian and German question (the 1866–1870 years).
Krieg mit Frankreich. Aufrichtung des Deutschen Reiches — the war with France and the founding of the German Empire (1870–71).
Kulturkampf; Bund und Bruch mit den Liberalen — the Kulturkampf; the union with and break from the Liberals (the turn of 1879).
Auswärtige Politik im Neuen Reich — foreign policy in the new Reich (the alliance system).
Innere Politik im letzten Jahrzehnt. Ausgang — domestic policy in the last decade, and the end: the conflict between Kaiser and Kanzler, the tragic solution of 18 March 1890 (Bismarck’s dismissal), his retirement to Friedrichsruh, and his death (“als die Rieseneiche im Sachsenwalde stürzte” — when the giant oak of the Sachsenwald fell, in 1898), closing with a summing-up (Die Summe) of his work.

The volume ends with the Anmerkungen (notes) section, Berichtigungen (corrections), and the printer’s colophon.

sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t11.title: Ollivier — L'Empire libéral, Tome XI (Livre XIX, La Veillée des armes)
sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t11.content:
Ollivier — L’Empire libéral, Tome XI (Livre XIX)
Émile Ollivier, L’Empire libéral; études, récits, souvenirs, tome onzième. Paris: Garnier frères, 6, rue des Saints-Pères, 1907. On the Internet Archive as lempirelibral11olliuoft (identifier spelling libral without the second e; University of Toronto / Robarts copy). The half-title band names the subject La Veillée des armes. The body opens Livre XIX.
The volume is Ollivier’s continuous memoir-history of the Second Empire in the two years that close the authoritarian system and prepare the liberal ministry and the war of 1870. Dominant years in the text are 1868–1869. The narrative runs from the abolition of discretionary press control and Rochefort’s Lanterne through the Spanish revolution, the Baudin affair, Eastern and Balkan crises, the Greek conference, Beust’s triple-alliance soundings, parallel Austrian and Prussian rearmament, Niel’s military work with the Emperor, the Belgian railway scare, Ollivier’s book Le 19 Janvier, the elections of 1869, and the first moves of the Hohenzollern candidacy. A short block of éclaircissements follows the twenty-one chapters.
Livre XIX — La Veillée des armes
Chapitre premier — La Lanterne — La France nouvelle — Les irréconciliables — La politique radicale de Jules Simon — Prophéties de malheur
Abolition of the discretionary press regime emboldens existing party papers and breeds new hostile sheets; on 31 May 1868 Rochefort’s red pamphlet la Lanterne appears on the boulevards at ten centimes. Government handling of the pamphlet; causes of its success; Paul de Cassagnac as Rochefort’s adversary. Condemnation and Rochefort’s flight to Belgium; the hostile current continues — Cavaignac’s son refuses to be crowned by the Prince Imperial; election of Jules Grévy; failure of Dufaure; Prévost-Paradol’s La France nouvelle and its bellicose character. Creation of the Irréconciliables; Jules Simon’s Politique radicale supplies their programme; Ollivier’s conversation with Gambetta and Jules Ferry; the irréconciliables separate from the republicans of 1848. Death of Walewski (23 September 1868); Thiers’s judgment; prophecies of misfortune for the liberal Empire.
Chapitre II — La révolution espagnole — Prim — Napoléon III — Bismarck
European anxiety over an expected Franco-Prussian war magnifies every word of the Emperor and of the King of Prussia. Portrait of Isabella II; causes of her unpopularity; Prim’s ambition and successive pronunciamientos under Narváez and O’Donnell; death of O’Donnell; González Bravo; arrest of Serrano and exile of Montpensier. Topete’s conspiracy; Prim and the fleet (September 1868); battle of Alcolea; flight of Isabella; Serrano at Madrid and Prim’s ¡Abajo los Borbones! Search for a king — Ferdinand of Portugal refused; first indication of a Hohenzollern candidacy, which Prince Anthony rejects “because France would not tolerate it”; Olózaga ambassador at Paris. Napoleon III’s abstention: he will recognise any government born of popular election, even Montpensier, and prefers Alfonso as the reasonable solution. Role Europe attributes to Bismarck in the Spanish revolution; Bismarck’s conversation with Clarendon disclaiming any part; Napoleon’s reiterated warning that Prussia will not be allowed to cross the Main; Bismarck will later use Spain against that casus belli. Dissent of Bismarck with Heydt; the King sides with the finance minister.
Chapitre III — L’affaire Baudin — Gambetta — Sa plaidoirie — La souscription — Refus d’Émile Ollivier — Les réunions publiques
Delescluze and Blanqui; their plan to move the bourgeoisie through the Baudin affair. Scene at the Montmartre cemetery (2 November 1868); opening of the subscription; adhesions of Odilon Barrot, Prévost-Paradol, Berryer and others. Prosecutions under the law of general security; portrait of Gambetta; his plea; Clément Laurier. Death of Berryer (8 November 1868). Newspaper trials and acquittals; revolutionary manifesto of 3 November; difference between the revolutionaries of 1848 and those of 1868. Ollivier’s situation after the session of 1868; preparation of Le 19 Janvier; letter to the Emperor and the Emperor’s reply (29 September 1868); summons to subscribe. Why Ollivier refuses: nothing justified a revolution against the Empire; dangers of attempting one. Letter of refusal and its consequences. Public meetings of 1868 — oppressive and anarchic character; government tactics.
Chapitre IV — La Turquie — Aali, Fuad — Bourée
Europe’s October 1867 declaration leaving Turkey to herself proves a service. Fuad and Aali as reforming statesmen; obstacles in the Sultan, the harem, and Russian intrigue; the Tsar’s relative moderation. Bourée’s beneficial action at Constantinople; Cretan firman (29 February 1868); Christians enter administration; Council of State; collective demarche of the ambassadors; Gorchakov’s incredulity; tobacco-régie affair.
Chapitre V — Bismarck et la Roumanie
Prince Charles of Romania as Prussia’s sentinel on the Danube; Prussian army organisation; German engineers; encouragement from King William and consul Kaysserling. Bratiano’s perturbing policy; French and Austrian protest; Prince Napoleon at Bucharest; Beust’s momentary counsel of Turkish menace withdrawn on Moustier’s representation. Fall of Bratiano (16 November 1868) on Bismarck’s order — Bismarck seeks Hungarian goodwill with a view to the war he is preparing against France.
Chapitre VI — Fin de l’insurrection crétoise
Last efforts of the Cretan rising; Greek obstacles to repatriation of exiles; Petropavloski’s bands and corsair ships; Turkish resolutions and ambassadors’ demarche; Turkish ultimatum (14 December 1868); rupture of relations; capitulation of Petropavloski; general amnesty (23 December 1868). Gorchakov’s ambiguous line on the Principalities and his need of Bismarck’s diplomatic help over Greece.
Chapitre VII — Ministère Gladstone–Clarendon — Ministère Forcade–La Valette — Rouher maître absolu du gouvernement
Disraeli’s Reform bill of 1867 and his fall; Gladstone and the Irish Church; Gladstone ministry with Clarendon at the Foreign Office (10 December 1868). In France: resignation of Pinard (16 December); La Valette to Foreign Affairs; Forcade de la Roquette to the Interior; Gressier to Public Works; Moniteur universel replaced by the Journal officiel from 1 January 1869; Rouher absolute master of the government.
Chapitre VIII — La conférence sur la Grèce
Bismarck, to serve Gorchakov, proposes a conference on the Turco-Greek dispute (18 December 1868); France accepts; Clarendon hesitates then accepts provided Turkish territorial integrity is not questioned; Greece admitted only in a consultative capacity. Conference (9 January–18 February 1869); declaration against Greece, which accepts; Ollivier judges the work ephemeral for want of applying the principle of nationalities — Sweden as contrasting example. The Emperor’s taste for European conference-parliamentarism.
Chapitre IX — Politique de Beust vis-à-vis de la Prusse, de l’Italie, de la France — Négociations pour un traité d’alliance franco-austro-italien — Dispositions de Bismarck
After Bismarck’s “two sweeps of the broom” in Romania and Greece, friction with Beust over historical revelations of 1866 (Usedom note). Beust does not want war — Austria is not ready, Hungary does not want it, and peace seems the surest bar to North German absorption of the South — yet seeks to bind France without binding himself. Difficult Italian situation of the Menabrea ministry; anger at Pius IX over the execution of two Garibaldians; failed attempts to end the French occupation of Rome. Through general Türr, Beust opens talks for a defensive triple alliance of France, Austria, and Italy. Bismarck’s quarrel with the King; offer and withdrawal of resignation (26 February 1869); apparent calm; Post article and Reichstag speech; Pourtalès’s warning that the calm is a deception and that war is being prepared.
Chapitre X — Préparation autrichienne
Under war minister Kuhn, complete reorganisation of the Austrian army: three laws on the active army, landwehr, and landsturm (5 December 1868) — personal obligatory service without replacement, one-year volunteers, twelve-year total obligation, contingent of 93,000. Parallel Hungarian law; honvéds. Correction of the errors of 1866 and improvement of mobilisation. (Body OCR reverses the roman numerals of Chapitres X and XI; titles and the table control.)
Chapitre XI — La préparation prussienne — Nouvelle tactique de l’artillerie et de la cavalerie — Arrangements avec les États du Sud — Plan de Moltke
Prussia after 1866 does not sleep on victory; Roon refines the instrument, Moltke its employment; the old King multiplies inspections and cabinet work. Application of the federal army law; eleven corps plus Saxony and the Guard; perfection of every service including mobilisation. Steel guns debate; Stoffel’s erroneous report; fortifications and Mainz. Instruction of the men; royal leave effectively shortening the three-year infantry term; Hindersin and artillery; initiative among officers. New cavalry and artillery battle tactics. Military accords with the South German states. Moltke’s plan and Ollivier’s judgment on it.
Chapitre XII — L’Empereur et l’armée
A recruiting law supplies elements; organisation is the sovereign’s work. Napoleon III’s constant care for the soldier’s well-being; circular from Biarritz (1 August 1854); Vaillant. Restoration of the Guard. Impotent struggle of the Emperor’s reforming spirit with bureau routine under Randon; attempt to reform the 1791 manœuvre regulation; little profit drawn from the Italian war.
Chapitre XIII — Niel et l’Empereur
Sadowa awakens Napoleon III; with Niel he attempts serious organic reform — restoration of cadres suppressed in 1863, abolition of elite companies, summer and winter contingents, instruction. The chassepot. Revelation of Prussian artillery superiority; mitrailleuses. Fortresses — Metz works and Blondeau’s provisioning. Defects of French mobilisation versus regional organisation; the Emperor wants permanent brigading, Niel opposes. Mobilisation of matériel, depot battalions, divergences between Emperor and Niel. Subsistence, train, central magazines. Remarkable letter of the Emperor to Niel (22 November 1867); regulation of 16 March 1869; Niel’s combat instructions. Offensive tradition versus Niel’s defensive counsel. Strategic plan — the Emperor studies but does not fix a definitive plan. Conclusion: Napoleon III shared equally with Niel in one of the greatest military efforts France had made; judgment on Stoffel’s reports.
Chapitre XIV — Après l’œuvre de Niel — Étions-nous prêts?
The Emperor assures the country the army is ready (opening speech, 18 January 1869); Niel confirms in repeated declarations (March–April 1869). Ollivier’s judgment: the Emperor and Niel were right — the army was magnificent and was beaten only by the incapacity of its chiefs.
Chapitre XV — L’hallucination des chemins de fer belges
Portrait of Frère-Orban and of La Guéronnière at Brussels. Cession of the Grande-Luxembourg line to the Compagnie de l’Est (8 December 1868); further Est–Guillaume-Luxembourg treaty; Belgian emotion and bill forbidding cession of railways to foreign companies without authorisation; reciprocal French emotion. Emperor’s letter to Niel (19 February 1869); military preparations. Clarendon’s intervention; French and Belgian declarations; Frère-Orban in Paris; Rouher wants to pose the casus belli; the Emperor, again pacific, calms him. Belgians wish to invoke the guaranteeing powers; Clarendon restrains them and warns France; La Valette receives the warning badly. General pacification.
Chapitre XVI — Lamartine, Berlioz, Rossini
Last days and funeral of Lamartine (d. 28 February 1869); definition of music; characters and works of Rossini and Berlioz.
Chapitre XVII — La responsabilité ministérielle au Sénat — L’administration de la ville de Paris — Haussmann et Rouher
Imperial speech as electoral programme: “I will not go back, but I will not go forward.” Ministerial responsibility in the Senate — Rouher and Maupas. Haussmann and the city of Paris in the Corps législatif — three networks, bons de délégation, Crédit foncier treaty (11 April 1867); Thiers, Picard, Rouher on the extraordinary budget; Haussmann defends himself in the Senate.
Chapitre XVIII — La veillée des armes au Corps législatif — Les officiers du parquet — La loi militaire — La responsabilité ministérielle — Pension aux anciens militaires
Budget discussion as complete inventory of questions since 1863 ahead of the elections. Embarrassed ministers versus an opposition at ease. Official candidatures — Forcade, Ollivier. Thiers demonstrates the need to restore the constitutional regime; Rouher’s protest; Thiers’s double language on liberal concessions as progress or comedy; La Valette’s pacific declaration. Pension for former soldiers — Buffet, Pelletan, Glais-Bizoin.
Chapitre XIX — Le 19 janvier
Publication of Ollivier’s Le 19 Janvier (3 March 1869); press charivari. Digressions on the je and the moi in history and on the abuse and use of quotations. Public success; letter of Sainte-Beuve. Diplomatic conversation between Rome and Paris over Mgr Darboy’s letter as reported in the book. Earlier imperial attempt, through Fleury and Prince Napoleon, to stop the publication; offer of neutrality in the Var and later the Ministry of Justice; Ollivier publishes anyway.
Chapitre XX — Les élections de 1869 — Le programme de Belleville de Gambetta — Les destructions nécessaires de Jules Ferry — Bancel et Émile Ollivier à Paris — Séance du Châtelet
Character of 1869 elections differs from 1863 on both sides: government invents “officieux” candidates; official candidates themselves liberalise and criticise Mexico, Sadowa, and armaments; opposition intransigence and antimilitarism. Paris elections run by intransigent papers; Gambetta against Carnot; Jules Ferry against Guéroult; sentence of exclusion against Ollivier. Gambetta’s Belleville programme; Ferry’s “necessary destructions.” Ollivier’s candidacy at Lodève and polemic with le Siècle; candidacy in the Var against Laurier; Mistral; Bancel raised against Ollivier at Paris; challenge and Châtelet meeting; revolutionary agitation; strange police attitude; withdrawal of the two government competitors — Ollivier is not thereby an official candidate. Girardin’s offer of a hall; Bancel retained in the Drôme by illness; Robert Mitchell; attitude of opposition deputies; last-hour manœuvre. Ollivier’s failure at Paris and election in the Var. Departmental elections not revolutionary; failure of Prévost-Paradol and Renan; Gambetta beats Lesseps at Marseille; disorders at La Ricamarie and Paris. Meaning of the elections: condemnation of the authoritarian Empire represented by Rouher and victory of the programme of the liberal Empire associated with Ollivier.
Chapitre XXI — Les négociations entre l’Autriche, l’Italie et la France sont suspendues — Lettres de Napoléon III, François-Joseph, Victor-Emmanuel — Commencements du complot Hohenzollern — La monarchie sans roi — Bismarck et le « fatal parlementarisme » — Conversation du roi de Prusse et de Nigra à propos de la ligne du Mein
Twelve-article draft treaty (March 1869); impossibility of agreement on Rome; negotiations suspended; letters exchanged among Napoleon III, Francis Joseph, and Victor Emmanuel. Cadiz insurrection (3–13 December 1868); monarchical elections to the constituent Cortes; Prim and Olózaga in search of a king; new refusal of Ferdinand of Portugal (3 April 1869); Serrano fails to carry Montpensier. Bismarck’s Spanish policy — counterbalance French influence and, if possible, install a German prince; he floats Leopold of Hohenzollern through the press; Benedetti’s demarches to Thile (31 March 1869) and to Bismarck (11 May 1869); imperial instructions. Bernhardi sent to Spain; candidacy introduced via Steyssal; Salazar y Mazaredo as first agent; Kanitz’s denial; royalty without a king — Serrano regent, Prim president of the council (1 June 1869). Bismarck’s struggle in the Reichstag; he curses the orators without condemning “fatal parliamentarism”; resigns the Prussian presidency of the council and takes leave (30 June 1869). King of Prussia at Baden; conversation with Nigra on the Rhine frontier; impression on Napoleon III.

Documentary notes supporting the narrative:

Lettres diverses
Élections de 1869 — Séance du Châtelet — Circulaires de Renan
Lettres diplomatiques

sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t14.title: Ollivier — L'Empire libéral, Tome XIV (Livre XXII, La Guerre)
sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t14.content:
Ollivier — L’Empire libéral, Tome XIV (Livre XXII)
Émile Ollivier, L’Empire libéral; études, récits, souvenirs, tome quatorzième. Paris: Garnier frères, 6, rue des Saints-Pères, 1909. On the Internet Archive as lempireliberal14olli (series dating in metadata from 1895; this volume’s imprint is 1909). The half-title band names the subject La Guerre: explosion du complot Hohenzollern; déclaration du 6 juillet; retrait de la candidature Hohenzollern; demande de garantie; soufflet de Bismarck; réponse au soufflet; déclaration de guerre. The body opens Livre XXII (the table of contents OCR mislabels it “Livre XIV”).
The volume is Ollivier’s continuous memoir-history of the July 1870 crisis in which he served as head of the liberal ministry. It runs from the premature revelation of Leopold of Hohenzollern’s acceptance of the Spanish crown through the French Chambers’ vote of war credits. An avant-propos frames the whole as a defence against the postwar charge that he went to war “au cœur léger.” The narrative is organised as five “moments,” then a conclusion and a block of éclaircissements.
Livre XXII — La Guerre
Avant-propos
Ollivier opens with a July 1870 café telegram that once paired his name with Cavour and Bismarck, then with the reverse judgment after defeat: a mediocre talker, “au cœur léger,” whose presumptuous ineptitude lost two provinces. He cites Machiavelli and Guicciardini on judgment by outcome rather than by the wisdom of counsel, and sets the volume as justification of the ministry’s conduct in the Hohenzollern affair and the decision for war.
Chapitre premier — Le guet-apens Hohenzollern éclate — son effet en France et en Europe
Salazar reaches Madrid with Leopold’s acceptance (telegraphed 26 June); Prim is away hunting; the news leaks through Zorrilla to la Época and the Puerta del Sol before the Cortes can be packed for an immediate vote. Prim returns in the night of 30 June–1 July and already judges the candidacy compromised: the plan with the King and Bismarck had been secrecy until a Cortes vote that would stun the Emperor. Prim tries to recover by charming Mercier; Mercier’s language remains correct. A letter of Prim to Olózaga. The news bursts on Paris like a bomb (3 July); Mercier’s dispatch; Gramont informs the Emperor; the Emperor’s surprise; Gramont’s letter to Ollivier; Ollivier’s despair; the government resolves to turn aside the candidacy. Prim answers French protests by summoning the Cortes for 20 July to elect Leopold; at Berlin, Thile tells Lesourd the Prussian government knows nothing and evades; Bismarck organises a press campaign. Unanimous French indignation — Doudan, Jules Favre, Jules Simon, Thiers, Gambetta — mirrored among foreign statesmen. The French press; this state of opinion does not discharge the Emperor’s responsibility alone.
Chapitre II — Les principes du droit international — le cabinet décide de les appliquer à la candidature
After 1815 each great power had bound itself not to seize exclusive influence by placing a family member on a vacant throne without European consent; examples; protest is addressed to the reigning family, not to the electing nation. The rule weighs still more on Spain and on Leopold, given that prince’s dynastic Prussianism. France therefore had reason to stir. The French cabinet resolves to confine the quarrel to the Hohenzollern candidacy and to set aside older grievances; German allegations of personal motives in the Emperor and especially the Empress are denied.
Chapitre III — Premier moment : déclaration ministérielle du 6 juillet
The aggression being plain, the ministry forgoes immediate military reprisals and tries to undo the trap by diplomacy. Conference and direct negotiation with Prussia both look impossible before Prim’s 20 July election date; the cabinet decides to speak from the tribune. Cochery, on Thiers’s advice, asks to interpellate (5 July); the government accepts. Le Bœuf is asked whether the army is ready and affirms that, acting without delay, France can win. Alliances: the Emperor holds out hope of Austria and Italy. Drafting of the declaration; Ollivier corrects it; reading in the Chamber (6 July); the Left pretends to hear a declaration of war; Ollivier restores the true sense. Universal enthusiasm in the French and English press. The ministry redoubles efforts for peace against Prim’s manœuvres; the Emperor approaches Serrano; Gramont approaches the powers; Olózaga approaches the Hohenzollern princes. In the Chamber the Left hampers pacific action; in the Senate warlike excitement; Parisian effervescence; bellicose language in le Pays, la Liberté, le Moniteur universel.
Chapitre IV — Suite du premier moment — Négociations avec les puissances et avec Serrano
Russia (Gorchakov) shows little eagerness and even malice — “France needed a lesson” — though the Tsar writes moderating counsel to King William. Beust pays in words; Italy is circumspect; the South German states unfriendly; the English cabinet withholds help it might have given. Demarches at Berlin and Madrid fail; the Emperor’s personal negotiation with Serrano yields a result: Serrano sends his nephew López Domínguez to the Hohenzollerns.
Chapitre V — Suite du premier moment — La négociation à Ems
Thile’s attitude forces the sending of Benedetti to negotiate at Ems; portrait of Benedetti; the ministry refuses to make him and Mercier scapegoats for not having pierced the plot in March 1870. Bismarck sees with anger the King’s reception of Benedetti. The King will not order Leopold’s renunciation but tries to obtain it by hint; French instructions all ask the same thing. Interviews of Benedetti and the King. The King’s delays look like duplicity; the Emperor takes military measures with Le Bœuf. Thiers’s demarche through the marquis de Massa and the duchess de Mouchy offering his help to the Emperor (10 July) is not received as it should have been. The King continues to let Benedetti hope for withdrawal without ordering it. In the Chamber Emmanuel Arago allows that the 6 July declaration was not a declaration of war; the Right grows more bellicose; Benedetti handles Ems with flexibility; the King commits himself officially by sending Werther to Paris.
Chapitre VI — Second moment — La renonciation — 12 juillet
Strat, Olózaga’s envoy, goes to Sigmaringen; Prince Anthony renounces for his son; Leopold resists; Strat has Anthony send three telegrams (to Prim, to Olózaga, to the Berlin papers) announcing renunciation (11 July). Prim’s envoy, come to offer the crown officially, still demands Leopold’s own official withdrawal; violent scenes between father and son; Leopold submits and hands his renunciation to the admiral. Bismarck’s wrath against the authors of the renunciation; his despair; he offers the King his resignation; the King persists in accepting Leopold’s withdrawal and closing the affair.
Chapitre VII — La demande de garanties — 12 juillet
The Emperor learns of the withdrawal during the morning council and conceals it from the ministers; Ollivier hears it on the way to the Chamber; Olózaga confirms; Ollivier tells the deputies and rejoices. The war party is discontented; Clément Duvernois asks to interpellate on guarantees for the future. The Emperor would have Ollivier present the renunciation as the King of Prussia’s work; Ollivier prefers to wait; the Emperor admits the King had no part in the withdrawal and, still for peace, promises nothing will be done before the next day’s council. Gramont receives Anthony’s telegram through Olózaga, is struck by its gaps, and in the interview with Werther tries to draw an admission that the King contributed; Werther denies energetically; the supposed letter of apology demanded of the King. At Saint-Cloud the Court is over-excited at the insufficiency of the renunciation; the Emperor forgets his promise, decides with Gramont alone (no other minister present) to send a demand of guarantees, dispatched about seven in the evening — the work of the Right, lacking serious grounds. Ollivier learns of the demand by chance; the Emperor orders Gramont to harden it; Ollivier advises the reverse — attenuate and confine it to the present. Ollivier is violently tempted to resign; he stays in order not to harm the country and to neutralise the demand’s effects.
Chapitre VIII — Quatrième moment — Le soufflet de Bismarck
Benedetti receives the order to ask guarantees; he disapproves but fails to send his objections and presses the King on the promenade (13 July); the King receives him ill yet remains courteous. In Paris a pacific Constitutionnel article affirms Ollivier’s pacific resolutions; Le Bœuf, furious at the demand of guarantees, wants the reserves called out — immediate war; Ollivier, backed by seven colleagues, has that rejected and decides that rejection of the guarantees by the King will not be a casus belli, to be read the same day in the Chamber. Violent scene with Le Bœuf; impolite attitude of the Empress; Gambetta to Mitchell: “Votre satisfaction est scélérate”; the Chamber receives the declaration with discontent; Thiers confers with Mège, Richard, Louvet, Segris, Chevandier and fears above all a general conflagration; bellicose Senate. Bismarck summons the King to receive Benedetti no more; the King is already so disposed; Werther’s report is not the cause; Abeken’s telegram to Bismarck; the King has Radziwill draw two reports; Abeken’s telegram poisons the narrative and authorises Bismarck’s perfidious disclosure. Bismarck seeks in vain in Werther’s report and in the French declaration of the 13th a pretext for war; he reworks Abeken’s dispatch until the falsified telegram becomes an unbearable outrage for France — a soufflet (13 July). He has it posted and published; all Germany treats war as inevitable. The French ministry still works for peace; Cassagnac, l’Univers, the Gazette de France, Girardin, Albuféra push war; Gramont continues to ask Benedetti for guarantees; the powers disapprove. Propitious news from Spain; Ollivier with Mitchell declares the incident finished; the Right organises a coalition with the Left — Gambetta and Clément Duvernois at its soul. On the morning of the 14th Ollivier believes peace sure; Gramont announces Bismarck’s soufflet; council at the Tuileries at half-past noon; the ministers still seek a pacific issue and decide on an appeal to a congress. The appeal is reprobated; council at Saint-Cloud (four ministers absent); no final decision, but war is recognised as inevitable after dispatches from Berne and Munich showing Germany is informing foreign powers of the King’s refusal to receive Benedetti; the congress appeal is dropped. Lyons foresees that France cannot bear the Prussian outrage; spontaneous violent manifestations of opinion; Benedetti offers himself to a further impertinence by seeking reception at the Ems station.
Chapitre IX — Cinquième moment — Notre réponse au soufflet de Bismarck — Déclaration du 15 juillet
Friday 15 July, nine in the morning: council at Saint-Cloud with the Empress present; all ministers free; no irrevocable public act yet done. Gramont reads the draft declaration framed so that the decisive grievance is only the public outrage of the posted Ems telegram — not Prague, not Luxembourg, not the refusal of future guarantees as such. The Emperor and all the ministers without exception decide for war. Despite the Constitution they will not declare war without the Chambers’ assent. Meeting with Benedetti. Ollivier reads the declaration in the Chamber of Deputies; general acclamations except sixteen deputies of the Left. Thiers’s speech: right not to tolerate the Hohenzollern candidacy, wrong to make war on a futile circumstance. Ollivier’s reply — le cœur léger. The Chamber, all bellicose, hears further explanations impatiently. Thiers speaks again: justly attacks the demand of guarantees, repeats that this occasion to avenge Sadowa is not propitious. Refutation; Gramont and Kératry; Buffet and J. Favre demand communication of the agents’ dispatches; a commission is named. Ollivier is absent when Gramont communicates dispatches to the commission; Gramont’s very innocent error on one dispatch and the calumnious use made of it. Guyot-Montpayroux for war; Gambetta’s equivocal speech still demanding public communication of dispatches; diplomatic impossibility of that; vote of the war credits — the Chamber was mistress to prevent war by refusing them; an imposing majority decides it. Gramont’s declaration in the Senate meets only acclamations; the Senate’s deputation to Saint-Cloud organised by Rouher; Rouher’s compromising speech. Explanation of the opposition’s attitude; Thiers had warned no minister that he thought the army unready. Gambetta, in reality bellicose, dared not separate from his party; the people of Paris and the provinces show themselves ardent patriots. The government notifies the declaration of war to Prussia expecting immediate entry into campaign. The King of Prussia re-enters Berlin amid warlike ovations; Lesourd’s conversation with Bismarck; Bismarck’s Reichstag speech of 19 July, his lies, the Reichstag’s patriotic unanimity.
Chapitre X — Conclusion et résumé
Historians who make Bismarck innocent of the war diminish him; those who restore his premeditation enlarge him; Bismarck’s own admissions confirm the latter. Ottokar Lorenz, Delbrück, Scherr, Schultze and serious historians generally lay responsibility on Bismarck. The German thesis that if Bismarck wanted war it was because France was herself preparing it is empty; Prussia alone needed the war to make her unity. Bismarck alone organised the Hohenzollern candidacy and falsified the Ems dispatch, without which there would have been no war. Summary of the French government’s conduct — correct and loyal against the Prussian government’s provocative disloyalty; impossibility for the French government of bearing the Prussian outrage. What would have followed had France borne it. Justification of the war; Ollivier acted with knowledge and solely in his country’s interest.
Éclaircissements
Documentary and polemical notes supporting the narrative:

Interpellation Cochery
La déclaration du 6 juillet
L’Empereur et Le Bœuf
L’Empereur et Thiers — témoignage de la duchesse de Mouchy et du duc de Massa
Le rapport Werther, 12 juillet
Thiers et la réunion des ministres dans un bureau, 13 juillet
Découragement de Bismarck après la renonciation
Erreur des mémoires d’Abeken sur le 13 juillet
Rencontre de Comminges-Guitaut avec le ministre prussien
Les conseils du 13 au 14
Conseil du 14 au soir — Plichon et Le Bœuf
Le cœur léger
C’est ma guerre
Souvenirs de Robert Mitchell

sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t16.title: Ollivier — L'Empire libéral, Tome XVI (Livre XXIV, Le Suicide)
sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t16.content:
Ollivier — L’Empire libéral, Tome XVI (Livre XXIV)
Émile Ollivier, L’Empire libéral; études, récits, souvenirs, tome seizième. Paris: Garnier frères, 6, rue des Saints-Pères, 1912. On the Internet Archive as lempireliberal16olli (UCLA / University of California Library copy; series dating in metadata from 1895; this volume’s imprint is 1912). The half-title band names the subject Le Suicide — premier acte: Wœrth–Forbach; renversement du ministère par la majorité impérialiste. The body opens Livre XXIV.
The volume is Ollivier’s continuous memoir-history of the opening disasters of the Franco-Prussian War and of the parliamentary overthrow of his own ministry of 2 January. Dominant year in the text is 1870, with narrative focus on 4–11 August. It runs from Mac-Mahon’s Alsatian campaign (Wissembourg, Wœrth) and Frossard’s action at Forbach through the double crisis at Metz and Paris, the Chamber session that forces the cabinet’s resignation (9 August), the formation of Palikao’s ministry, the Emperor’s loss of effective command to Bazaine, the German concentration toward Metz, and the diplomatic formation of the Ligue des neutres. A block of éclaircissements and a short errata for tome XV close the volume.
Livre XXIV — Le Suicide
Avant-propos
Ollivier opens with the conviction, drawn from the study of facts, that no government is destroyed by its enemies — enemies prop the edifice like the flying buttresses of Gothic churches — and that governments perish only by suicide. Since 1789 successive powers have destroyed themselves: the Constituants exclude themselves from their work; the Girondins deliver themselves; the Jacobins annihilate one another; the Directors put their Republic up for auction; Napoleon I abdicates twice; Charles X abdicates and departs; Louis-Philippe abdicates and flees. These failures are contrary to honour. The volume frames the first act of the liberal Empire’s self-destruction: military reverse paired with the overthrow of the ministry by the imperialist majority.
Chapitre premier — Wissembourg
Narrating a war one has declared is a double torment; Ollivier alone can restore certain unknown or ill-known facts. Disposition of Mac-Mahon’s army in late July: Abel Douay at Haguenau, Ducrot at Reichshoffen, Lartigue and Raoult at Strasbourg (Mac-Mahon’s headquarters); Félix Douay under the marshal. Mac-Mahon organises his advance toward the Lauter in four echelons. Description of Wissembourg; Abel Douay’s arrival on the evening of 4 August; he leaves Liaud’s battalion in the town and places the rest on the heights; his quietude; Mac-Mahon’s warning. March of the Crown Prince’s army on 4 August; Bavarian division Bothmer opens fire from the heights dominating Wissembourg (8 a.m.); dispositions of Liaud; general Pellé descends to his aid; Vth and XIth corps support the Bavarians; Abel Douay orders retreat and is killed; Pellé replaces him; Liaud, not having received the order, clings to resistance, falls, and his battalion surrenders (2 p.m.). Retreat of Pellé; taking of the Geissberg and Schafbusch; judgment of the combat; losses; Mac-Mahon’s dispositions. Napoleon III returns incompletely to Niel’s abandoned project of three armies and places Failly under Mac-Mahon.
Chapitre II — Entre Wissembourg et Wœrth
German uncertainty over Mac-Mahon’s situation after Wissembourg; preparation to act south or west; conviction that he is camped on the heights of Wœrth; conversion westward and decision to attack on 7 August after a day of rest. Description and real value of the Wœrth position; how Mac-Mahon disposes his troops. Failly’s various movements until placed under Mac-Mahon; on the evening of 5 August Mac-Mahon orders him to Reichshoffen with his whole corps as soon as possible; Failly disobeys, holds a council of war, and decides to send only Guyot de Lespart’s division. Mac-Mahon believes he faces only 40,000 enemies and, awaiting Failly and Conseil-Dumesnil, makes 6 August a day of rest; Raoult, Ducrot, and Leusse urge withdrawal on Lemberg; Mac-Mahon consents and gives orders of retreat, then hears cannon toward Wœrth, rides there, and orders battle. The cannonade proves only a reconnaissance; Bavarian Hartmann treats it as the signal to enter battle; Bose on the left and Kirchbach with the Vth corps make the action general.
Chapitre III — Wœrth
Kirchbach’s artillery silences the French guns while chassepots throw back troops trying the Sauer; the Crown Prince orders Kirchbach to stop; he continues, becomes critical, and is refused help by Bose and Hartmann before Bose finally sends Schkopp. Alternating success and reverse of Bose’s fractions; eastern edge of the Niederwald and Morsbronn taken; distress of Lartigue; Mac-Mahon promises Guyot de Lespart and puts Michel’s cavalry division at his disposal. Charge of Michel’s brigade. Arrival of the Crown Prince; imperfect execution of his instructions; Bose joins Kirchbach; struggle between Mac-Mahon and Kirchbach. Bavarians against Raoult; Suzzoni’s turcos hold them; Bose takes Elsasshausen and with Kirchbach menaces Frœschwiller; enveloping order of the Crown Prince. Heroic obstinacy of Mac-Mahon; charges of Bonnemain’s cuirassiers, of the artillery reserve, and of the 1st Algerian tirailleurs; arrival of the Württemberg brigade. State of the field; what Failly’s arrival would have produced; slowness of Guyot de Lespart; taking of Frœschwiller by the Bavarians; Mac-Mahon’s retreat (4 p.m.). Last resistances; Raoult will not leave the field and is killed; German losses. Mac-Mahon’s retreat; the Germans do not pursue; how he pushes the retreat as far as Sarrebourg. Failly during the day of the 6th. Causes of the defeat of Wœrth; grandeur of the battle.
Chapitre IV — Bataille de Forbach
Description of the triangular massif between Sarreguemines, Saarbrücken, and Saint-Avold (Éperon and neighbouring heights). Continued uncertainties of the French general staff. How Frossard disposes his troops. German movement; Kameke engages the battle. Bazaine during the morning of the 6th. First manœuvres of Kameke; intervention of Bataille’s reserve; Alvensleben’s judgment; occasion of victory offered to Frossard, which he does not use. Reinforcements reach Kameke; Alvensleben takes direction of the battle; his plan is not realised and the French keep their positions. Frossard, though not beaten, constitutes himself as beaten; appeals to Bazaine, who sends Castagny, Montaudon, Metman. Causes of Frossard’s panic: approach of the advance-guard of the Prussian 13th division; he loses his head and flees toward Sarreguemines. Bazaine’s reinforcements arrive after Frossard’s departure; oscillations of the Guard; Prussian and French losses.
Chapitre V — Qui est responsable : Frossard ou Bazaine ?
Mac-Mahon had accused no one, not even Failly, and had silently accepted full responsibility. Frossard tries to cover his nullity by charging Bazaine with not having succoured him in time. Examination: was Bazaine bound to go onto the field of battle? Ollivier weighs Frossard’s claim that the combat was to French advantage until four in the afternoon and that timely reinforcements would have turned failure into a magnificent advantage.
Chapitre VI — Comparaison entre les deux armées
Above the particular facts of Wœrth and Forbach, judgment on the value of the two armies still under transformation. The new doctrinaire military school attributes French reverses to bad doctrine; Ollivier refutes that view and compares spirit of solidarity, initiative, and obedience in the two armies. Have the French shown less offensive spirit than the Prussians?
Chapitre VII — L’Invasion
Real numbers of the German troops that invaded French territory. At the Prussian headquarters the news of Wœrth arrives incomplete in the night (“Deux aigles…”); Radziwill, Verdy du Vernois, and Brandenstein reconstruct the sense of the telegram.
Chapitre VIII — A Metz après les défaites
Through 6 August sensational news succeeds at headquarters: morning rumour of a great French victory; Mac-Mahon’s dispatch that if Failly rallies he can take the offensive next day; Frossard attacked; station-master of Reichshoffen telegraphing retreat; Frossard first reassuring then crying distress. Prostration of the French staff. The Emperor’s idea of retiring on Châlons; Le Bœuf’s plan; the Emperor first rejects it, returns to it on Jérôme David’s intervention, then renounces again. Le Bœuf at Saint-Avold; in his absence the Emperor orders the Châlons retreat and asks the Council what effect it will produce at Paris; Le Bœuf’s intolerable situation and resignation; the Emperor’s consolations to Mac-Mahon. Prince Napoleon and Castagny counsel the Emperor’s return to Paris; opposition of the Prince Imperial; the Emperor spontaneously renounces the Châlons retreat; new ministry dispatch on the effect of that retreat; constitution of two centres, Metz and Paris; Bazaine’s plan; fatigues of the army in concentration on Metz (Montaudon’s testimony); Franceschini Pietri’s dispatch to the Empress asking the Emperor’s return to Paris; arrival of Changarnier at Metz.
Chapitre IX — A Paris après la défaite. — Patriotisme ou partiotisme
How peoples bear reverse foreshadows their destiny — Greeks, Romans, English, French under the old kings, after the civil wars and the Revolution. Partiotisme set against patriotisme. Struggle of the two after Waterloo — Talleyrand, Lafayette, Carnot. Historians’ judgment (Mignet, Berryer, Barbès, Tocqueville) condemning partiotisme. Jules Simon’s admission that ministers, the majority of the Corps législatif, and the Opposition itself had regarded the French army as the first in the world.
Chapitre X — A Paris. — Journée du 6 août
The Empress had promptly communicated the Saarbrücken skirmish (2 August) but was slower with Wissembourg: she received it at Saint-Cloud in the night of the 4th and only at eleven the next morning sent Conneau with a sealed packet for Ollivier. Effect at Paris of the defence of Wissembourg on the 5th; Trochu’s letter to Plichon. False news of a Mac-Mahon victory and its effect; Emile Ollivier on the balcony of the Ministry of Justice.
Chapitre XI — La nuit du 6 au 7 août à Paris
About eight o’clock Chevandier sends a first Metz dispatch: Frossard is engaged, too far for help, hope not lost. Ollivier to Pietri: after today’s emotion tomorrow will be terrible. Police reports of rising fermentation; a long column descends the boulevards singing the Marseillaise and chanting “Ollivier!” — some cry “Ollivier à la lanterne! Vive la République!” and even “Vive la Prusse!” The ministry learns Frossard’s retreat and Mac-Mahon’s defeat; immediate measures for national defence. Arrival of the Empress at the Tuileries; ministers go to her; convocation of the Chambers fixed for 11 August despite the opposition of Ollivier and Chevandier. Second council at ten in the morning; the Council claims the Prince Imperial’s return; the Empress seems to consent and then dissuades the Emperor.
Chapitre XII — A Paris — Journée du 8 août. — Activité des ministres et des partis
(Body OCR heading sometimes reads “journée du 7”; the table and sequence fix the 8th.) True sentiment of the Paris population and its patriotic attitude; the parties organise revolution. Programmes of the deputies of the Left, Centre-left, and Right; three distinct currents — against the Empire, against the Cabinet, against Le Bœuf. Appeal to Schneider and how he answers. Third council at nine in the evening; request for imperial authorisation to offer the War Ministry to Trochu; Ollivier’s report on public opinion; firmness of Baraguey d’Hilliers maintaining calm in the streets. Manifesto of deputies and journalists in le Siècle; resolutions on arming citizens; Trochu’s atrabilious disposition; interview of Ollivier and Trochu; Trochu’s refusal; contrast with Changarnier. Schneider asks Ollivier for the Cabinet’s resignation and is refused; Schneider offers the ministry to Trochu, who also refuses; Ollivier’s visit to the Empress and the questions she puts; he counsels offering War to Cousin-Montauban. De Pierres, the Empress’s écuyer, comes to ask Ollivier’s resignation; evening council interrupted by a deputation demanding the ministry’s dismissal; the Empress refuses; disorderly attempts repressed by Baraguey d’Hilliers. National-defence measures of the 8th begin to execute; Duvernois reproaches the ministers for lack of confidence in the Left.
Chapitre XIII — Projet d’un coup de justice
In the first hours of the night after the terrible days of the 7th and 8th Ollivier walks his cabinet asking what to propose to the Council and the Chamber. First evidence: the bad fortune of the opening is due to the Emperor’s pitiful health and to the effect of his personal command. Chevandier proposes to arrest the revolutionary chiefs during the night; Ollivier adopts the plan in modified form. Return of Maurice Richard from Metz and his report on the situation there. Conference at the Tuileries among the Empress, the Prefect of Police, Chevandier, and Ollivier; Ollivier and Chevandier demand the Emperor’s return to Paris; Pietri supports them; the Empress after refusal seems to consent. Council of ministers; Persigny’s opposition to the Emperor’s return; in Ollivier’s absence (drafting with Dejean the declaration to be read to the Chambers) the Empress’s telegram calling the Emperor to Paris is withdrawn. Arrival of Palikao at the end of the council; short dialogue with the Empress and Ollivier.
Chapitre XIV — Le renversement du ministère
From ten in the morning compact masses of workers descend from Belleville and other quarters onto the Place de la Concorde and the quays; four or five thousand communists, anarchists, and Blanquists are organised and resolved among them, mixed with plain republicans, Orleanists, and the usual curious. Baraguey d’Hilliers holds the approaches. Ollivier’s dispositions going to the Chamber; he reads the ministerial declaration from the tribune; insults of the Left; silence of abandonment from Centre and Right; violent emotion; he puts the question of confidence; Schneider sends his secretary to the Tuileries to announce that the fall of the ministry is certain. New dispositions of the Empress; she offers Palikao the formation of a new ministry; he accepts. In the Chamber: proposals of Latour Dumoulin and Jules Favre; Granier de Cassagnac’s apostrophe against Favre’s proposal; fury of the Left. Jérôme David declares that France was not ready; Talhouët’s proposal, rejected by the ministry, is voted by the Chamber. Baraguey d’Hilliers represses an attempt to invade the Chamber; Ollivier’s conversations with Thoinnet de la Turmelière and with Persigny. Duvernois finds a formula that unites all parties against the ministry; impossibility for Ollivier to speak; vote by rising and sitting on the Duvernois motion. Ollivier reads the ministry’s resignation from the tribune; attitude of the deputies toward him; Jules Simon’s interpretation — the Empire exists only in name. The Empress asks the Emperor for Le Bœuf’s dismissal; summary dismissal of the Cabinet by the Empress. The fall of the ministry of 2 January has been a national catastrophe.
Chapitre XV — Cinquième victoire prussienne. — La haine du partiotisme l’emporte sur l’abnégation du patriotisme
The sitting of 9 August was like a military reconnaissance revealing the enemy’s dispositions. Jules Simon’s frank admission: until the fall of the Empire it was neither a man nor a meeting of men that commanded, but hatred. Paul Déroulède’s severe judgment on the opposition parties dominated by personal passions at such an hour. Patriotic attitude of the comte de Chambord, of the prince de Joinville, of Changarnier. Role Thiers might have played and the one he did play.
Chapitre XVI — A Paris : journées des 10 et 11 août. — Le ministère du suicide
Portrait and career of general Cousin-Montauban, comte de Palikao — uncertain name forms, birth at Paris 27 June 1796, marriage, physique, service record. Schneider proposes to the Empress a “ministry of last prayers”; Palikao wants a different one; his difficulties; the Empress’s expansion with Segris. Palikao ministry; judgment on those who compose it; replacement of Baraguey d’Hilliers by general Soumain. Diverse national-defence measures — forced course of banknotes, armaments, permanence of the Chamber accepted by the ministry.
Chapitre XVII — Metz. — Effet du renversement du cabinet du 2 janvier. — Destitution de l’Empereur
The Emperor is afflicted by the fall of the ministry: the Empress had given too wide a latitude to her authorisation of necessary changes; he had believed a partial change of persons, not the overthrow of the Cabinet itself, and had accepted Palikao as war minister in their cabinet, not as head of a new one. He measures the consequences and feels himself struck in the men to whose devotion he had counted; Le Bœuf is with him when the news arrives. Sentiments of Changarnier; mission of Duperré; increase of Bazaine’s powers; the Emperor persists in not delivering Le Bœuf. He renounces the constitution of two different corps at Paris and Metz and returns to concentration on Metz; defective manner of that concentration; what the true plan ought to have been. Summons of the ministry to the Emperor to dismiss Le Bœuf; the Emperor abandons the command and imposes it on Bazaine, who had refused it; letter of the Emperor to Emile Ollivier.
Chapitre XVIII — Le commencement du suicide
Joy and hope that the Court had drawn from the ministry’s fall are short-lived. The happy battle that was to cast the fallen ministers into public contempt and halo their successors does not come; the unanimity the Court thought to obtain for the Emperor by sacrificing the cabinet to opposition hatreds and anarchist plots is not obtained; it has been necessary to sacrifice the Emperor after them and strip him of his command. The slide has begun — royal majesty sinks more easily from the summit to the middle than it climbs again.
Chapitre XIX — Marche des Allemands sur Metz
Moltke’s fundamental plan has not been completely achieved: two French corps are beaten and entry on French territory is open, but the principal French army has not been annihilated between the three German armies. He rejoices nonetheless for distant consequences (“Eine victory is always welcome…”) and resumes what remains: march on Paris, crush the army met, prevent it from gaining the south, cut it from its communications. Germans organise to throw French forces back on Metz so as to march on Paris without hindrance. Surrender of Lichtenberg; heroic resistance of Bitche and Phalsbourg. Cavalry used more regularly for scouting; painful German march; constant expectation of French attack and stupefaction at being left the field free.
Chapitre XX — Effet à l’étranger. — La Ligue des neutres
Success makes enterprises appear just; the day after Wœrth and Forbach the French are treated as culprits duly chastised. Americans speak aloud of a government that aided the Secession rebels and tried to plant a monarchy on the southern frontier; in Europe some do not hide their satisfaction. Hidden or open joy of neighbouring nations; sadness of Victor Emmanuel, who consults La Marmora on the possibility of aid; Sella carries the cabinet to refuse all help; Italian public opinion hostile to intervention for France. Italy proposes to England a Ligue des neutres; England fears being drawn into action and first refuses; Cadorna makes clear that the League will on the contrary permit non-intervention; Granville and Gladstone adhere. Visconti’s explanation of the League. Ollivier’s attempt with his Italian friends to decide an intervention; futility of his journey; regrets of Victor Emmanuel and La Marmora.
Éclaircissements
Documentary and polemical notes supporting the narrative:

Le général Cousin de Montauban, comte de Palikao — ses états de service
Lettre à Emile Ollivier (15 février 1870)
Un récit faux de Palikao
Ordre général de service pendant l’absence de Sa Majesté l’Empereur
Une nouvelle argutie allemande — lettre d’Emile Ollivier au docteur Heinrich Seeholzer
Témoignage d’un socialiste allemand sur la guerre de 1870 — August Bebel
Gramont et Saint-Vallier
Gramont et Vitzthum
Lettres du premier Président de Toulouse G. Piou à Emile Ollivier
Lettre du prélat hongrois Mgr Haynald à Emile Ollivier
La solidarité ministérielle
Conversations

A short Errata corrects notes in tome XV (Corcel / Courcel; des Pallières / des Fallières; punctuation).
Notes

Imprint: Paris, Garnier frères, 6, rue des Saints-Pères, 1912. Typ. Ph. Renouard, 19, rue des Saints-Pères (and rear printer’s mark Desfossés).

Body OCR scrambles several roman numerals (e.g. Chapitre II as “H”, VI as “M”, VII as “Vil”, VIII as “Mil”, XII as “Xll”, XIV as “X”, XVI as “XjVl”); titles and the table of contents control.

(Sarrebruck, alliances). Tomes V and VII sit in the 1800–1865 wiki.

sources/oriani-la-lotta-politica-in-ital.title: Oriani — La lotta politica in Italia, Vol. I
sources/oriani-la-lotta-politica-in-ital.content:
Alfredo Oriani — La lotta politica in Italia, Volume I
Alfredo Oriani (1852–1909), La lotta politica in Italia. Origini della lotta attuale (476–1887), Quinta edizione, curated by Achille Malavasi and Giuseppe Fumagalli, who adhered faithfully to the original Turin edition prepared by the author himself while also consulting the original manuscript kindly placed at their disposal by the author’s son, Ugo Oriani. Three volumes; this is Volume I, containing Libri I–III. The text of this wiki is the Project Gutenberg Italian eBook (EBook no. 43022, released 24 June 2013, prepared by Carlo Traverso, Claudio Paganelli, Barbara Magni and the Distributed Proofreading Team from Internet Archive page images), 203 pages per the source PDF.
Dominant years in this volume are 476–c. 1825, the long age of Italian particularism and foreign domination down to the reaction of the Holy Alliance.
Libro Primo: Il federalismo municipale
Capitolo primo: La fusione barbarica — the fusion of Roman and barbarian worlds: the survival of Roman and Christian individuality in the federative structure of the empire, the foundation of the Lombard kingdom, the pact of Charlemagne and Frankish domination, and the catastrophe of the kingdom. Capitolo secondo: I Comuni — the origins of the communes: bishops and consuls, municipal wars, the descents of Frederick Barbarossa, the cities’ war against the castles, the podestà, Guelfs and Ghibellines, the captain of the people, Ezzelino da Romano, Charles of Anjou, the tyrants, and Boniface VIII with Henry VII of Luxembourg. Capitolo terzo: Le Signorie — the rise of the signorie: their first attitudes, Robert of Naples and Bertrand du Pouget, Louis the Bavarian and John of Bohemia, the triumph of the signori, Cola di Rienzo, Cardinal Albornoz, the ideal Italian unity, Petrarch and Boccaccio. Capitolo quarto: Venezia nella storia italiana — Venice in Italian history. Capitolo quinto: La rivoluzione militare — Italy’s military incapacity, the masnadieri (banditti), the condottieri, the effects of the military revolution in the republics, the triumph of the capitals, and its consequences for the rest of Italy. Capitolo sesto: I principati — the fifteenth century, the impossibility of a kingdom, Lodovico il Moro and Alexander Borgia, Leo X and Luther, Lodovico Ariosto and Niccolò Machiavelli, and the retrogradation of Italy.
Libro Secondo: Gli Stati
Capitolo primo: L’epoca della Riforma in Italia — the age of the Reformation in Italy: spiritual conditions, political repercussions, the Jesuits, and the activity of Piedmont amid the decay of the other Italian states. Capitolo secondo: La rinnovazione dello spirito nazionale — Torquato Tasso, the political writers, Giordano Bruno and Tommaso Campanella, and the scientific emancipation. Capitolo terzo: I regni del Piemonte e delle due Sicilie — the century of Louis XIV, Venice, Genoa and Corsica, the other Italian principalities, Piedmont in the wars of succession, the Papacy, and the new Italian problem. Capitolo quarto: Genio e carattere nazionale durante la formazione dei due regni — the political schools, Giambattista Vico, Pietro Giannone, Metastasio and Goldoni. Capitolo quinto: Il periodo delle riforme — European influence, the two Sicilies, Parma and Piacenza, Tuscany, Lombardy, Piedmont, the Papal State, the suppression of the Jesuits, Giuseppe Parini and Vittorio Alfieri.
Libro Terzo: La democrazia moderna
Capitolo primo: Le repubbliche — the French Revolution, the condition of the peninsula, the descent of Napoleon, the republican constitutions, the revolutionary settlement, and the Austro-Russian reaction. Capitolo secondo: Fine delle repubbliche — the French consulate, the battle of Marengo, the Concordat, and the Consulta of Lyon. Capitolo terzo: I regni francesi in Italia — the French empire, the fourth and fifth European coalitions (1807–1809), and the political changes in Italy. Capitolo quarto: Caduta di Napoleone — the Russian campaign, the catastrophe of the French kingdoms in Italy, the Hundred Days, and the writers of the French revolutionary and imperial age — Vincenzo Monti, Ugo Foscolo and the dialect poets. Capitolo quinto: L’Italia sotto la reazione della santa alleanza — the Treaty of Vienna, the Italian conditions, and liberalism under the Restoration.

sources/oriani-la-lotta-politica-in-ital.title: Oriani — La lotta politica in Italia, Vol. II
sources/oriani-la-lotta-politica-in-ital.content:
Alfredo Oriani — La lotta politica in Italia, Volume II
Alfredo Oriani (1852–1909), La lotta politica in Italia. Origini della lotta attuale (476–1887), Quinta edizione, curated by Achille Malavasi and Giuseppe Fumagalli (see the note to Volume I). This is Volume II, containing Libri IV–VI. The text of this wiki is the Project Gutenberg Italian eBook (EBook no. 43023, released 24 June 2013, prepared by Carlo Traverso, Claudio Paganelli, Barbara Magni and the Distributed Proofreading Team from Internet Archive page images), 203 pages per the source PDF.
Dominant years in this volume are 1821–1860, the full arc of the Risorgimento from the revolutions of 1821 to the eve of the Expedition of the Thousand.
Libro Quarto: Il Risorgimento
Capitolo primo: I moti del 1821 — European influences; the Neapolitan revolution of 1820–21; the Piedmontese revolution of 1821; the absolutist repressions. Capitolo secondo: Trame ed insurrezioni del ‘31 — the liberal incubation; the uniform conditions of the governments; the rising of the centre (Modena, the Papal States, Parma). Capitolo terzo: Il pensiero politico nel moto letterario — the first groups; the literary dualism; Colletta and Botta; Rosmini and Gioberti. Capitolo quarto: Giuseppe Mazzini e la Giovine Italia — Mazzini and the Young Italy. Capitolo quinto: Conati ed imprese rivoluzionarie — the expedition into Savoy (1834); the general state of the peninsula; the Bandiera brothers (1844); the reformers.
Libro Quinto: L’ultima rivoluzione federale
Capitolo primo: I prodromi — the effervescence of opinion; Pius IX; the agitation in the other states; the constitutions (statuti) of 1848. Capitolo secondo: Le sommosse popolari e la guerra regia — the Five Days of Milan; the adhesions to the war; the Piedmontese campaign of 1848. Capitolo terzo: La reazione federale — the papal allocation; the betrayal of Ferdinand II; the annexations to Piedmont; the military disasters; the constitutional catastrophes; Pellegrino Rossi; the second Piedmontese campaign (1849). Capitolo quarto: Schemi repubblicani — Florence; the proclamation of the republic; the fall of the Roman Republic (with a section on Giuseppe Garibaldi); the last republic of Venice.
Libro Sesto: L’egemonia piemontese
Capitolo primo: Le ristorazioni — the recovery of opinion; the Neapolitan kingdom; the Papal State; the Grand-Duchy and the duchies; the Lombardo-Veneto. Capitolo secondo: La preparazione piemontese — the first parliamentary difficulties; the Count of Cavour. Capitolo terzo: La politica dell’egemonia — Cavour’s ministry; the Crimean War; the Congress of Paris; the adhesions to Piedmont. Capitolo quarto: L’opposizione rivoluzionaria — the defeat of Mazzinianism; Carlo Pisacane and the Sapri expedition (1857). Capitolo quinto: La mediocrità politica e letteraria — the decline of the national genius; the new schools; Luigi Carlo Farini.

sources/oriani-la-lotta-politica-in-ital.title: Oriani — La lotta politica in Italia, Vol. III
sources/oriani-la-lotta-politica-in-ital.content:
Alfredo Oriani — La lotta politica in Italia, Volume III
Alfredo Oriani (1852–1909), La lotta politica in Italia. Origini della lotta attuale (476–1887), Quinta edizione, curated by Achille Malavasi and Giuseppe Fumagalli (see the note to Volume I). This is Volume III, containing Libri VII–IX. The text of this wiki is the Project Gutenberg Italian eBook (EBook no. 43024, released 24 June 2013, prepared by Carlo Traverso, Claudio Paganelli, Barbara Magni and the Distributed Proofreading Team from Internet Archive page images), 203 pages per the source PDF.
Dominant years in this volume are 1859–1887, from the eve of unification to the African adventure, the work closing on the battle of Dogali (24 January 1887) and Oriani’s closing synthesis of Italian history.
Libro Settimo: La rivoluzione unitaria
Capitolo primo: La grande vigilia — the exhaustion of the reaction; the last difficulties of Piedmont; the Napoleonic idea; the Franco-Sardinian alliance. Capitolo secondo: La conquista regia — the Franco-Sardinian war of 1859; the French peace; the catastrophe of the Piedmontese idea. Capitolo terzo: Prime integrazioni rivoluzionarie — the provisional governments in central Italy; dictatorial initiatives; the annexations of central Italy; the cession of Nice and Savoy. Capitolo quarto: La conquista rivoluzionaria — the Thousand of Marsala; the last resistances of the Bourbon and Piedmontese governments; the enterprise of Naples; the Piedmontese campaign in the Marches; the annexation of the kingdom.
Libro Ottavo: Il regno d’Italia
Capitolo primo: Il primo assetto — the historical insufficiency of the new monarchy; the data of monarchical policy; parliamentary characters; political difficulties. Capitolo secondo: La proclamazione di Roma capitale — diplomatic negotiations; the Buoncompagni order of the day; the last struggle between Garibaldi and Cavour; the Regions. Capitolo terzo: I luogotenenti di Cavour — the political environment; the first ministries; legislative empiricism. Capitolo quarto: La reazione del brigantaggio nel mezzogiorno — the brigandage reaction in the South. Capitolo quinto: La tragedia d’Aspromonte — the adventure of Sarnico; the second Garibaldian expedition; the Italian monarchy and the Papacy. Capitolo sesto: Soluzione monarchica del problema di Roma — Rome during the revolution; the September Convention (1864); the transfer of the capital to Florence. Capitolo settimo: La prima guerra italiana nel veneto — royal and democratic conspiracies; the Prussian preparation; negotiations and equipment; the campaign of 1866; Garibaldi in the Tirol; the battle of Lissa; the Peace of Vienna. Capitolo ottavo: Ultima ripresa rivoluzionaria — the last brigand reaction at Palermo; ecclesiastical policy; the Rattazzi ministry; Mentana (1867); parliamentary reactions; the last Mazzinian attempts. Capitolo nono: La crisi finanziaria — the economic environment; Quintino Sella; the danger of bankruptcy. Capitolo decimo: La presa di Roma — the rivalry of France with Prussia; the end of the temporal power; the Franco-Prussian War; monarchical hesitations; the annexation of Rome (1870); the entry of Victor Emmanuel into Rome; Garibaldi in France; the Law of the Guarantees (1871). Capitolo undecimo: L’opposizione ideale — literary decadence; Giosuè Carducci.
Libro Nono: Il secondo periodo monarchico
Capitolo primo: Le due monarchie — the exhaustion of the Right; the prisoners of the monarchy; the last Minghetti ministry; the advent of the Left (1876). Capitolo secondo: La conquista africana — the attraction of European history; European influence on Africa; the Italian initiative; diplomatic difficulties; the battle of Dogali (24 January 1887). Capitolo terzo: L’Italia in Europa — the closing synthesis of the whole work: Oriani’s reflection, ranging back over the entire course of Italian history from the Etruscans and Rome through the barbarian invasions and the medieval and modern ages, on how the Italian nation, risen again and constituted, had taken its place again in Europe.

sources/peguy-notre-jeunesse-1910.title: Péguy — Notre jeunesse
sources/peguy-notre-jeunesse-1910.content:
Charles Péguy — Notre jeunesse (1910)
Charles Péguy (1873–1914), poet, essayist and founder of the Cahiers de la Quinzaine, wrote Notre jeunesse as the twelfth cahier of the eleventh series of his review, published in 1910. It stands as his fullest statement on the meaning of the Dreyfus affair — which he calls “our youth” — and on the difference between the mystique of republican and revolutionary faith and its degeneration into politique. The essay, addressed in part to his collaborators Daniel Halévy and Jean Variot, is written as an “examen de conscience,” a public self-examination of the generation that had fought for the revision of the Dreyfus trial a decade earlier.
The Milliet family and the tissue of republican faith
Péguy opens by recounting how Paul Milliet brought to the Cahiers the archives of his republican, Fourierist family — letters from Victor Hugo and Béranger, papers touching the conquest of Algeria, the Mexican expedition, the Crimean war. What Péguy insists he wants is not the letters of the great men, of which he says the libraries are full, but precisely the letters of ordinary people, “the admirables troupes” behind the great republican leaders. He seeks “l’histologie ethnique” — the tissue of an ordinary republican family, taken “à plein drap, à même le drap,” to see what the people and the bourgeoisie and the republic were when “les républicains étaient héroïques et que la République avait les mains pures.”
He recalls the generation of his youth as the last carriers of a “mystique républicaine,” a lived faith rather than a set of propositions. The intermediate generation, he holds, has lost the instinct of republican mystique — “ça fait vingt ans.” Péguy situates himself as “l’arrière-garde,” a rear-guard “un peu isolée,” the last generation that possessed the republican mystique. The Dreyfus affair was, for him, the last surge of this heroism, “le dernier sursaut, le soubresaut suprême de cet héroïsme et de cette mystique.”
The modern world against culture
Péguy contrasts his generation with what he calls “le monde moderne,” those who “ne croient plus à rien, qui s’en font gloire et orgueil,” who make a virtue of believing nothing — “pas même à l’athéisme.” He insists the movement of the de-republicanisation of France is the same deep movement as its de-Christianisation, a single movement of “démystication,” by which the people no longer believes in the Republic or in God. This is “la stérilité moderne,” which dries up equally the political city and the Christian city. The modern world, he writes, opposes not only the ancien régime but every old culture together: “c’est la première fois dans l’histoire du monde que tout un monde vit et prospère, paraît prospérer contre toute culture.”
He does not say this is forever — “cette race en a vu bien d’autres” — and hopes the following generation will be “enfin une génération mystique.” But for the present, the Republic has ceased to be lived and has become a “thèse”: “quand un régime, d’organique est devenu logique, et de vivant historique, c’est un régime qui est par terre.” What had been for his fathers a living instinct is for the young a set of propositions, logical rather than organic.
The great dichotomy: men of eternal salvation and men of temporal salvation
The heart of the essay is Péguy’s account of what divided the two sides in the Dreyfus affair. His adversaries, he says, spoke the language of reason of state, of the temporal salvation of the people and the race — that one must not sacrifice a whole people for one man. The Dreyfusards, by contrast, spoke in a deep Christian movement: “une seule injustice, un seul crime… suffit à rompre tout le pacte social, tout le contrat social.” One blot dishonours a whole people; “l’honneur d’un peuple est d’un seul tenant.” He draws the corneille and Christian maxim, “je rendrai mon sang pur comme je l’ai reçu.”
The true division of the affair, for Péguy, was between “les hommes du salut éternel” and “les hommes du salut temporel.” The Dreyfusards “ne voulions pas que la France fût constituée en état de péché mortel.” To illustrate, he invokes the passage of Joinville’s life of Saint Louis in which the saint tells the clerk that he would rather be a leper thirty times over than commit a single mortal sin — for the leprosy of the body is cured at death, while the leprosy of the soul in mortal sin endures as long as God is in paradise. Péguy reads the Dreyfusards’ refusal to accept an official injustice as precisely this Christian preference for the health of the soul over the body.
Bernard-Lazare and the prophet of the affair
Péguy honours Bernard-Lazare — “né à Nîmes le 14 juin 1865; mort à Paris le premier septembre 1903” — as the prophet of the affair, the first to defend Dreyfus and the one whose word he calls “le mot décisif de l’affaire.” He recounts how, even as some Dreyfusards grumbled at the returned captain’s imperfections, Bernard-Lazare defended him “avec cet admirable aveuglement volontaire de ceux qui aiment vraiment”: “Il est innocent, c’est déjà beaucoup.”
Mystique and politique
Péguy closes by drawing the distinction that gives the essay its enduring fame. The political parties, he writes, can speak only the political, parliamentary language, and they translate, betray (traducunt, tradunt) everything that is done for the mystiques. “La mystique républicaine, c’était quand on mourait pour la République; la politique républicaine, c’est à présent qu’on en vit.” Since the degradation of the Dreyfusard mystique into Dreyfusard politique, Péguy says he and his collaborators have known fifteen years of poverty defending Christian consciences and republican liberties, only to find reactionary politicians forbid them being republicans and republican politicians forbid them being Christians. He answers that the Cahiers are “une compagnie parfaitement libre d’hommes qui tous croient à quelque chose.”
Addressing the royalists of the Action française, he concedes that the only force of a traditional monarchy is that the king is loved — “la seule force, la seule valeur, la seule dignité de tout, c’est d’être aimé” — and finds in Maurras’s phrase “nous serions prêts à mourir pour le roi” the one thing that speaks to him, for it is a truth of faith rather than an argument. Yet he holds that one founds no culture on derision and sarcasm. The essay ends with the words of Michel Arnauld at a gathering of the Cahiers: the royalists are but “une menace imprécise et théorique,” and “le jour où ils deviendraient une menace réelle ils verraient ce que nous sommes encore capables de faire pour la République.” Péguy closes with “FIN.”
Historical significance
Notre jeunesse is one of the defining texts of the Dreyfusard generation, and a central statement of Péguy’s intellectual and spiritual position in the decade before the First World War. In it he aligns the republican mystique with the Christian, sets the eternal above the temporal salvation of France, and warns of a “monde moderne” that prospers against every culture — a theme he would carry into his later poetry and essays before his death at the Marne in September 1914. The essay belongs to the wider quarrel over the meaning of the Republic and the Dreyfus affair that occupied French intellectuals in the years between the affair and the war.

sources/recouly-histoire-grande-guerre-1.title: Recouly — Histoire de la grande guerre, 1914-1918
sources/recouly-histoire-grande-guerre-1.content:
