Recouly — Histoire de la grande guerre, 1914-1918
Raymond Recouly (1876–1950), Histoire de la grande guerre, 1914-1918. Paris: Les Éditions de France, 20, avenue Rapp, 1934 (© 1934 by Les Éditions de France). A single-volume synthesis of some four hundred pages, drawn from the BnF scan (barcode 3 7502 00662084 5) via Anna’s Archive; the raw text in this wiki was obtained by OCR of the 416 scanned images (no embedded text layer). Recouly, a war correspondent and historian of the Third Republic, wrote the book “vingt ans après” — for the generation born at the moment the first shots were fired, who know nothing of the war at first hand, and for his own generation of soldiers and civilians who lived it. He declares his method at the outset: against the “anarchic and enfeebling theories” of Tolstoy, war is directed and conducted by chiefs; the intelligence and will of commanders matter as much as, if not more than, the courage of the commanded. The book rests on the published memoirs of the principals (Joffre, Foch, Pétain, Gallieni, Weygand, Haig, French, Pershing, Hindenburg, Ludendorff, von Kluck, von Kuhl, von Hausen), the official histories of the belligerent staffs, and a closing Bibliographie.
Dominant years in the text are 1914–1918.
Introduction — Vingt ans après
Written in 1934, twenty years after the outbreak. A generation has passed; thousands of young men entering the barracks were born at the first shots and know nothing of the war personally. Recouly proposes to gather, in a short space, the dominant features of the drama and its principal points, which like milestones mark the long road. His central thesis: Germany, for all its marvellous military preparation, was finally defeated by France and her allies because, too sure of its warlike superiority and committing its habitual sin of pride, it entered the conflict in bad diplomatic conditions and ranged too many enemies against itself. Conversely, the political (not military) defection of Russia brought victory within two fingers of Germany; the grave blunder of its military chiefs — ignorant of politics — in deciding on unrestricted submarine warfare and so provoking American intervention, added one more enemy. Only the threat of catastrophe compelled the Allies to accept a single command, confided to “a soldier of genius,” Foch. The Introduction also gives summary definitions of military terminology for readers unfamiliar with it (the division as the base unit of military organisation).
Chapitre premier — Causes et responsabilités
Opens on Sunday morning, 28 June 1914: the archduke-heir of Austria, Francis Ferdinand, and his morganatic wife assassinated at Sarajevo, capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the province occupied and then annexed by Austria, peopled chiefly by Slavs and Muslims. The double assassination in a distant Balkan town, “barely European,” provoked within a few weeks a war that lasted fifty-two months and in which the most powerful nations of the world were engaged. The chapter examines the causes and the responsibilities for the war.
Chapitre II — Mobilisations et déclarations de guerre
After the exchange of diplomatic notes that held the capitals in suspense during the tragic decade, the “chassé-croisé” of mobilisations and declarations of war. After a partial mobilisation, Austria’s declaration of war on Serbia opens the series of bellicose acts. General mobilisation of Russia, quickly followed — before the news reached Vienna — by the general mobilisation of Austria-Hungary. General mobilisation of Germany and of the other powers in turn.
Chapitre III — Les plans de campagne
The German plan. Germany, wedged between France and Russia, faces the problem of a war on two fronts, east and west. Almost on the morrow of the victories of 1870, Moltke the victor reflected on it, seeing in it “the most formidable test” that could threaten the existence of the new empire. The chapter sets out the pre-war strategic plans of the powers.
Chapitre IV — Concentration des armées — Premiers combats
Joffre, entirely won over to the idea of the offensive, on grounds both moral, political and military: the offensive answers to the French character and temperament; an army that has not fought in Europe for half a century can only regain confidence in itself through advance and attack. Formal engagements had been concluded between the French and Russian staffs binding both armies to attack the German forces as soon as they were ready. The chapter covers the concentration and the first combats of the frontier battles.
Chapitre V — La bataille de la Marne
Nothing is more complicated or confused than the battle of the Marne, if one tries to follow it in detail; nothing simpler or clearer if one holds to its great lines. A great battle always more or less partakes of chaos — like the hero of La Chartreuse de Parme wandering, blind, all day across the plain of Waterloo, which beside a modern battlefield seems no bigger than a pocket handkerchief. The skill and sang-froid of the French generalissimo, and the mistakes that excess of confidence made the German generalissimo commit, turned the situation; the battle of the Marne was lost, and at a stroke the German machine was half-dismantled — the war that was to have been short instead embarked on a long duration.
Chapitre VI — La course à la mer
The exploitation of victory having not given the results Joffre expected, he sought to accent the German retreat and free the territory, operating in the still-free country north of the Oise — a continuation of the manœuvre of the Marne. It collided with an analogous manœuvre by the enemy, and the two opposed movements tended to cancel each other out. In this race to the wing the Germans had an appreciable advantage, resulting from the very shape of the situation.
Chapitre VII — La guerre sur le front oriental
The decision that could not be obtained on the western front — the principal theatre, where the Germans had hoped the war would end in a few weeks — was equally impossible on the eastern front. There too, from the eddies of battle, after alternatives of victory and defeat for the Central Powers, the struggle threatened to drag on. It can be summarised thus: the German army, even with relatively reduced forces, almost always beat the Russian army, which was clearly inferior in high command and in certain qualities.
Chapitre VIII — Le mauvais bilan de 1915
On the western as on the eastern front, war everywhere came to a standstill. Winter, with its cold, fogs and rain, fell on the trenches, where millions of half-buried human beings lived like troglodytes, with no one able to foresee the end. War, until then dynamic, became static. The stabilisation of combat, imposed by the obstacle, by fortifications and the power of fire, was not in principle an absolute fact. The chapter weighs the poor balance-sheet of 1915 for the Allies.
Chapitre IX — Le redressement de 1916 — Verdun, la Somme, le plan des alliés
At the beginning of 1916, the third (though not the last) year of the war, how does the situation present itself for each of the two enemy blocs, and under what aspects to Joffre examining it at his headquarters at Chantilly with robust and clear common sense? The year that was ending had marked a setback for the Allied cause; yet the failures they suffered, especially in the East (for on the front in France they amounted only to a missed gain), were not catastrophic. The chapter covers Verdun, the Somme offensive, and the Allied plan of 1916.
Chapitre X — La disgrâce de Joffre et la révolution russe sauvent l’Allemagne
Judgment on Falkenhayn. The German failure before Verdun; the great Somme offensive which, on Ludendorff’s own admission, subjected the German armies to a most disquieting attrition; the entry of Romania into the war on the Allied side — three characteristic setbacks for the Central Powers within a few months, three very hard blows falling on the German staff. Yet the disgrace of Joffre and the Russian revolution were to save Germany.
Chapitre XI — Les offensives de Ludendorff
“La veillée des armes” (winter 1917–1918). After the military collapse of Russia, after the defeat of Romania, Germany could be said to have won the war, three-quarters of the way, on the eastern front; only the inter-Allied army of Salonika, maintained and reinforced thanks to the clairvoyance and energy of the French, prevented it from having won entirely. By the peace treaties signed with Russia and Romania (February–March 1918), Germany obtained what it sought. The chapter covers Ludendorff’s offensives of the spring of 1918.
Chapitre XII — Les offensives de Foch
There is in Casanova’s Mémoires a penetrating observation on man: he had only climbed, he said, up to a certain moment; from that point he begins to descend, and in a descent the more rapid the nearer he approaches the end — motus in fine velocior. The failure of 15 July followed, three days later, by a still graver failure, marks for Ludendorff the beginning of the descent that would become ever more rapid and soon vertiginous. The chapter covers Foch’s counter-offensives that broke the German army in 1918.
Chapitre XIII — Guerre et paix
To follow the unfolding of the war in its great lines, to understand the laws that determine it, one must observe it from above: it resembles an immense rugged landscape, with its summits and hollows, and one must dominate it to grasp its unity. In this unbroken sequence of events, at once political and military, there are very clear points of bifurcation where, according as the chiefs and the troops proved superior or inferior to their adversaries, merit or failure gave the facts a different direction from what they would otherwise have taken. The war became nearly inevitable the day the civil chiefs of Germany, the Kaiser first of all, seized by a contagious collective intoxication, were persuaded that Germany had not in the world the place to which it had a right; having developed its strength to the extreme limit, they awaited and seized the occasion to use it. The first battles of the frontiers seemed to give them reason; but the skill and sang-froid of the French generalissimo, and the errors of over-confidence by the German, turned the situation at the Marne. The chapter closes with the aftermath: a badly conceived and still worse executed treaty, and the “sombre perspective” of a new war only sixteen years after a war that had nearly laid France low. The tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Berlin bears the inscription of the scholar Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, INVICTIS VICTI VICTURI (“to the unconquered soldiers, today’s conquered who will be tomorrow’s conquerors”) — a lapidary phrase illustrating the state of mind of Germany on the morrow of its defeat. Germany proclaimed aloud that militarily it had suffered no defeat, that its soldiers had not been vanquished on the field by enemies from without but stabbed in the back by the triumphant revolution from within; and Recouly asks how those who had vanquished it with such difficulty, France first, could have committed the folly of not taking more solid precautions against it.
Bibliographie
A closing bibliography lists the works most frequently consulted: the official histories (the French Les armées françaises dans la grande guerre of the Service historique; the Reichsarchiv, der Weltkrieg 1914-1918; the Official History of the War; the Belgian Bulletin belge des sciences militaires; the Russian staff’s La Grande Guerre translated by Commandant Chapouilly, 1926; Österreich-Ungarns letzter Krieg), the memoirs of Foch, Joffre, Pétain (La Bataille de Verdun), Gallieni, Weygand (Le Onze Novembre), French, Haig’s dispatches, Pershing, Hindenburg (Aus meinem Leben), Ludendorff (Souvenirs de guerre), von Kluck (La Marche sur Paris), von Kuhl (La Campagne de la Marne en 1914), von Hausen (Souvenirs de la campagne de la Marne), and others.
Series note
This volume is a single, self-contained history of the whole war. It stands at the chronological end of the 1866–1919 period covered by this wiki — the First World War as the culminating event of the era treated by Sybel, Delord, Ollivier, Hanotaux, and the Russian works. Written from the perspective of 1934, it is a retrospective French synthesis (contemporary to interwar France) rather than a contemporary record of the war years themselves.

sources/redlich-osterreichische-regierun.title: Josef Redlich — Österreichische Regierung und Verwaltung im Weltkriege (1925)
sources/redlich-osterreichische-regierun.content:
Josef Redlich — Österreichische Regierung und Verwaltung im Weltkriege
Josef Redlich (1869–1936), Österreichische Regierung und Verwaltung im Weltkriege. Wien: Hölder-Pichler-Tempsky A.-G.; New Haven: Yale University Press, 1925. A volume of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Wirtschafts- und Sozialgeschichte des Weltkrieges (Economic and Social History of the World War), Austrian and Hungarian series, under the general editorship of James T. Shotwell and the Austrian editing committee of Friedrich Wieser, Richard Riedl and Richard Schüller. Redlich, professor of public law at the University of Vienna and a former minister, wrote the culminating study of the Habsburg state’s government and administration at war. The raw text in this wiki is the scanned copy (University of Michigan library), 398 pages, already OCR’d, concatenated in page order. The narrative runs from an Einleitung through nine chapters, followed by the Literatur-Angaben, a Kapiteverzeichnis, and an Anhang setting out the plan and publication list of the Carnegie series.
Einleitung
Redlich announces his subject: the Austrian war government as both political organ — bearer and expression of a particular conception of the Austrian state — and as supreme administrative organ. He notes the peculiar pre-war condition of Austrian government: the ministry in Vienna had long exercised in practice the legislative power too, meeting the unavoidable needs of legislation through the emergency-notification provision of the constitution (Article 14) by imperial decree; the ministry had resolved to keep this system through the war, the Reichsrat having been sent home in the spring of 1914 on the renewal of obstructionist tactics among the Slav parties. He frames the whole as the last chapter of three and a half centuries of Habsburg government and administration — for the state that bore it disappeared entirely with the war, the Allied war aim of destroying the Habsburg realm having been realised in the peace treaties.
I. Regierung und Verwaltung in Österreich vor dem Kriege: ihre Organisation, ihre Aufgaben und ihr politischer Charakter
The pre-war system, in seven sections: the foundations of state power; the Emperor and the question of the monarchy; the ministries and ministerial responsibility; the Reichsrat, the upper and lower houses, and the nationality struggles within them; the organs of self-government and the provincial (crown-land) administration; the place of the officials and the political character of the civil service; and the relations between government and parliament on the eve of the war. Redlich describes an administration already working largely by Article-14 decree and marked by the deepening nationality conflicts.
II. Die legislatorischen Vorsorgen der österreichischen Regierung für den Kriegsfall
The legislative preparations made before 1914 for the event of war: the emergency statutes and decrees prepared for war, the penal and censorship provisions, the contemplated suspension of civil liberties, and the readiness of the whole apparatus of state to pass into a war footing at the outbreak.
III. Die letzte Friedensregierung in Österreich
The last peace government: disappointment at the supposed healing effect of the universal suffrage of 1907; the precarious position of the officials’ ministries before the house elected under it, as visible signs of the national-political decomposition of the realm in both Hungary and Austria; the influence of the struggle over the annexation of Bosnia in sharpening national antagonisms in Hungary, the intensification of the conflicts with Croatia and the perpetual keeping-down of the nationalities by the Magyar gentry; the growth of an anti-parliamentary mood at court, among the generals and in the conservative circles of Austria; the unceasing accession of national radicalism among the Czechs, South Slavs and Ruthenians; the worsening of the Monarchy’s position toward the Western powers, Russia and Italy since the annexation of Bosnia; the reflux of all this on the separatist and dissolving currents among South Slavs, Poles and Ruthenians and on the nationalist democracy of the Czechs, with symptoms during the Balkan wars of 1912–1913; and the influence of these phenomena on the political strivings of the Germans of Austria and of the Magyars.
IV. Die österreichische Kriegsregierung und der Geist ihrer Administration
The outbreak and the war government: the suppression of the Austrian parliament at the opening of the war; the issue of the emergency decrees; the passing of civil public power to the Armeeoberkommando over wide areas; the transformation of civil into military administration over a great part of the state territory, and the consequent permanent tension between the Austrian government and the supreme army command; the opening conflicts between population and army leadership, above all in Galicia, toward Poles and Ruthenians alike; the army command’s constant efforts to extend its powers; the unconstitutional transfer of jurisdiction over wide fields of civil justice to military courts; the suspension of jury courts throughout the state; the complete militarisation of the railways; the dictatorship of the army leadership over the civil population; the office and activity of the Kriegsüberwachungsamt (war surveillance office); and the system of the Austrian war government down to the assassination of the minister-president Count Stürgkh in the autumn of 1916. Redlich traces the supremacy of the Hungarian government and of Count Tisza, the subordination of Austria, Stürgkh’s tenacious anti-parliamentary policy supported by the German-bourgeois parties, the consequent suppression of public life, and the strictly bureaucratic character of the war government with its ruinous effect on the whole public condition of the state.
V. Die österreichische Kriegsregierung und ihre Verwaltungstätigkeit
The war government at work: the dictatorial legislation and administrative activity; the government’s provision for the victims of war (Kriegsfürsorge); the participation of the population in relief for those stricken by war-need and want of food; the organisational measures for raising the war loans, supported among the German population alone by the forces of society; the beginning of resistance and conflict with the authorities in the non-German lands; and the growing difficulty of carrying through the state food administration in the hinterland.
VI. Die öffentliche Verwaltung und die Kriegswirtschaft
The public administration and the war economy: the nature of the economic tasks that the modern popular war imposed on the state; the concept of the war economy as the inevitable consequence of the mass war; the blockade and its influence on the formation of the Central Powers’ war economy; Austria’s economic position at the opening of the war; the government’s concern for the feeding of the people from the very outset; the conduct of Hungary in regard of export to Austria — Austria’s complete economic isolation by Hungary; the introduction of a planned state raw-materials economy and the rationing of foodstuffs; the organisation of the Kriegsgetreideverkehrsanstalt (war-grain traffic institute); the creation of the new central authority for food, the Amt für Volksernährung; the administrative apparatus for securing the food supply; a survey of the laws and decrees by which the state food economy was carried out; the Wirtschaftszentralen as the second principal form of the war-economy organisation, extended over the whole field of industrial production and trade, with their statistics, types and tasks; the character of the state war economy as a whole and its practical consequences for the social condition; its nature as a price-police, the principle of maximum prices first fixed in the grain economy; the securing of raw materials for the war industry; the rise of the industrial war economy and the step-by-step abolition of free economic intercourse, first in the cotton and then in the metal industries; the rise of the special war associations (Kriegsverbände) of the several branches of industry and trade; and the progressive militarisation of industry through the administration of the Zentrale.
VII. Die Kriegswirtschaft und der Staatssozialismus des Krieges in Österreich
The war economy and the state socialism of the war: the middle position of the Austrian government between the Armeeoberkommando and the war ministry on one side and industrial production and the consuming population on the other; the enormous extension of the whole war-economy apparatus and its capacity; the new organisations created in the war ministry; the militarised civil bearers of this war economy, and the double organism of military and civil war-economy leadership; the difficulties and defects of the civil administrative authorities in face of the war economy; this practical war-state-socialism as a theory developed in Germany and Austria; the further formation of this theory in the doctrine of the necessity of a transitional economy (Übergangswirtschaft) at the coming of peace; the creation of the Generalkommissariat für Kriegs- und Übergangswirtschaft as the high point of the intellectual development of the war economy in Austria; the retrospect on the rise and development of the war economy in the Denkschrift of the ministry of commerce of 1917; the connection of its ideas with the movement founded by Friedrich Naumann for a Mitteleuropa on a political and economic unity under Prussian-German leadership; and the failure of the war economy in Austria as a consequence of the overstraining of the physical, moral and spiritual forces of the population and of the excessive length of the war.
VIII. Die zweite Periode der Kriegsregierung
The second period of the war government: the death of the Emperor Francis Joseph and the accession of Emperor Charles; the weakening of the army command’s influence on the Austrian government and on the shaping of home politics; the ministry of Koerber as the transition from the “unpolitical” to a political war government; the formation of the ministry of Count Clam-Martinitz for the purpose of a dictatorial remodelling of the constitution in a German-national sense; the programme of the German-nationals for the future home and foreign policy of Austria and the peace-of-victory policy after the outbreak of the Russian revolution; the convocation of parliament and the appearance of separatist strivings among Czechs and South Slavs; the return of the Clam-Martinitz government to the system of officials’ ministries and its permanent difficult position in parliament; the retirement of the Kriegsüberwachungsamt and the softening of the war dictatorship; the political standing of the several nations, the struggle of the Slav parties and of the social democracy against the absolutist war government and against militarisation; the uncertain attitude of the Polish club toward the government; the conflicts between the two houses of the Reichsrat; the reaction of the army command’s early measures against the non-German peoples on their political conduct; the amnesty granted by Emperor Charles and the deep resentment of German-Austrian public opinion at it; and the juxtaposition of dictatorship with a house of deputies in its majority hostile to the war, the rapid sinking of the government’s authority, the growth of anti-dynastic currents, the successes of foreign propaganda among the non-German peoples and the recognition of the Czechs as a belligerent nation, the October Manifesto of the Emperor as the last attempt to preserve the Reich, the paralysis of parliament and its dissolution into purely national groups, the beginning of the catastrophe in September 1918, the collapse of the state food economy in the war zone and in the hinterland alike, the peace offers of the foreign minister Baron Burian and the ministry of Lammasch, the increasing paralysis of the central government and the dissolution of the Austrian state — the collapse of Reich and state.
IX. Der Untergang des Reiches, die neuen Nationalstaaten und das altösterreichische Amtentum
The fall of the Reich, the new national states and the old-Austrian officialdom: the adaptation of the old-Austrian civil service to the new conditions created by the collapse; the survival of the bureaucratic institutions in the national states and the quiet continuance of the officials’ work; the nationalisation of the old-Austrian officialdom in the provinces during the last two decades of the Reich; the reaction of the war economy on the independence of the provincial administration; the reaction of the political forces set free by the war on the officials’ attitude toward the idea of the unitary state; the growing democratisation and nationalisation in the disposition of the state’s officials long before the war, at length penetrating the German officialdom too; the loosening of the whole administrative apparatus, wholly so during the war government; the retrospect on the principal moments in the dissolution of the central state organisation; and the extinguishing of the state idea at length in the bureaucracy as in the free intelligence and the masses of the several nations. Redlich concludes that the October Manifesto of Emperor Charles was the formal, legally valid dissolution of the historic unitary state: by his word the Emperor himself — exercising for the last time the right of autocratic constitutional legislation that the house of Habsburg had always claimed — called the complex of new national states into being, and thereby released the officialdom of every nationality for its share in the revolutionary steps that followed. The dissolution of Reich and state went forward on a formally legal path; the last act of the dynasty gave the new states, ready formed in the person of their national officials, the organs with which to begin independent government, and so made the parting and the first independent steps of the peoples easier than they would otherwise have been.
Literatur-Angaben
A brief account of the material on which the work draws, disclaiming any exhaustive bibliography: the daily press of Vienna, Prague and the other provincial capitals as a principal source for the war period (its value lowered by the strict censorship), the radical press as the richest source for the historian; the weekly Der österreichische Volkswirt of Walter Federn and Gustav Stolper as an unequalled treasury and running commentary for all the economic phenomena of the war years; and the works and reports of the war administration itself — the printed emergency statutes and decrees, the handbooks of the war-economy organisations and their activity reports, the Denkschrift of Richard Riedl on the transitional economy, the report of the commissions that examined the war-economy organisations, and the protocol of Friedrich Adler’s trial before the exceptional court of May 1917.
Anhang
The plan of the Wirtschafts- und Sozialgeschichte des Weltkrieges: the editors and national editing committees (Austria-Hungary under Wieser, Riedl and Schüller with Shotwell as chairman; Germany under Melchior, Bauer, Bücher, Duisberg, Mendelssohn Bartholdy and Sering; Belgium under Pirenne; France under Gide; Great Britain under Beveridge, Davis, Jones, Keynes, Hirst and Scott; Italy under Einaudi; Jugoslavia under Bajkitsch; the Netherlands under Greven; Rumania under Mitrany; Russia under Vinogradoff; Scandinavia under Westergaard and Heckscher), and the list of publications of the series — the Austrian volumes on the government and administration (Redlich’s own), on industry, on the regulation of food and agriculture, of labour, on the railways, on coal supply, on crime and war, on the influence of the war on the spirit and manners of society (Seipel), the volumes on the war costs, on foreign economic policy and the exhaustion and dissolution of the Monarchy, and the corresponding Hungarian and public-health volumes.

sources/sabatier-orientation-religieuse-.title: Sabatier — L'orientation religieuse de la France actuelle
sources/sabatier-orientation-religieuse-.content:
Sabatier — L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle
Paul Sabatier (1858–1928), L’orientation religieuse de la France actuelle. Paris: Librairie Armand Colin, rue de Mézières, 5, 1911 (© 1911 by Max Leclerc and H. Bourrelier, proprietors of Librairie Armand Colin). A volume of the Bibliothèque du Mouvement social contemporain (series secretary Charles Rolland), in-18, 3 fr. 50. The raw text in this wiki was taken from the University of California scan (call no. BR846 S=4; UC-NRLF shelfmark YB 71304) via Anna’s Archive; the scan already carries a text layer of 364 page-files, here reassembled in numerical order. Sabatier, the Protestant pastor and historian whose Vie de saint François d’Assise had earned him the Institut’s grand prix décennal Lefèvre-Deumier in 1905, writes here not as an ecclesiastic but as an observer of the “mouvement social contemporain” — in the words of the series programme, “faire connaître et comprendre le mouvement social, exposer les faits et les interpréter, sans jamais se substituer à eux.”
Dominant years in the text are 1870–1911.
Introduction — Dans quel esprit est écrit ce livre
The term “orientation religieuse” is not synonymous with “affaires religieuses” — the latter designates what is most exterior in religious and ecclesiastical facts, what they become when carried onto the political markets and used in the quarrels of parties, a chronicle written day by day and left to the newspapers. The book proposes instead to discover “des aspects de réalité et de vie.” Sabatier takes up the antique formula Historia magistra vitæ and gives it an ampler meaning: history no longer gives only examples of individual conduct, it rises to the conception of the living germs that the past contains and that the present must select as the seeds of a new century. He warns of the infidelity of every historical image and the difficulty of the historian in freeing himself from himself, and dismisses “la légende du Français léger.”
I — Religion et orientation religieuse
A search for a definition of religion that holds for the present time and civilisation. What many simple minds seek in religion is a fundamentally moral foundation. The spontaneous and unconscious symbolisation of dogma. The religious movement always works itself out at the expense of the churches. The Catholic Church and the rights she has to the recognition of France; her activity to conquer the direction of political opinion — the Bonne Presse; the uselessness of its efforts. The new religious orientation.
II — Ce qu’on trouvera dans ce livre, et ce qu’on n’y trouvera pas
The impossibility of being complete. The true significance of the Dreyfus affair. Scientific activity in the Catholic Church; essays of reform and of new religion. Reasons why portraits and proper names find little place here; the unconscious collaborators of the religious movement; certain saints whom it would be dangerous to name; the value of anonymous confidences. The question whether the several churches should receive a place proportional to their numerical importance; conversions; the negative impression produced on some spectators by the missionary zeal of certain converters. The exclusion of eccentric or morbid phenomena.
III — Les circonstances qui ont déterminé l’orientation religieuse actuelle
The effects of the war of 1870 on the conscience of the country. As individuals the priests showed themselves admirable citizens, but the Church, on the morrow of the disasters, did not know how to rise to the height of its task. The disposition of France before 1870 toward Germany and toward Protestantism; the Prussian conquest dealt an irreparable blow to the prestige of the Reformation.
IV — Malentendus de plus en plus graves entre l’Église et le peuple
The attitude of Alsace and of France transformed the political question of the annexed lands into a moral question. The inexactness of the formula that patriotism has become the religion of France; the new notion of patriotism, which the Church did not create. The flowering of certain ideas once sown by her seems sometimes to work against her. Among the other factors that strongly influenced the religious orientation must be counted the laic school — accused of being the nursery of crime. The error of the apologists of religion who seek to make of the fear of the “apache” a motive for a return to the faith. The Church, by appealing ceaselessly to the limitless devotion of her children, answers — and answers alone — the most powerful instinct of the human heart.
V — Les déficits de l’antireligion
The necessity of not confounding free thought with anticlericalism. The impression produced on rural populations by certain manifestations of the latter; a profound antipathy for clericalism found among certain peasants who yet refuse to join anticlerical organisations. Civil and religious funerals. The incapacity of anticlericalism to understand what the Catholicism of the rural populations is. The Church gives the sense of discipline, of solidarity, of harmony. The little success of the essays of scientific religion. Easter.
VI — La philosophie contemporaine et l’orientation religieuse
It is not the philosophers who created the present religious orientation. The efforts of the national elite, both in the labouring classes and among the intellectuals, to place itself before the living social reality. Christianity at its origins was a popular movement, not provoked by philosophical views. The efforts of MM. Pillon, Renouvier, Secrétan — their high value recognised in intellectual circles — had no appreciable practical influence. Why the present generation attaches itself to the thought of Bergson, Boutroux, William James. The tendencies of the new philosophy.
VII — Les vues philosophico-religieuses de J.-M. Guyau et d’Émile Boutroux
Guyau and his Irréligion de l’avenir, a work of ever-growing importance; his thoughts on a new notion of the love of God, of prayer, of doubt, on what is eternal in religions. Boutroux goes still further in the way of realism, of the comprehension of living truth and the love of institutions; without affirming the absolute perfection of the churches, he sees their effort toward the ideal and manifests to all a sympathy at once disinterested and efficacious, very new among philosophers. His definition of religion; the philosophy of contingency and the historical significance of its success; his thought on the postulates implied by every life conscious of itself, on the results of religious evolution, on rites and the religious future.
VIII — L’orientation religieuse dans l’art et la littérature
The constant solicitation of our attention by the most superficial facts. Segantini, Bœcklin, Courbet and the Enterrement à Ornans; Eugène Carrière and his Premier voile, his biography by M. Gabriel Séailles, his ideas on art and its union with life. The little religious influence in France of Russian and Scandinavian literature, and the causes. Sully Prudhomme; Maeterlinck; Charles Péguy.
IX — Les caractères et la direction du mouvement religieux actuel
Man today has above all the sense of life, and comprehends at once its power and the limits of his freedom. History tends to invade all intellectual domains and even to substitute itself for metaphysics; but the contemporary spirit does not oppose, under pretext of reality, a materialist conception of history to its dogmatic conception — it takes consciousness of life in history, and from then on the guiding thread is found. To whom does the child belong? Neither to the Church, nor to the State, nor to the parents. The historical sentiment in the toast of a village mayor. The lineaments of a laic morality and religion proceeding from the new conception of history. The irremediable weakness of certain religious reforms.
X — Notre orientation religieuse actuelle est essentiellement française
The unity of France is not above all political; how it affirms itself in the movement under study. Our present religious orientation is not of foreign origin. The mediocre enthusiasm of the country for industrial and commercial successes. The impossibility for France of entering into intimate relations with the German mentality, whether political or theological. Renan, precursor of present tendencies; Dr Harnack; the manifesto of a liberal German pastor proclaiming the piety that may exist among atheists; why “unconscious Christianity” would have no success in France.
XI — Ses manifestations dans le catholicisme
Two catholicisms coexist in the Church. Her great force is having created the sentiment of unity and of tradition. Students of the Catholic institutes at the lessons of the professors of the State; the prohibition of Rome. The Modernism. The administration of the Church in the hands of a committee of public safety. The success of the new tendencies. The diocese of Milan accused of being a nursery of modernism, as is the University of Fribourg (Switzerland). A page of the R. P. Sertillanges. A note on the Sillon.
XII — Ses manifestations dans le protestantisme
One should rather say the absence of manifestations. The unity of the Protestant character amid its ecclesiastical divisions; individualism. The Separation of Church and State permitted new schisms in the Reformed Church. Why the most evolved Catholics show themselves so severe toward Protestantism. Its situation as attested by the pastors Lafon and Morize. Are the Protestants as misjudged as they believe? Pastor Wagner and the abbé Lemire; Dean Auguste Sabatier. What wounds the sentiments of France in Protestantism. Is Protestant liberty complete? Pastor W. Monod, and how he grasped the religious character that atheism can have.
XIII — Ses manifestations dans la libre pensée
That free thought is not essentially anti-religious. Free examination according to Séailles and F. Buisson. The significance of the success of the Cahiers de la Quinzaine; the École des Hautes Études sociales and its section for the study of religion in its relations with society; the Union of freethinkers and free believers.
XIV — La création de l’École laïque
If the war of 1870 influenced our school organisation, the soul of the laic school comes from farther and higher — it is the new incarnation of a secular religious effort. In 1882 it was far from being anticlerical. The crusade preached against it by the conservative parties; its results. It is now put on notice to give children the spiritual nourishment they do not find elsewhere.
XV — L’enseignement moral à l’École
The laic effort toward an efficacious and solidly constituted morality. The moral anarchy from which we suffer. The efforts of Guyau, Pécaut, Wagner; the course of Jules Payot; the essay of M. Delvolvé and his generosity toward religious teaching. Are the hesitations of laic pedagogy the proof of a failure? Laic mysticism.
XVI — L’École et l’Église
The impossible neutrality. The place and role of the history of religions in education; the new conception of history; the attitude of our contemporaries toward religious questions. The re-possession of the Bible; the return of admiration for the churches and the monuments of the past; a non-Catholic historian at mass at Notre-Dame de Paris.
Conclusion
To sum up the present religious situation of the country one must note two facts in appearance contradictory: the rapid progress of indifference and an unexpected awakening of religious aspirations — often to be observed in one and the same individual. It seems that we have arrived at an epoch of reconstitution, one might say of religious revenge, somewhat analogous to the origins of Christianity. If the Roman Church appears to have been struck more than any other by the political and intellectual crisis, yet in the midst of the spiritual ruins that surround us present thought goes to seek, to make the foundations and columns of the new temple, ideas and sentiments of undoubted Catholic origin: the sentiment of the mystery that envelops and grips us, of the unity and solidarity of all existences through time as through space; the great law of tradition; the certitude that man has a duty and that this duty is to give his harmonious note in the eternal concert; the conviction that every effort is worth only in the measure that it is disinterested and that the most living man is he who gives, forgets, sacrifices himself. All these sentiments are those of the present generation, and it is the Church that sowed their seeds in its heart. The Roman Church, despite its failures and appearances, keeps in the heart and conscience of the elite of the coming generation a unique, incomparable place, because alone it has taken consciousness of the unity and eternity of its life.

sources/sosnosky-die-balkanpolitik-oster.title: Sosnosky — Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866, Band I
sources/sosnosky-die-balkanpolitik-oster.content:
Sosnosky — Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866, Band I
Theodor von Sosnosky (1866–1930), Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866. Erster Band. Stuttgart: Deutsche Verlags-Anstalt, 1915. With two maps and an appendix. A contemporary account of some three hundred and thirty pages, drawn from the scanned copy (University of California, Berkeley; Google/Anna’s Archive scan, oclc 2757943) via the already-OCR’d Fraktur page texts; the raw text in this wiki is that scan (330 pages). As Sosnosky states in his preface, the purpose of the work is a clear, connected account of the share that the Habsburg monarchy took in the Oriental Question from 1866 down to the most recent Balkan crisis; because the causal connection of the events would not appear unless the historical background were supplied, he opened with a retrospect (Rückblicke), and he dwelled with deliberate emphasis on the military side — recalling that war is nothing but the continuation of politics by other means.
Dominant years in the text are 1866–1878 (with the long retrospect to 1526), the decisive term being the occupation of Bosnia in 1878.
Vorwort
Sosnosky sets out the aim of the whole work — a connected narrative of the Habsburg share in the Oriental Question from 1866 to the most recent Balkan crisis — and justifies the historical retrospect with which Band I opens, without which the account would hang in the air. He explains why some episodes (the Crimean crisis, the diplomatic mine-war that preceded the occupation of Bosnia) are treated only briefly, and why the military side is so strongly emphasized: war is the continuation of politics by other means. He cites the example of Friedjung’s Der Kampf um die Vorherrschaft in Deutschland, whose second volume is nearly all military history, and remarks that a statesman such as Kaiser Wilhelm I rose to his historical greatness only with Roon and Moltke beside him to translate his great thoughts into great deeds.
Erster Abschnitt: Rückblicke
I. Die Angriffskriege der Türken, 1526–1718 — the age of Turkish attack: from Mohács (1526) through the sieges of Vienna and the long wars of reconquest, down to the treaties that rolled back the Ottoman advance. II. Die Verteidigungskriege der Türken, 1719–1792 — the period of Turkish defence, as the monarchy and Russia pressed the retreat of the Porte in the eighteenth century. III. Von Kaunitz bis Beust, 1792–1866 — Austria’s Balkan policy from Kaunitz to Beust: (1) Der serbische Aufstand — the Serbian rising under Karađorđe and Miloš; (2) Die griechische Frage — the Greek war of independence; (3) Konservierungspolitik — Austria’s conserving, status-quo policy in the East; (4) Der neue Kurs — the new course; (5) Österreich im Krimkriege — Austria’s part in the Crimean War.
Zweiter Abschnitt: Der Aufstand der Bocchesen
The insurrection of the Bokelj (Bocchesi) in the Bay of Kotor in 1869 — an episode to which Sosnosky devotes a special section because of its dramatic and exemplary character in the history of the monarchy’s South-Slav policy.
Dritter Abschnitt: Die bosnische Frage
I. Nach 1866 — Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Austrian horizon after Königgrätz. II. Vor dem Sturm — the gathering of the crisis. III. Die Zustände in Bosnien und in der Herzegovina — the condition of Bosnia and Herzegovina under Turkish rule: the anarchy, the agrarian misery, the confessional hatreds. IV. Sturmboten — the portents of the storm. V. Österreich und Bosnien — the Austrian claims and policy toward Bosnia. VI. Andrássys Balkanprogramm — the Balkan programme of Gyula Andrássy. VII. Beschwichtigungsversuche — the attempts at appeasement. VIII. Von Reichstadt nach Konstantinopel — from the Reichstadt agreement with Russia to the diplomacy at Constantinople. IX. Österreich-Ungarn und Rußland — the Austro-Russian rivalry and understanding. X. Andrássys Balkanpolitik und die Volksvertretungen — Andrássy’s Balkan policy before the Hungarian and Austrian parliaments. XI. Der Berliner Kongreß — the Congress of Berlin (1878) and the mandate given to Austria-Hungary to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina. XII. Vor dem Einmarsch — the eve of the entry of the occupation troops.
Vierter Abschnitt: Die Okkupation
The military occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the late summer of 1878: I. Der Schauplatz der Okkupation — the theatre of operations; II. Die Streitkräfte der Insurgenten — the forces of the insurgents who met the Austro-Hungarian army; III. Die militärischen Vorbereitungen Österreich-Ungarns — the military preparations of the monarchy; IV. Die Mittelkolonne — the central column; V. Die rechte Kolonne — the right column; VI. Die linke Kolonne — the left column; VII. In der Herzegovina — the operations in Herzegovina; VIII. Der Marsch auf Sarajevo — the march on Sarajevo; IX. Die Einnahme von Sarajevo — the capture of Sarajevo (19 August 1878); X. Neugruppierung der Streitkräfte — the regrouping of the forces; XI. In der Posavina und Župa — the operations in the Posavina and the Župa; XII. Wieder in der Herzegovina — the renewed fighting in Herzegovina; XIII. In Südbosnien — in southern Bosnia; XIV. In Nordwestbosnien — in northwestern Bosnia; XV. Heimkehr — the return home; XVI. Resumé — the summing-up of the campaign, its cost and its meaning.
Anhang (Appendix)
I. Denkschrift des Feldmarschalls Grafen Radetzky vom 30. August 1856 — the memorandum of Field Marshal Count Radetzky of 30 August 1856, on the military and strategic value of Bosnia and the South-Slav lands. II. Ordre de bataille der Okkupationstruppen, Anfang August 1878 — the order of battle of the occupation troops at the beginning of August 1878. Followed by a Personenregister (index of persons).
Series note
This is the first band of Sosnosky’s two-volume account of the Habsburg monarchy’s Balkan policy. It carries the Eastern thread of the 1866–1919 period from the aftermath of Königgrätz through the great crisis of 1878 — the Congress of Berlin and the occupation of Bosnia — which is the very hinge of the period’s Eastern Question, and it pairs with the second band, Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866, Band II, which carries the same policy from the Berlin settlement down to the Peace of Bukarest (1913). It is the Austrian counterpart, along the Eastern road, of Sosnosky’s own Die Politik im Habsburgerreiche and of Hanotaux’s account of the Eastern Question through Berlin.

sources/sosnosky-die-balkanpolitik-oster.title: Sosnosky — Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866, Band II
sources/sosnosky-die-balkanpolitik-oster.content:
Sosnosky — Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866, Band II
Theodor von Sosnosky (1866–1930), Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866. Zweiter Band. Stuttgart und Berlin: Deutsche Verlags-Anstalt, 1914. With one map. A contemporary account of some four hundred and thirty pages, drawn from the scanned copy (University of Michigan; Google/Anna’s Archive scan, oclc 2757943) via the already-OCR’d Fraktur page texts; the raw text in this wiki is that scan (432 pages). In his preface Sosnosky states that he has kept the boundary line drawn in the preface of the first band and closed the whole work with the Peace of Bukarest (August 1913); he resisted the temptation to carry the Balkan events down to the immediate present, above all for reasons of space and time, given the enormous wealth of the material. He also records his special attention to the relations of the monarchy to Italy in so far as they concern Balkan policy, depicted, as he says, without embellishment, as they actually are, not in the artificial limelight in which the leading daily press likes to show them.
Dominant years in the text are 1878–1913, the decisive terms being the Bulgarian crisis of 1885–1888, the annexation crisis of 1908–1909, and the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913.
Vorwort
Sosnosky explains that this band too needs a preface: he has held to the boundary drawn in the first volume and closes the work with the Peace of Bukarest (August 1913), resisting the temptation to bring the story down to the immediate present for reasons of space and time — the material is overwhelming. He further notes his special attention to the monarchy’s relations with Italy in their bearing on Balkan policy, drawn as they truly are rather than in the flattering light of the press, and protests that this implies no antipathy toward the Italians.
Erster Abschnitt: Nachwehen
Einleitung: Nach dem Berliner Kongresse — the condition of the Balkan peninsula and of the monarchy’s policy in the years immediately after the Congress of Berlin. I. Andrássy als Angeklagter — Andrássy under attack at home for the policy that had led to the occupation. II. Novibazar — the Sandjak of Novi Pazar, its garrison and its significance for the Austro-Hungarian position. III. Der Aufstand vom Jahre 1882 — the rising of 1882 in the annexed lands.
Zweiter Abschnitt: Assekuranz-Politik
The “insurance policy” of the monarchy in its alliances: I. Österreich-Ungarn und das Deutsche Reich — the Dual Alliance with Germany; II. Italien auf dem Scheidewege — Italy at the crossroads, the making of the Triple Alliance; III. Österreich-Ungarn und Rußland — the Austro-Russian entente of the Dreikaiserbund and its limits.
Dritter Abschnitt: Die bulgarische Frage
The Bulgarian question, the great trial of the monarchy’s Eastern policy under the chancellorship of Gustav Kálnoky: I. Der Staatsstreich — the coup in Eastern Rumelia (1885); II. Bulgarien und Rußland — the estrangement of Bulgaria from Russia; III. Der Serbisch-Bulgarische Krieg — the Serbo-Bulgarian War of 1885; IV. Rußlands Rache — Russia’s revenge; V. Die Balkanpolitik des Grafen Kálnoky — Kálnoky’s Balkan policy; VI. Kálnoky und Bismarck — Kálnoky and Bismarck; VII. Die Erneuerung des Dreibunds — the renewal of the Triple Alliance; VIII. Um den bulgarischen Thron — the contest over the Bulgarian throne; IX. Bismarck und Rußland — Bismarck and Russia; X. Der deutsch-russische Geheimvertrag — the secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887; XI. Bismarcks Rede vom 6. Februar 1888 — Bismarck’s great Reichstag speech of 6 February 1888; XII. Die Lösung der bulgarischen Frage — the solution of the Bulgarian question.
Vierter Abschnitt: Wetterleuchten
The “summer lightning” of the new century: I. Kreta — Crete and the Greco-Turkish troubles; II. Mazedonien — Macedonia and the rising of the komitadjis, the murky ground of Austro-Russian agreement (Mürzsteg); III. Die Sandschakbahn — the projected Sandjak railway.
Fünfter Abschnitt: Die Annexion
The Bosnian annexation crisis of 1908: I. Der Annexionsakt — the act of annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (October 1908) by Aehrenthal; II. Das Echo — the reaction: among the Powers (England, France, Russia, Italy, Germany) and on the Balkan itself (Turkey, Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria, Greece); III. Der Verlauf der Krise — the course of the crisis, the Serbian clamour and the Austro-Hungarian mobilization, and the settlement; IV. Der Friedjung-Prozeß — the Friedjung libel trial (1909) over the forged documents against the South-Slav leaders; V. Ährenthals Annexionspolitik — an assessment of Aehrenthal’s annexation policy.
Sechster Abschnitt: Die Balkan-Katastrophe
The Balkan Wars of 1912–1913: I. Seltsame Bundesgenossen — the strange allies; II. Albanien — the Albanian question and the rising of 1912; III. Tripolis — the Italo-Turkish war over Tripoli (1911); IV. Der Balkanbund — the formation of the Balkan League of Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro; V. Der Status quo — the status-quo diplomacy of Count Berchtold; VI. “Der Balkan den Balkanvölkern” — the watchword “the Balkans for the Balkan peoples”; VII. Die legitimen Interessen Österreich-Ungarns — the legitimate interests of the monarchy; VIII. Die Affäre Prochaska — the Prochaska affair; IX. Pourparlers — the negotiations of the Powers; X. Um Albanien — the struggle over Albania; XI. Friedensverhandlungen — the peace negotiations; XII. “Entspannung” — the (illusory) relaxation; XIII. Montenegro und Österreich-Ungarn — Montenegro’s relation to the monarchy; XIV. Montenegro und Europa — Montenegro before Europe (the naval demonstration at Scutari, Montenegro and Russia, Nikita’s triumph); XV. Montenegros Rückzug — Montenegro’s retreat; XVI. Kriegspause — the pause between the wars (the question of intervention, the road to peace); XVII. Rumänien und Bulgarien — Romania and Bulgaria; XVIII. Die Balkanbündler untereinander — the Balkan allies among themselves, the seeds of the second war; XIX. Bulgarien in Not — Bulgaria in distress; XX. Der zweite Balkankrieg und die Mächte — the second Balkan War and the Powers; XXI. Der Friede von Bukarest — the Peace of Bukarest (August 1913); XXII. Finale — the finale; XXIII. Die Balkanpolitik des Grafen Berchtold — Berchtold’s Balkan policy (the non-occupation of the Sandjak, the creation of Albania, the policy toward Romania, the Prochaska affair).
Nachwort: Rückblick und Ausblick
Sosnosky’s closing retrospect and prospect: he looks back over the monarchy’s Balkan policy from the Congress of Berlin to the Peace of Bukarest and out to the future — the position of Austria-Hungary in the Balkan world, the sources of its interest in the peninsula, and the gathering storm that he discerned on the horizon before Sarajevo. The volume closes with a Personenregister (index of persons).
Series note
This is the second and concluding band of Sosnosky’s two-volume account of the Habsburg monarchy’s Balkan policy, carrying the Eastern thread of the 1866–1919 period from the Berlin settlement of 1878 through the Bulgarian crisis, the annexation crisis of 1908, and the Balkan Wars down to the Peace of Bukarest (August 1913) — the immediate prelude, in time and in temper, to the July crisis of 1914. It completes Band I and stands alongside Sosnosky’s own Die Politik im Habsburgerreiche as the Austrian thread of the wiki’s Eastern and Central-European coverage in the years before the First World War.

sources/sosnosky-die-politik-im-habsburg.title: Sosnosky — Die Politik im Habsburgerreiche
sources/sosnosky-die-politik-im-habsburg.content:
Sosnosky — Die Politik im Habsburgerreiche
Theodor von Sosnosky (1866–1930), Die Politik im Habsburgerreiche. Randglossen zur Zeitgeschichte. Zweite, durchgesehene Auflage. Berlin: Allgemeiner Verein für Deutsche Literatur (Hermann Paetel Verlag), 1913. A two-volume contemporary survey of roughly seven hundred and sixty pages, drawn from the scanned set preserved in a library copy (Google/Anna’s Archive scan, oclc 2179412) via the already-OCR’d Fraktur page texts; the raw text in this wiki is that single complete two-volume scan (762 pages). Sosnosky, a German publicist and political writer in Vienna, wrote deliberately not as strict scientific history but as a living “Randglossen” commentary on the politics of the Habsburg monarchy — moved, as his preface says, by the surprising poverty of the German literature on so rich and dramatic a subject, and treating the present and the immediate past.
Dominant years in the text are 1878–1913 (with the long retrospect on Austrian policy from Schwarzenberg onward and the Magyarization politics of the Dualist era).
Band I — Erster Teil: Äussere Politik
Vorwort (Band I)
Sosnosky opens on the superabundant, dramatic and passionate material of the politics of the Habsburg monarchy, and on the strange poverty of the German literature devoted to it — pamphlets there are in plenty, but books for the day that treat the subject thoroughly are few, and other languages have more on it than German. He declares that his work “shall not be a history”, at least not in the strict scientific sense, but a commentary on the politics of the present and the immediate past.
I. Von Schwarzenberg bis Aehrenthal
A review of Austria-Hungary’s foreign policy from the age of Prince Felix zu Schwarzenberg and the reaction after 1848 down to the chancellorship of Alois Lexa von Aehrenthal (1906–1912) — the retreat from the German Question after 1866, the Eastern orientation, and the shift of the monarchy’s weight toward the Balkans that culminated in the Bosnian crisis.
II. Die Annexion
The annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (October 1908) and its international consequences — the Aehrenthal policy that tore up Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin, the crisis with the Porte, the storm in Serbia and Montenegro, and the stand of the Great Powers.
III. Österreich und das Deutsche Reich
The relations of the monarchy to the German Empire — the Dual Alliance of 1879 and its working, the standing of Austria-Hungary in Bismarck’s and then Wilhelmine Germany’s system of alliances, and the growing frictions and dependencies between the two empires.
IV. Österreich und Italien
Austria-Hungary’s relations with Italy — the unredeemed irredenta and the contest for the Adriatic, and the place of the Italian alliance in the Triple Alliance.
Band I — Zweiter Teil: Innere Politik (in Österreich)
Einleitung: Das System
The constitutional system of the Austrian half of the monarchy after the Ausgleich — the character of the Reichsrat and of the parliamentary life of Cisleithania, the frame within which the national struggles of the Austrian peoples unfolded.
1. Der nationale Hader (a) Allgemeines
Das nationale Prinzip — the rise of the national principle as the governing force of the age, and its effect upon the multi-national state; Nationalität und Sprache — the identification of nation with language and the struggles that followed.
(b) Besonderes: Die nationalen Strömungen
I. Alldeutschtum — the pan-German movement within Austria and its contest against the other nationalities. II. Panslawismus — the pan-Slav current, examined in turn among the Tschechen (Czechs), Südslawen (South Slavs), Polen, and Ruthenen. III. Irredenta — the Italian irredentist movement in the Austrian littoral and Tyrol.
(c) Resumé
I. Die Symptome and II. Die Ursachen — the symptoms of the national malady of the Austrian state and its deeper causes, as diagnosed by Sosnosky at the close of the first part.
Band II — Die Politik in Ungarn
Vorwort (Band II)
Sosnosky explains the changed disposition of the second band, occasioned by the ever more significant and louder events within the lands of St. Stephen’s Crown: he was moved to treat these affairs far more fully than originally intended, and — bound by contractual limits of space — to “amputate” elsewhere in order to keep the treatment of Hungarian conditions from being cramped. He also answers the attacks that certain quarters had made upon his first band: he would not trouble his readers over merely adverse judgments, nor over the personal barbs, but replies to the malicious attempts to injure him in business that accompanied them.
Einleitung: Magyarische Politik
An opening portrait of Magyar politics and character — the passionate, domineering temper of the Hungarian political nation, its self-absorption, and the attitude toward the non-Magyar peoples of the kingdom.
Erster Abschnitt: Ungarn und Österreich
I. Los von Österreich! — the “Away from Austria!” movement in Hungary, its adherents and its programme. II. Der Ausgleich — the Compromise of 1867 as it stood within Hungary, the Deák settlement and its opponents. III. Ungarn und Österreich — the real relation of Hungary to Austria under the dualism. IV. Die Magyaren und die Krone — the Magyar attitude to the Crown and the monarch. V. Der Kampf um die Armee — the long struggle over the common army, its language of command, the Hungarian military demands, and the crisis this provoked.
Zweiter Abschnitt: Der nationale Hader in Ungarn
Einleitung: Der “magyarische Nationalstaat” — the Magyar conception of the national state, against the background of which the subject-nationalities of Hungary were treated.
I. Die “Nation” — under A. Panmagyarismus and B. Magyarisierung: the general theory (the school, the courts, the electoral system, the results of Magyarization, and the “Talmi-Magyaren” — the sham or half Magyarized). II. Die “Nationalitäten” — the subject peoples: the Deutschen (Germans), the Rumänen (Romanians), the Slowaken (Slovaks), the Ruthenen (Ruthenians), and the Serben (Serbs), and the working of the Magyar national state upon each. III. Kroatien und Ungarn — Croatia-Slavonia and its relation to the Hungarian kingdom under the nagodba of 1868.
Resumé: Die österreichische Frage
I. Die politische Bedeutung des Habsburgerreichs — the political weight and the raison d’être of the Habsburg monarchy within the European state-system. II. Die Entwicklungsmöglichkeiten des Habsburgerreichs — the possible futures of the monarchy as Sosnosky surveyed them on the eve of 1914: (1) Revision des Dualismus — a revision of the dualism; (2) Groß-Ungarn — the greater-Hungarian solution; (3) Trialismus — the trialist reorganization, chiefly with the South Slavs; (4) Groß-Österreich — the federal plan (of Aurel Popovici) of a “Greater Austria”. His closing argument — reached after weighing these alternatives — is that the future of the monarchy lay in an inner reform that should reconcile the peoples with the state; the work closes on the motto that he held before the Habsburg monarchy: to attain unity through multiplicity, and so to embody the watchword of its ruler — viribus unitis (“with united forces”).
Series note
This work stands as the Austrian–Hungarian political thread of the 1866–1919 period: it is a contemporary German account of the internal and external politics of the Dual Monarchy from the age of Bismarck down to the crisis years before Sarajevo, written by a Vienna-based German publicist. It complements the constitutional-juridical Hungarian view of Beksics, A dualismus with a German-national perspective on the same monarchy, and it looks forward along the Balkan road that Sosnosky’s own Die Balkanpolitik Österreich-Ungarns seit 1866 traces in detail, down to the eve of the First World War.

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 4
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Chapters
Dreizehntes Buch: Spannung zwischen Österreich und Preußen (Tension between Austria and Prussia)
Covers the escalating tensions in the German Confederation following the Danish War (1864), the growing rivalry over the administration of Schleswig-Holstein, and the diplomatic manoeuvring that poisoned relations between the two great German powers.
Vierzehntes Buch: Bruch zwischen Österreich und Preußen (Break between Austria and Prussia)

1. Kapitel: Allseitige Rüstung (Arming on all sides) — Details the military preparations undertaken by both Austria and Prussia, including mobilisation schedules, troop concentrations, and financial measures for war.
2. Kapitel: Letzter Einigungsversuch (Napoleon’s congress proposal, Gablenz mission) — Napoleon III’s proposal for a European congress to settle the German question peaceably, and the Gablenz mission as a last-ditch attempt at Austro-Prussian accommodation.
3. Kapitel: Österreich und Frankreich (Secret negotiations) — The secret diplomatic exchanges between Vienna and Paris, including Austrian overtures for French neutrality or support, and the quid pro quo of territorial compensation.

Fünfzehntes Buch: Preußisch-italienisches Bündnis (Prussian-Italian Alliance)
The negotiation and conclusion of the alliance between Prussia and the Kingdom of Italy (April 1866), the terms of the treaty, Bismarck’s strategic calculations, and Italy’s expectation of Venetia as the prize for joining the war against Austria.
Sechzehntes Buch: Übereinkunft und Gastein (Agreement and Gastein Convention)
The Gastein Convention (August 1865) as a temporary expedient to partition administration of the Elbe Duchies, its terms, its reception by the German states and the European powers, and its ultimate failure to prevent the inevitable clash.

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 5
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Chapters
Siebzehntes Buch: Italien (The Italian theatre)

1. Kapitel: Die beiderseitigen Heere (Benedek, Austrian army at Olmütz, deficiencies) — Analysis of the opposing armies: the Austrian Northern Army under Feldzeugmeister Ludwig von Benedek, its concentration at Olmütz, organisational problems, logistical deficiencies, and the command controversies that hampered its effectiveness.
2. Kapitel: Unterwerfung Norddeutschlands (Hanover, Langensalza) — The Prussian campaign against the German allied states of the Confederation: the occupation of Hanover, Saxony, and Electoral Hesse; the Battle of Langensalza (27 June 1866) and the capitulation of the Hanoverian army.
3. Kapitel: Custoza (Italian defeat at Custoza) — The Italian campaign: the Austrian victory under Archduke Albrecht at the Battle of Custoza (24 June 1866), the operational failures of the Italian army under General Alfonso La Marmora, and the strategic consequences for the Italian alliance.

Achtzehntes Buch: Böhmischer Krieg (The Bohemian campaign)
The main theatre of war: the Prussian advance into Bohemia in three separate armies (Elbe, 1st, and 2nd Armies under Herwarth von Bittenfeld, Prince Friedrich Karl, and Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm), the battles of Gitschin (Jičín) and Münchengrätz, and the climactic Battle of Königgrätz/Sadowa (3 July 1866) — Moltke’s masterpiece of concentration and the decisive defeat of the Austrian army, with detailed tactical analysis of the Prussian needle-gun advantage and Benedek’s failed defence.
Neunzehntes Buch: Unterhandlungen und Kämpfe (Negotiations and fighting)
The post-Königgrätz period: the armistice negotiations, the preliminary Peace of Nikolsburg, simultaneous military operations against the southern German states (Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden), the Prussian campaign on the Main, and the diplomatic interventions of Napoleon III as would-be mediator.
Zwanzigstes Buch: Grundlagen des neuen Reichs (Foundations of the new Reich)
The Peace of Prague (23 August 1866) and its terms: the dissolution of the German Confederation, Austrian exclusion from Germany, Prussian annexation of Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, and Frankfurt, the formation of the North German Confederation, and the constitutional groundwork for a unified German state under Prussian leadership.

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 6
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Chapters
Einundzwanzigstes Buch: Reform des Bundes (Reform of the Confederation)

1. Kapitel: Die neuen Zollvereinsverträge (New Zollverein treaties) — The renegotiation of the Zollverein (Customs Union) treaties in the wake of Prussian hegemony: the economic integration of the annexed territories, the pressure on the southern German states to accept new terms, and the link between economic unity and political unification.
2. Kapitel: Befestigung der Zollvereinsfrage (Consolidation of the Zollverein question) — The consolidation of the Customs Union as an instrument of Prussian policy, the Federal Customs Council (Zollbundesrat), the resistance of particularist interests in the south, and the interplay between tariff policy and the drive toward a unified German nation-state.

Zweiundzwanzigstes Buch: Norddeutscher Bund (North German Confederation)

1. Kapitel: Preußisch-deutsche Politik. Anfänge (Prussian-German policy. Beginnings) — The initial phase of Prussian statecraft under Bismarck after the war: the drafting of the North German Confederation constitution (the Augustenburg draft and Bismarck’s revisions), the relationship between the Federal Presidency (Bundespräsidium) and the Federal Council (Bundesrat), and the balance of power between Prussia and the smaller north German states.
2. Kapitel: Italien und spanische Händel (Italy and Spanish affairs) — Italian politics after the 1866 war: the acquisition of Venetia, internal instability in Italy, and the early stirrings of the Spanish question that would later culminate in the Hohenzollern candidature of 1870.
3. Kapitel: Deutsche und orientalische Frage (German and oriental question) — The interaction between German unification and the Eastern Question: the Cretan Revolt (1866–1869) against Ottoman rule, the great-power rivalries in the Balkans, and Bismarck’s emerging policy of limited engagement in oriental affairs.
4. Kapitel: Weitere Kapitel (Further chapters) — Subsequent chapters covering the first session of the North German Reichstag (1867), the debates over the federal constitution, military budgets, the Indemnity Bill, the military conventions with the southern German states (Baden, Bavaria, Württemberg, Hesse-Darmstadt), and the consolidation of the new federal institutions.

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 7
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Chapters
Dreiundzwanzigstes Buch: Deutschland und Frankreich (Germany and France)

1. Kapitel: Das erste Zollparlament (First Customs Parliament, Reichstag legislation) — The first Zollparlament (Customs Parliament) convened in 1868, bringing together deputies from the North German Confederation and the southern German states; the legislative work of the North German Reichstag, including military laws, fiscal legislation, and the gradual harmonisation of legal and economic frameworks.
2. Kapitel: Schwankungen der französischen Politik (Fluctuations in French policy, Ollivier, Napoleon’s reforms) — The internal political evolution of the Second French Empire: the liberal reforms of Émile Ollivier, the shift toward a ‘Liberal Empire’, the weaknesses of Napoleon III’s foreign policy, French public opinion, and the growing tension between Paris and Berlin.
3. Kapitel: Die luxemburgische Frage (The Luxembourg question) — The Luxembourg Crisis of 1867: Napoleon III’s bid to purchase Luxembourg from the Netherlands, Bismarck’s initial encouragement and subsequent denunciation, the threat of war, and the London Conference (May 1867) that guaranteed Luxembourg’s neutrality and led to the dismantling of its fortress.
4. Kapitel: Die Militärkonventionen (Military conventions with southern states) — The secret military conventions between Prussia and the southern German states (Baden, Bavaria, Württemberg, Hesse-Darmstadt) placing their armies under Prussian command in wartime — a crucial step toward military unity that would prove decisive in 1870.

Vierundzwanzigstes Buch: Ursprung des französischen Kriegs (Origin of the French War)
The immediate origins of the Franco-Prussian War: the offer of the Spanish crown to Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen (1870), the diplomatic crisis that followed, Bismarck’s role in promoting and then managing the candidature, the Ems Telegram (the ‘Ems Dispatch’), its deliberate editing by Bismarck to provoke French outrage, the French declaration of war (19 July 1870), and the mobilisation of the North German Confederation and the southern German states in a unified war effort against France.

sources/tivaroni-litalia-degli-italiani-.title: Tivaroni — L'Italia degli Italiani, Tomo II (1859–1866)
sources/tivaroni-litalia-degli-italiani-.content:
Tivaroni — L’Italia degli Italiani, Tomo II (1859–1866)
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. L’Italia degli Italiani. Tomo II (1859–1866). — Torino: Roux Frassati e Co., 1896.
The second volume of the series-within-the-work bearing the title L’Italia degli Italiani. It carries the national story from the war of 1859 through the making of the Kingdom of Italy in 1860–1861 and the first five years of the constitutional monarchy, closing on the eve of the war of 1866. Where the first volume had surveyed the restored absolutisms and the constitutional Piedmont, this volume is taken up almost entirely with the armed unification of the peninsula and with the ministries that governed the new Kingdom after the death of Cavour.
Tivaroni divides the volume into eight Parti (Parte III through Parte X, the numbering continuing from the two Parti of the first volume). The opening Parti treat the war against Austria and the annexations of central Italy; the middle of the volume follows the expedition of the Thousand and the fall of the Bourbons; the closing Parti follow the successive ministries of the new Kingdom — Ricasoli, Rattazzi, Farini-Minghetti and Lamarmora — down to 1866.
The volume is approximately 500 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive). It is the 506-page digitization.
Content Summary
Parte III — La guerra del 1859
The war of Italian independence against Austria.

The secret meeting of Plombières between Cavour and Napoleon III (1858)
The excitements and the plan for a European congress
The battle of Magenta (4 June 1859)
The battle of Solferino and San Martino (24 June 1859)
Villafranca and the peace

Parte IV — L’Italia Centrale
The revolutions and annexations of central Italy in 1859–1860.

Capitolo I — Le quattro rivoluzioni — the risings in Florence (27 April 1859), Modena, Parma and Bologna
Capitolo II — Bettino Ricasoli e Luigi Carlo Farini — the Tuscan and Emilian provisional governments
Capitolo III — Le Assemblee Costituenti — the constituent assemblies of the central states
Capitolo IV — L’imbarazzo del Governo di Torino — the embarrassment of the Piedmontese government
Capitolo V — La cessione di Savoia e di Nizza — the cession of Savoy and Nice for the annexation of central Italy

Parte V — L’anno decisivo
The decisive year of 1860: the expedition of the Thousand and the conquest of the south.

La spedizione dei Mille — the Sicilian precursors; the decision; the landing at Marsala; Calatafimi (15 May 1860) and the astonishing capture of Palermo (27 May 1860); Milazzo (20 July 1860); the crossing of the Straits of Messina; Naples in 1859 and 1860; the invasion of the Marches; the battle of the Volturno (1–2 October 1860); the Plebiscite (21 October 1860); the capture of Gaeta; the conclusion
La morte del conte di Cavour (6 June 1861) — the financial recklessness; Naples within the Kingdom of Italy and the brigantaggio; the negotiations of Cavour with the Holy See
Il primo Parlamento d’Italia — the opening of the first Italian Parliament

Parte VI
This Parte (its title is partly illegible in the OCR’d Indice) carries the early consolidation of the Kingdom through the first Parliament: the finances of the new state, the southern brigandage, and the negotiations with the Holy See over Rome.
Parte VII — Il Ministero Ricasoli
The ministry of Bettino Ricasoli (12 June 1861 – 2 March 1862).

The financial question
The solicitations of Ricasoli to Napoleon and to the Pope
The Comitati di provvedimento

Parte VIII — Il Ministero Rattazzi
The ministry of Urbano Rattazzi (3 March – 1 December 1862).

Sarnico — the Garibaldian rising in the north
Aspromonte — the wounding and capture of Garibaldi

Parte IX — Il Ministero Farini-Minghetti
The ministry of Luigi Carlo Farini and Marco Minghetti (9 December 1862 – 23 September 1864).

The enquiry into the southern railways
The September Convention (15 September 1864) with France over the Roman question

Parte X — Il Ministero Lamarmora
The ministry of Alfonso Lamarmora (23 September 1864 – 20 July 1866).

The armed bands in the Veneto
The ratification of the Convention

Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume and is partly garbled, so the structure above also draws on the running part-headers within the text. Tivaroni writes throughout from the perspective of the Risorgimento: the unification of the peninsula is treated as the culmination of the national movement, and the ministries after Cavour’s death are judged by how far they advanced the remaining national goals of Venice and Rome. The volume ends on the eve of the war of 1866, which the third volume takes up.

sources/tivaroni-litalia-degli-italiani-.title: Tivaroni — L'Italia degli Italiani, Tomo III (1866–1870)
sources/tivaroni-litalia-degli-italiani-.content:
Tivaroni — L’Italia degli Italiani, Tomo III (1866–1870)
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. L’Italia degli Italiani. Tomo III (1866–1870). — Torino: Roux Frassati e Co., 1897.
The third and final volume of the series-within-the-work bearing the title L’Italia degli Italiani, and the closing volume of the whole Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. It opens with the war of 1866 against Austria, which completed the acquisition of the Veneto, and carries the story through the long struggle of the Roman question to the breach of Porta Pia and the annexation of Rome (20 September 1870) — the last great act of Italian unification. The volume then turns from narrative to retrospect.
Tivaroni divides the volume into four Parti (Parte XI through Parte XIV, continuing the numbering from the two previous volumes of the series). The first two treat the war of 1866 and the Roman question; the third is a synthetic account of the development of the national idea across the whole Risorgimento; the fourth and last offers a gallery of biographical portraits of the leading figures of the movement, closing with the three great protagonists — Cavour, Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel II.
The volume is approximately 550 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive). It is the 572-page digitization.
Content Summary
Parte XI — La guerra del 1866
The third war of Italian independence, fought in alliance with Prussia.

The treaty of alliance with Prussia
The battle of Custoza (24 June 1866)
The inaction after Custoza
Garibaldi in the Trentino
The naval battle of Lissa (20 July 1866)
The cadeau du Veneto and the rising of Palermo

Parte XII — La questione romana
The long struggle over Rome between the Italian Kingdom and the Holy See.

The Syllabus (8 December 1864)
The ministry of Urbano Rattazzi (11 April – 19 October 1867)
The conspiracy in Rome
Mentana (3 November 1867)
The ministry of Luigi Federico Menabrea (27 October 1867 – 19 November 1869)
