The ministry of Giovanni Lanza and Quintino Sella (15 December 1869 – 20 September 1870)
The negotiations for alliance with Austria and France
The 20 September 1870 — the breach of Porta Pia and the occupation of Rome
Conclusion

Parte XIII — Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale
A retrospective survey of the growth of the national idea across the Risorgimento.

The height of Mazzini’s prestige
The germs of monarchical unity (Vincenzo Gioberti)
The murattismo
The Società Nazionale Italiana
The year 1859
The decisive year (1860)
The moderates and the partito d’azione
Culture in the Risorgimento
The question of Rome
The good and the evil

Parte XIV — Gli uomini del Risorgimento
A gallery of biographical portraits of the principal figures of the movement.

Nino Bixio, Agostino Bertani, Francesco Crispi, Benedetto Cairoli, Giorgio Pallavicino, Cesare Correnti, Antonio Scialoja, Silvio Spaventa, Giuseppe Pasolini, Aurelio Saffi, Agostino Depretis, Carlo Matteucci, Francesco Arese, Mariano D’Ayala
The Cardinal Antonelli
Massimo D’Azeglio, Angelo Brofferio, Giovanni Lanza, Quintino Sella, Marco Minghetti, Urbano Rattazzi, Alfonso Lamarmora, Luigi Carlo Farini
The Barone Ricasoli — the first part of his life; Ricasoli as unitario
The Conte di Cavour — his youth; the journalist, deputy and minister; the judgements upon him; his mind; the judgement of posterity
The Generale Garibaldi — the adventurer; the hero; Garibaldi the general; his doctrines; Garibaldi at Caprera; the judgement of history
Vittorio Emanuele — Re Galantuomo; the good and intelligent King; the first King of Italy

Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. Tivaroni writes throughout as a historian of the national movement, and this closing volume is the most explicitly retrospective of the series: the final Parti look back across the whole Risorgimento and sum up the significance of its principal actors, treating the completion of unification in 1870 as the culmination of the national achievement.

sources/witte-vospominaniya-t1-detstvo-a.title: Witte — Memoirs, Vol. 1 (1849–1894). Childhood. Reigns of Alexander II and Alexander III
sources/witte-vospominaniya-t1-detstvo-a.content:
Witte — Memoirs, Vol. 1 (1849–1894)
Count S. Yu. Witte (1849–1915) — Воспоминания. Vol. 1: (1849–1894). Childhood. Reigns of Alexander II and Alexander III. — Moscow: Publishing House of Socio-Economic Literature, 1960.
Introductory article and general editorship of commentary and index — A. L. Sidorov. Commentary on the volume — R. Sh. Ganelin and B. V. Ananich. Print run 75,000; set 15 March 1960, signed for press 31 August 1960.
Place in the set. The Soviet 1960 reissue arranged the memoirs in chronological order across three volumes:

























1960Period on titleChapters (running numbering)Vol. 1 (this file)1849–1894; childhood; Alexander II and III1–18Vol. 21894 – October 1905; Nicholas II19–51Vol. 317 October 1905–1911; Nicholas II52–70
Vol. 1 covers career to the death of Alexander III — Tiflis and the Caucasus, Odessa and the South-Western railways, the “Holy Brotherhood,” Borki, the department of railway affairs, the Ministry of Ways of Communication, the Ministry of Finance under Alexander III. Nicholas II begins in Vols. 2–3.
Contents of the volume. First-person testimony: ancestors (Witte, Fadeevs, Dolgorukys); the Caucasus under Vorontsov and Baryatinsky; education; service on the Odessa / South-Western railways; railway “kings”; 1 March 1881 and the “Holy Brotherhood”; Kiev under Drenteln; Alexander III’s journeys and the catastrophe at Borki; director of the department of railway affairs and journey to Central Asia; minister of ways of communication; cholera of 1892 and second marriage; Vyshnegradsky and appointment as minister of finance; portraits of persons in power; subordinates and activity of the Finance Ministry; Murman; extended characterization of Alexander III.
Character of the edition. Memoir text in new (Soviet) orthography; 1960 apparatus (Sidorov’s introduction, Ganelin–Ananich commentary, index). OCR medium–good: running heads “N Chapter …”, confusion of Roman/Arabic numerals and individual letters (П/Н, Ш/Щ); chapter headings restored from the table of contents and chapter openings.
Raw volume: ~2.32 MB, 32,036 lines. Internet Archive item: 3-1960_202510 (file Vol. 1 (1960)).
Raw text: wiki/raw/witte-vospominaniya-t1-detstvo-aleksandr-ii-iii-1960.txt.
Adjacent volumes of the same edition: Vols. 2–3, 1960. Junction with Kornilov, Part 3 (to 1891/92) and Granat, Vol. 8 (economy of the 1890s).

Chapters 1–18
Before chapter 1 — introductory article by A. L. Sidorov, “Count S. Yu. Witte and His ‘Memoirs’” (assessment of Witte as a figure of the era of transition to imperialism and the revolution of 1905–1907; character of the memoir text).
Chapter 1. On ancestors
Birth in Tiflis, 1849. Father — Yuly Fyodorovich Witte, director of the department of state domains in the Caucasus. Mother — Ekaterina Andreevna Fadeeva, daughter of a member of the chief administration of the Caucasian viceroy; on the Fadeev line — Princess Elena Pavlovna Dolgorukaya (senior branch of the Dolgorukys from Grigory Fyodorovich). Grandfather Fadeev came to the Caucasus under Prince Vorontsov; earlier managed foreign colonies in New Russia and was governor of Saratov. Sisters; a woman writer in the family circle (E. A. Gan and others).
Chapter 2. Rostislav Andreevich Fadeev
Uncle — only son of grandfather Fadeev; cadet corps; blow to an officer-instructor; exile as a soldier to a battery at Bendery under Nicholas I; later military and publicistic career. Family affection for “Rostik”; Fadeev’s role in the nephew’s fate.
Chapter 3. Caucasian viceroys
Baryatinsky; appointment of Grand Duke Mikhail Nikolaevich. Recollections of the visit of the heir-tsesarevich Nikolai Alexandrovich with Count Adlerberg. Life and youth of the viceroy’s staff; a boy’s observations in Tiflis.
Chapter 4. Recollections from childhood and youth
Early recollections (epidemic; grandfather on horseback); wet-nurse and nanny; family life; relatives’ laughter at the infant’s “impossible” memory. Transition to adolescence.
Chapter 5. Early upbringing. Gymnasium. University
Grandmother Dolgorukaya teaches reading and writing; free-hired wet-nurse and serf nanny; pictures of household drunkenness. Gymnasium; university course (pure mathematics); intention to remain at the chair.
Chapter 6. My service on the Odessa railway
University graduation (~1870). Prussia’s war with France; arrival of uncle Gen. Fadeev. Family objections to a professorship (“not a nobleman’s business”). Entry into railway service in Odessa; first years of practice.
Chapter 7. On the railway kings
After the war: unprofitability of the Odessa, Kiev–Brest, and Brest–Grajewo lines; merger into the Company of the South-Western Railways. Competition of private companies; “kings” and superfluous figures when administrations were united (Odessa, Kiev, Białystok). Witte’s place in the new structure.
Chapter 8. On the society “Holy Brotherhood” and my participation in it
1 March 1881: news in the Kiev theatre; letter to uncle Fadeev (comparison of the workshops’ “steam hammer” with the state’s powerlessness against anarchists). Participation in the “Holy Brotherhood”; Kiev context.
Chapter 9. My service in Kiev
Governor-general and commander — Gen.-Adm. Drenteln (army rear in the Turkish war; chief of gendarmes; transfer from Odessa). Drenteln’s wife. Witte’s service in Kiev on the South-Western; local society and administration.
Chapter 10. On Emperor Alexander III’s journeys over the South-Western railways. The catastrophe at Borki
Early visit of Alexander III with wife and sons Nicholas and George to Kiev. Escort of the imperial train (Andreevsky; replacement by Witte). Catastrophe at Borki; consequences for the Ministry of Ways of Communication and Witte’s career.
Chapter 11. My appointment as director of the department of railway affairs. Journey to Central Asia
Vyshnegradsky at the head of finance after Posyet’s departure; request for views on the profitability of the network. Idea of controlling tariffs of private companies (higher charter norms; competition for freights). Appointment as director of the department of railway affairs. Journey to Central Asia.
Chapter 12. My appointment as minister of ways of communication
After Borki: resignation of Adm. Posyet; Pauker. Characterization of Posyet (tutor of Grand Duke Alexei Alexandrovich; collision on the German Sea). Witte’s path to the Ministry of Ways of Communication.
Chapter 13. Journey to the cholera epidemic. Second marriage
Spring 1892; cholera on the Volga. Alexander III’s commission to the “youngest minister” to inspect measures (waterways and railways; general powers). Secretary; Prof. Pavlovsky in Samara. Second marriage in the same years.
Chapter 14. Ivan Alexeevich Vyshnegradsky. My appointment as minister of finance
Tsion’s memorandum against Vyshnegradsky (including accusation of a 500,000-fr. Rothschild bribe on the Paris loan); Witte’s report to the sovereign. Circumstances of Witte’s appointment as minister of finance in succession to Vyshnegradsky.
Chapter 15. On public figures and persons in power while I was department director and minister
Portraits: Count D. A. Tolstoy (MVD; “extreme right”; two fleeting meetings); other ministers and dignitaries of the end of Alexander III. Assessment by actions, not by personal acquaintance.
Chapter 16. On my subordinates and my activity as minister of finance
State Bank — Zhukovsky (reputation as a “leftist” from the 1860s Sovremennik; mediocre manager). Pleske — credit chancery, then bank manager; later Witte’s deputy as minister of finance. Recruitment of staff and first steps in the ministry.
Chapter 17. On my journey to the Murman coast
Alexander III’s attraction to the Russian North (type of peasantry; famine-relief committee while still heir). “Murman steamship company” and figures of the heir’s circle (Sheremetev and others). Witte’s journey to Murman.
Chapter 18. Emperor Alexander III
Summary characterization: “a great emperor”; undervalued by contemporaries; only 13 years of reign. Was not prepared for the throne (heir — elder brother Nicholas); circumstances of upbringing. Assessment of foreign and internal policy; death and reception in Russia and abroad. End of the first volume — on the threshold of Nicholas II’s accession (continues in vol. 2, ch. 19).

Completeness and relation to other volumes





















QuestionAnswerDoes Vol. 1 (1960) close Witte’s career to 1894?Yes — from birth and the Caucasus to the death of Alexander III and the emperor’s characterization (chs. 1–18).Is there material on Nicholas II after 1894 in 1960 Vol. 1?No — Nicholas II begins in Vol. 2 (ch. 19 “Beginning of the reign”).Is chapter numbering continuous?Yes across the whole 1960 three-volume set: 1–18 | 19–51 | 52–70.

Sources

Witte, S. Yu. Воспоминания. Vol. 1: (1849–1894). Childhood. Reigns of Alexander II and Alexander III. Moscow: Publishing House of Socio-Economic Literature, 1960. Internet Archive: 3-1960_202510 (Vol. 1). Raw: wiki/raw/witte-vospominaniya-t1-detstvo-aleksandr-ii-iii-1960.txt

Neighbors: Kornilov, Part 3; Granat, Vol. 8

sources/witte-vospominaniya-t2-3-nikolay.title: Witte — Memoirs, Vols. 2–3 (1894–1911). Reign of Nicholas II
sources/witte-vospominaniya-t2-3-nikolay.content:
Witte — Memoirs, Vols. 2–3 (1894–1911)
Count S. Yu. Witte (1849–1915) — Воспоминания. Vols. 2 and 3 of the Soviet three-volume set 1960 (Publishing House of Socio-Economic Literature, Moscow). Continuous chapter numbering 19–70 covers the reign of Nicholas II from the death of Alexander III to Kokovtsov’s premiership after the assassination of Stolypin (~1911).

Contents of the block. Finance and the Far East; spirit monopoly and gold currency; Bezobrazov and the 1903 resignation; Russo-Japanese War and Portsmouth; 9 January; Manifesto of 17 October; half-year premiership; loan of 1906; First and Second Dumas; 3 June 1907; Stolypin; Kokovtsov. Zhevakhov — Memoirs of a Deputy Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod, Vol. 1
Prince Nikolai Davidovich Zhevakhov (1874–1946) — Воспоминанія. Товарища Оберъ-Прокурора Св. Синода. Первый томъ. Сентябрь 1915 г. — Мартъ 1917 г. Munich: R. Oldenbourg Press, 1923.

































AuthorPrince N. D. Zhevakhov — official of the State Chancellery; from autumn 1916 deputy ober-procurator of the Holy Synod (under Ober-Procurator N. P. Raev)EditionMunich, 1923 (emigration); pre-reform orthographyIA idzhevahovndvospominanijaoberprokuroras2 (oras2 ≠ “volume 2” — this is the first volume)PeriodSeptember 1915 – March 1917 (to release from arrest by the Provisional Government)StructureChapters 1–94 + Conclusion; ~26,410 OCR linesNext volumeVol. 2 (1928) — March 1917 – January 1920
Contents. First-person testimony of a senior synodal official of the monarchy’s last year and a half: the Brotherhood of St. Joasaph of Belgorod and delivery of the Nechaian Icon to Stavka (Mogilev, October 1915); audiences with Nicholas II and Alexandra Feodorovna; Metropolitan Pitirim; resignation of A. N. Volzhin and Zhevakhov’s appointment as deputy ober-procurator (autumn 1916); synodal commissions and the Duma (speeches of Miliukov, Lvov); an extended sketch of Rasputin and “God-seeking”; journey to the Caucasus (January–February 1917); return to Petrograd in the February days; memorable sitting of the Holy Synod of 26 February; arrest of 28 February, confinement in the Ministerial Pavilion, news of the abdication, release by Kerensky.
Character of the source. Monarchical, church-mystical émigré memoir; the author defends the line of the Sovereign and the Empress and explains the collapse through a “fateful epoch” and the struggle against “tsarism.” Not an operational-staff monument (cf. Denikin, Essays on the Russian Troubles), but a view from the Synod and Tsarskoe Selo. Chronologically joins the end of Witte, Vols. 2–3 (1960) (Witte breaks off ~1911) and the beginning of Denikin’s volume (February–September 1917).
OCR. Medium: Roman chapter numerals often distorted (ГЛАВА Г. / ИП. / УГ.); Ѣ/Е, І/И; «Тоасафъ» = Joasaph; years sometimes “1945/46/47” for 1915–17. Headings below reconstructed from the table of contents and repeated forms in the body; raw stream is in the raw file.

I. Path to Stavka and the court (chs. 1–23) — autumn 1915 – early 1916
Chapter 1. General meeting of the Brotherhood of St. Joasaph, 4 September 1915. Report of Colonel O.
Meeting of the Brotherhood of Saint Joasaph of Belgorod on the anniversary of the glorification; chairman Gen. L. K. Artamonov; vice-chairmen — Archpriest A. G. Malyarevsky and Zhevakhov. Author’s absence from the meeting; on the evening of 5 September Malyarevsky recounts a report that became a “turning point” — the seed of the mission with the icon.
Chapter 2. Mistress of the Robes E. A. Naryshkina
Chapter 3. Count Ya. N. Rostovtsov
Court intermediaries; Rostovtsov as a channel to the Empress.
Chapter 4. Meeting with Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod A. N. Volzhin. Farewell conversation with Archpriest A. G. Malyarevsky. Departure from Petrograd
Malyarevsky insists on a visit to Volzhin before removing the icons; formal mission and telegrams to the Most Reverend of Kharkov and Kursk.
Chapter 5. Belgorod and Kharkov. Reception and farewell of the Nechaian Icon of the Mother of God
Chapter 6. On the way to Stavka. Conversation with priest Aleksandr Yakovlev
A rural priest-companion; piety of “seeing the Tsar Batiushka.”
Chapter 7. Arrival at Mogilev
Headquarters of the Supreme Commander; procession of the cross; name-day of the Heir (5 October) as the calendar frame of the icon’s arrival.
Chapter 8. At the Officers’ Assembly
Chapter 9. Protopresbyter G. I. Shavelsky
Military clergy at Stavka; Shavelsky’s attitude to the “holy object” in Zhevakhov’s account.
Chapter 10. Name-day of the Heir Tsesarevich
Chapter 11. Archbishop Konstantin
Chapter 12. Imperial breakfast
Chapter 13. Conversation with the Sovereign Emperor
Audience; the Sovereign recalls the first meeting at Tsarskoe Selo before the glorification of Joasaph. The author stresses Nicholas II’s dislike of strained court etiquette and his own “unconstrained speech” about the Saint.
Chapter 14. Return to Petrograd
Chapter 15. Report to Count Ya. N. Rostovtsov
Chapter 16. In the State Chancellery
Return to ordinary service; Shavelsky’s attitude to the holy object as a theme of reflection.
Chapter 17. Thoughts
Chapter 18. Audience with Her Majesty
Tsarskoe Selo station; court uniform; joint journey with a general “to Her Majesty.”
Chapter 19. The truth
The author’s “truth” about the court and the Empress — “afterward so criminally distorted.”
Chapter 20. At sister’s
Chapter 21. Meeting with A. N. Volzhin
Information of S. P. Beletsky; relations with the ober-procurator still before the break of 1916.
Chapter 22. Departure for Stavka
Mid-December 1915 (about the 15th).
Chapter 23. On the eve
“Ill omens” on the eve of 1916.

II. Pitirim, Volzhin, appointment as deputy ober-procurator (chs. 24–39) — 1916
Chapter 24. His Eminence Pitirim, Metropolitan of St. Petersburg and Ladoga
Corruption of the “mechanism” of power “at the top”; ministers “in captivity” to the Duma and the press; contrast with the still-holding lower police. Pitirim as a church-political figure of the capital.
Chapter 25. Appointment of N. Ch. Zaionchkovsky
End of 1915; the ober-procurator “still has not found” the needed people.
Chapter 26. Old songs to a new tune
Chapter 27. Imperial audience
Sister of mercy; modest attire at court.
Chapter 28. Candle congress. Visit of A. N. Volzhin. State Secretary S. E. Kryzhanovsky
Chapter 29. Break with A. N. Volzhin
Consideration in the Duma of the Synod’s estimate; conflict with the ober-procurator.
Chapter 30. Optina Hermitage. Elder Anatoly
Chapter 31. Conversation with Elder Anatoly
“Batiushka Father Anatoly, I can make nothing out” — spiritual counsel at a moment of service crisis.
Chapter 32. Resignation of A. N. Volzhin. New Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod N. P. Raev. Imperial ukaz on my appointment as deputy ober-procurator
Summer 1916 in the countryside without newspapers; at Liuban station — news of Volzhin’s resignation and of his own appointment. Raev — new ober-procurator; Zhevakhov — deputy ober-procurator.
Chapter 33. Conclusions
The author’s summing-up of the Volzhin history.
Chapter 34. Imperial audience. Departure for Belgorod. Archbishop Tikhon of Kursk. Governor A. K. Baggovut
Chapter 35. Belgorod. At the shrine of Saint Joasaph. The Most Reverend Nikodim, Bishop of Belgorod
Chapter 36. Arrival in Kharkov. Archbishop Antony and the vicar, Bishop Theodore of Starobelsk. E. N. Geitsig
Headmistress of the Kharkov diocesan girls’ school — an important figure for the author (see also ch. 74).
Chapter 37. The press on my appointment
Two weeks’ absence from Petersburg; reaction of the newspapers.
Chapter 38. Entry into office and first impressions
30 September 1916 — first entry into the Synod in the new rank.
Chapter 39. Abbess Margarita (Mariia Mikhailovna Gunaropulo)

III. Synod, Duma, Protopopov (chs. 40–53) — autumn 1916
Chapter 40. Political mood of Russia. Church-state activity of Metropolitan Pitirim
Chapter 41. Speech in the chambers of the St. Petersburg metropolitan on presentation of the Feodorov Icon of the Mother of God
Chapter 42. Visit to the Synodal infirmary named for the Heir Tsesarevich and speech to the wounded (5 October 1916)
Chapter 43. Interdepartmental commission on drafting a statute on clergy pensions
Chapter 44. Commission of inquiry into abuses in the purchase of wax abroad
Chapter 45. Loyalty of synodal officials
Chapter 46. Thoughts of the past. The fateful epoch. Deputation of former colleagues of the State Chancellery
Chapter 47. Speech of member of the State Duma P. N. Miliukov, 1 November 1916
The famous speech “stupidity or treason” as perceived by the synodal deputy ober-procurator.
Chapter 48. Member of the State Duma V. P. Shein. “Memorandum” of the deputy procurator
Chapter 49. Speech of member of the State Duma V. N. Lvov, 29 November 1916. Meeting with A. N. Volzhin
Lvov — future ober-procurator of the Provisional Government; collision of lines.
Chapter 50. Conversation with Chairman of the Council of Ministers A. F. Trepov
Chapter 51. Audience with Her Majesty
The Empress’s response to the blow dealt by Volzhin.
Chapter 52. Minister of Internal Affairs A. D. Protopopov
Characterization of Protopopov; “who is able to see beyond outward expressions.”
Chapter 53. Speech to former colleagues of the State Chancellery

IV. Rasputin and “God-seeking” (chs. 54–70) — December 1916
An extended excursus: not only a chronicle of the murder, but an apology for “eldership,” a portrait of Alexandra Feodorovna, and a critique of the “exposures.”
Chapter 54. Rasputin and Dobrovolsky
Chapter 55. Day of St. Joasaph, 10 December 1916. Summons to Tsarskoe Selo to Her Imperial Majesty
Chapter 56. Russian God-seeking
“Every fact becomes intelligible only in historical…”
Chapter 57. Religious atmosphere of Petersburg. Predecessors of Rasputin — Archimandrite Mikhail, priest Grigory Petrov, and “tongue-tied Mitya”
Chapter 58. Nature of the Russian soul. Russian problems of the spirit. Truth
Chapter 59. Holy foolishness in Christ. Its content and psychology
Chapter 60. Appearance of Rasputin. Eldership and its nature
Chapter 61. First steps of Rasputin
Chapter 62. At Baron Rausch von Traubenberg’s
Rasputin “let himself go widely” in secular society — contrast with the imperial circle in the author’s version.
Chapter 63. Audience of the Sovereign Emperor granted to Rasputin, and impression on the Tsar
Chapter 64. Parents of the Sovereign Empress Alexandra Feodorovna
Chapter 65. Arrival of the Sovereign Empress Alexandra Feodorovna in Russia and her first impressions
Chapter 66. Spiritual aspect of the Empress Alexandra Feodorovna. A. A. Vyrubova. Her Majesty’s acquaintance with Rasputin
Chapter 67. Rasputin’s ill fame and its consequences
Chapter 68. The “exposures” and the attitude of the Sovereign and the Empress to them
Chapter 69. Struggle against “tsarism” and its methods
“The second period ended” — a programmatic chapter on the methods of the opposition.
Chapter 70. Murder of Rasputin
“The third period ended. The fourth began” — the murder as a break toward catastrophe in the author’s scheme.

V. Caucasus, return, February, arrest (chs. 71–94) — January–March 1917
Chapter 71. Audience with Her Majesty. Journey to Novgorod
Return to the personal chronicle after the Rasputin excursus.
Chapter 72. The year 1917. Report to Her Majesty on the journey to Novgorod. Imperial rescript to E. N. Geitsig
Chapter 73. Departure for the Caucasus. The Tuapse Iveron-Alekseev women’s community
Chapter 74. Evgeniia Nikolaevna Geitsig
“Spiritual uplift” of the meeting; the Kharkov school headmistress.
Chapter 75. Arrival in Rostov. Deputation of Galicians. Prof. P. Verkhovsky. “The worst pupil”
Chapter 76. Arrival in Tuapse. Chief administrator Sorokin. Nun Mariam. Priest Krasnov. Elder Sofrony
Chapter 77. The Iveron-Alekseev community. Inquiry
Inspection/inquiry in the community accompanied by Sorokin and the ober-secretary.
Chapter 78. Novorossiysk, Ekaterinodar, and Stavropol
Vice-governor and local authorities.
Chapter 79. Taganrog. Legend of Elder Theodore Kuzmich
Chapter 80. Return to Petersburg and first impressions
24 February 1917 — return to the capital on the eve of the collapse.
Chapter 81. First steps of the revolution
“The next day was still more terrible than the previous.”
Chapter 82. Memorable sitting of the Holy Synod, 26 February 1917
Sitting appointed for the 26th; the Synod at the moment of the street break.
Chapter 83. Round-ups
27 February — “the genuine picture of the revolution.”
Chapter 84. Triumph of the boor
28 February; “the cabinet almost in full…”
Chapter 85. My arrest
28 February; rumours of the day’s victims; arrest of the deputy ober-procurator.
Chapter 86. First day of confinement
The “Ministerial Pavilion” at the Duma as the place of detention of arrested dignitaries.
Chapter 87. Observations and notes
Cellmates; a social cross-section of the overthrown power.
Chapter 88. Abdication of the Sovereign
News of the abdication reaches the prisoners.
Chapter 89. A terrible night
Rising fear among the arrested.
Chapter 90. Conversation with a soldier
The guard; attempt to soften the regime.
Chapter 91. Resurrection of a boy
Inserted tale (miracle/tradition of priest Gnevushev) — the religious register of the memoirs even in prison.
Chapter 92. Release
Kerensky “casting lightning glances about him” — the scene of release.
Chapter 93. Sister
First hours at liberty; apartment on Liteiny.
Chapter 94. The soldier and his nephew
Life of the first days after release.
Conclusion
“Results…,” “Judgment of God” — closing pages of the volume (per the table of contents).

Completeness of the set

















LayerStatusA. Continuous block “Synod / court to the collapse”Yes — September 1915 → March 1917, chs. 1–94, closed by this volumeB. In the preface to Vol. 2 the author mentions a possible Vol. III (European literature on the “Jewish question,” etc.) — not extracted, pending an IA id

sources/zhevakhov-vospominaniya-tovarish.content:
Zhevakhov — Memoirs of a Deputy Ober-Procurator of the Holy Synod, Vol. 2
Prince Nikolai Davidovich Zhevakhov (1874–1946) — Воспоминанія. Товарища Оберъ-Прокурора Св. Синода. Томъ II. Novi Sad (Novyi Sad): Russian Press of S. Filonov, 1928.

































AuthorPrince N. D. Zhevakhov — former deputy ober-procurator of the Holy Synod (autumn 1916 – February 1917); in Vol. 2 — witness of the South, the civil war, and the first emigrationEditionNovi Sad, 1928 (emigration); pre-reform orthographyIA idzhevahovndvospominanijaoberprokuroras3 (oras3 = second volume of the same work; not “volume 3” of a separate composition)PeriodMarch 1917 – January 1920 (personal chronicle) + extended essays on Soviet Russia and the Church (into the mid-1920s by newspapers cited)StructureChapters 1–61 (~27,188 OCR lines): chs. 1–25 — memoir core; chs. 26–61 — publicistics/history (Cheka, famine, Church, autocracy)Previous volumeVol. 1 (1923) — September 1915 – March 1917
Contents. Continuation after arrest and release: life with his sister, Kiev, the countryside, death of his mother (30 October 1917), siege of Kiev, murder of Metropolitan Vladimir (25 January 1918), arrival of the Germans, Hetman Skoropadsky, “satanists”/Petliurists, the Pokrovsky Monastery, the Skete of the Most Pure; 1919 — Professor Armashevsky, Prince P. V. Zhevakhov, G. A. Shechkov; path Kharkov — Rostov — Pyatigorsk (metochion of the Second Athonite Monastery, Metropolitan Pitirim) — Ekaterinodar (death of Pitirim) — Novorossiysk (January 1920). Second half of the volume — systematic survey of “methods of extermination” (Cheka, famine, moral tortures), condition of the Church (Council, Patriarch Tikhon, persecutions, the Abroad Synod, Metr. Sergius / Metr. Antony), nature of autocracy and “lessons of the revolution.”
Character of the source. The same monarchical and church-mystical line as in Vol. 1; in the second half — open émigré publicistics of the 1920s (including antisemitic constructions of “Jewish” dominion — to be recorded as the author’s position, not as established fact). The memoir core (Kiev 1917–19, Pitirim in the South, the exodus) joins Denikin, Essays on the Troubles calendar, but from a synodal-ecclesiastical and Kievan, not staff, angle.
OCR. Medium/heavy: Arabic chapter numbering relatively stable; Ѣ/Е, І/И; «Юевъ» = Kiev; gaps (ch. 27 barely marked in the stream). Headings reconstructed from the table of contents and body.

I. After arrest — Kiev 1917–1918 (chs. 1–17)
Chapter 1. Trials
From March 1917 — “a period of trials that fell upon me…” after the capital arrest and release.
Chapter 2. After the arrest
